en: The *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, Scroll One; also titled *The Present Retribution*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter One: Universal Praise (1). Chapter One: Universal Praise.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Universal Victory Hall in the realm of Magadha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—ten thousand bhikṣus and fifteen thousand bodhisattvas—all of whom were great sages gathered there like clouds.

Endowed with all virtues, they do not abandon the dhāraṇīs; their resolve is vast and universal, encompassing all things without exception. Their eloquence is thorough and penetrating, removing the net of doubt; they roam within the supernormal powers to expound profound meanings. Using skillful means to transform others according to what is appropriate, their compassion extends even to the lowly as they reach the further shore, proclaiming the Tathāgata’s samādhi and right meditative absorption.

Praised by all Buddhas and revered by devas and humans, their aspirations are sovereign and unimpeded; they travel everywhere through sublime and extraordinary realms, possessing the full array of miraculous powers and transformations, subduing all demons and thoroughly awakening to the wisdom of the Dharma.

Discriminating all phenomena, they deeply understand their ultimate limit; observing the original roots of sentient beings from the past, they expound upon the factors of enlightenment—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. They remain unstained by the eight worldly concerns and, further, employ great compassion to rescue and protect sentient beings. Guarding body, speech, and mind, they are free from false views; their resolve is exalted and diligent, and their mind is like a diamond.
Though he exerts diligent effort throughout incalculable eons, his mind remains ever courageous and free from weariness.

Among the great assemblies, he manifests the majestic power of a lion, subduing heterodox teachers so that they do not retreat, and seals them with the epithets of the sages. He traverses all the dwelling places where the Buddhas roam; these are all the practices cultivated by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.

The sanctified site of practice is majestic and immeasurable; whether walking or sitting, one enters bottomless wisdom. The mind is always joyful and never timid. The Dharma preached is impartial and non-dual; regarding those who have achieved it and those who have not, one views them as equals. Merit, renown, and fame are always attained with mastery. One cultivates the profound essentials of the Dharma and instructs others through the Way and its teachings. When amidst the great assembly, one’s majestic appearance is radiant, and divine wisdom is subtly penetrating beyond all calculation.
In the space of a finger-snap, he traveled to immeasurable Buddha-lands and made offerings to the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the ten directions.
Their names were as follows:

The Bodhisattva Joyful Radiance, the Bodhisattva Mountain Thunder, the Bodhisattva Dense Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Universal Clarity, the Bodhisattva Delivering Others, the Bodhisattva Total Retention, the Bodhisattva Vajra, the Bodhisattva King of the Grinding Stone, the Bodhisattva Thunderous Resonance, the Bodhisattva Drizzle of Rain, the Bodhisattva Skillful Calculation, the Bodhisattva Accumulated Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Supreme Dharma, the Bodhisattva Quiescent Mind, the Bodhisattva Dispelling Illusions, the Bodhisattva Good Renown, the Bodhisattva Space Treasury, the Bodhisattva Awesome Power, the Bodhisattva Blazing Light, the Bodhisattva Discerning Capacities, the Bodhisattva Exhausted Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Boundless Limit, the Bodhisattva Firm Resolve, the Bodhisattva Moonlight, the Bodhisattva Blazing Dharma, the Bodhisattva Unseen, the Bodhisattva Peerless, and the Bodhisattva Sun of Increasing Radiance.

In this way, bodhisattvas from the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions gathered like clouds, coming to the Sahā world to hear the Tathāgata preach the *Adornment of the Dharma* (*Dharmālaṃkāra*), which is the gateway to the roots of great wisdom and the entrance to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka—an inconceivable manifestation of immeasurable skillful means.
And during the Bhadrakalpa, Maitreya and Mañjuśrī, the sixteen great sages such as Bhadrayaśas,
the eight great divine beings, Śakra and the Four Heavenly Kings, along with the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven,
the Nirmāṇarati heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, the son of Māra, the Guide, and Brahmā.
The King, the Brahmā Śuddhāvāsaka King, the Brahmā Śubhakṛtsna King, the Brahmā Parīttābha King,
the Mahābrahmā King, the Śuddhāvāsa Devas, the Vimalaprabha Devas, up to the Ekasupratiṣṭhita Devas and the Anabhraka Devas,
as well as the tree spirits, mountain spirits, garuḍa spirits, and all other [spirits].
All the great and honored deities, each one more venerable than the next, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans,
each accompanied by their retinues, came to where the Buddha was; having prostrated themselves, they stood in attendance.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās each paid their respects; they came forward, prostrated before the Buddha, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of followers.
The Buddha ascended the majestic, pure, lofty, and expansive lion throne and preached the *Sūtra of the Necklace of Dharma* for the great assembly.

The Buddha was in the midst of the assembly like Mount Sumeru; he shone resplendently like a mass of gold, his majestic spiritual radiance surpassing the world and peerless. His virtue, conduct, and dignified demeanor were lofty and immeasurable, emitting a great light that illuminated everything without exception.

Furthermore, moved by his spiritual transformations, there immediately appeared in the air hundreds of thousands of precious jeweled canopies, interspersed with various rare treasures that completely covered him above. Priceless jewels and "illuminating the void" pearls were suspended in mid-air; light issued forth from these pearls, their colors and forms beyond compare.
In the sky, subtle clouds arose and rained down various fragrant flowers.
At that time, the flowers accumulated in the air up to the knees, and a great sound issued forth, filling the entire world.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Puzhao (Universal Illumination). Receiving the Buddha’s sacred command, he immediately rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"The divine manifestation we have witnessed now is something never before seen or heard. What auspicious omen is this that has reached such an extent?"
"I only pray that the Great Sage will expound upon this meaning, so that all those gathered here may forever be free from doubt.
The Buddha told Puzhao: "Return to your seat."

I shall explain to you, one by one, the meaning of the Dharma-garland; by cultivating and establishing the gates of the faculties, you shall transcend delusive thoughts and draw near to the stage of all-knowledge and the various supernormal wisdoms.

At that time, the World-Honored One again employed his supernormal powers to observe the meditative states entered by the bodhisattvas; the name of that dharma is "The Garland of the Bodhi Tree. It purifies the sites of enlightenment for all great beings, awakens them to the true dharma of the Way so they are free from fear, allows them to roam through the various noble wisdoms with mastery, and ensures that those who enter the gates of the Way do not lose their eloquence.
Furthermore, he adorned his seat with the璎珞 (necklaces/ornaments) of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), eloquently expounding and analyzing the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).

He understood that the single dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*) is empty and non-existent. Observing the sharp or dull natures of sentient beings, he fortified their minds and resolved all dharmas. He removed worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) in accordance with the essentials of the Dharma; his words were trusted and relied upon, being free from any defiled attachment. In responding to others, he was without doubt, sending them forth as they came and went. He spoke with unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*), forever departing from bondage and attachment. Having accumulated merit and virtue without harboring expectations, the various dharmas he taught were true and profound suchness (*tathatā*). He did not calculate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as having something to be accomplished; for him, marks (*lakṣaṇa*) were no-marks—how could there be the raising of marks?
He clearly understands the profound and subtle twelvefold dependent origination, investigating its source until it can no longer be delimited.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance rose again from his seat, stepped forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; if you would deign to listen, I shall then set forth my words."
The Buddha said: "Excellent! Ask whatever you wish.
If there is any doubt, express it clearly; the Tathāgata shall provide a thorough explanation for you."
At that time, Samantaprabha, seeing that he had been granted leave, was filled with joy and immediately asked:
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s body adorned with the dharma-garland?
What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s elimination of false views?"
What is meant by a bodhisattva giving rise to supramundane dharmas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva traveling through the worlds?
What is meant by a bodhisattva drawing near to the Tathāgata?
What is meant by a bodhisattva not dwelling in a mother’s womb?
What is meant by a bodhisattva whose consciousness is never confused at birth?
What is meant by a bodhisattva possessing profound faith?
How does a bodhisattva not act for his own sake?
What is meant by a bodhisattva rescuing sentient beings from suffering?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s gift of Dharma and gift of material wealth?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s discernment of the meaning of emptiness?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s removal of the hindrances and coverings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s extensive and blazing cultivation of the Dharma-precepts?
What is meant by a bodhisattva never being weary of hearing the Dharma?
What is meant by a bodhisattva sporting in śamatha and vipaśyanā?
What is meant by a bodhisattva reverently practicing the prohibitive precepts?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s vow to remain detached from worldly dharmas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva not dwelling in household affairs?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being without attachment?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s sitting down and rising up?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s secrecy of speech while the mind is otherwise?
Such is the essential meaning of what was asked.
The Buddha said, “Puzhao! Excellent, excellent!”
He then asked the Tathāgata about this meaning.
"Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well!
Keep it gathered within your heart, and do not let it be discarded through the conduct of ordinary worldlings."
Pu Zhao replied, "So be it,
World-Honored One! I wish and desire to hear the Dharma of the Great Sage."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Puzhao, saying: "One who practices the Bodhisattva path should keep ten virtues in mind to adorn their person.

They shall not speak of the faults of others regarding body, speech, or mind; they shall not give rise to contempt or arrogance toward their fellow students; their mind shall be as level as space, without increase or decrease; they shall abandon all evil destinies and refrain from harming others; they shall regard other sentient beings as no different from themselves; and their resolve shall be such that what is known through the body is inexhaustible."
Furthermore, they instruct sentient beings by means of the Four Noble Truths, maintaining a tranquil mind to awaken them and bring them to fulfillment.

Moreover, using the wondrous gateways adorned with the jewels of manifold wisdom, they train and transform those of the Two Vehicles so that they reach their respective goals; they encourage the study of the Mahāyāna, observing and penetrating all phenomena, and cultivate the meritorious virtues of the Tathāgata’s conduct, guiding others through gradual stages rather than through forceful or reckless means.

Reflecting upon one’s own faults without censuring the shortcomings of others, transcending all manifold difficulties, always delighting in the Dharma, remaining in tranquil concentration without distraction, eliminating all doubts and speculative views, causing those who are hesitant to attain timely awakening, and never abandoning the roots of virtue cultivated through the aspiration for the Way.

Furthermore, they teach and transform others so that they do not violate the precepts; they constantly preach the sutras for the sake of others with great compassion; wherever they travel in the worlds, they never depart from the presence of the Buddhas; and they proclaim the prohibitions and precepts until they attain all-knowledge.

Furthermore, they used radiant necklaces to adorn the pure jewel-adorned bodhimandas of all Buddhas; these luminous necklaces pervaded everywhere, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm and eclipsing the light of the sun and moon, such that even the majestic splendors of the divine and wondrous Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings could no longer appear.
The light of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, is unfathomable; it shines alone and manifests alone, with nothing that can equal it—this is called "Universal Illumination.
He adorns himself by wrapping himself in the ten virtues of the Bodhisattva path as a jeweled necklace.
Constantly mindful of all Buddhas, they make offerings to the Tathāgatas, extol the holy teachings, and exhort and transform sentient beings to enter the gateway of the Way.

They further instruct sentient beings to give rise to great vows; wherever they turn, upon hearing the names of the Buddhas, they nurture the multitudes with the wish to be born in those lands. Their resolve is vast and universal, free from cowardice; they penetrate deeply into holy wisdom and do not shrink from humble inquiry. They always delight in the subtle and wondrous, their speech is gentle and harmonious, and they are free from self-importance. They take pleasure in seclusion, eliminating all greed and envy; seeing those who practice the Way, they rejoice on their behalf. With the power of merit, they adorn the tree of the Path; through the power of retribution, the power of the mind, and the power of nourishment, as well as the power of liberation in which all sages dwell, they constantly sustain sentient beings with these dharmas, protecting them with kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, never abandoning them.

Protecting against attachment to all conditions, one uproots them at their source; observing that the three periods of time—past, future, and present—are devoid of coming or going, one sees that the retribution of good and evil is entirely non-arising. Phenomenon after phenomenon extinguishes itself and phenomenon after phenomenon arises of itself; phenomena do not perceive extinction, nor do they perceive arising. The mind is free from conceptualization, devoid of self, person, or life-span; there is neither coming nor going, nor any destination to which one returns. Furthermore, one adorns the sense faculties with the garland of the dharma of emptiness.
"In the past, when I attained Buddhahood, it was entirely through the perception of pure emptiness and non-existence that I personally realized perfect enlightenment.

By practicing the roots of goodness without creating various conditions, by giving rise to wholesome dharmas without heedless conduct, and by distancing myself from worldly affairs without dwelling in mundane laws, I have caused what I expound to spread throughout the ten directions. Having personally attended upon and paid homage to all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, my practice of giving is pure, having abandoned greed and desire; my mind is fresh and clean, free from defilement; my wisdom is boundless and my vision is penetrating; and the three obstructions and the six sense objects have been forever extinguished. This is called the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-garland."

“Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of great vows and adorn themselves with the necklace of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). According to the capacity of their original vessel, they bestow the Dharma; as soon as they have heard the wisdom, they are able to establish it. One who acts in accordance with this will not regress, maintaining a firm resolve and following virtuous friends.”

The teachings they practice are never false or deceptive; their mindfulness is always reverent and diligent, never contravening the work of the sutras. Their minds cultivate profound wisdom, receiving it without loss; they always concentrate the single mind so that thoughts are not confused. Discerning the depth or shallowness of an illness before administering medicine, they delight in patience and their gait is deliberate and careful.

The wealth and goods bestowed as gifts are without partiality; his intention is pure and subtle, free from agitation or confusion, and as he trains in the fundamental [teachings], his mind does not wander.

When people wish to hear the Dharma, he constantly provides instruction to lead them to know the essential path. Should he see those in distress who cannot save themselves, he is able to bestow gifts even at the cost of his own precious treasures. Furthermore, through the roots of goodness and various wondrous practices, he exhorts others to uphold the precepts, so that the wisdom they hear may bring them to the path of a Bodhisattva.

"Suppose a student of the Way dwells among the brahmins and is further able to establish awakening such that what arises does not depart from forbearance; having renounced worldly affairs, he cultivates diligence, penetrates the root of impermanence and dependent origination, and regarding all hatred and love, he gives rise to no dualistic thoughts. His conduct is impartial, leading all classes of sentient beings to attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas."

Constantly able to rely upon their boundless great compassion, they gradually instruct and exhort others through the Dharma of the Great Vow, bestowing it upon all beings so that they may hear and know it; with minds and natures serene, they realize there is no self, and through single-minded meditative contemplation, they give rise to wisdom, ensuring it never ceases.

Whatever they establish does not depart from the four debts of gratitude; they rescue those in peril and distress, leading them to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); they guard against transgressions of body and speech, refraining from the three types of misconduct; they establish the true and unsurpassed Dharma, and cultivate the cessation of thought and the tranquility of mind according to the nature of *tathatā* without ever losing it. This, O Universal Radiance, is what is called [the practice].
All these are established by means of the bodhisattva’s jeweled necklace. Furthermore, Puzhao!

A bodhisattva should further contemplate, calculate, and measure the infinite: practicing giving, cultivating precepts, maintaining a serene countenance, practicing patience, exerting diligence, abiding in tranquility, and not losing the foundations of mindfulness.

Furthermore, with holy wisdom and a mind fixed in single-minded concentration, one deeply examines the nectar-like path of the Four Noble Truths until reaching the unconditioned state where no further falsehood remains; this is called the adornment of wisdom.

"One should always maintain single-mindedness and purify the mind; one should give away all that one possesses without stinginess, cultivating the merit of transformation and liberation through the gate of emptiness.

Whether engaged in practice or providing instruction and admonition, one should extensively receive sentient beings and deliver them according to their needs, possessing the sublime virtues of benevolence and harmony."

He clearly understands the various categories of timely circumstances; he proclaims his compassionate heart, remaining unattached to suffering or pleasure; he pities all beings without avoiding even the most severe hardships; he awakens those sentient beings through the teachings of the True Dharma; with a mind of giving that fills the world, he protects them until they achieve fulfillment; the radiance of his jeweled ornaments shines everywhere without exception; universally pitying all, he causes them to cross over to the other shore.

Even if there were someone in a hidden place, he would eliminate their darkness so that nothing remains; with the power of fearlessness, he compassionately nurtures all beings, removing their old age and illness, and ensuring they practice without negligence.

Wherever the Teacher goes, there are none who do not follow his instructions; he holds [the Dharma] within like the ocean and bestows what he has heard upon others, transforming their worldly afflictions so that they are free from delusive thoughts.

His dwelling place is like a flower, free from attachment; he realizes that all phenomena are tranquil and pure, and in the teachings he expounds, he analyzes causes and conditions, cultivating and bringing to fruition the roots of virtue he has created.

"Out of compassion for the suffering of the world, he instructs all living beings that empty space is neither substantial nor truly existent; understanding that worldly phenomena are like bubbles and illusions, sentient beings remain unawakened, habituated to them and failing to relinquish them."

Though dwelling in the household life, he is able to remain free from the perils of birth; his path-eye is pure like a lotus flower, and his divine virtue is so lofty as to be beyond measure. Even if all the various classes of sentient beings in the world were to join in praising him, they could not know its source.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Puzhao:

"Now, the practice of sitting on the Way involves the realization that there is no coming or going; if one perceives coming and going, this constitutes conceptual attachment. Even the discernment of demerit and merit has neither arising nor ceasing; all these are naturally empty and non-existent."

When one realizes that the marks of existence abide without a master and lack beginning or end, and that there is nothing to be sought or obtained through aspiration, and can thus personally evaluate such a Dharma—this is called a bodhisattva proceeding toward the noble path.

Furthermore, one should discern the phenomena of the three periods of time, understanding that they are non-dual, devoid of self, and devoid of persons, and that all objective realms are empty and non-existent.
If one perceives something coming, this is the dharma of dependent origination through retribution; that which is without arising and without cessation accords with the Way and its teachings.

To reckon that sound possesses tone, yet tone has no form or image—to discern written characters as being entirely without reality—this is to achieve complete clarity and understanding, reaching unimpeded mastery in all things.
“The Bodhisattva’s necklace is true and without falsehood, and likewise without obstruction; it removes the hindrances of the aggregates so that they are entirely non-existent.

If one establishes what is to be given wherever it is desired, even if there is no such establishment, this corresponds to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*); with a mind of careful vigilance, one abandons all that is improper.”

One who maintains this mind accords with the precepts; they thoroughly understand that all phenomena are naturally non-abiding and without a fundamental limit. Diligently practicing contemplation to establish a foundation, they apply themselves with vigor to meditative reflection to restrain body, speech, and mind. With the radiance of wisdom shining forth of itself, they eliminate all defiled conduct; thus, they accord with true wisdom.

"Pu Zhao! Furthermore, know that the reach of supernormal powers and their resulting retributions are attained through the celestial eye, which enables one to see clearly; all of this arises from practicing and upholding the prohibitive precepts, constantly conforming to right view, and never committing any transgression."

By practicing the Dharma-ornament, they attain the divine ear; through mindfulness, conduct, and exhortation, they give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. Furthermore, they achieve the supernormal power of recollection, whereby they naturally remember all past lives; for the sake of sentient beings, they accumulate merit and virtue.

Every day he reproached himself for failing to attain those realizations, while harboring within him infinite supernormal powers and transformations; having abandoned all attachments to consciousness and contemplating meditative concentration as equal and non-dual, he understood the fruits of causes, conditions, and retribution.

By means of wisdom and supernormal powers, he extinguishes all defilements; through his samādhi, he thoroughly masters the noble Dharma and enters into non-duality. He exhausts all outflows while never losing the resolve for the Way, leading people to cultivate virtue. Furthermore, he encourages them to aspire to the merit of worldly giving; though he bestows such grace, he does not expect recompense, causing countless people to rejoice and devote themselves to the Dharma.

They are able to know all things without obstruction and enable others to practice the Dharma of Bodhisattvas; all this arises from diligence and the absence of indolence, through which they compassionately protect others so that everything is accomplished.

For the sake of sentient beings, they do not spare their own bodies or lives; they do not covet the treasures or wealth of their own persons. In whatever place they are born, they follow the principles of the Way; regarding what others seek, they harbor no doubt or difficulty. Hearing the wisdom of the teachings, they bestow faith and offerings without hesitation; all their words and instructions are trusted and honored by all.

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is free from all obstructions; his conduct is tranquil and devoid of negligence. He is firm in patience and delights in dwelling in seclusion. Furthermore, he transforms sentient beings while reproaching himself for falling short of their needs. His meditative contemplations, liberations, and samādhis are undisturbed; he constantly roams through supernormal powers for his own enjoyment. Moreover, by means of the merit of infinite radiance, he appropriately and timely distinguishes the meanings and principles of all chapters and phrases. He extinguishes all afflictions without concealment, and with constant single-mindedness, he opens the way to noble wisdom, demonstrating the fruits of retribution to countless people."

Endowed with all virtues, one cannot be assailed by the power of valor; having realized that the three periods of time are entirely non-existent, and that matters of the past, future, and present neither increase nor diminish, one then accords with the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).

By means of being able to practice giving, they have personally resolved upon the path; desiring to bring universal peace to all sentient beings, they themselves disperse all fetters and do not concern themselves with their own bodies.

If others strike them with staves or clubs, they are able to endure it all, and they likewise transform others, causing them to practice patience. Endowed with the roots of all virtues and furthered by single-mindedness, they cultivate the teachings of the Buddhas and exhort all classes of living beings to leave the household life and study the Path.
Observing for oneself the impurity of all things as decaying corpses, one immediately develops revulsion for the miserable realms until one’s merit reaches its ultimate fulfillment.

The wholesome karma one performs brings joy to the mind; wisdom penetrates deeply so that no resentment is harbored, and through firm faith in the prohibitions and precepts, one personally attains virtuous qualities.

Furthermore, with a harmonious mind, a sense of shame and remorse, and freedom from delusion, one constantly governs the spirit and will so as not to harbor coarseness or ferocity. One contemplates the agonizing sufferings of boiling water and fire in the hells, and admires the infinite bliss of receiving merit in the heavens; thus, becoming tranquil and free from sorrow, one no longer harbors greedy desires.

When practicing giving, one eliminates the three perceptions; the mind does not lean inward nor grasp external objects. One cultivates the path of the Dharma until all expectations come to rest, and through discerning wisdom, one awakens to one's own mind. By establishing the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—one removes inversions and remains free from harm; this is called "Universal Illumination."
The Bodhisattva’s jeweled necklace is a mind free from attachment.
Its intention is equanimous, empty, and all-pervading; it harbors no deluded thoughts, and through generosity it is fully prepared, with a mind that is harmonized and tranquil.
When preaching the Dharma for others, he does not depart from the meaning of emptiness; his compassionate pity for all beings is practiced without omission or failure.
He observes the consciousnesses through which sentient beings receive the Dharma, and knowing their dispositions and natures, he transforms and guides them.
In whatever place he travels, he guides all beings, practicing holy wisdom and manifesting the meaning of the Way.

With infinite great compassion, he brings others across; furthermore, through the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he enters among the various heterodox paths and schools, conforming to their rules and following their sacrificial rites. Observing their inclinations, he enables them to attain liberation, causing the brahmins to generate immeasurable merit.

Or, among wicked factions and bandits, he leads them and guides them to manifest his conduct; through this, he transforms and delivers countless sentient beings. Having already perfected his merits in past ages, all who see him rejoice and are not without reverence. He rains down the flavor of the nectar of the Dharma, removing the knots of hatred and resentment within sentient beings.

Furthermore, if another person comes to offend one with various provocations, one does not feel aversion toward them, but instead teaches them the Dharma of tranquility, knowing that what has arisen is neither true nor real.
"In this way, Samantaprabha!

The bodhisattva cultivates the mental adornment and dwells within it, always delighting therein; yet he does not perceive anything to be delighted in, nor does he find delight in anything, for he finds entertainment in the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā)."

Clearly knowing the fundamental inclinations of sentient beings, he rescues and delivers them so that they may transcend all worldly afflictions, ensuring that the perils of harm are forever eliminated without remainder.
Governing their minds with equanimity like space, he discerns the arising and ceasing of the four great elements, desiring to transform and instruct sentient beings.
What is taught is authentic and free from hatred or attachment; it subdues and abandons all minds of false views, serving as a firm mental ornament and a banner of steadfastness.
One battles against various categories of dharmas like a valiant general of a great army, subduing external adversaries and causing them to enter the Dharma and Vinaya.

If one enters the conventional teachings established by worldly convention—such as the giving of gifts which brings retribution, the observance of precepts leading to rebirth in heaven, and the fact that all virtues performed entail a corresponding result—one uses these to deliver beings, leading them to the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).

Now, as a bodhisattva, one naturally accords with the *adornment* (vaijayanta-mālā); from the very beginning, the mind never follows the words of evil friends, and only then does one fully perfect the conduct of a Mahāsattva.

With a mind harboring purity and ultimately free from the notion of "self," one maintains the mind like a mountain and acts without flaw or leakage; wisdom pervades all things like the first light of the rising moon.
If one is among the great assembly such that none can equal them, this, O Puzhao, is called the Bodhisattva’s necklace that completely fulfills all things.

To realize that all is void, tranquil, and non-existent; to always see radiance wherever one is born; to understand immediately whatever is heard until the attainment of the Buddha-way; to constantly contemplate the proclamation of the essentials of the sense-gates (*indriya-mukha*); to establish one's own karma without causing harm to others; to perceive the nature of the fundamental self as naturally arising and ceasing; to transcend the eight worldly dharmas without obstruction; and for body, speech, mind, and thought never to have practiced deception—this is it.

Furthermore, by means of skillful wisdom, they rescue and deliver sentient beings, causing those in dire straits to be fully satisfied. They maintain a mind like the earth, refraining from the three transgressions; they advance daily in the Way without indulging in negligence. Attaining a firm mind that does not regress, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) manifests before them.

Possessing the ten powers, they fearlessly awaken to the path of right contemplation; they cast off the notions of self, person, and life-span; they discern and contemplate the dharmas of existence and non-existence; and they move and transform immeasurable Buddha-lands through their mastery of supernatural powers.

The Bodhisattva’s proclaimed garland of words transcends all views and is free from further expectations; the mind is directed toward the right path and is without inversion; his eloquence is unimpeded and without stagnation; as he moves to and fro, he gives rise to no conceptual attachments; he eliminates all fetters, bonds, and latent tendencies, such that pride and self-importance are forever extinguished without remainder.

The resonance of his voice is like the roar of a lion and like the crashing of thunder, such that there is no sound it does not reach; it establishes him eternally in the ultimate state until final nirvana. From it issues the cloud of infinite *vimala* ornaments, proclaiming the thunderous roar of the Dharma and the lightning-flash of the Dharma drum.

Raining down the flavor of liberation, proclaiming the seven factors of enlightenment, maintaining pure mindfulness of the Dharma without departing from the Three Jewels, with a mind like the bright moon free from defilement, penetrating the coming and going without abandoning right action, and being fully endowed with the various marks of the most excellent Dharma—this, O Universal Radiance, is called [the practice].
The Bodhisattva’s jeweled necklace is inexhaustible;

it is excellent in its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, penetrating and benefiting all in between. Possessing a radiant brilliance, they do not lose their prohibitions and precepts; among the sages as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past and the future, there are none who do not praise the virtues of this Bodhisattva.
"Thus it is, Universal Radiance!
This treasury of the sublime Dharma of the factors of the path of the noble ones, this gate of precious jewels, is inexhaustible.

**Chapter Two: On Consciousness and Samādhi** (1) *The Bodhisattva’s Necklace Sūtra*, Chapter Two: On Consciousness and Samādhi. At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Jewel King (*Ratnarāja*) seated in the assembly. He immediately rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!

The necklace of mental consciousness practiced by Bodhisattvas awakens many and none fail to receive deliverance. Just as with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all those who have entered parinirvāṇa in the past, future, and present—how should one cultivate and study the chapter on the Necklace Precepts so as to reach the other shore and cause all classes of sentient beings to universally perceive its fragrant influence?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Jewel King, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!"
"I shall now expound its meaning for you.
A bodhisattva practices the ornament of the aggregate of precepts; perfumed by the fragrance of their merit, they adorn their own bodies.
Jewel King replied:
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The World-Honored One told him:

"To uphold and follow the Way and its Dharma, one cultivates the wisdom of precepts, concentration, and liberation, and exhorts all classes of sentient beings to have profound faith in the precepts. May their aspirations and natures each fulfill their wishes; may they understand how to act appropriately according to circumstances without losing their original vows, while simultaneously eliminating all deluded and ignorant minds."

One should purify the site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) and provide all necessary requisites, ensuring that no coarse or unruly thoughts pass through the mind, while constantly aspiring to reach the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

One should uphold the treasury of the profound and far-reaching True Dharma (*saddharma*), with the mind perpetually sporting in hundreds of thousands of samādhis; its power to move and transform is beyond comparison. All things in the ten thousand phenomena are entirely impermanent, and rare treasures cannot be relied upon as a refuge.

They exercise skillful means without abiding anywhere; yet sentient beings’ minds are deluded and fail to understand the Right Path, for their hearts cling to a self and they do not comprehend impermanence.

The Bodhisattva vows to explain this through analysis, clarifying that all things are empty and devoid of reality. Although they revere the Great Way, they do not abandon the Two Vehicles. In every land where they travel, there is none that does not receive blessings. They further increase their diligence, redoubling their practice of the path, and eliminate all false imaginings regarding the various scriptures and teachings.

The essential principles of the Bodhisattva do not depart from the ten stages; proceeding sequentially through the higher levels without overstepping their order, one employs wisdom to eliminate all worldly afflictions, and those who have not yet reached the Way naturally attain entry into the gateway of the Way.
Constantly mindful and self-reproachful, he thinks to himself:
"Who is it that gives?
Who is the recipient?"

"Just as one observes that all wealth and treasures have no owner, so too, if one encounters insult or humiliation, one should restrain one's own mind; later, if one receives a retribution of exquisite and wondrous physical beauty, everyone who sees one wherever one goes will be filled with joy."

"If one sees those who are impoverished and naked, one shall personally enter the sea to procure a wish-fulfilling jewel; one shall speak to them with the True Dharma so that they may know how to turn back from their ways, and by means of the nectar-like Dharma, one shall exhaust all their hardships and ensure their mindfulness does not wander astray."
Therefore, O Jewel King!

Adorned with the fruits of the bodhisattva path, their minds attain mastery; furthermore, through teachings of courageous and great power, they establish instruction and guidance such that none fail to comply.

Whether walking or sitting, do not depart from the ten recollections; let the mind dwell upon the Triple Gem without ever neglecting it. Fully comprehend the agonizing suffering of the hells, and with a sincere and tranquil heart, remove the defilements of worldly toil. Commit no evil and remain unswayed; accord with the correct principle and reverently cultivate the prohibitive precepts. Thus, the light of virtue will shine universally, and all shall receive its nourishing moisture.

He reckons all that he possesses as having nothing to be covetous of or begrudge; when giving to the Buddha and the Sangha, he does not give rise to conceptual attachments. Or, using skillful wisdom, he may associate with kings and is always able to cause them to renounce their high positions. If anyone comes to beg for his head, eyes, ears, nose, or mouth, he is immediately able to bestow them, never opposing the person's wishes.

At that time, all the disciples and bodhisattvas in the assembly, hearing of these merits of the *guṇa-mālā* (necklace of virtues), leaped for joy beyond measure. Their contemplation became profound and wholesome minds arose within them; each paid homage and they all together made offerings, scattering various famous flowers and diverse precious jewels. In unison, they praised his virtue, saying:
"By virtue of our past merit, we have encountered this excellent benefit and have heard this most wondrous instruction on the *mālā*."

If sentient beings were to hear this Dharma teaching, which exhorts them to develop the essential knowledge and concentration of a bodhisattva, their meritorious virtues would be immeasurable, and they would dwell securely in the truth as it has been expounded, without falsehood.

If there is a bodhisattva who encounters this "Adornment of Concentrated Consciousness," they will contemplate and comprehend all phenomena as being without location; with the adornment of concentrated consciousness, their spiritual mind becomes tranquil, no longer craving food or taking pleasure in the thought of food, and they shall instead encourage and assist others in generating meritorious karma.

"In the past, I offered five hundred flowers to the Buddha and established a vast vow to attain Buddhahood for myself; thus, the fruit of the Way has become imperishable and the True Dharma has been made to flourish.

Furthermore, by means of the prohibitive precepts, I have eliminated all defilements and rescued others from their manifold sufferings as if putting out a fire on my own head, ensuring that all who face calamities and hardships shall surely attain deliverance."

He reflected: "In the past, when I entered the sea to seek jewels, I encountered a makara fish and a mountain of water-forms. I, as the leader, entered the *vijñāna-samādhi-avalokita-maṇi* (the pearl-necklace of consciousness-concentration), whereupon a benevolent deity immediately showed me the auspicious path; thus, with joy and in safety, I returned to my native land."

This arises from the non-retrogressive vigor of one's vows and aspirations, entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samāpatti*) free from manifold perceptions—the hall wherein the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, dwell—and exhorting sentient beings to be born in the Brahma heavens and the heavens of non-perception; all of this is brought about by the necklace of consciousness-concentration (*vijñāna-samādhi*).

"If, within the human realm and the lands of the ten directions, they follow worldly customs to transform and guide others by preaching the Way that transcends the world; furthermore, using the ten wholesome paths and the fruits of realization to benefit sentient beings and lead them to the wisdom of emptiness; proclaiming all things in accordance with the holy teachings; understanding that all is fundamentally empty and nothing is created; and planting roots of virtue not for their own sake, but so that all may obtain the fruits of the Dharma."

He is capable of bearing the heavy responsibility of establishing the Dharma even in the face of decline; though he encounters suffering and affliction, he is forever free from grief and lamentation, nor does he harbor deluded thoughts or a mind of attachment. He nourishes his body and speech so that they do not leak or fail, and through skillful means, he enters deeply into the cycle of birth and death to preach the flavor of the eight liberations and right meditative attainments, thereby establishing the mundane world’s aspiration for and reverence toward the Buddha-way.

Whether expounding a single teaching or various chapters, they lead beings to enter the discipline of the noble ones; gradually guiding and instructing them, they bring them to parinirvāṇa, enabling the True Dharma to abide for many eons.

There are other sentient beings whom he causes to reach the remainderless, tranquil nirvana, free from the afflictions of birth, old age, death, and the assumption of physical form, and no longer dependent upon the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.
To those groups who dwell in wrong views and are deluded by ignorance, he demonstrates the Dharma of the single path of right view.

If they dwell in seclusion practicing the twelve dharmas of diligent and ascetic conduct, sitting in quietude beneath trees without dependence on anything, contemplating the methods of dhyāna with emptiness as their sole task, their minds will be tranquil and concentrated, free from error.

The Bodhisattva’s jewel-ornament of concentration of consciousness likewise does not dwell upon whether forms have marks or are markless; for marks are inherently empty and quiescent, and the primary and secondary marks are likewise so. Distinguishing between the internal and external, he realizes them as one; the three periods of time are empty and still, devoid of past, future, or present, thereby concentrating the mind through consciousness.
Furthermore, one contemplates the nature of the five aggregates, the sense-fields, and the bases of perception: from where do they come, and into what do they cease?
By discerning each of these individually, one knows them to be skillful fabrications; realizing they possess neither arising nor ceasing, one no longer gives rise to longing or hope.

Furthermore, one does not perceive existence or non-existence; the Way and its teachings do not arise through the mind or consciousness. When consciousness arises, it arises; when consciousness ceases, it ceases. One perceives no marks or appearances, nor is there any notion of self.
Furthermore, one does not cling to or abide in any location; the same applies to the six internal and external sense objects.
Even the ears and eyes, when analyzed, are found to be non-existent; how much more so could there be any matters of seeing or hearing?

This is not so. "O Jewel King, you should know that the bodhisattva’s necklace-like mental consciousness and its fixed dharmas neither arise nor cease, and have no beginning or end. They arise when conditions arise and cease when conditions cease; yet in their arising there is no perception of arising, and in their ceasing there is no perception of ceasing. Internally contemplating the thoughts of increase and decrease, one has no notions of suffering or pleasure."

The reason for this is that, having departed from the notion of a self, even while remaining amidst the manifold afflictions of desire, his mind is free from defilement; because he has distanced himself from the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, his will is like a diamond, indestructible.

Knowing the fundamental past lives and their ultimate origins, one severs all fetters without finding it difficult; seeing neither the finite nor the infinite—this is called the Bodhisattva’s Necklace of Consciousness-Samadhi.

Following worldly instructions and respectfully serving elders without expecting recompense; diligently practicing vigor for hundreds of thousands of kalpas; fully accomplishing the dharmas of the wisdom of the Way; proclaiming the impartial upholding and patience of all bodhisattvas; reciting and mastering them until they are thoroughly understood, receiving them with clarity so as never to forget.

The nature of the fivefold qualities of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is fully and clearly manifested in each instance, without artificial adornment in speech; his words are always accompanied by a smile, his mind is free from attachment, and he does not give rise to the dualistic views of annihilationism or eternalism.

Even when among the great assembly, he is without partiality or attachment; regarding the empty and non-existent dharmas, he is free from conceptualization. Though his inner being is truly full, he outwardly manifests as one who receives instruction. He does not give rise to the thought, "I am excessive in my practice while others are deficient," and he remains detached from all gain and honor, harboring no expectations.

He constantly reflects upon himself, knowing that the body has no master; from head to foot, he thoroughly realizes it is fundamentally non-existent. He practices the six perfections, understanding they have no fixed location; he calculates all dharmas as being merely provisional designations, knowing they possess neither form nor substance. All dharmas cannot be seen, and even when distinguishing sounds and echoes, there is nothing heard.
“Thus it is, O Jewel King!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the Dharma-garland of the meditative concentration on consciousness, he does not rejoice upon seeing the good nor feel dejection upon hearing of evil; only then should he correspond to the garland of diligence, entering hundreds of thousands of concentrations in tranquil non-conceptuality. Even amidst the thunder of heaven, earthquakes, dragon lightning and peals of thunder, the collapsing of mountains, the flooding of waters, or the roaring of lions, his mind remains silent and settled, forever free from confusion.”

At times, when a bodhisattva enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and right reception (*samyaksamāpatti*), they may remain for as long as one kalpa or even a hundred thousand kalpas; their physical form remains supple and beautiful, and they no longer require food, for through the power of this concentrated mind, they take the joy of dhyāna as their nourishment and the eight liberations as their drink.
At times, the Bodhisattva further enters samādhi by means of his supernormal powers; the name of this samādhi is "Universal Illumination.
He beholds the Buddha-lands of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where he pays homage, serves, and makes offerings to the Buddhas without losing his dignified deportment.

Likewise, in the southern, western, and northern directions, in each of the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he is able to make offerings to all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and eloquently expound upon the contemplation of the *vijñāna-samādhi-maṇi-alaṃkāra*.
"Thus it is, O Jewel King! Such is the power experienced by a Bodhisattva entering meditative concentration.

Let alone the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—suppose each of those lands were filled with dust, and one were to take a single grain of that dust and place it upon the Buddha-lands; even if all such grains of dust were exhausted, the Buddha-lands would still be immeasurable."

The Bodhisattvas, through their samādhis, behold all the assemblies and hear that Buddha expound upon the *mālā* (garland) of the conscious mind’s concentration. They understand that the root of all dharmas is empty, quiescent, and without a master; from the first arousal of the aspiration for learning until reaching the site of enlightenment, they contemplate and resolve to adorn the tree of the Way. Having completely transcended the fetters of the diseases of lust, anger, and delusion, their minds are firm and unshakable. Even if the celestial Māras were to lead billions of myriads of followers to come and destroy this concentration of the conscious mind, they would ultimately never be overcome by them, nor would they be led astray by the factions of evil. Their intent is as vast as the ocean, accepting all without exception; they fully accomplish the *mālā* of manifold virtues and constantly preach impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, saying: "If the permanent is not truly permanent, how could there be a self?"
Those who cling to the notion of permanence are far removed from meditative concentration; they fall into the cycle of birth and death and cannot save themselves.
"The Bodhisattva’s cultivation is dedicated solely to the Way; his mind is tranquil and forever free from manifold thoughts, never departing from the meritorious deeds performed by the Buddhas."

His mind is like Mount Tai, immovable and unshakable; he walks alone through the world without fear. With the eloquence of the four types of knowledge, he encompasses all dharmas and instructs sentient beings on the essentials of the Way and wisdom. Internally, his nature is substantial and upright, free from flattery or deceit.
The reason for this is that it is by virtue of its fundamental purity.

Since all defilements are absent and all darknesses have been extinguished, the light of wisdom shines everywhere, such that none fail to receive its benefit. The mind is vast and expansive, without limit or shore; it bathes away the impurities of thought until they are made bright and clear. It is able to accomplish whatever the world desires, and having approached the foot of the Bodhi tree, one cultivates the Dharma and its meaning for oneself.

He harbors no doubt regarding any phenomenon; he is fully accomplished in all compassionate wisdom; he accords with what he has heard to rescue those of little knowledge; with his mind adorned by meditative concentration, he delivers those who are distracted; and in whatever he practices, he constantly attains tranquil stability. He cultivates the factors of the Noble Eightfold Path and establishes all people so that they may see the True Truth. This, O Jewel King, is called [the perfection].
This is the essential adornment of the Bodhisattva’s concentration of consciousness.

If there are those who hear and uphold it within their hearts, they shall never be separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and shall attain non-retrogression on the path to unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.

When the Buddha spoke this "Adornment of Consciousness-Samadhi," immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans in the assembly all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Furthermore, there were sixty-two thousand bodhisattvas from other regions who attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Additionally, eight thousand laymen and laywomen, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye;
five thousand bhikṣus had their outflows exhausted and their minds liberated.
Ninety thousand devaputras became free from all greed and desire.
Chapter Three: Adorning the Bodhi Tree (*Bodhisattvālaṃkāra-sūtra*) At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the worthy ones:

"In the past, throughout incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I accumulated merit and cultivated practice to refine the pure Dharma. Whether sitting, lying down, or walking, I did not abandon the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*). In a single moment, a single action, or a single thought, I cultivated ten dharmas."

What are the ten? First, when descending from the Tuṣita Heaven to take birth, they see all the countless Buddha-fields of the ten directions; they see all the bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood, who have all gone to the tree of enlightenment to cultivate the pure *vimala-alaṃkāra* (pure ornaments). When they are about to lift their right foot to proceed to the site of enlightenment out of compassion for sentient beings, the trichiliocosm shakes throughout.
The Bodhisattva reflects to himself:
"My former vows have now been fulfilled; I shall destroy the adornments of Māra's realm and establish the Buddha-field.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s great compassion-garland, advancing toward the site of enlightenment with a mind that does not regress.

"Second, they exhaustively perceive the thoughts and mental activities of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas throughout the trichiliocosm; furthermore, they enter the samādhi of concentrated mind without distraction. They may see a bodhisattva attaining enlightenment in emptiness, or see them at a secluded place beneath a tree, or see them entering the water-light-emptiness-realm samādhi, adorning the Bodhi tree while never departing from great compassion. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s great compassion necklace, advancing toward the site of enlightenment with a mind that does not regress."

"Third, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally beholds the trichiliocosm and advances toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) without abandoning a joyful mind, thinking: 'I shall now certainly attain Buddhahood, without doubt; by means of the fundamental dharma of my practice, I shall universally moisten all things, and together with all sentient beings, I shall possess a golden hue, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and be surrounded before and behind by immeasurable multitudes; I shall destroy the net of Māra and establish my own land. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivating the necklace of joy, a mind that does not regress."

"Fourth, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva desires to proceed to the site of enlightenment and approach the foot of the Bodhi tree, they see all the incalculable lands (*asaṃkhyeya-kṣetra*) of the ten directions and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*). They fully cultivate and protect the mind to adorn the Bodhi tree, causing countless sentient beings to likewise protect their minds as they do. Without abandoning any of the *samādhi* concentrations of the various necklaces of jewels, this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s progress toward the site of enlightenment through the protection of the mind and the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the non-retrogressive mind."

"Furthermore, fifthly, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again beholds the countless lands of the ten directions, where Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood all turn the wheel of Dharma through the practice of non-retrogression. This Dharma is without verbal expression and without form; it is a single mark that is markless, an empty realm without shape. Since even emptiness is itself empty, how much more so is there no dharma-realm? This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s necklace of the Dharma of emptiness, non-existence, and formlessness."

"Sixth, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally observes the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where sentient beings possess penetrating wisdom and their faculties are mature and refined; their intentions are set upon the Three Vehicles and they do not abandon the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*); they practice the six profound dharmas through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; they possess the four unhindered wisdoms and the patience of the single-minded path, and thus know for themselves that they have received the prediction of enlightenment."
Furthermore, when he sees others receiving their predictions—whether the prediction of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha—the Bodhisattva reflects to himself:

"Throughout countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, from body to body, my successive existences have all been illusory transformations and not real dharmas; yet now I receive this prediction, advancing toward the unsurpassed, right, and true path to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment."

"Traversing through space, coming and going without any obstruction, one attains the samādhi of dhāraṇī at a single time and in a single place. Regarding that which all Buddhas praise—the Truths of Suffering, its Origin, its Cessation, and the Path—one realizes: 'This suffering is not suffering; from what does suffering arise?'"

To understand suffering as being without suffering accords with clear wisdom. Habitual tendencies arise from craving; yet craving is fundamentally formless and invisible. Birth is fundamentally without birth—how much more so could there be the extinction of dharmas?

Sentient beings are deluded and confused; they arise from renewed contact (*sparśa*) and practice this grasping (*upādāna*). To understand that there is no practice and no grasping is to accord with clear wisdom. All phenomena are without arising and are subject to the law of extinction; that which is exhausted is without arising and likewise without exhaustion.

All phenomena are inexhaustible; yet sentient beings, out of ignorance and delusion, claim that what is inexhaustible is exhausted. Within this, they give rise to conceptualizations, failing to realize that phenomena do not change. That which is truly exhausted is indeed exhausted; this is called clear wisdom.

The Way has no marks or characteristics; it cannot be seen by the realm of the eye. It is the eightfold right path, level, upright, and unimpeded; this is called clear wisdom. This is what is meant by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva advancing toward the Tree of Enlightenment with a mind that does not regress.

"Seventh, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thoroughly observes the three thousand great thousandfold world systems, examining the roots and origins of sentient beings—their heights and depths, their greatness and smallness. Some share the same mental orientation as the Tathāgata; their fundamental practices are in accord, and their wisdom neither increases nor decreases. Adorned with the garlands of great kindness and great compassion, they possess the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, along with skillful means, the sixteen sublime practices, and hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇīs. Their minds are vast and not narrow; even when they see the conduct of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, their minds remain free from attachment and they do not follow them. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva adorning the tree of enlightenment with a mind that does not regress."

"Eighth, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the dharma-gate of the virtue of eight hundred dhāraṇī-dharma-gates; when a bodhisattva attains this dharma-gate, all practices are fully perfected and they adorn the tree of enlightenment."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Universal Patience; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door universally moistens all beings by raining down the nectar of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Signlessness; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door fully enters the practice of emptiness and the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Sound and Resonance; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door is endowed with the eightfold equanimous practices and hears no discordant sounds.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Physical Conduct; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door maintains pure physical conduct and does not commit any evils.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of verbal conduct; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate commits none of the four transgressions and has no other evil deeds.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of mental conduct; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate does not let the mind wander in discursive thought, but remains tranquil and utterly extinguished.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-thought; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate enters the meditative absorption of cessation and perceives that all forms are non-existent.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Ultimateity; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate proceeds from this shore to reach the other shore.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-attachment; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate does not give rise to defiled attachment toward the phenomena of birth and death.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-obstruction; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate penetrates the coming and going [of saṃsāra] without being hindered by birth and death.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Resonant Response; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate proceeds according to their practice without disparaging the reception [of others].
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Divine Power; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate transforms at will to pay homage and serve all Buddhas.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of purity; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate purifies their wisdom such that they have no conception of a land.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of the practice of emptiness; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate understands and knows that all phenomena are false and not real.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Illusory Transformation; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate perceives that the provisional and deceptive aggregations of sentient beings are beyond all conceptual grasp.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Formlessness; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate realizes that the fundamental source of the faculties of sentient beings is inexhaustible.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Paths of Practice (*mārga-vidyā*); a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) without interruption.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Applications of Mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate contemplates the internal and external body, moment by moment, without interruption.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Abandonment of Mental Intentions; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate observes all phenomena without any notion of multiplicity.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Divine Footsteps; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate dwells for an incalculable number of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Faculties (*indriya*); the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate possesses a path-wisdom that is profoundly deep, firm, and unimpeded.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Spiritual Power (*ṛddhi-bala*); the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate dwells securely in all phenomena, such that they cannot be undermined or destroyed.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Factors of Enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). A bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate uses the flowers of the factors of enlightenment so that they are not defiled by dust or grime.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Path-factors (*mārgāṅga*). A bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate enters meditative concentration without obstruction, and their mind does not become confused.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Emptiness-Wisdom; the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate establishes sentient beings in peace, causing them to forever leave behind desire and anger.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Signlessness; the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate causes the various classes of sentient beings to conceive the aspiration for the Path.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Bodhisattvas who attain this Dharma-gate transform and guide sentient beings, causing them to eliminate all desires and aspirations.

This is called the eight hundred dhāraṇīs of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; to briefly state their essentials: they advance toward the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and adorn the Bodhi tree, with a mind like a diamond (*vajra*) that cannot be destroyed.

"Ninth, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates this trichiliocosm—beings with one foot, two feet, three feet, four feet, up to those with countless feet; those with minds of desire and those without minds of desire; those with minds of anger and those without minds of anger; those with minds of delusion and those without minds of delusion; those with minds of suffering and pleasure and those without minds of suffering and pleasure—he is able to distinguish them all in a single moment, a single arising, and a single thought-instant. For their sake, he preaches the absence of suffering, emptiness, and the non-existence of self or person. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the concentration of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samādhi) as he advances toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree."

"Tenth, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further contemplates that the minds and faculties of the future, past, and present throughout the trichiliocosm are tranquil, and their conduct accords with the unsurpassed, truly correct path; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment and adornment of the Buddha-tree."
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first lifts his right foot to take the first step, he practices ten dharmas therein, advancing toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree."

What are the ten? First, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva lifts his right foot to tread upon the ground, he proclaims his own name and title as the Most Honored One of the Three Realms; all Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have likewise walked seven steps, and all Buddhas of the future shall do the same.

I now appear in the world, uniquely honored throughout the three realms and without equal; the defining characteristics of all Buddhas must not be omitted or lost. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Buddha-tree.
"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva raises his right foot to step upon the ground, he forms this thought:
'I have now attained the stage of non-retrogression; I shall cause all sentient beings to follow the same path as I, never abandoning my vast and great resolve of the great vow.'"
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s adornment of the Bodhi tree and proceeding to the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva first lifts his right foot and treads upon the ground, he again reflects:
"The Buddhas of the past all practiced this Dharma first; I should now observe which Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood (Ekajātipratibaddha) shall succeed me, and what will be his name?"
He then turned his body to the right and looked back at Maitreya, saying:

"After you, you shall attain Buddhahood like me before long. Upon hearing this, hundreds of thousands of devas and humans were all filled with joy; they turned in one direction and spoke with one voice, praising him boundlessly.
How wonderful!
O Hero of the World!
The lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed.

At that time, eleven nayutas of devas and human beings, seeing Maitreya receive the seal of investiture, all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s adornment of the Bodhi tree and his advance to the site of enlightenment.
"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva first lifts his right foot and treads upon the ground, he forms this thought:

'I have now attained mastery over all wisdom; my spiritual insight is unimpeded and my eloquence is thoroughly penetrating. Yet these sentient beings have long harbored doubts, submerged in worldly defilements, and do not seek liberation.'"
"I shall now use the fire of wisdom to burn away the thicket of doubt within my mind.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva adorning the Buddha-tree and proceeding toward the site of enlightenment.
"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva first lifts his right foot and steps upon the ground, he reflects:

'I have now attained unconditioned liberation (asaṃskṛta-vimukti); I shall further lead across those who possess conditioned liberation (saṃskṛta-vimukti). All the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, were entirely identical to me in their unconditioned liberation; the Buddhas of the future shall likewise attain this Dharma.'"
"How wonderful!
The retribution of merit is never severed; delusive thoughts are exhausted, and there is nothing further to crave.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree.
"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first lifts his right foot and steps upon the ground, he again gives rise to this thought:
'Sentient beings dwell eternally in false views and inversion; they do not perceive the wisdom of the three gates of liberation, which is empty and non-existent.'"

I shall now expound upon the purity of the protective mind: the nature of phenomena is empty and tranquil, devoid of applied and sustained thought; it is the foundation of all practices, characterized by shame and remorse; it is suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the absence of a person or a life-span; one should use this mind to universally encompass all things.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to adorn the tree of awakening.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva first lifts his right foot, desiring to proceed to the bathing pool—surrounded by gardens and pavilions of seven treasures such as lapis lazuli and crystal, filled with various extraordinary birds like ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks, and followed by an immeasurable multitude of devas leading the way—this is likewise so.

"It is not appropriate for me to remain in this state of nakedness; should I enter a city or a village among the crowds of people, they would say I am naked and devoid of shame. I ought to seek a *kāṣāya* robe to cover my body."

At that time, there was a son of heaven named Puṇyaketu (福蓋) who, immediately perceiving the thoughts in the Bodhisattva’s mind, promptly presented him with eighty-four thousand gold-threaded robes woven from fine silk.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"What were the Dharma-robes of the Buddhas of the past?
What methods did they employ in their progress, movements, and comings?"
The Ākāśadevatā joined her palms and said:
"The Buddhas of the past all wore kashayas woven with golden threads, just like those offered by the devas today."
The Bodhisattva then accepted the eighty-four thousand robes woven with golden thread and, through his spiritual power, merged them into one.

When the robe was placed upon his body, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics were all manifested externally; this resulted from his past practice of giving without conceptualization and his cultivation of the perfection of giving. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree.
"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva lifts his right foot, he gives rise to this thought:
'The natures and conducts of sentient beings are manifold and diverse.
I shall now, with the radiance of wisdom, universally illumine the trichiliocosm.'"
He immediately emitted light from the mark upon his crown, which universally illuminated the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
All classes of sentient beings who beheld this light came together like clouds to the Sahā world, where they attended upon the Tathāgata and made offerings of incense and flowers.

Through the inspiration of his majestic spiritual power, he causes heaven and earth to tremble six times; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s progress toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree.
"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva lifts his foot, a thought arises in his mind:

'The conditions for birth are exhausted and I shall no longer undergo conception; I am uniquely honored within the three realms with no equal, and I shall be known as a Buddha, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.'"

"In the lands of the ten directions, the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, each within their own realm, addressed the fourfold assembly, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans:

'Today, Śākyamuni Buddha has appeared in the Sahā world-system; his manifold marks are fully perfected like the moon among the stars. He brings blessings and deliverance to sentient beings, and gods and humans receive his protection. Those who wish to arouse reverence and make offerings to that Buddha should know that now is the time.'"

At that time, bodhisattvas endowed with supernatural powers and eloquence from the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—who had attained the gate of dhāraṇī—numbering one thousand seven hundred and seventy-seven koṭis of nayutas, all came together like clouds to this Sahā world, offering such veneration that the flowers reached up to their knees.
Furthermore, there were eight million *nayuta* of celestial Māras, Pāpīyans, who all came to the Sahā world to present offerings and attend upon the Bodhisattva.
Additionally, there were hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* of dragon kings with supernatural powers, each having seven heads, who offered fragrant water for the Bodhisattva’s bath.

This arises from having, in the past, preached the Dharma of the ambrosia that is never tiresome; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s progress toward the site of enlightenment and the adornment of the Bodhi tree.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought within himself:

"Sentient beings have long been attached to existence and deluded; if they hear the Dharma of emptiness, non-substantiality, and profound stillness, their minds will harbor fear and their hair will stand on end."

The Buddha-dharma is profound and inconceivable; I shall gradually explain, in due order, the source of the path and distinguish the origins of the various faculties of sentient beings. With profound insight into the arising and ceasing of phenomena throughout the three periods of time, one eliminates conceptual attachments and the mind of greed and stinginess. From the accumulation of practices over incalculable kalpas until now, the reason one has not attained the Way is entirely due to craving and affection.
"I shall now uproot the thorn of affection and craving, deliver sentient beings, and establish them in the state of non-action.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s progress toward the site of enlightenment and his adornment of the Bodhi tree.
“In this way, son of good family!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva descends in spirit to be born and places his right foot upon the ground, he contemplates ten dharmas during that interval, adorning the tree of enlightenment and remaining non-regressive.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!
