When the Bodhisattva was first born, he descended to the ground and took seven steps toward the golden stand. Then, raising his left foot, he reflected within himself:

'The words and meanings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are immeasurable; the Dharma of the Path is pure and refined. It is the Dharma of the Infinite Deliverance, free from arising and ceasing. Its practice is beyond birth and death and inconceivable; it is not something that can be attained by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.'"

The Way requires single-mindedness; manifold thoughts are not the Way. The Way requires few desires; many desires are not the Way. The Way requires contentment; much seeking is not the Way. The Way requires right view; wrong views are not the Way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again had this thought:
"What is meant by the True Dharma practiced by the Buddhas of the past?
He then further had this thought:

"In the past, the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, appeared in the world; through their supernormal powers, they manifested their majestic virtue, and the ten fundamental meanings were inconceivable."
"What are these ten? In this regard, noble son!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva first raises his left foot, it pervades the entire realm of the three thousandfold world-system. It does not disturb sentient beings who lack awareness; yet, any sentient beings who behold the marks upon his feet all resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path. This is due to the retribution of their past acts of veneration. This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s progress toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Buddha-tree."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
At that time, as the Bodhisattva’s left foot touched the ground, a thought arose in his mind:
'When the Buddhas of antiquity preached the Dharma, how did they distinguish the phrases, the words, and the meanings? "

What are the rules of deportment for the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—their advancing and halting, their coming and going—by which a single phrase of meaning can bring forth the immeasurable treasuries of the Buddhas' Dharma, such that from eon to eon, even unto a hundred eons, one cannot exhaustively fathom the meaning of that single phrase?
"The secret essentials of the Tathāgata are inconceivable; they cannot be fathomed by those of minor capacity.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to adorn the tree of awakening (bodhivṛkṣa).
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva emits light from a single pore, which universally illumines immeasurable Buddha-lands.

Within that light, he expounds the great Dharma of the equality of the six perfections, as well as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the patience of non-arising. He also causes sentient beings to become firm in their resolve, so that they all give rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment. This is called the Bodhisattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment and his adornment of the Bodhi tree."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
At that time, the bodhisattva reflects within himself:
'I shall now, through the correct reception of samādhi, travel everywhere throughout the space of the dharma-realm of all Buddhas.'"

At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately entered the meditative concentration of formlessness (*animitta-samādhi*), traveling throughout the void and the dharma-realm of all Buddhas, with celestial beings and worldly people as his attendants on both sides, none of whom were aware of it; they thought the Bodhisattva was merely advancing toward the golden throne. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to adorn the Bodhi tree.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

He transforms a single form that pervades the trichiliocosm, and then returns to his original state, such that no class of sentient beings perceives it. This is called the Bodhisattva’s progress toward the site of enlightenment and the adornment of the Bodhi tree."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
At that time, the light of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom shines universally throughout the trichiliocosm. From within each ray of light, a voice issues forth:

'Today, Śākyamuni Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—shall turn the Wheel of Dharma upon Jambudvīpa to deliver those not yet delivered, bringing benefit and merit to sentient beings, and his fame shall spread far and wide.'"
This is called the Bodhisattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and the adornment of the Buddha-tree.
Furthermore, son of good family!

At that time, in a single moment of thought, the Bodhisattva causes all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, each to extend their hand to support and receive the Bodhisattva; the entire assembly sees this. This is called the Bodhisattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment and the adornment of the Buddha-tree.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas is profound and difficult to fathom; I shall now sequentially manifest the paths of the three vehicles—the Pratyekabuddhas, the Śrāvakas, and the Bodhisattvas. Upon hearing the Dharma, one awakens and never again becomes obstructed midway. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment and adornment of the Bodhi tree."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the three periods of the past—all those who now wish for me to accomplish the unconditioned Great Way—shall all bear witness and enable me to attain enlightenment."
All the Buddhas praised him well and stood before him, saying:

"For incalculable eons, you have performed countless ascetic practices; you have fully perfected the six perfections of giving, ethical discipline, and so forth, never begrudging your kingdom, wealth, wife, or children. Now you shall attain Buddhahood and extensively deliver all sentient beings."
"We shall support and escort you until you attain Buddhahood, not allowing you to stop midway.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and the adornment of the Buddha-tree.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
The Bodhisattva discerns the past, present, and future as empty, signless, and wishless; this too is the Dharma that all Buddhas should practice."

From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, one must cultivate the three vehicles, the four immeasurables of great compassion, and the eight paths of non-obstruction to adorn the body; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s advancement toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"When the Bodhisattva next raises his right foot and is about to tread upon the ground, he should be fully endowed with these ten inconceivable wisdoms of the divine feet."

What are the ten? There is a wisdom of spiritual power called "Non-attachment. When a bodhisattva attains this wisdom, they traverse the profound and essential Dharma-treasuries of all Buddhas; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva advancing toward the site of enlightenment and adorning the Bodhi tree.

"Furthermore, there is a divine wisdom called Formless; when a bodhisattva attains this divine wisdom, they enter the meditative concentration of insatiability and receive the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions."

"Furthermore, there is the non-dual divine wisdom; the bodhisattva who attains this divine wisdom exhorts and inspires sentient beings to achieve unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, rather than taking the path of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha."
"Furthermore, there is the divine wisdom of emptiness; when a bodhisattva attains this divine wisdom, they thoroughly contemplate the world as empty, devoid of self or person.

Furthermore, there is the divine wisdom of signlessness; when a bodhisattva attains this divine wisdom, they eloquently expound upon all phenomena, understanding them as having a single characteristic—signlessness—and being free from the dharmas of arising and ceasing, or attachment and severance."

"Furthermore, there is the divine wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness; when a bodhisattva attains this divine wisdom, they see all Buddha-lands, whether forming or decaying, as clearly as one gazes at a jewel in the palm of one's hand."

“Furthermore, there is the divine wisdom of relinquishing life. A bodhisattva who attains this divine wisdom contemplates the karmic retribution of the conditions of life, thereby relinquishing the physical form and receiving a new form.
Furthermore, there is the divine wisdom of ineffability. A bodhisattva who attains this divine wisdom preaches the Dharma without the notion of dharmas, nor does he have any discursive thoughts.”
“Furthermore, there is the divine wisdom of neither near nor far; when a bodhisattva attains this divine wisdom, they do not perceive the nearness or farness of the nesting places of all phenomena.

Furthermore, there is the divine wisdom of neither arising nor ceasing; when a bodhisattva attains this divine wisdom, they discern the root of the twelve links of dependent origination, wherein both that which arises and that which ceases are entirely non-existent. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s tenfold divine power of wisdom for advancing toward the site of enlightenment and adorning the Bodhi tree.”
The Buddha again addressed the son of noble family:
"When a Bodhisattva first takes his left foot upon birth, he should further fulfill ten karmas of infinite ultimateity. What are these ten?"

In this regard, son of good family! This is that which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have practiced: the Tathāgata manifests his form and appears in the world to teach and transform; he discerns the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time, and the defilements, fetters, and attachments of the three realms and five destinies. He bathes away all knots so that there is forever no dust or obscuration. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the first practice for advancing toward the site of enlightenment and adorning the Bodhi tree.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When the Tathāgata appears in the world to transform sentient beings, he establishes them in the three vehicles according to their respective aspirations;
yet there may be some sentient beings whose inclinations lie toward arhatship and who do not turn toward the gate of the Buddha."
There may be sentient beings who practice the conduct of pratyekabuddhas and do not turn toward the path of the Buddha;
there may be sentient beings who cultivate the unsurpassed path but do not incline toward the vehicles of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or arhats;
and there may be sentient beings who retreat from the path of the Buddha and aspire instead to the Lesser Vehicle.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva entices and encourages those before him until they attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

There may be sentient beings who, remaining on the level of ordinary worldlings, do not seek the skillful means to ascend to the Three Vehicles; the Bodhisattva exhorts them to achieve the paths of the Three Vehicles. This is called the Bodhisattva’s second deed: advancing toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Buddha-tree."

“The Tathāgata appears in the world to disseminate and manifest his verbal teachings, employing skillful means (*upāya*) to transform sentient beings according to their needs, bearing heavy burdens as one who takes on the great responsibility for others.

He may manifest before sentient beings as a parent, brother, or friend; he may appear as a state preceptor, an elder, or a master of the Way; or he may appear as a wealthy householder or a powerful ghost-king. He provides for the poor and destitute by bestowing the seven treasures, expounds the path of the teachings to bring them to fruition in the three vehicles (*triyāna*). This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the three karmas to advance toward the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and adorn the tree of awakening.”

"When the Tathāgata appears in the world and turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, he does not lose the four analytical knowledges; observing the minds of sentient beings, he bestows the ten wholesome courses of action and analytically expounds upon suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."

If some give rise to delusion and sink into the three realms, the Bodhisattva employs skillful means to rescue them, enabling them to forever leave behind birth and death; this is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the fourth practice to advance toward the site of enlightenment and adorn the Bodhi tree.

“When the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, appears in the world, he constantly bestows his great compassion upon sentient beings, never abandoning them with a heart like that of a mother who loves her child.

For example, it is like the dragon king Elapattra, who dwells in a palace of seven treasures on the slopes of Mount Sumeru’s Golden Fortune Peak, sporting together with various dragon maidens. If he wishes to go to the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to present offerings, he manifests a body seventy thousand *yojanas* long with thirty-two heads; each head has seven tusks, and upon each tusk there is a jeweled bathing pool. In each pool grow seven hundred lotuses, and within each lotus are seven hundred jade maidens who sport together, performing music and song, with the sounds of lutes and harps never ceasing.”

Furthermore, it rains the seven treasures down to the knees; likewise, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through the four immeasurable minds, bestows grace upon sentient beings, raining down the inexhaustible wealth of the Dharma—the seven factors of enlightenment—so that according to their inclinations, they all achieve the fruit of the Path. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the fifth practice: advancing toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree.

“The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, employs skillful means to transform beings according to the timing; he knows when to walk and when to sit, when to speak and when to remain silent. He enters universally into the thoughts within the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings, treating their ailments according to their specific conditions so as not to increase or decrease [the remedy], causing them all to dwell forever on the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the sixth practice for advancing toward the site of enlightenment and adorning the Bodhi tree.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When a Tathāgata appears in the world, he transforms and guides sentient beings not for his own sake; for the sake of even a single person, he undergoes hundreds of thousands of kalpas, enduring suffering on their behalf without weariness or fatigue, establishing them in the Buddha-wisdom and bringing them to the realization of the Unsurpassed Way. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the seventh practice: advancing toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree."

“The arising of all Buddhas does not destroy the dharma-realm; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus by itself, yet it is not so by itself. As such, the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) neither undergoes destruction nor does it not undergo destruction. To cultivate this without fear and without dread is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the eighth practice, advancing toward the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to adorn the tree of awakening.”

"When a Tathāgata appears in the world, he further fulfills the single characteristic of formlessness; in the space of a finger-snap, from among the dharmas of the past, future, and present, he gives birth to the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time—real, non-different, and immutable. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the ninth practice for advancing toward the site of enlightenment and adorning the Buddha-tree."

"The Tathāgata, appearing in the world out of compassion for sentient beings, causes the duration of a single day to become one kalpa spanning the three periods of time; yet among the sentient beings therein, none perceive it. This is called the Bodhisattva’s first birth, falling to the ground and lifting his left foot to practice the ten deeds, proceeding toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Buddha-tree."
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

“When a Bodhisattva is first born and takes seven steps upon the ground, during that interval he should further contemplate ten dharmas: subduing non-Buddhists, destroying the net of Māra, being attended by the devas, proceeding toward the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree, and never abandoning these practices until his final nirvāṇa.”
What are these ten?

In this regard, noble son, one should first subdue Māra; donning the armor of loving-kindness and benevolence, grasping the sword of wisdom in hand, guided by skillful means, and wearing the flower garland of fearlessness upon one's head, one shall destroy the hosts of arrogance and forever eliminate haughtiness.
This is what is meant, son of good family:
one should first cultivate this foremost dharma that is difficult to attain.
Furthermore, son of good family:

Furthermore, one should contemplate the profound and vast meaning, sever the outflows, and realize the fruit of enlightenment; one should gather those heterodox practitioners and become their leader, augmenting this with immeasurable supernormal powers and spiritual might. Should they manifest one [miracle], I shall manifest two, thereby leading those of the heterodox factions to abide securely in right view.
This is what is called, son of good family!
A bodhisattva should mindfully cultivate this second dharma that is difficult to obtain.
"Furthermore, son of good family!"

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva transforms and delivers sentient beings, receiving the joy of the Dharma, they will certainly reach steadfastness and not turn toward other paths; this is called the third dharma difficult to attain practiced by a Bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The constant practice of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is to observe sentient beings during the four periods of day and night. In the space of a finger-snap, they pervade the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, returning again and again without attachment to the triple world. This is called the Bodhisattva’s fourth dharma that is difficult to attain."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Practicing unimpeded wisdom that pervades the trichiliocosm, one delivers sentient beings yet perceives no one who is delivered; this is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the fifth dharma that is difficult to attain."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

By means of the power of the supernormal bases, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva travels throughout the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, universally observing the thoughts and consciousnesses of sentient beings. He may transform a single body into hundreds of thousands of bodies and then merge them back into one, such that no one perceives it. This is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of the sixth dharma that is difficult to attain."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Bodhisattva contemplates the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*), which is not something cultivated by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, nor is it something that can be attained by the eight classes of beings, such as devas, nāgas, or yakṣas. This is called the seventh dharma difficult to attain practiced by a Bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The supernatural power of the Tathāgata is inconceivable: he can enter the pore of a single atom with the immeasurable Buddha-lands of the ten directions, moving back and forth without any obstruction; yet when he returns to his original state, no one perceives it. This is called the Bodhisattva’s eighth dharma that is difficult to attain through practice."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has attained the four analytical knowledges and the wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing, which pervades the trichiliocosm; this is called the ninth dharma difficult to attain in the bodhisattva's practice."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cover all sentient beings with the Dharma-door of the inexhaustible Dharma. The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas—this is called the tenth dharma difficult to attain practiced by Bodhisattvas, whereby they advance toward the site of enlightenment and adorn the Bodhi tree."
The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Scroll One.
The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Scroll Two. Also titled *Pratyutpanna-vipāka*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Dragon King Bathes the Prince (2). Chapter Four: The Dragon King Bathes the Prince.
The Buddha again addressed the sons of noble family:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva ascended the golden throne; his complexion was serene and his countenance was composed."

The devas above scattered flowers and burned incense, performing celestial music to entertain the Bodhisattva; the people below stood in attendance on his left and right, their voices rising in unison to shake heaven and earth, while eighty billion gandharvas struck bells and chimes and sang to delight the Bodhisattva.

At that time, eighty-four billion dragon kings—including the Dragon King Manasvin, the Dragon King Vāsuki, the Dragon King Elāpattra, and the Dragon King Anavatapta—all came together in a great assembly like clouds.
Then the dragon kings praised him with this verse:
"Today, free from worldly defilement, you have descended to be born in Jambudvīpa;
Following worldly custom, you dwell within your mother’s womb; We pray that you bathe and remove the dust of the world."
In the past, throughout incalculable kalpas, you accumulated merit and performed manifold deeds;
now that your vows have borne fruit, we pray that you will permit us to bathe your holy body.
Eighty-four billion nayutas of dragons have come from the ten directions.
Each desiring to make offerings to the Honored One, we present vases and offer fragrant water.
Throughout countless kalpas, you, O Honored One, have practiced austerities for the sake of sentient beings;
your sublime virtue is boundless—may you look upon us with compassion and deign to hear us.
For a long time I have yearned for the Hero of the World, weary of the suffering of birth and death;
now I behold the Wise and Noble One, like the sun shining across the void.
You, O Honored One, originally made a great vow, desiring to deliver those not yet delivered.
The Most Victorious One is already liberated; he shall further liberate those not yet liberated.
The Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as those of the future and the present, possess immeasurable merit; the Honored One has now fully perfected it all.
Even if one were to proclaim the teachings of the Honored One among Men from kalpa to kalpa, how could the light of a firefly dare to compete with the sun that is the Buddha?
The void may be fathomed to its limit, and Mount Sumeru may be weighed; yet [the Buddha’s merit] remains beyond measure.
The waters of the sea may be exhausted, But the virtue of the Honored One is boundless.
Compared to the light of the sun and moon, Or the mani-jewel and the bright moon-gem—
Though these illuminate external darkness, They cannot eliminate ignorance.
Today, you who are peerless, with the radiance of a single hair,
universally illuminate the heavens and the world, removing the stains of lust, anger, and delusion.
The six Tathāgatas of the past were all born in Jambudvīpa.
Having received all our offerings, you bathe your venerable form with fragrant waters.
Now we have encountered the Teacher of Gods, who appears but once in billions of kalpas;
now each of us prostrates at your feet, praying only that you will bathe at this time.

“May all the devas and the people of the world, desiring to hear the True Dharma, listen as the profound root of the Dharma is expounded; they should pay homage to the Honored One of the Three Realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed directly toward the east with a serene and joyful countenance, and spoke these verses to the various dragon kings:
"From this day forward, I shall manifest my form and traverse Jambudvīpa,
rescuing those suffering in affliction through the four immeasurable states."
The golden body possesses clear evidence; its manifold marks are like the radiance of the sun.
Those who have not yet awakened should now awaken; before long, you shall attain Buddhahood.
Contemplating births through countless ages, the forms one has assumed have not been of a single kind.
Though there be superior, middling, and inferior, none have ever appeared like this.
How joyful is this firm vow! Holding fast to one’s resolve without impairment, the manifested results of retribution are fundamentally pure like space.
In the world there are three things considered firm: body, life, and wealth;
yet even these are not ultimate, for they cannot be relied upon from beginning to end.
I now renounce these three; the Dharma-body is empty and formless.
Without end and without life, it naturally becomes the root of the Way.
Worldly treasures are full of perils; like illusions, they do not endure long.
Now that I have obtained the wealth of the seven jewels, it is formless and inexhaustible.
The mind, intellect, and consciousness of sentient beings were once shrouded by the three defilements;
now they have attained the threefold clear knowledge, having mastered the beginning, the middle, and the end.
For the sake of all gods and humans in the world, they shall now turn the Dharma of the Deathless.
The Wheel of Dharma covers the great trichiliocosm, its benevolent and compassionate heart universally moistening all.
Bound by the four fetters in taking birth, one does not escape the afflictions of the three periods of time;
now that the four Noble Truths have been attained, there are no fetters and one is no longer defiled.

With wisdom one contemplates the Noble Truth of Suffering; through the awakening of wisdom where there was ignorance, the pure nature becomes like something stainless, and one attains the realization of eternal tranquility.
Former habits give rise to renewed pleasure, and attachment to craving remains inexhaustible.
Those external objects my mind receives, Their entanglements thus grow ever more intense.
I now contemplate their fundamental purity; The perception of pleasure and the perception of suffering are extinguished.
Tranquil, free from sorrow and joy, I am forever parted from birth and death.
In the past there were three modes of conduct, the very source from which delusion and craving arise;
once these are exhausted, one no longer dwells therein, and the mind is free from defilement.
In the present there are sixty-four [factors], which drag one into the gathering of the dark chamber.
Forever relinquishing them, one does not dwell with them, And attains the sixty-four clarities.
The dust of innumerable future eons Obscures the minds of men;
The Dharma-cloud spreads throughout the three realms, Moistening all that has not yet reached it.
The mouth of one who teaches purity is supple, and their voice is like that of a mournful phoenix;
this arises from practicing without deceit and preaching the Dharma without flaw or omission.
Sentient beings harbor the five hindrances and act with frivolity, lacking shame and remorse.
Now, for the first time, I have attained shame and remorse, destroying my arrogant mind.
Since the Buddha appeared in this world, he has subdued all the hosts of the heterodox;
ascending the seat, he roars the lion's roar and expounds the causes and conditions of his past lives.
The Buddhas of the past have bestowed their prophecies, as have those of the future and the present;
in this world of the five turbidities and decline, there shall be a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
Now, observing myself, I find that my aspirations and nature are extraordinary compared to the common.
Since his name is not in vain, his father calls him Siddhārtha;
thus, standing amidst the assembly, he gazes levelly with no fear.
Having attained the wisdom of pure dhāraṇī, he acts to deliver those who are unworthy.
Not perceiving the fundamental nature of all phenomena, Arising and ceasing have no location, nor do they possess success or failure;
In this profound stillness, one should respond with wise observation.
Universally discerning all phenomena, One finds that none have any place of abode or nest.
Serene and without destination, this is the practice that accords with the Vinaya.
Not seeing through the lens of "seeing" or "non-seeing," there is no seeking and nothing to be guarded.
Self and person are stilled in meditative concentration; signlessness and aspiration are likewise so.
Those who wish to drink insatiably of the subtle and wondrous flavor of ambrosia,
Who eliminate signs and remove all attachments— these correspond to the wisdom of a bodhisattva.
Being without a person and without a life-span, They accomplish the treasury of all Buddhas.
Crushing the arrogant mind, one does not give rise to self-importance.
The person of supreme wisdom does not cling to numerical categories, nor does he calculate the notion of permanence.
When sentient beings give rise to defiled minds, he illuminates them so they may realize pure wisdom.
The noble ones comprise various classes, for the faculties of sentient beings differ;
yet when one observes the future with wisdom, there are ultimately no diverse paths.
The Buddha-dharma possesses profound essentials, and its wisdom is boundless.
Only emptiness is free from defilement; this is called the purity of the Dharma-realm.
Having passed through one life, a hundred lives, and even incalculable eons, I now renounce them forever;
turning my back on them, I move forward to realize the realization.

Even if, in the interim, I were to calculate my lifespan as being equal to the number of Ganges sands of Buddhas who have passed away, yet remain attached to the nature of phenomena, I would not tread upon the wisdom of emptiness.
Constantly subduing my own mind, I shall discern the teachings of written words.
Therefore, having awakened by myself, I established the great and vast vow.
In the past, when I first resolved my mind, I aspired to seek the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas for forty-four billion kalpas in a secluded and pure place where no people dwelt.
For seventy kalpas there was no Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha;
later, he encountered Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, who eloquently expounded the traces of the Mahāyāna.
Having first heard of this unprecedented matter, he realized the immeasurable awakening of noble wisdom.
With compassion, you protected the four immeasurables; thus did you gain a slight understanding of the faith.
From that time onward, you established meritorious deeds, making offerings to countless Buddhas for nineteen kalpas.
Later he became a great king, a Wheel-Turning Emperor;
seven treasures preceded and followed him, and his thousand sons were endowed with talent and skill.
He made offerings to pure persons who diligently practiced the holy life.
Ninety-seven billion *ya* (koṭi-nayuta), with minds liberated and free from attachment;
he bestowed gifts upon the poor of the land, the orphaned, the destitute, and those with no place to turn.
From his treasuries he brought forth precious jewels, providing for all so that none lacked anything.
Furthermore, throughout incalculable eons, he personally cultivated pure conduct;
relinquishing his throne to the crown prince, he left the household life and donned the dharma robes.
By nature patient, harmonious, and gentle, he dwelt in seclusion in silent tranquility, free from discursive thought.
Gradually the mind grows weary, like a person drowning in a deep abyss.
The roots of goodness gradually diminish, like fruit that falls when ripe.
One undergoes the suffering of birth and death through repeated cycles, receiving retributions in countless transformations.
If the mind lacks the great vow, it merely seeks to escape physical suffering;
when the karma of the mind is buffeted by the winds of conceptualization, it wavers and fails to reach the ultimate.
Thus remaining within birth and death, one revolves in saṃsāra and cannot escape.
Again, after sixty kalpas had passed, he encountered the Buddha Ratnamālā.
Through skillful means he transformed and delivered beings; there was but the One Vehicle, no second path.
They heard not even the name of the "lesser vehicle"; through the wisdom of emptiness, they exhausted all outflows.
He expounded the single mark of the Way, the profound and purely virtuous practice;
from the moment he first resolved his mind upon it, his heart of great vows was difficult to deter.
From that time until today, seven hundred million asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed.
"Protecting and upholding the True Dharma, I have now finally awakened to it myself.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva, together with all sentient beings—the eight classes of gods, dragons, ghosts, and spirits—as well as the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions endowed with supernatural powers, recited this verse and received its profound and wondrous meaning."

At that very seat, eighty-four koṭis of people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and furthermore, countless sentient beings attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this single verse, recite, chant, read, and uphold it, and explain and analyze its meaning for others, they shall not be taken advantage of by the various māras."

Why is this? It is because these sentient beings have all, through their past deeds, fully perfected their practice; they have previously made offerings to countless Buddhas and, with pure and refined vows, each made this aspiration:

"In my future lives, I must hear the True Dharma from a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood (Ekajātipratibaddha), and immediately upon that Buddha, I shall attain great, clear awakening and realize the dharma that is unborn and without arising or ceasing."
"How so? Son of good family!
Suppose there were a person who spoke these words:"
"I have now realized that the formless Dharma is taught through forms, and the characteristic of emptiness is taught through substantiality.
Could this person not achieve such an intention by establishing it?
At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Abhayamahanātha. Beyond this trichiliocosm, there was a buddha-field named Bhadraśūra, and the Buddha there was named Samantabhadra.

The Bodhisattva Abhayamahāparipālaka, having come from that land, attained the dhāraṇīs and established himself in non-retrogression; he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To teach the formless Dharma through forms, and to teach the signless void through signs—this is exceedingly difficult, indeed most difficult;
it can never be fully attained. Why is this so?
"Space is formless and cannot be defiled; how much less could it be made to possess physical substance?
This matter is not so.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Fearless Great Protector:
“Son of good family!
This may still be obtained; however, to hear this Dharma from a Bodhisattva who is in his final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) is ultimately impossible. Why is this?
All phenomena are numberless; how could one find a numbered phenomenon within that which is numberless?
Can there be a phenomenon with conditions and counterparts within a phenomenon without conditions and counterparts?
Does the nature of empty space possess form or substance?
This matter is not so.

It is simply because the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, widely disseminates his great compassion to transform sentient beings and establish them in firmness; he expounds the Way and its teachings and distinguishes all dharmas, yet remains without words and without speech.

In the world, many are deluded and give rise to minds of right and wrong, thinking: "This is a dharma with outflows; this is a dharma without outflows. This is a dharma of causal opposition; this is not a dharma of causal opposition. This is to be guarded and maintained; this is not to be guarded and maintained. This dharma has a self; this dharma is selfless. This is a worldly dharma; this is a dharma of Nirvana. This dharma is defiled and attached; this is not defiled and attached. This dharma is finite; this dharma is infinite. This dharma is subject to annihilation; this is not subject to annihilation. This dharma is turbid; this is not turbid."
Furthermore, they admonished one another, each saying these words:

"Practice this, abandon that; study this, set aside that. These are dharmas of training, these are dharmas not of training; these are the dharmas of śrāvakas, these are the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas; these are not the dharmas of śrāvakas, these are not the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas; these are the dharmas of bodhisattvas, these are not the dharmas of bodhisattvas."
"One does not achieve supreme perfect enlightenment by means of this contemplation.

Why is this? Contemplation that clings to marks is not the foremost contemplation of emptiness; rather, it is when there is no seeking, no marks, and no cognition or vision that one achieves the contemplation of emptiness."

"Now, to observe that all phenomena are without self and without life-span, not perceiving lands or discriminating realms, being without support and without that which is supported—this is the contemplation of dharmas, which is empty and non-existent."
One who contemplates in this manner perceives that all phenomena are quiescent, the fruits of the Path are quiescent, and the realization itself is quiescent.

If a bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness is thus, they will be free from inversion regarding all expectations; they will bring benefit and aid to sentient beings by giving rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), establishing the Buddha-dharma, and although they deliver sentient beings, they maintain no conception of "sentient beings."
How could a Bodhisattva who contemplates emptiness perceive one who is delivered? This is not so.
If there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who attains this contemplation of emptiness, they will then obtain the fulfillment of the ten dharmas of non-self.
What are these ten? In this regard, Abhaya!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva—whether a son of noble family or a daughter of noble family—does not perceive purity or impurity within the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, nor gives rise to thoughts of "this" or "that," such as "this is the dharma-body" or "this is the body of desire"; and if they know the past before and examine the future after, perceiving all these as pure and free from the notion of self—this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness and non-self.
"Furthermore, Abhaya!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with his dharma robes properly arranged and his alms bowl held, observes the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the future, past, and present, entering cities to teach and transform beings—seeing neither the noble and wealthy nor the lowly—and therein gives rise to neither the view of self nor the view of other, this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness and non-self."
"Furthermore, Abhaya!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives from afar the countless Buddha-fields and adorned pure lands as level, even, and upright. He does not speak of the defilement and evil of the present Buddha-field; he maintains a pure resolve free from manifold conceptions, remaining one-pointed in every thought-moment with consciousness that does not wander. This is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness and non-self."
"Furthermore, Abhaya!

When sentient beings are defiled by attachment and rely upon the body to understand emptiness, the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s wisdom of emptiness has no reliance across the three periods of time; this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness and non-self."
"Furthermore, Abhaya!

For a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, although the various teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, differ, their fundamental purity is neither different nor distinct. This is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness and non-self."
The Buddha told Abhaya:

“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, whether a son or daughter of noble family, practices the infinite dharma-treasury of the perfections (pāramitās) and adorns themselves with the flower-garlands of various jewels, such that they do not perceive even this infinity as being exhausted—yet within this they achieve the realization of both the exhausted and the inexhaustible—this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness and non-self.”
"Furthermore, Abhaya!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate that the physical forms of all Buddhas are immeasurable; they enter the quiescent dharma of the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), discerning its meaning and intent to understand that form is fundamentally non-existent. They universally enter the dharma-realm to transform and guide sentient beings, yet do not perceive any physical form as being that which transforms sentient beings. This is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness and non-self."

"Furthermore, Abhaya! When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains the profound treasury of the Buddha’s noble wisdom, possesses the four kinds of fearlessness, and leaves behind the eight fetters to attain the eight liberations; when he rains down the Dharma to provide nourishment, being free from old age and death; when he utters the lion’s roar with a will as adamantine as a vajra; and when he is detached from 'this,' 'that,' and 'the middle,' remaining unstained by attachment—this is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness and non-self."

"Furthermore, Abhaya! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva shall gradually draw near to and cultivate the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Observing countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he beholds various Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in such-and-such lands. Although these Buddhas manifest *nirvāṇa*, they do not enter final extinction; they purify the traces of sentient beings without harboring indolence, and they do not weary of sentient beings because of the number of kalpas. Nor do they seek to enter extinction out of a desire for the bliss of *nirvāṇa*. Their minds are like space, incapable of being defiled. This is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness and non-self."

"Furthermore, Abhaya! A bodhisattva mahāsattva rescues sentient beings with boundless wisdom. Even if they are extremely far away, beyond the sands of the Ganges—where every single grain of sand is itself as vast as the sands of the Ganges—and even if one were to calculate this process again and again until it has filled the eight directions, above and below, and traversed the immeasurable realms of empty space, the bodhisattva must rescue sentient beings so that they do not fall; yet he does not praise his own attainment of the fruits of supernatural powers and wisdom. This is called the tenth dharma of non-self for a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"One who has exhausted the stage of gestation as a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood should indeed practice in this manner.
At that time, among those seated there, nineteen *koṭis* of devas belonging to the realm of form and desire immediately attained the patience of the summit (*mūrdha-kṣānti*);
furthermore, countless other devas and worldlings attained the practice of the contemplation of emptiness and the conduct of ultimate faith.
The yakṣas, nāgas, and ghosts, having faith in the Three Honored Ones, received the three refuges.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"At that time, while the Bodhisattva was upon the golden table, the king, householders, devas, nāgas, spirits, and bodhisattvas from the ten directions each gave rise to reverence and desired to bathe the Bodhisattva."

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Candrarasmi, who was the foremost among the assembly of bodhisattvas. Maintaining his majestic deportment and dharma robes with composure, he rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and praised him in verse:
“O Honored One, your body is now unimpeded, Untainted by the dust of the three realms.
You have bathed it in the waters of the eight liberations; How could the waters of the world ever suffice?”
When the defilements of the mind are exhausted, it becomes clear and bright;
Without obstruction within or without, the sources of oceans, rivers, and springs— A bath such as this does not bring purity for long.
Formerly, when I was in the Lapis Lazuli Pond, And dwelling at that time in the Dragon Palace of Chan-tou,
With single-minded resolve, you set out upon the Mahāyāna, vowing to extinguish the demons of craving and desire;
now that you have fulfilled your original vow, peerless throughout the three realms,
I pray that you ascend the seat of fearlessness.
Why manifest this bathing?
For sixty-two *nayuta* kalpas, throughout the eons of those born in heaven, the five kinds of celestial music shall arrive; the resonance of merit is the natural retribution.
The Dharma-body is endowed with all wisdoms; expounding the unimpeded path, he has completed his cycle and taken birth here in the city of Kapilavastu.
Though there are three calamities in this world, he shall extinguish them through the retribution of the three supernormal knowledges.
The three wisdoms penetrate the three types of supernormal knowledge; The three essentials are now fully possessed.

With the three equalities, you contemplate the three periods of time; Unstained by the existence of the three realms, And endowed with the three parts of the Dharma-body— I prostrate before the Honored One of the Three Realms.
The sentient beings gathered from all quarters, The devas, asuras, and ghosts,
All harbored a sense of exultation; Reverently receiving him, they raised offerings,
Guarding him with purity and wonder before and behind, As he proceeded to the Lapis Lazuli Garden.
Reaching up with his right hand to grasp a lotus branch, he descended in spirit to be born in Jambudvīpa.
At the moment of birth, as he fell to the ground, he was as pure as purple-polished gold;
the heavens and earth shook in six ways, and moved by his divine power, the devas arrived.
The various tortures and lashings in the hells all ceased at once;
pure and free from defilement, like a lotus flower untouched by water.
In the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, the Tathāgatas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, [were likewise present].
In each of their respective lands, they proclaimed to the fourfold assembly:
"Today, in this Sahā world, the Hero of the World has appeared;
out of compassion for all sentient beings, he who have long remained in the three miserable realms."
When he turned the Wheel of the True Dharma in the clear and pure Deer Park,
he moistened those long parched with the nectar of the Dharma.
The Honored One alone awakened to the Eightfold Path and thoroughly exhausted the twelve links of dependent origination.
The inexhaustible treasures of the rivers and seas satisfy all people.
Even if every Buddha were to praise their virtue from kalpa to kalpa, they could not fully proclaim it; how much less so my own glow-worm light?
In the past, while in the realm of Abhayā and within the Buddha-field of Animiṣa,
I first contemplated the ineffable Dharma; yet, as I had not yet attained the wisdom of non-arising,
I vowed to be born amidst the teachings of speech to expound the inexhaustible Dharma.
"Today the appointed time has arrived; I pray that you will turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva’s mind was serene and tranquil; he gazed silently and intently without speaking, reflecting within himself:
"If I were to preach the Dharma for people today, expounding upon the pure stage of non-retrogression, I would not harbor a sense of selfhood."

It is the same with all dharmas arising spontaneously: one preaches the Dharma according to the roots and capacities of individuals. The nature of dharmas is inherently such that it undergoes no change; how much more so for sentient beings who receive the Dharma?

Sentient beings are fundamentally pure and do not see defilement; they establish wisdom and give rise to the heart of great vows, investigating that all sentient beings are entirely pure—fundamentally pure by nature, selfless by nature, formless by nature, and the nature of both persons and things.
What is meant by "primordial purity and spontaneity"?

Since time immemorial, while transmigrating through birth and death, from the initial resolve to seek the Way up until Nirvana, one is fundamentally pure from the very beginning; this is what is called primordial purity and spontaneity.
What is meant by "selflessness and spontaneity"?

That which existed originally is now non-existent; that which exists now did not exist originally. One does not say, "I am," nor that "I was born from existence," nor again that "existence is born from me. I do not know myself as being without self, and existence does not know itself as being existent. This is what is called "selflessness and spontaneity."
What is meant by "formless spontaneity"?
That which is formless consists of consciousness (*vijñāna*), spirit (*śen*), and life-force (*shòu*).

The meaning of these three phrases exists eternally and undergoes no change: when in emptiness it is emptiness; when in form it is form; when in existence it is existence; when in marks it is marks; and when in the markless it is the markless. This formless consciousness is the spontaneous nature of emptiness; this is what is called "formless spontaneity."
What is meant by the spontaneity of persons and things?

Upon investigating persons and things, one finds no nest or lair; consciousness is a magical illusion that fails to reach its source. Ignorance and delusion are passed down through generations as people speak of father and mother; they gradually give rise to manifold thoughts regarding national wealth, wives, and children, becoming stained and attached to the three realms of existence.

I have now relinquished [all attachments] and shall never again dwell therein. By means of this spontaneous and penetrating wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*), and because the wisdom of emptiness is spontaneous, all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise so.

Since all phenomena are spontaneous, even the one who attains perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is likewise spontaneous. All phenomena are merely provisional names; that there are names due to designations is also spontaneous. To discourse upon spontaneity is itself discourse; it is a phenomenon without arising or ceasing. This is what is called the spontaneity of persons and things.

If I were now to preach the Dharma of emptiness and stillness, sentient beings would not believe it and their webs of doubt would double; even if I were to further preach the Dharma of form and substance, I could not exhaust its root and source, let alone speak of its cessation and nirvana.

"It is fitting that we remain tranquil and that the noble ones maintain their silence. At that time, there was a son of heaven named Ratnāvalī (寶瓔), who had attained mastery of the noble mind and shared the same nature and conduct as the Buddha. His six supernormal powers were pure and penetrating; he understood the single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and was forever free from the eight worldly dharmas, dwelling not amidst the dust of worldly toil. He was capable of turning the wheel of Dharma and proclaiming the Buddha’s teachings. Through the noble wisdom of the Four Truths, his defilements were suddenly removed; he was fully endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body of the Tathāgata and had attained the fruits of the six unimpeded spiritual powers (*abhijñā*). His physical form and spirit traveled together without obstruction or hindrance. Adorned by the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), he was complete in the eightfold path and possessed qualities unique among all dharmas. Having attained the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), his power was like a diamond (*vajra*), indestructible and unshakable. Because he knew that the Bodhisattvas and noble ones were maintaining their silence, he did not expound the teachings of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Then, the devaputra Ratnakaṇṭha rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I do not now view the classes of sentient beings with the Buddha-eye, the Dharma-eye, the wisdom-eye, or the divine eye; rather, I should view them according to the laws and regulations of the noble ones.”

Now, with my physical eye, I behold the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions; I see those who are ready for realization, those practicing meditative concentration, and those ranging from the first to the tenth stage. Furthermore, I see good sons on the verge of attaining Buddhahood, having reached the stage of non-retrogression and being born only once more before succession to the position of a Buddha, proceeding to the site of enlightenment to adorn the Bodhi tree.

Those of such a kind should hear the Dharma of equality—that all phenomena are non-dual—from a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood; thus, their aspirations for the Path will all be fully accomplished.
At that time, the Devaputra Ratnakaṇṭha earnestly entreated him three or four times, and further praised him with this verse:
“Your golden countenance is peerless and honored; Your facial features resemble a hundred-petaled flower.
When you descended to earth, you proclaimed your own name; Your voice surpasses the sound of Brahmā.”
He establishes a deep pool of wisdom, preaching the Dharma beyond existence and non-existence.
Sentient beings harbor notions of permanence; he remains serene, giving rise to no duality.
His radiant light shines throughout the ten directions, so that all in the darkness behold clarity.
The Honored One among Men is rare to encounter; for this reason, I now take refuge in him again.
Having practiced austerities for countless eons, his compassion is peerless;
his merits are fully perfected—now I take refuge in him once more.
Even if one were to praise his venerable feet—his calves, heels, knees, thighs, and waist;
how his skin and hair are even across the seven parts; how he stands upright with his limbs balanced on both sides;
how his arms and fingers are slender and delicate; and how the lines on his palms are joined by a web-like membrane.
With fearless and broad long tongue, marked with the pattern of a thousand-petaled lotus;
possessing forty square teeth, their color like white snow or jade;
when he preaches the Dharma, his lips shine like pearls and fire.
The eightfold voice is neither male nor female, Nor is it the sound of a bird or a beast;
It moves the ten directions, And those who hear it never tire.
Upon her ears are twin pendants, Like bright moon-pearls in the sky.
The eyes gaze upon the division between white and black, blinking both upward and downward;
the hair is deep blue-black in color, and the *uṣṇīṣa* curls to the right.
His marks and signs are boundless, appearing like a mountain of gold when gazed upon intently.
With bodies adorned by a garland of manifold virtues, Like a profusion of blossoming flowers, They extinguish all dust and defilement;
The Honored One walks alone throughout the three realms.
Beings such as these, from every direction in the ten quarters, Have gathered here together.
We wish to hear the Honored One’s True Dharma, the essential core of the unsurpassed supreme path.
Gods, humans, nāgas, and spirits all thirst and long to hear the Dharma;
out of compassion for all beings, we pray that you will swiftly turn the Wheel of Dharma.

At that time, among the Great Brahma Kings of the worlds of the ten directions, the eighty-four billion Śikhin Kings were foremost. They rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with palms joined before the Buddha, and praised him in verse, reciting this hymn:
"Unattached, you have cast off all defilements; With outflows extinguished, you are untainted by desire.
Practicing the one path, you respond to the Honored One’s teaching; Your mind roams in emptiness and wisdom."
Originally in the Tuṣita Heaven, you preached the Dharma like a rushing torrent;
why now are you so silent, failing to open the flower of wisdom’s light?
Your honored radiance illuminates the darkness, cleansing away the gloom of the three periods of time.
The One Possessing the Ten Powers is untainted; we only pray that you will expound the Dharma at this time.
Today, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, all the venerable Bodhisattvas have assembled, desiring to hear entirely the Dharma never before turned.
With a pure mind and untainted conduct, like the moon among the stars, you have transcended both the signless and the wishless;
we pray that you will preach the Dharma at this time.
Beings are now drowning, wandering through the ocean of birth and death.
I vow to use this boat of equanimity to rescue those drowning and submerged.
His wondrous light is most majestic, eclipsing the brilliance of the sun and moon;
it suppresses the affliction of feverish distress, being pure and free from all blemishes.
The Honored One originally formed his vow, Courageous and without deficiency;
With a mind of equal compassion, He preached the Dharma without addition or subtraction.
Perfecting the precepts through meditative stillness, His supernormal powers are fearless.
The dharma of fearlessness characterized by emptiness, Wandering through the realms in right meditative absorption;
Practicing the dharma of the six perfections from the beginning, Without harboring a mind of sorrow or grief;
With humble intent, one pays respectful homage, Serving and honoring teachers and elders.
Therefore, none dare look directly upon the Honored One’s uṣṇīṣa;
how much less could they wish to offer their hearts, beholding the Tathāgata’s crown?
Out of compassion, the One of Ten Powers has appeared in the world, descending his steps to deliver all sentient beings.
"The multitude all look up with longing; Please deign to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma King Śikhin had praised him with this verse, he rose, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and returned to his original seat.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and three times proclaimed his own name:
"I am Śakra, the Lord of Devas, named Kauśika."
Standing before the Bodhisattva, he praised him with these verses:
"Silence accords with tranquility; Non-instruction accords with self-perfection;
Non-practice accords with the boundless; Spontaneity accords with the unconditioned."
Having practiced the signless giving in the past, you now obtain the fruit of emptiness;
you should pay homage to the deity of space, who is tranquil and without trace of speech.
Awakened first while in the world, you bring peace and security to those in peril and distress.
Guiding us along the path of right view, may those in blindness receive the practice of rectitude.
Sentient beings have been deluded for a long time; desiring to hear the Dharma of ambrosia, I pray you open the inexhaustible treasury, so that its moisture may reach both gods and humans.
Practicing loving-kindness and cultivating the roots of virtue, With skillful means that neither increase nor decrease,
He proclaims and spreads the teaching of non-action, Satisfying all people.
The birth of a World-Honored One is difficult to encounter, And the True Dharma is likewise difficult to meet.
To encounter an assembly of worthy sages is likewise impossible to obtain.
The Tathāgatas of the past attained perfect enlightenment here;
pray, O Honored One, deign to come at this time—why do you crave the glories of this world?
The Honored One originally delighted in seclusion and purity, contemplating the Way of non-action;
having already fulfilled his original vows, why do you remain amidst such clamor?
The five cauldrons of Jambudvīpa boil more violently than a raging fire of boiling water.
I only pray that you will quickly leave the household life, To be freed from the bonds of worldly desire.
Reflecting on my past lives, when the various Buddhas attained equal enlightenment, They immediately went beneath the King of Trees; Sitting in the morning, they achieved the Way by evening.
If you now have doubts and still desire the pleasures of birth and death—wherein affection is like a decaying city—how can such pleasure be worth coveting?
In this world there is the affliction of birth and death; only the Way is eternally tranquil.
Affectionate love is like a flash of lightning; Illusory transformations are not real.
The world is entirely shrouded in darkness, Covered by the five obscurations.
I only pray that you will open the light of wisdom, Shining universally so that all may obtain the eye.
You manifest countless transformations, responding appropriately to sentient beings before you;
according to their original practices and vows, you cause each to fulfill their meditative and ascetic efforts.
Why do you now remain in stillness, rather than turning the supreme Wheel of Dharma?
I only pray that you will expound [the Dharma] in due time, so that those who thirst may be fully satisfied.
Recalling the merit I previously cultivated, it was indeed but slight;
yet by its power, I have attained the rank of Heavenly King, with dominion over boundless realms.
I have made offerings to all the Tathāgatas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, of the past—
four Buddhas and one who was in his final birth— as well as to those venerable ones who were not yet to come.
For countless billions of nayutas of eons, they had been submerged and obscured within the cycle of birth and death for a long time.
I pray you take up the chariot of the great vow, To ferry us across to the further shore.
Now I entreat you only to preach The nectar-like Dharma that never tires;
The eight liberations free from attachment, Untainted and unstained by the dust of the world.
Venerable One, you have now entered meditative absorption and do not deliver those who should be delivered in this realm;
I pray that you first transform those of this kind whose minds are fixed and unshakable.
The nature of space is unstained, equal, serene, and one.
There is no destination to be seen; may you have no doubts.
This profound, wondrous, and boundless treasury is not something those of inferior capacity can guard or hold.
Now that we have encountered the Teacher of Gods and Men, we pray that you will open it and manifest its contents.
"Your Reverence originally made the vow to deliver others; how could you fail to act on that same day?
Why do you now remain silent? Having saved yourself, why do you not save the rest?
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra, having praised the Buddha with these verses, circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to his original seat.
At that time, the Māra named Krodhahantṛ rose from his seat together with his host of māras, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May it please the World-Honored One!..."

For a long time we have harbored doubts and failed to attain the True Way; now we wish to hear the exposition of the peerless Wheel of Dharma. We pray only that you will deign to show us compassion by unfolding the sublime teaching. For a long time we have dwelt outside the Law and Discipline; though each of us has had hearts that yearn for and aspire to the wisdom of emptiness, we have yet encountered the great transformation and the instructions of the scriptures.
At that time, Māra spoke before the Buddha in verse:
"Only once in hundreds of thousands of millions of eons does one free from attachment appear;
like a lotus flower detached from dust and water, your mind is pure and transcends even that."
The number of kalpas is without end; having undergone accumulated ascetic practices, he does not abandon the four great vows, which are as indestructible as adamant.
His mouth proclaims the eight kinds of unimpeded eloquence, filling the heavens and the world.
Those who receive [this teaching] shall be forever satisfied, free from the afflictions of old age and death;
from one birth to a hundred births, they shall fully know the origins of all names,
clans, and faculties, transforming others through incomparable wisdom.
The ten stages return to the original limit; though they may regress, they advance once more.
The Most Victorious One transcends these difficulties; at this time, expound [the Dharma] without doubt.
Having departed from Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they have all roamed within this grove.
Turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, you deliver beings beyond measure.
Even in future ages, when all Buddhas attain the fruit of the Way,
they shall all, at this very spot, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
I have heard of the Tathāgatagarbha, the secret and essential wisdom of the Tathāgata, titled the *Puyanyantu* (Universally Adorned Land) Bodhisattva-Necklace Sūtra.
Today is precisely the right time; it is difficult to encounter and impossible to find.
Delivering them from all suffering and calamity, he spreads forth the wisdom of the Path from this point.
There may be beings who, weary of the suffering inherent in bodily existence,
desire to hear the subtle and wondrous Dharma so as to eliminate the phenomena of the four great elements.

desiring to hear the way of emptiness and non-existence, they fully understand that nothing exists.
Again, there are those who dwell in mountain caves, guarding themselves with no other thoughts.
Considering that this body is but a transient vessel, do not give rise to conceptual attachments or discursive thoughts.
Although you may contemplate the roots of the Path, if you have not yet heard [the Dharma], you shall not attain awakening.
I only pray that the Honored One will descend with his spirit, so as to cause them to be free from doubt and obstruction.
His eyes are like blue lotuses; his vision penetrates all without obstruction.
He observes the suffering of the three periods of time and those defiled by the dust of afflictions.
Regarding what the Honored One has undergone in the past, he made offerings to all the World-Honored Ones.
Humblest among the humble, he has now attained the formless knot.
Not clinging to marks within marks, nor relying on manifold beautiful colors,
for this reason, none of the many sages and saints can see the crown of his head.
From between his brows shines a pure light, universally illuminating countless lands;
those who behold this light have their feverish afflictions removed, as if encountering deep shade in the summer heat.
With a single lion’s roar, the Honored One subdues all heterodox paths.
He shatters the forest of false views, Just as light eternally dispels darkness.
His words are never false; His aspirations will surely be fulfilled.
He teaches the Dharma, the true reality, The ultimate path and the source of the Way.
In the past, one hundred million Honored Ones resided here for twelve intermediate kalpas;
passing from one to another in succession, they maintained the lineage of the Wheel-Turner without interruption.
Following their teachers to seek supreme brilliance, they gathered various forms of wisdom.
The adorned body is infinite, formless and beyond naming.
Establishing faith where there was none, with faculties and powers undiminished,
fearless and free from the duality of self and other— only pray, expound this at this time.
The Honored One of the Three Realms is infinite; as the Righteous Dharma, he governs all.
Having destroyed unrighteousness to achieve the Way, he has forever eliminated the notion of self.
All people are greedily attached to the body, indulging in it and unable to let go.
Enmeshed by the sufferings of the world, by what means could there be an end?
When the light of wisdom illuminates the world and uproots the heart of craving and attachment—
delivering oneself and rescuing others— such a one is exceedingly rare among men.
Bestowing gifts without a sense of self, having already transcended the three realms,
with a single thought at one time, they are equal and without distinction of male or female.
Sentient beings harbor inverted views and fail to realize the wisdom of emptiness.
With minds set upon the five desires, they reckon the body to be substantially real.
Because of this, they fall into the five realms of existence and do not perceive the realization of impermanence.
Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, he extinguishes those notions of existence and non-existence.
Entering meditative absorption, he is unattached to craving; forever casting off worldly glory and adornment, he contemplates this impermanent form as being neither existent nor non-existent.
With great compassion, he rescues sentient beings, vast and without bound.
Your long-cherished vow has now borne fruit; arise quickly and take your seat.
Behold this person burning with passion, wandering in saṃsāra without self-awareness.
Why do you, O Venerable One, remain in silent stillness, neither speaking nor saying anything?
There are five difficulties within the defilements of the world: not seeing the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
possessing physical faith; being born in a central land; having parents as the fifth factor;
and [possessing] the radiance of form and the formless, yet not perceiving their physical shapes or images.
As he was about to enter the meditative absorption of cessation, all became silent and free of sound.
The great assembly gathered from afar— the Kālayas, Gandharvas, and Kumbhāṇḍas—
listening without weariness to the Honored One’s discourse on the unconditioned, delivered with his broad and long tongue.
There is a Dharma inconceivable, wherein transformation occurs without the transformed being aware of it;
yet, in order to make known its beginning and end, this too is unprecedented.
That a bodhisattva does not regress, even though they have not yet attained that Dharma—this is likewise marvelous.
How much more so for those who turn toward the Gate of the Way—how could they wish to know its fundamental essentials?
Honored One, you now observe the fourfold assembly, whose inclinations and pursuits are of many kinds;
we pray that you will expound the Dharma for them, so that each may receive deliverance.

Sentient beings are defiled by the three realms of existence; desiring to seek liberation from their bonds, they contemplate permanence as impermanence, all of which he illuminates and leads toward extinction.
Though there be billions of devils and spirits who come from the ten directions, [he remains unshaken].
Having attained faith and the patience of non-arising, they practice on the stages without regression.
Furthermore, there are billions of beings whose inclinations follow ours;
these sons of noble family will surely reach the stage of firm stability.
Furthermore, there are countless people who walk upon the earth without attachment;
all seek emptiness and signlessness, advancing toward the site of enlightenment.
The Arhats, feeling self-disdain, enter among the common folk according to their kind.
The suffering described is not slight; ultimately, there is no one with all-encompassing wisdom.
This too is the seal of the Bodhisattva, sealing the fruit of the attainment of the Way.
Having received and practiced the Mahāyāna, it is fundamentally non-existent and without variety.
When the Honored One first resolved his mind on enlightenment, he cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness;
in his practice of the stages, there was no high or low, for the Way follows through wisdom alone.
Even throughout countless kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [he remained thus].
Through ascetic practice and without wrong thoughts, all his vows have now borne fruit. As for those of the future,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who likewise desire to attain Buddhahood—
if they do not abandon these vows of self and others, they will surely reach awakening just as he has now.
The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, Sacrificed his life not for himself;
His giving was equal, without high or low, Thus he perfected the wisdom of the six perfections.
Past, future, and present— Birth and extinction are fundamentally without end.
Those who are born are born of themselves; no one knows their original root.
When the ten practices leave the human body, the five practices become the Dharma King.
Through contemplation, one extinguishes the original root and compassionately expounds the Great Dharma.
Furthermore, at other times, whether walking, sitting, or lying down, he remains mindful;
this arises from his attainment of dhāraṇī and his boundless four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Out of compassion for all beings, the Bodhisattva does not harbor notions of permanence.
Reflecting that the world is impermanent, he has attained eternal peace and security.
With his supernormal powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eightfold path of awakening,
and the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata— the World-Honored One is now fully endowed with them all.
"Sentient beings give rise to thoughts of their own accord, That there is nothing to be gained and nothing that can be attained;
Consequently, they fall into a deep abyss And do not turn toward the gate of liberation.
At that time, the Māra King Krodhahantṛ, having spoken this verse, circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to his original position.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, leading their celestial hosts, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and stood to one side.
After a short while, they stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We possess great merit from past deeds, O World-Honored One, to have encountered your holy countenance as you descended your spirit into Jambudvīpa to expound the Wheel of Dharma and reign over the three thousandfold world system."
Furthermore, they scattered flowers—
*kuṇḍalaka* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, and *sugandhika* flowers— over the Tathāgata. At that time,
the devas again praised him with these verses:
"The Hero of the World has now descended, ruling this Jambudvīpa;
though born in these eight states of non-leisure, the dwelling places of sentient beings,
he is forever free from defiled attachment and does not give rise to discursive thoughts within."
Breathless, tranquil, and extinguished, I pray you fully expound the Dharma.
Your venerable virtue is inconceivable, your meritorious achievements beyond reckoning;
your body is adorned with the various marks, like the moon shining among the stars.
Having exhausted all conditioned activities and not creating further roots, he sits upright in the site of enlightenment;
being himself devoid of mind and consciousness, how could he be stained by worldly attachments?
Having transcended the roots of all practices, his virtue fills all sentient beings.
His resonance surpasses that of Brahmā; I take refuge in the God among Gods.
His original creation arose from the four Māras; though Māra seeks to separate him from birth and death, he remains untainted by the eight worldly concerns. I take refuge in the Peerless One.
The Honored One now proceeds toward the single Dharma: Nirvāṇa, which is neither arising nor ceasing;
with the cessation of the mind, the mind does not arise, and one perceives no realization of karmic fruit.
The Honored One originally cultivated two practices: tranquility and the non-arising of insight.
Practicing until the end, yet seeing no end— The Hero of the World is foremost and supreme.
The Tathāgata’s three fundamental dharmas— Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
Advance toward the path of Nirvāṇa, Free from gain and free from defilement.
Their vows are exceedingly firm; they accumulate practices without transgression.
They do not dwell on non-attachment, nor do they abide within the three realms of existence.
Possessing the four bases of spiritual power, they sustain their lifespan according to conditions.
His conduct transcends all limits; his benevolence and kindness are supreme.
Having been born amidst the five turbidities, he gathers others without regard for right or wrong.
The True Person’s conduct is untainted; employing skillful means, he enters among sentient beings.
Equally practicing the five faculties—faith, wisdom, and the power of diligence—one is unstained by and abandons inverted views; such purity is supreme.
Your venerable virtues surpass those of gods and men; you are forever unattached to the eight worldly concerns.
With a concentrated mind, unconfused, he thus pays homage to the Most Victorious One.
When the Honored One descends to take birth, he causes the three thousand worlds to tremble;
awakening sentient beings who have long slept, they leave behind the afflictions of these three realms of existence.
At that time, after the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven had praised the Buddha with these verses, they circumambulated him three times and returned to their original seats.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected within himself:

"Now this assembly is gathered in its entirety; from the worlds of the ten directions, those possessing the six supernormal powers and noble wisdom, those in their last birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), and those fully endowed with the four immeasurable states have all assembled like clouds, desiring to hear the Dharma and attain the stage of non-retrogression."
"Now I should instead grasp the fearless Dharma and adorn my body with the roots of virtue from all practices, following the methods practiced by all Buddhas of the past.
Thereupon, while seated, he entered the Samādhi of Innate Non-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and with a discerning and concentrated mind, he contemplated the conduct of the Buddha.

The Bodhisattva’s jeweled necklace consists of eighty thousand categories; its virtues are so extraordinary that they can be compared to nothing else. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains this Dharma-gate of the Necklace, they are able to advance with single-minded resolve toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
“Sentient beings who have not yet entered the path of the Dharma can be enabled by me to reach the other shore.
