At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue, its radiance universally illuminating the trichiliocosm, and addressed the fourfold assembly—
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
I shall expound for you the Bodhisattva’s Adornment of Formlessness."
"If good sons or good daughters obtain this necklace to adorn their bodies, they will be able to advance toward enlightenment without any hindrance.
**Chapter Five: The Dharma Gates** At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the sons and daughters of noble family:
"I shall now proclaim the eighty thousand dharma gates of the Bodhisattva Necklace."
What are the eighty thousand?

In this regard, noble son, there is a necklace called "Exhaustive Faith. When a Tathāgata attains this dharma-gate, it causes those sentient beings in the hells who are undergoing suffering and affliction to be free from all such calamities.

Furthermore, there is the *Samatā-maitrī-avalokita* (Equal Compassion) necklace; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it causes those who have taken the form of animals to never again suffer harm.

Furthermore, there is the *Asaṃpramoṣa* (Non-forgetfulness) necklace; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it causes the class of hungry ghosts to never again harbor thoughts of hunger or thirst.
Furthermore, there is the Necklace of Purity; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it causes deluded sentient beings to know the path.

Furthermore, there is the Necklace of Penetrating Hearing; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it enables sentient beings who have not heard the Dharma to hear the true teaching in its entirety.
Furthermore, there is the *svaprabodha-mālā* (Garland of Self-Awakening); when a bodhisattva attains this garland, it causes the minds of ignorant sentient beings not to become deviant or distracted.

Furthermore, there is the *cittasaṃyama-mālā* (Garland of Restraint of the Mind); when a bodhisattva attains this garland, they instruct and exhort sentient beings to practice the ten virtuous actions (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).
Furthermore, there is the necklace of upright faith; the bodhisattva who attains this necklace causes sentient beings with false views to dwell securely in right view.
Furthermore, there is the necklace of great vows; the bodhisattva who attains this necklace does not regard the duration of kalpas as distant.
“Furthermore, there is the Necklace of Transcendence; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it causes indolent sentient beings to uphold the true discipline.
Furthermore, there is the Necklace of Non-Anger; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it causes sentient beings who harbor anger and malice to practice patience.”
Furthermore, there is the Necklace of Valor; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it causes sentient beings who are arrogant and indolent to practice diligence without ceasing.

Furthermore, there is the Necklace of Single-mindedness; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it causes sentient beings with distracted minds to maintain meditative concentration without decline.
Furthermore, there is the blazing necklace; the bodhisattva who obtains this necklace causes sentient beings who are ignorant and deluded to achieve wisdom.
Furthermore, there is the firm necklace; the bodhisattva who obtains this necklace causes those who have not yet entered the tracks of the Path to establish themselves therein.
Furthermore, there is the necklace of extensive learning; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it causes sentient beings of little wisdom to possess strong memory and never forget.
Furthermore, there is the necklace of dignified deportment; when a bodhisattva attains this necklace, it causes shameless sentient beings to come to know shame and remorse.
Furthermore, there is the Necklace of Impurities; when a Bodhisattva obtains this necklace, it causes sentient beings attached to desire to realize its impurity.
Furthermore, there is the Necklace of Joy; when a Bodhisattva obtains this necklace, it causes sentient beings who harbor anger to sever it forever, leaving nothing behind.
Furthermore, there is the Universal Radiance Necklace; any bodhisattva who attains this necklace will fully reach the clarity of wisdom and forever eliminate all darkness.
Furthermore, there is the All-Pervading Necklace; any bodhisattva who attains this necklace will cause sentient beings with balanced dispositions to no longer give rise to doubt.

Furthermore, there are necklaces of transformed forms and colors; when a bodhisattva attains these necklaces, they behold immeasurable transformations of form and color, and all give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

“O son of noble family! These necklaces extend to eighty thousand Dharma gates; a bodhisattva could never exhaustively fathom them. I have now spoken of them only briefly and cannot detail all their particulars.”

"If there were sentient beings who, from kalpa to kalpa, even unto hundreds of thousands of kalpas, desired to exhaust the practices of the Bodhisattva’s *vaijayantī* (ornament), this would not be so.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Formless (*Anākāra*), established in non-retrogression, who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
How extraordinary!
This is something never heard before.
The transformations of the Tathāgata are inexhaustible; he is thus able to expound the wondrous Dharma of the *Ratnavyuha* (Necklace).
All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who uphold, recite, and chant the names of the *Avataṃsaka* are protected by all the Buddhas.
If there are good men or good women who encounter the *Avataṃsaka* of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma, they have thereby encountered the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the fourfold assembly:
"If there are good sons or good daughters who, with single-minded devotion, receive, uphold, recite, and chant [this teaching], they shall immediately attain ten kinds of unimpeded merit."

What are these ten? They are: attaining the profound penetration of the majestic deportment of the Gaganagañja; possessing powerful memory for what is heard without losing eloquence; observing and comprehending all thoughts as being like illusions or transformations; roaming the mind in liberation without reckoning them as permanent; constantly remaining free from the eight worldly dharmas and not dwelling in clamor or bustle; rejoicing immediately upon hearing the Dharma with a mind free of dualistic views; understanding emptiness and signlessness without clinging to signs; further being able to enter deeply into the meditative concentration of cessation; attaining unimpeded supernormal powers and swift wisdom; and knowing that phenomena arise of themselves, seeing neither their origination nor their extinction.
"This is what is meant by saying that good sons and good daughters are then able to be fully endowed with the ten unimpeded merits.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
All dharmas are formless and cannot be seen.
A formless dharma is not something that can be attained by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
Why, then, does the World-Honored One say, "If good men and good women uphold and recite the ten unimpeded merits, they shall immediately realize the fruit of the Way and enter the gate of Nirvana"?
"Is unimpeded nirvana not a distinct dharma?

Nirvana is unconditioned, unimpeded, and unattached; yet the Tathāgata, being presently present, has attained equal and right enlightenment. How then can he speak of nirvana by means of unimpeded merit?"
If sentient beings were to attain the ten unimpeded merits, they would have already attained nirvāṇa.
If sentient beings had already attained nirvāṇa, then that nirvāṇa would be neither nirvāṇa nor non-nirvāṇa.
"Why does the World-Honored One say:
'To attain the ten unimpeded merits is itself Nirvana'?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"What you have asked is entirely due to the Buddha's majestic spiritual power; it is not within your sphere of experience.
How so? Śāriputra!"
"Is Nirvāṇa form? He replied, "No."
“How is it, Śāriputra? Is nirvāṇa formless?”
He replied, “No. [The Buddha asked,] “How so?”
"Śāriputra! Is nirvāṇa form or is it formless? He replied:
"No, it is not. "In what way, Śāriputra?"
"Is nirvāṇa neither form nor non-form? He replied, "No."
"How is it, Śāriputra? Are these unimpeded dharmas permanent or impermanent?"
"Is there arising and ceasing? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“If one were to cause all unobstructed dharmas, even up to nirvāṇa, to be neither form nor non-form, neither form nor non-form, and furthermore to be without arising, ceasing, severance, or attachment—formless and invisible.”
"Why, then, do you further speak of Nirvana by name?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Nirvana is nameless; it cannot be seen as an object within the sphere of visual consciousness.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Śāriputra! As you have said, it is not something that can be seen within the sphere of visual consciousness. Why is this so?
"Śāriputra, does consciousness have form? He replied:
"According to their form and appearance.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"As you have said, according to their form and appearance, there is consciousness."
"Why, then, do you say it is not the domain of visual consciousness?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"That which follows from having form and characteristics is conditioned consciousness; that which follows from being without form and characteristics is unconditioned consciousness."

Unimpeded nirvāṇa is neither the characteristic of the conditioned nor the consciousness of the conditioned; it is neither the characteristic of the unconditioned nor the consciousness of the unconditioned.
"How so, Śāriputra?"

Unobstructed nirvana is neither the characteristic of the conditioned nor the consciousness of the conditioned; it is neither the characteristic of the unconditioned nor the consciousness of the unconditioned. It is the consciousness of the conditioned, yet the unconditioned is without consciousness.
“Nirvana is neither this nor that; is it something different from consciousness? Śāriputra replied to the Buddha, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Nirvāṇa is neither this nor that, nor is it something other than consciousness. Its characteristic is no-characteristic; how then could Nirvāṇa be established as a distinct name?”
If Nirvana were established under a distinct name, then consciousness would arise in accordance with its formal characteristics;
if Nirvana were not established under a distinct name, then there would be unconditioned consciousness in accordance with the characteristic of the unconditioned.

Why do you say that nirvāṇa has neither the characteristic of the conditioned nor the consciousness of the conditioned, neither the characteristic of the unconditioned nor the consciousness of the unconditioned, yet is not different from consciousness, nor is it established as a separate designation?
"How, then, can it now be called Nirvāṇa?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Nirvana, Nirvana. The Buddha asked,
"What do you mean by 'Nirvana, Nirvana'?"
Śāriputra said, "It is like the exhaustion of nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:
"How is it like the exhaustion of nirvāṇa?
Śāriputra replied, "It is like exhaustion being non-exhaustion."
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!”

As you have said, it was originally taught that unimpeded nirvāṇa is neither the characteristic of the conditioned nor the consciousness of the conditioned, neither the characteristic of the unconditioned nor the consciousness of the unconditioned, and furthermore, it is not a different consciousness; as for its characteristic, it is a non-characteristic and no separate name is established for it.
"Why, then, do you further say that unimpeded nirvana is like exhaustion and non-exhaustion?
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This is not within my realm; I speak of unimpeded nirvana, yet this unimpeded nirvana is neither exhausted nor inexhaustible.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"I shall now provide you with a simile, for the wise understand through analogies."
It is like a man shooting upward into the void, seeking emptiness within emptiness, and then saying to others:
"In the past, while wandering through the void, I fell into an abyss; now that I have found the void, I shall shoot back to take my revenge."
"How joyful! This is indeed my wish.
What do you think?
“Śāriputra! Is the aspiration and inclination of this person truly as such?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That person who shoots at empty space wishing to take revenge for a grudge does so with certainty and not in vain. “How so?”
“Śāriputra! If one shoots at emptiness with an arrow, will the arrow stick in emptiness? He replied:
"Not attached. The Buddha said:
"How can one seek retribution for an offense against emptiness?"
Śāriputra said, “Space is without marks; one does not perceive therein either retribution or the absence of retribution.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is. It is as you have said: space has no retribution.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Unimpeded Nirvana is also like this: when it is in the characteristic of the conditioned, it follows the consciousness of the conditioned; when it is in the characteristic of the unconditioned, it follows the consciousness of the unconditioned. It is not in this characteristic, nor is it in that characteristic; it is neither with consciousness nor without consciousness. This is called unimpeded Nirvana being neither with consciousness nor without consciousness.”

At that time, there were five hundred bhikṣus who, upon hearing this teaching on the inexhaustibility of space, immediately rose from their seats, took up their robes and bowls, and departed along the road.

Why is this? These bhikṣus seek emptiness within emptiness, desiring to repay the grudge of emptiness; their minds are reckoned as being stained by attachment, claiming that there is emptiness within emptiness. Even if, in the future, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to stand before them and preach the Dharma, these bhikṣus, being stained by emptiness within emptiness, would ultimately never attain liberation.

At that time, the ordinary persons, those established in faith, and those who were learners and non-learners seated there had not yet been able to exhaust suffering and reach the realm of the unconditioned.
Then, Śāriputra, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, addressed the fourfold assembly:
"What do you think?"
"Virtuous ones!
Do you truly understand this profound Dharma? They replied:
“Indeed it is so,
worthy Śāriputra! You have forever severed the afflictions and accomplished what was to be done.”
Śāriputra asked, "In what way are the afflictions exhausted? He replied:
"The various wisdoms are not intermingled, for they are neither created nor uncreated;
therefore, they exhaust all afflictions. Śāriputra said: "Excellent, excellent!"
Son of good family!

The category of afflictions is the very basis of sentient beings; within these sentient beings, one accomplishes the unsurpassed path and, within the field of merit of the Tathāgata, purifies all-knowledge.
Śāriputra said: "If even purity is without purity, how can one purify all-knowledge within the field of merit? He replied:
"Having not yet attained the fruits of the Path, one has not yet purified one's tracks regarding omniscience.
He asked again: "Śāriputra!
“How many categories are there for a bodhisattva’s purification of all-knowledge? Śāriputra replied,
“A bodhisattva’s purification of all-knowledge is not constrained by worldly dharmas.”
He asked again:
"How is it that one is not constrained by worldly dharmas? Śāriputra replied:
"All dharmas are without attachment, and one does not harbor inverted views.
He asked again:
"How is the Bodhisattva’s *ratnavyuha* (jeweled necklace) accomplished?"
He replied: "One does not lose the Buddha-way until it is ultimately accomplished, nor does one lose the bodhisattva’s necklace of adornments. O son of noble family!
This is because, through fundamental practice, one does not lose one's virtuous vows."
He asked again: "How is it so, Śāriputra?"
"How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva rely upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to accomplish the jeweled garlands of the various practices of a Bodhisattva?
He replied: "To be unstinting with one's body and life for the sake of all sentient beings—this is what is called a spiritual friend for a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
He asked again:
"By what kind of wisdom are the various practices accomplished as a jeweled necklace? He replied:
"Without severing the lineage of the Buddhas, one does not create anything new.
He asked again:
"How does one serve and make offerings to the Tathāgatas, and adorn the Buddha-fields?"
He replied: "Not taking kalpas as a measure of time—this is called adorning the Buddha-land.
He asked again:
“How is it that one remains in noble silence before the Tathāgata, giving rise to no manifold perceptions? He replied:
“One would rather lose body and life than fail in the precepts.”
He asked again:
"How does one distinguish the eight hundred faculties? He replied:
“Maintain the continuity of the mind, not losing the mindfulness of the breath as it enters and exits.
He asked again:
“How does one fulfill the six methods of steadfastness?”
He replied, "An unreal body and an unreal life can be exchanged for a real body and a real life.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'being endowed with the inexhaustible treasury'? He replied:
"Having attained the unimpeded necklace of a bodhisattva, one is then able to fully possess the seven inexhaustible riches."
He asked again:
"What is meant by having few desires and being content with what one has in this world? He replied:
"To not be in conflict with the various forms of knowledge is called having few desires.
He asked again:
"How does one dwell the mind in seclusion, untainted by the three realms of existence?"
He replied, "I do not seek or desire anything within the three realms.
He asked again:
"What is meant by using wisdom to awaken to the afflictions of the three periods of time? He replied:
"To exhaust the fundamental source of suffering so that worldly toil does not arise."
He asked again:
"How is it that one has no conceptualization regarding the three types of sensation? He replied:
"One does not perceive suffering or pleasure; there is neither suffering nor pleasure.
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva experience that which is not experienced?"
He replied: "One distinguishes the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
He asked again:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva deeply penetrating the fundamental nature of phenomena? He replied:
“To relinquish the six external sense bases and not to create the six sensory objects internally.”
He asked again:
"How does one cross by means of crossing? He replied:
"Distinguishing the various paths, yet not becoming stained by the fruits of those paths.
"How does a bodhisattva abandon stinginess and practice generosity without giving rise to conceptual attachments? He replied:
"He has no threefold obstruction in his mind toward all sentient beings.
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva maintain the precepts without deficiency?"

He replied: "From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, one does not abandon the mind of the Way and maintains the compliant patience regarding the Dharma.
He asked again:
“How does one cultivate patience so that anger and resentment do not arise? He replied:
“One subdues the mind and restrains the thoughts, contemplating emptiness and formlessness.”
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva apply mental diligence so as not to give rise to indolence? He replied:
"Discriminative reflection should be like extinguishing a raging fire.
He asked again:
"How is it that a bodhisattva’s meditative mind remains undiminished, traveling throughout the ten directions without error in thought?"
He replied, "The mind and its objects are non-dual; thus, wisdom is not lost.
He asked again:
“What is meant by the wisdom-eye universally illuminating without obstruction? He replied:
“Regarding all dharmas, one does not perceive their forms or characteristics.”
He asked again:
"How is it that a bodhisattva enters the meditative absorption of loving-kindness and so forth, gathering in sentient beings yet seeing no one who is delivered? He replied:
“[The Buddha said: ‘One contemplates the fundamental nature of the mind, intellect, and consciousness of sentient beings.
[Subhūti asked: ‘How does a bodhisattva feel compassion and weep for those who have not been delivered? He replied:”
"He does not give rise to the notion of dharmas, nor does he perceive distinctions of high and low.
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva enter immeasurable concentrations with an uninterrupted mind of joy?"
He replied: "The essence of practice is spontaneous; one does not perceive arising or ceasing.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'a bodhisattva practices the three samādhis and reaches the gate of nirvāṇa'?
He replied: "It means not abandoning the Tathāgata and the path of the Eightfold Noble Way."
At that time, Śāriputra, through countless skillful means, expounded for the members of the assembly the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Unhindered Necklace.
At that moment, one thousand two hundred bhikṣus, their faith firm and steadfast, established themselves in non-retrogression.
Furthermore, there were countless devas and humans who all resolved to attain unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Anuttara-lakṣaṇa (No-Top-Mark) who rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said:
"How extraordinary!..."
How extraordinary!
This is something never heard before!
As the worthy Śāriputra has explained the realm of wisdom, it is neither existent nor non-existent; one does not perceive the characteristics of phenomena such as love and hatred, joy and anger.

As I observe the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the worlds of the ten directions expounding the teachings of the Way: some proclaim the teaching of existence that gradually leads to the unconditioned; some proclaim the teaching of non-existence that likewise leads to the unconditioned; some speak of bodily suffering to bring about weary detachment; and some eliminate perceptions and thoughts to realize the primordial limit.
How does a bodhisattva universally enter all phenomena, discerning each one individually without giving rise to increase or decrease?

Now I hear that the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s physical marks is such that conditioned things are naturally so and their functioning is not subject to change, while the unconditioned is formless and cannot be measured.
Now I wish to hear about the fundamental nature of the Tathāgata’s *ratnāvalī* (jewel-garland); I only pray that you will explain it.
How many *ratnāvalīs* are there by which the conditioned form-body (*saṃskṛta-rūpakāya*) is adorned?
And how many *ratnāvalīs* are there by which the unconditioned form-body (*asaṃskṛta-rūpakāya*) is adorned?
“How many necklaces adorn the conditioned formless body?
And how many necklaces adorn the unconditioned formless body?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
That you are able to let out a lion’s roar before the Tathāgata— now I shall analyze this for you in detail, point by point.”
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!

From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should always fully maintain restraint over body, speech, and mind. Adorning the six perfections, they realize that form is fundamentally non-existent; not perceiving the fundamental nature of form, they adorn form with the dharma of the six necklaces, thereby attaining the Tathāgata’s profound treasury of necklaces.

“What are the six? In this regard, when a son or daughter of good family sees a form with the eye, they recognize that the arising of that form is due to the lust, anger, and delusion of sentient beings; they advance when it is appropriate to advance and retreat when it is appropriate to retreat. The eye is not that form, and the form is not the eye. They maintain mindfulness to eliminate that form and do not give rise to perceptions of the eye. This is called the first dharma: the Pure Ornament.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The nature of form is spontaneous, and consciousness is also spontaneous. When that form and my consciousness do not give rise to the dust and toil of affliction, one swiftly understands those fetters and does not become stained by the notion of 'mine. This is called the pure necklace of the two dharmas."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Regarding all roots of goodness, one contemplates that form is formless; since the root is pure, form is also pure. This is called the 'Adornment of the Purity of the Three Dharmas. "
"Furthermore, son of good family!
One is attached to form and stained by desire for form; yet there is no desire within form itself.
Since the nature of form is fundamentally non-existent, how much less so is sexual desire?"
These are called the four ornaments of pure dharmas.
Furthermore, son of good family!

To reckon that form is permanent and not within the realm of the eye, and for the conceptualizing consciousness to give rise to hesitation, reckoning it as permanent, impermanent, and so forth, even up to non-self—yet the nature of form is empty and quiescent, forever without arising or ceasing—this is called the five ornaments of pure dharmas.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Form is an external sense-field (*āyatana*), which eye-consciousness approaches and receives. There is form that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and form that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). If consciousness regarding conditioned form causes the roots of the Path to perish, while consciousness regarding unconditioned form achieves fruition, then the contemplation and discernment of the marks of existence and non-existence—this is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Six Dharmas. "
"Furthermore, son of good family!
There are six further matters regarding the internal collection of form-consciousness (*rūpa-vijñāna*). What are these six?

"In this regard, son of good family! The characteristics of consciousness are formless, yet they flow and rush toward myriad ends; when external objects appear before it, affliction immediately arises. If there is the good, there is the perception of good; if there is the evil, there is the perception of evil. Evil perception lacks goodness, and good perception lacks evil. When a Bodhisattva restrains the mind so that perceptions of good or evil do not arise, this is called the first dharma: the Pure Ornament."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When visual consciousness contemplates emptiness and perceives that nothing exists at all, it gives rise to the notion of emptiness and the absence of retribution for good or evil deeds. Not seeing that there is receiving of retribution in this life or in future lives, one gathers the mind within and does not give rise to inverted perceptions; this is called the second adornment of purity."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

To discern non-self, yet at times perceiving the impurity of the sense-gates and conceiving them as pure, or conversely, being mindful of the purity of the sense-gates and conceiving them as impure—to then restrain the mind within this state so that neither of these two perceptions arises, this is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Three Dharmas. "
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When one perceives that anger has both wholesome and unwholesome aspects—where 'wholesome' refers to what is always wholesome, and the same applies to the unwholesome—one who gathers the mind within this regard and fulfills patience, this is called the fourth ornament of pure dharma."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

To discern whether sentient beings incline toward the wholesome or do not incline toward the wholesome, whether they dwell firmly in the stages of practice or do not dwell firmly in the stages of practice, and to maintain mental focus therein so that the mind does not regress—this is called the 'Adornment of the Fivefold Purity of Dharma. "
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When observing the preceding forms, there is the path and the mundane; yet one sees the path but does not know it as the path, and sees the mundane but does not know it as the mundane. To collect the mind therein and skillfully distinguish between the path and the mundane—this is called the sixth adornment of pure dharmas."
“Furthermore, there are six matters regarding the conceptualization of the ear-consciousness. What are these six?
In this regard, son of good family!”

If, when hearing sounds through the eighteen transformations—whether hearing the sound of wind, trees, or mountain collapses, or at times the voices of birds, beasts, or music—sounds that may be good or evil, recordable or unrecordable—one gathers the mind therein so that the ear-consciousness does not err, this is called the first dharma: the Pure Ornament.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

There may be times when sentient beings attain mundane, penetrating hearing, reaching a hundred *yojanas* or two hundred *yojanas*, and even extending to countless Buddha-lands. It is like when the Valiant World-Honored One advances toward the site of enlightenment desiring to achieve equal and perfect awakening; at that time, heaven and earth shake in six ways, and all distinct sounds dissolve back into emptiness. To be able to withdraw the mind within this state and not give rise to conceptual attachments is called the second dharma: the Pure Ornament."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When the ear-consciousness hears sounds, they are originally non-existent; yet, various perceptions arise and manifold thoughts are produced. To collect the mind within this state so that there are no perverse thoughts—this is called the 'Adornment of the Threefold Purity of Dharmas.'"
"Furthermore, son of good family! The supernormal power of the ear is purified;

one knows that those who have received form are either pure or turbid. Seeing the turbid, one does not give rise to worldly afflictions; seeing the pure, one does not give rise to the mind of the Path. Within this, one gathers the mind and does not give rise to the notions of 'self' and 'other. This is called the fourth ornament of the purity of dharmas."

"Furthermore, son of good family! At times, the ear-consciousness hears the exposition of the fivefold Dharma-body in other lands and different realms; it manifests dwelling in the mother’s womb without being stained by worldly desires; it further manifests leaving the household life with an unchanging mind; and beneath the king of trees, it attains equal and perfect enlightenment, therein gathering the mind to distinguish between the monastic and the lay. This is called the 'Adornment of the Five Pure Dharmas. "
"Furthermore, son of good family!

With the ear-consciousness, one listens to and observes the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the lands of the ten directions as they turn the Dharma-wheel of space, delivering immeasurable classes of sentient beings in the mere twinkling of an eye. Yet, they do not claim for themselves that 'I have delivered anyone,' and within this state, they restrain their thoughts and do not calculate that they are transforming sentient beings. This is called the sixth ornament of pure dharma."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Anuttara-lakṣaṇa, saying:
"Based upon that ear-consciousness, one should practice six dharmas. What are these six?
"Therefore, noble son!

One who practices skillful means and records what was originally created, cultivating the *adornment* (*vimalakīrti*) without transgressing its proper sequence—this is called the first dharma, the Pure Adornment."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
To practice the conduct of non-self and not to calculate upon the origin of the body—this is called the second dharma, the pure ornament.
Furthermore, son of good family!"
To be fully endowed with six dharmas and not violate the nature of the precepts—this is called the third ornament of purity.
Furthermore, son of noble family!

When the ear-consciousness possesses profound discernment that penetrates all things without obstruction, and does not abandon the mind of great compassion and its vast vows—this is called the fourth ornament of purity.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When the ear-consciousness discerns and understands progress and movement, such that it distinguishes: 'This dharma is the path of goodness; this dharma is the path of evil; this dharma is conditioned; this dharma is unconditioned,' and the ear-consciousness does not err in its discrimination therein—this is called the fifth ornament of the purity of dharmas."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When the ear-consciousness discriminates the worlds of all Buddhas and hears the extraordinary, profound, and wondrous Dharma, and one serves each and every Buddha-Bhagavān, this is called the sixth ornament of pure dharma.
"Furthermore, there are six dharmas that you should mindfully practice. What are these six?

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses a pure form-body that is not a body of desire; his body emits various fragrances that pervade immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions. Each fragrance expounds immeasurable *kaṇṭhaka* (necklace) Dharma-gates. Without relying on sentient beings yet having no notion of sentient beings, he achieves and fulfills the faculty of olfactory consciousness therein. This is called the first dharma: the Pure Necklace.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses an immeasurable realm of fragrance; with the fragrance of his preceptual virtue, he pervades the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, therein gathering in immeasurable sentient beings. This is called the second ornament of the purity of dharmas."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Again, one uses the nose-consciousness to examine that realm of fragrance; one should sever all fetters and attachments through the three paths, without losing the fundamental basis for the functioning of nose-consciousness. This is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Three Dharmas.'
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Because of that supernormal power of the nose, one expounds immeasurable and profound teachings; with the purity of olfactory consciousness, all practices are fully perfected. This is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Four Dharmas.'"
"Furthermore, son of good family!

There are three aspects of nose-consciousness: entering the internal consciousness from the external realm, smelling fragrant and foul odors, and discerning the Eightfold Path and the sixteen noble traces. This is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Five Dharmas.'
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When the nose-consciousness smells fragrances, with a single thought and a single intention, it knows the dharmas contemplated by the minds of those sentient beings, expounding and clarifying each one through immeasurable Dharma-gates; this is called the sixth ornament of pure dharma."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa, saying:
"Furthermore, one should be fully endowed with six dharmas: the marks of a Buddha are signless and cannot be maintained; one adorns oneself by accomplishing the path through adornment."
What are the six? In this regard, son of good family!

One cultivates the single mark while seated beneath the Bodhi tree, observing that the conduct of sentient beings does not abide [in reality]. From the Tuṣita Heaven, one descends by spirit into the mother’s womb; though manifesting worldly transformations, one does not lose the state of a worthy sage. The fragrance of the Tathāgata’s prohibitions and precepts pervades immeasurable worlds. This is called the first dharma: the Pure Ornament.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Cultivating the characteristics of olfactory consciousness, one universally knows the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions and understands that the forms received by beings in their various rebirths are not the same; furthermore, using supernormal powers to transform and teach them—this is called the second dharma: the pure necklace."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The nose-consciousness discriminates the marks of marks without weariness; furthermore, one contemplates the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and sees that the fragrance of Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood (Ekajātipratibaddha) completely fills the worlds of the ten directions. Within this, one gathers the mind and does not allow it to scatter; this is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Three Dharmas. "
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When he first sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he reflected within himself:
'Now my attainment of Buddhahood is certain and beyond doubt.'"
By what means of verification shall the devas,
nāgas, and spirits, and even the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, know that I am now seated beneath the Bodhi tree?

He immediately emits from every single pore all manner of fragrances, causing those in the worlds of the ten directions to come and provide lodging, guard, and protect the Bodhisattva until he attains Buddhahood; this is called the fourth dharma: the pure necklace.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Having attained perfect enlightenment beneath the King of Trees, endowed with all the marks of excellence, he perfected the three types of supernormal knowledge within a single night."
During the first watch of the night, he thought to himself:
"The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained enlightenment here in the past; what Dharma did they first expound?
How did they teach and transform beings?"
Reflecting thus, he reached the middle watch of the night and thought:
"In ancient times, the Buddhas of the past attained enlightenment here and all taught the immeasurable *pāramitās*; I too should now act in accordance with the Dharma of those Buddhas."
He then entered the meditative concentration of "Universal Fragrance and Formlessness.
Emerging from that concentration, he further reflected:
"Although the Buddhas of antiquity attained enlightenment at this very place, whom did they deliver first?"
"How does one preach the Dharma?
At that time, he heard the voices of all beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, each delivering teachings to those ready for deliverance.

Furthermore, he contemplated each of those matters one by one until the final watch of the night; thus, he did not retreat nor was his perception of the realm of fragrance deficient. This is called the "Fivefold Pure Ornament."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Having attained the mark of the nose, he reflects within himself:
'Worldly fragrances are impermanent and are of the nature of birth and death; by what skillful means may I seek the fragrance of the Way and its virtue?'"

He then entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and, through discerning wisdom, distinguished the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharma-kāya*). By means of consciousness, he proceeded to differentiate them: the fragrance of precepts (*śīla-gandha*) gathers the body; the fragrance of concentration (*samādhi-gandha*) gathers the mind; the fragrance of wisdom (*prajñā-gandha*) gathers distraction; the fragrance of liberative insight (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) gathers inverted views; and the fragrance of the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*) gathers ignorance (*avidyā*). This is called the Tathāgata adorning his body with the necklace of the fivefold Dharma-fragrance; this is called the necklace of the purity of the six dharmas.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa, saying: “The tongue-mark of the Tathāgata is the most sublime among all marks;

when he proclaims and disseminates his verbal teachings, they are free from the four faults. Because of his original vows, he teaches the Dharma to transform and guide others; his oral instruction is pure and does not lose the faculty of the tongue-consciousness. This is called the first dharma: the Pure Ornament.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Having fundamentally cultivated the pure observance of the three modes of conduct, one knows the destination of the consciousness of those sentient beings and immediately preaches the Dharma without losing its proper sequence; with the purity of the tongue-consciousness, this is called the second ornament of the purity of dharmas."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Although one speaks the Dharma with speech that has instruction and resonance, and words issued from consciousness are immediately received by those being transformed, one further adopts their language to preach the Dharma for them; therein, one internally restrains the tongue-consciousness so that it is pure. This is called the 'Adornment of the Purity of the Three Dharmas. "
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The tongue possesses manifold characteristics, each distinct from the others; every transformed consciousness preaches the Dharma inexhaustibly, never losing the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The tongue-consciousness is pure, such that even throughout immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whatever words are spoken or uttered are received with faith. This is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Four Dharmas. "
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Suppose there is a person who hears that teaching of the Dharma—whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, or whether it speaks of wrong views or right views—and is further able to cross-examine and investigate its underlying meaning, remaining fully endowed with an undiminished faculty of tongue-consciousness therein; this is called the fifth ornament of the purity of the Dharma."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

The teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the past possessed practice, wisdom, and the path of rebirth; the Buddhas of the future will possess practice, wisdom, and the path of rebirth; and the Buddhas of the present possess practice, wisdom, and the path of rebirth."
What are the practices, the wisdom, and the destinies of the Buddhas of the past?
In this regard, son of good family!
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past had their bodies extinguished, their marks extinguished, and their forms extinguished.

What is meant by the extinction of the body? The bodies of past Tathāgatas do not abide permanently; their physical forms undergo transformation, being neither one nor two. As they arise, they naturally perish; though they may eventually be extinguished after a long time, the name "body" still persists without ceasing. This conditioned body does not enter the realm of the unconditioned.

The body of the Tathāgata is the nature of the fivefold Dharma; it is eternally settled and unchanging whether a Buddha exists or not. This is what is meant by "the extinction of the body," which does not mean the extinction of the fivefold body.
As for what is called the "extinction of marks," there are marks with form and marks without form.
What is meant by "having signs and having form" and "having signs but no form"?
That which is the objective sphere of eye-consciousness and the basis of the six external sense bases is called "having signs and having form.

As for "having signs but no form," it refers to all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, as well as determinate and indeterminate phenomena, which are not the objective sphere of eye-consciousness; this is called "having signs but no form."
Regarding what is called the cessation of form (*rūpa-nirodha*): there are three categories of form—visible form, invisible form, and increasing form. What is visible form?
It refers to the teachings uttered by the mouth and the activities constructed by the mental consciousness, which follow along with prior attachments; this is called visible form.
What is meant by "formless" (*arūpin*)?
It is as when one says that there is good and there is evil, and that there will certainly be retribution in the future, without any doubt.
Yet, while existing in the present, one performs past and future formations (*saṃskāra*) which are not seen by the present visual consciousness; this is called "formless."
What is meant by "increasing the existence of form"?

There is that which is the inexhaustibility of form and the exhaustibility of the non-form; there is that which is both the exhaustibility of form and the exhaustibility of the non-form. This is called increasing the existence of form.
"In this way, son of good family,
one is fully endowed with the six dharmas of the pure necklace.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What is the verbal teaching of tongue-consciousness? It brings forth immeasurable fundamental wisdom and concentrated intent; yet tongue-consciousness is neither consciousness nor is it equanimity. All sounds are the domain of ear-consciousness; external forms and images are the domain of eye-consciousness; various fragrances, whether pleasant or foul, are the domain of nose-consciousness. The words spoken by the mouth have sound but no form; the subject cognizes external phenomena but does not cognize itself. How, then, can tongue-consciousness receive the characteristics of ear-consciousness?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa,
saying: "What do you think, noble son?"
"Does sound emerge from the ear, or does it come from the outside?
He replied, "It is external consciousness; it does not arise from internal consciousness."
He asked again:
"When verbal teachings are uttered, whether great or small, are they heard by the ear-consciousness through the mouth, or are they not heard by the ear-consciousness through the mouth? He replied:
"Either heard through the mouth, or not heard through the mouth.
He asked again:
"What does it mean to hear through the mouth?"
"Is it not heard by means of the mouth? He replied,
"When sounds and echoes issue from the mouth, these are heard by means of the mouth."
"Earth, water, fire, wind, mountains, rivers, and stone walls—these are not heard through the mouth.
He asked again:
"The sounds produced by the mouth can be called consciousness; can earth, water, fire, and wind be without consciousness?"
He replied: "Earth, water, fire, and wind are not objects of oral cognition.
He asked again:
"What constitutes the accomplishment of oral consciousness? He replied:
"The four great elements."
He asked again:
"The mouth is not composed of the four great elements; do you now say it is composed of the four great elements? He replied:
"One speaks of the four great elements with consciousness, but does not speak of the four great elements without consciousness.
He asked again:
"Why do you say 'four great elements with consciousness' and not 'four great elements without consciousness'?"
He replied: "The four great elements with consciousness are those perceived by the mouth;
the four great elements without consciousness are earth, water, fire, and wind."
He asked again:
"The four great elements that possess consciousness—would these not be earth, water, fire, and wind? He replied:
"So it is. He asked again:
"What are the four great elements that are without consciousness?"

He replied: "When earth is separated from water, there is no consciousness; when water is separated from fire, there is no consciousness; when fire is separated from wind, there is no consciousness; when wind is separated from space, there is no consciousness; when space is separated from consciousness, there is no consciousness. This is what is meant by the four great elements being devoid of consciousness."
He asked again:
"Regarding the sounds produced by the four great elements that possess consciousness, do they arise from earth or from water?"
Is it fire? Is it wind?
Is it space?
"Is it consciousness?
He replied, "It is the universal collection."
He asked again:
"Apart from the four great elements, where does consciousness reside? He replied:
"Consciousness has nothing upon which it relies.
He asked again, "Earth, water, fire, and wind all have the same sounds and the same echoes; do you not speak of consciousness [in this regard]?"
He replied, "Consciousness is solitary and without companion; therefore, there is no consciousness.
He asked again:
"Is consciousness alone designated as 'consciousness'?
He replied, "Consciousness alone is not consciousness."
He asked again:
"If consciousness alone is not consciousness, how can it rely upon earth, water, fire, and wind?
Is it conditioned?"
"Is it unconditioned? He replied, "It is so."
He asked again:
"Once consciousness has departed from the womb at death, is there another place for it? He replied:
“There is. He asked again:
“What is it that exhausts the root of suffering?”
He replied, “It is the inexhaustible consciousness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttaraketu asked again:
"Is consciousness the great accomplishment,
or does consciousness accomplish the great? He replied:
"Great accomplishment is consciousness.
He asked again:
"Upon what does consciousness depend?"
He replied, "The great elements.
He asked again:
"In earth, water, fire, wind, and space, or apart from earth, water, fire, wind, and space,
where does consciousness abide? He replied, "Consciousness has no abode."
He asked again:
"Is it extinguished? He replied:
"No," he replied.
He asked again,
"Is it not cessation?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
“Consciousness neither goes nor does not go; is this dharma not nirvāṇa? He replied, “No.”
He asked again:
"Is there a difference between consciousness and nirvāṇa? He replied:
"Not different.
He asked again:
"Are there the four great elements of nirvāṇa?"
He replied: "In nirvāṇa, there are no four great elements.
He asked again:
"Is there a consciousness of nirvāṇa?
He replied: "There is a consciousness of nirvāṇa."
He asked again:
"What is the distinction between the consciousnesses of earth, water, fire, wind, and consciousness, and the consciousness of nirvāṇa? He replied:
“The transformation of earth, water, fire, wind, and consciousness occurs, whereas the transformation of nirvāṇa-consciousness does not; this is called their distinction.
He asked again:
“When earth, water, fire, and wind are separated from consciousness, and nirvāṇa is separated from consciousness, what is the difference between them?”
He replied: "The four great elements are separated from consciousness, yet they do not depart from the past, future, or present;
Nirvana is separated from consciousness, and it eternally departs from the past, future, and present."
He asked again:

"Apart from the consciousness of the four great elements and apart from the consciousness of nirvāṇa, is this consciousness—which is neither within the four great elements nor within nirvāṇa—anything other [than them]?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
“Are the four great elements separate from consciousness, and is nirvāṇa separate from consciousness?
Are they not different? He replied, “They are not different.”
He asked again:
"When consciousness abides in nirvana, it constitutes an unconditioned dharma; when consciousness abides in the four great elements, it constitutes a conditioned dharma.
Are these not distinct? He replied:
"Not distinct. He asked again:
"If they are not distinct, how is it that this is conditioned consciousness and this is unconditioned consciousness? What difference is there between them?"
He replied: "Conditioned consciousness accomplishes the four great elements, whereas unconditioned consciousness does not accomplish the four great elements; therefore, there is a distinction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The consciousness apart from the four great elements and the consciousness apart from nirvāṇa are neither one nor two. Why is this?
When consciousness abides within the four great elements, there are then the past, the future, and the present;
when consciousness abides in nirvāṇa, there is no longer past, future, or present.
Is this consciousness different from that consciousness?
He replied, "Not different.
He asked again:
"Why do you speak of this consciousness of the four great elements and this consciousness of nirvāṇa?
He replied: "These are provisional designations; they are not the teaching of ultimate truth."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttalakṣaṇa thought to himself:
"Regarding my present question concerning the retribution of formations dissociated from consciousness within the four great elements, he has now answered me with the absence of such retribution."
"Is it not that you have asked whether 'non-self' is incorrect?
Is it not that you have reported 'self' to be incorrect?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa, addressed the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa, saying:
“Consciousness of the conditioned four great elements is not consciousness of the unconditioned four great elements;
consciousness of the unconditioned four great elements is not consciousness of the conditioned four great elements.
Why is it that consciousness of the four great elements is neither this nor that?”
He replied, "No. He asked again:
“Is it that consciousness is not the four great elements, nor is it the consciousness of nirvana, yet it is not the absence of consciousness?
He replied: “Consciousness ceases, yet consciousness does not cease.”
“What is the cessation of consciousness? He replied:
“It is not the present.”
"What is meant by 'consciousness does not cease'? He replied: "The present."
He asked again:
"Does consciousness have cessation? He replied:
"Present. He asked again: "Are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) also present?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"Are conditioned phenomena also present? He replied, "No."
He asked again:
"The characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned are neither manifest nor non-manifest;
upon what do they depend? He replied:
"By relying on that which has no basis.
He asked again: "Excellent!"
“Does consciousness have a basis? He replied,
“Consciousness has no basis.”
He asked again:
"How is it that consciousness has no support?
Is there a realm?"
He replied: "There are three realms:
the realm of the body, the realm of phenomena, and the realm of space; these are called the three realms."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttalakṣaṇa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"There is defiled consciousness and undefiled consciousness.
How is it that undefiled consciousness becomes defiled consciousness?"
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa:
"The movement of defiled consciousness constitutes undefiled consciousness; undefiled consciousness does not become defiled consciousness."
Why is this? Because the nature of consciousness is eternally abiding and immutable, free from arising, ceasing, attachment, or annihilation.
For this reason, the moving consciousness becomes the abiding consciousness, and the abiding consciousness does not become the moving consciousness.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa:

"I have now attained Buddhahood as the uniquely honored one within the triple world, fully endowed with all marks, possessing the four fearlessnesses and the eighteen unique qualities; with all virtues universally complete, I now abide in the consciousness of stillness, having not yet attained the consciousness of movement."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttalakṣaṇa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does one abide in consciousness so as not to move consciousness?”
The Buddha said:
"What is called 'moving consciousness' is the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*); what is called 'abiding consciousness' is the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).

It is not that unconditioned consciousness becomes conditioned consciousness; rather, for this reason, moving consciousness becomes abiding consciousness, but abiding consciousness does not become moving consciousness."

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke these words, the Bodhisattva Wu-ding-xiang (Anūnatvāpūrṇatva) and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all gave rise to the resolve for supreme awakening and established themselves in the practice of consciousness;
countless sentient beings likewise gave rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"Endowed with all marks, he has perfected the body of a Tathāgata; Unattached to the three realms, like space, he is without self."
Having already removed the defilements of the mind, his supernormal powers are sovereign; because he has attained the consciousness of movement, he does not attain the consciousness of abiding.
The dharma-realm is empty space and likewise undergoes no change; after how long, O Tathāgata, will you attain the consciousness of abiding?
The Tathāgatas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, did they all move their consciousness in order to abide in consciousness?
I now have a doubt and do not yet comprehend the Dharma-realm; I only pray that you will look upon me with compassion and cause my deluded thoughts to cease.
The inclinations and natures of sentient beings differ; hearing the teaching of wondrous emptiness, they do not investigate its fundamental source.
Emptiness is signless and practices a single equality; how can one dwell upon consciousness and yet claim it is pure?
Now that the time has come, it is fitting to expound upon the ultimate limit and penetrating wisdom, which is most marvelous and rare.
The fourfold assembly, free from fear, all desire to hear and know [this], as well as the abiding consciousness and the moving consciousness, and to discern their natures.
The Buddhas of the past were always thus; the Dharma-realm is equal and impartial. The sages of the future shall likewise have such a nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Just as sentient beings of the present enter into stillness without distraction, from what consciousness do they obtain this concentrated mind?
Now, this state of meditative concentration is eternally tranquil and soundless; is it the abiding consciousness, or is it the moving consciousness?
I pray that you explain each of these one by one—the very root of the Dharma-realm—so that all knots of doubt may be forever severed and no further hesitation be harbored.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa with these verses:
"The Tathāgatas of the past, Whose spiritual wisdom was inexhaustible,
Though their bodies entered parinirvāṇa, Their abiding consciousness remained unchanging."
Moving consciousness has two categories: that which abides and that which does not abide;
even if one enters the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one perceives neither of these two designations.
The Tathāgata is free from attachment; as immovable as Mount Sumeru, he remains steadfast and serene.
His conduct is peerless; out of compassion, he delivers those who are inferior.
Throughout the kingdoms and all the villages, wherever the Benefactor has passed, no one fails to recognize it;
yet they are moved by doubt regarding their own consciousness and its stability.
Even if one were to spend countless eons attempting to calculate the consciousness of all the Tathāgatas—
whether it moves, remains still, or neither moves nor remains still—
the wisdom of the Buddha is boundless, and his consciousness pervades immeasurable dharmas.
The physical marks and great vows are complete, yet being signless, they cannot be seen.
When I was first born, heaven and earth were suddenly illuminated;
I held fast to my heart with firm vows, formless and non-active in consciousness.
The Honored One among two-legged humans is like an elephant freed from its hook and chains;
celestial music and performances naturally fill the void of space.
Countless devas and humans each offer their own respectful salutations.
Each, with several verses, sang praises of the Tathāgata’s virtues.
Having attained equal and perfect enlightenment, his gaze was never satiated;
he turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and expounded the incomparable teaching.
All classes of sentient beings revere and honor his sublime teaching;
Transcending past, future, and present, the Hero of the World is like a lion.
Having accumulated merit for countless eons, he never loses the practice of *dhāraṇī*.
The four immeasurables and fearlessnesses nourish and benefit all people.
Adorned by the fruits of the Path, they do not calculate in terms of life-span or self;
being without conceptual correspondence, they are perfectly awakened, like space covering all without obstruction.
Today I have attained the five eyes; Not abiding in non-abiding, I embrace that which is free from inversion.
Without abiding, there is no perception of consciousness.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous and extraordinary wisdom Seals all with the dharma of signlessness.
When practice is complete and without deficiency, there is no wealth that is not worldly glory.
With a single intention and a single thought, the Bodhisattva observes without distraction;
while the moving consciousnesses are manifold and wondrous, the abiding consciousness is not the foremost.
Contemplating the Buddhas of the past, And those yet to come in the future,
Just as I exist in the present, They are not established by depending on consciousness.
The Tathāgata’s threefold knowledge Is peerless and has no companion.
"Conduct passes away and cannot be extinguished; one does not perceive where consciousness resides.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"There is no body and no body-consciousness; the body is without body-consciousness. These dharmas are sixfold."
What are the six?

If there are good sons or good daughters whose bodies encounter the sixteen external defilements of sensation, and their body-consciousness discerns each one individually, even unto the pure ground, this is called the first dharma: the Pure Ornament.
"By means of consciousness that is without body, one gives rise to bodily consciousness; within this, all discrimination arises from contact. This is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Two Dharmas.'"

"I formerly made a vow: 'I shall cultivate my physical marks through one hundred and five practices; these are called the physical marks, and when another one hundred and five are fulfilled, they constitute the physical marks. This is called the Threefold Dharma Adornment of Purity."
"In the distant past, when sentient beings had already perished, they received bodies therein—whether conditioned or unconditioned, with activity or without activity;

whether beautiful or ugly, with suffering or with pleasure. They individually discerned what was the dharma-realm and what was not the dharma-realm, identifying 'this is the body-consciousness of the dharma-realm' and 'this is the body-consciousness that is not the dharma-realm. This is called the Adornment of the Purity of the Four Dharmas."

“Regarding the body-consciousness creating form, there are further ten matters: the true body and the transformed body likewise have no beginning or end; knowing that this body-consciousness tends toward nowhere to which it tends—this is called the Fivefold Dharma Adornment of Purity.”

"To realize that the fundamental consciousness of the body differs across ages, that the former body and the present body are subject to change and do not abide, and to know that the form originally received is likewise subject to change—yet to be able to remain undeluded regarding this consciousness of the body amidst these changes—is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Six Dharmas.'"
"Furthermore, son of good family!
There are another six matters. What are these six?

To have pure conduct of body and not commit any evils, to have purity of speech and not utter wrong actions, and to cultivate purity of mind and not create any defilements—this is called the first ornament of purity.

"When the past body has already ceased, there are both wholesome and unwholesome [actions]. One distinguishes wholesome consciousness through a wholesome body and wholesome merit, and unwholesome consciousness through an unwholesome body and unwholesome karma. To contemplate each instance of wholesome and unwholesome bodily consciousness one by one is called the 'Pure Ornament of the Two Dharmas.'"
“The six bodily characteristics transcend both good and evil, yet they can further give rise to mindfulness without abandoning bodily consciousness.

Furthermore, at times sentient beings reckon that because the body is pure there is a pure consciousness, or that because the body is impure there is an impure consciousness; within this, they differentiate between pure bodily consciousness and impure bodily consciousness—this is called the Threefold Dharma of the Pure Ornament.”

"To recollect the conditioned bodies and unconditioned bodies originally created, as well as the bodies of the past, future, and present, being able to discern them all without losing the consciousness of the body—this is called the fourth ornament of pure dharmas."
“The dharmas contemplated by the mind are neither one nor two; they are remembered with strength and not forgotten, arising from knowledge. This is called the Fivefold Pure Ornament.
Furthermore, there are five matters regarding the formless body of consciousness.”

What are the five? There is the defiled body and the undefiled body; the corporeal body and the incorporeal body; the conscious body and the unconscious body; the mundane body and the supramundane body; the singular body and the non-singular body. To discern each of these is called the "Pure Ornament of the Six Dharmas."
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Anuttaralakṣaṇa:
"There are further six matters. What are these six?"

The inexhaustible Dharma-body and the exhaustible Dharma-body; the discernment of existence and non-existence, and the purity of consciousness—this is called the first ornament of the purity of dharmas.

The unconditioned nature of phenomena neither increases nor decreases; knowing that phenomena have goodness and knowing that phenomena lack goodness; knowing there are phenomena that arise and knowing there are phenomena that cease; clearly understanding the consciousness of phenomena without losing the nature of phenomena—this is called the second ornament of the purity of dharmas. (In various editions, a third dharma is briefly mentioned.)

"There is an eternally abiding body and there is no eternally abiding body; one knows that dharmas are not eternally abiding, yet one also knows that all dharmas are eternally abiding; one contemplates that while all dharmas abide, consciousness has no abode—this is called the Pure Ornament of the Four Dharmas."

"All dharmas are quiescent; the form of all dharmas is likewise quiescent. Conditioned phenomena are not known by consciousness, yet there is consciousness of conditioned phenomena; unconditioned phenomena are not known by consciousness, yet there is consciousness of unconditioned phenomena. To contemplate without losing the dharma-realm—this is called the Fivefold Dharma Purification Ornament."

“The Dharma-body is incalculable, formless, and invisible; it is not comprised within the realm of the eye. From the first generation of the resolve for enlightenment, one does not give rise to dualistic thoughts, and by discerning all phenomena, one does not lose the Dharma-body. This is called the sixth ornament of pure adornment.”
The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Scroll Two.
The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Scroll Three. Also titled *Pratyutpanna-vipāka*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Six: The Realm of Consciousness (3). Chapter Six: The Realm of Consciousness.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva on the assembly named Hauxian (Māṅgalya), who had come from sixteen Ganges-sands of buddha-fields in the eastern direction to this realm to hear and receive the wondrous Dharma of the *Āmala-ka* (Necklace).
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his hands joined in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
If I may be permitted, I venture to submit this request."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
"I shall distinguish each point for you one by one.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Hauxian addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How does consciousness sustain the objects of the various consciousnesses?
As the Blessed One said:
"Consciousness arises from the conditioned, not from the unconditioned."
Furthermore, it is said:
"Consciousness arises from the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), not from the conditioned (saṃskṛta).
What, then, is this consciousness and that consciousness?
"Is it called the element of consciousness?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Hauxian:
"Consciousness is not something that possesses consciousness; consciousness arises from dharmas."
The noble and wise one addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is consciousness not consciousness, yet consciousness arises from dharmas? He replied:
"Consciousness is not a permanent consciousness; consciousness exists in accordance with phenomena.
He asked again: "What is consciousness?"
"To universally cognize all consciousness and know all phenomena—this is called 'consciousness that is not [ordinary] consciousness.
He asked again:
"Does consciousness possess wisdom?"
"Is it because they lack wisdom? He replied:

"Consciousness possessing wisdom is suchness; consciousness lacking wisdom is suchness. The consciousness of all sentient beings possesses wisdom as suchness; the consciousness of noble ones beyond training lacks wisdom as suchness."
"This is what is meant, son of good family!
There is suchness with consciousness and suchness without consciousness.
He asked again:
"What is consciousness? What is non-consciousness?
What is the suchness of consciousness?"
"What is the suchness (tathatā) of non-consciousness? He replied:
"To be able to fully discern the wisdom of consciousness and the wisdom of non-consciousness as suchness—this is called the discernment of the realm of consciousness."
The Bodhisattva Hauxian addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the Tathāgata now speaks of the meaning of ‘definitive’ and the meaning of ‘consciousness,’ my doubts have doubled.
The Buddha told Hauxian:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
There may be cognition of the wise and cognition of the non-wise; there may be cognition of phenomena and cognition of what are not phenomena."
What is consciousness of phenomena (dharma-vijñāna) and what is non-phenomenal consciousness?
From the ultimate truth up to the Pratyekabuddhas, this is called consciousness of phenomena.

From the stage of insight (darśana-bhūmi), the stage of refinement (tanu-bhūmi), the stage of nature (gotra-bhūmi), and the stage of non-obstruction (anāvaraṇa-bhūmi), up to the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood (eka-jāti-pratibaddha), this is called consciousness of phenomena.
The consciousness of phenomena (*dharmavijñāna*) further possesses five matters.

What are these five? First, the wisdom that proceeds toward the Path; second, the consciousness of past lives; third, the wisdom that proceeds toward discernment; fourth, entering the gate of emptiness; and fifth, contemplating the original nature of the mind. These are called the five matters accomplished by the consciousness of phenomena.
Furthermore, there are five things that accomplish the consciousness of the Dharma (*dharmavijñāna*).

What are these five? First, practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) without relying on the three poisons; second, dwelling in the womb without being defiled by birth and death; third, practicing the dharmas of signlessness (*animitta*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); fourth, cultivating supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) without obstruction; fifth, establishing the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) as having a single characteristic, which is the absence of characteristics (*animitta*). These are called the purities that accomplish the consciousness of the Dharma.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Hauxian:
"There are five further matters regarding the purity of the consciousness of dharmas. What are these five?

To contemplate the traces of learning with unchanging knowledge and insight, to see neither the state of no-more-learning nor its traces, to see no inclination toward phenomena (*dharma*), to see neither instruction nor non-instruction, and likewise to see neither the nature of the Path nor what is not the nature of the Path—whether the thought of the Path arises or does not arise—this is called the accomplishment of the five matters of the contemplation of the concentration on the consciousness of phenomena (*dharmavijñāna*).
“Furthermore, there are five matters. What are these five? First, the extinction of the fundamental defilements so that no locus is perceived;

second, mindfulness of the immeasurable, empty, and quiescent concentration of mind; third, establishing the foundation of the Path without meeting with the Path; fourth, severing thoughts from the mind while seeking to sit at the site of enlightenment; and fifth, cultivating fields of merit to eliminate delusive imaginings. These are called the five matters for the purification of the consciousness of phenomena.”
“The consciousness of the non-arising dharma has five further aspects. What are these five?

Consciousness contemplates the past and does not give rise to arising and ceasing; consciousness contemplates the present and does not see arising and ceasing; consciousness contemplates the future and does not see arising and ceasing; consciousness contemplates the beginning and the end and does not see arising and ceasing; consciousness contemplates the nature of suchness and does not see arising and ceasing. These are called the five aspects of the purity of the dharma-realm.”
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Hauxian:
“A Tathāgata, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, must further cultivate the consciousness of phenomena (dharmavijñāna); there are eleven modes of practice regarding the penetration of sounds.”

What are the eleven? The Dharma-realm is unattached and does not perceive the root of consciousness; within it, one is fully endowed with the practices of the path of the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*). One who wishes to purify and cultivate the consciousness of the Dharma-realm should, at the outset, have a mind like a mountain or a wall; gradually, through contemplation, they reach the point of knowing the origin of the body and realizing that the body is detached from the self.

Having further relinquished the body, one knows that the mind is detached from the mind; having further detached from the mind, one knows that emptiness is detached from emptiness; having further relinquished emptiness, one proceeds again from a single thought to a hundred thousand thoughts, being able to cultivate all thoughts not yet transformed; furthermore, one knows that the methods of transformation are non-existent—this is called the path of the supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) arising from the consciousness of phenomena (*dharmavijñāna*).

“By means of the consciousness of the body, one cultivates the practice of the consciousness of the body; or, by means of the consciousness of the body, one performs the practice of the consciousness that is not the body, discerning the consciousness of the body from the consciousness that is not the body—this is called the consciousness of phenomena cultivating the practice of the bases of psychic power.”

"To discern all phenomena within the non-dual Dharma and therein attain equal and perfect enlightenment; not perceiving the arising of consciousness as one attains equal and perfect enlightenment; being able to discern all the aggregates, bases, and elements throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of past eons; and not losing sight of the fundamental conduct and destinies of sentient beings—this is called the cultivation of the practice of the divine feet through the consciousness of phenomena."

“The dharma of non-transformation is not seen to undergo change; within it, the consciousness that constructs cannot be exhausted—this is called the cultivation of the bases of psychic power through the consciousness of dharmas.

Thereupon, one enters meditative concentration and discerns the realm of space, further reckoning one’s own body as being no different from it—this is called the cultivation of the bases of psychic power through the consciousness of dharmas.”

“Observing all worlds, one does not perceive their exhaustion; one is able to fully comprehend all worlds, whether they are in the process of forming or have already formed. This is called the cultivation of the bases of psychic power through the consciousness of phenomena.”

"Now, when the consciousness of the dharma-realm forms the five aggregates, there is arising and ceasing; yet, not seeing the five aggregates as having arising and ceasing—this is called the practice of the supernormal powers through the consciousness of the dharma."

“The Dharma-realm is without attachment and does not perceive forms or characteristics; past consciousness is not the present, and present consciousness is not the past. Not perceiving the beginning, middle, or end of the causal conditions of the present—this is called the cultivation of the practice of the bases of psychic power through the consciousness of phenomena.”

"To discern individually all phenomena arising from the nature of reality (dharmatā), seeing no nesting place for them; to withdraw the mind and extinguish conceptualization so that even wisdom does not arise—this is called the cultivation of the bases of psychic power through the consciousness of phenomena."

"All dharmas are unborn; one does not perceive their arising or ceasing, yet one can further contemplate these phenomena of arising and ceasing as being, by their very nature, spontaneously of a single mark which is markless.
This, noble son, is called..."
This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the bases of spiritual power.
The Buddha spoke again: “Noble son!
The attachment-free dharma-realm further comprises ten matters. What are these ten?
