When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, he is able to fully realize the perceptions of the body-consciousness throughout the three periods of time; this is called the practice of the non-self of the dharma-consciousness.

"To gradually transform sentient beings through the three methods of cessation, yet neither perceiving cessation nor perceiving non-cession—this is called the practice of the markless conduct of the dharma-consciousness.
To discern and fully understand each word and meaning, and further manifest original karma through expedient wisdom—this is called the practice of the markless conduct of the dharma-consciousness."

“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having analytically contemplated the four immeasurable wisdoms, does not perceive notions of annihilation or permanence; this is called the cultivation of the practice of non-self within the consciousness of phenomena.”
"Furthermore, to transform all sentient beings with wondrous wisdom while never abandoning great compassion—this is called the practice of the non-self of the dharma-consciousness.

To observe all sentient beings, seeing both those who are pure and virtuous and those who are not, and to transform them according to their kinds without abandoning their inherent natures—this is called the practice of the non-self of the dharma-consciousness."

“The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, employs expedient means to transform all sentient beings without perceiving any who are transformed; this is called the cultivation of the practice of non-self through the consciousness of the Dharma.

The Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and perceives neither success nor failure; that there is birth and extinction is not the original vow of the Tathāgata; this is called the cultivation of the practice of non-self through the consciousness of the Dharma.”

“The Tathāgata has a single characteristic; he is unstained by the past, future, or present. By practicing the conduct of non-reliance, he has attained true, perfect enlightenment. This is called the cultivation of the practice of non-self regarding the consciousness of phenomena.”

"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha takes countless billions of koṭis of kalpas as a single day; within that single day, he transforms and delivers sentient beings beyond all measure. This is called the practice of the non-self through the consciousness of phenomena."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Hauxian, saying:
“In the past, incalculable asankhyeya kalpas ago, I myself reflected upon and practiced the consciousness of formless dharmas.

There was a Buddha named Hongshi Wuyuan (Vast Vow Without Aspiration) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-sampanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who preached for me the practice of non-attachment to the dharma-realm.”
Now, the Dharma-realm consists of one hundred and seven matters. What are these one hundred and seven matters? They are: not seeking the practice of emptiness;

not dwelling on permanence; viewing the world as a dream; extinguishing the notion of self; ensuring that the arising of consciousness does not occur; discerning the characteristics of the realms; forever severing false views; ensuring the mind of giving is never lacking; keeping the mind always concentrated and undisturbed among the multitude; having no manifold thoughts regarding the consciousness of the body or the consciousness of emptiness; the Bodhisattva possessing a countable number of names yet not being attached to those appellations; observing and understanding that all dharmas are neither one nor two; and when sentient beings give rise to anger, employing skillful means to preach for them the practice of removing the non-existent fundamental consciousness, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the noble wisdom of the Four Truths, contemplating whether the root of suffering possesses a consciousness of suffering.
Is there no consciousness of suffering?
"At times there is consciousness abiding in the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
at other times there is consciousness apart from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
At times there is consciousness that, while attached to forms, does not defile the consciousness;

at times there is consciousness that, being unattached to forms, does not defile the consciousness—this consciousness is so subtle that it cannot be comprehended by Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained non-retrogression;
at times there is consciousness that, while attached to sounds, does not defile the consciousness.
At times there is consciousness that does not cling to sounds and does not defile consciousness, nor is there any resonance; therefore, it is called pure consciousness.
At times there is consciousness that clings to fragrances but does not defile consciousness;
at times there is consciousness that neither clings to fragrances nor defiles consciousness, discerning each part individually without losing the consciousness of the Dharma.
At times there is consciousness that, while attached to flavors, is not defiled by consciousness;
at times there is consciousness that, neither attached to flavors nor defiled by consciousness, further discriminates without losing its sequential order;
at times there is consciousness that, while attached to bodily contact, is not defiled by consciousness.
At times there is consciousness that does not cling to bodily contact and does not defile consciousness, discerning each part individually without giving rise to conceptual attachment;

at times there is consciousness that clearly knows all phenomena—those that arise and those that cease, conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena, those that are concentrated and those that are distracted. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s discernment of the nature of consciousness, which is likewise undefiled.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

One should discern the four immeasurable wisdoms—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and pervade all beings with them to rescue and sustain them, yet remain without attachment."

At times, there may be a son of noble family who enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and practices a single dharma. Having practiced this one dharma, he immediately attains hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gateways, which are like echoes and like illusions. Gradually, he reaches even the state of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). His bodily conduct is pure and he does not create the roots of evil; his mind contemplates loving-kindness and does not harbor any malice; and he understands the three periods of time, eliminating all fetters and attachments.
"O son of noble family! This is called the bodhisattva’s correct practice of arising and non-arising.

Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of meditative concentration in which all dharmas enter: there is the body, yet no perception of a body; there is mindfulness, yet no mind of mindfulness; it is neither one nor two, and likewise devoid of consciousness."

In the past, countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, when I first entered the Dharma and Vinaya, I accorded with this practice: I recognized that there are twelve factors of the Dharma which constitute the root of the causal conditions—from ignorance conditioned by volitional formations, up to old age and death—without seeing their arising or ceasing. This is called the concentration of mind named "Inexhaustible."

Having attained concentration of mind, they fully know all the destinies within the triple world; whether there are sentient beings who conceive notions of permanence or impermanence, notions of suffering or non-suffering, or notions of stability or instability, they distinguish each one individually without giving rise to defiled attachment.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should mindfully practice the essentials of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
What are these thirty-seven?
What are called the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) eliminate lust, anger, and delusion, thereby eternally extinguishing the three poisons.

One should further contemplate the four right efforts (catvāri samyakprahāṇāni), severing all thoughts of seeking and ensuring that no karmic retribution arises; only then does one attain the practice of the four bases of psychic power (catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ).
Having attained the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), he travels to the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions, yet he does not boast of his own supernormal powers.

The Tathāgata has perfected the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*): the body of precepts (*śīlakāya*), the body of concentration (*samādhikāya*), the body of wisdom (*prajñākāya*), the body of liberation (*vimuktikāya*), and the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanakāya*). This is called the Tathāgata’s fivefold Dharma-body, the indestructible Dharma-body of the Tathāgata’s divine wisdom.
“What are the five powers? They are the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. Regarding the power of faith:

it is single-mindedly unconditioned and unstained by the three realms. Even if as many Māras as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were to transform themselves into Buddhas, they could not move this mind; this is called the power of faith.”
What is the power of diligence? As for the power of diligence:

having heard of the Dharma known as the consciousness of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-vijñāna), whether it be located at a distance of one yojana up to a hundred thousand yojanas, or within the realm of a single Buddha or the realms of a hundred thousand Buddhas, to maintain one's faith, establish one's precepts, and not abandon one’s great vow—this is called the power of diligence.
What is the power of mindfulness?

As for the power of mindfulness, it means that mindfulness follows continuously before one’s mind without any other thoughts. Even if all the hosts of Māras, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were to come wishing to destroy this state of meditative concentration, they would only exhaust themselves in vain and fail to achieve their original intent; this is called the accomplishment of the power of mindfulness.
What is the power of concentration?

As for the power of concentration, it refers to a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva established in the stage of the superior faculties, who gathers the mind and eliminates perceptions without harboring doubt; this is called the power of concentration, which is likewise indestructible.
What is the power of wisdom?

That which is called the power of wisdom is the inconceivable, immeasurable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), which fully encompasses all forms of wisdom and the fundamental principles of skillful means (*upāya*). It does not destroy the practice of the wisdom-nature of the realm of phenomena; this is called the power of wisdom, wherein all virtues are complete.

Furthermore, one should further discern the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). One awakens to and comprehends all that is conceived by the mind and consciousness, whether with form or without form, from the desire realm up to the form realm and the formless realm—discerning what may be distinguished and what cannot be distinguished. To gather the mind so that it is not distracted is called the factor of concentration (*samādhi*).

“The nature of wisdom and the Eightfold Path are equal; they are likewise free from fear. Entering the samādhi of emptiness, there is a single practice without duality, having no beginning or end. Having already transcended the finite and the infinite, one is free from birth and death. No further knowledge arises; knowing the dharma of arising and ceasing as pure, one does not give rise to manifold conceptualizations. This is called the purity and non-duality of the Eightfold Path.”

"Furthermore, one should reflect upon the sixty-two views: the notion of permanence and the notion of impermanence; the notion of a path and the notion of no path; the notion that there is this world and the notion that there is no this world; the notion that there are parents and the notion that there are no parents; and the notion of self-identity and the notion of non-self-identity."

At times, there is consciousness that discerns the purity and flawlessness of the various paths, individually distinguishing the root of craving in three places, the root of desire in five places, and the practice of lust in seven places.

At times, there is practice in a secluded place—whether beneath a tree, in the open air, or among burial mounds—where one contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of breath, which at times is long and at times is short, and at times is cold and at times is warm; as all phenomena arise through the convergence of causes and conditions, one contemplates and discerns them with an undisturbed mind.

Therefore, the practitioner knows the inhalation and exhalation; they know when the breath is long and they know when it is short. They know the preceding breath as the preceding breath and the succeeding breath as the succeeding breath, gradually attaining the practice of the first dhyāna.

The Tathāgata’s noble and realized state of meditative concentration differs [from that of others]; by practicing the four dhyānas, he enters the cessation of perception and cognition (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*). Such a state of concentration is common to the three vehicles.
Furthermore, there is the unsurpassed state of concentration of the Tathāgata.
What is called the "unsurpassed concentration of mind"?

That which is called unsurpassed concentration refers to the fact that while the mind has superior, middling, and inferior levels, when the practitioner enters this concentration, there is no further entering or exiting, nor is there long or short breathing; they only discern the buddha-fields with single-minded focus.
He contemplates the past, future, and present, considering: "Which beings are those to be transformed by me, and which are not?
He further reflects:
"If I were to dwell in a secluded place without distinguishing among sentient beings, this would not be appropriate for me."
"Now I shall go to countless lands; by transforming myself and transforming others, I shall fulfill my vow.
This is called the first concentration, which likewise cannot be destroyed.

Furthermore, when the practitioner first enters the state of meditative absorption, they reflect within themselves that both suffering and pleasure originate fundamentally from the body. Having completed this practice, they must further propagate it so that all those sentient beings may fully understand it. This is called entering concentration and accomplishing the second practice.

"Furthermore, the mental phenomena (cittadharma) are neither existent nor non-existent; though lacking a body, one perceives a body. Without yet attaining the supernormal powers (abhijñā) to travel and transform throughout the ten directions, one restrains the mind, self-examines, and purifies one's spiritual lineage (gotra). This is called the concentration of mind that does not destroy the consciousness of the Dharma."

"When one possesses mind, consciousness, and thought to contemplate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, [one realizes] that since I myself am non-self, how could there be a sentient being? First knowing oneself to be empty, one then contemplates sentient beings; by means of the path of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), the mental spirit goes forth while the manifested body does not go there."

Furthermore, within the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, he delivers countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings through this concentrated mind, and therein he further cultivates the ten wisdoms of empty space.
What are these ten?

To teach the Dharma that shatters the palaces of Māra; to advance toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and achieve immeasurable awakening; and for the mind to be like space, without increase or decrease—this, noble son, is called cultivating the wisdom of space.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

First, one transforms those of various heretical and heterodox schools, removing their perverse karmas and establishing them in right view, causing them all to take refuge [in the Dharma] so that they no longer harbor stinginess or envy; this is called cultivating the wisdom of space."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, you transform the various classes of sentient beings, causing them all to fulfill their respective aspirations; yet, although you preach this Dharma, your mind remains unattached—this is called cultivating the wisdom of space."

Furthermore, by means of the path of unimpeded wisdom and supernormal powers, they travel to immeasurable worlds, manifesting all dharmas to transform sentient beings; yet they perceive neither sentient beings nor the act of transformation—this is called cultivating the wisdom of empty space.

“Furthermore, there is a Tathāgata wisdom called ‘Embracing Emptiness,’ which accomplishes the Dharma-realm without destroying its original nature; it maintains the mind like space so that no defilement arises—this is called cultivating the wisdom of space.”

“The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, may travel through the realm of empty space with a single body, or with innumerable bodies, or again manifest the extinction of *nirvāṇa*; yet he does not cling to a single body, nor give rise to the notion of multiplicity, nor does he cling to the extinction of *nirvāṇa*. This is called cultivating the wisdom of emptiness.”

“The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess seventy-two kinds of unimpeded eloquence and fourteen marks of retribution for their tongues; their wisdom in teaching and transforming sentient beings never halts, causing all classes of beings to achieve the clarity of insight.”
What are the seventy-two kinds of unimpeded eloquence?
In this regard, son of good family!
When the Tathāgata first cultivated the fundamental marks of merit, he himself made this great vow:

"If, after I have attained immeasurable, perfect enlightenment, the beings born in my land shall not even hear the names of ignorance, lust, anger, and delusion; may my land be as pure as space; may its inhabitants be like those in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens—having few desires and being content—and with their minds intent upon the Path, they shall encounter no obstructions therein, nor shall they be reborn in the eight states of no leisure."

Amidst the wealthy and noble, he does not become conceited, nor does he despise the lowly and humble; therein he restrains his mind and practices the merit of giving. If one seeks drink, he gives drink; if one seeks food, he gives food. He bestows even his national treasures, wife, and children, his heart unimpeded in its generosity, never giving rise to distracted thoughts.

Furthermore, they teach sentient beings to maintain the precepts in their entirety and to cultivate the six profound dharmas with diligence and single-mindedness. If there are sentient beings who encounter hundreds of thousands of sufferings, they are able to go forth at once to deliver them, ensuring they do not fall away or lose their status as noble and sagely beings.
These are called the eight dharmas for cultivating the wisdom of space.

When the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, desires to turn the wheel of Dharma, he first enters a state of meditative equipoise to collect his body and mind, knowing within himself that the time has come:
"I should now turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma for the sake of the classes of sentient beings."
"Roaming the mind through the six supernormal powers, one emits various radiances from every single pore, and only then turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

This is the unarisen and undestroyed dharma of non-attachment, the single characteristic of signlessness and the dharma free from defilement. What is taught is like space, with no trace of words appearing; one does not see sentient beings as increasing or decreasing. These are called the nine dharmas for cultivating the wisdom of emptiness."

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata attains equal and perfect enlightenment within the realm of non-arising; he perceives all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations, seeing no one who achieves the fruit of the Way, yet he does not lose his analytical wisdom of supernatural powers. The Tathāgata’s ten powers likewise remain unstained by attachment. These are called the ten dharmas for cultivating the wisdom of space."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the fourfold assembly:
“Each of you should, before the Tathāgata, personally proclaim the dharma of the wisdom of emptiness and non-attachment.”

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Ākāśacārin, who had come from a buddha-field located fifty-six *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* sands of worlds to the southeast of here. Having arrived at this land, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In that pure land, there is neither the teaching of dharmas nor the teaching of meanings; knowing both the pure and the impure to be entirely like empty space—this is called the unattached dharma of the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Anātman said:
"Non-seeing is not emptiness, and seeing is also not emptiness; neither seeing nor non-seeing is perceived—this is called the wisdom of emptiness, the dharma of non-attachment."
The Bodhisattva Dharmasthiti said:

"When the tracks of practice have not yet been established, defiled consciousness arises; though for incalculable kalpas there has fundamentally been no nature of consciousness, this is called the dharma of non-attachment to space."
The Bodhisattva Overcoming Conduct said:
"To not commit any evils through body, speech, or mind, and to never give rise to conceptual thoughts—this is called the practice of emptiness and the dharma of non-attachment."
The Bodhisattva Wu-xing said:
"The Dharma-body is inexhaustible; seeing no attachment or clinging, with a concentrated mind and single intent—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha said:

"To perceive neither the preceding nor the succeeding locations of the dharma-realm, and likewise not to perceive sin, merit, or the retribution for evil—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Practicing Suffering said:

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, fully know the past, the future, and the present; they enter into sovereign wisdom and do not give rise to false views. This is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Maitramati said: "The self has no form;

one focuses the mind on practicing the Way without other divergent thoughts. There is no dependence and no attachment to dharmas; they arise and cease spontaneously. This is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Ratnakalpa said:

"The practice of the four immeasurables is without attachment and without defilement; since there is a body, there is suffering, and perception and consciousness are also suffering; to understand that they neither arise nor cease is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Skillful Calculation said:
"I do not perceive any dharmas as having number or being without number.
How could dharmas have number or be without number?"

The mundane has number; the Way is without number. The conditioned has number; the unconditioned is without number. Not perceiving number or the absence of number—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness.
The Bodhisattva Jinsheng said:

"All dharmas are without arising, nor is any arising perceived; purity is devoid of the notion of purity. Birth and death have been exhausted, forever extinguished and no longer arising—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Brahmacharya said:

"To practice the three samādhis without thinking of receiving a body, to contemplate emptiness without departing from emptiness, to contemplate signlessness without departing from signlessness, to contemplate wishlessness without departing from wishlessness, and furthermore, not to think of receiving pure merit—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-lakṣaṇa said:

"To distinguish the three poisons as the dharma of darkness and not to perceive the three types of supernormal knowledge as the dharma of purity—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Kṛtaka said:

"To not perceive a single characteristic, to discern the absence of characteristics, to neither perceive suffering nor perceive the departure from suffering, and to be without suffering, without the absence of suffering, and without anything performed—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Unreceiving Form said:

"When there are no four great elements and one does not perceive the location of any objective realm, being single-mindedly unconditioned and not giving rise to the three types of thought—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Asama said:

"To remain detached from worldly pleasure and pain and unattached to the eight worldly dharmas; to feel no joy upon seeing praise, nor to harbor grief or sorrow even when facing defamation; and to have a mind of forbearance like the earth—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Vimala said:

"Not seeing the six internal sense faculties creating the six external sense objects, and not seeing the six objects and the six faculties as being in opposition—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."

The Bodhisattva Chóngguān said: "External forms do not give rise to internal consciousness, nor does consciousness cling to external forms. Consciousness does not know 'I am form,' and form does not know 'I am consciousness. It is the same for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharma*). Mental phenomena do not know 'I am consciousness,' and consciousness does not know 'I am mental phenomena. All dharmas are mutually ignorant of one another; this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness."
The Bodhisattva Dūrībhūta said:
"I do not perceive the five aggregates as having defilement or attachment. Why is this?"
“The nature of the five aggregates and the nature of all phenomena are eternally abiding and unchanging; this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness.
Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla said:

“The dhāraṇī of all phenomena does not perceive hope or hopelessness, nor does it perceive any phenomenon that can be spoken or cannot be spoken; it protects sentient beings by establishing them in non-retrogression—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness.”
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama said:

“All dharmas are eternally fixed and without diversity; one does not differentiate between the Buddha-dharma and the bodhisattva-dharma, the mundane dharma and the path-dharma, the conditioned dharma and the unconditioned dharma, or the dharma that can be protected and maintained and the dharma that cannot be protected and maintained. There is likewise no differentiation—this is called the practice of non-attachment through the wisdom of emptiness.”

At that time, the countless members of the fourfold assembly seated there, having heard this teaching on the dharma of emptiness, wisdom, purity, and non-attachment, became doubly suspicious and failed to reach a definitive understanding.
The World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts within their minds, perceived that they should be liberated through the wisdom of emptiness, yet the convergence of conditions had not yet arrived.

He then manifested a transformed body four hundred *yojanas* in height and emitted a great sound, addressing all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently preaching the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions:

"Those who wish to hear and receive the *Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra*, let them all gather like clouds; those who wish to go to the Sahā world, dispatch countless hosts of transformed bodhisattvas to pay homage to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions."
“Now, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, in the Sahā world-system, is expounding the Bodhisattva-Necklace (Bodhisattvamaṇḍala). We should all gather together in that land.
Thus, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, free from attachment, immediately assumed their respective forms and maintained their majestic deportment as they proceeded to the Sahā world-system.
Bodhisattvas who have established faith and attained the ten stages see all the Tathāgatas, pay them homage and make offerings to them, and each sits in turn upon the seat of fearlessness;

those who have not yet established faith remain on the level of ordinary beings, and as they have not yet attained the divine eye or perfected the various supernormal powers, they do not see the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Why is this? It is because the minds of ordinary people are narrow and they fear losing their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).

There may be a Tathāgata sitting in meditative concentration here whose body reaches as far as the Brahma Heaven; or there may be a Tathāgata who manifests transformations that pervade one thousand world-systems, two thousand world-systems, and even up to a trichiliocosm.
Why is this? Because sentient beings who receive transformation must see the form to receive the Dharma, and they must hear it to receive the Dharma.

At that time, to the east, beyond lands as numerous as the sands of two Ganges Rivers, there was a Tathāgata named Fundamental Purity (Mūlapariśuddha), who, together with a great assembly, spoke these words of the Dharma by means of verses:
"Space is boundless and shoreless; when one conceives of it through thought, doubt arises.
Since the practice of the primordial limit has been exhausted, there is neither duality nor equal peer.
If one wishes to describe the characteristics of space, its fundamental nature shows no sign of arising."
How can you doubt the wisdom of emptiness, desiring to seek non-existence within it?
Although I have now attained Buddhahood, I harbor neither existence nor non-existence and remain untainted.
With defilements exhausted, I have naturally reached the state of the Honored One; there is no longer any arising or ceasing.
Having entered the level and upright path, one does not follow narrow-minded views;
calculating that there is no self, one gives rise to the thought of non-arising, and through this, one attains the Way and attains extinction.
My lifespan spans many kalpas, and those whom I have delivered are beyond measure.
With the will severed, eternally extinguished and tranquil, how could there be a consciousness that saves others?
Adorned with the sevenfold contemplation as a jeweled necklace, the color of the Way’s flowers remains unchanging;
formless yet entering all realms of existence—this is called the practice of a Bodhisattva.

The Tathāgata has two kinds of activity: the fundamental path endowed with all virtues, and the manifestation of illusory dharmas through skillful means; thus he accords with that which neither arises nor ceases.
Among the classes of beings in the heavens and the world, there are no forms and no numbers.
How can one who possesses a physical form well understand the formless dharma?
The Hero of the World is an inexhaustible treasury; it cannot be exhausted by form or desire.
How much less, then, can those who have not yet attained the Way fathom his wisdom of equality?
Though passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they have never allowed their resolve to rest;
when sentient beings fall into indolence, they remain steadfast and do not falter in their intent.
As for the Mahāyāna Dharma of equality, how could its hearing and reception ever come to an end?
"Now I have briefly explained the wisdom of emptiness; why do you still harbor doubts regarding emptiness?
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, he suddenly vanished.

To the south, at a distance of eighteen hundred million *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of] Ganges rivers, there is a buddha-field named Adorned Purity (*Vyūhaśuddhi*). Therein dwells a Buddha named Vimala Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
Manifesting a physical form of infinite and towering majesty, he spoke these verses among the great assembly:
"I originally arose from the Way; Having heard the wisdom of the equality of emptiness, After twelve kalpas had passed, I finally attained this concentrated mind."
Contemplating their coming and going, the practices of the six perfections and four immeasurables all arise from the karma of wisdom in emptiness; thus they are the blazing foundation of all dharmas.
Though there are gradations in the initial resolve, there is no difference in the great vows.
With unattached wisdom and contemplation, he transforms beings without distinction.
Just as in the lands where I travel, adorned with exquisite and wondrous necklaces, he proclaims this extraordinary wisdom; in those lands, there are no three evil realms.
One practices only the conduct of the wisdom of emptiness, Without clinging to the positions of existence or non-existence.
Since I have no mental activity, How could I say that [anything] exists?
Just as intrinsic nature has no form or characteristic, The dharma-realm is likewise pure.
Having understood that [all things] are already exhausted and extinguished, there is therefore neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, beyond ten billion adorned and pure lands, in those realms this Dharma exists:
the practice of purity and unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*).
To speak of non-existence is itself a word; Not to dwell upon the basis of marks, one should thus remain in tranquil concentration.
When practice is exhausted, there is no name or designation.
The mind of sentient beings tends toward its objects, Arising as the fundamental consciousness according to its kind.
As I am forever serene and detached, I perceive neither existence nor non-existence.
Thus, throughout incalculable eons, I have severed all seeking and do not cling to existence;
desiring neither arising nor cessation, I have finally attained fulfillment.
Now, though empty and without body, he manifests forms according to where beings go;
the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless and never becomes defiled.
His nature is naturally pure, and he perceives no notion of permanence.
Endowed with the wisdom of the Path and all virtues, he is therefore named Vimala (Stainless).
Since attaining the fruit of the Way, he has traveled throughout the realms of empty space;
at times he became Śakra, Lord of Devas, and at other times the Great Honored One, Brahmā King of Gods.
Therefore, manifesting transformations of form, he converts those attached to existence,
leading them all toward the wisdom of non-arising, until they reach ultimate purity.
He further becomes a Wheel-Turning King, ruling over countless cities.
Having renounced the world to practice the Way, one realizes that such knowledge is not enduring.
Returning once more to the company of the śrāvakas, appearing as if one has not yet attained the Way,
one immediately receives instruction from a teacher and severs all fetters of conceptual attachment.

He further proceeded to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and expounded the root of pure conduct, so that they might relinquish the blessings of those celestial realms; for these beings do not exhaust suffering.
As for the formless sentient beings, they conceive the notion of permanence and do not depart from such thoughts.
Those who are arrogant and self-indulgent are all led to enter the gateway of the Way.
The Original Non-being, the Perfectly Awakened One, has no manifested form through which to transform others;
yet, until the root of birth and death is exhausted, he will never abandon them to enter quiescence.
"How much more so for you fourfold assembly now, who have become indolent upon first hearing this?
Such as these have their own appointed time; it cannot be brought to fulfillment quickly.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, he suddenly vanished.

To the west, beyond a hundred billion Ganges-sands of Buddha-fields, there is a land named Crystal. Its Buddha is named Pure Honored One Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. The sentient beings of that land uphold but a single dharma, and they lack the foundation of various practices such as the six perfections. Furthermore, amidst the great assembly, he spoke this verse:
"The eightfold path has no high or low; It extends straight to the ultimate extinction.
Casting off one body to receive another Only increases the defilements of dust and toil."
In space there is no duality of dharmas; it has no abiding place and leaves no trace.
The wisdom of the Eightfold Path is the sphere where all Buddhas roam.
In the past, I myself established this practice and turned the Dharma through my great vows.
Embodied in faith, he returns to the non-existent, and now has attained the status of the Honored One among men.
The lands where the Buddhas dwell differ in their skillful means and teachings;
appearing in every place, they manifest in order to transform all living beings.
Bound and attached by sensual pleasures, one dwells forever in a dark chamber;
only when one follows the path that has been vowed since the beginningless past can one finally attain liberation.
As for the people of my land, they restrain their minds and do not commit evil.
In the end, one honors non-action; thus, one draws near to the Way.
When the defilements of lust, anger, and delusion are thin, one does not need to exert great effort;
naturally one enters into the practice of the precepts, like a flower blooming in its season.
The intent for the Way is unshakable; the mind is forever severed from suffering and pleasure.
Traveling to and visiting various buddha-lands, they exhaustively cultivate the wisdom of emptiness.
Since I have now practiced this single path, those multitudes are likewise not different.
Now that I have heard of the Honored One, the Able Benefactor, I therefore manifest the cultivation of equal wisdom.
The Great Sages have all gathered like clouds; though they are noble and honored, there is no distinction of high or low.
Although they manifest different lands, that which they cultivate is the same Dharma.
Now observe the beings of the five destinies, obscured by ignorance and karmic formations;
submerged in birth and death, they increase their toil and suffering all the more.
Why do you not establish your own resolve and embody the path of wisdom in emptiness?
"One shall swiftly attain liberation, Just like the sentient beings of other lands.
After the Tathāgata had spoken this verse, he suddenly vanished.

Three *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddha-lands to the north of here, there is a land named Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*). There dwells a Buddha named Skillful Eloquence (*Pratibhānavatī*) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who further addressed the great assembly in verse:
“The Way of the Tathāgata has but a single characteristic; it originally arises from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Through diligent toil over countless eons, one finally exhausts the afflictions of worldly dust.
It is like a person wishing to cross the void who does not seek skillful means.”
One merely recollects and hopes for empty dharmas, yet there is no means by which the fruit can be attained.
Bound as one is by conceptual thought, failing to reckon that all things are impermanent,
to seek the ground of immortality— this too has never been achieved.
Abiding in detachment, one does not dwell in the realms of existence or non-existence;
having attained the wisdom that treads upon emptiness, one is naturally free from defilement and attachment.
The Way arises from the very source of the body, and only thereafter is perfect enlightenment realized.
Deluded in mind and heart, one errs by seeking emptiness outside the mind.
Though external suffering has its name, it does not exist apart from its perception and ideation.
The path of the pure Dharma-realm corresponds to pure wisdom.
Sentient beings dwell within birth and death, Sunk and drowning, unable to pull themselves out;
If they wish to be free from all afflictions, They must first eliminate the mental consciousness.
That which is manifested by the Tathāgata Is the thorough exposition of the incomparable Dharma.
The single characteristic is undefiled; by what means could emptiness be defiled again?
With the most supreme threefold knowledge, having transcended obstructed forms, his present mindfulness is not the original mindfulness;
it is a mindfulness that arises in dependence upon sentient beings.
All dharmas are inconceivable; they neither exist nor do they not exist.
As there is an echo only because of sound, so there is a Buddha only because of sentient beings.
Those sentient beings who receive transformation constantly feel weary of and loathe their own bodies.
“The Path can extinguish what is not the Path; there is nothing that is not the True Dharma.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken this verse, he suddenly disappeared.

To the northeast, ninety-two billion *koṭis* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* worlds away, there is a land named Pure Contemplation (*Vimaladarśana*). There dwells a Buddha named Dharma-Contemplation Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who, before this great assembly, spoke these verses:
"Form is fundamentally without form, Nor does it possess the characteristics of form;
Sensation and phenomena have no arising or ceasing, Nor do they arise from renewed contact."
Consciousness is like a wild horse; like bubbles on water, it does not remain for long.
When there is no body, wisdom is naturally pure; this is called the emptiness of equality.
With a single contemplation and a single application of mindfulness, one practices the pure and honored holy life.
I am attached to the notion of a self, yet I have not reached the realm of existence or non-existence.
Having awakened myself and awakening others, I cause them to attain the wisdom of emptiness;
because sentient beings do not awaken themselves, they harbor doubts.
Natures are of superior, middling, and inferior grades; good and evil are always in opposition.
Abandoning evil to practice good, one must not lack the wisdom of emptiness.
Being able to see neither good nor evil, the mind is upright and free from inversion.
Thereupon, he believed and understood emptiness, Attaining pure and pristine wisdom.
From a fundamentally equanimous mind, He perceived no distinction among the various classes of beings;
After a long time, he attained self-realization, Responding to the Unsurpassed Way.
Insightful observation removes greedy attachment; The mind is washed clean and free from stain.
With benevolence and wisdom like the wisdom of space, It is therefore called the Dharma of the True Person.
Out of compassion for the beings of the world, He expounds the Way of emptiness and non-existence.
Not dwelling on the opposition of good and evil, Without form and without conceptual thought.
I originally followed the mind of equanimity; The Tathāgata received this Dharma from me.
Upon hearing it, I immediately attained the wisdom of emptiness, And contemplated the transformation and purification of the buddha-fields.
"Having received the mandate for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*), he preached the Dharma until the end to transform beings;
leading countless people, he caused them to enter this fundamental realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One suddenly vanished.

One hundred million buddha-fields to the southeast of here, there is a land named Supreme Wonder, where the Buddha is named Subtle and Wondrous Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. He further spoke in verse:
"Consciousness fundamentally arises from the five aggregates;
Through the convergence of causes and conditions, It wanders through countless kalpas, Arising spontaneously and ceasing naturally."
Foolish and deluded sentient beings, failing to comprehend the root of birth and death,
dwell forever within the womb and do not seek to escape calamity and affliction.
Just as in the space of a single thought-moment, they produce nothing but inverted views.
Bondage and attachment have thus become exceedingly rampant; how much less could the roots of the Path arise?
When I contemplate the various classes of sentient beings, they delight in the source of the three poisons.
The five hindrances obscure the mind and spirit; without eyes, how can there be vision?
The Tathāgata holds the great torch, extinguishing the root of worldly desires;
yet though they behold his wisdom and brilliance, they still fail to give rise to firm faith.
As I observe the worlds of the ten directions, I resolve my mind to seek the Way.
When karma is exhausted, one undergoes rebirth once more, destined again for the afflictions of the three miserable realms.

These four stations are not one's original vow; one casts oneself into the four abysses, never departing from the gates of the four modes of birth, and failing to achieve the fruits of the four paths.
Sometimes, separated from the four dharmas, one gives rise to the five aggregates of clinging;
without attachment, yet possessing overweening pride, one does not exhaust heedless conduct.
Gradually reaching countless states, one fails to behold the source of noble practice.
Just as a person’s mind wanders astray, failing to guard or reflect upon itself,
so too the Tathāgata’s six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are neither empty nor distinct from emptiness;
having forever removed the root of birth and death, he thus accords with the wisdom of equality.

Fundamentally, there is no birth or death; yet, through the flow of transmigration and attachment to form, one eventually becomes the form of the *dharmadhātu*. To extinguish existence is not to cling to non-existence.
Where there is a path, there is consciousness; this consciousness is not originally non-existent.
When one is able to not perceive the consciousness of the Path, one then accords with the dharma of wisdom and concentration.
Since the Path arises from the further enjoyment of consciousness, it manifests in countless transformations;
when one knows for oneself that concentration and wisdom are perfected, one then accords with the transformations of the various marks.
Abiding nowhere and unchanging, free from doubt and hesitation, having subdued all afflictions, one then accords with the wisdom of equality.
When people act, there are three obstructions: they do not relinquish conceptualization and fail to realize emptiness.
"Without having first established the foundation for all practices, this karma will not achieve fulfillment.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, he suddenly vanished from sight.

Thirteen billion buddha-fields to the southwest of here, there is a land named Vast Excellence (*Viśiṣṭa*). Therein dwells the Buddha named Wondrous Trace (*Vicitrapada*) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who, amidst a great assembly, spoke these verses:
“The arising of awakening is an illusory dharma; It does not reside within the profound essentials of the Dharma.
If even the Path has no name or designation, How much less can one perceive the traces of words in emptiness?”
The various external and internal sense bases, when analyzed, are entirely non-existent;
formless and invisible, they accord with pure wisdom.
One does not follow the mind in calculating desires, nor does one cling to emptiness.
Mutually free from defilement and attachment, they attain the most perfect enlightenment.
The ignorant, not yet seeing the light, reckon that [delusion] arises from mind and consciousness;
as the six dharmas give rise to the six sense objects, from this they give birth to thoughts of doubt.
Due to consciousness, one receives this body, Naturally forming the four great elements;
Revolving through the five destinies, One does not understand the dharma of emptiness.
It is like a person who thinks, And says to himself that defilement is fundamentally non-existent.
Body and mind arise together with obstruction; how could one penetrate the notions of existence and non-existence?
With wondrous contemplation, they illumine the three periods of time, manifesting and teaching all dharmas.
The essence and wondrous teaching of all Buddhas are neither existent nor non-existent.
The suffering of the world arises from ignorance; it is equal, empty, and without dependence.
By contemplating and understanding existence and non-existence as equal, it is called the wisdom of equality.
When consciousness perceives existence and non-existence, this is not the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Untainted by either self or other, the mind is as level as an echo responding to a sound.
The Eightfold Path exhausts the source of suffering; the eight liberations wash away the dust of the mind.
The eight echoes all return to emptiness; the eight wisdoms give rise to no further birth.
Detaching from oneself and further detaching from that, with no obstruction in between;
following what consciousness is stained by and attached to—this is called equalizing wisdom (*samatā-prajñā*).
Humans originally abide in empty space, yet their stained consciousness leads them through the three realms of existence.
The Tang dynasty has long been shrouded in the dust of worldly toil, failing to enter the fundamental realm of non-limitation.
From the very first generation of the aspiration for enlightenment, the wisdom of the nature of emptiness has never diminished;
yet, after passing through immeasurable eons, one finally attains this samādhi.
I understand the minds of this assembly: they seek emptiness apart from consciousness.
Why do you not reflect upon consciousness itself—that it is empty within and likewise without?
As phenomena are without marks according to the Dharma, so too is the vision of wisdom.
Through mindfulness and concentration, one removes distraction; this is called impartial wisdom.
This body entirely returns to emptiness, eternally quiescent and without arising or ceasing.
The Tathāgata, with his universal great vows, delivers these multitudes of living beings.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One suddenly vanished.

To the northwest, beyond lands as numerous as the sands of fifty-four billion Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-field named *Anuvartana*. There dwells a Buddha named *Viśvarūpa*, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who, amidst the assembled multitude, uttered this verse:
"As I contemplate the practice of emptiness, My single mind is without high or low."
Existence and non-existence, right and wrong—all these arise from birth and death.

Those who seek the Buddha’s profound treasury and wish to exhaustively investigate the root of all conditioned phenomena have never been able to fully fathom it; only the Tathāgata’s divine wisdom penetrates it.
Suppose there were a man who, from eon to eon, for hundreds of thousands of millions of such eons, neither increased nor decreased in number.
That person possessed all his faculties, with no deficiency in the six sense organs.
If one wishes to hear the wisdom of the Tathāgata, it will not be easily or suddenly attained;
how much more so for those who have only recently resolved their minds and wish to reach that wisdom of equality?
They will only suffer further decline, gaining no benefit for the Dharma.
One must cultivate great compassion, protect oneself through skillful means and wisdom, and maintain firm and fearless vows; only then can the mind be subdued.
Even if one travels through the worlds wishing to make offerings to the Buddhas, [one must first achieve this].
Without giving rise to the effort of conditioned action, one naturally accords with holy practice.
The Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers of a sage, subdues all false views;
through the patient realization of the markless self, he has attained the status of the Honored One among men.
Realizing that phenomena abide yet do not abide, One does not perceive the practice of merit;
Exhausting birth so as never to receive it again— This is the realm of the Hero of the World.
Desiring to perfect the various marks and signs, One must not sever the roots of all goodness.
To extinguish the mind and not give rise to conceptualization—this is called impartial wisdom.
When I observe the various classes of sentient beings, they are unaware of time and emptiness;
for this reason, they are constantly exhausted and do not enter the state of eternal stillness.
"If you wish to swiftly attain the fruits of the Path and adorn your body with manifold virtues, simply contemplate severing the root of the mind; why then give rise to doubt?
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One suddenly vanished.

Countless Buddha-lands away from here, extending to the very limits of the realm of sentient beings, there is a world-system named Revolving. There dwells a Buddha named Sound-like-Voice Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who, amidst a great assembly, spoke these verses:
"Space has no form or consciousness; It possesses neither this shore nor the other.
Since no sentient beings are perceived, How much less could there be one who wanders through the Dharma-realm?"
Those seeking the Way now wander in emptiness seeking the empty;
having already recognized what is impure, they further seek external emptiness.
Compassionately mindful of such people, whose minds do not understand noble wisdom, [I teach them].
Contemplating this wisdom-observation, one also attains the path of impermanence.
Now receiving a body within the three realms, one distinguishes through penetrating wisdom;
with concentration and consciousness free from formal conceptions, the severing of seeds constitutes the intent of the Path.
A person reflects upon consciousness itself; the four great elements serve as its nesting place.
Even if it were to exist outside in emptiness, it would not differ from the four great elements.
It is simply that one has not yet attained wisdom and has not yet fully understood internal and external conditions.
These beings are worthy of compassion; the World-Honored One does not reproach them.
This Great Man is without equal; his practice transcends the sphere of non-ideation—this is called the Dharma of all Buddhas.
Deluded, one reckons oneself as a self; yet fundamentally there is no dharma of arising or ceasing—ultimately all is utterly pure.
The holy life (brahmacarya) is ultimately pure; one does not give rise to thoughts of the three periods of time.
What was previously said is not what is said now; moment by moment, things change and transform of their own accord.
This may serve as proof; why then do you give rise to doubt?
Since I did not claim for myself, but merely assumed the guise of an ordinary person, I contemplated these four great elements and considered from where the phenomena of consciousness arise.
I shall proclaim the phenomena of the past, which are formless and invisible.
Although future consciousness exists, it has not yet received the four great elements.
The present consists of two categories; I shall now explain each one in detail.
Each of you should not harbor doubts regarding this wisdom of equality.
To discern past consciousness: that which died was not the present form;
yet this consciousness does not decay, and thus it is designated as "past consciousness."
If consciousness exists in the present, A combination of the four great elements as causes and conditions,
And this consciousness remains forever unchanging, Yet you still call it "present consciousness.
Furthermore, if one abandons the present, The future has not yet arisen.
That consciousness is not of the present; by what means could it be called belonging to the three periods of time?
The nature of consciousness always abides in itself; it has no past, no future, and no present.
If one seeks the root of consciousness, where is its nest and lair?
The Tathāgata’s peerless wisdom has realized that the source of consciousness is fundamentally non-existent;
the nature of emptiness is tranquil and one—do not harbor further doubts or conceptions.
If you wish to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment, do not be stained by conceptual attachments or conditioned activities.
"Fully knowing the nature of non-consciousness, he is therefore called Equal Wisdom.
When the Tathāgata had spoken this verse, he suddenly vanished.

Eleven *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands] of *kalpas* below this place, there is a land named *Anūnatva*. Therein dwells a Buddha named Samantapraṇidhāna Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. In that assembly, he spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions gather, Equal and without duality;
They all preach the samādhi of emptiness, Tranquil and without activity."
Sentient beings harbor the notion of permanence, Claiming that emptiness is finite;
Realizing that the fundamental is untainted, This is called returning entirely to emptiness.
Without attachment in the mind of giving, One loses the practice of the original vow.
Thus they give rise to the karma of slander, [claiming] there is no Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha.
The Tathāgata’s body of precept-virtue is pure and without blemish;
having delivered those yet to be delivered, it is beyond conceptualization throughout the three times.
Empty consciousness has its own name; it arises spontaneously and ceases spontaneously.
This arising is not empty consciousness, and the cessation of consciousness is likewise so.
Because they do not penetrate the fundamental source, people wander about in pursuit of the characteristics of consciousness.
Conventional emptiness is designated as consciousness; how could emptiness and consciousness be different?
The characteristics of the body are like formlessness; one birth follows another in succession.
It is only for the sake of deluded and ignorant people that consciousness arises in its various forms.
The multitude of wisdoms constitute the essence of the Dharma; the marks and signs naturally adorn the body.
When the body perishes, wisdom returns to emptiness—how then could one say that consciousness exists?
Upon investigation, the three periods of time are not found; there is no consciousness and no four great elements.
One then attains the ability to roam the Dharma-realm, knowing that existence is neither existent nor non-existent.
The immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas manifests through skillful means without increase or decrease;
by means of this form beyond consciousness, one travels everywhere throughout the buddha-fields.
"This doubt has long existed; it is not unique to you, but I am the same.
Only when universal wisdom shines upon all can one truly recognize a Buddha.
When the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, he suddenly vanished.
At that moment, eleven nayutas of sentient beings present in the assembly all attained the contemplation of the wisdom of universal emptiness.

Furthermore, immeasurable numbers of sentient beings—including devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits—upon hearing this teaching of the Dharma, all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.

Chapter Seven: The Exhortation and Assistance of All Buddhas (3) The Bodhisattva-āraṇyaka Sūtra, Chapter Seven: The Exhortation and Assistance of All Buddhas. At that time, the World-Honored One ascended the Seat of Fearlessness and emitted the radiance of the mark of the tongue, which universally illuminated the trichiliocosm, as well as the countless Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. It also reached the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts throughout the ten directions—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—extending even to all sentient beings within the void of the ten directions, so that they all beheld this light.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of countless rays of light. Those various sentient beings said to one another:
"For a long, long time, we have never seen such subtle and wondrous light; neither the stars, nor the sun and moon, nor the deva-sons possess such radiance."
How extraordinary! How marvelous!
Never before have we heard such a thing, nor have we ever seen it.
At that time, sentient beings in the various lands throughout the ten directions each gave rise to this thought:
"Could it be that a Buddha has appeared in the world?

Then, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts within the minds of the sentient beings of the ten directions, manifested various radiances, each of which featured a transformation Buddha. Each of these transformation Buddhas was surrounded before and behind by immeasurable multitudes who listened as they preached the Dharma.
What is called "preaching the Dharma" refers to a Dharma that has no form or characteristics, no verbal teaching, and is a Dharma without birth, aging, sickness, or death.

Thereafter, those who have not seen the light or perceived forms and colors shall all hear the resonance of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma—the wisdom of emptiness and the wisdom of phenomena—which speaks of the unattached mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the fourfold assembly gathered there, saying:

"Do you all behold this inconceivable dharma of the radiance from the mark of the tongue, which reaches throughout the countless *asaṃkhyeya* lands of the ten directions like the sands of the Ganges, universally illuminating immeasurable classes of sentient beings and causing various emanation Buddhas to preach the Dharma? Do you, sentient beings, see it or not?"
At that time, all the bodhisattva mahāsattvas endowed with supernormal powers addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We have all seen it."
Those ordinary beings who were attached to desire further spoke to the Buddha themselves, saying: "World-Honored One!
Although we have seen this radiance, we do not know what auspicious omen this light portends."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings and wishing to remove their doubts and eliminate their attachments to false imaginings, addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mṛdusvara, saying:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One of Unsurpassed Right Enlightenment, possesses a body of golden hue with a circular halo seven feet in diameter; his voice is like that of the kalaviṅka bird—soft and flawless; and his body is adorned with all the marks of excellence. All of these result from the accumulation of merit and the practice of goodness over incalculable kalpas in the past, whereby he has become fully endowed with all virtues."

He does not commit verbal transgressions, and his spoken teachings neither exceed nor fall short of the truth; therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, now attains the retributive dharma of the fourteen marks of the tongue:
first, his speech and voice are sincere and free from deception;
second, whatever he says is immediately believed and understood upon being heard.
Third, his verbal conduct does not lose the gates of the faculties;
fourth, he knows the proper time and preaches the Dharma without omission;
fifth, he himself delights in expounding and disseminating the prohibitions and precepts.
Sixth, the sequential correspondence of names and phrases;
seventh, being empowered by great compassion so as not to abandon the mind of giving;
eighth, beholding the image of the Buddha without harboring doubt or hesitation.
Ninth, they attain the spiritual powers of a Buddha and sport therein;
tenth, having entered the Dharma-realm, they do not abandon the wisdom of a Buddha;
eleventh, they obtain the inexhaustible treasury of immeasurable wisdom.
Twelfth, the Buddha’s mind is formless, yet all enter it completely;
thirteenth, his skillful means and wisdom are unimpeded, and he perceives no one being delivered;
fourteenth, abiding in the wisdom of ultimate truth, all people place firm faith in him.
These are called the retributions for the fourteen marks of the tongue.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who obtain these retributions for the fourteen marks of the tongue, they are then able to emit immeasurable light that illuminates all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions; this is entirely due to their having been free from deception in speech in the past.
The Buddha again addressed Mṛdusvara:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who uphold, recite, and chant this profound Dharma, they shall immediately obtain the ten marks of physical form that never weary."
What are these ten?
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha ascends the seat of fearlessness; first, through the contemplation of equality, he gathers his mind in silent stillness and reflects within himself:
"I am now among the assembly as a hero among men; sitting here upon this seat, there is much that can be accomplished."
He further reflected:

"The categories of sentient beings are inconceivable; some who are at the stage of faith may wish to regress, while others at the first through sixth stages may likewise wish to regress. It would be appropriate to set them aside for now and not include them within the ranks of the noble ones."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose minds are excessively bound and attached by lust, anger, and delusion; these are also distinguished as being outside the category of the noble ones.
Or there may be sentient beings whose minds revere wealth and nobility and do not cultivate the roots of virtue; these too are set aside and do not belong to the category of the noble ones.
There may be sentient beings whose ignorance is rampant and who give rise to conceited conduct; these are also set aside and not included among the ranks of the noble ones.

There may be sentient beings whose minds understand that all phenomena are illusory and who perceive the Tathāgata as an illusion that is not the Buddha; these are also set aside and not included among the ranks of the noble ones.

“Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who attain mundane supernatural powers and perceive the Buddha’s divine virtues as no different from their own; these are likewise set aside and not included among the ranks of the noble ones.

Or there may be sentient beings whose nature is such that they possess strong memories, yet do not believe in the Tathāgata’s practice of dhāraṇī; these are likewise set aside and not included among the ranks of the noble ones.”

There may be sentient beings whose inclination toward giving is predominant; upon hearing that the Tathāgata’s giving is no different from their own, they too are set aside and not included among the ranks of the noble ones.
There may be sentient beings who possess exclusively a mind for ethical discipline; upon hearing that the Tathāgata’s discipline is no different from their own, [they likewise are set aside].
This too is set aside and does not fall within the category of the noble ones.
Or suppose there were a sentient being whose mind was constantly compassionate and patient, thinking, "How is the patience of the World-Honored One now any different from mine?
This too is set aside and does not fall within the category of the noble ones.
"Or there may be sentient beings who exert themselves with diligence, thinking: 'How does the diligence of the World-Honored One differ from mine?
This too is set aside and not included among the ranks of the noble ones.
Or there may be sentient beings whose minds delight in the practice of dhyāna, thinking: 'How does the World-Honored One's practice of dhyāna differ from mine?'"
This too is set aside and does not fall within the category of the noble ones.
Or, there may be sentient beings who possess worldly eloquence and ask, "How does the wisdom of the World-Honored One differ from mine?
This too is set aside and does not fall within the category of the noble ones.
“‘There may be sentient beings who possess a partiality for loving-kindness (*maitrī*); how does the Tathāgata’s practice of loving-kindness differ from theirs?
This case, too, is set aside and not included among the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Or there may be sentient beings whose compassionate intention (*karuṇā*) is uninterrupted; how does the Tathāgata’s practice of compassion differ from theirs?’”
This too is set aside and does not fall within the category of the noble ones.
Or there may be sentient beings who constantly harbor joy, thinking, "What is the Tathāgata’s joy different from mine?
This too is set aside and does not fall within the category of the noble ones.
"Or there may be sentient beings whose minds are constantly characterized by relinquishment; how would the Tathāgata’s relinquishment differ from theirs?
This case, too, is set aside and not included among the ranks of the noble ones.
'Or there may be sentient beings whose minds are constantly mindful of emptiness; how would the Tathāgata’s practice of emptiness differ from theirs? "
This too is set aside and does not fall within the category of the noble ones.
Or there may be sentient beings whose minds are not inquisitive, thinking, "What difference would it make if the Tathāgata had no aspirations for me?
This too is set aside and does not fall within the category of the noble ones.
“Or there may be sentient beings who do not give rise to conceptual attachments, thinking: ‘The Tathāgata is without conceptualization; how is he any different from me?
This case, too, is set aside and does not fall within this category.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara:

"The inclinations and aspirations of sentient beings differ according to where they dwell; throughout all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—the mental thoughts of sentient beings are each distinct and not the same."

There may be sentient beings in the realm of desire who indulge in the five desires yet do not relinquish the five aggregates; these, too, are set aside and do not fall within the category of the noble ones.

There may be sentient beings who, while calculating [the nature of] form, maintain it in their minds and do not internally cling to desire; these, too, are set aside and do not fall within the category of the noble ones.
"Or there may be sentient beings who aspire to and delight in the formless realm; these too are set aside and do not fall within the category of the noble ones.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara:
"The mental consciousnesses of the various classes of sentient beings differ, and their practices are each distinct."
The reason for this is that they are all so steeped in perversion that they can suddenly be awakened.

As I observe the various classes of sentient beings today, I know where their minds are directed and what paths they seek; I travel to the countless lands throughout the ten directions, understanding each one clearly without error.
It is just as if a man with sight were to personally grasp a divine moon-pearl in his own hand, examining it clearly without confusion or any other distracting thoughts.
I am now likewise so disposed, discerning the fundamental course of the spiritual consciousness and past conduct of sentient beings.
There may be sentient beings who, in the space of a single thought-moment, perform one or two courses of action; these are also set aside and do not fall within the category of the noble ones.

There may be sentient beings who, within a single thought-moment, fulfill all various courses of action, yet those actions are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); these too are set aside and do not fall within the category of the noble ones.
There may be sentient beings who possess precepts but lack generosity, or who possess generosity but lack precepts; these too are set aside and do not fall within the category of the noble ones.
There may be sentient beings who are endowed with the six practices, or who are not endowed with the six practices; these too are set aside and do not fall within the category of the noble ones.
The countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, first perfected these three grades of practice and only thereafter preached the Dharma.
Were it even so for the future, all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who wish to preach the Dharma, shall likewise perfect these three grades of sublime conduct.

What are the three? First, observing that the thoughts of sentient beings differ from moment to moment; second, that the majestic and fearless *bodhimaṇḍa* of the Buddhas cannot be established by *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*; and third, [observing] that all dharmas are empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, and beyond conceptualization. This is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the three gates of liberation. What are the three? First, contemplating all dharmas as being like an illusion; second, contemplating all dharmas as being like a dream; and third, contemplating all dharmas as being like an echo. This is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the three gates of liberation. What are the three? First, contemplating all dharmas as being like a reflection; second, contemplating all dharmas as being like a mirage; and third, contemplating all dharmas as being like a phantom. This is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the three gates of liberation. What are the three? First, contemplating all dharmas as being like space; second, contemplating all dharmas as being like a flame; and third, contemplating all dharmas as being like a water bubble. This is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the three gates of liberation. What are the three?
