Third, regarding dharmas never heard before, the Tathāgata teaches them so that they all return to the wisdom of emptiness;
these are called the three kinds of sublime practices of the Tathāgata, which remain entirely without deficiency or omission when the Dharma is being preached.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that the three types of sublime conduct established by the Tathāgata differ from one another?”
At that time, the World-Honored One replied: "So it is, so it is;
it is just as you have said. I shall now explain to you one by one what are called the three kinds of sublime practices of a bodhisattva."

When the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, first enters the Samādhi of the Universal Marks of Concentration, he preaches the Dharma to the entire assembly for the sake of all sentient beings. For such immeasurable multitudes whose minds are of one consciousness and whose thoughts are likewise identical, they hear the meaning of suffering and no other teaching; thus, they attain entry into the rank of the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, son of good family!

The Buddhas of the past, future, and present know the thoughts within the minds of those sentient beings; they first attain supreme, right Dharma through equal enlightenment, yet they teach that there are dharmas which do not transcend conceptual attachment. This, too, should not be categorized among the examples of the noble ones.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, first gathers his ten mental states into undistracted contemplation before he expounds the profound and wondrous treasury of the Dharma, so that all classes of sentient beings may immediately understand the teachings they hear."

What are the ten? When the Tathāgata desires to preach the Dharma, he looks upon all sentient beings with single-minded unimpededness, considering which teaching would enable each to attain liberation.
Furthermore, since the dispositions of sentient beings vary in depth, by what skillful means can they be rescued and delivered?
Or, if the Dharma is taught as a single practice without duality, is this Dharma appropriate for these sentient beings or not?
Contemplating the immeasurable emptiness and consciousness of the mind’s thoughts, from what dharma do they arise?

Thereafter, one attains the liberation of the *vaiśāradya-samādhi* (the samādhi of valorous prowess), acting without stain or defilement. In a single thought-moment, all dharmas are fully present; one contemplates the entire Dharma-realm as being without beginning or end. One performs the deeds of all Buddhas without obstruction, universally moistening all things with immeasurable wisdom.

Once the assembly was settled, he used his supernormal powers to illumine their minds; having discerned their fundamental conditions, he preached the Dharma for them, which is indeed the standard practice of the sages.
"Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra!..."
When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha ascends the seat of fearlessness, he must further be fully endowed with ten inexhaustible dharmas. What are these ten?
The Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas is inconceivable; the Buddha-body is immeasurable, and the Dharma is likewise immeasurable.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, further possesses an inexhaustible ocean of formless dharmas through which he performs buddha-works; furthermore, there is that which is inexhaustible and not encompassed by visual consciousness, universally observing all forms and formless things throughout the ten directions.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through his skillful means and expedient devices, rescues and delivers sentient beings; never forsaking his original vow, he establishes all universally so that they may cultivate the ten wholesome actions.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, maintains constant internal one-pointedness of mind while externally manifesting the teaching of the Dharma; he does not employ a fixed state of quiescence, nor does he manifest confusion externally while teaching the Dharma."

"Furthermore, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha preaches the Dharma, he lets fall the rain of the nectar-like Dharma, universally moistening and nourishing all sentient and insentient beings, those with consciousness and those without."

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, while at home, achieved a physical appearance of such extraordinary excellence that even when the great assembly was seated on higher seats, they would humble their minds and remain lowly; he would not proclaim his own surname as noble and aristocratic, nor would he speak of the clan from which the Tathāgata originally descended when among those of lower status."

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the knowledge of past lives, perceives former existences that are infinite and immeasurable. He sees sentient beings who are difficult to deliver, born within the five destinies, having originally created these conditions; now, through the causal conditions of retribution, they attain awakening."

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, gives rise to the great, far-reaching vow and the four immeasurable minds, enabling all sentient beings with form throughout the ten directions to attain Buddhahood in a single day, fully endowed with the various marks; according to reality and as they wish, they shall all achieve the Way of the Buddha."

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, establishes his resolve with firm stability and does not abandon his original intention; he causes immeasurable Buddha-worlds to all attain parinirvāṇa on a single day, and it never deviates from what he has intended. This is called the tenth inexhaustible essential dharma of the Tathāgata."

Ascending the seat of fearlessness, one possesses this essential dharma; it proclaims the inexhaustible teachings of the Tathāgata, which neither Arhats nor Pratyekabuddhas are capable of proclaiming.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara,
saying: "What do you think,
son of good family?"

If there are good sons or good daughters who practice emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and all establish themselves on the stage of faith to cultivate the bodhisattva practices, would their merit not be great?
The Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”
"It is immeasurable and beyond all analogy.
The Buddha told Navaśūra:
"It is not as good as a son or daughter of good family who upholds and recites the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries; the merit of the latter surpasses that of the former."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara:
"What do you think,
son of good family?"

If there are good men or good women who, having already attained the second stage and perfected its various practices, do not harbor indolence or a sense of inferiority, and furthermore make offerings as previously established in their faith.
"In all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is exactly like this;
would not their merit be great? Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "It is exceedingly great, exceedingly great, beyond all calculation."

Why is this? If there were good sons or good daughters who practiced all dharmas, progressing from the stage of faith to the second stage, and if such individuals as these were to fill the immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions—how truly marvelous!
"How extraordinary!
It is beyond all analogy.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"Therefore, compared to these good sons and good daughters who uphold and practice the ten inexhaustible dharmas, their merit is far greater, far more abundant, and beyond all comparison."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara, saying:

"If there were good sons or good daughters who, practicing all dharmas, accomplished the three stages and caused them all to be fully perfected as the root of all dharmas—along with the previous stages of faith and the second stage—and if in every Buddha-land throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it were likewise so for all such beings, would their merit not be great?"
Mṛdusvara addressed the Buddha, saying:

If there were good sons or good daughters who, having practiced all dharmas, proceeded from the stage of faith to the second and third stages, and if such individuals as these were to fill the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions beyond all comparison.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"Therefore, it is not as [meritorious] as when a son of good family or a daughter of good family upholds and practices these ten inexhaustible dharmas; their merit is exceedingly great, exceedingly great, beyond all comparison."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara:

"If there were good sons or good daughters who, practicing the various dharmas, accomplished the fourth stage and caused them all to be fully endowed with the aforementioned first, second, and third stages of faith—would their merit not be great?"
Mṛdusiri addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"Therefore, it is not so; the merit of these good sons and good daughters who uphold and recite the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries surpasses that of those aforementioned good sons and good daughters."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdvin:
"What do you think,
son of good family?"

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, being fully endowed with the dharma of truth and free from doubt, did not abandon the five stages of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-seal, and practiced through the stage of faith up to the fourth stage, pervading the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions—would their merit not be great?
Mṛdusvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is exceedingly much, exceedingly much.”
The Buddha said:
"Therefore, it is not like this: the merit of a good son or a good daughter who upholds and practices these ten inexhaustible dharmas is exceedingly great, beyond all comparison."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara:

"Furthermore, setting this aside, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, having already reached the sixth stage and perfected all practices, have transcended those [realms of] emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—of this they are certain and have no doubt—and who, while practicing the stage of faith up to the fifth stage, pervade immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions."
What do you think,
son of good family?
Would that merit not be great?
Mṛdusvara addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Very much, very much.
The Buddha said:
"Therefore, the merit of these good sons and good daughters who uphold, recite, and chant the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries surpasses that of the former.
The Buddha again addressed Mṛdvin:
"What do you think?"
O son of noble family!

If there are good men or good women whose great vows are firm and steadfast, who abide in the seventh stage without falling back, who are fully endowed with all dharmas and free from the notions of "self" and "other," and who—from the stage of faith up to the sixth stage—are complete in all virtues and fully prepared in all practices.
"What do you think,
son of good family!
Would that merit not be great?"
Mṛdusvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
“Therefore, it is not as good as for these sons and daughters of good family to uphold, recite, and chant the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries; their merit surpasses that of the former.”
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara:
"If there were good sons or good daughters who, having already passed through the seven stages, were to advance toward Buddhahood;

and if I, now dwelling in the state where there is no thought of 'self' or 'other,' were to personally realize this with certainty and without doubt—suppose such beings as these were to fill the ten directions, and one were to make offerings to them as previously described, from the stage of faith up to the seventh stage: would their merit not be great?"
Mṛdusvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"Therefore, it is not as good as for these sons and daughters of good family to uphold and recite the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries; their merit surpasses that of the former."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara:

"If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has already attained the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing, whose mind is like space and cannot be defiled, he need only employ skillful wisdom to proceed beneath the King of Trees."

Those of such a kind, from the stage of faith up to the eighth bhūmi, having perfected all practices and being not long from attaining Buddhahood, will fill the three thousandfold world system throughout its immeasurable realms.
"What do you think,
son of good family?
Would that merit not be great?"
Mṛdusvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Because these good sons and good daughters, having already dwelled as companions of the Buddha, are themselves called Buddhas; how much more so those in the ten directions throughout immeasurable worlds, from the stage of faith up to the eighth stage!
"Therefore, it is not equal to the merit of a single thought-moment of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of the ninth stage.

The Buddha said, "If there are good sons or good daughters who uphold, recite, and chant the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries, even though I have today attained the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, they still do not possess these Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries."

If there are good men or good women who wish to practice the ten inexhaustible treasuries; who wish to fully know how the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all attain the Way at one time and simultaneously enter parinirvāṇa; who wish to completely extinguish the mental consciousness and conceptual attachments of sentient beings; who wish to attain Buddhahood first; and who wish to gather in sentient beings so that their minds become identical to the Buddha-mind—they should practice these ten inexhaustible treasuries.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, amidst the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"Though I have now attained Buddhahood, It is due to the retribution for my past exhortations and assistance.
The True Dharma cannot be shifted; The Great Way is without variation."

Reflecting upon my own past lives, I served and made offerings to all the Buddhas, encouraging and assisting them through the teachings of the Dharma; I cast off the physical form until reaching the formless.
Yet, throughout countless eons, I did not obtain the inexhaustible treasury.
With resolve established and free from conceptual thought, one gradually reaches the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possessing the three types of knowledge, the six supernormal powers, and wisdom,
encourages and assists in the fulfillment of all practices, whereby one attains the inexhaustible treasury.
The original vow has now received its fruition; Thus he is titled the God among Gods.
This arises from the merit of encouragement and assistance, Attaining for oneself the state of the Infinite Honored One.
The rivers and seas may be exhausted, And the mountains and rivers may crumble away;
The sun and moon have their waning and waxing, yet the Dharma-treasury can never be exhausted.
The path of the Buddhas’ skillful wisdom is of inconceivable power;
nurturing all sentient beings, they turn the Dharma out of compassion.
Or while dwelling within the mother’s womb, desiring to transform his parents, he further becomes a Wheel-Turning King, ruling over countless lands.
How joyful is this retribution! To have obtained this inexhaustible treasury.
Through cultivation, he attained Buddhahood, with manifestations beyond measure.
In countless past lives, he performed meritorious deeds;
his encouragement and assistance were foremost, and none surpassed him.
The complete array of the seven treasures, gold and silver, possesses a splendor beyond compare;
all arise from the retribution of encouragement and assistance, an inexhaustible treasury of dharmas.
Though space itself is nothingness, it manifests through the creation of form and color.
"This Dharma is profoundly subtle; its true reality cannot be destroyed.
At that time, after the Tathāgata Śākyamuni had spoken these verses, he further addressed the sons and daughters of good family:

"If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from their first aspiration until they attain Buddhahood, cause all sentient beings to be no different from themselves, they should practice these ten inexhaustible treasuries."

At that time, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, being about to preach the Dharma and turn the wheel of the Dharma, entered the meditative concentration of the Inexhaustible Treasury. He moved all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, so that they appeared before him at that very moment. Simultaneously, with one voice, each spoke this verse:
“The present Dharma transcends the four meanings; The Tathāgata practices without attachment. Cultivating the One, he attains the Buddha-way; In mindfulness and diligence, there is no indolence.”
The three gates turn toward the equality of emptiness, And are called the Inexhaustible Treasury;
Without abandoning the foundation of the ten practices, This is termed the Tathāgatagarbha.
The Buddha-dharma is inconceivable, Like space that receives all things.
My consciousness does not perceive a self; this is the inexhaustible treasury.
The Buddha’s practice is not subject to exhaustion; what he expounds is immeasurable.
Out of compassion for all beings, he manifests that which is non-existent.
The marks of the Tathāgatas and all Buddhas are accomplished without distinction;
yet, according to the inclinations of sentient beings, their marks are known to have degrees of height and depth.
Now I am without equal, having grown weary of the suffering of sentient beings.
Governing one's own mind through the Way, one subdues all those of external paths.
The source of all dharmas is without conditions and does not combine;
through the awakening to equality, one attains the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The Buddhas are inconceivable; the fundamental nature of phenomena is inconceivable;
causes, retributions, and conditions are inconceivable; and their discernment is inconceivable.
Even if I were to dwell for a thousand kalpas, Buddha after Buddha would praise me of their own accord.
We have not yet exhausted the treasury of the Dharma; there is not even a hair’s breadth of diminution.
We have already attained Buddhahood, fully endowed with the empty Dharmakāya.
Having cultivated the inexhaustible treasury in the past, we have personally become the Honored Ones among men.
The realm of desire abounds in afflictions; to sever desire is not found elsewhere.
That one can become free from desire within desire is entirely due to the inexhaustible treasury.
Though dwelling therein, one does not dwell; nor does one possess any marks of form or color.
The various consciousnesses are attached to conceptual discrimination, yet the Buddha’s consciousness has no form or characteristic.
The Tathāgata has no physical marks, yet he manifests forms for the sake of sentient beings;
being without attachment and without defilement, the body of the Tathāgata is likewise empty.
"Pervading the realms of the ten directions, like the present Samyaksaṃbuddha, the fundamental consciousness is inconceivable; it expounds inexhaustible meanings.
At that time, after the Buddhas of the ten directions had spoken these verses, the eight directions, above and below, shook in six ways.
Among those seated were six hundred bhikṣus who had originally been intent upon attaining arhatship; at that moment, they turned their minds back and attained the inexhaustible treasury.
Furthermore, one billion three hundred million sentient beings also attained the inexhaustible dharma-treasury.
Chapter Eight: The Tathāgata (3). The Bodhisattva-Necklace Sūtra, Chapter Eight: The Tathāgata. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“How do the sons of good family cultivate the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma?
The Buddha said,
“If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to cultivate the inexhaustible Dharma, they should cultivate the Dharma-gate of the five sufferings.”
What are the five gateways of the Dharma of suffering?

If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing the worlds of the ten directions, hear of the wisdom of suffering and the consciousness of suffering, they are able to go forth according to their forms to receive and deliver them; this is called the first dharma.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to contemplate that the thoughts of sentient beings in immeasurable worlds are empty and non-existent, and who wish to attain the wisdom of emptiness and suffering, they should establish this intention and not regress; these are called the two dharmas."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all attain an impartial mind and practice inexhaustible compassion—causing those who have not yet attained to attain, those who have not yet achieved to achieve, and those who have not yet been delivered to be delivered—these are called the three dharmas."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having achieved success in their domestic lives and likewise in their lineage, all possess the wisdom of suffering such that their minds do not dwell on pleasure—these are called the four dharmas."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who possess the Tathāgata’s immeasurable Dharma-gates, inexhaustible treasury of Dharma, and mastery over all wisdom—this is called the fivefold inexhaustible treasury of Dharma."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If there are sons or daughters of noble family who wish to attain the complete and inexhaustible treasury of Dharma, there are another five matters.

What are the five? The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always abide in meditative equipoise; at times they enter the contemplation of space to discern sentient beings—those who abide within the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones and those who do not—and are able to establish them all securely, each fulfilling their aspirations. This is called the first dharma.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If you wish to be born in the heavens, you should practice the precepts and dharmas of the devas. There are devas with desire and devas without desire; there are times when some devas are attached to sensual pleasures and others are not. One who can fulfill both these conditions while remaining entirely free from defiled attachment accords with the inexhaustible Dharma."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
You should further fulfill four types of karmic retribution practices, whereby you may ride upon spiritual powers to travel through immeasurable worlds.
What are these four karmic retribution practices?

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, always abide in profound stillness. If there are devas, nāgas, gandharvas, or asuras who wish to hear the truth from the Tathāgata, even before they have uttered their question, the Tathāgata already knows that this son of noble family intends to ask about this meaning. This is called the first dharma: the practice of the four fruits of retribution.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"If a son or daughter of good family has a mind that is tranquil and does not wish to hear the Dharma, the Tathāgata fully knows what may be followed and what may not be followed, as well as their desire or lack of desire to hear the Dharma. This, son of good family, is called..."
The second is the retribution of fruition.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If a son or daughter of good family has already received the seal of the Tathāgata, they are then able to seal the minds and intentions of sentient beings; this is called the third retribution of fruition."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If a son or daughter of noble family, having heard the True Dharma—which cannot be fathomed by the mind nor measured by thought—causes all things to be equal and free from dualistic conceptions, this is called the fourth retribution."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If you wish to attain the perfection of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), you should also contemplate the karmic fruition of these four matters.
What are the four bases of psychic power?

Thereupon, for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment through the first, second, and up to the tenth stage, there are distinct modes of practice regarding their supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda).

There may be a bodhisattva who, while already established in the first stage, attains the bodily consciousness that travels through the infinite worlds of the ten directions, yet has not yet attained the concentrated mind that knows the thoughts of sentient beings.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, having already attained the first stage, are fully endowed with the physical marks and secondary signs of a Buddha; they likewise travel through and observe the worlds of the ten directions, paying homage to, serving, and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Although they have attained the supernormal power of the body, they are not yet capable of teaching and transforming sentient beings or purifying Buddha-lands.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having already attained the supernormal powers, pay homage to, serve, and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and are thus able to preach the Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings.

“Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having already purified their buddha-fields while on the first stage (*bhūmi*), are yet unable to know for themselves the matters of that first stage.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have not yet fully cultivated the mind of the Great Vehicle’s vast vows; they give rise to hesitation and conceptual attachment therein, and those of such a kind will inevitably fall into the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who cultivate the pure practices of a single stage and, by means of their supernormal powers, travel extensively through the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, thoroughly knowing the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings; yet they are not yet able to deliver those beings and establish them securely within the restraints of the Path.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having already attained the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) upon the first stage (*bhūmi*):

the first base of power is called "Contemplation of Suffering. Bodhisattvas who attain this base of power constantly travel through the worlds of all Buddhas, enabling sentient beings who suffer to dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The second base of power is called "Resonance. Bodhisattvas who attain this dharma travel throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions; among all sentient beings, those who should be liberated through resonance will hear what the bodhisattvas preach and believe and understand it without exception.

Furthermore, there is a supernormal power (ṛddhipāda) called "Arousing the Intention. When a Bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, they travel throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions; whenever sentient beings arouse the intention to pursue the Path, they are immediately able to protect them and cause them to achieve success.

Furthermore, there is a supernormal power called "Moving and Stirring. When a Bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, they travel throughout the ten directions to observe the minds of sentient beings; for those who should be delivered through the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā), this is what is meant by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of the First Stage being fully endowed with these four practices of supernormal power.
"The Bodhisattva of the Second Ground further possesses four matters. What are these four?

The Bodhisattva has a supernormal power called 'extinguishing the seeds. Having attained this supernormal power, he travels throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, fully knowing the thoughts and mental activities of all sentient beings; he extinguishes the seeds of ordinary persons and enters the realm of the Noble Truths."

Furthermore, there is the supernatural power (ṛddhi-pāda) called "Extinction. One who attains this supernatural power travels throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, observing the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings to discern whether they harbor wholesome or unwholesome intentions;

being able to extinguish unwholesome intentions, they enter the Noble Truths. Furthermore, there is a supernatural power named "Removal of Defilement. One who attains this supernatural power travels throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, observing and knowing that the defiled desires within the minds of sentient beings have entangled their hearts; being able to eliminate the conscious perceptions of ordinary worldlings, they enter the Noble Truths. Furthermore, there is the supernatural power of the "Three Skillful Means.

A Bodhisattva who attains this supernatural power travels throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, observing and knowing the mental perceptions of sentient beings, and is able to establish their intentions by instituting the three types of equal Dharma.

This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, having attained these four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*), is able to travel to immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions, and thereby fulfills the practices of the second stage (*bhūmi*).
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

“When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is in the third stage, there are further four kinds of divine footprints (ṛddhipāda) like necklaces, by which they can transform this body into immeasurable forms and then merge them back into one.”

What are the four? There is the fundamental essential power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*); one who attains this divine foot travels throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, universally observing what is contemplated in the minds of sentient beings, and delivers them according to their own contemplations.

Furthermore, there is the power of the divine feet of the blazing and radiant Dharma-practice; a Bodhisattva who attains this divine foot travels throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, thoroughly observing what is contemplated in the minds of sentient beings—whether they have joy or anger, or neither—and transforms and teaches them through the blazing and radiant Dharma.

Furthermore, there is the formless supernormal power (*ṛddhi*); one who attains this supernormal power travels throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, observing what is conceived in the minds of sentient beings and teaching and transforming them through the absence of mental consciousness.

Furthermore, there is the threefold pure supernormal power; one who attains this supernormal power travels throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, observing and knowing the thoughts of sentient beings, and preaching the practice of the three dharmas so that they may extinguish the three perceptions.
What are the three modes of practice? First, emptiness;
second, consciousness.
"Third is the self.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s fulfillment of the practice of the four bases of psychic power while in the third stage.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the fourth stage, they must further possess these four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*). What are the four?

Furthermore, there is a base of spiritual power called 'signlessness' (*animitta*); a Bodhisattva who attains this base of spiritual power travels throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, from the Heaven of the Three Pure Abodes up to the limit of space, causing all sentient beings everywhere to attain the dharma of signlessness."

Furthermore, there is the supernormal power of removing greed; one who attains this supernormal power travels throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, fully observing the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings, and teaches and transforms them through the methods of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, there is the supernormal power of turning the wheel of Dharma; one who attains this supernormal power travels throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, turning the Dharma of the four fearlessnesses and the nectar of immortality, causing those who have long suffered from hunger and thirst to attain full satisfaction.

Furthermore, there is the supernormal power of equal wisdom; one who attains this supernormal power travels throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, fully observing the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings, and delivers and liberates them through the wisdom of equality.
"This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva abiding in the fourth stage and being fully endowed with the practice of the four bases of psychic power.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is in the fifth stage, there are furthermore four bases of psychic power."

What are the four? There is a supernormal power called the "Gate of Immeasurability. A bodhisattva who attains this Gate of Immeasurability perceives all that is thought within the minds of sentient beings and delivers them by means of the wisdom of liberation.

Furthermore, there is the supernormal power of conduct; one who attains this supernormal power travels throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, fully comprehends what sentient beings think, and immediately expounds the Dharma by means of the gateway of penetrating the source of phenomena.

Furthermore, there is the gate of supernatural power (ṛddhipāda) of receiving retribution; one who attains this supernatural power delivers and liberates others by means of manifesting the dharma of karmic retribution.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of these four practices of supernatural power while abiding in the fifth stage (bhūmi).
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"When a bodhisattva is in the sixth stage, they must further fulfill the practice of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). What are these four?

There is a supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) called "Causing to Fall. A Bodhisattva who attains this supernormal power travels throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and fully observes the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings. For those whose various evil karmic retributions should be transformed into purity and goodness, he gradually preaches the Dharma to cause them to fall [from their evil states]. Furthermore, there is the "Rootless" supernormal power;

one who attains this supernormal power travels throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and fully observes the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings, excavating their roots so that they are forever severed and do not arise again.

Furthermore, there is a supernormal power named "Stainless Path to Liberation"; one who attains this supernormal power travels throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and fully observes the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings, causing those beings to attain the essential path of liberation. [The Sanskrit manuscript is missing one item.]
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the seventh stage, which is called the stage of non-retrogression, they shall then fully possess the four bases of spiritual power."

What are the four? There is a supernormal power called "Impurity of the Body of Sentient Beings"; when a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, they can manifest the impurity of foul secretions to thereby transform countless sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is a supernormal power called "Virtue and Way"; when a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, they can use the right path to abandon the three paths and attain arhatship.

Furthermore, there is a supernormal power named "Awakening to the Right"; when a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, they are able to cause all sentient beings to establish themselves on the stage of faith and not regress.
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s possession of the methods of the supernormal powers while abiding in the seventh stage.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in the eighth stage, they are fully endowed with the four bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda), which are vast and boundless, beyond the reach of knowledge of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."

What are the four? There is a supernormal power (ṛddhi-pāda) by which beings who have not yet resolved their minds toward the Path, upon the Bodhisattva attaining this supernormal power, are led to first establish themselves on the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi), though other practices are not yet perfected.

Furthermore, there is a supernormal power called "Non-arising" (anutpāda); when a Bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, he observes each and every conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra) as being without self (anātman).
Furthermore, there is a supernormal power called "Attachment," which a bodhisattva who attains this power delights in the marks and signs of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, there is the supernormal power of "Exhausting Outflows," which a bodhisattva who attains this power can, with a single mind, sever all phenomena of outflow.
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possessing the four bases of spiritual power while in the eighth stage.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"When a Bodhisattva is in the ninth dwelling, he shall then fully possess the dharmas of the four bases of spiritual power."

What are the four? There is a supernormal power named "Ocean of Multitudes. When a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, those who possess the four types of craving and approach the gate—once their defilements are exhausted—they are able to enter the gate; those whose mental defilements are not yet exhausted cannot enter the gate. This is called a bodhisattva in the ninth stage possessing the four supernormal powers.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"When a bodhisattva dwells within the ten stages, they possess the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*). What are these four?

There is a supernormal power named "Radiance"; when a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, they travel through the countless Buddha-lands of the ten directions, fully observing the thoughts within the minds of all sentient beings, and sit beneath the King of Trees in the full lotus posture, thereby fulfilling their heart of great vows.

Furthermore, there is a supernormal power named "Infinite Gateways"; when a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, they distinguish the various destinations and lead them all toward the Single Vehicle.

Furthermore, there is a supernormal power named "Single Thought-moment"; when a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, they cause all immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions to achieve the Way in a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, there is a supernormal power called "Adornment. When a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power, within a single day they can completely adorn all buddha-fields, attaining enlightenment simultaneously at the same time and with the same name.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of the tenth stage possessing the dharmas of the four bases of psychic power.
*Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra-sūtra*, Scroll Three.
*Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra-sūtra*, Scroll Four; also known as *The Present Retribution*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Nine: On Sounds and Resonance (4). Chapter Nine: On Sounds and Resonance.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing again to proclaim extensively the immeasurable dharma-meanings of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers, then filled immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions with a single verse.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
“Existence and non-existence arise from emptiness; Those sounds are not mine.
Each sound is distinct from every other; Therefore, I proclaim the teaching of the Honored Dharma.”
"The Buddha’s conduct is immeasurable; It is neither existent nor non-existent.
With a single voice he expounds all dharmas; By this, one attains Buddhahood.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One beheld the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions, each praising him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

The pure practices of all Buddhas are identical and uniform. The peerless World-Heroes of countless worlds throughout the ten directions proclaim all dharmas with a single voice. Within each of the six perfections, there are the lineages of immeasurable Buddhas; these inexhaustible dharmas are inconceivable.”
What is the inconceivability of the lineage (*gotra*)?

It is like the Buddhas of the ten directions, who are all of one single resonance; by means of the meaning of a single verse, they cause immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions to all enter the inexhaustible Dharma-gate, such that they all share the same aspiration and attain enlightenment on the same day and at the same time.

Furthermore, with a single voice, they pervade immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing all sentient beings who hear this sound to spontaneously realize their fetters and attain eternal liberation.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Vyākaraṇa (Explanation), who rose from his seat and assumed a majestic demeanor. Having abandoned all worldly expectations and clearly understood all dharmas, he possessed mastery over various wisdoms and had attained the patience of non-arising. With his right shoulder bared, kneeling with palms joined, he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
How extraordinary!

Now we hear that within a single utterance, a single sound, and a single moment of the Tathāgata, he exhaustively expounds the scriptural teachings and fully encompasses all practices—something that neither Arhats nor Pratyekabuddhas can ever attain.

I now wish to ask: how is it that within the resonance of sound the dharmas of the Tathāgata’s manifold practices are fully contained, such that sentient beings first encounter these dharmas and subsequently, upon hearing this sound, attain awakening?
"Does the name of all dharmas emerge from within sound?
At that time, having heard the question posed by the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa, the World-Honored One replied:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Noble son! You now inquire about the dharma of emptiness and formlessness, which is beyond the reach of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; I shall now distinguish it for you point by point."
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Contemplate this well!
Because the resonance of the Tathāgata is like space and formless, the arising of all phenomena is inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa addressed the Buddha,
saying: “How is this so,
World-Honored One?”
“The resonance of the Tathāgata is like space, formless; how then can you say that it gives birth to all dharmas?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa:
“Is the resonance of the Tathāgata possessed of form?”
He replied, "Formless. He asked again:
"Sound and resonance have no form; from where does the resonance emerge?
He replied: "Due to the causal conditions of the four great elements, consciousness arises and makes distinctions."
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"Regarding what you have asked: the resonance of the Tathāgata is like space, formless; how, then, can all phenomena be produced from that which is formless?"
"Does the echo arise from the four great elements,
or is it not the empty Dharma-realm? He replied, "Not so."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa: "How is it so,
son of good family?"
"The resonance of the Tathāgata originally arises from the four great elements; when the resonance ceases, where does it return?
He replied, "The resonance has no place to which it returns."
The Buddha asked again:
"Is there some other space from which this echo emerges? He replied:
"No, it is not so; the sound does not emerge from a space other than this.
The Buddha said, "Nor is it from a space other than this, nor is it from this very space; rather, it is because the Tathāgata has no separate existence apart from you."
The Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, You Yourself have declared that the resonance of the Tathāgata is like space, formless, yet capable of giving rise to all dharmas.”
I clearly understand that all phenomena arise from the resonance of the Tathāgata; why, then, do you say that all phenomena also arise within the realm of empty space?
It is as difficult for a person in darkness to seek light as it would be to find it; my present doubt is now twice as great as that.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa, saying: "How is it,
son of good family?"
Now, regarding these phenomena called "arising," how do they exist?
Do they arise from emptiness,
or do they not arise from emptiness?

He replied: "Now, the dharma-nature of all dharmas is empty from the very beginning; emptiness itself is empty, and even the emptiness of emptiness is empty of its own accord. How, then, could there be any dharmas?"
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is.
As you have said, all dharmas of the Tathāgata are like space and formless; the sounds of the four great elements arise from the four great elements."
"Are the resonance of the Tathāgata and the realm of empty space not different? He replied, "Not so."
Regarding my question: it is not doubted that the sounds of the Tathāgata arise from the four great elements and thereby give birth to all dharmas.
But how can it be said that space, in turn, gives birth to all dharmas?
The Buddha said: "Stop, stop!
Son of good family!"
That you have now raised these questions is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
What do you think,
son of good family?
“Does the Tathāgata’s voice-sound exist? He replied, “It does not.”
“How is it, son of good family?
Does the Tathāgata’s voice not exist?”
He replied, “Suchness. The Buddha asked again:
"The resonance of the Tathāgata is neither existent nor non-existent; how should this dharma be named?
He replied, "This dharma should be called 'emptiness'."
The Buddha said:
“Emptiness itself is formless; it is neither this, nor that, nor is there anything intermediate between them.
How, then, can it be called ‘emptiness’?”
The Bodhisattva She-shih (Vimokṣaprajñā) addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata, with his broad and long tongue, has himself proclaimed the nature of emptiness as being neither existent nor non-existent, and lacking any plurality.
As I contemplate it, this emptiness does not fundamentally exist; how much less should I establish a name or designation for ‘emptiness’?”
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!

Emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is there anything intermediate between them. Just as I, today, am a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who am neither existent, nor non-existent, nor anything intermediate, so too are all dharmas that I have taught."
"Why do you slander the Tathāgata by claiming that the name 'emptiness' originates from the Tathāgata?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to resolve the doubts in the minds of the assembled multitude, addressed the fourfold assembly:

"The single voice of the Tathāgata is able to give birth to all dharmas; what he says is neither false nor non-existent. It is only because sentient beings harbor thoughts of attachment that they dwell in delusion, forever remaining within the four currents."

The divine wisdom of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; according to what the Buddha’s consciousness contemplates through the roots of immeasurable practices, he is able to fully know the karmic retributions that all sentient beings should receive—a realm that is not within the reach of arhats or pratyekabuddhas.
"Therefore, with a single sound, the Tathāgata is able to bring forth all dharmas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How extraordinary! How marvelous!
The realm of sentient beings is inconceivable.

Some possess great vows and incline toward the Mahāyāna; some resolve upon the mind of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha; some delight in the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and others take pleasure in dwelling among devas and humans to receive blessings. Such categories as these are inconceivable; for each sentient being, with their respective mental consciousnesses, what they contemplate differs and their practices are likewise not one.
"How is it that from a single sound all dharmas are produced, and how can they completely pervade all sentient beings?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa, saying:

"The divine wisdom of the Tathāgata is formless and cannot be seen. There is a wisdom called 'Swift Sovereignty' which is able to fully and universally know the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings—whether deep or shallow—and can distinguish them all."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The consciousness of sentient beings is neither existent nor non-existent; yet some reckon it as permanent, while others reckon it as impermanent. How is it that through the swift and sovereign wisdom, one is able to give rise to all-encompassing knowledge?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa:
"I shall now provide you with a parable, for the wise understand through parables. What is it?"

"Noble son! For example, the Sun Deity receives a body composed of the four great elements measuring twelve yojanas; the inner palace walls are seven yojanas distant from the outer walls, and the light shining between them is immeasurably more brilliant."

The second wall is seven yojanas distant from the third wall; the radiance diminishes further still, continuing in this manner until the seventh wall, each being separated from the next by seven yojanas, such that the illumination of each successive one is less than the preceding.
Outside the seventh wall, there is another protective wall at a distance of two *yojanas*, its radiance being even less than that of the former.
The first palace wall within is made of wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewels; the heat therein is like that of the rootless fire (*amūlaka-niraya*).
The second wall is made of *jvālānugata* jewels; its heat is like that of the Black Rope fire (*kālasūtra-niraya*).
The third wall is named Flame Light Shadow; its heat is like that of blazing fire.
The fourth wall is named Brave Flame Jewel; its heat is like that of boiling embers.
The fifth wall is named Ultimate Flame Shade; its heat is like that of copper-leaf fire.
The sixth wall is named Vaidūrya; its heat is like that of a red lotus fire.
The seventh wall is named Sphaṭika; its heat is like that of a blue lotus fire.
How is this so, son of good family?

This Sun Deity, in a single day and night, travels with extreme speed throughout the four regions; its radiance illuminates the four continents, and whether they be blue, yellow, red, or white, high or low, cities, villages, hamlets, surnames, and names—all these can be seen by itself and distinguished one by one.
"How is this so, son of good family?
Sentient beings have immeasurable forms and diverse natures; how is it that the radiance of the Sun Deity is able to illuminate them all such that they are entirely of one color?"
"Does it arise from within the sunlight that immeasurable light issues forth to illuminate immeasurable forms?
Or does it arise from a single light that illuminates immeasurable forms?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As I have asked, the Tathāgata produces immeasurable dharmas from a single sound; this voice issues forth from the four great elements. Regarding the words spoken in the future, the past, and the present, I have no doubt."
"Today, the nature and characteristics of this radiance are such of themselves; why then do you ask how they are identical to verbal teachings?
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"The sounds and resonances produced by the Tathāgata’s four great elements each possess their own teaching, and all are capable of giving rise to all dharmas."

When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma, they do not think or say, "I am saying this" or "I am establishing that. Their minds are tranquil and extinguished, free from any such thoughts.

It is like the Sun God, whose single light shines universally upon all regions, yet has no thought that "I am illuminating something. Those who receive the light each know their own destination. This, O Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa, is what is meant.
“The Tathāgata’s swift and sovereign wisdom brings great benefit; he universally knows the conscious beings with form throughout the ten directions and transforms them to deliver them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The sounds and voices produced by the Tathāgata—whether they be clear or unclear, dark or light—all enable one to advance toward and accomplish the Way of the Teaching.”
"The sun's light causes much injury to those who prefer darkness; how can this be used as a metaphor?
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"It is like a person wandering in the sky whose mind is so deluded that it is difficult to awaken; you are now just like this, not yet understanding my parable."

"What I have now spoken is that the resonance of the Tathāgata arises from the four great elements and is fully capable of giving birth to all dharmas; just as the light of the Sunlight Devaputra is able to universally illuminate all that has form—first, being able to give birth to all dharmas, and second, being able to universally illuminate all that has form."
"What distinction exists such that you harbor doubt?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viniścaya reflected deeply within himself and attained sudden, great enlightenment; he then addressed the Buddha again, saying: "Excellent!"
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, uses formless dharmas to teach through forms, and uses wordless teachings to teach through words.
Now I repeat my request: I only pray that the Tathāgata will dispatch [an envoy] at this time so that there may be no further doubt.
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!”
“Son of good family!
The Tathāgata shall dispatch them by means of skillful expedients. “In what way?”
“World-Honored One!

There is the supernormal power of permanence, the supernormal power of impermanence, the supernormal power of knowing one’s own past lives, the supernormal power of knowing the past lives of others, the supernormal power of visual consciousness, and the supernormal power of auditory consciousness. What is the distinction between the meanings of these six dharmas?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa: "So it is, so it is.
Just as you have asked, these six supernormal powers are each distinct and not different; I shall now explain them to you."

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of the permanence of existence, they observe that the production of all phenomena is uninterrupted: the prior birth is the prior birth and the subsequent birth is the subsequent birth. Whether passing through one kalpa or up to a hundred thousand kalpas, when a kalpa arises it arises, and when a kalpa ceases it ceases; yet they observe that this consciousness does not decay or perish.
Why is this? Because the root of ignorance is deep and cannot be destroyed.

Furthermore, regarding the supernormal power of impermanence (*anityatā-abhijñā*), one likewise observes all sentient beings who possess form—those born and those passing away—from one kalpa up to hundreds of thousands of kalpas. One sees that when a kalpa arises they arise, and when a kalpa ceases they cease; knowing that their assumed forms all return to extinction and do not endure eternally, this is called the distinction between the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal power of permanence and the supernormal power of impermanence.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa, saying:
"In this regard, son of good family!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of self-cognition, he is able to see for himself one body, two bodies, up to a hundred thousand bodies. From kalpa to kalpa, throughout all that he has experienced therein, he is able to fully recognize it: 'I was born in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a district; my name was such-and-such, and my clan was such-and-such.'"

Furthermore, one recognizes for oneself the initial reception of the four great elements and the formation of various physical forms, being able to discern all deeds of good and evil; this is called the supernormal power of self-recognition.
The Buddha again addressed the son of noble family:

“When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the knowledge of the supernormal powers of others, from this realm of desire and form up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, they are able to discern every single destination. From one year to hundreds of thousands of millions of years, from one kalpa to hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, regarding the places experienced through their formation and destruction therein, they are able to discern them all and know them completely; this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s knowledge of the supernormal powers of others.”
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of visual consciousness, he contemplates the trichiliocosm and knows those who have taken form and those who have not; he is able to see all that possesses form.”

From one year to hundreds of thousands of millions of years, and from one kalpa to hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they perceive and observe all of these without confusion; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva possessing the supernormal power of the divine eye while remaining free from attachment.
The Buddha again addressed the son of noble family:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of the ear-consciousness, they hear all sounds of sentient beings in the ten directions—those with voices of suffering or joy, those without voices of suffering or joy, those hearing the retribution of good or evil, and those not hearing the retribution of good or evil. They hear and know them all without confusion; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva being endowed with the supernormal power of the ear-consciousness while remaining unattached.”
"These are called the six dharmas, each distinct from the others.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

There is the Bodhisattva Constant Penetration; those who attain this penetration fully know that all things possessing form and substance arise and continue without end, whereas those lacking such penetration arise only to perish with each birth.
Now, observing that the previous life is not the subsequent life, how can it be said that birth and birth are uninterrupted?

Furthermore, the Tathāgata, having attained the supernormal knowledge of self-cognition that exhausts all past lives, perceives one body and two bodies up to hundreds of thousands of bodies, and one kalpa and two kalpas up to hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; he sees that the present body is not the future body, and this body is different from the previous body.
If the present consciousness is not the future consciousness, then this consciousness is different from the future consciousness.

If consciousness were separate from this consciousness, it would be the same as that of ordinary beings; why then does the World-Honored One speak of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives through one's own consciousness?

Furthermore, World-Honored One, regarding what you have said—that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others knows the locations of the mental consciousnesses of all sentient beings, and knows both their own mental consciousness and the minds of others; that one who possesses the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others also knows both their own mind and the minds of others—what is the difference between these two supernormal powers?

As the World-Honored One has said, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of the divine eye, they observe and behold the ten directions, from the desire realm up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, clearly seeing all those who possess form and those who do not, as well as those who receive the retribution of good and evil and those who do not.

Furthermore, it is said that Bodhisattvas who have attained the supernormal power of the divine ear hear all sounds of suffering and happiness, as well as sounds of neither suffering nor happiness, throughout the ten directions; they hear those who receive retribution for good and evil deeds, and those who do not receive such retribution.
The divine eye also sees, and the ear-consciousness also hears; what is the distinction between these two?
We only pray, World-Honored One, that you will explain and analyze this further, so that we may forever be free from doubt.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa:
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of permanence, they awaken to all dharmas and know that they abide within the dharma-nature without change."
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of impermanence, they realize that all phenomena are subject to change; this is called the supernormal power of impermanence.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is such that whether a Buddha appears or not, there is neither arising nor ceasing; this is called the supernormal power of permanence.

Furthermore, regarding the universal characteristic of impermanence of all phenomena: they all return to destruction and do not endure for long; arising again and again without staying, this is called the universal characteristic of impermanence.

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of permanence, they become fully endowed with all the dharmas of a Tathāgata: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; this is called the supernormal power of permanence."
Furthermore, all phenomena—whether future, past, or present, whether wholesome or unwholesome—are entirely non-existent; this is called the penetration of impermanence.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva further observes sentient beings who have set out upon the path of the Three Vehicles and should attain arhatship; they seek a teacher for awakening, and their attainment of the fruit will surely be as they wish, without doubt.
He further sees sentient beings who have set out with the mind of a pratyekabuddha, dwelling alone in the wilderness, and their attainment of the fruit will surely be as it is, without doubt.
Furthermore, seeing sentient beings give rise to the bodhicitta, he knows that their vows will certainly be fulfilled without doubt.
This is called the constant supernormal power of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

If there are good men or women who, having first sought the path of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha, or practicing the path of a Bodhisattva, subsequently regress from it and remain on the level of ordinary worldlings without achieving success, this is called impermanent supernatural power.

"Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has already attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), and by his own knowledge recalls countless past existences—how he first gave rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), established meritorious virtues, served and made offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and was certain to attain the fruit of the Way—and furthermore, if he personally recollects and recognizes that before receiving the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), he relied upon emptiness and did not cling to form (*rūpa*)—this is called 'recollecting one's own past lives. "

There may be a bodhisattva who possesses the supernormal knowledge of knowing the minds of others; he knows their various ways of receiving bodies and their various forms, yet he cannot know from where they originally came—this is called the mundane knowledge of others' minds.

Furthermore, there are sons or daughters of good family who, having attained the supernormal knowledge of knowing the minds of others, are fully endowed with both internal and external supernormal powers; this is called the distinction between the supernormal power of self-cognition and the supernormal knowledge of knowing the minds of others.

"If there are sons or daughters of good family who have already attained the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which is pure both internally and externally, they see exhaustively the fundamental dispositions of the faculties of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.

Some bodhisattvas, with their divine eye, see one thousand world-systems; some see two thousand world-systems; some see three thousand great thousandfold world-systems; and some bodhisattvas, with their divine eye, see one buddha-field, two fields, or three fields, within which they fully know those who are subject to regression and those who are not subject to regression. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attaining the supernormal power of the divine eye, knowing all realms while realizing that nothing truly exists."
The Buddha again addressed the son of noble family:

"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has already attained the supernormal power of the ear, he hears all sounds throughout the lands of the ten directions—sounds that are virtuous or non-virtuous, and sounds that are beautiful or not beautiful."

Furthermore, there are sons or daughters of good family who hear of one thousand, two thousand, or three thousand lands; or there are bodhisattvas who hear of the sounds and voices of one buddha-land, two buddha-lands, three buddha-lands, and even of countless buddha-lands.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa, saying:
"Regarding the six dharmas, one attains their fulfillment, each having its own distinction.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, speaks with immeasurable eloquence, analyzing and distinguishing the firm dispositions of sentient beings one by one. He speaks of the six supernormal powers as being inconceivable, such that they cannot be known or reached even by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.”
As the World-Honored One has said:
"While expounding the practice of the six supernormal powers and the dharma of non-attachment, they still harbor doubts.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"Those with permanent supernormal powers preach the Dharma of Nirvana; those with impermanent supernormal powers preach conditioned phenomena.
If good men and women were to possess conditioned supernormal powers, would their bodies and minds then immediately enter parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha said,
"It is not so. The Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa (Explanation) then spoke:
"All dharmas are without arising and without cessation; does the body-consciousness of the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa this very day?
Why, then, are there still further verbal teachings?
The World-Honored One replied:
"It is not that I do not say there is eternal nirvana, nor that I do not say there is impermanent supernatural power.
However, because my supernatural power knows both existence and non-existence, I speak of it thus."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the son of good family:
"If there be sons or daughters of good family who attain the supernormal power of permanence, they shall be named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"One who attains the supernormal power of impermanence may be on the stage of a noble one (*ārya*) or on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); these are called the two distinct differences.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has already attained the supernormal power of visual consciousness; being able to fully perceive and see all sentient beings of the three periods—past, future, and present—is what is called "supernormal power."
Furthermore, it is said that the ear hears the sounds of countless past, future, and present lifetimes.
If this is so, does the eye see past forms?
Past forms have already ceased to exist.
Is it future form? It has not yet manifested its signs.
As for the present dharma-realm of eye-consciousness, I have no doubt.
“I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you may cause those sentient beings who have not heard [the Dharma] to forever attain awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
I shall analyze its meaning for you."
How is this so? Noble son!

Suppose there are sentient beings who have already attained the divine eye; they observe all forms and appearances throughout existence, being able to discern them all completely and without any doubt.
When he recollects past forms, they suddenly appear before him; he perceives them all completely without any obstruction.
The supernormal power of the ear-consciousness is likewise: when he brings it to mind, it appears before him, and with no impediment to his hearing, he perceives everything entirely.
The Bodhisattva She-shih (She-shih) again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now that I have heard this, my doubts have doubled.
How is it that through the supernormal power of the eye and the supernormal power of the ear, one sees past events and hears past sounds?"
Just as I now personally recognize my past lives and am thus able to know the events of those past lives by myself, and just as my auditory consciousness knows present matters in the present,
how can one know the past and the future?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa:

"There may be those with the supernormal power of the eye who possess consciousness fixed on the eye, or there may be those with the supernormal power of the eye who do not possess consciousness fixed on the eye;

there may be those with the supernormal power of the ear who possess consciousness fixed on the ear, or there may be those with the supernormal power of the ear who do not possess consciousness fixed on the ear."

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of concentration regarding visual consciousness and the supernormal power of concentration regarding auditory consciousness, they are able to see from their first reception of form until their final body—whether large or small—and throughout that interval, they distinguish all things without losing the supernormal power of concentrated mind.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: entering this state of meditative concentration, he contemplates the realm of a single Buddha; then, having dissolved that realm, he contemplates countless buddha-fields, within which he manifests the accomplishment and non-accomplishment of the five aggregates.
Sometimes they manifest the five aggregates of the small [world], sometimes the five aggregates of the earth, sometimes the five aggregates of water,
sometimes the five aggregates of the four continents, sometimes the five aggregates of the jewel mountains, sometimes the five aggregates of Mount Sumeru,
sometimes the five aggregates of the Cakravāḍa mountains, and sometimes the five aggregates of the Mahācakravāḍa mountains; or they manifest...
The five aggregates manifest as the cities, fortifications, and villages of the human world; or they manifest as the five aggregates dwelling in pleasure gardens and bathing pools;
or they manifest as the five aggregates dwelling in the palaces of the devas; or they manifest as the five aggregates in the palaces of the nāgas;
or they manifest as the five aggregates of the eight classes of spirits and deities; or they manifest in the forms of sentient beings of the desire realm; or they manifest in the form realm.
They manifest in the form of beings of the form realm; or they appear in the formless realm, assuming formless forms;
or they appear as small worlds, assuming the forms of small worlds; or they appear as thousand-world systems, two-thousand-world systems, and even up to three-thousand great thousand-world systems.

Or they may manifest sentient beings experiencing or not experiencing the retribution of their karma—whether for a moment, a day, a month, or a year; whether during the kalpa of formation or the kalpa of destruction; whether in turbid or clear conditions, in the beautiful or the ugly, or in the happy or miserable realms; including the appearance of Buddhas in the world and the attendant bodhisattvas—they are able to discern all these things. This is called the supernormal power of the concentrated eye-consciousness and the supernormal power of the concentrated ear-consciousness.

They attain the power to move the divine consciousnesses of all Tathāgatas so as to reach the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, where they serve and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Furthermore, they see the various Bodhisattvas presenting offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, mattresses, and medicinal requisites for the sick and infirm.

Furthermore, he saw buddha-fields that were pure and those that were impure; he saw sentient beings practicing the holy life and those not practicing the holy life; and he saw the diverse ways in which beings of the five destinies receive and practice their training, each according to their different cultivation.

This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attaining the supernormal power of the concentrated eye-consciousness and attaining the supernormal power of the concentrated ear-consciousness, whereby they fully observe all matters of the past, future, and present without any omission.

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the supernormal power of visual consciousness, they can manifest through skillful means the inconceivable realms of countless sentient beings and is thus able to transform various kinds of rare treasures."
To all sentient beings who go there to take precious jewels, he gives them all away so that they are fully satisfied.
Furthermore, he may manifest the original pure practices of various Buddha-lands, which, being already completed, are no longer newly created.

"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attaining the supernormal power of the eye of concentrated consciousness and attaining the supernormal power of the ear of concentrated consciousness, being able to fully perfect all practices.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Having attained the supernormal power of the concentrated eye-consciousness and the supernormal power of the concentrated ear-consciousness, in what stage do these good men and good women abide?
For how long have they made offerings to the Buddhas?
The Buddha said:

“These sons and daughters of good family, who uphold and cultivate the supernormal power of the concentrated eye-consciousness and the supernormal power of the concentrated ear-consciousness, have already made offerings to the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past; they have already attained the dhāraṇīs and the practice of non-retrogression; their faculties are fully developed and their marks and signs are perfected; and they possess upright parents and a noble lineage.”

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, although they receive offerings from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and travel from one Buddha-land to another to serve and pay homage to those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have yet to attain the supernormal power of eye-consciousness or the supernormal power of ear-consciousness.

There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although they have attained the supernormal power of the divine eye, have not yet fully perfected the foundation of all practices; nevertheless, by means of their power of spiritual travel, they journey to immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions to serve and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although they have attained the supernormal power of the eye and the supernormal power of the ear, have not yet attained fixed consciousness; such individuals cannot fully know the thoughts of sentient beings, nor can they purify buddha-fields or transform sentient beings.

There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose six supernormal powers are pure and penetrating, with no obstruction between the internal and external, yet who are unable to fully perfect the practice of the four dharma-gates.

There may be bodhisattvas who, within a single buddha-field, travel about teaching and transforming others without any defilement or attachment, yet have not yet fully comprehended the fundamental dispositions of the faculties of sentient beings.

There may be bodhisattvas who purify their own buddha-fields such that no beings possessed of lust, anger, or delusion are born in their lands; yet, though born in those lands, they do not exhaust the root of suffering.
There may be bodhisattvas who give rise to a great vow, saying:
"If, in my future births, I am born in my own buddha-field, let there be no mention of the names of the Three Vehicles among the people of my land."
These bodhisattvas do not attain the supernormal power of the concentrated eye-consciousness or the supernormal power of the concentrated ear-consciousness.
