Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who give rise to the mind of great vows, thinking:
"By my original vow to seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path, may all the people of my country practice the same conduct, and may the land be pure with all beings having the same appearance."

"Having attained what they had vowed, they have no further doubts; yet such bodhisattvas have not yet attained the supernormal power of the concentrated eye-consciousness or the supernormal power of the concentrated ear-consciousness.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who give rise to a great vow of resolve:
'When I later attain Buddhahood, may all sentient beings within my realm achieve the Way and enter parinirvāṇa in a single day.'"
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as these have not yet attained the supernormal power of the concentrated eye-consciousness or the supernormal power of the concentrated ear-consciousness.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who give rise to the heart of great vows, thinking:
‘When I later become a Buddha, may all sentient beings in my land attain Buddhahood on the same day.’”
"In this way, such bodhisattvas attain the supernormal power of the concentrated eye-consciousness and the supernormal power of the concentrated ear-consciousness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!
Is there any bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has resolved upon this great vow:
"When I attain buddhahood, shall all sentient beings simultaneously attain buddhahood?"
The Buddha said: "There was!

In the past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Anālayasthita Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The land shall be named Dharma-Exquisite, and the human lifespan shall be thirty thousand years.

At that time, the Tathāgata Abiding in the Non-abiding shall have a lifespan of one hundred thousand years; he will give rise to a great vow to cause all sentient beings in his own land to attain the Buddha-way on the same day and at the same time, and on that very day, they shall all enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there any Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who has given rise to this great vow:
'When I later become a Buddha, shall I cause all the empty space and sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions to fully attain the Way of the Buddha'?"
The Buddha said: "No. Why is this?

The realm of sentient beings is inconceivable; the limits of space have no boundary or bottom; that which has perished in the past is immeasurable, and those who will be born in the future are likewise without limit.
The Buddha again addressed the son of noble family:

"In the past, before this Bhadrakalpa, after passing through incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and further passing beyond those incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there was a Buddha named Samatā Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who appeared in the world."
The human lifespan is one thousand years, and the land is pure.

Within a single day, he manifests throughout the ten directions, across the entirety of the realm of empty space, all sentient beings with form; they all simultaneously attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and within that same day, they all enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Once the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Equal Enlightenment has attained Buddhahood, may he further cause all sentient beings throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, as boundless as space, to all attain the Way of the Buddha on the very same day."
"How is it that today there are yet Tathāgatas and ourselves?
Are there all sentient beings?
How is it that there are furthermore the realms of gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-dwellers?"
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa: "Stop, stop!
Son of good family!"
"I have already stated previously that this refers to those who have attained a human body, not to other realms.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Is there any bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, having resolved upon the great vow, can cause the sentient beings of the five destinies to attain Buddhahood on the same day as themselves within a single day?
He replied: "There is none. Why is this?"
The natures, behaviors, and inclinations of sentient beings differ; how could one possibly attain Buddhahood through the forms of hungry ghosts, animals, or hell-beings? This is not so.

"Why is this? One can never become the Honored One among men by means of a non-body; it is through the manifestation of expedient transformation that one may provisionally provide universal salvation.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa, saying:

"Innumerable Buddhas of the past originally gave rise to a great vow, desiring that all sentient beings—every form of existence as well as the realm of empty space—should all attain Buddhahood and enter final parinirvāṇa."

However, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, on that very day, first transformed sentient beings of the three miserable realms, uprooting the source of their suffering and restoring them all to human form. Once they had attained the human path—with all faculties complete and the six senses fully intact—he, within a single day, led them all together to achieve the Buddha-way. Endowed with the various marks of excellence, just like me today as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, possessing sovereign spiritual wisdom and unimpeded eloquence, they all entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Bodhisattvas of Great Vows teach and transform sentient beings, performing ascetic practices therein for immeasurable kalpas.”
"For what reason do you not cause all sentient beings within the three realms of existence to immediately attain the Buddha-way?
The Buddha said,
"They cannot achieve the Way."
How so? Son of good family!
These three paths of rebirth are not the three wholesome paths.
"How can one wish to attain the Buddha-way therein?
This matter is not so.
It is like a person who, desiring to seek the seven treasures, abandons the heap of seven treasures and instead seeks them in the sky; could such a person obtain them?"
He replied: “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is,
son of good family!”
"To wish to cause those in the three realms of existence to attain the path of Buddhahood—this matter is not so.
Chapter Ten: Causes and Conditions (4) The *Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra-sūtra*, Chapter Ten: Causes and Conditions. The Buddha addressed the sons of good family:
"If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, recite, and chant the fixed eye-consciousness and the fixed ear-consciousness, they shall obtain ten merits."
What are these ten?

In this regard, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by means of an incomparable mind, attains the image of empty space; he does not transform sentient beings or purify buddha-fields through verbal instruction.

Good sons and good daughters, knowing for themselves the beginning and end of the countless forms and consciousnesses, and realizing that they are empty, quiescent, and entirely non-existent, give rise to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is about to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he will be able to fulfill the purity of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

This is because the Tathāgata is of a single characteristic and formless. There may be a bodhisattva who attains the seal of the one dharma (ekadharma-mudrā) and expounds the immeasurable teachings of the Tathāgata, awakening spontaneously without receiving them from a teacher."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
There is one fundamental dharma that is vast and bottomless: the production of all fundamental dharmas through the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).
How does signlessness give rise to that which has signs?"
The Buddha said:
"Just as there are external forms—blue, white, red, black, and yellow.
The Bodhisattva Vyākhyāna explained:

“The Tathāgata has taught that the spirit abides in empty space; it belongs neither to the past, the future, nor the present, and it does not even have the name of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Why, then, do you speak of blue, yellow, red, white, and black?”

“This law of dependent origination is inconceivable; it is because sentient beings themselves give rise to the perception of conditions that, with volitional formations (saṃskāra), there is consciousness (vijñāna). From consciousness arises delusion (moha), and thus a human body is formed.”
The Bodhisattva Vyākaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘Space is formless; it acquires form through the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind.’”
"I now ask the Tathāgata: what are these called—earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, white, and black?
As the World-Honored One has said:
'Just as blue, yellow, white, and black, along with space and consciousness, exist within space.'"
"Why do you not say that among blue, yellow, red, and white, blue, yellow, red, and white are all empty? He replied: "Not so."
Why is this? Because each is empty of itself; the nature of emptiness does not know the nature of existence, and the nature of existence does not know the nature of non-existence.

It is just as when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in a single moment of thought, knows the immeasurable Buddha-worlds of lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, knowing each one individually—both their kalpas of formation and their kalpas of destruction.

Understanding this, one perceives no other characteristics; all phenomena arise and perish through their own causes and conditions, while the primordial self arises from emptiness and is neither born nor extinguished.

Furthermore, one contemplates immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* lands, beholding the various Bodhisattvas who receive the adornment of wisdom in those lands, purifying the seeds of sentient beings, and propagating the teachings of the Way throughout those Buddha-fields.
The incalculable Buddhas, Tathāgatas, fully know the source from which they arise; they distinguish each one individually, yet remain free from the notion of a self.
Furthermore, regarding the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, they hear their profound essential teachings and receive them with devotion, never abandoning the root of all dharmas.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva does not perceive for himself either a self or a non-self; practicing the Bodhisattva conduct, he does not perceive a practice. This is called arising from existence toward the signless, yet within it, he does not personally extinguish signs."

Although the body gives rise to contemplation, one does not even perceive it oneself and has nothing to be cognized; having no cognition, the thought "I am" does not arise, and through such self-examination, one is able to discern all phenomena.

Ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions contact, and so on, up to birth, old age, and death, which are likewise conditioned in this manner.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samudrareṇu further thought: "All dharmas arise through the conditioning of causes and conditions, and they cease through the conditioning of causes and conditions.

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, he contemplated and thoroughly understood the characteristics of all dharmas: when conditions arise, they are born; when conditions cease, they perish. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.

To state the essentials: the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are the root of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). They are non-reliant and cannot be relied upon; yet one knows the origin from which they arise. Therein, one inwardly contemplates the various dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*); through the purity of the wisdom of dharmas (*dharmaprajñā*), one does not abandon eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas contemplate and analyze the twelve links of dependent origination, how is it that ignorance conditions volitional formations?

In this regard, sons or daughters of good family, by virtue of ignorance as the root, they perform wholesome and unwholesome actions; these exhaustively give rise to the twelve bases of non-virtue, which gradually form the five aggregates of clinging. This is called "ignorance conditions volitional formations."
At that time, the bhikṣu Atītagaṃsī rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Regarding the profound Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination as I have studied it, I shall now speak of it.”

With ignorance as condition, formations arise, thus producing twelve; with formations as condition, consciousness arises, thus producing twelve; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises, thus producing twelve; with name-and-form as condition, contact arises, thus producing twelve; with contact as condition, the six sense bases arise, thus producing twelve; with the six sense bases as condition, craving arises, thus producing twelve; with craving as condition, feeling arises, thus producing twelve; with feeling as condition, existence arises, thus producing twelve; with existence as condition, birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise, thus again producing twelve.

According to my understanding of the twelve links of dependent origination: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!

Without destroying the nature of phenomena, it is like a magician who, standing upon this ground, manifests his illusory arts; yet those illusory arts do not damage this ground, nor does the ground damage the illusory arts."
However, this illusionist creates these transformations without distinction between day and night, and all who see this illusion believe and understand it.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this, employing the power of supernormal faculties to discern the twelve links of dependent origination.

A land without a Buddha manifests as its own buddha-field; that which was originally without a world now manifests as having a world. Furthermore, by means of a buddha-field with a Buddha, it can manifest a buddha-field without a Buddha; by means of a formless buddha-field, it manifests as having form and color. It does not destroy the one by means of the two, nor does it destroy the two by means of the one.

Why is this? Just as those illusory phenomena can cause all worlds to become entirely like magical illusions—just as all worlds, according to what people prefer, are entirely composed of illusory phenomena—so too, illusions consist of various manifestations rather than being a single, fixed phenomenon.

"There may be an illusory dharma called 'The Gateways of Infinite Dharmas. When a bodhisattva attains this illusory dharma, they are able to manifest that all dharmas are like illusory dharmas. Having attained the illusory dharma, they attain illusory wisdom without forgetting it; having attained illusory wisdom, they attain illusory practice, which can exhaust all suffering."

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have already attained illusory wisdom and practice within illusion, they are able to discern all activities therein through that illusory wisdom. Contemplating each one individually, they do not lose the original limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Just as those illusory phenomena do not rely on an internal ground, yet manifest as external phenomena without relying on the external, they cause all sentient beings to perceive the existence of internal phenomena.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: they do not make internal or external distinctions regarding emptiness, saying, "I shall transcend all worlds."
Nor does one regard the world as existing within or outside of empty phenomena. Why is this?
Because the nature of space is such that it does not destroy the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm does not destroy the nature of emptiness.

"The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the nature of emptiness within this; he contemplates all dharma-realms in various ways, yet neither contemplates the dharma-realm nor destroys the dharma-realm. Not only does he not perceive this world as having any particular form, but he also does not perceive the retribution for the good or evil deeds of sentient beings. He analyzes and investigates each matter individually, [finding that] their nature is empty by its very own nature, such that nothing can cause it to be otherwise."

Having observed this, one further observes and analyzes the three realms of existence (*tribhava*). Within them, one calculates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*): from ignorance (*avidyā*), eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arises, and therein are three modes of activity (*trividha-kriyā*).
What are these three?

It is just as, son of good family, when the eye sees external forms, whether they be wholesome or unwholesome, one does not make any discrimination; this arises from the defilement of fundamental consciousness by ignorance and volitional formations.
Alternatively, a son of good family or a daughter of good family may give rise to the three unwholesome dharmas of body, speech, and mind, whereupon their minds gradually awaken to this realization:
"Alas! That which I originally created was rooted in ignorance; it is now that it has brought about the twelve links of dependent origination."
"Knowing that one cannot reform oneself through ignorance, [one reflects:
'Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family, conditioned by delusion (moha), volitional formations (saṃskāra) arise; the root source of all offenses arises from offense:
"I shall now contemplate a tranquil and concentrated mind, and observe whether these twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) arise from delusion?"'"
"Does it arise from volitional formations? He further reflected:
"How could the dharma that is undifferentiated, tranquil, and hidden—namely ignorance—give rise to the various conditions of attachment?"
"If it is not created by the actions of my own body or speech, how can it arise?
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s discernment that the three types of action are non-existent.

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains the meditative concentration of the contemplation of emptiness, he discerns the twelve links of dependent origination: conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations, and thus there is the retribution of conditions. Since ignorance is not the fundamental origin, by what means could volitional formations exist?
The three factors of body, speech, and mind depend upon one another to give rise to all phenomena.

Therefore, although the Tathāgata has contemplated and analyzed the twelve links of dependent origination throughout incalculable eons, it was only upon attaining Buddhahood that he first achieved true faith and understanding.

"When I first resolved to seek the Bodhisattva path, I underwent successive births and deaths, analyzing the twelve links of dependent origination; yet though I contemplated the root of suffering, I had not exhausted its source.
Now that I have attained the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, I have finally been able to fully comprehend the twelve links of dependent origination."
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣu Atītacaryā:
"Although you have now spoken of the twelve links of dependent origination before the Tathāgata, you have not yet fully grasped their fundamental source."
Why is it fundamentally non-existent?

Even if a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to remain for as many eons as the sands of the Ganges and proclaim the twelve links of dependent origination, he could not exhaust them; how much less so can you now hope to do so?
At that time, the bhikṣu felt profound shame before the Tathāgata,
thinking, "Could it be that I have lost my supernormal power?
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew.

11. Chapter on the Mind (4). *The Bodhisattva’s Necklace Sūtra*, Chapter Eleven: On the Mind. At that time, the devas of the desire realm, the devas of the form realm, as well as gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas seated in the assembly, having heard the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, preach this most profound Dharma, were all filled with yearning and aspiration to behold the Tathāgata’s upright mind and concentrated intent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts within the minds of the sentient beings, desired to cause the assembly to enter the samādhi of mental concentration.
Thereupon, while seated upon his throne, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi of Manifesting the Face, causing all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to behold it.

Fifteen times the number of sands of the Ganges away from here, there is a buddha-field named Like an Illusion. There, a Buddha resides, named Tathāgata Equal-Mind, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans; he is called Buddha, World-Honored One.

That land is pure and free from attachment or conceptualization; it contains no realms of hungry ghosts, animals, or hell-beings. Its conduct is consistently profound and sincere, devoid of self-conceit; the mind does not incline toward the Lesser Vehicle, nor are there any sounds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
He caused everyone in the assembly to see it all.

At that time, the World-Honored One arose from that samādhi and again entered the meditative state of the "Full Moon," causing all sentient beings to see everything as golden in color and hear the Buddhas of the ten directions proclaiming the practice of signlessness:
"What is meant by signlessness?"

All dharmas are quiescent, tranquil, and formless; all dharmas do not arise, enduring all anger and rage; all dharmas gather the mind, giving rise to no external thoughts; all dharmas stabilize the intent, manifesting the purity of one's own land; all dharmas are skillfully contemplated, not limited by the calculation of kalpas; all dharmas are joyfully practiced, forever departing from affection and craving; all dharmas manifest clarity, giving rise to no deluded thoughts.
All dharmas transcend greed, thereby fulfilling the perfection of giving;
all dharmas are without transgression, thereby fulfilling the perfection of ethical discipline;
all dharmas give rise to no thoughts of anger, thereby fulfilling the perfection of patience.
In all dharmas, one exerts diligence without indolence, thereby fulfilling the perfection of vigor;
in all dharmas, one does not give rise to distracted thoughts, but gathers the mind without wavering and constantly delights in dhyāna, thereby fulfilling the perfection of meditation;
in all dharmas, one completely eliminates ignorance and delusion without other divergent thoughts, thereby fulfilling the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, there is that which is called the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
What are these four foundations of mindfulness?

If there are good sons or daughters who practice the foundation of mindfulness regarding the internal body, they distinguish it part by part from the head down to the feet, contemplating the impurity of its arising; they contemplate their own body and the bodies of others, they contemplate their own mind and the minds of others, and all internal and external phenomena are likewise treated in this way."
Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas for himself:

the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; this is called the signless practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having observed his own body, observes the bodies of others, discerning each part from head to foot and giving rise to the perception of impurity. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s contemplation that both internal and external bodies are entirely non-existent."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses in praise:
"Not relying on mind, thought, or consciousness, One discerns the root of all conditioned formations;
When the Way abides in the absence of conceptualization, Then one accords with the Noble Truth."
The Buddha’s wisdom is boundless, seeing neither union nor separation;
Buddhahood arises from the signless, thus responding to the practice of the fruit.
The Way of the Buddha is fundamentally non-dual, and likewise possesses no single characteristic.
The True Person’s benevolence is universal; he manifests various teachings.
Fundamentally, there is no self and nothing created by a self; through defilement, the five aggregates come into being.
With the immeasurable wisdom of the Noble Truths, one advances toward the spontaneous cessation of the mind.
Neither existent nor non-existent, yet arising from birth and death through defiled attachment;
by extinguishing these marks, one spontaneously becomes a Buddha, and is thus titled the God among Gods.
It is difficult to be born with a human body, and difficult for the six sense faculties to be complete.
It is difficult to extinguish the twelve links of dependent origination; it is difficult to be born in heaven and receive its blessings.
It is difficult to encounter the worthy and the holy; it is difficult to enter meditative concentration and eliminate conceptualization.
It is difficult to contemplate the body internally and externally; it is difficult to receive the holy teachings face-to-face.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking these verses, all those present in the assembly—the devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and the eight classes of beings—conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; furthermore, countless sentient beings attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Chapter Twelve: The Four Noble Truths (4). *The Bodhisattva’s Garland Sūtra*, Chapter Twelve: The Four Noble Truths. At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:

“In the past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mahākāya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”

The land is named Śūnyapraśānta; it was precisely here that he attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and preached the subtle Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to the fourfold assembly, extensively transforming sentient beings so that they all reached the realm of nirvana without remainder and attained parinirvāṇa.
"What are the Four Noble Truths?

First is the Noble Truth of the Immeasurable. When a Bodhisattva attains this Noble Truth, within a single thought-moment they personally extinguish the defilements of their own mind and can likewise extinguish the defilements of others' minds; they do not perceive any dust or defilement as having an end or being inexhaustible.

Second is the Noble Truth of the Exhaustion of Conduct. When a Bodhisattva attains this Noble Truth, within a single thought-moment they cause all sentient beings to fully awaken to the conduct of body, speech, and mind—whether good or evil—and lead them all toward the gateway of the Path, causing every sentient being to reach the realm of Nirvana without remainder."

The third is the Holy Truth of Swift Action. A bodhisattva who attains this holy truth can cause all sentient beings to fully achieve the Buddha-way in the space of a finger-snap; they can further cause infinite, immeasurable, and incalculable numbers of beings in a single day to attain the Way, and cause the various classes of beings in countless *asaṃkhyeya* lands to each give rise to a virtuous mind and offer respectful worship to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—with incense, flowers, silken banners, and the performance of music—transforming *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-lands into a single precious canopy used for offering, surpassing all that of devas and worldlings, and being able to provide, in a single thought-moment, all the natural food and drink, clothing, beds, bedding, and medicinal treatments for the sick found in the heavens.

The fourth is called the Noble Truth of Equality. When a bodhisattva attains this noble truth, they can cause all sentient beings to become entirely of one course, devoid of any manifold characteristics, and enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder. It is like a flame, a phantom, or a mirage; the world is empty and quiescent, formless and ungraspable.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: while teaching and transforming sentient beings and purifying Buddha-lands, he does not perceive any sentient beings who have attained deliverance, nor does he perceive any who receive transformation;
yet it is not that sentient beings do not exist, nor is it that they do not exist; it is not that there are no pure sentient beings, nor is it that there are no pure sentient beings.
It is not that turbidity does not exist, nor is it that turbidity does not not exist; it is not that there is no conception in a womb, nor is it that there is no non-conception in a womb;
it is not that existence does not exist, nor is it that existence does not not exist; it is not that birth and death do not exist, nor is it that birth and death do not not exist.
To distinguish each of these individually, they are all found to be non-existent; knowing the twelve links of dependent origination is likewise thus. From...
Ignorance through to the twelve links of dependent origination are neither existent nor non-existent; they are like a mirage. The world cannot be grasped or maintained;
it is neither near nor far. Although one transforms sentient beings, one does not perceive any who have been transformed.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: when contemplating all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, he perceives neither their arising nor their cessation; they possess neither marks nor are they without marks.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the dharma of signlessness, teaches and transforms sentient beings and purifies the Buddha-lands.

Although there is a Buddha, he has no perception of a Buddha; although there is the Dharma, he has no perception of the Dharma; although there is the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, he has no perception of the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. This, Mañjuśrī, is called—
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained the dharma of signlessness, they abide in non-retrogression without any obstruction.
It is, for example, like a person who, while dreaming, becomes either a king or a wheel-turning sage king; upon waking, they remember what they did in the dream and do not forget it.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he contemplates all sentient beings as having become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; yet he does not perceive a characteristic of becoming, nor does he perceive a characteristic of non-becoming.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"Was that Tathāgata Mahākāya, who preached the Dharma that is pure, formless, and invisible, anyone other than this person?"
Do not form such a view.
Why is this? The Tathāgata Mahākāya of that time is none other than the present Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In incalculable past ages, there was a Buddha named Mahākāya (Great Body).
He attained perfect enlightenment here, and no faction of heterodox practices existed."
Constantly employing the dharma of signlessness, he discerns the Four Noble Truths;
manifesting expediently as he wanders through the worlds, he appears to receive instruction.
The Buddha-way is inconceivable, and his supernormal powers are inexhaustible.
I transform and guide all classes of sentient beings, until they are all made one in appearance.
Now I have attained Buddhahood myself, the foremost honored one in the three realms;
unstained by those things, I shall no longer undergo birth, old age, or death.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking these verses, immeasurable sentient beings all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Chapter Thirteen: Attaining the Way (4) The Bodhisattva’s Necklace Sūtra, Chapter Thirteen: Attaining the Way At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Fearless (Abhaya), who had made offerings to countless Buddhas of the past and had already attained *dhāraṇī*, discerning the destinies of the rise and fall of the three periods of time. He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, knelt on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is so, World-Honored One!”
Now I have heard the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, preach the four dharmas of the noble ones that are difficult to encounter—dharmas never before heard and never before seen.
If there are good men or good women who receive, uphold, recite, and chant the names of the Four Noble Truths, they will then be able to serve as a field of merit and blessings for others.
Why is this? World-Honored One!

These good men and women have established great vows not for their own sake, desiring to deliver sentient beings within the realm of emptiness, so that all may reach the realm of nirvana without remainder and enter parinirvāṇa.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain these Four Noble Truths, they contemplate and realize that sentient beings are entirely non-existent. Through the contemplation of emptiness, the Bodhisattva perceives neither a self nor sentient beings; yet, maintaining the mind of great vows, they employ emptiness to raise up emptiness, accumulating merit and virtue over countless kalpas until they behold the appearance of Buddhas in the world.

One discerns that all phenomena have no form or appearance; one does not cling to worldly interests—gain or loss, defamation or praise, renown or insignificance, suffering or pleasure—and furthermore, one knows the minds and consciousnesses of sentient beings across the future, past, and present, discerning each one so as to bring them to fulfillment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhayamati again addressed the Buddha,
saying: "How is it so,
World-Honored One?"

The classes of sentient beings are beyond calculation or record; they are not within the reach of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas. Among the countless Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, were there any who resolved to seek the Bodhisattva path and declared:

"In the distant future, I shall surely attain the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path. I shall be able to exhaust the limits of space and know the fundamental nature of sentient beings within those limits; having already been able to distinguish the sentient beings within space, I shall further be able to distinguish their consciousnesses regarding the realms of existence and non-existence, such that all these sentient beings may be led to attain the Way within a single day"?
“Is there such a thing?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Fearless, saying:

“The consciousnesses of the future, the past, and the present are not within the sphere of your discernment; that you have now posed this question is entirely due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.”
"Why is this? Only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is able to expound each and every profound dharma.
The Buddha said:
“Son of good family!

Regarding past consciousness as you have asked, one can fully know the transmigration of consciousness through the four paths among devas and humans, and even exhaustively discern all that consciousness has experienced and all where it has proceeded throughout the eight classes of beings.”
The Bodhisattva Abhaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has given rise to the mind of great vows, fully capable of rescuing and delivering all beings of the past, future, and present.”
"How can one attain Buddhahood in a single day?
The Buddha said, "The question posed by the Bodhisattva Fearless is most profound; I shall now explain it to you in full detail, so that you may understand its purpose and what has been asked."

Past consciousness does not, within the past, cause past consciousness to attain Buddhahood; it does not, within the present, cause present consciousness to attain Buddhahood; nor does it, within the future, cause future consciousness to reach Buddhahood.
Why is this? Past consciousness is not the original past consciousness; future consciousness is not future consciousness; present consciousness is not present consciousness.
"Fearless Bodhisattva, you should know that there are three practices for attaining Buddhahood in the past."
What are the three?
There is the initial mind, the generative mind, and the sentient-being mind.
What is the initial mind?

Fearless Bodhisattva, you should know that although there is originally no Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, he nevertheless teaches and transforms beings therein, such that they all attain the Buddha-way on the same day and at the same time; this is called the initial resolve.
What is meant by "arousing the mind"?
That which is called "arousing the mind" refers to having already received the defilements of sensory objects, and now intending to extinguish the mind and eliminate those defilements.
What is the "mind of sentient beings"?
Suppose there are sentient beings who, from eon to eon, even unto hundreds of thousands of eons, further exhaust countless births, deaths, and afflictions;
yet this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva must surely extinguish those countless afflictions and deliver countless sentient beings.
This is called, Fearless Bodhisattva!
the accomplishment of three matters within the past.
"Fearless, you should know that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall likewise possess three dharmas in the future."
What are the three? It is as follows:
the future mind has not yet received the present; this too can be further advanced. Furthermore, Abhaya!
The mind of the future already possesses defilements within a single day; therefore, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva must extinguish these defilements of a day.

Son of good family, you should know that as the future shifts from one kalpa to a hundred kalpas, even unto incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha knows this bodily consciousness along with its afflictions. This is called being endowed with these three dharmas within the future.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in the present, shall likewise be endowed with these three dharmas.”
What are these three?
First, when the initial consciousness is present and not yet defiled by worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), one causes that consciousness to attain *nirvāṇa* in a single day.
If, however, after one or two moments it gives rise to worldly afflictions, one must be able to extinguish those one or two moments as well as the afflictions; only then can one attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:

"If, in the present, from one body up to a hundred thousand bodies, various afflictions (*kleśa*) arise, this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva being fully endowed with the three dharmas within the present."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Abhaya:
"He who was liberated in a single day by his initial resolve in the past is none other than the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Viśvada in the past."
The one who, in a past life, was granted deliverance by his mind is none other than the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Anupama.
The sentient beings of the past who were granted salvation are none other than the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mūlapratiṣṭhāna.
Those who receive deliverance through the initial resolve in the future are the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha *Śūnyarūpa*.
Those who receive deliverance through the first or second [levels] in the future are the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha *Śūnyamukha*.
Those who will attain deliverance through countless future bodies are the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha of Fixed Intention.
Those who attain deliverance at the initial moment of the present are the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha of No Body.
Those who are now delivered through a single or double body are the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sunakṣatra.
Those who are now delivered through innumerable bodies are the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candraprabha.
"What is it, son of good family?
Among the nine grades, what is your aspiration?"
Is it because of the initial mind of the past?
Or the minds of past births?
Or the minds of past sentient beings?
Is it because of the first thought-moment of the future?
Or the one or two thought-moments of the future?
Or the thought-moments of incalculable eons of the future?
Is it from the initial thought of the present?
Or from one or two thoughts of the present?
Or from countless thoughts of the present?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhaya came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I first resolved my mind to seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path, I was not yet able to know for myself which path I was seeking."

Now that I have heard the Tathāgata explain the nine grades of practice, I now wish to give rise for the first time to the great mind of universal vows, desiring to deliver those from the past who have not yet been defiled by the dust and grime of the world.
The Buddha said: "Stop! Stop!"
"O son of good family!
You have now already fallen away from the initial resolve; how then can you hope to achieve unexcelled, perfect enlightenment based on that initial resolve?
This is not possible."
The Bodhisattva Abhayamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Although I have already fallen away from the initial resolve of the past, I now wish to seek the mind that delivers sentient beings of the past, and through the wisdom that is universally equal toward all beings, to achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
The Buddha said:
"You have now transcended this realm and fallen to a lower stage; you have not yet accomplished the task of rescuing sentient beings to achieve unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhayamati again addressed the Buddha,
saying: "How is this so,
World-Honored One?"
"Regarding sentient beings burdened by afflictions in the past, did you not give rise to the great vow-mind and thereby achieve unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment? The Buddha said, "No."

Why is this? The countless past [eons] have already ceased and been exhausted; it is not by exhausting those afflictions within the present body that one attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. For this reason, one cannot achieve unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now find nothing whatsoever in the three periods of the past.
Because it exists neither above nor below, I do not attain the unsurpassed, truly real, equal, and right enlightenment."
"Why is this? Because you originally gave rise to a great vow-mind that is neither 'that' nor 'this,' it cannot be accomplished.
The Bodhisattva Abhaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is this so, World-Honored One?

Now that I wish to relinquish one or two [eons] of the future and relinquish the afflictions of the future, would it still be possible to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment starting from the present initial resolve?"
The Buddha said: "No.

Originally, when you first resolved [to attain enlightenment], your mind was bound to specific existences; the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha perceives lands according to their transformations, responding appropriately to those bound existences, which was not your original vow."
The Bodhisattva Abhayamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the future, one relinquishes one mind and two minds; furthermore, in the future, one relinquishes sentient beings afflicted by defilements; and furthermore, in the present, one relinquishes present sentient beings. Is it possible, within the present, to cause sentient beings of one mind and two minds to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?”
The Buddha said: "There is none. Why is this?"
"Your original aspiration was that your mind remained attached to existence; it was not your original vow.
The Bodhisattva Abhaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Furthermore, having set aside one mind and two minds, and having further set aside the afflictions (*kleśa*) of future sentient beings, and having further set aside the initial mind of the present, and having further set aside one mind and two minds of the present—now, if you wish to make a vow for the sake of sentient beings currently beset by afflictions, is this possible?
The Buddha said: "No. Why is this?"
"We have already passed beyond this realm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Fearless addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Where among the nine grades does the Tathāgata abide today?
The Buddha said,
"I have relinquished the three of the past, the three of the future, and the three of the present."

“Furthermore, can one attain equal and perfect enlightenment at the initial moment of mind in the future, thereby causing sentient beings at the initial moment of mind in the future to attain equal and perfect enlightenment?
The Buddha said: “No.”
Why is this? Your body does not exist in the future.
How then can you seek to attain equal and perfect enlightenment in order to deliver sentient beings of the future?
"This matter is not so.
The Bodhisattva Abhaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Now that I have fallen back to the initial mind of the future, do I wish again to give rise to great vows so as to attain equal and perfect enlightenment within one or two minds of the future?
The Buddha said,
"Indeed you do!"
"Your wish shall be fulfilled. Why is this?

Because throughout countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past, you have constantly given rise to a vast and great mind of solemn vows; therefore, in this very body, you shall ascend to the pure world of the upper direction and attain Buddhahood there, bearing the name Fearless Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, just as you do now."

Having received this individual prophecy, the Bodhisattva Abhaya leaped for joy; he immediately beheld the Pure World with his own eyes, and the sentient beings therein transformed by him appeared no different from himself.
Why is this? It is because the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power causes them all to see it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Fearless addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now further resolve upon a great vow to make offerings to countless Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. I pray that I may deliver the sentient beings of future defilements and attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment therein—would this be possible?”
The Buddha said: “No.

Since you first sought the Way, your mind has not dwelt in the middle; rather, having eliminated the two extremes, you have remained among sentient beings in the midst of worldly afflictions, attaining the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, and being titled Buddha, the World-Honored One.”
The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Scroll Four;
The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Scroll Five. Also known as the *Pratyutpanna-vipāka*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.

Chapter 14: On the Birth of Buddhas (5) At that time, there was a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva in the assembly named Vibhajyavāda-dāna (Discerning Explanation of Giving), who had cultivated the roots of all virtues under immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. He rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
“Excellent, excellent!
“World-Honored One!

Is there any Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who, within a single moment or a single day across the past, future, and present, can know the three matters of the past and the three matters of the future and present, and thereby attain Buddhahood?”
He replied: "There is none. Why is this?"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, observes and beholds lands according to his transformations; it is only by adapting to sentient beings that he brings them to accomplishment.
It is just as when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not regard lands as lands, nor sentient beings as sentient beings, but discerns them through the dharma-knowledge born of the dharma-realm.

The Tathāgata’s divine wisdom is not mundane wisdom; mundane wisdom refers to that which extends from the desire realm and the form realm up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception. This is what is called mundane wisdom.
Today, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has already transcended this wisdom; how then does he give rise to all dharmas and achieve the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha?
This matter is not so.
Why? Because the Tathāgata is suchness.

As is the suchness of the Tathāgata, so is the suchness of the world; as is the suchness of the nature of all phenomena, the inconceivable suchness, the suchness of the future, and the suchness of the number of eons in that world.
The Tathāgata’s eons are suchness; this suchness is one and not two.
All suchnesses and the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena are likewise neither born nor extinguished, and are without attachment or cessation.

The names and titles bestowed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout kalpas that are infinite, immeasurable, and beyond calculation, are seen neither as long nor as short; they are seen neither as arising nor as ceasing. How, then, do they give rise to all phenomena?
Being formless and invisible, they do not arise in the future; being indeterminate, they are not seen as determinate.

Just as formless phenomena are of various kinds, so too are the groups of names (*nāmakāya*) and phrases (*padakāya*); the groups of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) are likewise. There are no distinct individual name-groups, no distinct individual phrase-groups, and no distinct individual phoneme-groups.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are each empty; they possess neither good nor evil, neither merit nor the absence of merit, and they may involve either action or non-action.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Akṣayamati who had realized this nature of emptiness, suchness, and the non-existence of phenomena. He rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am now able, before the Tathāgata, to expound the dharma of having practice and being without practice, which is like the nature of emptiness and suchness."
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
“Speak as you wish.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there are good sons or good daughters who cultivate both conditioned practice and unconditioned practice, they will be able to fulfill all dharmas and attain equal and perfect enlightenment.”
What is meant by "with practice" and "without practice"?
That all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and that there is no past, future, or present—this is called "without practice.
To definitively conclude that one discriminates among the past, future, and present of all phenomena—this is called the Bodhisattva’s "with practice."

There are immeasurable name-bodies (nāmakāya) whose beginning and end are not perceived; there are immeasurable phrase-bodies (padakāya) whose beginning and end are not perceived; there are immeasurable syllable-bodies (vyañjanakāya) whose beginning and end are not perceived—this is called the non-practice of a bodhisattva.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family knows that the dharmas of the three periods of time have arising and ceasing, yet discerns within them that nothing at all exists, this is called the bodhisattva’s practice with activity.
At that time, Akṣayamati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“To bring to ultimate completion those dharmas that have not yet reached completion, and to bring to total extinction those dharmas that have not yet been extinguished—this is called the bodhisattva’s non-action.”
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, regarding the past, future, and present, perceives neither measure nor lack of measure, this is called the "practice with activity" of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, good sons and daughters!

When one first gives rise to the mind of the Way and practices the unsurpassed, right, and true path, one does not take pleasure in praise or blame, suffering or joy, gain or loss, defamation or fame; this is called the 'non-practice' of a bodhisattva."

If all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm were to focus their thoughts and minds as one, analyzing the dharma of annihilation throughout the three periods of time, this is called the bodhisattva’s practice with activity.

"Furthermore, good sons and daughters who, throughout immeasurable kalpas, practice diligent and ascetic austerities desiring to hear and receive the Tathāgata’s teachings—this is called the bodhisattva’s non-action."

Furthermore, sons or daughters of good family who practice the four immeasurable minds (catvāry apramāṇāni) yet do not praise themselves on account of those four immeasurables—this is called the bodhisattva’s practice with activity.
“Being unstained and unpolluted, without past, future, or present—this is called the bodhisattva’s non-practice (*apracāra*).

If, noble son or daughter, one is neither meaningful nor meaningless, neither established nor unestablished, neither having an opposite nor lacking an opposite—this is called the bodhisattva’s practice (*pracāra*).”
"Alternatively, if one purifies the buddha-field without being stained by anything, yet does not perceive that the field has been accomplished, this is called the bodhisattva’s non-practice.
Furthermore, if one does not give rise to false views regarding any phenomena and remains without origination, adorning oneself with inexhaustible dharmas, this is called practice."
To neither exist nor not exist—this is called the bodhisattva’s non-practice.

Furthermore, son or daughter of good family, to contemplate a single buddha-field as no different from space, and not to fixate upon other fields as being within that one nation—this is called the bodhisattva’s practice.

Furthermore, one observes for oneself that there are originally Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Mahāsattvas of the three periods of time—past, future, and present; this is called the bodhisattva’s non-practice.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If a son or daughter of good family discerns each [element] individually, realizing that the realms are not my realms, the world is not my world, and existence is not my existence—this is called the bodhisattva’s practice with activity."
Furthermore, son of good family!
To discern the activities of the three realms as being without activity, neither seeing action nor seeing non-action—this is called the bodhisattva’s non-activity.
At that time, the Tathāgata asked the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:
"In what dharma do you abide to speak thus?
Does non-practice give rise to practice?"
“Is there practice that arises from non-practice?
By what means does the Tathāgata himself speak of both practice and non-practice?
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This has originated from self-awakening, and now its fruit is finally realized; we only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and elucidate it.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! As you have spoken, reflect upon it well; today the Tathāgata shall expound its teaching for you. How so?"
Son of good family!
When you first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, was it through conditioned practice,
or was it through unconditioned practice?
He replied: "Neither by way of conditioned activity, nor by way of non-activity.
The Buddha said:
"How is it, son of good family?
If one does not proceed by way of existence nor by way of non-existence, how can one attain equal and perfect enlightenment?"
He replied, “There is suchness, and suchness is also such-like; therefore, it does not proceed from existence nor does it proceed from non-existence.
The Buddha said:
"Why did you not ask this question earlier?
I have already previously explained both the practice and the non-practice.

Chapter Fifteen: On the Beginning and End (Part Five). *The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen: On the Beginning and End. At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to manifest the conduct of a bodhisattva, immediately entered the Samādhi of Original Purity, causing all sentient beings to see the beginning and end of all dharmas of the past, future, and present.

Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to see the various Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in immeasurable worlds—those who have attained accomplishment and those who have not; those from the first stage up to the tenth stage; and those whose bodily activities are manifest and those whose bodily activities are not manifest, causing all sentient beings to discern each of these individually.

At that time, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, desiring to deliver sentient beings, smiled; from his face there issued forth a great radiance that illuminated immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extending from the Desire Realm upward to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, such that all beheld the light.
From that radiance, the fundamental basis of immeasurable sentient beings is manifested.
What constitutes the beginning and end of sentient beings?
In this regard, when good sons and good daughters practice a single dharma, they will be able to fulfill immeasurable wisdom, purify Buddha-lands, and transform sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of those who practice the conduct of non-attachment:
"What is the conduct of non-attachment?
From the first generation of the aspiration for enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, one practices the non-attachment to emptiness through fifty-four dharmas."
Therefore, sons and daughters of good family should constantly contemplate this without being parted from it for even a moment.
What are these fifty-four?

First, one discriminates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): knowing their arising when they arise, and knowing their cessation when they cease; yet those five aggregates may have birth or be without birth, may possess noble practice (*ārya-caryā*) or lack noble practice, and may involve the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) or lack the contemplation of emptiness.
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family discerns the five aggregates: by what cause do they arise?
By what cause do they cease?

Form was originally without arising, yet now it has arising; one understands that form is neither existent nor non-existent, whether there is the existence of form or the fundamental nature of form. Past, future, and present forms are likewise thus."

Fundamentally there is no form, and thus one does not perceive a "basic" form. Within the past, one does not perceive past form; within the future, one does not perceive future form; within the present, one does not perceive present form. Past form is not present form, nor is it future form; future form is not past form, nor is it present form; present form is not past form, nor is it future form. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is fully able to discern each of these and knows them all completely.
"Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family!

One should analytically discern the dharma of sensation (vedanā) and understand that sensation has no arising. One contemplates that past sensation was originally non-existent; one also knows that this sensation does not possess a past, for past sensation is neither future nor present, future sensation is neither past nor present, and present sensation is neither past nor future."
Why is this? Because future sensation originally lacks such sensation.

If a son or daughter of good family contemplates present sensation as neither prior sensation nor subsequent sensation, neither past sensation nor future sensation, and realizes that sensation itself does not know sensation, only then do they come to know that it is pure at its root and pure at its end.

“Furthermore, if a son or daughter of good family should further contemplate the perception of the five aggregates of the past, they should realize that, by their very nature, these perceptions do not exist. The perception of the five aggregates of the past does not know the perceptions of the future or the present; the perception of the future does not know the perceptions of the past or the present; and the perception of the present does not know the perceptions of the past or the future. Thus, perception is without perception.”

"If a son or daughter of good family, within the future, discriminates the perception of the future, that perception of the future does not know itself as the perception of the future; the perception of the future does not know the perceptions of the past or the present; the perception of the future or the past does not know the future; and the perception of the past does not know the perceptions of the future or the present."

"If a son or daughter of good family, within the present, discerns the perception of the past yet has no perception of the past; discerns the perception of the future yet has no perception of the future; discerns the perception of the present yet has no perception of the present; within the present and the past, there is no perception of the past; within the present and the future, there is no perception of the present or the future; and even within the perception of the present, there is no perception—[this is so]."

"If a son or daughter of good family further contemplates the past analysis of the five aggregates: by what cause do they arise? By what cause do they cease? Past formations (*saṃskāra*) are not themselves formations;

one analyzes past formations as not being past formations. Past formations are not future formations nor present formations; future formations are not past formations nor present formations; present formations are not past formations nor future formations. Past and future formations are not past and future formations; past and present formations are not past and present formations."
Why is this? Because practice is fundamentally non-existent, and yet there is no practice.

"If a son or daughter of good family, in the future, were to fully possess future practice, they would not perceive past practice within the future, nor would they perceive present practice within the future; they would not perceive future-past practice within the future, nor would they perceive future-present practice within the future, nor even perceive future-future practice."
Why is this? Because fundamentally there is no such practice.

If a son or daughter of good family were to further analyze within the present, they would find that past practice has no past practice, nor does it have future practice, nor does it have present practice.

Contemplating present formations, one does not perceive past formations; contemplating present formations, one also does not perceive future formations. Thus, one contemplates that all formations are entirely non-existent.

"If a son or daughter of good family, regarding the past, contemplates past consciousness and does not perceive past consciousness; regarding future consciousness, they do not perceive future consciousness; regarding present consciousness, they do not perceive present consciousness; regarding past consciousness, they do not perceive past or future consciousness; and within the past, they do not perceive past or present consciousness, nor do they perceive consciousness at all."

"If a son or daughter of good family, within the future, does not perceive past consciousness as future consciousness, nor perceive future past consciousness within the future, nor perceive future present consciousness;..."

If a son or daughter of good family does not perceive the past consciousness within the present consciousness, nor perceive the future consciousness; and within the present, does not perceive the past consciousness, nor perceive the future consciousness within the present—this is called the discernment by a son or daughter of good family that the five aggregates are empty from beginning to end.

16. Chapter on Neither Consciousness Nor Non-Consciousness (5). *The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Chapter Sixteen: Neither Consciousness Nor Non-Consciousness. At that time, the Bodhisattva Pratibhāsa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I have just heard that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has already explained the fundamental nature of sentient beings.
Today, relying upon the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, I wish to speak of those with consciousness and those without consciousness.
"I only pray, World-Honored One, that you will grant me leave; having received it, I shall venture to speak.
The Buddha said:
“Noble son! Speak as you wish.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Rūpa-pratibhāsa (Form-Echo) immediately praised the Buddha before him in verse:
“The World-Honored One’s great vow, Knowing the fundamental capacities of all beings,
Today we have been granted the opportunity to hear The oral teachings from the mouth of the Divine Honored One.
From countless Buddhas in the past, I have constantly sought to hear this essential Dharma.”
Now I have heard the teaching of the Holy Honored One, and I have listened to the discourse on existence and non-existence.
In the past, throughout countless eons, I served various Holy Honored Ones;
as a result, I have now attained the foremost eloquence in vocal resonance.
Marks themselves have no marks; neither existence nor non-existence is perceived.
Free from dust and all defilements, you are now hailed as the Honored One among Men.
Since birth itself is fundamentally non-birth, how could there be further birth for me?
Because I lack the intent for [profound] meaning and wish only to explain the basis of limited wisdom,
I do not dare, out of my own ignorant sentiments, to proclaim the teachings of the Tathāgata.
Recalling the roots of my past conduct, I listen only and do not dare to doubt.
“Birth and death are without measure; receiving body after body, one remains in a state of perpetual doubt until the very end. Pray, listen as we expound upon this.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva Xingxiang (Form-Echo) stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To understand the primary meaning (paramārtha) without distinguishing between that consciousness and this consciousness is called ‘consciousness and non-consciousness.

Not seeing the grasping of existence, nor seeing the grasping of non-existence, wherein all dharmas are of a single mark—neither entirely non-existent nor entirely existent—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s consciousness and non-consciousness.”

Distinguishing between spiritual lineages, [the Bodhisattva] discerns that "this consciousness is pure" and "this consciousness is not pure," that "I have accomplished the primary and secondary marks" and "that one has not accomplished the primary and secondary marks. To be able to perceive and understand all these things while realizing they are non-existent—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s having consciousness and yet having no consciousness.

When discerning the passage of time, one beholds the various Buddhas, seeing that there are Buddhas in this kalpa and no Buddhas in that kalpa; yet one does not harbor joy because there is a Buddha, nor does one feel sorrow even when there is no Buddha. This is called the bodhisattva’s having consciousness and being without consciousness.

Furthermore, I observe among the classes of sentient beings those who possess skillful means and those who lack skillful means; yet within this, I give rise to no conceptualization or mental activity. This is called the bodhisattva’s having consciousness and being without consciousness.

Furthermore, he observes sentient beings and knows the limits of their lifespans: there are sentient beings who should attain liberation through a past kalpa, those who should attain liberation through a future kalpa, and those who should attain liberation through the present kalpa; yet he does not perceive this kalpa as having either those who are liberated or those who are not. This is called the bodhisattva’s having consciousness and being without consciousness.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Saṃpūrṇalakṣaṇa who rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I, too, am capable of speaking before the Tathāgata concerning the conscious and the unconscious."
Furthermore, he spoke these verses in praise:
"Having performed these manifold meritorious deeds before Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
He brings to mind the Perfectly Enlightened Ones and, through his accumulated practices, recognizes his past lives."
Not clinging to self, person, or life-span, birth and death have no fundamental root;
the marks of the Way are without form or sign—now I have encountered the Honored One among Men.
With the wisdom that is equal throughout the three times, it is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness.
When all conditioned activities have ceased and no further karma is created, one then bestows the final prediction upon the disciple.
When even a single consciousness is found to be non-existent, one awakens to the profound essentials of the Dharma and transcends all Buddha-fields and immeasurable buddha-lands.
Throughout countless past lives, it was only upon hearing this teaching that I attained awakening.
I pray that before the Tathāgata, you will explain the distinction between consciousness and non-consciousness.
Having analyzed this profound and subtle Dharma, I have now encountered the Honored One among Men.
"Having fully reached the realm of Nirvana, I only pray that you will grant me leave to speak of it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Just as I am today called "Endowed with All Marks," yet when these marks arise I do not know they are arising, and when these marks cease I do not know they are ceasing—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva having consciousness and being without consciousness.
The Bodhisattva Samantavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I recall, in the past I heard this essential teaching from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jñānaprajña: ‘If there are sentient beings who, from their first aspiration until their attainment of Buddhahood, do not perceive the characteristics of consciousness, this is called a bodhisattva having consciousness yet being without consciousness.’”

If a son or daughter of good family discerns each of the six decays (āyatana) and six sense bases individually, knowing that past decay is not past decay, knowing that future decay is not future decay, and knowing that present decay is not present decay, and does not give rise to conceptual attachment or perception therein—this is called "consciousness with non-consciousness."
The Bodhisattva Jāti-jāta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Today, in the presence of the Tathāgata, I have heard the Bodhisattva Ghoṣa-vatsa speak of consciousness and non-consciousness, and I have further heard the Bodhisattva Lakṣaṇa-samudgata speak of consciousness and non-consciousness.”
"How so? World-Honored One!
Regarding that which is called 'consciousness,' what constitutes consciousness?"
The Buddha said,
“It is equal to space.
The Bodhisattva Jātiga then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In what way is it equal to space?
The Buddha said:
"It is neither born nor extinguished; it is neither attached to nor severed.
The Bodhisattva Jāti-gotra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now ask the Tathāgata about the origin of consciousness; why do you answer me with emptiness?"
The Buddha said: "It is not so.
I now declare that consciousness is neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, it is called 'consciousness with consciousness' and 'consciousness without consciousness.'"
The Bodhisattva Jāti-prabhava asked,
“Is consciousness characterized by marks, or is it markless?
The Buddha said:
"Consciousness, moreover, has neither marks nor is it markless.
The Bodhisattva Śrigarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way does consciousness have neither marks nor is it markless?"

The Buddha said: "Originally there was no characteristic, nor is there a characteristic now; therefore it is said that the original consciousness is not the present consciousness, and the present consciousness is not the original consciousness.
Thus, consciousness has neither a characteristic of existence nor a characteristic of non-existence."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jātinirghoṣa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If having marks is not consciousness and being without marks is not consciousness, for what reason do you say ‘consciousness cognizes’?”
The Buddha said: “It arises in accordance with the arising of consciousness.
When consciousness arises, it arises; when consciousness ceases, it ceases. Therefore, it is neither characterized by existence nor characterized by non-existence.”
The Buddha again addressed the son of good family:
"What do you think,
O Bodhisattva born of the lineage?"
"Do you now perceive consciousness? He replied, "No."
"Why is this? It has no form and no image; it does not exist in the present, nor did it exist in the past, nor will it exist in the future.
The Buddha said:
“You have yourself stated that consciousness has no consciousness—neither in the present, nor in the future, nor in the past. Who, then, are you speaking of now?
He replied, “If one wishes to speak of it as consciousness...”
"From what lineage is this consciousness born?
The Buddha said, "I do not ask from what lineage this consciousness of a bodhisattva is born; I only ask whether this consciousness exists or does not exist."
He replied, "Consciousness is neither existent nor non-existent.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, son of good family! At that time, the Bodhisattva Jātinirvṛta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One? Regarding the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha as he is today, do you speak of him as existing or as non-existing based on consciousness?"
"Do you ask this of the Tathāgata based on whether [existence or non-existence] is spoken of apart from consciousness?
The Buddha said: "By what meaning do you question the Tathāgata?"
The Bodhisattva Jāti-jāta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have just asked the Tathāgata:
‘Do you now speak of consciousness or non-consciousness?’”
"Is there a future, a present, and a past?
Or is there no future, no present, and no past? I replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
Just as the World-Honored One has now said that present consciousness does not exist, so too future and past consciousness do not exist."
"Where, then, does consciousness reside in me and the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:

"I have already stated previously that there is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness; it is only for the sake of awakening sentient beings that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, employs various dharmas."
How so? Son of good family!
If a son or daughter of noble family understands this Dharma in its essence, they will be able to fulfill all dharmas.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Balavardhana who rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I, too, am capable of explaining that which possesses consciousness and that which lacks consciousness."
The Bodhisattva Balavikrāmin then spoke in verse before the Buddha:
"From the Honored One of Ten Powers, I have heard this teaching on existence and non-existence,
The Eightfold Path of the noble ones, and the eloquent exposition of unimpeded wisdom."
Their voices are each distinct, and the realms of sentient beings differ;
yet bestowing grace without thought of inequality, they are titled the Ten Powers.
If, after my passing, I attain Buddhahood and discern all dharma-realms, [may I likewise be so named].
From the single practice there is no duality; I only pray that you will listen as I explain its cognition.
The Way fundamentally arises from the self, yet through the self, cognition is not produced.
When one calculates and realizes there is no conceptual thought, it is neither cognition nor non-cognition.
Accumulating small acts leads to greatness; through practice, one eventually attains awakening.
Birth and death are immeasurable, and how could the spiritual consciousness ever be exhausted?
Now, relying upon the Honored One’s divine power, I shall briefly expound this for myself.
"I only pray that I may remain in Your holy presence and attain proximity to the treasury of all Buddhas.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Balavikrama had spoken this verse, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "How is it so?"
“World-Honored One!
If there is a conceptualization that the Tathāgata’s ten powers are indestructible, how is it that the Tathāgata’s ten powers are indestructible?
