First, the Tathāgata’s resolve to seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is indestructible; this is called the bodhisattva’s having consciousness and being without consciousness.”
Furthermore, knowing that in the union of self and other, neither the beginning nor the end is seen—this is called the Bodhisattva’s having consciousness and yet being without consciousness.

Observing the fundamental conduct of sentient beings and realizing it is spontaneous, thereby knowing the immeasurable origins from which they come—this is called the Bodhisattva’s having consciousness and yet being without consciousness.

All dharmas are fundamentally without form; it is through the accumulation of delusion that this consciousness arises. One discriminates this delusion without knowing its origin or cessation; this is called the bodhisattva’s having consciousness yet being without consciousness.

Distinguishing the various forms of knowledge, there are three matters that serve as the basis for practice; from the presence of illumination, one may still fall back into the four inversions. Regarding these four inversions, they are seen as illusory transformations; thus, one neither perceives inversion nor perceives non-inversion—this is called the Bodhisattva’s having consciousness and yet being without consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding four matters, when one observes that sentient beings are fundamentally and ultimately endowed with the five practices (*pañca-dharmas*), they are immediately able to contemplate them, whereby these become five matters.
If a son or daughter of good family, within the original absence of practice, practices the traceless practice.
What are the five? First, mindfulness;
second, the turning of mindfulness.
Third is the fundamental;
fourth is delusion;
fifth is inexhaustibility. These are called the consciousness and non-consciousness of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Furthermore, there is another inconceivable dharma of consciousness: there is a skillful means that cannot be fathomed by ordinary people, which involves four modes of practice. By beholding the arising and ceasing of all Buddha-fields, one is then able to accomplish the non-perception of arising and ceasing; this is called the bodhisattva’s consciousness that is both conscious and non-conscious.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, observes the past, the future, and the present, yet he does not perceive a fundamental basis for the past, the future, or the present.

If one is born into the five destinies and assumes the forms of sentient beings within those five destinies, one is able to discern the five destinies according to where they enter; furthermore, one is able to discern the possession of physical sense faculties or the lack thereof.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has already received the faculty of a deva and not that of a nāga, yet wishes to receive the faculty of a nāga, he is able to bring down the rain of all dharmas.

If a son or daughter of good family obtains the faculty of a yakṣa, and having left that yakṣa-faculty receives the faculty of an asura, they are further able to be fully endowed with both consciousness and non-consciousness.

They relinquish those faculties of the asuras and receive those faculties of the gandharvas; having relinquished those faculties, they are then able to be fully endowed with both consciousness and non-consciousness.
It is the same for the caṇḍālas, the māhaurakas, humans, and non-humans. This is called the inconceivable mastery of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva over the entire treasury of the Dharma.

17. Chapter on the Immeasurable (5). *The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Chapter Seventeen: The Immeasurable. "Furthermore, good sons and good daughters, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are further able to fully know that the teachings established by the Buddhas are sometimes fixed and limited, and sometimes immeasurable."
How so? Son of good family!

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas enter this samādhi along with the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, they fully know the finite and infinite teachings established by all Buddhas; they are able to fully know all that the Buddhas speak regarding the activities of speech, the activities of body, and the activities of mind.

Furthermore, they may manifest traveling through the worlds of the ten directions: crossing over the immeasurable worlds of the east and those realms to be saved therein, without failing to uphold the teachings established by the Buddhas of the east;
crossing over the immeasurable worlds of the south and those realms to be saved therein, without failing to uphold the teachings established by the Buddhas of the south;
and crossing over the immeasurable worlds of the west and those realms to be saved therein, without failing to uphold the teachings established by the Buddhas of the west.
He traverses immeasurable worlds in the northern direction and crosses over the realms therein, never failing to uphold the teachings established by the Buddhas of the north;
he traverses immeasurable worlds in the northeastern direction and crosses over the realms therein, never failing to uphold the teachings established by the Buddhas of the northeast;
he traverses immeasurable worlds in the southeastern direction and crosses over the realms therein, never failing to uphold the teachings established by the Buddhas of the southeast.
He traverses immeasurable worlds in the southwestern direction and crosses over the realms therein, yet he does not lose the teachings established by the Buddhas of the southwestern direction;
he traverses immeasurable worlds in the northwestern direction and crosses over the realms therein, yet he does not lose the teachings established by the Buddhas of the northwestern direction.
Furthermore, he travels to the immeasurable worlds above to deliver those who are to be delivered, never failing to uphold the teachings established by the Buddhas of the upper realms.
He likewise proceeds to the immeasurable worlds below to deliver those who are to be delivered, never failing to uphold the teachings established by the Buddhas of the lower realms.

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue and emitted a great radiance, universally illuminating countless worlds in the ten directions. He caused the entire assembly to hear the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as he expounded the profound established teachings to deliver those who were to be delivered:
"In this there are eighteen clarities of wisdom."
Thus, sons and daughters of noble family!

They are able to fully embody the teachings established by the Tathāgata; they can cause what is a realm to be perceived as not a realm, and they can cause what is not a realm to be perceived as a realm. By preaching the Dharma of a single contemplation within those worlds, these good men and women are said to have accomplished one dharma among the eighteen illuminations of wisdom.
"Furthermore, good man or woman!

To foresee countless matters of future worlds, and to know the Buddhas and non-Buddhas, as well as the Bodhisattvas and non-Bodhisattvas, of the past and present—this is called the second dharma accomplished by a Bodhisattva through the eighteen kinds of wisdom-illumination."
"Furthermore, good sons and daughters!

In the past, there were immeasurable, unconditioned, and innumerable [eons] such that their exhaustion could not be seen and their arising could not be seen. This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the three dharmas within the eighteen wisdom-illuminations."
"Furthermore, good sons and good daughters!

To internally and externally discern the four practices of impermanence, and therein personally observe that one's own bodily conduct is complete—this is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the four dharmas within the eighteen illuminations of wisdom."
"Furthermore, good sons and good daughters!

The Buddha-realm is immeasurable and inconceivable; one who can discern the two matters of all Buddhas—delusion and craving—and fully knows their nature to be empty, is called a good son or good daughter who, among the eighteen kinds of clear wisdom, has accomplished five dharmas."
"Furthermore, good sons and good daughters!

If they can contemplate each instance of internal and external emptiness—realizing that 'I do not exist in them, nor do they exist in me'—and know each instance to be empty, quiescent, and non-existent, this is called the good sons and good daughters accomplishing the six dharmas within the eighteen dharmas."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Space is without characteristics and cannot be characterized by space itself. In this regard, those who internally discern their own bodies as being equal to that space—such sons of good family and daughters of good family are said to have accomplished seven dharmas within the eighteen dharmas."
"Furthermore, good sons and good daughters!

Whether there is form or no form, whether there is sound or no sound, within these, all conceptual distinctions are entirely non-existent. This is called the good sons and good daughters accomplishing the eight dharmas among the eighteen dharmas."
"Furthermore, good sons and good daughters!

To know the dhāraṇī of the noble Dharma of the Four Truths arising from the seven contemplations, and to practice the eighteen kinds of emptiness—this is called the good sons and good daughters accomplishing the nine dharmas within the eighteen dharmas."
"Furthermore, good sons and good daughters!

To know that the nature of formless dharmas exists both in the born and in the unborn, and to realize that within this there is nothing whatsoever to be differentiated—this is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the ten dharmas through the eighteen clear wisdoms."
"Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family!

One contemplates immeasurable worlds and knows that they have arising and ceasing, just as a magician observes a reflection in a mirror. This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the eleventh dharma among the eighteen clear wisdoms."
"Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family!
You should further know the seven roots of suffering.
What are these seven?
First, knowing that this mind does not emerge from that [other mind], and that other mind likewise does not exist within this one;
second, knowing that the suffering mind of the other is without self and without person, and that this suffering mind is likewise without self and without person;
third, knowing that the worlds of all Buddhas are inconceivable, and that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas are fully able to measure them all.
Fourth, if a son or daughter of good family internally contemplates suffering, emptiness, and non-self, they do not perceive the existence of a body, being like a mirror reflecting an image;
fifth, if I receive a physical form, I sever the dharma of the ten bodies, yet I do not perceive that these ten bodies originally arise from me;
sixth, by means of the dharma of fearlessness, one does not disturb the perceptions of others, and the minds of those who receive the teaching remain unshakable.

Seventh, there are the contemplation-practice, the practice of non-practice, the fundamental practice, the self-practice, the future practice, that which is neither existent nor non-existent, and that which is neither non-existent nor not non-existent; these are called the seven ascetic practices.
This is what is meant by a bodhisattva accomplishing the twelve dharmas within the eighteen clear wisdoms.
"Furthermore, good sons and good daughters! Contemplate immeasurable emptiness;
regarding the perception of immeasurable emptiness, do not give rise to thoughts within yourselves, nor perceive those thoughts."
Why is this? Because immeasurable worlds are empty and signless.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of thirteen dharmas within the eighteen luminosities of wisdom.
"Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family!
You should further contemplate the four immeasurable sufferings.
What are these four sufferings?
Within Jambudvīpa, he contemplates the fundamental sources of the various sufferings of immeasurable sentient beings:
first, the suffering of birth, knowing its beginning and end and constantly mindful of the perils of the womb;
second, the suffering of old age, wherein the physical form changes, the complexion fades, and youthful vigor no longer remains.

Third, regarding the suffering of illness: when one of the four great elements increases, one type of illness increases; when all four great elements increase, all four types of illness increase. When one of the four great elements subsides, one type of illness subsides; when all four great elements subside, all four types of illness subside.
"How is it, son of good family?
Is illness something that arises and ceases, or is it something that does not arise and cease?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva named Mūlaniruddha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The four great elements are fundamentally extinguished; they are not subject to arising and ceasing.”
The Buddha said:
“Noble son! How is it that the four great elements are fundamentally extinguished and not subject to arising or ceasing?”
He replied: "Originally there were no four great elements; what now exists was not originally present. Therefore, it is fundamentally extinguished, not subject to arising and ceasing.
The Buddha said:
“Noble son! What is fundamental cessation?
What is arising and cessation?”
He replied: "Fundamentally there is no form and fundamentally there is no arising; not perceiving suffering and not perceiving what is not suffering—this is called 'original cessation.
As for what is called 'arising and ceasing,' it is when my mind is present and I am able to cause this mind to remain latent and not arise—this is called 'arising and ceasing.'"
The Buddha said: "How is this so,
son of good family?"
The past mind and the present mind: the past mind is not the present mind, and the present mind is not the past mind. How, then, can that which was originally extinguished give rise to extinction?
He replied: "The fundamental is without cessation; that which arises is without cessation.
The Buddha said:
“Noble son! From what do the origination and cessation of that which is fundamentally extinguished arise? He replied:
"Because there is no arising, there is arising.
At that time, World-Honored One,
he praised the Bodhisattva Fundamental Extinction, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are indeed able to speak these words so eloquently before the Tathāgata.”

"What is called the suffering of death: when one is on the verge of dying, having abandoned the present body and before receiving a new body, one remains in an intermediate state, not yet knowing where one will go—whether in the future, the past, or the present—at that moment, the spirit becomes terrified; this is called the suffering of death."
This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of fourteen dharmas within the eighteen types of clear wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If a man or woman discerns non-self, suffering, emptiness, and non-substantiality—possessing these four practices, they are able to receive the Tathāgata’s prediction.
What are the four? In this regard, son of good family!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family calculates that the self is non-self, neither possessing form nor being formless, and understands that which is nothingness—this is called "non-self."

Furthermore, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family contemplates that the dharma-realm is suffering without a fundamental basis, and explains that there is neither suffering nor arising and ceasing, this is called the discernment of suffering as being without suffering.

Just as the immeasurable perceptions of sentient beings pervade the realm of empty space, one thoroughly knows that these perceptions are produced by the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) and are all exhausted within emptiness; this is what constitutes emptiness.

What is meant by "non-body"? It refers to the non-body wherein one conceives of a self, yet there is no self; one discriminates a self, yet there is no self. One perceives no self, sees no self, hears no self, and perceives neither seeing nor hearing. This is called the non-body. This is what is meant when a bodhisattva accomplishes fifteen dharmas within the eighteen clear wisdoms.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as my suchness is the suchness of all Buddhas' dharmas, it is not different from the suchness of all Buddhas' dharmas; nor is there a state where Buddhas' dharmas do not exist and suchness does not exist, for that too is not different. This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the sixteenth dharma among the eighteen clear wisdoms."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If a son or daughter of good family [knows that] the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding his original vows and practices, knows the degree of the three poisons in beings of equal disposition, yet does not perceive the three poisons as being distinct from the three pure dharmas—this is called the seventeenth dharma accomplished by a Bodhisattva through the eighteen clear wisdoms."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family reflects upon their own past incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, knows the present incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and knows the future incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—discerning each of these one by one yet finding nothing therein—this is called a bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the eighteen dharmas through the eighteen clear wisdoms."

"If a good man or a good woman, having distinguished the eighteen kinds of clear wisdom, remains fearless amidst the great assembly—just as a brave and powerful king who has subjects under his command, and all those who are attached to him receive the king's instructions without any failure."

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: having attained the teachings of the noble wisdom and being sealed with the Dharma-seal, they are then able to fully master immeasurable gateways of wisdom.
What is the gate of immeasurable wisdom?

The Buddhas are inconceivable; the Buddha-fields are inconceivable; all phenomena are inconceivable; the dharma-nature of all phenomena is inconceivable; the community of bhikṣus is inconceivable; the dharma of the Saṃgha is inconceivable; and the fields of the Saṃgha are inconceivable.
Regarding such practice of the Dharma, there are furthermore four matters. What are these four?
First, from time immemorial throughout the limits of countless kalpas, one has always maintained a single-minded focus without error.

If there are good sons or good daughters who, guarding the root of the single practice, know existence and exhaustion as well as non-exhaustion, and know that all Buddhas possess both existence and exhaustion as well as non-exhaustion, they will then be able to fulfill the practice of the path of equality.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Candraprabha who rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I am now able to expound the practices of the Dharma-gates concerning that which is exhaustible and that which is inexhaustible."
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by being fully endowed with the five practices regarding the four fundamental dharmas, come to thoroughly know the root of the Tathāgata?
What are these four?

First, to fully understand all matters of coming and going while in the world, and to distinguish between the dharmas of the Path and the dharmas of the world—this is called accomplishing the first dharma.

Furthermore, by means of a concentrated mind free from form and characteristics, to influence various lands, and within those lands to teach and transform sentient beings by manifesting the teaching of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—this is called a son or daughter of good family accomplishing the second dharma.

"Furthermore, good sons and daughters, when one does not perceive a self within the phenomena of one's own body, yet is able to deliver immeasurable sentient beings without ever abandoning the dharma-realm of sentient beings—this is called accomplishing the three dharmas."
"Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family, one should discern the three foundations of the Tathāgata’s practice of the Dharma.
What are these three foundations of the practice of the Dharma?

First is walking meditation (*caṅkrama*): when it is time to go, one knows one is going; when it is time to come, one knows one is coming; when it is time to sit, one knows one is sitting; thus fixing the mind on clear perception so that the heart is not confused."

Second, regarding seated meditation: if one wishes to go to one's seat and sit in the full lotus posture, one should immediately eliminate all discursive thoughts and unify the mind so that the body does not shift, maintaining the meditative concentration until its completion without initial distraction;

if one further engages in performing various virtuous deeds, what is undertaken will surely be accomplished without other extraneous thoughts. This is called accomplishing four dharmas within three dharmas.

"Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family, by fully knowing all that has been born, is yet to be born, and has already been born throughout the past, future, and present, they are able to let out the lion’s roar therein without losing the dharma of their original practice; this is called accomplishing the five dharmas."

"Furthermore, good sons and daughters, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should further awaken to and know the three practices of the Tathāgata: the Tathāgata’s meditative concentration is not the mundane dhyāna, nor is it the dhyāna of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, nor is it the dhyāna of the first, second, up to the tenth stage."
"Why is this? Other forms of dhyāna are limited, whereas the Tathāgata-dhyāna is likewise without limit.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Moonlight Radiance, saying:
"What do you think, son of good family?
Is it the dhyāna of the mundane world, the dhyāna of those in training, or the dhyāna of those beyond training; or is it the dhyāna from the first stage up to the tenth stage?"
The Bodhisattva Candraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

According to what I have heard from the Tathāgata regarding these matters, if there are beings in the desire realm—whether men or women—who, from their first resolve until they attain Buddhahood, while still on the stages of the path and not yet established in the rank of a bodhisattva, immediately attain the three dhyānas:”
There is past dhyāna, there is future dhyāna, and there is present dhyāna.

Although these sons and daughters of good family have attained these three types of dhyāna, they can only know for themselves the past body within their own body, the future body within their own body, and the present body within their own body; they are not yet able to know the past body within the bodies of others, the future body within the bodies of others, or the present body within the bodies of others.
How does such a son or daughter of good family know the past body within their own body?
In this regard, World-Honored One,
when practicing seated meditation, they observe their own body and give rise to the perception of impurity, then reflect as follows:
"Alas! This body of mine is subject to decay and destruction.
With every thought and every moment, he perceives only impurity, yet he is not yet able to know its destination.
At that time, the sons and daughters of good family further reflect to themselves:

"Now that I have relinquished this body, I shall seek further contemplation. Just as I now understand through wisdom that this body is without self, I know that external objects are likewise so; when each is analyzed individually, they are all found to be non-existent."
This is called being able to contemplate the past and the future while within the present body.
Furthermore, son of good family or daughter of good family, having observed one’s own body and external objects, one should set aside this mind and further seek contemplation, thinking:
"This body of mine is entirely a conceptual construction, neither existent nor non-existent."
"Are those sentient beings like my own body?
Thus, he discerns the external and internal past bodies, exclaiming, "Alas, this body will soon perish," and thereby gives rise to the perception of impurity.
Having already produced the perception of impurity, one knows that the internal past body of another person is no different from one's own.
"If a son or daughter of good family, having set aside this internal past body of another person, should further give rise to this contemplation:
'From what does this person’s internal past mind arise?'"
"From what does it cease?
He further reflected:
"For now, let aside external objects and internal past thoughts."
He then further contemplated the internal future mind of others, thinking:
"Alas! From where has this body come?"
"From what does it cease?
This is called the way in which sons and daughters of good family who stand in the stage of a bodhisattva are able to fully accomplish the practice of the third dhyāna.
The Buddha again asked the Bodhisattva Moonlight Shining:
"How does one cultivate the dharma of the three dhyānas on the stage of training?
The Bodhisattva Moonlight-Illumination addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a good man or a good woman, already established in the stage of faith and thus termed a 'learner,' desires to advance toward the path they seek, they shall go to one of the six places of tranquility—whether beneath a tree, in a cemetery, in a secluded spot, or in an open-air pavilion—and there, assuming the full lotus posture, they shall concentrate their thoughts and contemplate with the intent to personally fulfill the practices of the three dhyānas."
At that time, the good man or good woman reflects within themselves:
"Observing my own past body internally, from what did it originally arise?
And by what does it cease?"
Again, he reflected to himself:
"Alas! This body is fundamentally without birth and fundamentally without cessation."
"Good sons and good daughters, having cast off this body, they further seek contemplation:
'From what is this present body of mine born?
By what does it perish?'"
"Is it the same for the future body?
He then reflected to himself:
"From what does the internal future body arise?"
"From what does it cease?
Then he thought to himself:
"This internal future body neither arises nor ceases."
This is called a son or daughter of good family who, within the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), is fully endowed with the three dhyānas regarding the internal body.
What is meant by a person in the stage of training observing the internal body and being fully endowed with the three dhyānas regarding the bodies of others?
At that time, the good man or good woman, having relinquished this body, contemplates the external body and the internal past body: from what did it originally arise?
From what did it originally cease?
He then reflected to himself: "Alas!
From what did that past body within another arise?"
"From what does it cease?
He further reflected:
"This internal past body neither arises nor ceases."
Having again relinquished this, he further seeks contemplation:
"This internal past body has already ceased to arise and has already ceased to perish.
From what does this internal future body arise?"
"From what does it cease?
He then gave rise to this thought:
"This internal future body neither arises nor ceases."
"This is what is meant by a son or daughter of good family being fully endowed with the three dhyānas regarding the past and future bodies within the bodies of others.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Moonlight Shining, saying:
"How does a son or daughter of good family on the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) become fully endowed with the three dhyānas?"
The Bodhisattva Candraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to proceed toward the stage of outflows and sever the dharmas without outflows, they should reflect within themselves and sit in the full lotus posture, contemplating internally:
'From what did this past body within arise?'"
"From what does it cease?
He further reflected to himself:
"This internal past body neither arises nor ceases."
At that time, the noble sons and daughters who have attained the state beyond training (aśaikṣa), having set aside this contemplation, further reflect:

"I have now contemplated my internal past body; I shall next contemplate my own past self. Yet, therein I see neither cessation nor birth, neither kalpas nor existence, neither birth-and-death nor buddha-fields."
"This is called a good son or a good daughter who, in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣabhūmi), is fully endowed with the three dhyānas.
The World-Honored One again asked the Bodhisattva Moonlight Shining:
"How does a bodhisattva of the first stage, without exhausting all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), become fully endowed with the three dhyānas?"

He replied: "By observing the mindfulness of the body through the contemplation of the non-existence of the body; by not losing the practice of mindfulness through the root of non-thought; and by not receiving sounds or echoes—having transcended the first stage of a bodhisattva, having passed three times beyond the stage of faith, and having surpassed all dharmas—this is called a good man or good woman who is fully endowed with the three dhyānas."
The World-Honored One asked the Bodhisattva Candraprabha: "How is it so,
son of good family?"
"Do you not see your own stage and the three dhyānas?
He replied, "I do not see any realm; therefore, I do not speak of them."
The Buddha asked,
"Is there no body? Or is there a body?"
"For what reason is it not taught?
He replied: "Because there is a body."
The Buddha asked again:
"Is the body the Dharma-body, or is it the body composed of the four great elements?"
He replied, “It is the body of my parents.
The Buddha said:
"How do you, with this body of a parent, achieve the third dhyāna?
The Bodhisattva Moonlight-Illumination addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first sought to become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, sitting beneath the King of Trees, I was without fear or dread, and I immediately contemplated the burning and blazing nature of the three realms."
He then reflected to himself:
"All the Buddhas of the past have entered parinirvāṇa; how many sentient beings were they able to deliver? How many who had previously attained the stage of srotāpanna?
How many who had previously attained the stage of sakṛdāgāmin?"
The past anāgāmins? The past arhats? The past pratyekabuddhas?
He further reflects: "In the future, it shall also be thus.
This is called the first-stage bodhisattva being fully endowed with the practice of the first dhyāna.

Just as a Bodhisattva of the first stage perceives the three realms, the fundamental practice of this first stage surpasses that of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; this is called a Bodhisattva of the first stage accomplishing the second dhyāna.

If a good man or good woman of the first stage distinguishes between the internal and external while maintaining the three emptinesses of the body, and expounds the teachings of the Dharma without error, this is called the accomplishment of the third dhyāna within the first stage.
The Buddha again asked the Bodhisattva Candraprabha:
"Why do you not speak of the three dhyānas of the Sakṛdāgāmin and the Anāgāmin? He replied:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having already attained the stage of vision, reflects thus:
'Within my own body, there is no past body, no present body, and no future body; therein is neither the notion of a Buddha, nor the notion of a Dharma, nor is the notion of a body perceived.'"
This is called the internal past body being fully endowed with the third dhyāna.
What is the internal future body being fully endowed with the three practices?

At that time, the Sakṛdāgāmin further observes both the internal and external, abandons all defilements, and fixes his mindfulness upon the stage of the third dhyāna without forgetting it. Although he has personally attained realization, he does not destroy its own characteristics; just as the self-characteristics of dharmas are such, he himself distinguishes the name-body, phrase-body, and syllable-body.

Furthermore, he contemplates immeasurable external sentient beings who do not yet conceive the thought of the Buddha; he brings them to the accomplishment of the thought of the Buddha, making them all equally pure and non-dual. He perceives no coming or going, and no proximity or distance. This is called the Sakṛdāgāmin being fully endowed with the third dhyāna within his future internal body.
Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family sit upright in contemplation and, having attained the path of the Non-returner (anāgāmin), reflect to themselves:
"I am now certainly situated on the ground of receiving realization; I shall not destroy the natural marks of all phenomena, but shall personally verify this for myself."
"I have already transcended one, already transcended two, and already transcended three; no longer coming and going, I abide within birth and death with a mind serene and unshakable."
"This is called a good son or a good daughter observing the past within their own body; the future is likewise so.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the Bodhisattva Moonlight Illumination:
"Does one who has attained the stage of Anāgāmin obtain the dharmas of the past?"
"Has he not yet attained the past dharmas? He replied:
"The Anāgāmin has attained the past dharmas, yet has not exhausted the past dharmas."
What is meant by "attaining past dharmas while not yet exhausting past dharmas"?
It is when an anāgāmin’s body exists in the past while his dharmas exist in the future; this is called attaining past dharmas while not yet exhausting past dharmas.
Furthermore, when the body of an Anāgāmin exists in the future and the dharma has already passed, this person also acquires past dharmas but has not yet exhausted past dharmas.

Moreover, son of good family or daughter of good family, if the body of an Anāgāmin has neither passed nor is currently present, while the dharma has already passed and the dharma is now manifest before him, this is called an Anāgāmin who acquires past dharmas but has not yet exhausted past dharmas.
The World-Honored One again asked the Bodhisattva Candraprabha:
"Does the Sakṛdāgāmin attain past dharmas and exhaust past dharmas? He replied:
“Although the Sakṛdāgāmin possesses a past body, he does not obtain past dharmas, nor does he exhaust past dharmas.
“In what way does the Sakṛdāgāmin possess a past body, yet neither obtain past dharmas nor exhaust past dharmas?”

He replied: "For the Sakṛdāgāmin, the past body has already ceased, yet past phenomena are not yet exhausted; regarding future phenomena, having observed them for himself, he realizes they have already passed away and those phenomena likewise do not exist."
Just as an Anāgāmin has no past body but possesses past dharmas, the Sakṛdāgāmin is not like this.
It is like observing the reflection of one's face in a clear mirror; it is not the same as seeing the face directly. For this reason, the Sakṛdāgāmin is not like [the Anāgāmin].
"The consciousness of an Anāgāmin is like refined gold, while the consciousness of a Sakṛdāgāmin is like unrefined gold;
therefore, there is a distinction. The Buddha asked again: "How so?"

"Noble son! Is it as you say—that an Anāgāmin attains past dharmas and exhausts past dharmas, attains future dharmas and exhausts future dharmas, and has already accomplished those dharmas not yet accomplished?"
He replied: "It is not so.
Although it is refined gold, it has not yet been fashioned into a vessel; it may still bear the name 'gold,' but it does not yet have a form."
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
You have well explained this point.
Just as a non-returner (anāgāmin) has no past dharmas and has exhausted past dharmas, and has no future dharmas and has exhausted future dharmas—
does a present arhat likewise obtain past dharmas and exhaust past dharmas?
"Does one acquire future dharmas and exhaust future dharmas? He replied:
"One acquires past dharmas but does not exhaust past dharmas; one acquires future dharmas but does not exhaust future dharmas. Therefore, there is a distinction."
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the Bodhisattva Candraprabha:
"How does a bodhisattva of the second stage fulfill the practice of the three dhyānas? He replied:

"Just as a Bodhisattva of the second stage, having resolved upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, perceives neither an internal body nor an external body, but maintains mindfulness before him and reflects thus:
'Do I now possess an internal past body within this internal body?'"
Is there no internal past body?
Is there an internal future body?
Is there no internal future body?
Having relinquished this contemplation, he further reflected:
"I now have no internal body and no external body; how can I seek an internal past body or seek an internal future body within the internal body?"
This is called the second-stage bodhisattva being fully endowed with the three dhyānas regarding his own internal and external body.
At that time, the second-stage bodhisattva further reflects:
"I have now thoroughly analyzed my own internal and external body; I should next observe whether the internal and external bodily dharmas of others differ from my own."
Turning one's attention forward to observe the internal and external bodies of others:
is there a past body? Is there no past body? Is there a future body?
"Is there no future body?

Those sons or daughters of good family who abide in the second stage perceive that others have no past body when observing their past bodies, and they perceive that others have no future body when observing their future bodies.
"This is called the second stage, wherein a son or daughter of good family accomplishes the third dhyāna within the past lives of others.
The World-Honored One again asked the Bodhisattva Moonlight Illumination:
"How do sons or daughters of good family in the third stage accomplish the third dhyāna within that third stage?"
He replied: "If a son or daughter of good family from the third stage sits upright and contemplates thus:
'In regard to the internal, does a past body exist when observing the past body?'"
Is there no past body? Contemplating the future body internally, is there a future body?
Is there no future body?
He further reflected:

"Within the first stage, I have no past body nor a non-past body; likewise, within the first stage, I have no future body nor a non-future body. Furthermore, within the first stage, there is no past body nor a non-past body belonging to another; likewise, within the first stage, there is no future body nor a non-future body belonging to another."
Again, he contemplates within the second stage: does a past body exist? Does a past body not exist?
He contemplates within regarding the future body:
does a future body exist? Does a future body not exist?
"Is there no future body?
He further reflected:

"Within these two stages, I have neither a past body nor a non-past body; likewise, I have neither a future body nor a non-future body within these two stages. Furthermore, within these two stages, there is neither another's past body nor a non-past body; likewise, there is neither another's future body nor a non-future body within these two stages."
As I observe now, within my own three stages, there is no internal past body;

furthermore, observing my own internal future body, there is no internal future body. Within these stages, observing another's internal past body, there is no other's internal past body; observing another's internal future body, there is no other's internal future body. How much less, then, could I have a body or be without a body?
"This is called the way in which good sons and good daughters fulfill the three dhyānas within the third stage.
At that time, the World-Honored One again asked the Bodhisattva Moonlight Shining:
"How do good sons and good daughters fulfill the three dhyānas within the fourth stage?"
He replied: "If a son or daughter of good family from the fourth stage sits upright and contemplates:
'In observing the past body within, does a past body exist?'"
Is there no past body? Contemplating the future body internally, is there a future body?
Is there no future body?
He further reflected to himself:
"I have no past body in the first, second, or third grounds, nor do I have a future body; how much less could there be a past body within the fourth ground?"
"In the fourth stage there is no past body; in the fourth stage there is no future body; in the fourth stage there is no future body.
This is called the accomplishment of the three dhyānas by a son of good family or a daughter of good family within the fourth stage.
At that time, the World-Honored One again asked the Bodhisattva Moonlight Shining:
"How do good sons and good daughters at the fifth stage fulfill the three dhyānas within the fifth stage?"
He replied: "If a son or daughter of good family on the fifth stage sits upright in contemplation, thinking:
'Observing internally the past body, is there a past body?'"
Is there no past body? Contemplating internally the future body: is there a future body?
Is there no future body?
He further reflected to himself:

"I have now already relinquished the first stage, the second stage, and even up to the fourth stage. Within these four stages, when observing the past body internally, there is no past body; when observing the future body internally, there is no future body."

Having further relinquished this, one contemplates that within others' internal past bodies there is no past body, and contemplates that within others' internal future bodies there is no future body; how much less could there be a past body within my own internal [body] at the fifth stage? There is no past body.
Regarding others, one contemplates that their future bodies have no future bodies.
This is called a good man or a good woman who, within the fifth stage, is fully endowed with the three dhyānas.
The World-Honored One again asked the Bodhisattva Moonlight Shining:
"How is it that good sons and good daughters at the sixth stage fulfill the three dhyānas within that sixth stage?"
He replied: "If a son or daughter of good family in the sixth stage sits upright in contemplation, thinking:
'I observe that I have no self; within this selfless body, do I observe a past body existing internally?'"
Is there no past body? Contemplating the future body internally, is there a future body?
Is there no future body?
This is called the third dhyāna accomplished by good sons and good daughters in the sixth stage within the sixth stage.
Having relinquished the selfless body, do good sons and good daughters in the sixth stage perceive, within their contemplation of others, that there is a past body?
Is there no past body?
Within the internal contemplation of others, is there a future body?
Is there no future body?
Again, he reflects to himself:
"In observing another's internal past body, there is no past body; in observing another's internal future body, there is no future body."
"This is called the accomplishment of the three dhyānas by good sons and good daughters within the sixth stage.
The Buddha again asked the Bodhisattva Moonlight-Illumination:
"How do good sons and good daughters of the seventh stage accomplish the three dhyānas within the seventh stage?"
He replied: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, sitting upright in a secluded place, reflects thus:
'Observing the internal past body, is there a past body? "
Is there no past body? Furthermore, one contemplates the internal future body:
is there a future body, or is there no future body?
"Good sons and good daughters further form this thought:

'I have now relinquished, within the first stage, the past body internally as being no past body, and the future body internally as being no future body; and so on, up to the sixth stage, where the past body internally is no internal past body, and the future body internally is no future body.'"
"How is it that within the seventh stage there may be an internal past body or no internal past body?
How is it that there may be an internal future body or no internal future body?
This is called the accomplishment of the third dhyāna by a son of good family or a daughter of good family within the seventh stage.
The Buddha again asked Candraprabha:
"How do good sons and good daughters, within the seventh stage, contemplate the internal past body of another as not being a past body?"
"When observing another's internal future body, is it a future body or not a future body? He replied:

"Good man or good woman, when observing another's internal past body, there is no such thing as another's internal past body; when observing another's internal future body, there is no such thing as another's internal future body."
The Buddha said: "Stop, stop!
Son of good family!"
This is not within your sphere of experience. Why is this?

Sons and daughters of good family on the seventh stage observe that another’s internal past body does not exist as an internal past body, and they see only the non-existence of another’s internal future body.
"For what reason do you say that good men and good women, within the seventh stage, accomplish the internal future body of others?
The Bodhisattva Moonlight-Illumination again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As I contemplate the internal future body of others, it is neither existent nor non-existent; for this reason, I say they accomplish it."
The Buddha again asked the Bodhisattva Candraprabha:
"How do good sons and good daughters of the eighth stage accomplish the three dhyānas within that eighth stage?"
He replied: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family sits upright in contemplation and reflects:

'Observing the internal past body, there is no internal past body; observing the internal future body, there is no internal future body; observing another's internal past body, there is no internal past body; observing another's internal future body, there is no internal future body.'"

At times, when a son or daughter of good family contemplates their own internal past body, it is neither existent nor non-existent, being like empty space; yet they have not yet extinguished the internal future body.
At times, when contemplating the internal future body, they have not yet extinguished the internal past body.
At times, when contemplating another’s internal past body, they have not yet extinguished that other person’s internal future body.
"When observing another's internal future body, one has not yet been able to extinguish that other's internal past body.
This is called the accomplishment of the third dhyāna by a good man or good woman within the eighth stage.
The Buddha again asked the Bodhisattva Moonlight Shining:
"How do sons and daughters of good family in the ninth stage accomplish the three dhyānas within that ninth stage?"
He replied: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family sits upright in contemplation and reflects:
'Is there a past body within? "
Is there no past body?
Observing internally for oneself regarding the future body:
is there a future body? Is there no future body?
"Good son or good daughter, having relinquished this contemplation, they further contemplate another's internal past body: 'Does the past body exist?
Does the past body not exist?'"
He contemplates another’s internal future body: "Is there an internal future body?
Is there no internal future body?
Having relinquished this contemplation, he further reflects as follows:

"I originally have no internal past body, nor do I have a past body; originally there is no internal future body, nor is there a future body—how much less could there be an external other's past body that lacks a past body?"
He has no future body in his external future existence; his resolve is firm and steadfast, and he does not abandon his original vow.
This is called the accomplishment of the third dhyāna by a good son or good daughter within the ninth stage.

"Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family on the ninth stage should further cultivate the practice of the three dhyānas until they sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), without falling away from them.
What are these three? "
First is contemplation;
second is practice;
third is the fundamental basis.
If one accomplishes the third dhyāna, one is then able to fully attain the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
What is meant by contemplation (vipaśyanā)?
It is the discernment of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), knowing the fundamental roots of all things and adorning their various characteristics; this is called contemplation.
What is meant by "practice"?

It refers to approaching the Bodhi tree and manifesting the physical marks and characteristics, with all outflows extinguished and untainted by the dust and defilements of the world; it is the constant practice of the four dharmas of impermanence by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas—this is what is called "practice."
What constitutes the foundation?
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva reflects:
"I have now fulfilled my great vows; I shall cause all sentient beings to likewise fulfill these great vows."
"This is what is called the foundation.
If good sons and good daughters are endowed with these three practices, they will be able to fully attain the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Furthermore, good sons and good daughters!"

Furthermore, one must fully possess the three dhyanas to reach the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). What are these three?
