Second is the perception of emptiness;
third is the consciousness of emptiness.
If one possesses these three kinds of emptiness, one will be able to fully attain the site of enlightenment.
What is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*)?

That which is called emptiness refers to contemplating the emptiness of internal phenomena and the emptiness of external phenomena; contemplating one world, two worlds, and even up to incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds—this is called the dharma of emptiness.
What is the perception of emptiness?

It is when one enters a state of meditative concentration and observes the entire world exhaustively, yet gives rise to no thought of whether there is emptiness or non-emptiness, or a self or non-self; this is called the perception of emptiness.
What is meant by the "emptiness of consciousness"?
When entering a state of meditative concentration, one further forms this contemplation:
"Now, through the mindfulness of sentient beings, I have no other thoughts; I shall purify sentient beings so that they are no different from myself."
However, these sentient beings possess immeasurable consciousnesses; with which consciousness should I now transform those various consciousnesses?
I shall now employ the consciousness of emptiness to cause this world to become entirely like space, thereby causing those sentient beings to abandon their discriminative attachment to consciousness.
This is called the good sons and good daughters possessing these three dhyānas within the ninth stage.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas that should be practiced. What are the three?
First, the discernment of the world;
second, the discernment of the realm of sentient beings;
third, the discernment of the ultimate truth.
If one cultivates these three dharmas, one will be able to advance toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) without fear.
What is the discernment of worlds?

It is the ability to universally observe all realms—those that are pure and those that are impure—and to understand them all completely without error; furthermore, it is the selection and cultivation of Buddha-lands according to one's will. This is called the world.
What is the realm of sentient beings?

Furthermore, one should universally observe all sentient beings, constantly teaching and transforming them through skillful means, never abandoning the vast and great mind of the profound vow, and regarding the passage of kalpas as no hardship.
This is called the way in which good sons and good daughters bring sentient beings to maturity.
How do they bring them to maturity in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?

By discerning each and every aspect of the meaning and purpose of sentient beings, one finds that all ultimately return to emptiness; there is no self, person, or life-span, nor is there duality or unity. This applies even to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), which are likewise so. This is called the discernment of the ultimate truth.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family accomplishes three dharmas, they will be able to fully possess the qualities for advancing toward the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*).
What are the three?
First, through supernormal power, one knows the phenomena of the past;
second, through supernormal power, one knows the phenomena of the future.
Third, the supernormal power of knowing present phenomena.
If a son or daughter of good family is endowed with these three dharmas, they will be able to fully attain the site of enlightenment.
What is the supernormal power (ṛddhipāda) of knowing past phenomena?

Here, sons and daughters of good family on the nine stages perceive past phenomena as being like space. They discern past sentient beings—those whose minds were defiled by desire, anger, and ignorance, and those whose minds were undefiled by desire, anger, and ignorance—discerning each one individually without attachment. This is called the supernormal power of knowing past phenomena.
What is the supernormal power of knowing future phenomena?

In this regard, sons and daughters of good family on the nine stages know those sentient beings who will receive a physical form in the future: those whose minds are defiled by desire, anger, and ignorance, and those whose minds are not defiled by desire, anger, and ignorance. They distinguish each of these individually without attachment; this is called the supernormal power of knowing future phenomena.

Furthermore, a son or daughter of good family on the ninth stage knows that among all present sentient beings, there are those whose minds are defiled by desire, anger, and ignorance, and those whose minds are not defiled by desire, anger, and ignorance; they distinguish each one individually without attachment. This is called the supernormal power of knowing present phenomena.
This is called the ninth stage, wherein one accomplishes three dharmas to advance toward the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family at the ninth stage possess another three dharmas by which they reach the site of enlightenment.
What are the three?
First, purity of body;
second, purity of speech.
Third is purity of mind.
By possessing these three dharmas, one attains the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
What is purity of body?

Having already transcended immeasurable virtuous practices, their fundamental activities have been extinguished and they no longer create bodily formations; their bodies penetrate all things without obstruction—this is called the purity of body of a Bodhisattva in the Ninth Ground.
What is purity of speech?
It is the issuing of immeasurable teachings without ever impairing the profound and wondrous treasury; this is called purity of speech.
"What is mental purity?
It is the removal of defiled attachment and the non-acceptance of worldly dust; this is called mental purity.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Moonlight Shines spoke these verses:
"The body is pure and free from blemish, Without defilement within or without;
Virtue is so lofty there is no peer, Forever extinguished are the names of desire and anger.
The mouth is pure as it expounds all teachings, Leaking no faults whatsoever."
Until his final passing into nirvāṇa, his oral teachings shall never be exhausted.
With a mind purified of greed and attachment, his compassion neither increases nor decreases;
throughout immeasurable births, he awakens those who have not yet awakened.
The ninth stage transcends the dharma-realm; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Such sons of good family have already entered the domain of the Tathāgata.
Throughout immeasurable past eons, I diligently studied and followed my teachers and companions.
Since they have not yet trodden this path, how much less those who have fallen away?
By maintaining practice without attachment, one accumulates merit until attaining Buddhahood;
having transcended the three realms through such practice, one lets out the lion’s roar among men.
"This is called the nine stages wherein good men and good women accomplish three dharmas.
*The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
*The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Scroll Six; also known as the *Sūtra on Retribution in the Present Life*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter 18: On the Immeasurable Path (6). Chapter Eighteen: On the Immeasurable Path.
The Buddha said:

“Good sons and good daughters, those who uphold, practice, and cultivate the third dhyāna will attain the fullness of all virtuous merits and travel through various Buddha-lands to make offerings to and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, All relied upon the Dharma of the three dhyānas;
Through the signless and wishless dharmas, They accorded with the practice of the noble discipline."
The fundamental dharmas of the third dhyāna lead one to attain nirvāṇa by oneself;
even if one were to recite them immeasurably, one could not exhaustively master those dharmas.
Suppose there were a man who lived for immeasurable kalpas—
Among these, I wish to proclaim that which does not exhaust the root of the three dhyānas.
Observing consciousness of the past for oneself, it cannot be proclaimed by the mind.
Consciousness of the future is likewise: it is a consciousness that is neither existent nor non-existent.
Formless and invisible, yet it sows the seeds of the disease of birth and death;
by contemplating the dharmas of the ninth stage, one subsequently attains the peace of awakening.
Through the pure dharma of the holy life, one upholds and protects the teaching of the Tathāgata.
If one were to analyze each part in detail, the body of the Tathāgata could not be fully described.
The Honored One, peerless throughout the three times,
has shattered the net of all worldly desires and the entanglements of various fetters, exhausting them forever without remainder.
Observing the transformations of all existences in the world, Life after life, they never remain constant;
How much more so for one who seeks to know the root of consciousness, Which manifests as the six sense-bases.
The primal self does not create existence; It is through defiling existence that impurity arises.
All this arises from the Dharma of the third dhyāna, whereby he sat beneath the Bodhi tree.
If there were sons of noble family who, with a mind intent on calculation,
sought to analyze the body of the Tathāgata, they would find that it is as fine as a single hair.
All past dharma-realms, each and every one inconceivable,
Are named and designated only by virtue of these three meditations.
If one wishes to calculate the root of consciousness, One discerns that there are no phenomena that truly exist.
The destinations are countless and ever-changing, yet they accord with the practice of the three dhyānas.
Since my own birth has become peaceful, I am likewise able to bring peace to all people;
for human thoughts are manifold, I guide them so that they may understand.
From the fundamental state of equanimity, I practiced contemplation and realized the third dhyāna;
free from the perceptions of earth and consciousness, I transcended past formations.
Birth originally arises from the notions of self and person, causing one to transmigrate through the five realms of existence.
To be able to exhaust the defilements of a lifetime, one is said to correspond to the third dhyāna.
There are ultimately three dharmas: examining the essentials of original defilement;
the second is present wisdom; and the contemplation of the Path—these are called the three.
One who can exhaustively realize this meaning and engage in the immeasurable practices of the three dhyānas—
this too is inconceivable— and who thoroughly masters the practice of the three dharmas;
furthermore, one who understands the root of affection and gradually enters into meditative concentration.
Having already received [instruction] from the Teacher, he subsequently attained the awakening of the Way.
He may manifest throughout three thousand worlds, as clearly as one views beads upon the palm of a hand;
entering each and every pure contemplation, he bathes away all worldly afflictions.
If one attempts to fathom emptiness, wishing to measure it with pecks and bushels, though such a thought may be conceived, how could there ever be such a principle?
The mind’s thoughts are boundless; their arising continues without end.
Just as water flowing toward the ocean is seen neither to increase nor decrease,
how much less can a person hope to measure the fundamental source of the mind?
To seek out the thoughts within the mind— how could such a principle ever exist?
The reason the Sage descended was to manifest his appearance in the world;
thus, he wished to measure emptiness so that people might understand the measures of pecks and bushels.
He discerned the arising of every thought, whether preceding, succeeding, or occurring in between.
Each and every one he knows completely, severing the root of birth and death.
The minds of people are not of a single type; they create various kinds of karma, falling of their own accord from the ultimate limit and thus sinking into the abyss.
All the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
Whose dharmas were entirely equal, Attained the Unsurpassed Way through the practice of the three dhyānas.
The Tathāgatas of the future shall likewise uphold this practice.
Establishing all sentient beings securely, may they together attain the awakening of the Way.
Just as I have now become a Buddha and reign over these worlds,
so too shall they, through the wisdom of the three times, attain the Unsurpassed Way.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the sons and daughters of good family:

"In the past, during incalculable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared a Buddha named Drṣṭasamatā (Jianwu), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He also attained Buddhahood at this very place."
At that time, there was a king named Kṣemadatta who ruled over this land; the people were flourishing and the five grains ripened in abundance, and he possessed the seven treasures.
These so-called seven treasures were:
the jewel treasure, the wheel treasure, the precious queen treasure, the horse treasure, the elephant treasure, the treasury steward treasure, and the military commander treasure.
Furthermore, he had a thousand sons who were highly skilled, courageous, and fully proficient in the six arts.

At that time, King Kṣemamati, being advanced in years, wished to relinquish the throne and practice the pure life of brahmacarya under that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He then conferred the royal sovereignty upon his eldest son and proceeded to the presence of the Buddha Vipaśyin to seek the cultivation of the pure life. For twelve years he pursued that Buddha and practiced these three dhyānas, yet even then he had not yet understood the meaning of a single phrase.

Furthermore, from the time that Buddha passed into extinction until now, there were twenty great kalpas during which no Buddha appeared; subsequently, a Buddha emerged, and he again went to that Buddha to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). In this manner, he passed through twelve *koṭī-nayuta* of Buddhas, cultivating the pure holy life in the presence of each and every one of those Buddhas.

Furthermore, having come from that place, he made offerings to countless Buddhas; after a long time, he finally encountered the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhāsa, from whom he received the wisdom of the three dhyānas, which he has only now finally attained.
The Buddha addressed those gathered in the assembly:
"At that time, was King Puṇyavanta anyone else?
Do not harbor such a thought."
Why is this? The King Kṣemavat at that time was none other than I, Śākyamuni Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
From that time until now, I have finally attained these fundamental practices of the three dhyānas and have personally realized Buddhahood, sitting upon the site of enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"Reflecting on my accumulated merit, I have passed through the presence of countless Buddhas;
Yet encountering various afflictions, I was unable to extricate myself."
In the meantime, he further made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
giving away his wife, children, kingdom, and wealth, yet he had not yet attained these three dharmas.
Later, upon meeting the Honored One of Radiance, he finally obtained this sublime wisdom.
During that interval he cultivated pure conduct and first awakened to the Dharma of the three dhyānas.
Serene and free from sorrow or fear, without birth and without defilement, his manifold marks naturally adorned him; thus he is called the Honored One among Men.
"By means of my impartial wisdom, I give rise to no perceptions of manifold attachments;
I transform these gods and people of the world, as the Honored One who presides over the three realms.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings in the assembly all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Furthermore, there are devas and worldlings who each achieve their respective paths according to what they contemplate.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Viśuddha who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"A Wheel-Turning Sage King governs the four continents and is able to be fully endowed with the seven treasures; only then is he called a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses seven perfections (pāramitās); only then is he named the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Now I ask the Tathāgata!
"Are these seven dharmas material or immaterial?
The Buddha said:
"Stop, stop! Son of good family!
I now understand the eloquence of your skillful means."
Regarding what the son of good family has asked, the seven dharmas of the Tathāgata have no form.
Why is this? These dharmas are exceedingly profound and inexhaustible; it is only for the sake of sentient beings that they appear to have an end, yet these seven dharmas are without end.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do the seven treasures of the wheel-turning monarch possess form,
or do they lack form?"
The Buddha said:
"There are those with form that are sentient, and there are those with form that are insentient.
What are those with form that are sentient?"
The jewel of the jade woman, the elephant jewel, the horse jewel, the treasury jewel, and the military commander jewel—these are sentient beings with form.
What are those with form that are insentient?
"The wheel-treasure and the jewel-treasure are material and insentient.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

It is like the celestial throne of a Wheel-Turning Sage King: whatever he intends in his mind arrives immediately upon that thought. At that time, when there are forms and sentient beings, does the King’s thought arrive because of those sentient beings? Or does it arrive for the sake of sentient beings?
"How can that which is insentient arrive?
The Buddha said, "Although this is sentient, it arrives because the King thinks of it; it is not that the object itself knows the King's intention to come."
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Although they are sentient beings, how are they different from the wheel-treasure and the jewel-treasure?
The Buddha said:
"What do you think,
son of good family?
Although the wheel-treasure and the jewel-treasure also arrive through the power of mindfulness, do these two possess vocal sounds or verbal instruction?"
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha said,
"There is no verbal teaching.
The Buddha said:
“In this way, son of good family!
Although sentient beings arrive by virtue of their mindfulness, they do not grasp at verbal teachings.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is this so, World-Honored One?
If a Wheel-Turning Sage King merely thinks of them and they arrive, can it be that the wheel-treasure and the jewel-treasure are capable of giving verbal instructions?"
The Buddha said: “It is so. Why is this?
"It is by the power of the Wheel-Turning King that there is verbal instruction.
The Bodhisattva Jing said:
"The Holy Wheel-Turning King is neither pervasive nor responsive; how can he cause insentient things to have verbal instruction?"
The Buddha said:

"A Wheel-Turning Sage King attains worldly supernormal powers (*laukika-abhijñā*), enabling him to make worldly objects conform to his thoughts as required; however, he is not yet able to transform sentient beings into insentient things."
The Bodhisattva Jing replied again,
"How does one cause sentient beings to reach the state of non-sentient things?
The Buddha said:
“O son of good family!
I shall now explain to you in detail how sentient things are made to reach the state of insentient things, and insentient things are made to reach the state of sentient things.”
Reflect upon this well; I shall now explain it for you.
Just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King regards those sentient beings who possess form—those whom he loves and cherishes and is unable to abandon—and desires that they endure forever without ever changing.

One reflects that although one’s own body has received the noble status of a king, one perceives only its blessings and not its decay; this is called the desire for sentient beings to possess formless things.
Just as a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has already attained the path of practice constantly reflects:
"I now renounce what is old and no longer take pleasure in it; I wish to extinguish this form so that consciousness remains undefiled."
"This is what is called having form while being extinguished within the realm of emotion.
The Buddha said, "Noble son!"

As with the four dharma-realms, when one dharma-realm increases, the other realms suffer diminution; when all realms increase, one realm suffers diminution. This increase occurs by virtue of sentient beings, not by virtue of insentient things.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has spoken, I shall now explain the transition from sentient beings to non-sentient things, and from non-sentient things to sentient beings;

yet now the Tathāgata has only spoken of the transition from sentient beings to non-sentient things—I have not heard the Tathāgata speak of the transition from non-sentient things to sentient beings.”
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
That you have now posed these questions is entirely due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
I shall now question you in turn; you should answer me point by point. How is it so?

"Noble son! If there is a good man or a good woman who, while initially on the stage of training, accomplishes the seven pure contemplations (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) of the learner’s dharma—at that time, would there still be the past, future, or present mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is,
son of good family!"
"This is what is called being dispassionate toward sentient beings.
The Buddha again asked the Bodhisattva Vimala: "How is this so?"
"Noble son! When one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa) now cultivates the nine paths of purification, at that time, are there also seven untainted contemplations (anāsrava-vipaśyanā)? He replied:
“There is not, World-Honored One.
The Buddha spoke again:

“Noble son! When a non-retrogressive bodhisattva attains the contemplation of space and cultivates the sixteen noble practices, at that time, does one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa) not cultivate the nine paths of purification?”
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is,
son of good family!"
"This is what is meant by being dispassionate toward sentient beings.
The Buddha asked again: "How so?"

"Noble son! Just as a bodhisattva at the eighth stage attains the physical marks of a Buddha and acquires the thirty-two noble truths, does there, at that time, further exist a ninth path of purification?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is,
son of good family!"
"This is what is called being dispassionate toward sentient beings.
The Buddha again asked the Bodhisattva Viśuddha: "How is this so?"
"Noble son! At that time, does the bodhisattva of the ninth stage also possess thirty-two noble truths? He replied:
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, son of good family! This is what is meant by being dispassionate toward sentient beings."
The Buddha again asked the Bodhisattva Viśuddha: "How is it,
son of good family?"
Now that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has finally subdued the fourteen types of dust and defilements, at that time, do the three dhyāna-practices still exist?
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is,
son of good family!"
"This is what is meant by 'the insentient being toward the sentient.
" The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Jing:

"I have now explained for you the sentient being toward the insentient and the insentient being toward the sentient; thus one can fully possess the teachings of the Tathāgata, ascend to the rank of Bodhisattva, and advance toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). This is like the light of the moon among the stars, universally illuminating all so that none fail to receive its radiance."

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva possesses this quality of sentient beings being non-sentient and non-sentient beings being sentient, they are then able to fulfill the noble conduct of the Tathāgata; their bodies become golden-hued with towering virtues, like a mountain of purple-polished gold, and they attain mastery over all wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Today, does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possess sentience or is he insentient?”
"Are you indifferent toward sentient beings?

At that time, having heard the Bodhisattva Viśuddha ask this question, the World-Honored One emitted radiance from the joints of his limbs, which universally illuminated immeasurable Buddha-fields, causing them all to become the color of gold.
He withdrew his radiance and addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddha, saying: "Excellent, excellent,
son of noble family!"
Now you ask the Tathāgata about this meaning by means of the dharma of signlessness.

Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has already transcended the nine stages, sentient beings [attain] insentient things up until the attainment of Buddhahood and the site of enlightenment; this is what is meant by "insentient things [arising] from sentient beings."
"Why is this? It is because all sentient beings possess the conceptualization of attachment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has taught, one remains dispassionate toward sentient beings for the sake of sentient beings; has the Tathāgata not yet abandoned this today?
The Buddha said, “I have already abandoned it; though I abide therein, I am not defiled.”
He asked again: "How is this so,
World-Honored One?"
“The Tathāgata distinguishes between the sentient and the insentient so as to cause the insentient to act toward the sentient; is it only that the insentient acts toward the sentient?
The Buddha said, “Noble son!”
The Tathāgata has no further separate sentiments; rather, he is "without sentiment" toward those who possess sentiment.
It is only because of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) that he is without sentiment toward those who possess sentiment.
The Bodhisattva Jing then asked again:
“What is meant by ‘regarding the insentient,’ and what is meant by ‘regarding the sentient’?
The Buddha said:
“Son of good family!
I have no mind of a pratyekabuddha or an arhat; yet I possess compassion, sympathetic joy, and protection—this is what is meant by being dispassionate toward sentient beings.”
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha said:
"If the Tathāgata today has no affection for sentient beings, could he possibly have no affection for that which is non-sentient?
The Buddha said:
“There is. The Bodhisattva Viśuddha asked: “What is it?”
The Buddha said, "My mind is now extinguished and entrusted to the unconditioned; this is called being dispassionate toward the dispassionate.
The Bodhisattva Jing asked:
“Is it that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is sentient, or that the insentient is also sentient? Is this merely a provisional designation?
Why is it, World-Honored One, that you say: ‘Now my mind has ceased and is entrusted within the unconditioned’?”
The Buddha said, “Noble son! So it is, so it is.”
"As you have said, all dharmas are merely provisional designations; thus, the sentient exists within the insentient, and the insentient exists within the sentient.
The Bodhisattva Jing again addressed the Buddha, saying, "As the World-Honored One has taught, all dharmas are disordered, all dharmas are indeterminate, and all dharmas are impermanent."
"How is it that within the dharma of provisional designations, one further speaks of the insentient as being sentient,
and the sentient as being insentient? The Buddha said, "How so?"
"Noble son! I shall now question you regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and you should answer me point by point.
Do you currently possess a sentient being?"
"Are they insentient?
He replied, "They are sentient."
The Buddha asked,
"Upon what do you base your position? He replied:
"Stand amidst the insentient.
The Buddha said, "You are now sentient; how can you stand amidst the insentient?"
He replied: "By abandoning existence and tending toward non-existence, one establishes oneself in the insentient.
The Buddha said:
"If insentient things do not exist, upon what could they be established?
He replied, "They are established on that which has nothing to be established."
The Buddha said,
"By what dharma do you now establish that which is established as having nothing to establish? He replied:
"I now perceive neither sentient beings nor non-sentient things; therefore, I establish that which is established as nothing.
The Buddha said, "Noble son!"
You say that all phenomena are merely provisional designations.
How can one speak of sentient beings within phenomena that are mere designations, or speak of insentient things as being sentient?
If that were the case, all phenomena would be disordered, all phenomena would be indeterminate, and all phenomena would be impermanent;
yet you now further state that they are neither sentient nor insentient, and thus establish nothing at all.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddha remained silent and did not reply.
The Buddha said,
"Son of good family!
"What meaning do you perceive that causes you to remain silent and not reply?
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha replied, "I perceive that within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there is neither speech nor discourse; therefore, I remain silent."
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is,
son of good family!"

All dharmas are merely provisional designations; within these dharmas of provisional designation, there is neither reality nor existence. Because their minds are defiled, sentient beings fail to realize this and each claims, "This is nirvāṇa" or "This is saṃsāra.
However, for one who observes with the pure contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is neither nirvāṇa nor saṃsāra.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"All realms of phenomena are fundamentally non-existent and nothing at all;
Failing to perceive this through the vision of birth and death, One claims that phenomena are inherently so."
Throughout the three mundane worlds, those who advance in seeking the Bodhisattva path and yet regress are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
how could there be anyone who reaches the fundamental non-arising?
The One of Ten Powers manifests in this world out of compassion, pitying all classes of beings equally.
To expound the Dharma of provisional names, so that they may know the clarity of the ultimate Way;
liberation is without peer, and he swiftly proclaims the sound of the Dharma,
filling immeasurable classes of sentient beings with the nectar of the Dharma.
The Great Way has no form or image; it is neither sentient nor insentient.
Yet, by giving rise to defiled thoughts, one fails to attain the foundation of the three dhyānas.
If you wish to cultivate this foundation, purify the seven untainted states.
Proclaiming and expounding the nine stages of purity—this is called the gateway to the Path.
When first desiring to approach the site of enlightenment, one is bound by fourteen mental states;
these must be extinguished upon attaining Buddhahood, and only then is the fruit of the Path realized.
The sixteen noble truths, the dharmamudrās of the bodhisattvas,
and the bestowal of the nectar-like wisdom— thereby he is named Tathāgata.
The thirty-two fundamental dharmas and the supernormal wisdom of the bodhisattvas.
Extinguishing the afflictions of the three periods of time, one gradually attains *nirvāṇa*.
Those who wish to seek the Buddha-way, adorn the various *kṣetras*,
and have their voices pervade the worlds of the ten directions, must practice *dhyāna* to achieve this.
The practice of the three untainted dhyānas is the profound treasury of all Buddhas;
for the sake of sentient beings, they make a vow and preach the deathless Dharma.
When practice is exhausted, no further practice is created; even the fruit is without retribution.
The Way proceeds from the wisdom of equanimity, with a mind free of even a single deviant thought.
The fourfold faith is the treasure of the Tathāgata; the six sense objects are the dust of the world.
The seven factors of enlightenment are a garland of purity; when the eightfold path is cultivated, perfection is achieved.
The five mundane supernormal powers are like a bird soaring through the void;
though its life-force is tethered to the great earth, it cannot escape the perils of birth and death.
The sixfold path of the Mahāyāna sports freely within the profound depths of the void.
Ultimately non-retrogressive, this peace leaves nothing further to be attained.
With wisdom-vision reaching pure clarity, he illuminates all within the darkness;
unattached and untainted, he is therefore titled the World-Honored One (Tianzun).
The Way does not arise of itself; it exists only through causes and conditions.
Phenomenon after phenomenon lacks self-awareness; how can empty stillness be called the Way?
Human beings fundamentally dwell within birth and death, wandering on without self-awakening.
With diligence and without indolence, one gradually accords with the holy discipline.
The jewel of the mind is inherently luminous; it does not depend on external light.
When the sun and moon are obscured by the five veils, how can they illuminate anything?
The Buddha’s fundamental conduct is pure; his mind and wisdom are free from the dust of defilement.
Having saved himself, he saves others; wherever he goes, there is no obstruction.
He is able to sever all cravings and eliminate all fetters and attachments.
Illuminated by the light of all dharmas, the darkness of ignorance and folly can no longer be known.
The nature of nirvāṇa is pure and clear; one perceives neither coming nor going.
Profound and subtle, it cannot be seen; it is tranquil and immutable.
Entering into meditative concentration with a single-minded resolve, he moves all throughout the ten directions;
his power of spiritual travel and the strength of the Way are mighty, and the eightfold path remains unimpaired.
For this reason, he gives rise to great vows, shedding tears of compassion for all sentient beings.
All contemplate suffering on their behalf; this is truly extraordinary.
People do not reckon with impermanence, yet they greedily cling to the splendors of the three realms;
like leaves blown by the wind, they wander and transmigrate wherever they are led.
Space is boundless, and the practice of the Way is likewise boundless;
it manifests as sound through emptiness, yet is void and still, without root or foundation.
When a person first emerges from the mother’s womb, they follow their conduct and become defiled within the five destinies.
Good and evil follow the form of a person, Just as a shadow follows the body.
If one can extinguish the five aggregates, The consciousness returns to emptiness;
No longer subject to birth, aging, or death— This state is truly blissful.
If one knows the treasury of all Buddhas, profound and inscrutable,
transcending realms and surpassing the three periods of time, one gazes upon the shores of birth and death.
Originally, due to my own folly and delusion, I entered this blazing cauldron.
Now that I have escaped this calamity, I sport in the pure abyss.
Although I am now freed from suffering, while I am liberated, others are not;
solitary goodness is no grand vow—why must I take final nirvana?
Returning again to manifest birth, he employs skillful transformations within the realm of affliction;
his vast salvation knows no bounds, and he never tires of the duration of kalpas.
Daily he delivers beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, acting as their peerless companion as if they were himself.
Not calculating even as much as a hair’s breadth, one proclaims and spreads one's own meritorious achievements;
one does not consider those already delivered as near, nor those yet to be delivered as distant.
With the mind and consciousness serene and unified, one ultimately remains free from all hindrance.
The physical marks are the equipment of his body; his comeliness is peerless and beyond compare.
His faculties have become fully matured, even unto great joy.
Possessing sharp faculties and complete conduct, his awakening still proceeds by degrees.
To encounter one who is deluded is truly most difficult.
When a Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, they do not dwell on thoughts of existence or non-existence;
walking alone without fear, their virtue surpasses all mountains.
The practitioner has five stages, the methods for advancing, retreating, and remaining in the middle.
One’s resolve should be like Mount Sumeru, firm and unshakable.
With the great wisdom of the six perfections and the divine feet that travel to and fro, one proceeds.
The Dharma-realm has no threefold thought, Thus it is able to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
Originally accumulating immeasurable goodness, One naturally attains the Sage within benevolence.
The Way is equal and has no threefold basis; The mind reckons the purity of both internal and external.
Natures and conducts vary in their diversity, yet the Dharma practiced is without distinction;
it is only for the sake of those who debate in the world that distinctions of grades are made.
Though they have passed through many kalpas of conduct, they have never once given rise to conceptual thoughts.
Therefore, the wandering mind is boundless, and in emptiness there is no obstruction.
Earth is the foundation of ultimate sincerity; it can endure impurity yet remains untainted.
The wisdom-mind contains all within its vast embrace, seeing neither those who are saved nor those who are not.
The conduct of the Sages is most extraordinary; they are able to endure these manifold sufferings.
Having practiced meritorious deeds for billions of eons, they have thereby perfected the root of the One Dharma.
Through the three concentrations—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they practice all dharmas.
With the wisdom of the multitude and the ten powers, he transcends the realm of non-arising.
Having fundamentally cultivated the wisdom of sounds and echoes, his eightfold voice is exceedingly pure and wondrous;
analyzing the activities of the five aggregates, he eliminates conceptual thought and craving.
Sinking into and mired in the root of birth and death, one does not seek the path of transcendence;
yet by not abandoning the three roots, one emerges through the essentials of the Way.
Through the supernormal power of knowing past lives, the Dharma-body is inconceivable.
The destruction of existence and the attainment of non-existence— this power cannot be thwarted.
Throughout the infinite realms of space, which are neither one, nor two, nor three,
he follows his original vows to purely cultivate all wondrous paths.
The dharma of the turbid sludge of birth and death is what the foolish delight in;
with wise observation free from defilement, one forever eliminates the dharmas of delusion and ignorance.
The Bodhisattva delights in tranquility and contemplates immeasurable dharmas.
Now, neither arising nor ceasing, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
With the wisdom that knows one's own past lives, one contemplates the root of birth and death;
like a person standing on the edge of a river or the sea, one then trembles with fear.
The Great Vow of Boundless Deliverance, practicing the path of the level and upright ground;
sitting or reclining, one enters deep concealment, always remaining far from defiled conduct.
Earth, water, fire, wind, and space—the consciousness relies upon and dwells within them.
Seeking the dwelling of a meditation cave, one does not know where the spirit-consciousness goes.
It is the same with human beings: through the convergence of causes and conditions, consciousness departs from the four great elements into emptiness, yet one does not know where each has gone.
The ocean of Dharma has no shore; it receives and contains internal and external dust.
Its fundamental nature is inherently pure, without distinguishing between defilement and purity.
The Great Way is fundamentally without dharmas; one contemplates the internal and external purity of all phenomena.
He does not dwell on the past, future, or present; his worldly wisdom is peerless and without equal.
He understands all the voices of the multitude and all phenomena, whether finite or infinite.
Since even the eons themselves are subject to decay and extinction, how could there be anything that remains forever?
Able to sever the calamities of sentient beings, Forever departing from the realm of the four māras;
Since greed and envy have no inherent nature, Only then should one practice pure contemplation.
Originally seated beneath the King of Trees, So too was it during the middle watch of the first night.
With single-minded concentration, his mind was fixed and free from further distraction.
For seven days his body did not lean; he thoroughly examined the dharmas of the three periods of time.
Extinction is one and non-renewal is another; it is from this that one attains awakening.
Now that you have attained Buddhahood, out of compassion for those not yet liberated, you have turned the unsurpassed Dharma wheel at the Deer Park.
First, you proclaimed the wisdom of the Four Truths: the wisdom of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
For those who have not yet awakened, it is accomplished through three recitations.
All the infinite multitudes, upon first hearing the Dharma of the Ambrosial Nectar, all attain the mind of non-arising; henceforth, there is no further birth or cessation.
Although manifesting birth in this life, his spirit roams through immeasurable realms;
turning the wheel of Dharma everywhere, he manifests transformations in every place.
Here he appears as a Buddha, dwelling in his mother’s womb for ten months.
The Sage is free from dust and defilement, and does not indulge in the five desires.
Therefore, he studies with diligent effort, mindful of transcending the consciousness of existence and non-existence.
His essential nature and conduct are spontaneous, and he does not destroy the Dharma-realm.
Those who have passed away are immeasurable, and those yet to come are inexhaustible;
even those in the present are subject to change—where, then, does the consciousness reside?
Consciousness is the root of birth and death, wandering through saṃsāra without end.
Desiring to reach the shore of the unconditioned, the third dhyāna is foremost.
May I attain the formless dharmas and be dyed in formless robes;
finding delight in the non-existent, I do not wish to dwell within the three realms of existence.
Recalling my original firm vow, for the sake of sentient beings at the primordial limit,
I again conform to worldly people, yet never fail in the heart of my great vow.
When Bodhisattvas practice the three roots, they may harbor thoughts of mutual superiority or inferiority.
I have now attained realization myself, being the foremost among those who practice with diligence.
The transformations manifested by the Tathāgata cannot be fathomed;
at times he dwells amidst rocky crags, silent and without speech.
Discerning the six internal sense-fields, one is free from the notions of self or person;
external phenomena are likewise so—perceiving them as permanent, yet they are impermanent.
From the moment I first resolved my mind, I established my practice not for myself alone.
Although I have now attained awakening first, am I not one among the rest?
Therefore, I exert myself in study, fearing that I might fail my original vow;
thus, I shall deliver those not yet delivered—this is called the Tathāgata’s pledge.
The Buddha originally made his vow, not minding the difficulty of kalpas;
though he dwells amidst worldly desires, this suffering shall not last long.
The True Dharma is fundamentally one, yet its classifications bear three names.
The Way shines like the sun and moon, Without high or low, superior or inferior minds.
One wisdom and one insight Are fundamentally accomplished through a single vow;
Because I now do not abandon this oneness, I am thus called the Foremost Honored One.
The two contemplations arise from a single dharma; through mindfulness, one transcends the three sufferings.
Fundamentally, there is no realm of suffering; it is the Dharma-body that makes distinctions of its own accord.
The Bodhisattva, wielding skillful wisdom, teaches people to be free from the notion of dharmas.
The mind of the True Person is ever pure, Not dwelling on arising or non-arising.
Constantly with a heart of great compassion, He does not dwell on the deficiencies of sentient beings;
From this he is adorned with the self-adornment, Possessing the wisdom that fully realizes the meaning of the Dharma.
The Way is fundamentally without self; this has issued from the mouths of sentient beings.
One must not, for the sake of sentient beings, preach that it is fundamentally without self.
Now I shall speak of practice, gradually leading them to perceive the traces of the Path.
Causing them to know the perception of impermanence, they shall long awaken by themselves.
Practicing the noble conduct while in the world, they never lose the root of the meaning;
it is not for the sake of mere words that they manifest before the people of the world.
Receiving instruction from all Buddhas, He sports in various meditative concentrations;
With the gait of a divine dragon among men, He has attained the four fearlessnesses.
The Tathāgata possesses distinct truths, Each and every one inconceivable.
Without dependence and without defilement, he is thus called the Honored One among Men.
An ordinary person may study worldly scriptures and reach the state of non-conception;
yet this is not equal to the meaning of a single phrase [of the Dharma], which does not dwell within the realm of birth and death.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One said:
"What do you think,
son of good family?"
"Have you thoroughly understood this meaning regarding sentient and insentient beings? He replied, "I have."
“World-Honored One!
Truly there is none equal to it.

If there are good sons or good daughters who can recite, uphold, and maintain the meaning of ‘sentient beings being non-sentient’ and ‘non-sentient things being sentient,’ they will be able to fully possess all dharmas.”
Why is this? Because all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and all worthy sages have attained Buddhahood through this very principle.

From this day forward, we, these sons and daughters of good family, shall all protect and defend those sons and daughters of good family who uphold, maintain, recite, and chant [this teaching], whether they treat sentient beings as non-sentient or non-sentient beings as sentient.

Why is this? As I observe what the Tathāgata has taught, all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have attained accomplishment through this very principle; we, too, shall surely reach this meaning of the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Avīkṣaṇa who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, knelt on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We eight shall, within this Bhadrakalpa, protect these good men and good women who uphold, recite, and chant these phrases and meanings; they shall then obtain ten meritorious blessings."
What are the ten? First, attaining the dharma that is without form or characteristics;
second, deeply entering the treasury of the Dharma.
Third, having the foremost eloquence;
fourth, attaining immeasurable dharmas;
fifth, acquiring swift and nimble wisdom.
Sixth, not abandoning the mind of great vows;
seventh, mastery over meditative concentration;
eighth, knowing the thoughts of sentient beings in advance.
Ninth, establishing the mind of non-arising;
tenth, practicing that which is fundamentally natural.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, recites, and chants the meaning of these phrases, they shall immediately obtain ten merits.

Even if one were to cause all the sons and daughters of good family who fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems to achieve and attain the bodhisattva path, it would not be equal to this son or daughter of good family receiving, upholding, and reciting the meaning of this single phrase.
"Why is this? Because all virtuous merits arise from this.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddha:
"What do you think,
son of good family?
If all the sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to become Śakra Devānām Indra, would their merit and blessings not be great?"
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not equal to the merit and blessings of a faithful son or daughter of good family who cultivates the foundation of the third dhyāna; their merit and blessings are exceedingly great, exceedingly great."
The Buddha said: “How is it so,
son of good family?”

If all sentient beings in the three-thousandfold world system were to become Brahmā deities, and each Brahmā deity possessed immeasurable divine virtues—would their merit and blessings not be very great?
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much so, very much so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

"It is not equal to a bodhisattva-mahāsattva on the first stage who practices the cultivation of the three dhyānas; the merit and blessings thereof are immeasurable and cannot be compared by means of analogy."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddha, saying:
"What do you think,
son of good family?"
If good sons or good daughters have already attained the title of Bodhisattva on the first stage and fill the trichiliocosm, would their merit and blessings not be great?
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

"Therefore, it is not equal to the merit and blessings of a bodhisattva mahāsattva on the second stage who cultivates the practice of the third dhyāna; that merit and blessings are incalculable. Why is this?

The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddha, saying:

Noble son! If Bodhisattvas of the second stage were all brought to fulfillment and filled the entire trichiliocosm, would their merit and virtue not be great?
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”

The Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:

World-Honored One!”

The Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:

World-Honored One!"

The Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Bodhisattva Viśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:

What do you think?

World-Honored One!

"By means of these three dhyānas, all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, attain the full perfection of all dharmas.

Now, regarding these sixteen dharmas, one finds delight within them;
not relying on the root of the three poisons, one accords with the ten points of meaning.
Transcending immeasurable realms, one does not lose the fundamental practice of contemplation.
To deliver all sentient beings—this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
All phenomena are like dreams and illusions; neither existent nor non-existent, they transform all classes of beings—this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.

With the twelve peerless wheels, one eloquently expounds the practice of original non-being.
To receive and enter the fundamental states—this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
Birth and death are without measure; not lingering in the three realms of existence, the consciousness-nature transforms spontaneously—this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
Once a person knows that all is impermanent, they do not cling to worldly glory or honor;
the True Person severs both this shore and the other—this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
Sentient beings are not sentient beings, and non-sentient things are likewise so.
The path of practice transcends the three realms; this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
Birth and death originally have no sign; all phenomena arise through causes and conditions.

Compassionately and universally nurturing all, Without attachment to the fundamental notion of a self,
The nature of phenomena has no high or low— This is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
The fundamental practice of a bodhisattva Consists solely in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Possessing the perfection of giving, one rescues those who are lowly;
fulfilling their every aspiration—this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
Guarding the precepts without transgression, like protecting an auspicious vase.
Moment by moment, thoughts are not intermingled; this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
The root of the practice of patience is that the mind remains unchanging when encountering objects of sensation;
Being without thought like empty space—this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
Exerting diligence for countless kalpas, never harboring indolence, one instructs and transforms all classes of sentient beings; this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
Abiding in the meditative absorption of the third dhyāna, the single-pointed mind remains unchanging.
Moving the ten directions with inspiration— this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
A deep ocean of wisdom, equal and without duality,
having eliminated all false imaginings— this is called the practice of the third dhyāna.
“Skillful means have no fixed method; Manifestations are beyond measure.
Without reckoning of noble or base, This is called the practice of the third dhyāna.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings all gave rise to the unsurpassed resolve and attained the practice of the third dhyāna.

Chapter Nineteen: Following in Practice (6–7) The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Chapter Nineteen: Following in Practice. At that time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, each gave rise to this thought:
“We wish to behold the Tathāgata’s divine wisdom and immeasurable transformations, as he travels through various worlds and returns to his original place without anyone being aware of it.”

At that time, there was a Brahmā named Zun Fu Zun (Most Honored of the Honored) who had come from a Buddha-field in another direction. Having traversed the third dhyāna and being free from all fear, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, knelt down, and spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One possesses the threefold knowledge; He fully perceives the root of the three periods of time.
Having severed delusions and removed doubt, He manifests for us the path of spiritual wisdom."
Such is their nature, spontaneous and natural; Their practice transcends the three realms of existence.
The wisdom that is the bodhisattva’s necklace— Of what general practices is it composed?
The tree of the Way is the root of all dharmas; The mind of non-arising is supreme.
Awakened by oneself without a teacher’s instruction, through what practice was this attained?
Having transcended the inferior stages, one aspires upward to the Bodhisattva path;
proclaiming the four essential dharmas, the foundation of pure Brahma-conduct.
The various classes of beings in the world of gods, In every thought-moment, are each different;

Not seeing that the beginning and the end are empty—this is called attaining through practice.

Now, having received this great radiance, it is said that one attains [realization] by following one's practice.

Like a person viewing the five colors, their own perceptions and conceptions arise;

Complete with the fivefold Dharma-body, perfected through precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation,
one is perfumed by the fragrance of virtue and conduct, which dispels the foul stench of the world.
If a person understands how to cultivate clear wisdom and remains untiring for billions of eons, they shall attain this.
All virtues are naturally complete, hence he is titled "Peerless.

In the past, throughout countless lifetimes, I cultivated the path of a bodhisattva.

At that time, all Buddhas assemble, coming from every direction throughout the ten quarters;

Grasping the four paths of skillful means, riding upon the wisdom of the four fearlessnesses,

Its form is like that of a plantain tree; though it has bark, there is no core within.

yet you are not defiled by worldly dust, remaining unattached like a lotus flower.

Within, one adorns the body and mind with the Dharma of the Eightfold Right Awakening;
without, one embellishes all lands with the various marks and signs of excellence.
Cultivating the two contemplations through clear wisdom, one naturally adorns oneself with these marks and signs.
Originally formed from the four great elements, their formation and destruction are non-existent;
the preceding thought is not the succeeding thought, yet moment by moment they form the dust of affliction.
Bestowing the mind of giving upon all beings, one encounters no opposition from the high or the low.
Internally endowed with the perfections (pāramitās), he is without dependence and has no fixed abode.

he upholds all virtues and moral conduct, never failing in the nature and practice of the precepts.
The third stage possesses ten dharmas, formless and invisible;
through skillful means and expedients, one enters birth and death, manifesting the paths of the world.
One undergoes the manifold sufferings and afflictions of life, with countless anxieties and fears amidst constant change.
The Sage can come and go, yet does not consider this perilous.
The Great Way is fundamentally formless; it is neither existent nor non-existent, yet gives birth to wisdom.
Through the infinite crossing of sign after sign, one adorns the body with its own radiance.
The eyes gaze upward and downward with blinking; seeing afar without limit, one practices the Perfection of Purity and attains this reward of non-obstruction.
The heels are fine, level, and upright, having cultivated the seat of the Great Sage.
Now having attained this stainless retribution, he is endowed with the perfection of the Way.
His calves are like gold set inlaid; they neither retain dust nor water.
When he lifts his feet, they are like whirlwinds; his joints and mechanisms move without obstruction.
The lotus of the mind is unstained by dust; internal joy radiates outward.
All this results from the retribution of forbearance, and is thus called the Perfection of Forbearance (Kṣānti-pāramitā).
Holding the mind as firm as a vajra, one expounds the dharmas of the stages of the Way.

being sincere and unstained by existence—this is called the perfection of non-deception.
The Way proceeds from the contemplation of the three views; One can thereby attain impartial wisdom.
When the mind does not cling to right or wrong, One should cross over to liberation in the unarisen.
When first giving rise to the heart of great vows, It is not for the sake of a few people alone.
Spontaneously attaining the realization of the Way—this is called being endowed with the perfection of emptiness.
Wandering through Buddha-lands by means of the supernormal powers, body and mind are without limit or obstruction;
with a single intent that never shifts, this is the infinity of the perfection of supernormal powers.

Regarding the phenomena of sensation, there are internal and external; they are neither suffering nor are they pleasure.
Eliminating all internal and external phenomena is the perfection of non-action (apramāṇa-pāramitā).
The five faculties possess five dharmas; they fundamentally rely upon the eighteen elements (dhātus).
By discerning and removing five [of these], one attains the perfection of no-retribution (avipāka-pāramitā).
Guarding body, speech, and mind, Restraining them so they are not negligent;
The Pure Resonance shines everywhere— This is the Immeasurable of the Eightfold Path.
Not relying on the three types of mental application, Nor having arising or ceasing,
With the cessation of mental activity, rebirth no longer arises; this is the Perfection of Silence.
Pure as a lotus flower, one’s vast learning remains untainted;
constantly training and transforming sentient beings, this is the Perfection of Pure Teaching.
With equanimity and non-dual thought, One harbors no biased or narrow mind;
Like the sun shining upon the void, This is the *prajñā-pāramitā* of wise observation.
Benevolence and wisdom are immeasurable, And the unarisen is invisible.

Knowing that birth has no inherent master, and that all phenomena arise through causes and conditions, one achieves the path of both existence and non-existence; this is the perfection of equanimity.
Through the unimpeded path of dhāraṇī, one attains the wisdom of liberation.
Discriminating the notion of non-self is the perfection of emptiness and purity.
The five hardships within birth and death, and attachment to worldly dust—
Wandering through the infinite realms of space is the perfection of skillful wisdom.
Already liberated from the bonds of birth and death, He sports within liberation;
pure and free from distracted thoughts, His fruition is the *pāramitā* of infinite transcendence.
While manifesting ascetic practices in the world, He maintains a mind as firm as a diamond.
Having already transcended the three realms of existence, one naturally attains the *pāramitā* of liberation.
Whether abiding in the realm of empty space, one contemplates the Dharma without distracted thoughts;
like the void that contains all, one attains the *pāramitā* of formlessness.
How joyful is the Way of Non-arising! It forever severs all worldly afflictions;
Seeing neither coming nor going, This is the Perfection of Non-action.
The supernormal powers have four aspects, Constantly roaming through the lands of the ten directions.
Body and mind both empty and tranquil, The perfection of clear wisdom.
Originally arising from a mind of equanimity, With a single intent free from all defilement;
The mind transcends immeasurable realms, The perfection of the subtle and wondrous.
Contemplating the suffering of birth in the world, one realizes that all phenomena are of a single nature and nothing arises;
the mind of the Way is irreversible—this is the *vajra-pāramitā*.
Having attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one cultivates the holy life and transcends the nine successive stages.
When practice is consummated and no longer burns with craving, this is the *yoke of adornment* (*mālā-vimokṣa*).
When the Path proceeds from the contemplation of the three types of wisdom, distinguishing the practices of meditative concentration,
and the mind naturally subsides without arising, this is the *yoke of the immeasurable* (*apramāṇa-vimokṣa*).

Rescuing and delivering those in the four evil realms, Transcending stages without awaiting formal realization, Spontaneously extinguishing ignorance— This is the perfection of equanimity (*samatā-pāramitā*).
The Way of the Teacher is truly subtle and wondrous; Diligence cannot be surpassed.
The dharma of equality and non-duality is the perfection of all practices.
Amidst the many sufferings and hardships of birth in the world, one constantly cultivates the unsurpassed path;
seeing neither the traces of existence nor non-existence is the perfection of all mental conceptions.
Birth and death abound with many constraints, And the light of wisdom is not seen;
Through the power of the Way being proclaimed, The practice of infinite accumulation is perfected.
Having accomplished the nine dhyāna methods, One remains unstained by worldly knowledge.
Discerning each and every perception is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
To manifest the Dharma out of compassion for all people,
seeing neither one who is saved nor one who is not saved, is the perfection of tranquility of mind (*śānta-citta-pāramitā*).
Wandering through immeasurable realms, serving all the worthy sages,
receiving their teachings without ever forgetting them— this is the perfection of dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, being able to manifest transformations that move and inspire all Buddha-fields.
Nor does he harbor self-conceit; this is the perfection of the extinction of mental activity.
Recalling past lives and universally cultivating the bodhisattva path, he remains unattached to internal outflows; this is the perfection of contemplative practice.
Cultivating and purifying all Buddha-lands, making them stainless and free from defilement;
delivering immeasurable beings—this is the Infinite Deliverance of the Dharma-realm.
The faculties of sentient beings are infinite, yet their bodies are supremely pure.
Unstained by existence internally or externally, one realizes the *dharma-pāramitā*.
Knowing that birth is not worth craving, one manifests expediently without fixed direction;
not giving rise to manifold conceptualizations, one attains the *asama-pāramitā*.
Though the dharmas of the body are manifold, they do not give rise to defilement;
adorning the marks of the physical form is the perfection of merit.
Having accumulated the roots of the Dharma through incalculable eons, [he has perfected this].
Accumulating merit not for oneself is the Infinite of Supernatural Powers;
The six sense-faculties not clinging to existence, discerning immeasurable wisdom,
and reaching beyond the limits of empty space, is the Infinite of Single-mindedness.
Difficult is it to be born among humans; though one receives countless bodies, the eye does not cling to external forms—this is the perfection of non-conceptualization (*asaṃkalpa-pāramitā*).
Holding the mind without greedy attachment, one’s births continue without ceasing.
Spontaneously extinguishing all internal conditioned activities is the *apramāṇa* of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Being fearless and without attachment, not perceiving internal or external phenomena,
and having no diversity in the aspiration for the Way— this is the *apramāṇa* of spiritual wisdom (*jñāna*).
The Buddha’s body is inherently pure, Untainted by dust or defilement;
His wisdom reaches beyond a hundred kalpas— This is the perfection of the mindless.
The former mind is not the present mind, Yet birth after birth it continues without end.
With a single mind, nothing arises; this is the Great Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā).
Though hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings are delivered, one does not perceive even those who are delivered.
When mental thoughts are free from all that is non-rectitudinous, this is the Perfection of Delightful Play (Ratipāramitā).
Having exhausted all practices, one realizes suffering and penetrates the root of the three periods of time;
harboring no thoughts of the Lesser Vehicle, this is the *mūlaparyavasāna-pāramitā*.
Not dwelling on suffering as suffering, one thoroughly understands the four marks of impermanence.
Exhausting birth so that no further body remains is the Perfection of the Noble Truths.
Having received the prophecy from immeasurable Buddhas that one shall become a Buddha,
yet feeling no personal joy or celebration, is the Perfection of Equal Giving.
The mind is fundamentally inconceivable, its virtue transcending all measure;
through the contemplation of existence and non-existence, one attains the perfection of tranquility.
It is the source of the manifold sufferings of the five realms, where pure and wholesome dharmas do not arise.
The practice of the eightfold noble path is the *apramāṇa* of manifesting the body;
the human body is fundamentally without dharma, and not perceiving the marks of the *dharmadhātu* is the *apramāṇa* of supreme wisdom transcending a hundred practices.
In the space of a single thought-moment, one receives realization without difficulty;
forever free from all defiled phenomena, the Great Sage’s perfection is infinite.
From beginning to end, he is eternally detached, nor does he perceive a self.
Spiritual power like space is the perfection of contentment;
Self-mastery of dignified conduct and non-attachment to marks and signs is the perfection of self-restraint;
Guarding oneself without transgression is the perfection of intimacy.
For countless eons, I have made offerings to all the World-Honored Ones;
without violating the realms of phenomena, I practice the perfection of wishlessness.
Furthermore, I harbor no expectations nor do I seek fortune within any phenomena.
Non-existence gives rise to nothing; this is the perfection of accumulated practice.
Not dwelling on either shore, one transcends the sea of birth and death;
having thoroughly exhausted all roots, this is the perfection of inexhaustibility.
The sixteen inconceivables are also called the sixteen wisdoms;
from suffering to the non-existence of dharmas, they constitute the perfection of non-attachment.
Birth and death have no bottom; beings emerge or sink away within them.
Being able to fully observe and understand that the nature of things is emptiness is the perfection of emptiness (śūnyatā-pāramitā).
Being able to discern each of the thirty-two marks of the physical body as defiled and impure practices is the perfection of non-attachment (asaṅga-pāramitā).
Visual consciousness has internal and external aspects; not receiving external bodily sensations, one is fearless and unmoved—this is the perfection of loving-kindness.
As I sit beneath the Bodhi tree, adorning the diamond throne,
Subduing Māra without fear, his great compassion is infinite.
Pitying all classes of sentient beings, he delivers people without perceiving anyone delivered;
his vast salvation knows no bounds, and his self-detachment is infinite.
The past does not arise again; one is unstained by the dust of the future.
With a mind of wisdom that has neither interior nor exterior, this is the perfection of non-doubt.
Regarding the internal and external aggregates, elements, and sense bases, no defilements of dust are produced.
Guarding the One with heedfulness is the Perfection of Divine Power;
The eye does not cling to external forms, nor does the tongue perceive flavors;
Eliminating thoughts of greedy attachment is the Formless Perfection.
Discerning the bodhisattva mind, Pure contemplation is free from attachment;
The Path proceeds from equanimous wisdom, The perfection of majestic deportment.
Through the knowledge of recollecting past lives, One knows the origins from which one has come.
Not giving rise to further conceptual thoughts is the *apramāṇa* of manifest birth;
the wise transform the world while remaining in it, exhausting all suffering without remainder.
Uprooting and severing the root of birth and death is the *apramāṇa* of ascetic practice.
Compassion surpasses that of a mother’s nurture; wisdom is universal, without high or low.
Internally not perceiving a self, this is the perfection of non-attachment.
Virtue wanders through immeasurable realms, yet there is no one who perceives it.
Nor does he praise himself; this is the *Dharmakāya-pāramitā*.
Furthermore, from all Buddhas he receives the immeasurable Dharma of the wisdom of emptiness;
naturally exhausting the limits of suffering, this is the *Anutpāda-pāramitā*.
The Way proceeds from the wisdom of equanimity; Untainted by the perceptions of the three realms of existence, One thereby attains the divine feet: This is the perfection of non-self.
Ordinary people are bound by the four attachments, And do not escape the afflictions of the triple world.
Exhausting birth so as never to create it again is the perfection of transcendent wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Throughout incalculable eons, the concentrated mind remains undisturbed and the will remains unchanging;
this is the perfection of the ultimate limit (*koṭipāramitā*).
Divine wisdom is boundless, forever eliminating attachment to existence;
having attained the patience of non-arising, one reaches the infinite nirvana.
With the insight of the Way, one contemplates the seven stages; within the dharma-realm, there is no disparity.
The single mark is invisible; this is the *apramāṇa* of formlessness.
Nirvāṇa is without birth or extinction; its traces are non-existent.
Being able to transcend both "this" and "that," this is the *apramāṇa* of following practice.
Ignorance is the root of all formations; it flows through the twelvefold ocean.
Not being defiled by consciousness is the perfection of non-attachment.
Just as these Four Noble Truths give rise to the fruits of all paths.
The extinction of the mind through the four dhyānas is the perfection of concentration;
The Tathāgata’s eight liberations, being neither suffering nor pleasure,
can extinguish present fetters— this is the perfection of freedom from affliction.
Not clinging to the three realms, yet manifesting within the dust and toil of the world;
cultivating supernatural powers and wisdom, this is the perfection of bliss.
Abiding nowhere and coming or going not, nor destroying the nature of phenomena—this is the perfection of bliss.
Eternally extinguishing the field of worldly toil is the *apramāṇa* of immutability.
Just as form is fundamentally without form, and the nature of form is eternally spontaneous,
to fully comprehend the suffering of the three periods of time is the *apramāṇa* of the cessation of thought.
Not receiving the defilements of external objects, with a concentrated mind free from other thoughts, birth is exhausted and no further karma is created; this is the perfection of non-reception.
Manifesting infinite transformations, yet never acting for one's own sake—this is the perfection of non-attachment.
The wisdom of the Way is free from the three obstructions; this is the Perfection of the Ultimate Limit.
Entering meditative absorption to eliminate the three perceptions, one perceives no self, person, or life-span;
holding to faith without wandering, this is the Perfection of Multitudinous Wisdom.
The dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, Contemplating the samādhis and the noble path, Tranquil, extinguished, and unified in mind—this is the perfection of embracing [the Dharma].
The Path gives rise to immeasurable dharmas; From this, one arrives at that [other shore].
Profoundly comprehending the suffering of the three periods of time is the *apramāṇa* of receiving joy;
knowing that birth is a great calamity and that all dharma-realms are leaking and porous,
yet relinquishing the one [self] without defiled attachment, is the *apramāṇa* of manifold wonders.
The four immeasurable minds of compassion universally moisten all beings;
in their transformation and guidance, there is neither high nor low—this is the Great Perfection of Wisdom.
The forms produced by the causes and conditions of the four elements have a nature that cannot be altered.
Seeking to reach the gates of liberation, one practices the perfection of the three vehicles.
Even when the kalpa is about to end in flames, one harbors no heart of fear;
naturally attaining the power of the Way, this is the perfection of non-conceptualization.
Nor does he give rise to thoughts, nor does he discriminate among various perceptions;
the Buddha’s wisdom is inexhaustible, like the Great Ocean of the *pāramitā*.
His meritorious achievements surpass all practices, and his fundamental karma is immeasurable.
Not seeing one thing as not one, this is the *apramāṇa* of detachment from the crowd.
Fulfilling the vows of the great resolve, observing that the body has no form or characteristics,
and destroying the afflictions of the four Māras, this is the *apramāṇa* of adornment.
Non-conceptualization is the fundamental nature of all dharmas; nirvāṇa is tranquil and pure.
This is the realm where all Buddhas dwell—the profound treasury, the *pāramitā* of depth.
Without marks and invisible, one attains Buddhahood through this single principle.
Departing from the mind and returning to the fundamental Dharma is the *ekārtha-pāramitā*.
Exhaustively investigating the fruits of all paths, one has no threefold nesting place;
wisdom shines forth without limit—this is the *mūlasthiti-pāramitā*.
Amidst all the hardships of birth and death, one dwells in the tranquil peace of the unconditioned;
by not giving rise to the defilements of the five sensory objects, one attains the *dhāraṇī-pāramitā*.
Wandering through immeasurable worlds, one teaches and transforms all classes of sentient beings.
Experiencing the suffering of birth and death, he attains the *apramāṇa* of severing suffering;
Manifesting within a mother’s womb, he is truly unstained by attachment;
His mind is pure as space, the *apramāṇa* of fundamental wisdom.
Not perceiving any recipient of retribution, one realizes the fruit of all-encompassing wisdom;
by discerning the root of the four paths, one practices the perfection of bearing burdens.
Originating from immeasurable ages, the dharma-realm is inconceivable.
With a mind of equality and non-duality, one attains the perfection of vast wisdom (*vipula-prajñā-pāramitā*).
The Buddha-dharma is profoundly subtle and wondrous, beyond the reach of the two vehicles;
by transcending immeasurable practices, one attains the perfection of being free from doubt (*aniścaya-pāramitā*).
First purifying the faculty of the eye, Purifying and cultivating the fundamental practice of the mind,
Aspiring to reach the path of the Bodhisattvas— This is the Perfection of Purified Intention (*cetanā-pāramitā*).
Holding the will as firm as a vajra, Pure and free from all blemish,
Permanently detached from the realms of existence and non-existence, this is the perfection of the fruit of the Way.
When the World-Honored Ones of antiquity sat beneath this most auspicious tree, they subdued the four demonic enemies; this is the perfection of the power of patience.
The divine consciousness dwells in the void, Primordially free from any mind of anger, Nor giving rise to any defilement; This is the perfection of transcendence.
Divine power surpasses the immeasurable, Throughout all worlds.
Nor does one cling to what is desirable; this is the perfection of stainlessness (*vimala-pāramitā*).

To thoroughly investigate emptiness, being pure within and likewise without, and to discern that all perceptions are impermanent—this is the perfection of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-pāramitā*).
The radiance illuminates all realms, dispelling all darkness and obscurity;
by not giving rise to manifold conceptualizations, one attains the perfection of severing defilements.
