Through the wisdom-observation of the three dharmas, one eternally eliminates desire, anger, and ignorance.
Unstained by form, this is the perfection of wisdom-conduct;
Even throughout billions of kalpas, with a mind of vast vows,
Not perceiving any class of sentient beings, this is the perfection of pure teaching.
Practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, Free from the notion of self within and without,
The Buddha-realm and Dharma-realm are pure— This is the Immeasurable Liberation.
If people fundamentally cultivate this practice, They will uproot and sever the twelve links of dependent origination.
Eliminating greed and not clinging to existence is the *apramāṇa* of single-mindedness.
If one wishes to cultivate the practices of the human path, one must first guard body, speech, and mind;
this is the *apramāṇa* of the ten wholesome actions, the foundation of all practices that accord with the Dharma.
I originally did not create delusion; that which serves as its fundamental basis is the ten wisdoms and immeasurable knowledge—the perfection of primordial non-existence.
The Dharma-realm is inconceivable, and one thereby accomplishes the state of fearlessness.
Exhausting the root of birth and death is the *apramāṇa* of the heavy burden;
the Tathāgata’s compassion and wisdom are equal, nurturing all without distinction of high or low,
and removing the defiled mind is the *apramāṇa* of being without expectation.
Generating the aspiration for the Mahāyāna, He rescues and delivers all those who are obstructed;
Seeing no fundamental basis to birth and death, This is the perfection of detachment.
Upholding his great vows through diligent effort, He sports within various states of meditative concentration.
Constantly harboring a mind of reciprocity is the *apramāṇa* of repaying kindness;
The wisdom of the equality of all sentient beings, which fully knows all fundamental roots and harbors no mind of worldly desire, is the *apramāṇa* of skillful wisdom.
The Great Way is most wondrous; it is not moved by worldly desires.
Having relinquished its original intent through the three emptinesses, it reaches the ultimate *pāramitā*.
Within this Bhadrakalpa, the various Buddhas have arisen in the world.
Uprooting suffering without the three obstructions, he practices the *paramitā* of universal circulation;
Emitting impartial light from his body, he receives and delivers countless multitudes;
Knowing birth yet remaining unstained by birth, he practices the *paramitā* of the virtuous friend.
Desiring to accomplish the unsurpassed path, one draws near to virtuous friends;
being able to exhaust the very limit of suffering is the perfection of inexhaustibility.
In the four paths there is no coming or going, abiding for the duration of countless kalpas.
To exhaustively investigate the root of the Way is the *apramāṇa* of immutability.
To exhaustively investigate the cycle of birth and death, one must not harbor a regressive mind;
being courageous and invincible is the *apramāṇa* of establishing resolve.
Practicing giving without attachment, one does not give rise to the three perceptions;
since both the beginning and the end are entirely empty, this is the perfection of wisdom.
The power of the Way is like space; one does not calculate the body of the five aggregates.
Form is fundamentally not form; this is the Infinite Purity.
The source of all wisdom is non-arising; the notion of permanence is not true.
Seeing no one to be taught, this is the Infinite Power of Wisdom.
Innumerable kalpas in the past, there was a Buddha whose name was the same as mine;
he cultivated the root of the Dharma of equality, the Perfection of Formlessness.
When the Tathāgata Mahāprajñā appeared, he extinguished the dust of craving and desire.
Instructing the multitudes of sentient beings is the perfection of the faculty of faith.
There was a Buddha named Unobstructed who practiced austerities for immeasurable eons;
restraining his mind and remaining heedless was his perfection of ethical discipline.
Next is the Buddha named Mahāpraṇidhāna (Vast Vow), who teaches without distinction of high or low;
his mind is equal like space, and he possesses the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
There is a Buddha named Mahāpraṇidhāna who has thoroughly exhausted the root of birth and death.
Manifesting countless transformed bodies, The Perfection of Diligent Deliverance.
The Way is fundamentally pure by nature; One does not perceive the wisdom of space.
Formless and invisible, The Perfection of Compassionate Deliverance.
The eighty-six modes of contact are what the Bodhisattva practices;
since they have no root in the three poisons, there is the perfection of non-arising.
Through the sixteen minds of the noble ones, one fully knows that nothing exists.
Not destroying the various dharma-realms is the perfection of bodilessness.
Within a single mind and a single thought, not departing from meditative concentration and contemplation,
yet arising again from that single intent, is the perfection of non-conceptualization.
Space is boundless and shoreless; with a tranquil mind free from defilement, relinquishing all and clinging to nothing, one attains the perfection of meditative concentration.
I have long practiced this path, remaining serene and free from discursive thought.
The present state of tranquility of mind is the perfection of non-obstruction;
Through meditative concentration, one extinguishes the self-will, and through pure contemplation, one extinguishes the three perceptions.
The wisdom of the Path is naturally pure; this is the perfection of removing defilement.
The realm of the Buddha is inconceivable, and the realm of sentient beings is likewise so;
the nature of phenomena is naturally quiescent—this is the perfection of formlessness.
Able to cross over the perils of birth and death, one does not dwell upon the suffering of the three realms.
With a mind of forbearance, one does not give rise to conceptualizations; this is the *apramāṇa* of serenity.
Entering the meditative concentration of the three periods of time, one fully knows the faculties of all sentient beings;
observing the body internally and externally, this is the *apramāṇa* of wishlessness.
Within the realms of the eight classes of spirits and deities, he transforms them according to their needs;
manifesting the power of his spiritual feet, he reaches the *apramāṇa* of the cessation of traces.
Skillfully employing expedient means to teach sentient beings, he never departs from the emptiness of both the root and the branches.
Discerning the four fearlessnesses is the perfection of selflessness.
Contemplating the internal and external body, discerning emptiness and non-wisdom,
and not perceiving a self is the perfection of the mental faculty of phenomena.
To be born encountering sages and saints is joy; The eight liberations are free from attachment.
Not giving rise to manifold conceptualizations— This is the perfection of illusion (māyā-pāramitā).
In the True Dharma there are no men or women; The mind arises from ideation.
The profound Dharma is invisible; this is the *aśubha-darśana-apramāṇa*.
He manifests infinite forms through emanation, then returns and merges them into one;
none are able to perceive this—this is the *kāya-guhya-apramāṇa*.
The Tathāgata is endowed with all marks; his form-body wanders through the world, teaching and transforming beings through spiritual powers—this is the perfection of non-reliance.
Ordinary people who have not yet entered the path of training do not contemplate the body internally or externally.
The noble wisdom is profoundly subtle, With the marks and signs of the infinite transcendence.
Originally arising from the supernormal powers, The mental dharmas have no high or low;
The Bodhisattva’s formless contemplation Is the peace and bliss of infinite transcendence.
In meditative concentration, one awaits without thought; with a stilled mind, there is no attachment.
One sports in the pool of the eight liberations; this is the perfection of utmost sincerity.
When people know the nature of the five sufferings, they look up and cultivate the Way of non-action.
The six supernormal powers and untainted dharmas are the Perfection of the Sages;
Wandering through the world with spiritual powers while constantly practicing the discipline of the sages,
Without observing internal or external phenomena, is the Perfection of Namelessness.
Practicing without arrogance, harboring no perverted thoughts,
and not giving rise to the various fetters— this is the perfection of purification.
Furthermore, through the contemplation of a corpse, one does not dwell on the pure or the impure.
Being unattached to either the internal or the external, one attains the *pāramitā* of non-arrogance;
Maintaining dignified conduct in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya, and acting without falsehood,
one attains the *pāramitā* of self-protection through manifold wisdom.
Taking formlessness as the essence of the Way, Unstained by the dust of the world,
With mind always settled whether sitting or reclining— This is the Infinite of Self-Maintenance.
The Sage takes pity on the mundane world, Raining down the Dharma of Ambrosia.
Expounding and elucidating immeasurable wisdom, he attains the *pāramitā* of transforming through reception;
Practicing extensive giving with abundant benevolence, his contemplation and observation eliminate the root of the mind,
Dispelling all afflictions and sufferings, he attains the *pāramitā* of the battle for victory.
The mind contemplates immeasurable dharmas and manifests immeasurable transformations;
by recollecting the source of supernormal wisdom, one attains the *vaiśāradya-pāramitā*.
When internal dharmas are free from thought, yet constantly defiled by external objects, [one realizes their true nature].
By means of that knowledge of non-arising, one proceeds from the perfection of aspiration.
Adorned by various concentrations as one’s own necklace, the visual consciousness does not give rise to conceptualization;
since even that does not exist inherently, one proceeds from the perfection of immutability.
Cultivating all forms of wisdom, one attains liberation through the transcendence of knowledge and vision;
desiring to drink the nectar of immortality, one reaches the *pāramitā* of ambrosia.
Through pure contemplation free from attachment, the wisdom of emptiness is non-dual with the *pāramitā*.
Discerning the four fruits of the path is the Perfection of Transmigration;
like a man who can endure the dust of worldly toil,
with a mind and wisdom untainted by defilement, this is the Perfection of Fulfilling Vows.
Each mark has its own retribution; there is neither active practice nor existent dharmas.
Transcending the practices of the four dhyānas is the perfection of the extinction of birth.
Due to fundamental practices in previous lives, one harbors no anger toward others.
Spontaneously free from the eight difficulties, one attains the *paramita* of transcendence;
That which ordinary people contemplate— meeting and then parting—
is not the vast vow-mind of the Sage, which is the *paramita* of discernment.
By means of non-illumination, one perceives what is originally present;
Thoroughly seeing that nothing exists externally, the burden of form naturally ceases—this is the *apramāṇa* of non-seeing.
Proceeding to the realm of empty space, one moves with swift speed and without obstruction.
Not dwelling on intermediate phenomena is the perfection of discipline;
realizing that the fundamental is a single dharma, yet the inclinations of each differ,
and following the world while not being stained by its colors is the perfection of liberation from bonds.
Discerning the root of the three poisons, one should practice until all conditioned formations are exhausted;
knowing that the root is not "mine," this is the perfection of the body’s fundamental nature.
When the mind roams with mastery, it perceives desire as a blazing fire.
Extinguishing the five destinies is the *śītalāpāramitā*.
Having no aspirations within the three realms of existence and being forever detached from the eight states of no leisure while clinging to the dharmas of the five desires is the *vyavahārapāramitā*.
Arising and ceasing have no fixed limit; The dhāraṇī is never forgotten.
With all wisdom complete, This is the perfection of extensive learning.
There are four grades of receiving wisdom: Others awaken while one does not know for oneself.
By relying on this, one attains the seven emptinesses, the perfection of swift progress.
The Buddha-way is difficult to fathom; it cannot be measured by the mind.
To fully know that there is no path to be observed is the perfection of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Discerning the thirty-seven factors, the noble path of the Tathāgata,
with a single mind free from conceptualization— this is called the perfection of the body.
Comprehending all phenomena, both near and far, without dwelling on the unimpeded path— this is the perfection of the body.
Each of the ten titles is distinct, representing the countless *pāramitās*.
Preaching the profound and essential Dharma, his mind harbors no timidity;
he does not seek after formlessness—this is the *jñānapāramitā*.
Entering the wisdom of the eightfold noble path, one does not destroy the practice of emptiness;
contemplating the Dharma within oneself, one attains the perfection of the fruit.
As name-and-form undergoes various transformations, craving enters the sickness of worldly defilement.
Unable to reach the fundamental non-existence is the perfection of skillful examination;
The ten dharmas are empty and unchanging, yet the mind’s thoughts are bound by conceptions.
Not dwelling on thoughts and removing external intrusions is the perfection of impartiality.

Compassionately mindful of those in the world suffering, whose anxieties and fears are endless and manifold, he establishes expedient means and manifests transformations; this is the perfection of liberation through manifestation.
His mind is as firm as a vajra, incapable of being destroyed by anything conditioned.
Irrigating with the Dharma of ambrosia, the profound and essential *pāramitā* of deliverance;
fundamentally relying on the wisdom of emptiness, liberation without obstruction;
the clarity of knowledge removing dust and defilement, the *pāramitā* of seeing and hearing.
Knowing how to uphold the discipline of the sages, with precepts, learning, wisdom, and a concentrated mind,
and possessing the strength of the power of the Path— this is the perfection of non-deficiency.
Knowing that the body is fundamentally formless, one endures the torments of the laws of birth and death.
Tranquil, they return to emptiness and stillness; Unbinding themselves, they attain the Infinite.
The wise adapt to worldly changes, Yet never cling to renewed pleasure;
Eliminating fetters and severing the root of suffering— This is the Supreme Vehicle of the Infinite.
The World-Honored Teacher among men has practiced through immeasurable eons;
with utmost sincerity and free from deceit, his speech accords with the Infinite Deliverance.
His mental reflections are inconceivable, as he has exhausted the profound treasury of the Dharma.
Discerning the realm of the Tathāgata is the perfection of the path of awakening;
the tenfold meaning of the Tathāgata is each devoid of form and characteristics,
tranquil and without sound— this is the perfection of bestowing the prediction of enlightenment.
Contemplating the body as empty and formless, pure and unstained, with no fundamental dharma to increase—this is the perfection of the exhaustion of conditioned activity.
The Tathāgata bestows the prophecy: suchness is immutable and unchanging.
Not perceiving the root of arising and ceasing is the *pāramitā* of primordial purity.
That which is taught by the Perfectly Awakened One—
never abandoning any being and causing all to obtain protection— is the *pāramitā* of the peerless.
Acting as a bridge for all beings, he exhaustively investigates all dharmas;
gradually entering the profound treasury, he attains the *apramāṇa* of transcending suffering.
He teaches and transforms all classes of sentient beings, never departing from the realm of Dharma.
Advancing toward the site of enlightenment is the perfection of self-maintenance;
that which all sentient beings take as their refuge and turn entirely toward the gateway of the Way is the perfection of freedom from affliction through sovereign wisdom.
Acting as a torch of light for the world, serving as eyes for sentient beings,
causing them to know where to turn for refuge— this is the Great Way of Infinite Deliverance (*mahāpatha-aparimita*).
Manifested in the world by the One of Ten Powers (*daśabala*), it uproots and severs the sorrow and suffering of humanity.
Wisdom destroys all states of existence; this is the perfection of spiritual wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Delighting in secluded and tranquil places, one cultivates the practices originally undertaken;
being able to manifest transformations for the sake of sentient beings, this is the perfection of the path (*mārgapāramitā*).
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, he endured suffering without forsaking it;
having perfected the ten treasures of the Dharma, he attained the perfection of non-receding.
His contemplation and concentration were equal to space, universally capable of illuminating all things.
Observing oneself and further observing others is the perfection of equanimity.
Observing all Buddha-fields and adorning oneself with manifold wisdom,
traveling everywhere throughout the realms of the ten directions, is the perfection of tranquility.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable dharmas proclaimed by the Tathāgata, which extinguish the root of all that is unrighteous; this is the perfection of firmness.
Sentient beings who are ready for transformation awaken as soon as they hear the Dharma.
These beings possess the sharpness of past consciousness; this is the perfection of swiftness.
The root of all dharmas is neither existent nor non-existent;
the Way arises from the signless; this is the perfection of the eightfold dharma.
Wisdom illuminates the infinite; like a lion, it is fearless.
Contemplating the dharma of impermanence, one attains the *apramāṇa* of non-arising.
In preaching the Dharma, there is no preaching; in delivering beings, there is no delivering.
Skillful means surpassing a hundred kalpas, The Perfection of Non-defilement;
Neither sinking nor exhausting, It illuminates all people.
Proclaiming the wisdom of the Tathāgata, The Perfection of Desirelessness.
Teaching the Dharma without the notion of dharmas, Not perceiving a self, a person, or a being,
Great compassion transcends existence and non-existence— This is the perfection of the wheel-turning king.
As various birds delight in the pond Amidst blue lotuses and water lilies,
Through meditative stillness, perceptions are forever eliminated; this is the perfection of non-action.
In preaching the Dharma there are three matters: by removing both root and branch through emptiness, one crosses over these immeasurable realms; this is the perfection of non-reliance.
Contemplating the roots of others and observing their mental consciousness, they do not depart from the Bodhisattva vow; this is the perfection of ultimateity.
Acting with skillful means according to the occasion, they do not allow suffering to enter their minds.
Forever abandoning the mind of increase and decrease is the perfection of acting according to the Dharma.
When illusory arts are attached to the visual consciousness, one does not see anything being born;
when the auditory consciousness hears those sounds, understanding emptiness is the perfection of liberation.
If that great illusionist manifests various foods and drinks,
and the nose-consciousness discriminates them, this is the perfection of fragrance.
Just as that which is created by transformation, its meaning is inconceivable.
Those who wish to exhaustively investigate [the truth] attain the *asaṃkhyeya* of flavor and cognition.
Originally, it is I who create renewed pleasure; the body perceives all dharmas as fundamental.
When the mind is gathered and naturally subdued, one manifests through skillful means the *asaṃkhyeya* of deliverance.
With a pure and resonant sound, it pervades the realms of the ten directions;
the fragrance of the virtue of precepts is likewise, representing the perfection of non-transgression.
Illusions are not real, deceiving the ignorant and deluded.
Guiding others toward the true Dharma is the perfection of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Probing and seeking the faculties of sentient beings is something no one but the Sages can fathom;
the Great Sage’s skillful transformation is the perfection of establishing the teachings.
Pure as a lotus flower, Never receiving dust or defilement,
Transcending all other practices in succession— This is the Infinite Practice of Restraining the Mind.
*The Bodhisattva-āraṇyaka Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
The *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, Scroll Seven; also titled *The Present Retribution*;
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
The Nineteenth Chapter, "On Following Practice," Part Two.
"Transcending and passing beyond the three realms, formless and invisible to the eye,
universally illuminating the three thousand worlds— this is the Infinite Compassion of the Dharma.
In the space of a single thought or a single moment, one is fully endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence."
Untainted by worldly defilements, this is the *akṣaya-pāramitā* of the realm of emptiness.
If one can eloquently proclaim the Dharma, universally moistening all living beings,
and perceives the Four Noble Truths according to their true nature, this is the *akṣaya-pāramitā* of the exhaustion of suffering.
The Buddha-lands are universally pure, Without the mind of the three vehicles;
Spontaneously attaining the Way’s teaching— This is the *samādhi-dhyāna-pāramitā*.
Human beings originally arise from emptiness, And the Dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases.
Not contravening the fundamental nature of all dharmas is the perfection of skillful means.
Illusions and transformations are not real; practicing beyond the three realms, transcending immeasurable lands is the perfection of penetration.
The beings in the realm of non-perception rely on consciousness and do not understand wisdom;
the noble ones who attain the stage of coming and going possess the perfection of subtle consciousness.
By nature they are thus, and the wisdom of the Dharma brings great benefit.
The four great elements are naturally so; this is the Infinite Perfection of Beginning and End.
Not perceiving self, person, or individual, nor the life-span—the root of all conditioned phenomena—is the Infinite Perfection of Formlessness, wherein the single mark is without marks.
Countless Buddha-fields, Adorned as Buddha-places of enlightenment,
Radiating the light of the Buddhas— The Immeasurable Excellence of the Dharma Jewel.
With a mind gathered and free from distraction, Forever eliminating the three poisons of the heart.
Equanimity without variation is the perfection of sincerity and faith;
Dependent consciousness proceeds through the five realms, unable to unravel its fetters and attachments;
To uproot the source of suffering is the perfection of remoteness.
Though dwelling within the womb, he is not defiled by desire;
forever free from lust, anger, and delusion, he possesses the liberation that is the *pāramitā*.
The Buddha-dharma is profoundly subtle and wondrous; his spiritual power transcends the three realms.
Manifesting forms within the five turbidities is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, when encountering suffering or joy, one does not give rise to a mind of increase or decrease;
maintaining the will like empty space is the boundless perfection of non-limitation (*anantapāramitā*).
The Way does not arise from emptiness, nor does it depart from the human mind;
its manifestations fill all of space—this is the *apramāṇa* of Extinction.
Not perceiving self, person, or other, yet not destroying the fundamental mark of non-existence.
Attaining perfect enlightenment in a single practice is the *apramāṇa* of observing the world;
neither arising nor ceasing, with no root of birth and death,
one goes from this shore to the other shore— this is the *apramāṇa* of transcendence.
The root of all suffering has no form; fundamental wisdom arises from its objects.
The mind-consciousness cannot be destroyed—this is the *māyācaryāpāramitā* (Perfection of Illusory Practice).
There are two roots of illusion: the illusion of practice and the illusion of profound wisdom.
Being able to understand this illusory dharma is the perfection of non-doubt;
Wisdom-illusion transcends the three realms, and the illusion of practice is likewise so.
The purity of the Eightfold Noble Path is the perfection of the factors of enlightenment.
The world is an illusion and not real; the noble sages are untainted by attachment, while the foolish harbor notions of permanence—this is the perfection of universal wisdom.
Beyond the six sense objects are the six sense bases; these twelve factors are bound together in mutual dependence.
Name-and-form arises from contact; this is the perfection of perception.
Volitional formations arise from delusion; they flow and race through countless thoughts.
If one contemplates their formal nature, this is the perfection of completeness.
Space is boundless, and no traces of its movement can be seen;
yet one may find the shore of birth and death, naturally attaining the Infinite.
Human lifespans vary in length, whether in this world or in future lives.
Only the Way is tranquil and secure; in this tranquility, one transcends to the infinite.
Each within the dharma-realm has its own nature, yet no place of reception or entry is seen.
Without dependence, one cannot be defiled; in this absence of longing, one transcends to the infinite.
The Buddha-lands are infinite in number; The wisdom of the Dharma is inconceivable.
The ocean of insight is immeasurable; This is the perfection of receptivity.
Human wisdom neither increases nor decreases; The conduct of the worthy and sages is equal.
Discerning emptiness without [clinging to] wisdom is the perfection of the aggregates (skandha-pāramitā).
Having practiced asceticism for immeasurable eons since beginningless time,
without reckoning the duration of kalpas, is the perfection of tranquility (viveka-pāramitā).
Mindful while dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, he expounded the formless Dharma and guided immeasurable beings; this is his second *apramāṇa*.
He does not rejoice in the presence of pleasure, nor does he grieve when abiding in suffering.
Realizing the path through the vision of the truths is the perfection of reality;
Descending his spirit within Jambudvīpa and turning the Dharma at Rṣipatana,
Completely abandoning worldly defilements is the perfection of severing all longing.
The Bodhisattva’s practice is perfected; unattached to the six defiling objects, he studies the profoundly deep Dharma—this is the firmness of his *pāramitā*.
With wisdom, skillful means, and expedient methods, he penetrates deeply without obstruction.
Discriminating immeasurable bodies, one reaches the perfection of wherever one delivers beings.
Valiantly transcending immeasurable kalpas, one exhausts the root of birth and death;
Adorning the purity of Buddha-lands, one reaches the perfection of subtle wonder.
If a person can believe in the source, they will not be obstructed by birth and death;
with a correct mind free from distracted thoughts, this single thought is the *apramāṇa* of crossing over.
When practicing giving, one does not perceive the act of giving, nor does one harbor thoughts of coming or going.
Contemplating all things as empty space is the perfection of non-attachment;
Contemplating the world as not being a world, yet seeing no suffering in the three evil realms,
Saving oneself and saving others through great compassion is the perfection of great kindness.
When he sees beings of various kinds, stained by attachment within the three realms of existence, he exhorts them with the True Teaching; this is the Great Compassion that is Infinite.
Wandering through immeasurable worlds, he maintains faith as steadfast as Mount Sumeru.
With a serene countenance and constant single-mindedness, one attains the *pāramitā* of joy;
when a bodhisattva first resolves their mind, they do not act for the sake of a single person,
but provide vast salvation without limit, thereby attaining the *pāramitā* of relinquishment.
When I was first born, the Buddha-field was the color of gold, adorning the site of enlightenment;
this is the infinite excellence of spiritual resonance.
I do not extinguish the perception of names and concepts, nor do I cling to the notion of a life span.
Emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—these are the gates of the senses, the *pāramitās*.
Originating from the wisdom of equality, one now attains perfect enlightenment;
not abandoning the adamantine mind, these are the three contemplations, the *pāramitās*.
Diligent in the Way and its virtue, constantly practicing walking meditation day and night, expounding the Dharma and its meaning—this is the perfection of progress.
Contentment is the foremost path; relinquishing worldly thoughts, one has no craving.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the perfection of the unconditioned.
The Bodhisattva’s buddha-field is pure, and his lineage is free from confusion;
Always being born into a truly noble family is the perfection of the aristocratic clan.
Descending his spirit into the mother’s womb, he manifested the form of an infant;
with a mind held pure and stainless, this was the perfection of transformation.
Having emerged from the mother’s womb, he took seven steps as soon as he lifted his feet.
Fully traversing seven *koṭis*, he manifests the Perfection of Manifestation;
Ever remaining upon the golden stand, he appears to bathe with scented water;
Innumerable Buddhas assemble, exhorting him toward progress—this is the Perfection of Exhortation.
Endowed with the thirty-two marks and adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, the earth and heavens trembled in six ways; such is the perfection of physical appearance.
Though all dharmas are formless, he manifests through the dharma of physical forms.
Walking alone without companion, the Most Honored One’s *pāramitā* of Deliverance;
contemplating each and every dharma-realm, never failing his original essential vow,
regarding all dharmas as if deaf, the Silent One’s *pāramitā*.
The noble eightfold path, the practices of tranquility and insight, and the practice of non-conceptualization—
never abandoning emptiness and wisdom— is the single entry into the perfection of liberation.
Constantly employing the Dharma of the wondrous Way, he expounds and transmits all the various gateways of the Dharma.
Exhorting all people, the Dharma-sound reaches the infinite;
The ten wholesome deeds are the root of all practices, Unattached and incapable of being defiled.
Cultivating one, one attains completion; Non-retrogression reaches the infinite.
Worldlings harbor stinginess and greed, dwelling forever in the dark realm;
one should guide them with immeasurable dharmas, practicing the perfection of learning.
The Tathāgata is free from attachment, receiving the Dharma without ever abandoning it.
Forever departing from the abodes of sentient beings, he attains the *apramāṇa* of solitary deliverance.
Though dwelling in his father the King’s palace, he remains in silent contemplation of the Way;
not craving the pleasures of the five desires, he attains the *apramāṇa* of freedom from defilement.
Contemplating the body as dry tree bark, And like long-decayed ashes,
observing for oneself that it lacks consciousness— This is the *anilambha-apramāṇa* (the infinite of exhalation).
Counting one without departing from one, Stilling and contemplating are the fundamental practices and vows.
The intent lies right before one’s eyes; this is the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
People have long dwelt within birth and death, failing to reckon that both the root and the branches are empty.
To be able to relinquish them and not dwell with them is the Perfection of Total Retention (Dhāraṇīpāramitā).
Thus one attains the four analytical knowledges, the swift wisdom of Dharma and its meaning,
and proclaims immeasurable truths, responding appropriately with boundless skill.
Innumerable great sages assemble, hearing the Dharma without ever wearying.
The universal penetration of great wisdom is the perfection of equanimity;
even if one were to exhaust the countless eons of formation and destruction,
the Tathāgatagarbha remains inexhaustible— this is the perfection of detachment.
Whether in one lifetime or a hundred thousand lifetimes, there has never been anyone like those who seek to exhaustively fathom the virtues of the Tathāgata—
those whose practice is vast and reaches the infinite.
Even if space had a limit, and Mount Sumeru could be weighed, [the virtues of the Buddha would remain beyond measure].
How could there be a Great Teacher, Whose measure is limitless and boundless?
Throughout incalculable eons, He has accumulated all roots of virtue;
His practice is complete and no more is created— This is the perfection of the flow of liberation.
The Hero of the World’s compassionate canopy is universal, Its moisture reaches all classes of sentient beings;
Hearing the Dharma without doubt or stagnation, This is the perfection of faith and understanding.
Courageous and surpassing all others, Without any inferiority complex,
Subduing the hosts of Māra, this is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
In the past, I made a vow; not begrudging my own body or life, I alone emerged [from the womb], this is the perfection of the adamantine (vajra-pāramitā).
If there were doubt in the interim, one would not achieve supreme perfect enlightenment;
yet having accumulated immeasurable merit, the Honored One among Men attained the Infinite.
Only then was the Way profound and subtle, and the Treasury of Dharma inconceivable.
Transcending the manifestations of the three realms of existence is the perfection of maturation;
The single characteristic being invisible, such is the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*);
Abandoning the root to follow the branches is the perfection of non-obstruction.
Awakening spontaneously without being taught, possessing all-knowledge without a teacher,
uniquely virtuous and free from anxiety, he is blameless and has reached the ultimate limit.
He has destroyed the sixty-two views and the various nets of craving and desire.
Closing the gates of birth and death, one attains the infinity of blissful liberation.
Quieting the mind and extinguishing its own volitions, one harbors no defiled thoughts;
holding the mind as steadfast as the great ocean, one attains the infinity of non-transgression.
Contemplating the body as an enemy, with all its orifices flowing with impurity, one discerns internal and external phenomena;
this is the perfection of understanding the fundamental.
In the space of a single thought-moment, the mind rushes about, impossible to restrain.
Reaching the place beneath the King of Trees, his great vows are the *apramāṇa* of deliverance.
His practice of the Dharma is like the lotus flower; he constantly teaches by means of the three vehicles.
Though dwelling therein, he is unstained and unattached; this is the *apramāṇa* of single-mindedness.
With an even mind like the Great Way, forever eliminate the narrow-minded heart;
when the thirty-three dharmas are exhausted, one attains the Immaculate Perfection.
A person should seek the essential way out, discerning the internal and external dharmas.
Contemplating without abandoning [the practice] is the Perfection of Vigor;
observing the body as one observes dharmas, and the coming together and dispersal of the five aggregates,
like a person looking at a jewel in the palm of their hand, is the Perfection of Truth.
Shattering the defilements of the four māras, Crushing the mountain of arrogance,
The fire of wisdom incinerates the three poisons— This is the perfection of relinquishment.
If you all have any doubts, Each of you should proclaim your own original account.
With the light of wisdom, he illuminates; this is the *pāramitā* of radiance.
The various marks beneath his feet are luminous, and the patterns of the seals appear brilliantly clear;
all who behold these marks receive his grace—this is the *pāramitā* of benevolence.
His calves are like vajras, appearing luminous both within and without;
his feet stand firm without leaning, and his majesty is infinite.
His skin is exceedingly soft and fine, like a red lotus that remains unstained by water.
Each and every mark of excellence is complete; this is the perfection of conduct.
When I lift my foot to enter the city for alms, bestowing blessings regardless of whether one is poor or wealthy; this is the perfection of non-discrimination.
Having completed his alms-round everywhere, he returns to his quiet chamber;
delighting in the Dharma by himself, he contemplates the *apramāṇa* of deliverance.
Day and night he constantly practices walking meditation, observing who should be delivered first.
Not transgressing one’s original great vow is the *pāramitā* of purity.
Therefore, one constantly cultivates oneself, does not contend with worldly affairs, and detaches from both self and others;
this is the *pāramitā* of detachment from the realms of rebirth.
The four great elements each have their own nature, And their heights and depths are likewise different;
Through the discernment of the consciousness-spirit, This is the Dharma-meaning *pāramitā*.
The Bodhisattva contemplates emptiness for himself, Examining it without missing even the most subtle detail.
Guarding against all evil karma is the perfection of wisdom-vision;
Contemplating all buddha-fields without giving rise to notions of suffering or pleasure is the perfection of the profound understanding of all phenomena;
Understanding the extreme profundity of all dharmas is the perfection of wholesome qualities.
One may advance and know that one advances, yet harbor no doubt;
the essential exit has but one path—this is the *vimala-dhāraṇī* (the Perfection of Emptiness and Quiescence).
One thoroughly observes the root of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and the retribution received is likewise pure.
Seeking no meritorious karma, one forgets the Perfection of Giving;
The past does not arise again, and the future cannot be seen;
The present is the nature of things—this is the Perfection of Aspiration.
Nirvāṇa has no intrinsic nature, nor is there any place of entry;
by contemplating the retribution of all dharmas of sensation, one knows the perfection of the fundamental [wisdom].
With the mind stilled in samādhi, one is forever parted from a distracted mind.
Impermanence, suffering, and non-self—these are the practices of the *pāramitās*.
Observing phenomena as they truly are, one knows that the One is immovable;
not destroying the fundamental mind of phenomena is the *pāramitā* of spontaneity.
Fully knowing that all phenomena lack self, they do not perceive birth in any successive arising;
turning the wheels of Dharma in their practice, they exercise the boundless liberation of vast salvation.
They are able to extinguish the nature of all phenomena, yet they do not even seek personal liberation.
Truly and faithfully traversing the five realms of existence is the perfection of exhausting all births;
the Tathāgata’s most secret practice is such that his mind, intellect, and consciousness are likewise so—
attaining the mind of non-arising is the perfection of thorough realization.
When I reckon my original practice, Abiding for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, My meritorious labors were naturally manifest; The traces of my conduct are the Infinite Practice.
That which life and death originally proceed from Is like an illusion, devoid of reality.
Quiescence is undefiled; this is the *gocara-viśuddha* (Purity of Sphere) *pāramitā*.
The twelve categories of the noble ones all return to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
Non-arising is eternally non-arisen; this is the *caryā-viśeṣa* (Excellence of Practice) *pāramitā*.
Recalling how in the past, in the Fragrant Grove, he sat upright contemplating the Way,
his body neither leaning nor slumping— this was the *dhyāna-pāramitā* of the first dhyāna. Furthermore,
originally at the Lion’s Wide and Universal Lecture Hall, he sat thus.
Guarded by the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought, he attained the *pāramitā* of the Second Dhyāna.
Furthermore, during this Bhadrakalpa, within the Great City that Protects the Dharma,
he concealed himself to seek the Way of the Teachings, thereby attaining the *pāramitā* of the Third Dhyāna.
Now, at this very seat, you extensively expound immeasurable dharmas;
with no obstruction internally or externally, you have reached the perfection of the four dhyānas.
In practicing the Way, you remain untainted, giving rise to no manifold thoughts.
Therefore, he causes one to attain the state of honor; this is the Perfection of Transcending the World.
Like the sun first emitting its light, it enables people to see for themselves;
now I expound the Way and its teachings, manifesting the Perfection of Illumination.
Innumerable asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable Tathāgatas,
each and every one spreading the path of the Dharma, possess the perfection of non-arising.
Even if hundreds of thousands of millions of the seven treasures were to fill the world-realm, [it would not equal this].
It is not equal to a single moment of focused thought; this single-mindedness is the *apramāṇa* (infinite) practice.
Neither arising nor ceasing, one knows the origin from which all things come;
having understood and realized the contemplation of the three periods of time, this is the *apramāṇa* practice of the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*).
If one can honor the root of wisdom, following the sequence without overstepping its order,
practicing the Way with a single-minded resolve, this is the *practicing the Way without dualistic mind* (mārga-bhāvanā-advaya-citta) *paramita*.
With inconceivable great compassion, universally rescuing the multitudes of sentient beings, this is the *inconceivable great compassion* (*mahāmaitrī-acintya*) *paramita*.
The lion’s single thunderous roar, universally heard, is the perfection of liberation;
All classes of sentient beings who believe and delight in the dharma of emptiness,
Following principle without transgression, constitute the perfection of practice.
Cultivating the six profound dharmas within, delighting in stillness and not dwelling in clamor, one recognizes the conduct of past lives; this is the perfection of knowing the origin.
Regarding the portion of conception in this present life, one diligently practices to bring desire to extinction.
Once the life-faculty and consciousness are lost, there is the perfection of receiving the prediction of enlightenment.
All dharmas are without disturbance; practicing the pure and white dharmas, one contemplates birth as being fundamentally free from birth—this is the perfection of being without basis.

When humans wander through the depths of the five realms of existence, it is like a river rushing toward the great ocean—swift and surging, never to return; thus they turn toward the Infinite Deliverance (pāramitā).
Constantly mindful of the suffering of the world, they contemplate detachment and do not remain joined with it.
Departing alone without harboring sorrow, this is the *apratihata-gati-pāramitā* (the perfection of unimpeded passage).
Just as when various seeds are sown—rice, hemp, and various flowers and fruits—the original seed is not what produces the sprout;
this is the *pariṇāma-gati-pāramitā* (the perfection of transformation).
If one does not study the Way during life, there will be regret at the moment of death;
desiring liberation, do not be indolent—study the Perfection of Progress.
If you wish to uproot the fundamental, do not plant its consciousness again.
This exhaustion is unsurpassed; it is the *gandhavāsanā-pāramitā*.
Contemplating all worldly phenomena as entirely empty and non-existent, one should contemplate these as non-dharmas; this is the *akṣobhya-pāramitā*.
Exhorting and assisting in all meritorious deeds, Each and every one is without obstruction;
Ascending the throne of the ten stages of practice, This is the *ekajātipratibaddha* (one-life) *pāramitā*.
Thoroughly observing all dharma-gates, One maintains total retention (*dhāraṇī*) without forgetfulness.
Corresponding with all dharma-realms, one attains the perfection of severing the fetters.
If one wishes to roam through space, possessing unimpeded supernormal powers,
and is free from the notions of self and other, one practices the perfection of cultivation.
Contemplating each and every dharma, Leaping lightly without obstruction,
Measuring space with the body— This is the perfection of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Observing the fundamental nature of persons as they truly are, Acting according to the Way without transgression—
Not associating with a mind of dualistic views is the perfection of right concentration;
like observing the reflection of one’s face in a mirror, once faith is free from blemish,
the afflictions naturally perish— this is the perfection of the hundred blessings.
Long-cherished vows are inexhaustible; through the accumulation of practice, they are now attained.
Sincerity and faith are like the rising sun; the selection of the Dharma is boundless.
With diligent mindfulness, one enters the profound essentials; one searches for and seeks the immeasurable teachings.
With a mind of humble and lowly reverence, one attains the perfection of firmness.
The Bodhisattva possesses eight dharmas; by practicing them, they reach the site of enlightenment.
Understanding wisdom without clinging to emptiness is the perfection of non-conceptualization.
If one wishes to rely on the wisdom of emptiness, knowing that emptiness is not a substantial reality,
and that the essence of wisdom knows the three obstructions— this is the Perfection of the Characteristic of Emptiness.
There is a dharma called the "Battle Array," which is the fearless samādhi of vigorous exertion.
Nor does one harbor cowardice; this is the perfection of manifold wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Causes and conditions arise from one another; birth and death are the very root of the Way.
These two matters are inseparable; this is the perfection of uprooting suffering (*duḥkhoddhāra-pāramitā*).
A single lifetime is not the fundamental root, nor do sentient beings possess such roots;
when the consciousness and spirit become defiled by attachment, it is called the "Infinite Deliverance through Provisional Designation.
The True Way has no form or substance; it is subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable.
The Way is truly not a "Way," which is the *cankrama-vikṣepa-aparimita*.
Contemplating the purity of all Buddha-lands, which are stainless and free from defilement,
and always employing the Path of Equanimity, is the *abhijñā-aparimita*.
The Bodhisattva constantly observes, Not clinging to phenomena of form and appearance;
Knowing that birth involves the transmigration through the five realms, This is the Perfection of Namelessness (Anāmakatā-pāramitā).
Or there may be one who cultivates a single dharma, Transcending the surface of all practices.
Supreme spontaneous realization, the perfection of transcending stages;
Contemplating all people as empty, with a stilled mind free of thought,
Responding to all without defilement, the perfection of equanimity.
The Great Sage’s virtue is immeasurable; he is not defiled by worldly desires.
Having thoroughly exhausted the source of afflictions, his boundless deliverance is infinite.
Originally there are no five realms of existence; they arise only from the dust and grime of defilement.
The perception of illusion and transformation is the perfection of holy wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Entering into the characteristics of all phenomena is the practice cultivated by Bodhisattvas;
not seeing the root of all sufferings is the perfection of non-self (anātmapāramitā).
Nor does it reside within the span of kalpas; birth and death have no form or sign.
That which comes will not remain forever; this is the boundless speed of deliverance.
One discerns the four marks of impermanence: suffering, emptiness, and the non-self of the body.
Adorning oneself with wisdom is the perfection of cultivation;
Like a person wishing to travel through space, One attains the fruit by practicing dhyāna.
With a concentrated mind free from confusion, This is the perfection of resolve.
The mouth emits immeasurable sounds, yet does not violate the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
like the moon among the multitude of stars, this is the perfection of fruit (phala-pāramitā).
His supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda) are unfathomable, and his ocean of wisdom is like the sands of the Ganges.
Mastery in gathering through skillful means is the perfection of receptivity.
If one wishes to transform sentient beings, one enters meditative concentration to observe their minds;
first guiding them with skillful wisdom, one gradually manifests the perfection of deliverance.
The Buddha’s scriptures are beyond counting; only the Buddha can record them.
The characteristics of the mutual correspondence of all dharmas constitute the perfection of exhortation and joy.
Delivering all sentient beings, he does not limit himself by the distance of kalpas.
The True Way has neither male nor female; it follows the Single Practice to the Ultimate.
If one wishes to cultivate the Bodhisattva path, first purify body, speech, and mind.
Do not follow the ten unwholesome actions; this is the Fundamental Purity to the Ultimate.
With single-minded devotion to the Way of the Teachings, one forever leaves behind the activities of the realm of desire;
by not giving rise to conceptualizations in the interim, one attains the *apramāṇa* of extinguishing desire.
All dharmas are without names or titles, yet those who cling to form seek after merit and reward.
Form, too, is not originally non-existent; this is the perfection of detachment from form.
When a bodhisattva receives the prediction of enlightenment, it is the seal of approval from the Tathāgata;
having exhausted all conditioned activity and no longer creating further karma, this is the perfection of the position of the successor.
The finite and the infinite, and likewise the infinite itself;
arising yet not seeing arising—this is the perfection of severing the fetters.
Cessation and birth are not truly born, and non-birth is likewise so.
Knowing that arising is non-arising is the perfection of non-arising;
that there is no fundamental existence and that non-existence is likewise so—
understanding both existence and non-existence is the perfection of the single direction.
The one is fundamentally not one; the absence of one is likewise so.
The one is fundamentally without abiding; this is the Perfection of Namelessness.
Provisional designations emerge from original non-being; expedient means are not the ultimate reality.
Asaṅga returns to the extinction of cessation, Embracing the Way, he attains the *apramāṇa*.
Humanity fundamentally arises from the accumulation of practice;
Contemplating the world as an illusion or a transformation, He does not harbor manifold conceptions, Thus attaining the *apramāṇa* of severing traces.
Passing through all kalpas, one is uprooted and transcends the reckoning of kalpas;
not clinging to any sounds is the *apramāṇa* of soundlessness.
It is like a person’s eye beholding forms; form is fundamentally not an object of the eye.
Still perceiving the distinction between internal and external is the *apramāṇa* of non-perception (*asaṃjñā*).
Sound, fragrance, taste, touch, as well as mental objects (*dharma*), are likewise so;
that these perceptions are fundamentally non-existent is the *apramāṇa* of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Contemplating all phenomena as formless, Without the arising of sensation or contact, Fully endowed with dignified deportment and all practices— This is the perfection of the formation of deeds.
Originally there was no such birth; Yet craving and consciousness delight in this birth.
Taking birth according to physical form is the perfection of severing greed;
The spiritual consciousness is fundamentally formless, its nature naturally quiescent from the start;
Later, one undergoes the suffering of the six sense bases—severing these entrances is the perfection of severing the bases.
Mindful of leaving the abyss of the five realms, Contemplating the meditation on emptiness, He erects the great banner of the Dharma; This is the infinite excellence of Radiance.
Without conceptualization and without arising, He receives no teachings from a teacher.
Being able to awaken from within this state is the perfection of transcending stages.
All phenomena are like empty space; they do not fall within the category of thought or desire.
Fully understanding all sounds and echoes is the perfection of hearing the Dharma.
His voice is pure, wondrous, and excellent; what he speaks is without obstruction.
He does not give rise to the six sense-contacts; this is the *dharmaparyāya* of the Infinite.
All phenomena are immeasurable, yet the Tathāgata has completely transcended them.
The wisdom of the Path penetrates the three types of supernormal knowledge; this is the Perfection of Right Contemplation.
Manifesting as a teacher to receive the teachings, one harbors no thoughts of high or low;
with the mind transcending the three realms, this is the Perfection of Solitary Progression.
There is no practice, nor is any practice created; practice is fundamentally without causes or conditions.
When conditions are exhausted, there is no practice—this is the Infinite Power of Divine Virtue.
The three types of suffering arise from pleasure and pain; retribution follows its own law.
Neither suffering nor pleasure, the cessation of sensation is the *apramāṇa* of transcendence.
Accomplishing the seven contemplative practices, the three bases are naturally extinguished;
the aggregates and sense-bases no longer arise—this is the *apramāṇa* of the cessation of craving.

Investigating form, one finds it originally arises from emptiness; It gives rise to the conceptualization of all dharmas, yet it is not I who originally created them—this is the perfection of seeing correctly.
There is neither action nor retribution; Sitting upright, there is nothing to be thought of.
Contemplating until one spontaneously attains the Way is the Perfection of Constant Abiding;
Holding the will so it cannot be moved, serene as empty space,
Neither existent nor non-existent, is the Perfection of Extensive Practice.
Even when entering final nirvana, his concentrated mind remains undisturbed;
he does not harbor thoughts of permanence, yet he extensively practices the *pāramitā* of deliverance.
He turns the Dharma without a notion of "Dharma," let alone a person who receives it.
Understanding that all things are entirely empty and quiescent is the perfection of knowing the proper time.
His voice fills the entire world as he proclaims the sounds of the wondrous Dharma;
since the essence of sound is originally unborn, this is the perfection of the absence of sound.
Guarding the body and protecting the speech, Let the mind not dwell on what is wrong or perverse;
Not being in opposition to the Way, This is the perfection of non-hatred.
Contemplating all realms of phenomena, Without destroying the practice of the Wheel of Dharma— This is the perfection of non-hatred.
Fully possessing the nine successive stages is the perfection of the Dharma-realm;
Fearlessness is inexhaustible, without interior or exterior, near or far.
Transcending the four types of sensation is the immeasurable perfection.
Not destroying the nature of form and color, nor being conjoined with them;
not subverting the natural marks—this is the perfection of conjunction (*saṃprayoga-pāramitā*).
The Path of Practice is fundamentally non-dual, profoundly deep and immeasurable.
Adapting to the root causes for transformation, according to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
For those who wish to understand the Dharma, there is the manifestation of the Dharma with its objective sphere;
thus they are able to trace back to the root cause, which is the perfection of inexhaustibility (akṣayapāramitā).

Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, he teaches and transforms all classes of sentient beings, desiring that they all achieve fulfillment; this is the *upāya-pāramitā* (Perfection of Skillful Means).
Manifesting skillful means according to the occasion, he remains unstained by the three realms of existence.
Uprooting and severing all the veils of the aggregates, one attains the perfection of equanimous wisdom.
Mastering the gateways of all dharmas and not losing the root of right practice, one does not praise oneself; this is the perfection of fulfillment.
Phenomena that arise do not truly arise; phenomena that cease do not truly cease.
To know that arising and ceasing are fundamentally non-existent is the Perfection of the Echo in Emptiness.
Just as the voice of a person, so too are the teachings spoken by the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
All returns to emptiness and nothingness; this is the perfection of reality (*tattva-pāramitā*).
The faculties are not confused; guarding mindfulness and possessing all marks, one returns to the fundamental non-being through purity;
this is the perfection of the wisdom of the Way (*mārga-jñatā-pāramitā*).
Beings are bound by immeasurable fetters, which nothing else can destroy;
yet they naturally attain the penetration of the sages—this is the perfection of transformation and birth.
The Tathāgata, the Most Perfectly Awakened One, profoundly discerns the dharmas of the past.
Spontaneously transforming in various ways, this is the *gambhīra-guhya-pāramitā* (Perfection of the Profound Secret).
Regarding the source of future births, where suffering is immeasurable,
employing skillful means to sever the future and bring the root to exhaustion is the *mūla-kṣaya-pāramitā* (Perfection of the Exhaustion of the Root).
Presently practicing immeasurable deeds, the sentient beings are beyond measure;
manifesting in accordance with their forms to transform and guide them, the purification of lands is infinite.
When one preaches this chapter on the Dharma-gate, its merit and blessings shall never be exhausted.
Not hoping for rewards of merit or fortune, this is the *apramāṇa* of the Bodhi-tree;
The divine feet have their foundation in practice, and the teachings proclaimed are not uniform;
Manifesting the Dharma with its variations of increase and decrease, this is the *apramāṇa* of universal circulation.
Immeasurable wisdom is unimpeded; what is taught is without deficiency.
The resolve for the Way is profoundly firm; this is the infinite practice of eloquent exposition.
The Buddha-dharma has no dual characteristics; it exists solely in the purity of body and mind.
The sphere of phenomena is without attachment; it is the perfection of non-abiding.
Though one may attain the supernormal powers, not practicing the methods of calculation is the perfection of coming.
When practice is completed yet not fully perfected, it is not the perfection of coming.
In reality, there is no single entity, nor is there any notion of multiplicity;
by exhausting all conditioned formations, one attains oneness—this is the perfection of making offerings.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained mastery over all phenomena.
Attaining mastery over emanation bodies, he reaches the ultimate of dharma-to-dharma deliverance.

Having known the incalculable past and the immeasurable kalpas that are difficult to reckon, his teaching exhausts itself only to flow forth again in transformation; thus he attains the ultimate of unhurried deliverance.
In future incalculable eons, knowing that the diligent efforts of immeasurable classes of sentient beings will not be in vain,
he universally receives and delivers them through the perfection of universal reception.
He observes the various kinds of past immeasurable Buddhas.
It is also taught that the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is the perfection of non-reliance;
Reality is neither originally real, nor does reality arise spontaneously,
nor is reality eternally abiding— this is the perfection of the transformation of the body.
The Dharma of the Path of Characters: In one's conduct, there is no doubt or difficulty;
Not doubting the suffering of the three periods of time, This is the Infinite of the Body’s Original Deliverance.
Not calculating the original non-existence of dharmas, Wisdom arises from the immeasurable.
Contemplating that all worlds are but delusion is the perfection of teaching;
from the first moment of generating the resolve, one constantly pities the classes of sentient beings,
not dwelling in cities or towns, which is the perfection of detachment from the multitude.
Discerning the limbs and joints of the body, And the various impurities of its physical form, One understands that it is fundamentally formless; This is the perfection of non-attachment.
The nature of phenomena is not permanent, Nor does it belong to this world or the next.
Not attaining the fruit apart from the Dharma is the *apramāṇa* of the future;
Nor abiding in the same place, with paths each distinct,
yet all returning to *nirvāṇa*, is the *apramāṇa* of equanimity.
True emptiness cannot be abandoned; how much less so the absence of true emptiness?
Through the power of mindfulness of the good and diligent study, one reaches the Perfection of Skillful Means.
Possessing all marks, they are fundamentally non-existent as a single form.
The Dharma is attained through the wisdom of emptiness; this is the perfection of self-arising.
Recalling the Buddha Abhaya from the beginning, and the Honored One Sugata until the end of life, thereby one now attains Buddhahood; this is the perfection of establishing the resolve.
Though his physical form was subjected to slander, he was not bowed down by honor or disgrace;
thus he is called the Honored One among Men—this is the Infinite of Restraining the Mind.
Before receiving the wisdom of original non-existence, the resolve for the Way may still shift and change.
Manifesting light throughout the world, he has set forth the *cintā-viśuddhi-pāramitā*.
There are four grades of *parinirvāṇa*, all of which stem from the root of the three poisons;
being named the Honored One among Men, he has attained the *jāti-viśuddhi-pāramitā*.

The Way likewise has three aspects; as the fundamental nature of True Suchness (tathatā), one attains the three rewards in the present, thereby accomplishing the Perfection of Deliverance (dāna-pāramitā).
Regarding the Tathāgata’s true Dharma, there is none who can protect and uphold it.
Discerning that the body is empty from its origin is the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.
Attaining the supernormal powers that are unfathomable, with both mind and form abiding thus,
Refining the path to remove the defilements of the mind is the *gati-āgati-pāramitā*.
Fundamentally there is no mind or intent; it arises spontaneously and ceases naturally.
I, too, was originally non-existent; this is the *śūnyatā-śānti-aparimita*.
The Buddha does not depend on the three periods of time, nor upon the path of the future or the present.
Transforming and shifting without constant rest, the *śīghratā-aparimita* (Infinite Speed) is reached.
The characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) dwell eternally in themselves, while the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*) flows on;
neither a land nor possessing a land, the *praśama-jñāna-aparimita* (Infinite Tranquility of Wisdom) is reached.
The dharmas of the body have six modes; they are not created by the mind of non-conception.
The thirty-seven practices of asceticism constitute the proclamation of the *pāramitās*.
These were not created by me; for them, I have preached impermanence and emptiness.
The manifestation of all Buddha-dharmas is the *loka-dhātu-pāramitā*.
Divine wisdom and the broad, long tongue, whereby what is spoken accords with the teaching, are accomplished through merit; this is the *citta-prativedha-pāramitā*.
Generosity, knowing gratitude and righteousness, and being careful not to harbor expectations;
protecting oneself through the Way alone—this is the perfection of the present dharma.
The profound meaning of the Dharma practiced on the Path, the supernormal powers, liberation, and meditative concentration—these constitute the perfections.
Transforming according to the times through skillful means, this is the *apramāṇa* of manifold virtues.
Contemplating the Dharma-body as a desire-body is not the most ultimate reality;
attaining that nature of *nirvāṇa* is the *apramāṇa* of extinguishing form.
Adapting to circumstances to transform others before them, Never yielding to the dust of worldly toil;
Through extraordinary and marvelous transformations, The Infinite of Subduing and Delivering.
From the beginning, there was no need for arduous suffering; His creative power cannot be matched.
The body of precepts is naturally complete; this is the perfection of virtue.
With faith directed toward the Triple Gem, one remains humble and does not exalt oneself;
Reaching the root and exhausting suffering, this is the perfection of removing delusion.
Discriminating consciousness and all forms of wisdom, He does not cling to the dharma of a self;
Naturally attaining holy penetration, He personally reaches the perfection of deliverance.
He proclaims and elucidates the twelve links of dependent origination, Discerning and distinguishing each one.
Using the three medicines to eliminate the three cravings is the perfection of restraint in speech.
Manifesting transformations throughout all lands and expounding the wisdom of emptiness,
yet remaining unattached to the body, is the perfection of observing sentient beings.
Delivering people as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Dharma they hear is immeasurable;
wandering through the realms of empty space, they attain the equality of the boundless and the measureless.
Delivering through the non-arising of the eight worldly dharmas, their skillful means illumine all things.
Not perceiving the characteristics of all phenomena is the perfection of constant dharma;
Wisdom being unimpeded in all things is the perfection of cultivation that removes further craving;
The spirit returning to the Great Way is the perfection of the gate of direction.
The total retention consists of ten matters; body, speech, and mind are the foundation.
By eliminating the ten and accomplishing the ten, one attains the *pāramitā* of retribution.
Able to manifest supreme wisdom for the sake of all classes of sentient beings, [one fulfills this practice].
Virtue surpassing the manifestations of all sages, The perfection of transcending suffering;
Pure, empty, and formless, Not perceiving even the path of perfect awakening—
Leading beings toward liberation, The perfection of the path’s progression.
Even if one were to reverently serve sages and saints for a hundred kalpas,
it would not equal the "Infinite Compassion of Bestowing the One Path's Foundation.
When I first received my prediction of enlightenment in the past, I first attained the wisdom of non-arising.
Like the passage through kalpas, it is the perfection of the wisdom of emptiness.
The original aspiration for perfect enlightenment accomplishes the basis of the ten titles;
having attained that which was sought, it is the perfection of the bridge.
His holy virtue surpasses that of heaven; his radiance is boundless.
Through profound transformation he delivers sentient beings; his pure grace is infinitely vast.
Though he teaches while remaining amidst the secular world, his solemn instructions are as they were vowed.
Extensively proclaiming immeasurable jewels, this is the *apramāṇa-dāna* (immeasurable giving) of the time;
If one does not contemplate the world, its impermanence and various transformations,
yet their lifespan accumulates immeasurably, this is the *kalpa-sthiti-apramāṇa* (immeasurable abiding through kalpas).
According to what I have experienced, and what I now behold for myself, I feel weary of this body of the five aggregates; this is the *pāramitā* of pure contemplation.
Though I desire to seek *nirvāṇa*, I eliminate all attachments and perceptions of the body.
Meditating on the present concentration is the perfection of non-transgression;
The eighteen fundamental dhāraṇī-dharmas, Mindfulness of cessation and entering the dharma of conditions—
For one who does not give rise to deluded thoughts, this is the perfection of auspicious medicine.
The Dharma of Receiving has three meanings: To take exclusive charge of one’s own body, speech, and mind;
To sever seeking and not dwell on emptiness—this is the perfection of penetration.
To discern each and every part of the body, And likewise for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Entering meditative concentration to contemplate all perceptions is the boundless *pāramitā*.
The inexhaustible treasury of all Buddhas produces immeasurable concentrations;
universally observing all realms is the ultimate *pāramitā*.
The constant deportment of all Buddhas, Cultivating the precepts as supreme,
With the dharma of dignified composure in coming and going, Is the perfection of mental restraint.
If one desires to produce a spiritual response, One must first enter meditative concentration.
Thoroughly knowing that both the root and the branches are empty is the perfection of equanimity (*samatā-pāramitā*).
That which the Buddha originally practiced— contemplating the body as having nothing to crave,
thereby benefiting oneself and others— is the perfection of the limit of conduct (*caryā-pāramitā*).
Observing phenomena before and after, one transcends the realms of existence and non-existence;
with mastery over all conceptualizations, they are stilled—this is the *apramāṇa* of manifold teachings.
Regarding the body and its phenomena, there are three matters: not committing killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct.
Diligently seeking the Dharma-realm is the perfection of fundamental practice;
Not committing the four verbal transgressions and not speaking falsely,
Protecting oneself and protecting others is the perfection of equal enlightenment.
When the mind and dharmas possess these three qualities, one does not give rise to various distracted thoughts;
attaining the dwelling place of the Buddhas is the perfection of steadfastness.
Having originally come from the equality of space, one brings transformation and instruction to fill the entire world.
Severing seeking and not clinging to emptiness is the perfection of reality as it is.

Conduct arises from the three periods of time; bound by the defilements of craving and desire, one realizes the dharma of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), thereby accomplishing the perfection of vows.
With the wisdom of the three penetrations and five superknowledges, he moves everywhere without hindrance;
purifying buddha-fields and transforming sentient beings, his practice of the liberation of consciousness is infinite.
Originally non-existent, there is existence today; yet this existence is not born from the original state.
Conditioned by formations, suffering and pleasure arise; this is the perfection of the transcendence of conditions.
Fundamental awakening is inconceivable, manifesting transformations beyond measure;
the divided bodies return to unity—this is the perfection of divine wisdom.
Neither abiding in this nor in that, nor dwelling in the dharma-realm, one contemplates the body as being without a body; such is the perfection of action (karma-pāramitā).
Attachment gives rise to the immeasurable, and through conditions, it leads to birth, old age, and sickness.
Both internal and external are entirely empty and quiescent; this is the perfection of non-self.
Fundamentally arising from the wisdom of equality, one perceives no coming or going;
understanding that the three [realms] are devoid of the three [characteristics], this is the perfection of equanimity.
The three practices have three aspects: vitarka and vicāra, and the absence of vitarka;
they advance along the path to Nirvāṇa, manifesting the perfection of universal manifestation.
Through the seeds of all dharmas within vitarka and vicāra, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are produced.
Advancing upon the path to Nirvāṇa is the perfection of peace and security;
The dharma of non-learner’s investigation and analysis likewise perceives neither arising nor ceasing;
Moving with mastery whether sitting or reclining is the perfection of non-arising.
Observing persons, there is nothing to be observed; one does not see a master of dharmas.
In actual activity, there is neither arising nor ceasing—this is the immeasurable *pāramitā*.
Human beings encounter manifold sufferings and pass through countless bodies.
Wishing to extinguish these manifold difficulties, one practices the *pāramitā* of cultivation;
having received this body of the four great elements, wishing to extinguish them yet finding no means,
one uses wisdom to reach full observation and cuts off desire— this is the *pāramitā* of severing desire.
The full maturity of all phenomena purifies the karma of all meritorious deeds;
by accumulating these, one attains Buddhahood—this is the perfection of purification.
Fulfilling the aspirations of sentient beings, it causes each to achieve their realization.
All things return to cessation; this is the perfection of the prohibitive precepts.
In the places where the Buddha teaches and transforms, he takes emptiness as the fundamental basis;
preaching non-existence and the non-perception of existence, this is the perfection of joy.
If there are sentient beings who wish to cultivate the five virtuous practices, they should gather together immeasurable dharmas; this is the perfection of wisdom.
They should cultivate the fivefold Dharma-body: precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Measure exhausted, there is no measure; this is the *Dharmapāramitā*.
From the beginning, there has been no birth; there is neither Buddha nor assembly.
Actions are fashioned through conditions; this is the *Svayambhūpāramitā*.
One shall undergo immeasurable suffering, with the manifold pains of birth and old age;
though formless, one enters the womb—this is the Perfection of Vigor.
The Buddhas constantly abide in meditative concentration, shedding tears for the sake of sentient beings.
The Dharma of the Three Grades and Six Perfections is the Infinite Reaching of Severing Expectations.
Cultivating the roots of all virtues, awakening the mind to enter various meditative concentrations,
and being able to remain detached from birth despite being born— this is the Infinite Reaching of the Characteristics of Consciousness.
His meritorious deeds exceed a billion kalpas; he clings not to any further worldly pleasures.
Mindful of the good, he cultivates the root of the Way; this is the infinity of detachment from dust.
Entering meditative concentration, he attains joy; his mind roams through immeasurable emptiness.
Distinguishing each and every characteristic of the assembly is the perfection of attaining the Way.
To possess the profound treasury of Dharma, one first cultivates emptiness and signlessness;
teaching and admonishing with the virtue of the divine feet is the perfection of purification.
The Tathāgata, with all-encompassing wisdom, knows that the beginning and end of humanity are empty;
for their sake, he preaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—this is the perfection of the fruit.
The Great Sage, the Honored One among men, provides vast instruction without limit.
The wisdom-action accomplishes the five dharmas; this is the perfection of the treasure casket.
The five actions accomplish the five elements; the five vows sever the five paths.
The five natures and the five bodies of manifestation; this is the perfection of the five actions.
If one can cultivate virtuous deeds, seeking the root where fundamentally no karma exists,
yet blazing forth the fruits of the various paths, this is the Infinite Radiance.
With the ten wisdoms and the path of the ten joys, the ten dharmas are all fully perfected.
The ten stages and the ten bases from which they arise, and the ten wondrous perfections (pāramitās).
With three thousand two hundred merits, each and every mark of excellence is fully possessed;
his countenance is peerlessly beautiful—this is the perfection of self-purification.
With compassion, he exhorts all beings, striving to bring them to the fruit of the Path;
through immeasurable virtues accumulated over countless eons, he attains the ultimate perfection of deliverance.
He establishes the root of all manifold virtues, yet perceives no self, person, or individual.
Therefore he is titled the Honored One among Men, With infinite and boundless deliverance.
The transformations effected through skillful means Are inconceivable in their ingenuity;
Revealing or concealing the Dharma according to the time, He exhausts all births—this is the perfection of deliverance.
The retribution of merit within the three realms does not distinguish between various kinsmen;
manifesting the majestic deportment and virtues of a Buddha, one achieves the *pāramitā* of deliverance.
I now proclaim this *ratna-avalambana*, the precious seal of all Buddhas.
Adorning the purity of the Buddha-lands is the *puṣpamālā-pāramitā*.
Those who receive and uphold this Dharma obtain twenty virtues of merit;
calculating the fullness of body, mind, and consciousness, they accomplish the *siddhi-pāramitā*.
The ears and eyes are naturally clear and bright; one naturally recognizes what has been experienced in the past.
Discernment and wisdom are penetrating and beneficial; this is the *pāramitā* of the knowledge of past lives.
One constantly beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions and receives this *dhāraṇī*.
Upon hearing the Dharma, one immediately attains understanding; this is the Perfection of the Essential Dharma.
What one says is trusted by others, and one is never subjected to slander;
the body is fully endowed with all its parts—this is the Perfection of the Fragrance of Precepts.
**Chapter 20: On Radiance (7)** *The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Chapter Twenty: On Radiance* At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the good sons and good daughters:

“If there be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who receives, maintains, recites, and chants the inconceivable dharma of the meaning of the phrases asked by the Most Honorable Great Brahmā Heavenly King, they shall immediately attain the Dharma-gate of the non-duality of bodily marks; their visual faculty shall become pure, and they shall attain mastery over the Dharma-realm.”

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter meditative absorption with a concentrated mind, they manifest mastery over the Dharma-realm from every single pore of their own bodies; they thus bring across and deliver sentient beings without end, never impairing the pure conduct of the Dharma-realm.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters this meditative concentration, they will be able to fully realize all dharmas and manifest all dharmas as being like illusions.
