They will be able to know the origins of all dharmas within the worlds, traveling from one buddha-field to another, even across countless billions of hundreds of thousands of eons, discerning the fundamental dispositions of the faculties of sentient beings in every detail.
Furthermore, they are able to contemplate proper deportment and etiquette, knowing when it is appropriate to sit and when it is appropriate to lie down.

Moreover, throughout that incalculable number of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, they discern the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*), the meaning of suffering (*duḥkha*), the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the meaning of formlessness. For their sake, they preach the contemplation of emptiness, the contemplation of namelessness, internal contemplation, external contemplation, the contemplation of non-sentient beings, and the contemplation of the pure and the impure; they practice the Mahāyāna path with equanimity and non-duality, advancing toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the stage of non-retrogression.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to resolve the doubts of those gathered there, immediately emitted light from the pores of all his limbs and joints while seated upon his throne, illuminating immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.
Among them, all sentient beings—whether flying, crawling, or moving, and all forms of living creatures—saw this light and came to recognize for themselves the fundamental laws of their past lives.

Furthermore, within that radiance, they heard these teachings on the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, and the meaning of formlessness; immediately in that eon, they saw the events of a hundred eons, knew the events of a thousand eons, knew the events of ten million eons, knew the events of ten billion eons, knew the events of infinite eons, knew the events of asaṃkhyeya eons, knew the events of immeasurable eons, knew the events of boundless eons, knew the events of incalculable eons, knew the events of limitless eons, knew the events of ineffable eons, knew the events of inconceivable eons, knew the events of unmeasurable eons, and knew the events of inexhaustible eons; furthermore, they knew the events of the arising and passing away of sentient beings throughout infinite, immeasurable, and incalculable Buddha-fields across all eons.
Furthermore, he beheld the rules of conduct, deportment, and etiquette practiced by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as they single-mindedly cultivated them without deviating from their original vows.

At that time, upon seeing this radiance, the Bodhisattva’s mind was opened and liberated; he then entered into a state of meditative concentration within the pores of his own body, whereupon he further beheld the fundamental practices cultivated over hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis* of eons by immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again arose from that samādhi and beheld the light of the Buddhas, no different from before.

Then, there was a bodhisattva named Jyotirvikhyāta (Illumination) who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have just witnessed the light from every pore and limb of the body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, which completely illuminates immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions, causing all sentient beings to recognize their own past lives and immeasurable worldly affairs; it also enables all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain mastery over spiritual powers and to enter the meditative concentration of the body’s pores and limbs, thereby knowing the past lives of sentient beings in the ten directions.
How extraordinary!
How unique! How inconceivable!
“I only pray, World-Honored One,
that if you would grant me leave to ask what I have in mind, I may then set forth my words.
At that time, the World-Honored One, already knowing his intention, addressed the Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha, saying:
"What you have asked is entirely within the realm of the Tathāgata.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!"
"Do you know what you have asked? He replied,
"It is so, World-Honored One!"
"The Tathāgata is the treasury of all dharmas; I pray that you will expound them fully so that there may be no further doubt.
The Buddha said, "Noble son!"

Regarding what you have just asked: the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat—the World-Honored One who is the Benefactor of the Multitudes—today emits light from all the joints of his body, which shines throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, causing all classes of sentient beings to recognize their own past lives and their origins. Through the power of this single radiance, immeasurable beings are delivered; from ordinary persons on the stages of training up to those beyond training, all receive this light and attain liberation.
Why does the Tathāgata not constantly emit this light to deliver and save immeasurable classes of sentient beings?
What do you think,
O Bodhisattva Illuminator!
"Is it not as you have asked? He replied, "It is so, it is so."
World-Honored One!
How marvelous! How extraordinary!
"What you have asked is of this meaning. How so,
son of good family?"
The Tathāgata shall respond to you with this meaning: that the manifestation of light reveals the various dharma-gates of meditative concentration, which cannot be taught through verbal instruction.
You, in turn, should report to me: "How is it so?"
"Bhagavān! Now these sun and moon illuminate the four continents; there is nowhere that does not receive their light.
At times, do the light of the sun and moon sometimes benefit and at other times harm?"
I then replied: "No, noble son!"
The Buddha said, "Is it not as you have asked? He replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
"At that time, you should further ask this question:
'The light of the sun and moon shines everywhere and is never diminished; yet today the Tathāgata emits a great radiance—does it sometimes diminish and sometimes not?'"
I shall further respond to you with this principle: "How is it so,
son of good family?"
"Can that which is illuminated by the sun and moon be made night by day, or day by night? You should answer me: "No."
“World-Honored One!
The radiance of the sun and moon cannot turn day into night or night into day. I said:
“O son of good family! It is so, it is so.
The radiance of the Tathāgata can turn day into night and night into day; this is what is meant by their respective distinctions.”
"O son of noble family!
You should again question me with this meaning: 'How is it?'"
“World-Honored One!

If dust, mist, and the five obscurations veil the light of the sun and moon so that they have nothing to illuminate, does the radiance of the Tathāgata likewise possess such dust and obscurations? I replied:
"No, son of good family! Why is this?
"The Tathāgata’s radiance penetrates both internally and externally; it is not obstructed by dust or mist, and having transcended the three realms, he is the Unsurpassed Honored One.
What do you think?
"O Illuminator!
You should further ask this question:
'The Tathāgata’s radiance is unobstructed; are the three poisons of sentient beings not like dust and cataracts?'"
"If these are merely dust and obscurations, how do they differ from the five obscurations of the sun and moon?
At that time, I replied:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Noble son! It is well that you have spoken these words; I shall now distinguish them for you one by one.
The Tathāgata’s radiance is inconceivable, transcending the triple world and being without equal. As for the radiance of the Dharma, it possesses ten treasuries of practice."
What are the ten? First, the courageous seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) wherein one does not disparage any phenomena;
second, the inexhaustibility of all phenomena through which one attains the four fearlessnesses.
Third, possessing eloquence that is fluent and penetrating, one remains free from the eight worldly dharmas;
fourth, thoroughly mastering the six supernormal powers so as to be without any obstruction;
fifth, expounding the sublime Dharma without harboring any timidity or weakness.
Sixth, by not practicing negligence, they are forever free from the five hindrances;
seventh, through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, they universally pity all beings;
eighth, they travel to the various Buddha-lands to transform and guide all.
Ninth, they are endowed with the faculties and do not delight in what is inferior;
tenth, they cultivate the unsurpassed path and do not abandon the intention for the Dharma.
These, O son of good family, are called [the ten qualities].
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha cultivates these ten dharmas, thereby corresponding to the ten luminous wisdoms of a Tathāgata.
It is just so, son of good family!

The spiritual power of the light of the maṇi jewel is immeasurable; its radiance illuminates one world-system, two world-systems, three world-systems, and four world-systems; its radiance illuminates a thousand world-systems, two thousand world-systems, and three thousand world-systems; it illuminates the small thousand-world system and the medium thousand-world system, and further illuminates the great trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, there are those who obtain the divine maṇi jewel, which illuminates one Buddha-world, two Buddha-worlds, three Buddha-worlds, and even up to countless trichiliocosms.
The virtue of that radiance is beyond measure.
Such is the virtue of even inanimate light;
how much more so for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who emits a great radiance that universally illumines immeasurable Buddha-lands?

Among those sentient beings who possess physical form, anyone who beholds this radiance shall be cleansed of the three defilements and all shall resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Furthermore, O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānaprabha!
If there are good sons or good daughters who, with sincere faith, receive and uphold the Tathāgata’s wisdom and attain great radiance, they possess ten modes of practice. What are these ten?
The Tathāgata fully knows all unprecedented phenomena; this is called the first matter.
The unprecedented skillful means he employs can manifest the Buddha-dharma for the realization of the assembly; this is called the second matter.

"Regarding external phenomena, they have not yet attained mastery; each harbors doubts and gives rise to a mind of right and wrong, claiming to see what is not seen, claiming to bind what is not bound, claiming to liberate what is not liberated, claiming to uphold what is not upheld, and claiming to accomplish what is not accomplished. Yet, regarding all dharmas, they have attained complete mastery—truly as it is, thus as it is, truly without falsehood—and cause the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, to attain complete mastery over all dharmas, being without any obstruction within the dharma-realm. These are called the three matters."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

It is like a person who, in a single moment of thought, purifies all defilements of the mind and awakens with vast clarity; no longer requiring the passage of kalpas, they travel from one Buddha-land to another, teaching and transforming sentient beings without hindrance, and transcend the three realms of existence entirely without finding it difficult—this is called the fourth matter."
"Furthermore, O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jyotirvid!

Even when the kalpa is consumed by fire and the interval between worlds is desolate—when the preceding Buddha has passed away and the succeeding Buddha has not yet appeared—the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains eternally present without change. At such times, there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of great vows who are able to settle their spirits in tranquil concentration within the void, and do not enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder."
The reason for this is that their fundamental, essential, and solemn vows are profound; these are called the five matters.
Furthermore, O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānaprabha!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, observes those whose minds are ready for transformation and those who are not; the Tathāgata knows all this as it truly is, without error. From this realm of desire up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, the Tathāgata fully knows whatever thoughts arise in the consciousness—whether good or foul, suffering or joy—and is thus able to teach and transform them therein, leading them to liberation. These are called the six matters.
"Furthermore, O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jñānaprabha!

The transformation body of the Tathāgata is unfathomable; it wanders through immeasurable Buddha-fields and practices dhyāna, liberation, and the nine successive stages of attainment—these are called the seven matters."
"Furthermore, Illumination Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva!

If there are good sons or good daughters who cultivate the five virtuous practices and maintain a mind of forbearance, neither mocking nor accepting [the insults of others]; furthermore, they do not give rise to the thought, 'I am superior and they are inferior,' nor do they give rise to the thought, 'They are superior and I am inferior'; or they may give rise to the thought, 'They are equal to me' or 'I am equal to them. These are called the eight matters."
"Furthermore, Illuminating Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can, within the space of a finger-snap, fully know the inconceivable immeasurable dharmas and the thoughts dwelling in the minds of those within the five destinies."

There is a mind with delusion and a mind without delusion; a mind with craving and a mind without craving; a mind with hatred and a mind without hatred—discerning each of these individually and knowing them all completely; these are called the nine matters.
"Furthermore, O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jyotirvikrāmin!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family travels through the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, exhorting and inspiring people to perform the work of Buddhas, they shall then speak of the afflictions of receiving physical forms within the five destinies."

Although rebirth in the heavens is not the eternal way, the human condition undergoes a hundred transformations with immeasurable cycles of birth and death; one may collide headlong into the realm of animals with no end to liberation; as a gluttonous hungry ghost, one receives a hideous form; and in hell, one suffers retribution until the karmic debt is exhausted before finally emerging.
Only Nirvana offers incomparable bliss; it points out the direct path for advancing toward the unconditioned.
"Thus it is said, O Illuminating Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva!
These ten matters of practice are not within the reach of knowledge of the followers of the Two Vehicles.

**Chapter 21: On Non-Conceptualization (A-saṃjñā)** At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra was seated in the assembly. Having heard the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, expound upon the ten lights of wisdom, he leaped up with joy, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If I may venture to ask a question, provided that your reverence will grant me leave, I shall then set forth my inquiry.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra, saying: “Noble son!”
"Now this great assembly has gathered and all are free from fear; whatever doubts or difficulties you may have, you may ask about them.
Then the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
What is perception and what is non-perception?
What is volitional activity and what is non-activity?
What is sensation and what is non-sensation?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra: “Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!”
That which you have asked is all sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
"I shall distinguish each point for you one by one.
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra said:
"I wish and desire to hear it."
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!
I shall now question you; you should answer me one by one."
How so? Son of good family!
Does the Most Perfectly Awakened One possess conceptual thought?
"Is it that he is without perception?
Bodhisattva Dharmakāra replied,
"Does the Most Perfectly Awakened One possess perception?"
"Is it not the state of non-perception? The Buddha said, "How so?"
Son of good family!
Is the pure dharmakāya possessed of conceptualization,
or is it devoid of conceptualization?
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The pure Dharma-body possesses perception; it is not without perception.”
The Buddha said: “How is this so,
son of good family?”

“Are the aggregate of precepts, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation possessed of perception,
or are they without perception?
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Buddha asked again:

Are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold noble path, and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—from the stage of stream-enterer up to Buddhahood—possessed of conceptualization?
"Is it non-conceptualization?
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"From all dharmas up to Buddhahood, they all possess conceptualization; they are not without conceptualization.
The Buddha asked again: "How so?"
"Noble son! From all dharmas up to and including perfect enlightenment, are they all characterized by conceptualization and not devoid of conceptualization?
What, then, is that which is devoid of conceptualization?"
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The wisdom of original non-existence and the wisdom of *nirvāṇa* without remainder—this is called 'non-conceptualization' (*asaṃjñā*).
The Buddha again questioned the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra, saying:
"How is it, son of good family!
Have you now attained the wisdom of original non-existence and the wisdom of nirvana without remainder?"
He replied: "No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said,
“Son of good family!
How does one know that the wisdom of original non-existence and the wisdom of nirvana without remainder are without conceptualization and not characterized by conceptualization?”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra replied with a verse:
"In the past, from the God among Gods, the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
I heard the teaching on the wisdom of original non-existence and the path to Nirvāṇa without remainder."
Non-arising is not arising; it is tranquil and free from conceptual attachment, serene and unchanging, peaceful and without birth or extinction.
Now I therefore report to the Tathāgata: fundamentally there is no existence, nor is there any conceptualization.
"Being without attachment, one cannot be defiled; how much less so when there are manifold thoughts?
The Buddha again replied to the Bodhisattva Dharmākara in verse:
"The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge without obstruction."
The conceptualization of various phenomena has not yet exhausted its root;
Nirvana is tranquil and fixed, and the nature of phenomena is indestructible.
If conceptualization exists whether it turns or does not turn, how can there be "no-thought"?
“The Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, taught the Dharma with this same meaning:
if all things are fundamentally non-existent and devoid of conceptualization, how can one transform and guide sentient beings?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is ‘having perception’?

"The four foundations of mindfulness, up to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—from the stage of stream-enterer up to the Buddha—the seeker is characterized by conceptualization, while the attainer is without conceptualization.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
From all dharmas of the pure *dharmakāya* up to perfect enlightenment, are they possessed of form,

The Buddha said: "Stop, stop!
Son of good family!"
"I now ask you: does this realm of empty space have form, or is it formless?
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This realm of empty space is empty like emptiness; it is neither with form nor without form.
The Buddha said:
“Noble son! In what way is emptiness like emptiness—neither having form nor being formless?
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Internal and external dharmas are empty like space, whether they have form or are formless; there is no path to nirvāṇa that remains. This is called neither having form nor being formless.”
The Buddha again asked the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra:
"In what way is *nirvāṇa* without remainder neither with form nor without form?
Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The realm of space is subsumed within eye-consciousness; viewed in this way, it is neither with form nor without form.
The Buddha again asked Dharmakāra, "Is the eye, then, empty?"
"Is it not empty? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha asked again:
“If visual consciousness were not empty, how could one know emptiness through that consciousness?”
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra said:
"Because consciousness is not empty, one knows that emptiness is like emptiness—neither having form nor being without form.
The Buddha asked again:
"How is it, son of good family?

Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"The Tathāgata is originally non-existent.
The Buddha asked again:
“What is meant by the Tathāgata Primordial Non-existence?
“Because he does not abide, does not undergo change, and does not destroy the dharma-realm, he is called the Tathāgata Primordial Non-existence.”
The Buddha asked again:
"Noble son! It is neither destroyed nor does it abide, noble son!"
"Is it by means of the fruit? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“How do you know that non-abiding is the fundamental non-existence of the Tathāgata?”
Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The past has no form; the present does not abide; the future has not yet arrived.
The Buddha said:
“Have you now attained this Dharma-nature? He replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“If one does not yet know whether the dharmas of the three periods of time abide or do not abide, how can one know whether they have form or are formless?”
Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: does he abide in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*?"
"Or am I in nirvana without remainder?
The Buddha said,
"I am now both in nirvana with remainder and in nirvana without remainder."
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that one is both in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and also in *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*?”
The Buddha said:
"As I have attained this physical body with its thirty-two marks, there is *sa-upādiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
To contemplate that the past Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were formless and invisible, is *an-upādiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*."
Dharmakāra asked again: "How so,
World-Honored One?"
“Is there anything within the dharma-realm of nirvāṇa that can be designated or cannot be designated?
The Buddha said, “Noble son!”
“The Dharma-realm of Nirvāṇa cannot be defined.
Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha:
“If Nirvāṇa is undefined, why do you say that there are as many as the sands of the Ganges, beyond counting, which are called ‘Nirvāṇa without remainder’?”
The Buddha said: "Stop, stop!
Son of good family!"

As you have said, this Dharma is provisional and deceptive, lacking any name or essential nature; that which is called Nirvana is neither existent nor non-existent, neither with form nor without form. It is only because sentient beings are attached to emptiness and defiled by emptiness, attached to the dharma-realm and defiled by the dharma-realm—failing to know how to go from having form to being without form, and failing to know how to go from being without form to having form—that the Tathāgata has taught this meaning!
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If emptiness is made to be like emptiness, it is both with form and without form.”
Does the Tathāgata today have a physical form as his essence,
or does he have no physical form as his essence?

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra: "Excellent,
son of good family!"

As you have said, the Buddhas of the past, the present, and the future are each devoid of conceptualization; the past is not the future, the future is not the past, the past is not the present, and the present is not the past. The meaning of what I have taught is exactly thus.
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding past perception and non-perception, present perception and non-perception, and future perception and non-perception—are they different or not different?"
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra:
"The past is not the present, and the present is not the future; each is without distinction.
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by ‘with activity’?
What is meant by ‘without activity’?

“The pure Dharma-body is called ‘with practice’;
that which is apart from the pure Dharma-body is called ‘without practice.

if one is detached, there is no practice.
Dharmakāra said: “The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha now speaks of practice with activity and practice without activity. What is meant by practice with activity?
What is meant by practice without activity?”
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!
The earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these are called 'conditioned activities' (saṃskāra)."
“Emptiness, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and formlessness—these are called non-practice.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, abides both in practice and in non-practice.”
What is meant by "with activity" (sābhoga) and what is meant by "without activity" (anābhoga)?

The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is it that when there is the realm of a Buddha, there is practice;

The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra:

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is 'having sensation' (vedanā)?
What is 'being without sensation'?
The Buddha said:
“Initially desiring to practice giving is called suffering; giving without regret is called freedom from suffering.
Training in the precepts without transgression is called suffering; having a firm resolve in the precepts is called freedom from suffering.”
To hold the mind as steadfast as the earth and not abandon patience is called "pain"; to be able to harmonize the assembly without creating distinctions between self and other is called "no pain.
To serve the Dharma with earnestness, never wavering or regretting, is called "pain"; to advance in the Dharma as one did before and not forsake the root of the Way is called "no pain."

Although one attains long-term concentration, for the mind to abide in the signless is called "having pain"; for the root of the Path not to be destroyed and the mind to remain single-pointed without distraction is called "being without pain.
To transform and guide sentient beings by gathering them through the One Path is called "pain"; to not perceive a self and to abandon attachment to signs and the mind is called "being without pain."

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Viśuddhadarśana who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

Why is this? Because these are the practices cultivated by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, and those of the future shall likewise study these dharmas and attain accomplishment.
"Just as I, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaim this Dharma today, using skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to transform and guide sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhadarśana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who proclaims this Dharma and disseminates it among people of the world, their merit shall consist of twenty aspects."
What are these twenty?
The necklace of dhāraṇī, which does not destroy the dharma-realm;
the necklace of spiritual lineage, which achieves fulfillment within the household life;
The necklace of skillful means does not diminish or exhaust any phenomena;
the necklace of transformation-born birth is not received from a womb;
the necklace of pure teaching contains no deceptive or contentious dharmas.
The necklace of the Dharma-body is the purity of the nature of understanding;
the necklace of reception and entry is the accomplishment of the practice of emptiness;
the necklace of sentient beings exists for the sake of transforming all.
The necklace of extinction is so called because it is free from dust and defilement;
the necklace of the exhaustion of birth is so called because it is fundamentally devoid of mind and consciousness;
the necklace of the immeasurable is so called because its impurities are naturally pure.
The kalpa-counting necklace, because there is no distance or nearness;
the knowledge-of-birth necklace, because it praises original non-existence;
the morality-and-virtue necklace, because practice is self-extinguished.
The necklace of the Mahāyāna, because all faculties are fully perfected;
the necklace of liberation, because no sentient beings are perceived;
the necklace of the Dharma King, because the teaching of the Dharma is inexhaustible.
The necklace of insatiability, because one never tires of receiving the Dharma;
the necklace of letters, because of strong memory and non-forgetfulness;
the necklace of the dharma-realm, because of the perfection of practice.
The *dharmamūla* necklace, because it is fundamentally *nirvāṇa*;
the *dharmatā* necklace, because it is without arising or ceasing;
the *mahāpraṇidhāna* necklace, because it is the self-nature of the path.
The necklace of True Suchness (*tathatā*), because it is fully endowed with the roots of goodness;
the necklace of Purity, because it is free from birth and fundamentally non-existent;
the necklace of Non-obstruction, because it penetrates the coming and going [of all phenomena].
The Dharma-Origination Necklace is so called because it is not attached to the three places.

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who receive, uphold, recite, and chant this Dharma-necklace, they shall immediately become fully endowed with twenty meritorious qualities of the dhāraṇī-dharmaparyāya.

The Bodhisattva Viśuddhadarśana addressed the Buddha, saying:

who practiced the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; who cultivated twelve dharmas with minds free from delusion; who were capable of teaching and transforming others; who practiced four dharmas and performed seven contemplations; who cultivated five pure dharmas and performed five contemplations; and who further cultivated eight dharmas, eighteen dharmas, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—would their merit and blessings not be great?

Arriving at the place of the World-Honored One, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.

To the south, ten billion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of] Buddha-lands away, there is a Buddha named One Path (*Ekamārga*). Having seen the light, he immediately dispatched eight thousand great bodhisattvas to come to this Sahā world; they arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and sat down to one side.

To the west, beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in seven Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha named Unobstructed Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Seeing this light that shines everywhere, he immediately dispatched twelve hundred great beings, all of whom had attained supernatural powers and were able to pass through the realm of Māra. They arrived in the Sahā world at the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.

To the north, at a distance of thirteen billion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of] Ganges rivers from here, there is a buddha-field named Tathāgatamūlapratibhāsa. Its Buddha is named Samyaktvārtha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He too saw the light shining universally throughout the trichiliocosm, and immediately dispatched fifty thousand bodhisattvas—all of whom possessed the supernormal powers and the six penetrations with perfect clarity—to come to the World-Honored One in this Sahā world-system. They prostrated themselves at his feet, paid homage, and sat to one side.

In the northeastern direction, at a distance of as many *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* sands from here, there is a buddha-field named Vimala. Its Buddha is named Samacaryā Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Having seen this radiance, he dispatched seven thousand great bodhisattvas to the Sahā world; they arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.

Three hundred million buddha-fields to the southeast of here, there is a buddha-land named Accumulated Jewels (*Ratnasaṃcaya*). Its Buddha is named Well-Accumulated Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Having seen the light, he immediately dispatched seven hundred virtuous men (*satpuruṣa*), all of whom had attained supernatural powers and acquired unimpeded wisdom; they came to this Sahā world and, having reached the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads and sat to one side.

To the southwest, ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Buddha-lands away from here, there is a Buddha-land named Ekavyūha. Its Buddha is named Samatājñāna Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Upon seeing this radiance, he immediately dispatched fifteen hundred great bodhisattvas to the Sahā world; they arrived at the place of the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.

To the northwest, at a distance of fourteen hundred million *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Buddha-lands from here, there is a land named Pure (*Vimala*). There, a Buddha named Guṇasamudra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having seen this light, immediately dispatched five thousand bodhisattvas to the Sahā world. Upon arriving at the place of the World-Honored One, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.

Above this world, passing beyond realms of sentient beings and further across worlds as numerous as the sands of two Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-field named Universal Compassion. Its Buddha is named Mahāsamata Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Having seen this radiance, he immediately dispatched five thousand bodhisattvas to come to the Sahā world; they arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.

Thirty-two billion Ganges-sands of world-systems below this place, there is a buddha-field named Sthira. There dwells a Buddha named Anikṣiptamahāpraṇidhāna Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Seeing that Śākyamuni Buddha had emitted a great radiance, he dispatched ten thousand mahāsattvas from the region below to come to the presence of the World-Honored One; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the assembly was seated and settled, addressed those gathered there:
"I shall now discourse upon practice and non-practice.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
Reflect upon this well!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, from the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat, have not yet attained the Tathāgata’s treasury of the wisdom of the Way, such individuals do not belong to the category of the noble ones.

At that time, there were ninety-two thousand unattached Arhats on the assembly who had come from various other worlds to this Sahā world, desiring to hear from the Tathāgata the *Dharmaparyāya of the Garland of Practice and Non-practice*.

Now that I have heard such a teaching from the World-Honored One, I realize that if good sons or good daughters—from those at the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhat—have not yet trodden upon the treasury of the Tathāgata’s path and wisdom, they do not belong to the ranks of the noble ones.
At that time, ninety-two thousand Arhats who had attained the Way, whose outflows were exhausted and whose fetters untied, realized as it truly was that they would no longer undergo rebirth.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Piṇḍola, Mahākātyāyana, Revata, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and the rest of the assembly of ninety-two thousand people, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Tathāgata, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and each knelt down before him, addressing the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"Although we have attained the four fruits and our six supernormal powers are clear and penetrating, we are still not equal to ordinary practitioners.
This is because we have now heard the Tathāgata speak of the profound treasury of the wisdom of the Path, which is not a realm that we can enter."
“May we, World-Honored One,
be granted the opportunity to hear this Dharma, so that sentient beings who have long been asleep may forever be free from hesitation.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not respond.
Then Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Although we Arhats have attained the title of 'sons of the Buddha,' this is entirely the fault of the Tathāgata and not our own transgression."
For what reason?
If the Tathāgata had vowed that there were no three vehicles, would we not have attained equal and perfect enlightenment?
Why then has the Tathāgata not permitted us to be included among the ranks of the sages?
At that time, Mahākāśyapa and ninety-two thousand *ṛṣis* all removed their monastic robes and, wailing and weeping with grief, prostrated themselves on the ground.
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, gandharvas, humans, and non-humans marveled at this unprecedented event.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to dispel the doubts in the minds of the people, extended his right hand to support Kāśyapa as he rose, and then directed each of them to sit down again.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The Tathāgata’s karma was originally non-existent; The treasury of the wisdom of the Path is foremost."
With the immeasurable wisdom of the various perfections, they gradually enter the realm of the Tathāgata.
In the Great Way there are no three vehicles, much less four fruits of the path.
Contemplating purity as being like empty space—this is the Elder Kāśyapa.
I now observe this mind: it is neither existent nor non-existent;
it manifests many infinite transformations, yet never abandons the Buddha’s great vow.
Since time immemorial, I have cultivated the ornaments of the supernormal powers.
The Dharma of the six perfections is vast and great; how could there be such a thing as the name "śrāvaka"?
The Buddha-realm has no boundaries, yet those who are transformed are likewise diverse;
thus sentient beings are deluded, claiming that the Way is manifold.

At that time, upon hearing these verses spoken by the Tathāgata, there were immeasurable sentient beings in the assembly who all resolved their minds; with faith and joy, they desired to hear the profound treasury of the path-wisdom and the most deep-seated Dharma, and they all gave rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable sentient beings who, with upright minds, attained liberation and achieved the practice of ultimate faith.

Chapter Twenty-Four: On Practice and Non-Practice (8) The Bodhisattva’s Necklace Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Four: On Practice and Non-Practice. At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttara-lakṣaṇa rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his hands joined in *añjali*, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I am capable of expounding upon practice and non-practice before the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!”
"If there is one who can speak [of this], now is precisely the right time.
The Bodhisattva Anuttalakṣaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who understands that fundamental non-existence is what is called "having practice," and that fundamental non-existence is naturally empty, quiescent, and formless—this is called "non-practice."
The Bodhisattva Vipula-gati said:
"To manifest miraculous powers to teach and transform beings in that buddha-field is called 'with practice'; not perceiving a land while transforming sentient beings is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Jñānotpāda said:
“To know that nirvāṇa is quiescent and without arising or ceasing is called ‘with practice’; not perceiving nirvāṇa or the characteristics of nirvāṇa is called ‘without practice.’”
The Bodhisattva Dharmaratna said:
"To speak of the path as non-path is called 'having practice'; likewise, neither to have a path nor to lack a path is called 'non-practice'."
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhasūkṣma said:
"To contemplate the pure dharma is called 'with practice'; not even perceiving the contemplation of the pure dharma is called 'without practice.
The Bodhisattva Mārgagāmin said:
"To see the Buddha’s supernatural power is called 'with practice'; likewise, neither seeing the Buddha nor [seeing] supernatural power is called 'without practice. Bodhisattva Pushi said:

"To manifest entry into meditative concentration is called 'with practice'; likewise, neither seeing the cultivation of practice nor seeing entry into meditative concentration is called 'without practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Moonlight-Illumination said:
"To see the physical marks of the Buddha’s body filling the trichiliocosm is called 'with practice'; likewise, not seeing the Buddha nor his marks and signs is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Karuṇāloka said:
"To have a self and a life-span is called 'with activity'; likewise, not perceiving a life-span and not perceiving a self is called 'without activity'."
The Bodhisattva Abhaya said:
"To preach the Dharma while maintaining the notion of dharmas is called 'with practice'; likewise, not perceiving dharmas yet not being without dharmas is called 'without practice'."
"In this way, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding both practice and non-practice, attains the complete adornment of a bodhisattva.
An immeasurable number of bodhisattvas said:
"That which transcends the measure of the Buddhas and cannot be limited is called 'practice'; furthermore, neither perceiving a measure nor perceiving a non-measure is called 'non-practice'."
The Bodhisattva Mindfulness said:

"To travel through the various Buddha-lands by means of the six supernormal powers without praising oneself or extolling those powers is called 'with practice. To not perceive any lands as being subject to reception or deliverance is called 'without practice.'"
Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla said:

"To be able to transform all things so that they entirely take the form of a Buddha is called 'with practice'; furthermore, neither perceiving the transformation nor perceiving the Buddha is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Anantapāra said:
"To possess immeasurable dhāraṇīs of the Buddha-realm without forgetting them is called 'with practice'; that there is fundamentally no dhāraṇī and no Three Jewels is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Constant Compassion said:
"When sentient beings give rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna, this is called 'having practice. Furthermore, when there is neither the Mahāyāna nor the path, this is called 'non-practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Acintya said:

“The inconceivability of the Buddha and the inconceivability of the True Dharma are likewise; the inconceivability of receiving retribution is also thus—this is called ‘having practice. Furthermore, neither perceiving the conceivable nor perceiving the inconceivable is called ‘non-practice.’”
The Bodhisattva Zhouxuan said:

"The wisdom of emptiness is one; it is not that there is no wisdom—this is called 'having practice. Wisdom is also empty and quiescent; it is neither the presence of wisdom nor the absence of wisdom—this is called 'non-practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Dharmakāra said:

"That the Tathāgata is one true limit (bhūtakoṭi) is likewise called 'with practice' (sacaryā); yet, neither seeing the Tathāgata nor seeing the true limit—being neither one nor not one—is called 'without practice' (acaryā)."
The Bodhisattva Skillful Means said:
"To discern all dharmas through the observation of wisdom is called 'with practice'; likewise, to have neither the observation of wisdom nor any dharmas is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Without Equal said:
"The single mark being without marks is called 'with practice'; neither seeing marks nor seeing no-marks is called 'without practice'."
"In this way, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding both conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) and non-activity, is able to fully possess the bodhisattva’s jeweled necklace.
The Bodhisattva Merit said:
"Neither perceiving birth nor perceiving non-birth is called 'conditioned activity'; that birth is itself non-birth and further lacks the birth of birth is called 'non-activity'."
The Bodhisattva Awakening said:
"To perceive permanence and impermanence is called 'with activity'; likewise, neither perceiving permanence nor perceiving non-permanence is called 'without activity'."
The Bodhisattva Accomplishment said:
"To not engage in bodily actions and to have no attachment is called 'with action'; likewise, neither perceiving engagement nor perceiving non-engagement is called 'without action'."
The Bodhisattva Prārthanā said:
"To not engage in verbal actions and to have no attachment is called 'with practice'; to neither perceive engagement nor perceive non-engagement is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Without Abode said:
"To not engage in mental activity and to have no attachment is called 'having practice'; likewise, neither seeing engagement nor seeing non-engagement is called 'non-practice'."
The Bodhisattva Unhindered Wisdom said:
"To awaken to that which is not awakened to is called 'with practice'; likewise, neither perceiving awakening nor giving rise to the notion of sentient beings is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Gandhavyūha said:

"To understand that the Way is fundamentally without dharma-nature and that there is no difference [between them] is called 'having practice. Furthermore, not perceiving the Way and yet having no dharma-nature is called 'non-practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Dharmacakrapravartana said:

"To proclaim and expound the realization of the fruits of the four paths while beneath the king of trees is called 'with practice'; to preach the Dharma without the notion of dharmas and without perceiving the four paths is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Self-Contemplation said:

"To speak of the emptiness of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is called 'with practice'; likewise, not perceiving the formation or disintegration of the five aggregates is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Zhongzhi said:

"To contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness and know that both the internal and external are empty is called 'with practice. To discern that the foundations of mindfulness originally come from nowhere, go nowhere, and reach nowhere is called 'without practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Bahusruta said:

"To kindle all dharmas, up to and including the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, is called 'with practice. Furthermore, not perceiving the kindling nor any of these dharmas is called 'without practice.'"
The Dharma-body Bodhisattva said:
"To perceive all dharmas as having movement or lack of movement is called 'with practice' (sa-caryā). That which is neither movement nor lack of movement is called 'without practice' (a-caryā)."
The Bodhisattva Anigha said:
"All dharmas are spontaneous, and the contemplation of dharmas is likewise; the contemplation of dharmas is spontaneous, and all dharmas are likewise—this is called 'with practice.
That from the beginning there are no dharmas and no contemplation of dharmas—this is called 'without practice.'"
The foremost bodhisattva said:
"To discern the Buddha’s wisdom and know its emptiness and stillness is called 'with practice';
to contemplate the Buddha’s profound wisdom as being naturally so by its very nature, without even a name or title, is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Daoyi said:

"To realize the fivefold Dharma-body without departing from it is called 'with practice'; to observe each [phenomenon] one by one as being inherently formless and without arising or ceasing is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Benzuo said:
“All dharmas likewise have nothing upon which to rely; not relying on internal emptiness nor relying on external emptiness is called ‘with practice.
To thoroughly understand internal and external emptiness as well as all dharmas, neither seeing arising nor seeing cessation, and being entirely without attachment—this is called ‘without practice.’”
The manifested Bodhisattva said:

"To travel back and forth, paying homage and serving the various Buddhas, yet not perceiving whether their Buddha-lands are pure or impure, nor the good or evil of sentient beings—this is called 'having practice.
Not perceiving one's own body or the good, evil, clarity, or turbidity of the various Buddha-lands—this is called 'non-practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Non-Conceptualization said:
"When all dharmas are undisturbed, tranquil, and immovable—when one does not calculate suffering or pleasure, permanence or impermanence, beauty or ugliness—this is called 'with practice.

When immeasurable wisdom entirely returns to emptiness, and one perceives neither disturbance nor concentration, neither suffering nor pleasure, neither beauty nor ugliness—this is called 'without practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Mahāmaitrī said:
"To not perceive that any phenomena have a destination or no destination is called 'with practice'; to never have a destination and not even perceive a destination is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Kṣānticārin said:
"To understand that emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as the realm of consciousness and the single nature of suchness, is called 'with practice.

That emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are themselves empty; that emptiness is also empty; and that signlessness and wishlessness further have no retribution—this is called 'without practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said:

"To enter a single state of meditative concentration and fully know the path of the majestic deportment and the rules of conduct of all Buddhas is called 'having practice. To enter dhyāna-concentration while never perceiving the marks of phenomena is called 'non-practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Xiqing said:
“When the roots of the three poisons arise and cease spontaneously, such that one does not know why they arise when they arise nor why they cease when they cease, this is called ‘with practice.
When one contemplates that the roots of the three poisons are inherently without form or sign, and are forever without arising or ceasing, this is called ‘without practice.’”
The Bodhisattva Guanjin said:
"To uphold the precepts without transgression and yet not perceive any transgression is called 'having practice.
That there is fundamentally no precept and no transgression, for such is the inherent nature of things, is called 'non-practice.'"
The Bodhisattva Constant Joy said:

"To analytically discern the twelve gates of liberation is called 'with practice'; furthermore, not perceiving that liberation or the various treasures of the Dharma have arising or ceasing is called 'without practice'."
The Bodhisattva Xuanchang said:

"That the arising of phenomena and the arising of suffering have fundamentally no locus is called 'with practice' (sābhoga). To know the ultimate limit of suffering while it cannot be perceived is called 'without practice' (anābhoga)."
The Bodhisattva Daoxiu said:
“The Great Way has a single characteristic; nirvāṇa is formless. Not perceiving the aspiration for the unsurpassed way is called ‘having practice.
When the teachings of the Way that one expounds lack subtlety and refinement, and the dharma-realm is spontaneous and cannot be turned back, this is called ‘non-practice.’”
The Bodhisattva Dharmadeśaka said:
"The path that is established is inconceivable; though one dwells amidst defilement, being as if dwelling nowhere is called 'having practice.
To thoroughly understand that the nature of the five purities and the five turbidities is empty and not real, and that they are likewise non-existent, is called 'non-practice.'"
At that time, the countless bodhisattvas from the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each having spoken of both practice and non-practice, returned to their respective seats.
Then Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and stepped forward to address the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I am also capable of explaining the practice with activity and the practice without activity; if you would grant me leave, I dare to declare what I harbor in my mind.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Now this great assembly has gathered and has been longing for this teaching for a long time; if you are able to speak it, now is precisely the right time.
At that moment, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who uphold the twelve dhūta practices of the true discipline—difficult to attain—and do not lose even as much as a hair’s breadth of them, nor give rise to thoughts or a mind of right and wrong, this is called the first type of practice.”
At that time, Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family focuses their mind with single-minded devotion and without forgetfulness, being able to expound the Way and its teachings so that each fulfills their aspirations, and never alters their great vow until they attain Buddhahood—this is also called the first practice."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who advance in study and cultivate the dharma-gate of meditative contemplation, remaining unstained by and unattached to various supernormal powers and wisdoms; who cause those seeking the Way to each find joy; and who are further able to guide and show them the path, fulfilling the aspirations of others according to their minds; and who, for those seeking the Mahāyāna, bring them to the ultimate fulfillment of their resolve without allowing them to fall or encounter obstacles along the way."

"If one further desires to attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha, one likewise protects and guards them so that they may attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this too is called the 'first practice with effort' (*prathamā savyāpārā kriyā*). Then, Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to cultivate the dharma of 'practice without effort' (*nirvyāpārā kriyā*), all sentient beings have roots of sin that are deep and firm, making them difficult to rescue. Yet these sinful persons have no affinity with me and no means by which they might be delivered. However, O World-Honored One, you subtly employ skillful means to gradually wait for their opportunity; knowing their movements and inclinations, you create the causal conditions for them to receive your protection and shelter—this is what is called 'practice without effort.'"
At that time, Mahākāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son or daughter of good family, originally lacking the mind for the Way while still on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), is able to be instructed and inspired to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and ultimately achieves success without ever falling midway into the two stages [of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha], this is called ‘non-practice.’”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If there are good men or good women who, having accumulated merit and virtue over incalculable kalpas, have made this great and solemn vow:
'When I attain the Way, may I be born in such-and-such a country, encounter such-and-such a Sage, and have disciples and attendants likewise as these. "

However, if those good men and good women encounter sages or Buddhas appearing in the world while deviating from their original vows, they attain parinirvāṇa under those Buddhas; this is called "non-practice."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa: "Stop, stop, Elder!
How could you, with your currently turbid and biased mind, be able to fathom this? Why is this so?

Even Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have established their faculties and attained power do not yet fully comprehend what constitutes practice and non-practice; how much less can you, with your minor virtues, hope to understand it completely?
"This is not so; return to your seat with your usual deportment.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa’s countenance changed from its normal state, and filled with extreme shame, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet and returned to his original seat.
At that time, the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya rose again from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!
I am now able, before the Tathāgata, to proclaim the teachings of the Way regarding both practice and non-practice."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, son of good family!"
"Now is the very time; speak freely on what you wish to say.
Then, Ājñātakauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If there are good sons or good daughters who cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path and do not give rise to doubt regarding these eight factors, this is called "having practice.

Furthermore, if good sons or good daughters attain the wisdom of immeasurable dharmas and discern that the eight factors are entirely non-existent—since originally not even a single dharma exists, how much less the Eightfold Noble Path? This is called "having no practice."
The Dharma that is without name or designation also has no dwelling place; this is called the foremost, most excellent Dharma of non-action.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, in the practice of the four dhyānas, contemplates each one with a mind that does not scatter, binding the mind to clarity and not losing the propriety of the Dharma, they will certainly attain its fruit without any doubt. This, World-Honored One, is called..."
First is the practice with activity.

Furthermore, if a son or daughter of good family, from beginning to end, sits upright and contemplates all formless dharmas, seeing no point of origin and no beginning, their names and titles being deceptive, neither true nor existent—this is called the dharma of non-activity.
Then, the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family discriminates the wisdom of emptiness yet their mind is not stained by emptiness, and seeks emptiness within emptiness, giving rise to perverted conceptions—this is called ‘having practice.’”

If one does not give rise to defilement regarding the wisdom of emptiness, does not engender false views or various mental constructions, and recognizes that there was originally no fundamental basis—how much less could there be a "now"?
This is called non-action.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If again a good man or a good woman internally contemplates the empty and quiescent concentration of wisdom, maintaining the mind with firm stability such that it neither increases nor decreases, this is called 'with practice' (sābhoga)."

To discern that the six internal and external sense bases have no master, that the six sense objects were originally non-existent yet now possess consciousness, and that this consciousness does not belong to the three periods of time nor cling to the three realms of existence—this is called "non-action" (anabhisamskāra).
At that time, after the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya had spoken thus regarding the practice and non-practice of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Noble son! To proclaim and expound the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata is most marvelous and extraordinary;
it is truly unprecedented."
"Return to your seat and assume your usual dignified demeanor.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, adjusted his dharma robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Having harbored doubts for a long time, I wish to ask something; I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it point by point.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "Excellent!"
“Son of good family!
If you have anything you wish to ask, now is precisely the right time; the Tathāgata shall answer each of your questions one by one.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘with activity’?
What is meant by ‘without activity’?”
As the World-Honored One has said, "If there is present creation, then there is activity; if there was originally nothing, then there is no activity.
Now I ask the Tathāgata: Is it that one proceeds from having activity to being without activity that is called "non-activity"?
Is it because there is permanence for those with practice and impermanence for those without practice that this is called "non-practice"?
If one says there is practice, then what the Venerable Mahākāśyapa has proclaimed regarding practice would be without error.
If there were no practice, there would be no verbal teaching; how then could one cause that which is a dharma without verbal teaching to possess verbal teaching?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this point by point.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "How is it, Śāriputra?"
“Is it not the case that the essential nature of conditioned formations is empty?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“The nature of conditioned formations is empty, like space.
The Buddha again asked Śāriputra: “How is this so?”
“Son of good family!
What is the emptiness of non-action?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The emptiness of non-action is precisely the emptiness of action.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If the emptiness of conditioned phenomena were identical to the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, why did Mahākāśyapa now speak only of the existence of conditioned phenomena and not of the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, nor speak of the existence of unconditioned phenomena, nor of the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does one practice the emptiness of nature?”
“What is the emptiness of non-activity?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Listen closely, listen closely!”
"Reflect upon this well!
I shall expound its meaning for you. He replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"What do you think, noble son?

When the body composed of the five aggregates and the four great elements has been fully formed and one abandons what was originally produced, such a sentient being may perceive external forms; within that visual consciousness, afflictions arise spontaneously. One should discern that this consciousness does not come from without, nor does it emerge from within; it is through the discrimination of consciousness that these afflictions are produced."
"How is it, son of good family!
Is the dharma-realm of the five aggregates not thus?"
Śāriputra said: “So it is, so it is,
World-Honored One!”
"All this arises from visual consciousness giving rise to these defilements.
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:
"What do you think?"
O son of noble family!
If there is a person with vision who contemplates the eye-consciousness as it discriminates the defilements, from where does it originally come?
By what means is it extinguished?
"If one seeks the nesting place of worldly afflictions, can it be found?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "No."
“World-Honored One!
Eye-consciousness has no form and cannot be seen.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Śāriputra! This is precisely what is called the emptiness of conditioned activity."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding emptiness, remains detached from emptiness and does not become stained by consciousness of emptiness; if they have stilled the mind so that it is eternally extinguished and no longer gives rise to conceptual attachments, remaining silent and without speech—this is what is called the emptiness-nature of non-practice.
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears external sounds with the ear, smells external odors with the nose, knows external flavors with the tongue, experiences external contacts as internal pleasure with the body, and cognizes external formations with the mental faculty of dharmas."
Contemplate this consciousness: it neither comes from without nor arises from within; rather, this affliction arises through false discrimination.
Why is this so, noble son?
"Are the five aggregates and the dharma-realm not thus?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
This arises from the dharma of consciousness giving birth to all afflictions.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"What do you think,
son of good family?
If there were a person with eyes who contemplated the consciousness of dharmas and analyzed their afflictions, from where would they have come?"
"Furthermore, from what do they cease?
If one seeks the nesting place of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), can it be found?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"No, World-Honored One!
The consciousness of dharmas is formless and cannot be seen."
The Buddha said:
“So it is, Śāriputra! This is precisely what is called the emptiness of conditioned activity.”
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding emptiness, remains detached from emptiness and does not become defiled by the consciousness of emptiness; if their mental activity is extinguished and eternally stilled so that no conceptual attachments arise, and they remain tranquil and silent with neither teaching nor doctrine—this is what is called the emptiness-nature of non-action."

The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra: "The nature of all phenomena abides without change; when a phenomenon arises, it arises; when a phenomenon ceases, it ceases. In arising, it does not know by what it arises; in ceasing, it does not know by what it ceases. Even a person with eyes who observes this sees neither arising nor ceasing. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān; he has transcended the three realms and is the Honored One among gods and men."

If there are good men or good women who receive, uphold, recite, and chant this profound essential of the Dharma—the fundamental teaching on practice and non-practice—they shall immediately attain the wisdom that is fully endowed with all marks.

When the Buddha spoke this Dharma of practice and non-practice, ten billion nayutas of sentient beings all abandoned their original practices and firm attachments, and advanced toward the stage of non-retrogression in the Buddha Vehicle.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable multitudes of devas and worldlings who had all attained the patience of the Way (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*) and transcended the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*).
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose again from his seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
“I, too, am capable of thoroughly expounding and elucidating the inconceivable Dharma of both practice and non-practice.”
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, son of good family!"
"If you would like to speak, now is the very time.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Now I hear that the Tathāgata encompasses all dharmas within his consciousness, regarding them as both with practice and without practice; yet as I contemplate and examine the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, it is not the case that we śrāvakas possess such practice or lack thereof.

The reason for this is that the faculties of disciples and pratyekabuddhas are already pure and refined; they no longer look toward or aspire to equal and perfect enlightenment, and thus I have no further practice to perform before the Tathāgata.

If the Tathāgata were to abandon the ocean of wisdom and depart from all the various knowledges, seeking instead the path of a disciple or a pratyekabuddha, then the Tathāgata would have no practice toward me.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has said:
"All dharmas are empty and quiescent, without arising, ceasing, attachment, or annihilation.
If this is indeed the case, why then do you restrict disciples and pratyekabuddhas from being included within the category of the noble ones?
Furthermore, as we ninety-two thousand people have all attained the six supernormal powers, our doubts have doubled.
Moreover, we have heard the Buddha say:
"My Dharma is vast and boundless; it does not reckon in terms of 'I' or 'mine,' nor does it cling to sentient beings."
"If it were so, the Tathāgata would today have a deficiency in the pure dharma-realm.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Noble son! You are indeed able to expound this gate before the Tathāgata.
I now question you; you should answer me one by one."
Maudgalyāyana replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
“How is it, Maudgalyāyana? Is there a retribution for action?”
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
Action has its retribution.”
He asked Maudgalyāyana again,
"What is the retribution for one's actions?
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"According to the conditions they encounter, there is a good retribution for good deeds and an evil retribution for evil deeds.
The Buddha asked again: "How is this so?"
“Maudgalyāyana!
Is there a good retribution for good deeds and an evil retribution for evil deeds?
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Undergoing the tortures and beatings of the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties is called an evil retribution;
the eternal stillness of Nirvana, where there is no further birth or extinction, is called a virtuous retribution.
The Buddha again questioned Maudgalyāyana:
“What do you think,
son of good family!
Has the Tathāgata of the present not attained his reward?”
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha asked Maudgalyāyana: "How is it so,
son of good family?"
"Now, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses a body of golden hue and is fully endowed with the various marks; what is the retribution for this?
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying, "This is the retribution for the physical form and the marks of excellence of the Tathāgata; it is not the retribution of Nirvāṇa."
The Buddha asked Maudgalyāyana:
"Is your body nirvāṇa? How do you know that there is a good retribution for good deeds, and that this is the retribution of nirvāṇa?"
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“All dharmas are merely provisional designations; they possess no reality.
That which is called nirvāṇa is likewise but a provisional designation; therefore, it is said that for nirvāṇa there must be good karma for the sake of good.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"For the Tathāgata, there is no 'practice' for you; this too is a provisional designation and not something possessing ultimate reality."
If you wish to seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there is no practice to be found within the Tathāgata, for he is but a provisional designation.
To attempt to differentiate between practice and non-practice within the dharma of provisional designations is not possible.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this Dharma of provisional designations, nine hundred million sentient beings gave rise to the mind of great vows, aspiring to attain the Bodhisattva Necklace of both conditioned practice and unconditioned non-practice.
Furthermore, immeasurable sentient beings attained the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.
Additionally, three hundred million sentient beings, with their outflows exhausted and minds liberated, attained arhatship.
At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola again rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“I am also capable of explaining the Bodhisattva’s Necklace of Practice and Non-practice, so that good men and good women may attain its cultivation.
The World-Honored One said,
“Excellent, excellent!”
“Son of good family!
If you are able to speak, now is precisely the right time.
At that moment, Piṇḍola addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son or daughter of good family, within the stage of the first dhyāna, discerns the foul impurities of the five aggregates and contemplates therein that there is nothing to be grasped or attached to, this is called ‘with practice.

If they enter a state of meditative concentration and contemplate that all things are non-existent, empty, and not real, and observe the bodies of others in the same way, this is called ‘without practice.’”
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a good man or a good woman experiences foul odors and impurities flowing from their current body, this is called "with practice.
To deeply contemplate its beginning and end and know it to be empty, this is called "without practice."
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a son or daughter of good family fulfills the four practices within the stage of the second dhyāna, this is called "with practice";
knowing that the stage of the second dhyāna ultimately reverts to emptiness, this is called "without practice."
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If a good man or a good woman is able to awaken themselves and teach all classes of sentient beings to depart from the pure mind and give rise to the perception of impurity, this is called "with practice.
To understand that the perception of purity is fundamentally non-existent is called "without practice."
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a good man or a good woman contemplates the third dhyāna to purify their afflictions, yet does not praise themselves for what they have accomplished, this is called "with practice.
Not perceiving whether afflictions are eliminated or not, this is called "without practice."
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If a son or daughter of good family, while in the stage of the four dhyānas, contemplates the five aggregates with focused attention and without forgetting, this is called "with practice" (sābhisamskāra).
To discern the four dhyānas as being eternally free from suffering and pleasure, and devoid of all fetters, bonds, and attachments, this is called "without practice" (anabhisamskāra).
"In this way, sons and daughters of good family, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the silent contemplation of the *adornment* (*vinyāsa*) of both conditioned activity and non-activity.
At that time, after the Venerable Piṇḍola had spoken this Dharma, he returned to his original seat.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am now able, before the Tathāgata, to speak of 'action' and 'non-action,' so that the various classes of sentient beings may practice them."
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family does not give rise to doubt regarding the sixteen noble practices, this is called "with practice.
To contemplate that bondage and attachment are by their very nature non-existent, and that even the name "sixteen noble practices" does not exist, is called "without practice."
Kātyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family uproots and severs the dharmas of the three poisons—lust, anger, and delusion—and examines what is being thought within the minds of those sentient beings, being able to distinguish without error whether there is a mind of ignorance or no mind of ignorance, a mind of craving or no mind of craving, and a mind of malice or no mind of malice, this is called 'with practice' (sābhoga).

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family contemplates and knows that the three poisons are fundamentally non-existent, seeing neither one who arises nor one who ceases, as they are empty, quiescent, and formless, this is called 'without practice' (anābhoga)."
Kātyāyanīputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family brings all the aggregates of fetters (saṃyojana-skandha) to ultimate cessation and no longer creates or gives rise to afflictions (kleśa), this is called 'with practice' (sābhisamskāra).

If one does not perceive within the fetters anything that is either ultimately ceased or not ultimately ceased, and likewise does not create or give rise to the suffering of afflictions, this is called 'without practice' (anabhisamskāra)."
"In this way, good sons and good daughters, for the Bodhisattva’s *ābharaṇa* (ornament), there is both practice and non-practice.
After Kātyāyanīputra had spoken these words on practice and non-practice before the Buddha, he rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and returned to his original seat.
At that time, the Venerable Revata rose from his seat, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, am capable of expounding upon the Bodhisattva’s *ābharaṇa* (ornament) regarding both practice and non-practice.”
The Buddha said to Revata,
"If you are capable of speaking, then speak.
