Holding the torch of the Four Noble Truths, He illuminates the root of that ignorance;
Constantly contemplating that there is no permanence, He reflects on removing the disease of fetters.
The number of kalpas has no end; It is inexhaustible, yet not subject to exhaustion.
It is only because sentient beings are deluded that they wish to know the original absence of mind.
Now, one who wishes to study must first hear and receive the profound and subtle Dharma;
this is not something that can be fathomed by the practices of the Two Vehicles.
The Buddha originally made a vow to himself, To eliminate the abyss of the five realms of existence;
Through the completion of his practice by means of an impartial mind, He is thus titled the Honored One among Men.
The Buddha’s wisdom has no boundaries, And his divine intelligence is immeasurable.
Not taking bodily suffering as fundamental, one eternally eliminates the hardships of the three periods of time.
This is the jeweled necklace dharma of all Buddhas, realized through self-awakening without receiving it from a teacher;
with a mind as stable as space, one constantly contemplates the perception of bliss.
For countless eons I have followed [the path], entering meditative concentration without departing from emptiness;
with a single mind I have perfected the One Way, and thus I am called the Honored One among Men.
Furthermore, for countless eons, I have served all the World-Honored Ones.
Exhausting all births, they attain non-attachment, And personally realize supreme perfect enlightenment.

The Buddhas appear in the world to transform beings; In the joy of practicing the Path of the True Dharma, They are able to purify all Buddha-lands, Unstained by the pleasures of the three realms of existence.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One further addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who uphold and practice the five inconceivable and profound dharmas, all the Buddhas of the ten directions will come to protect them, and no māras shall be able to find an opportunity against them."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the bodhicitta, they should practice five inconceivable dharmas."
What are the five? First, to universally bestow one’s own concentrated mind upon all sentient beings, so that they all abide in the state of Buddhahood without falling back;
second, not to rely on the three paths while receiving the realization of the fruit.
Third, immeasurable oceans of dharmas all manifest before them;
fourth, they possess the wisdom and eloquence that fully realize the dharma-gates of manifold characteristics;
fifth, through the transformation of their bodies to teach and convert others, they attain the wisdom of the six perfections.
"O son of noble family! This is called:
from the first generation of the resolve to practice the bodhisattva mind, by practicing these five inconceivable dharmas, one is able to fully perfect all the practices of a Tathāgata."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:
"If there are good sons or good daughters who contemplate and discern the five fundamental dharmas of suffering. What are these five?
First, by discerning the nature of form, one does not give rise to attachment toward consciousness;
second, by contemplating the hundred and eight pains, one finds neither suffering nor pleasure;
third, by forever severing all conceptualizations, one does not give rise to a distracted mind.
Fourth, understanding that the twelve links of dependent origination are fundamentally without this practice;
fifth, knowing that the consciousness-spirit is formless and cannot be exhausted.
These, O Bodhisattva Samacārin, are called [the five practices].

If a son or daughter of good family contemplates and discerns the fundamental nature of the five types of suffering, they will draw near to the Buddha-treasury and not depart from the source of the path of the assembly of sages and saints.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, cultivates the bodhicitta, there are furthermore five dharmas that are inexhaustible."
What are the five? First, his countless meritorious achievements are inexhaustible;
second, his eighty-four types of wisdom are inexhaustible.
Third, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the Dharma is inexhaustible;
fourth, the essential concentration on all phenomena is inexhaustible;
fifth, the eightfold melodic resonance is inexhaustible.
Thus it is said, O Samacārin Bodhisattva!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from the first generation of the mind, cultivates the bodhicitta and practices these five dharmas without end, they will be able to fully perfect the dharmas of a Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, cultivates the bodhicitta and practices the inconceivable Dharma of the six perfections.”
What are the six?

In this regard, good sons and good daughters do not begrudge their own bodies or lives; they comply with whatever is requested before them without opposing anyone's wishes, thereby fulfilling the *pāramitā* of giving (*dāna*).

Although he possesses the perfection of giving, he upholds those who observe the precepts and does not allow their nature of discipline to be destroyed; seeing those who are violent and rebellious, he exhorts them toward patience.
If people are indolent, he exhorts them toward diligence.

There may be sentient beings who are attached to the sixty-two views, whose minds are disordered, and who do not recognize emptiness, *nirvāṇa*, or the Great Way; [the Buddha] gathers those sentient beings into a single-minded meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), removes their distracted thoughts, and prevents the arising of dualistic views.

“Or there may be sentient beings who dwell forever in darkness, harboring minds of ignorance; by means of skillful expedients, one gathers in those sentient beings and causes them to see the light of wisdom.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:
“If there are good sons or good daughters who, from their first aspiration, cultivate the bodhicitta, they shall, within a single perfection, fulfill all six perfections of the infinite.”
How can one fulfill the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) within a single perfection?

There may be sentient beings who, with a single mind, uphold the precepts without violating their nature of discipline; within this upholding of the precepts, they fully realize generosity, and without disparaging those who receive their gifts, they constantly practice patience.

If there are sentient beings who see themselves being insulted or humiliated, they do not give rise to disordered thoughts or a mind of anger; day and night they apply themselves with diligence and without indolence.

Although they uphold the prohibitive precepts, their concentrated mind remains undisturbed; within the nature of the precepts, they do not neglect dhyāna, and they propagate wisdom to eliminate the mind of ignorance and darkness. This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the precepts (śīla-pāramitā), by which they are able to fully realize all six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who, from their first aspiration, cultivate the bodhicitta and attain the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), subduing their minds and thoughts so as not to harbor pride, they should further fulfill the six perfections within that perfection of patience."
One practices giving without abandoning the mind of patience; although there is something given, one does not give rise to conceptual attachments.
Within this, one fulfills the nature of the precepts: even if others strike or assault one, one does not give rise to distracted thoughts, but instead restrains and collects the mind.

They fully cultivate the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) and, with a concentrated mind, do not violate the dharma of meditation (*dhyāna*). Within the perfection of patience, they fulfill the practice of meditation.

Furthermore, if a good man or good woman has already attained the perfection of patience, they discern the arising of the formation and destruction of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); they contemplate the three poisons (*triviṣa*) and know them to arise from delusion and craving; and through the wisdom of the Path (*mārga-prajñā*), they observe that ultimately nothing is produced.
"This is called the way in which good sons and good daughters fulfill the six perfections within the perfection of patience.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who, from their first aspiration, cultivate the bodhicitta, they should further fulfill the six perfections within meditative concentration, gathering in sentient beings and eliminating their distracted thoughts."
How does a bodhisattva fulfill the six perfections within meditative concentration?

In this regard, a son or daughter of good family contemplates the empty nature of the body and perceives neither its arising nor its cessation; with a concentrated mind free from distraction, they practice giving. They perceive neither sentient beings nor material wealth, nor do they give rise to the thought:
"I shall now receive a great reward for what I have given," or "The adornment of the Buddha-land was originally not pure."
"One will then be able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Samacaryā:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who, from the first production of the thought [of awakening], cultivate the bodhisattva mind, they shall fulfill the six perfections within the perfection of wisdom."
How do good sons and good daughters fulfill the six perfections within the perfection of wisdom?

In this regard, when good sons and good daughters have already cultivated the perfection of wisdom, they discern the absence of conceptualization and the lack of other divergent practices; they individually discern the bodies of names and the bodies of phrases; they restrain their minds and maintain the precepts without violating the nature of the precepts; and even if others insult or humiliate them, they harbor no grief or resentment. This is called fulfilling the nature of the precepts within wisdom.

Furthermore, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices patience within the perfection of wisdom, their mind being like space and not receiving any defilement or evil, this is called attaining the mind of patience within the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family attains the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), restrains the mind with diligence, and abandons the mind of indolence; if they discern that the realm of the eye is inconceivable and, seeing those who are indolent, exhort them toward diligence—this is called being fully endowed with diligence within the perfection of wisdom."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:

"If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who attain the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), whose minds remain undistracted in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā), and who for a hundred thousand kalpas maintain a single-minded focus and a single thought, subduing their own minds through self-mastery, and who thoroughly discern all thirty-six perfections—this, O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samacārin, is called [the perfection of wisdom]."
"The root and source of all practices.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking these words to the Bodhisattva Samacārin, there were immeasurable sentient beings who had originally resolved their minds to pursue the path of the Pratyekabuddha; now they all turned their intentions toward the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path.
Furthermore, there were countless devas and worldlings who attained the practice of ultimate faith and did not depart from the Mahāyāna.
*The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Scroll Nine.
*The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Scroll Ten, titled "Present Retribution."
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-nine: The Assembly of Worthies and Sages (10). Chapter Twenty-nine: The Assembly of Worthies and Sages.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vicārin rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, am capable of proclaiming the pure practices of the six perfections.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Pravicaya:
"If you are capable, you may speak before the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vicaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who cultivate the pure dharmas of the six perfections and concurrently practice the various Buddha-prohibited dharmas of the eight gates, these good sons and good daughters will possess the complete and pure conduct regarding the dharmas of the six perfections.
The Bodhisattva Pure Intention addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to pay homage to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions, and who receive the true teaching to cultivate and practice it, such sons and daughters of good family will be fully endowed with purity in the Dharma of the six perfections.”
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there are good sons or good daughters who sever all fetters and afflictions so that no defilement arises, they will be fully perfected in the purity of the six perfections.”
The Bodhisattva Pure Dharma Realm addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are good sons or good daughters who understand the spontaneous nature of dharmas and do not destroy the gateway to the Way, they will fully possess purity in the six perfections."
The Bodhisattva Skillfully Understanding Illusion addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there are good sons or good daughters who, by discerning the eight worldly dharmas, eliminate honor and disgrace, and who are pure and complete in the dharma of the six perfections.”
The Bodhisattva Overmeasure addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, amidst the great assembly, turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, restraining their body, speech, and mind without any other distracting thoughts, and being fully perfected in the purity of the six perfections;”
The Bodhisattva Dharmākara addressed the Buddha, saying:

“To understand the four formless concentrations (ārūpyasamādhi) and be free from the notions of self and person, and to contemplate the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) without destroying the root of wisdom—this is called the complete purity of the six perfections.”
The Bodhisattva Pure Mind addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there are good men or good women who restrain the faculty of the eye and do not give rise to perceptions of consciousness, and likewise with the ear, nose, body, tongue, and mind, they will fully perfect the purity of the six perfections.”
The General Siṃha addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Sentient beings are submerged and obscured, dwelling forever in the darkness; may you spread forth the light of wisdom so that they may know the path to enlightenment, and may they become pure and complete in the Dharma of the six perfections.”
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Prajñācakṣus who asked Mañjuśrī:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva restrain body, speech, and mind so as not to violate the nature of the precepts, and become fully perfected in the purity of the six perfections?"
At that time, Mañjuśrī replied to Prajñācakṣus Bodhisattva:
“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas understand emptiness and non-self; they give gifts without expectation of reward, and they are fully perfected in the purity of the six perfections.”
The Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus asked again:
"How is this so, noble son?"

The Tathāgata’s form-body is fully endowed with all virtues, possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; his body is golden in color, like a heap of gold—is this a retribution born of conceptual thought?
"Is it a retribution of non-conception?
Mañjuśrī replied to Prajñācakṣus Bodhisattva, "The Tathāgata’s form-body (rūpakāya) is a retribution of conception; the Tathāgata’s dharma-body (dharmakāya) is a retribution of non-conception."
The Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus asked again:

"By giving away one's greedy seeking and purifying the inner mind, and by removing conceptual attachments, one attains the great fruit; yet the Dharma of the six perfections does not consist of a reward of non-conceptualization."
"How, then, is the retribution of the Dharmakāya accomplished?
At that time, Mañjuśrī replied to Prajñācakṣus Bodhisattva: "How so?"
"Noble son! Is the Tathāgata’s form-body existent,
or is it non-existent?"
The Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus replied:

"As the son of good family has said, the Tathāgata’s form-body (rūpakāya) is retribution-born and not non-retribution-born; yet, as I observe the body of the Tathāgata, it is neither retribution-born nor non-retribution-born."
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked again:
"In what way is the body of the Tathāgata neither retributive nor non-retributive?
Prajñācakṣus replied to Mañjuśrī:

"The body of the Tathāgata is endowed with a multitude of merits; adorned with exquisite form, one never tires of beholding it. All who see his physical form give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; this is called the retribution of the form-body."
What is meant by the Tathāgata’s form-body being without retribution? In this regard, noble son!

When the Tathāgata has finished his teaching while in the world, he withdraws his spirit into non-action, never undergoing change; possessing a single mark yet being formless, it cannot be obstructed or destroyed. This is called the Tathāgata’s form-body being without retribution.
At that time, Mañjuśrī again asked the Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus: "How is it so,
son of good family?"
"The physical form and characteristics of the Tathāgata are inconceivable;
is it because he possesses form that there is no retribution, or is it because he lacks form that there is no retribution? Wisdom-Eye replied:
“The body of the Tathāgata may have form yet lack retribution, or it may be formless and lack retribution.
What is meant by having form yet lacking retribution?

When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, dwells in the world to teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain the realization of the fruit and obtain the path of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)—this is called the Tathāgata’s material body having form yet lacking retribution.”
What is meant by "formless and without retribution"?

In this regard, while the Tathāgata’s physical body (rūpakāya) was in the world teaching and transforming beings, he manifested transformations of supernormal power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) and finally completed his preaching of the Dharma; then, within the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*), he attained parinirvāṇa. This is called the Tathāgata’s physical body being formless and without retribution.

At that time, Mañjuśrī knew that within the minds of all those sentient beings there were various doubts, and they had not yet been able to fully comprehend whether there is retribution or no retribution.
He asked again the Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus: "How is it so,
son of good family?"

The physical body of the Tathāgata is like an illusion and like a magical transformation; how can there be non-retribution within such illusory and transformative phenomena, yet all sentient beings attain the purity of the fruit of the Path through the nature of dharmas?
"If it is subsumed within the realm of the eye, how can it be that within the nature of the path of sentient beings it receives no retribution?

He further asked the Wisdom Eye: "The physical body of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; when his teaching of the Dharma has concluded, he enters quiescent parinirvāṇa, free from birth, old age, sickness, and death. Having already relinquished the physical body, he no longer assumes a form; he is of one mark yet markless, and thus invisible. Even the provisional designations established for him lack any ultimate reality."
“The Tathāgata is neither a Tathāgata nor a Buddha; how then, by means of the unconditioned path, can this physical body of the Tathāgata be without retribution? Mañjuśrī asked again: “How so?”
Son of good family!
The Tathāgata’s form-body is an unconditioned retribution, and nirvāṇa is an unconditioned retribution. Are these one or different?
If they were one, there would be no Tathāgata; how then could there be such a thing as "unretribution"?
"If these two non-existences were present, then the Tathāgata’s form-body would not be the retribution of Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Huiyan replied to Mañjuśrī, saying:

"Fundamentally, there is no form-body of the four great elements belonging to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; yet within the present dharma, it is both with retribution and without retribution, for its extinction in Nirvāṇa is called 'without retribution.'"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus replied again to Mañjuśrī:

“Regarding the practice of the six perfections by sentient beings, if a person practices giving yet has no thought of giving, and furthermore does not perceive anyone who receives the gift, this is called the perfection of the perfection of giving.”

Furthermore, if there is a person who is fully endowed with the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) and does not violate the precepts, yet does not perceive even one who maintains ethical discipline—this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) through the fullness of ethical discipline.
The Bodhisattva Wisdom-Eye spoke again to Mañjuśrī:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who constantly cultivate patience, who do not give rise to arrogance when encountering those who treat them with contempt, and who do not even conceive the thought that they possess patience, this is called being fully endowed with the perfection of patience."

If there are good sons or good daughters who apply themselves with diligent vigor to cultivate the sixteen noble practices, yet do not perceive anyone else as being diligently vigorous, this is called the perfection of the practice of vigor.
The Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus spoke again to Mañjuśrī:

"If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, having restrained the mind and entered meditative concentration, discerns the three contemplations, yet does not perceive anyone who has established that concentrated mind; and whose mind travels through the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions to serve and make offerings, observing all dharmas as being like illusions and transformations—this is called the perfection of the pāramitā of dhyāna."
The Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus spoke again to Mañjuśrī:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family proclaims the Tathāgata’s immeasurable dharma-realm, the purity of the eye-consciousness is inconceivable; yet, when each and every part is analyzed, none of it exists at all.”
If the ear hears sounds, it knows whence they come; if the nose smells fragrances, it knows whence they come—discerning each one individually, yet finding nothing therein.
If the tongue tastes flavors, it knows whence they come.
“The Tathāgata’s mental consciousness discriminates all dharmas with immeasurable spiritual power; this is called being fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus again addressed Mañjuśrī:

“Furthermore, there is a meditative concentration named the ‘Inexhaustible Dharma Gate. A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who attains this Inexhaustible Dharma Gate transcends the Three Vehicles and achieves the title of Bodhisattva.”
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Contemplation; when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain this Dharma-gate, they contemplate the Dharma-realm and do not abide in the two stages.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Form and Image; when Bodhisattvas attain this Dharma-gate, they accomplish the inexhaustible treasury of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-retrogression; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate transforms the pure Dharma so as not to perceive forms or images.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Vast Salvation; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate transforms those sentient beings without acting for their own sake.
Furthermore, there is the Buddha-dharma gate of Universal Resonance; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma gate rains down the nectar of the Dharma to moisten and nourish all beings.

Furthermore, there is the dharma gate of the Realm of All Buddhas; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma gate manifests and expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Manifesting the Teaching; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door adorns buddha-lands and achieves a retinue of followers.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of the Peerless; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door discerns the profound and abstruse meanings of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Essential Dharmas; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door proclaims and expounds the inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Roots of Goodness; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door discriminates the various faculties and forever leaves behind the five realms of existence.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Illusory Transformation; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate discerns the inexhaustible and vast Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Gathering Practices; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate discerns the meaning of phrases as being without form or image.
"Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of 'Accordance. Bodhisattvas who attain this Dharma-door are able to satisfy those who hold false conceptions.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of 'Attaining the Intention. Bodhisattvas who attain this Dharma-door bring their roots of goodness to full maturity and obtain the four fearlessnesses."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Ocean of Dharmas; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate is fully endowed with virtuous karma and does not abandon the nature of the Way.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Radiant Flames; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate universally manifests radiant flames to expound the Dharma inexhaustibly.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Divine Power (*ṛddhi*); a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate travels extensively through all realms without being defiled by the three paths.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Radiance of the Sun and Moon; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate shines universally upon those in suffering and affliction, delivering and liberating them.
"Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-arising; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate employs skillful means to guide and transform others, naturally flowing toward the ford.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Infinite Wisdom; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate transcends the afflictions of the triple world and perceives no one to be delivered."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Arising of Wisdom; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate fully knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-Attachment; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate dispels all darkness with the light of wisdom.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Fundamental Source; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate discerns the inconceivable practices of the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Dependent Origination; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate discerns the root of the twelve modes of deluded conduct.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Path-Wisdom; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate is not deficient in the three equalities of the Dharmatā Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Patience-Wisdom; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate sits beneath the King of Trees and subdues the palace of Māra.
"Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Great Vow; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate does not abandon sentient beings while seeking their own extinction.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Ascetic Practice; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate manifests the eating of sesame and rice, thereby perfecting all practices."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Solitary Pacing; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate manifests wonders of his own accord, such that none can equal him.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Purity of Mind; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate eliminates the defilements of the mind and remains free from all attachment.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Ultimateity; those Bodhisattvas who attain this Dharma-gate cause all sentient beings to enter and emerge from the essential path.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Desirelessness; those Bodhisattvas who attain this Dharma-gate eliminate greedy attachment and possess a mind free from defilement.
“Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Realm of Dharmas; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate takes pity on all beings and does not forsake their original vows.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Path of Practice; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate discerns the various faculties and establishes the dharmas of a superior person.”
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Non-retrogressive Mind; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate establishes themselves in non-retrogression upon generating the mind of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-Treasury; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate purifies their path-wisdom and realizes the fruit of wisdom.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Path of Transformation; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate gives rise to the mind of non-arising and perceives neither movement nor return.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-Necklace; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate adorns the Buddha-lands and purifies sentient beings.
“Furthermore, there is a profound dharma-gate; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate enters deeply into the treasury of the Dharma and is endowed with the seven factors of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of fearlessness; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate abides securely in all dharmas and expounds the conduct of the worthy and the noble.”
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Removing Defilements; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate abides peacefully in all phenomena without any attachment or defilement.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Pure Conduct; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate discerns the three gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Dharmakāya; the bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate discerns all practices of non-attachment and emptiness.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Power of Dharma; the bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate acquires great wisdom within the immeasurable realm of space.
"Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-obstruction; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate expounds the Way and its teachings without any hindrance.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Great Compassion; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate moistens and benefits all beings without abandoning their deluded thoughts."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Great Compassion; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate delivers others from suffering and hardship without giving rise to worldly afflictions.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Joyful Mind; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate eliminates all anger and resentment.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Protecting the Mind; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate discerns the non-dual nature of the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Extensive Giving; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate eliminates the three perceptions and does not reckon in terms of a self.
"Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of supernatural powers; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate travels extensively through immeasurable worlds in the ten directions.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of inexhaustibility; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate discerns the meanings and purports and cultivates the dharma of the three phrases."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Expounding and Elucidating; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door is fully endowed with merit because they embrace and bring forth the Way.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Purity; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door purifies verbal transgressions and does not give rise to the ten non-virtuous actions.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Ten Powers; the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate holds a vajra-mind that cannot be destroyed or defeated.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Immeasurable Roots of Goodness; the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate is then able to fully possess the supernatural powers of a Tathāgata.
“Furthermore, there is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gate of the Extinction of Practice; when a bodhisattva attains this Dharma-gate, they do not give rise to notions of self, person, or life-span.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Quiescence of the Mind; when a bodhisattva attains this Dharma-gate, they forever sever the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.”
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Augmentation; the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate causes all virtuous merits to increase day by day.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Joy; the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate satisfies all those who thirst for and yearn after the Way.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-Anger; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate eliminates mental attachments and is free from inverted perceptions.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Aspiration; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate accomplishes the three fundamental practices for maturing sentient beings.
"Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-thought; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate causes all sentient beings to be free from the thoughts of the three poisons.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Meaning of Dharmas; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate gives rise to all dharmas without losing their proper sequence."
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of swift action; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate discerns the fundamental roots and accomplishes the traces of the path to enlightenment.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of contemplation; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate discerns the impurities within and without.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Fragrant Incense; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate shall universally permeate all things with the fragrance of the virtue of their precepts.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Skillful Expedients; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate transforms beings according to their forms and circumstances, such that no one perceives themselves as being saved.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Illuminating Understanding; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate distinguishes sounds and voices to deliver beings.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-Self; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate understands that all phenomena are empty and non-existent.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of "Abiding Well. Bodhisattvas who attain this Dharma-door possess firm and resolute vows, such that their minds do not waver or shift.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of "Innumerable Bodies. Bodhisattvas who attain this Dharma-door distinguish each [being] individually, without limiting themselves to sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Skillful Entry; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door transforms all sentient beings so that they enter the laws and regulations.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Sovereignty over Dharmas; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door is capable of receiving the True Dharma and does not feel shame in asking humble questions.
"Furthermore, there is a pure and wondrous Dharma-door; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door wanders through the lands of all Buddhas without harboring any timidity.
Furthermore, there is a peerless Dharma-door; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door finds joy in inner stillness and does not disturb any being."
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of immeasurable merit; bodhisattvas who attain this dharma-gate achieve a retinue and obtain the fruit of the true retribution.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of emitting light.
A bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate universally illuminates all that lies in darkness.
Furthermore, there is the dharma-gate of non-deception; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate is fully endowed with verbal conduct and does not commit the four transgressions.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Encouraging Virtue; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate takes pity on those who have not yet reached it and rains down the Dharma of Immortality.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Reliance; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate causes all sentient beings to have a place of refuge.
“Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate called ‘Extraction and Rescue. Bodhisattvas who attain this dharma-gate increase their merit, and their minds become pure like space.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate called ‘The Boundless. Bodhisattvas who attain this dharma-gate do not perceive anyone who is being delivered or anyone who has attained accomplishment.”
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Equal Practice; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door distinguishes all forms of wisdom without limit.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Equality; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door does not speak of various vehicles within the different paths.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of the single intention; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate does not perceive anyone who generates the intention to enter the Way.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of empty space; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate enters into various states of meditative equipoise with an undistracted mind.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Blazing Radiance; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door extensively expounds all inexhaustible teachings.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Discerning the Dharma-realm; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door discerns, one by one, that which arises within the Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Transcending Boundaries; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate rescues and protects all beings, enabling them to reach the other shore.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Ultimate Realization; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate perceives no nesting place from which all phenomena arise.
"Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Pure Contemplation; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate does not disparage sentient beings when seeing the pure Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Fulfillment; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate does not regard the number of kalpas as being distant."
Furthermore, there is a Dharma-gate of transcendence; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate practices for all-knowledge without giving rise to the notion of dharmas.
Furthermore, there is a Dharma-gate of origination; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate brings forth the profound and subtle meaning of all dharmas.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of sharp faculties; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate hears the path of the single destination and establishes themselves in non-retrogression.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of sequential progression; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate cultivates all dharmas without losing their fundamental essentials.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Characteristics of Phenomena; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate discerns the characteristics of all phenomena one by one.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Formless Phenomena; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate has all phenomena manifest before them.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Counting of Kalpas; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate perseveres in ascetic practices and does not abandon birth and death.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Practice of the Path; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate contemplates the five elements and the perception of impurity.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Profound Entry; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door enters deeply into the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma-jewels.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Transformation and Guidance; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door nurtures and sustains all classes of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of coming and going; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door circulates through the world to teach and transform others with a mind free from indolence.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of accomplishment; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door brings the fruits of the Path to maturity while not abandoning the five realms of existence.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Penetrating Illumination; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate enters meditative concentration with a single mind, free from manifold perceptions.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Immeasurability; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate finds that the multitude of dharmas they practice is inconceivable.
Furthermore, there is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gate of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate practices the immeasurable conduct of emptiness in the present.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the responsive echo; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate fulfills all vows and forever eliminates conceptual thought.
"Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Transformation; the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate can manifest bodies and disperse forms according to their free aspirations.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-deficiency; the Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate thoroughly purifies the intentions and thoughts of the minds of sentient beings."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of penetrating the coming and going; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door purifies the realms of sentient beings from every single pore.
Furthermore, there is the Formless Dharma-door; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door teaches and transforms the formless realm of phenomena, making it pure.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of Non-obstruction; any Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door causes immeasurable sentient beings to transcend the four types of impermanence.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of the Sound of Suffering; any Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-door causes sentient beings habituated to suffering to forever leave behind their fetters and attachments.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Sound of Habituation; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate causes sentient beings bound by attachments to forever leave behind the traces of habituation.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Sound of Exhaustion; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate causes sentient beings within the realm of existence to reach inexhaustible Nirvana.
"Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Sound of the Path; if a bodhisattva attains this Dharma-gate, they will not give rise to the sixty-two types of afflictions.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Dignified Conduct; if a bodhisattva attains this Dharma-gate, they will never lose proper decorum in their advancing, halting, walking, or coming."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of True Nature; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate distinguishes his retinue and does not dwell in lowliness.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Direct Gaze; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate distinguishes the five aggregates and proceeds single-mindedly toward the Way.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Celestial Conduct; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate enters among devas and humans to cultivate the foundation of purity.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Human Conduct; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate enters among the beings of the human realm to guide and encourage them toward liberation.

Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of practicing among animals; those Bodhisattvas who attain this Dharma-door enter among them in accordance with their forms to transform them, so that all return to the gateway of the Way.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-door of hungry ghosts; those Bodhisattvas who attain this Dharma-door exhort them to eliminate greed and to have no expectations.
Furthermore, there is a Dharma-gate of the hells; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate manifests their body within the hells to transform beings and cause them to give rise to wholesome minds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wisdom-Eye (Prajñācakṣus) spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“Unattached and incapable of being defiled, Untainted by the existence of the three realms,”
The fragrance of virtue purifies all; the gateways of Dharma are inexhaustible.
The eight hundred practices of the six perfections were proclaimed by the Hero of the World;
he discerns the minds of sentient beings, whose inclinations and interests differ from one another.
Possessing immeasurable roots of virtue, you manifest expediently within the mundane world;
having spread the teachings of the Good Path, you have transcended to the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Today, with great compassion, you expound the Dharma without end.
The Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Expounded the Dharma just as they do now.
By cultivating meritorious deeds and the five virtues, They subdue those with inverted views;
The reward of the form-body being no-body Is the profound and secret treasury of all Buddhas.
There is no retribution, nor is there non-retribution; the nature of nirvāṇa is inherently empty.
Sentient beings give rise to thoughts of their own accord, dwelling their minds on retribution and non-retribution.
By eliminating discriminative conceptions through practice and contemplating the deeds of the Tathāgata, [one realizes this].
Neither arising nor non-arising, it is thus the gateway of the Bodhisattva.
The teaching of the Dharma is not a substantial dharma, nor is there any notion of a sentient being;
delighting in the thought of departure and abandoning the thought of suffering, birth and cessation are forever stilled.
The resonance of merit responds spontaneously, like space, free from attachment;
with a single mind one achieves perfect enlightenment, and the retribution of form becomes its locus.
Ruling over the heavens and the world, the True Truth is inexhaustible.
Entering meditative concentration, one manifests impermanence; ultimately, all returns to the source of cessation.
The mind of the Way is neither within nor without;
through various thoughts on the perception of suffering, one seeks the Way to exhaust its very root and origin.
Contemplating hundreds of thousands of concentrations, life after life, never ceasing;
when the mind is bound, the heart is severed— how could distracted thoughts arise?
The practices undertaken by Bodhisattvas are each different according to their Dharma-gates.
If you seek the immeasurable Dharma, you should seek it within sentient beings.
Phenomenon after phenomenon arises spontaneously; the wisdom of phenomena has no nesting place.
Seeking the origin of arising, one finds it is originally non-arising; how then can there be a fundamental source for phenomena?
Having accumulated wisdom for more than a hundred eons, Cultivating insight without indolence, And advancing to perfect the eightfold noble path, He is therefore called the Honored One among Men.
There is retribution, yet no retribution; Nor is there the mark of a physical body.
Adorned with the various karmas of wisdom, he manifests his body to teach and transform the mundane world.
His inner and outer appearance are like purple-gold; his voice is exceedingly gentle and soothing.
What he speaks is never in vain, and all who hear it attain liberation.
I am like the light of a firefly; it illuminates itself but benefits nothing else.
The Buddha-sun shines upon the great trichiliocosm, leaving no place in its vast darkness unknown.
How could I dare hope to increase the moisture of the rivers and seas with a mere drop of morning dew?
Relying upon the majestic power of the Great Sage Buddha, I shall now expound the gateway of the Bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattvas radiate the light of wisdom, Permanently eliminating the darkness of sentient beings;
They uproot the source of ignorance and delusion, So that the path of the sages lies before them.

**Chapter 30: The Three Paths and the Three Vehicles (10)** *The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Chapter Thirty: The Three Paths and the Three Vehicles* At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

“Observe this Bodhisattva Huiyan (Wisdom-Eye). Having attained the four kinds of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*) and mastery over all wisdoms, he has cultivated mental concentration (*citta-samādhi*). Amidst this great assembly, he expounds upon the profound and abstruse dharmas of the bodhisattvas.”
"How long will it be before this bodhisattva attains equal and perfect enlightenment?
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The vision of us śrāvakas is meager and slight; how could we possibly fathom the scriptural canon of the Great Sage?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and disseminate the transformative teachings of the Way, so that all those gathered here may hear its essentials.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
I shall proclaim the essential core for you."
Śāriputra said: “So it is, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"To the northwest of here, at a distance of fourteen *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges], there is a buddha-field named Viśvajñānavaśitā. There, the Buddha is named Prajñākṛta Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."
That Buddha-Tathāgata first resolved his mind upon the Way with a vastness that knows no bounds, surpassing all the various saints who have received individual predictions.
That Buddha-Tathāgata gave rise to this heart of great vows:
"When I attain Buddhahood and depart from birth and death, may I not dwell amidst the clamor of the five turbidities in their boiling surge; let my land be pure and without flaw."
"Once I have attained Buddhahood, my retinue shall be perfected, such that men and women shall each remain distinct and free from lustful desires.
He further made this vow:

"May all sentient beings in my land illuminate one another with their own radiance, such that there is no need for the light of the sun, moon, or stars; and may my land be adorned with the seven treasures—crystal, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, amber, gold, and silver."

May my land be as one with water and milk; may my realm possess a single bathing pool like that of the four continents, where wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks, all with bodies made of the seven treasures, warble in harmony with one another in mutual delight.

The place where the water flows from the eastern mouth of the bathing pool is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth; the southern mouth of the bathing pool is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth; the western mouth of the bathing pool is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth; and the northern mouth of the bathing pool is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. In the center of the bathing pool, there is a natural high seat made of the seven precious substances, measuring one thousand yojanas in height, width, and depth.

The Mahāyāna bodhisattvas from the immeasurable, limitless, and boundless lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, who have sat beneath the king of trees to forever sever the fetters of the mind, subdue the palaces of Māra, and accomplish the unsurpassed path—on that very day, they came to this world-system, proceeded to my bathing pool, ascended the seven-jeweled throne, and expounded the Mahāyāna practice of non-retrogression.
May all those who follow the Mahāyāna and have made great vows come to my land, so that in my realm there shall be no Mahāyāna bodhisattvas, no Mahāyāna pratyekabuddhas, and no Mahāyāna śrāvakas.
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:

"This Bodhisattva Huiyan now possesses a firm resolve in the Mahāyāna that is difficult to thwart or destroy; he shall be born in that land, attain equal and perfect enlightenment, and teach and transform sentient beings without end."

The lifespan of the people in that land is uniform for all, and none suffer premature death; if one wishes to know their life span, it is like that of the Buddha-lands of the Buddhas of Immeasurable Life. However, the male and female sentient beings there do not attain the Way as readily as those in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

At that time, Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; the entire assembly likewise harbored doubts. He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

Now that I have heard the Tathāgata expound upon the practices of non-retrogression in the Mahāyāna, and how the Mahāyāna retinue brings about the perfection of one’s own buddha-field, I wish most earnestly to hear this.
What constitutes a Mahāyāna bodhisattva?
"What is a Mahāyāna pratyekabuddha? What is a Mahāyāna śrāvaka?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Bodhisattvas have three vehicles, each with its own three grades; pratyekabuddhas also have three vehicles with their own three grades; and śrāvakas likewise have three vehicles with their own three grades.
In this regard, Śāriputra!”
If you wish to know the three vehicles of the bodhisattvas, I shall now explain them to you.
There is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva, the Pratyekabuddhayāna of the bodhisattva, and the Śrāvakayāna of the bodhisattva; these are called the three vehicles of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Regarding the three vehicles of the pratyekabuddha, there is the Great Vehicle of the pratyekabuddha-bodhisattva, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha-bodhisattva-pratyekabuddha, and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha-bodhisattva-śrāvaka; these are called the three vehicles of the pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding the three vehicles of the śrāvakas, there is the śrāvaka Mahāyāna, the śrāvaka Pratyekabuddhayāna, and the śrāvaka Anāsravayāna; these are called the three vehicles of the śrāvakas.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The land where Bodhisattvas with the wisdom-eye are born is precisely the realm of the Tathāgata Hui-zao (Wisdom-Creation).

If there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who give rise to the heart of great vows and do not delight in the Lesser Vehicle, they shall all be born in that land of Hui-zao, provided they fulfill their aspirations as described above."
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas for bodhisattvas?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"To the northwest of here, having passed beyond fourteen Ganges-river-sands of world-systems, and further passing beyond another fourteen Ganges-river-sands of world-systems, there is a buddha-field named Pure Tranquility (Jìngtài). There resides a Buddha named Akṣobhya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles."

The land is pure and free from lust, anger, and delusion; those above and below are respectful and submissive, valuing the cultivation of purity and emptiness. The sentient beings of that land all practice a single path, universally leaving the household life to study the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, cultivating equal enlightenment.

In the realm of that Buddha, there is a bathing pool, one Buddha-world in length and breadth. The eastern opening of the pool extends for hundreds of thousands of myriads of yojanas; the southern opening of the pool extends for hundreds of thousands of myriads of yojanas; the western opening of the pool extends for hundreds of thousands of myriads of yojanas; and the northern opening of the pool extends for hundreds of thousands of myriads of yojanas.
All those bodhisattvas who practice the Mahāyāna path of the pratyekabuddhas will be born in that land.

Hundreds and thousands of species of extraordinary and wondrous birds frolic within its ponds, while various fragrant incenses pervade the world; there grow trees made of the seven treasures, their flowers and fruits pure and fragrant.
In the waters of that pond, blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka) all grow within the water.

In the center of the pond there is a high seat made of the seven treasures, its length, breadth, and height exceeding the realms of sentient beings and encompassing all the abodes of the worthy and the holy.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
In that Buddha-land, there is no Bodhisattva Mahāyāna; there is only the Bodhisattva Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.

Why is this? It is because they are all born there by virtue of their past vows, where they distinguish the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas), delighting in one another and propagating the teachings of the Way.
"Thus it is said, son of good family!
This is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas; it is not something that can be reached by Bodhisattvas of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to Śāriputra:
“The Tathāgata is inconceivable, and all phenomena are each distinct;
the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas’ Mahāyāna and their buddha-fields are likewise diverse.
Yet the noble ones of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle are universally gathered together in a single flavor.”
Exhorting one another to manifest in teaching and conversion, they propagate the incomparable Dharma.
Uttering pure sounds with an impartial and non-dual mind,
they are born in that buddha-field as the fruition of their original vows from former lives.
Seated upon a high throne of the seven treasures, his thunderous roar shakes the three realms;
those he delivers are beyond measure, as he spontaneously accords with the laws of nature.
He does not calculate the root of birth and death, nor does he harbor thoughts of sorrow or joy.
They do not dwell on the practice of existence or non-existence, nor do they calculate the emptiness of the beginning or the end. Now, Śāriputra!
If you wish to know the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the lands, the names of the Buddhas, and the meaning of what is taught, it is as follows.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We have now fully understood the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattvas and the Pratyekabuddhayāna of the Bodhisattvas as spoken from the divine mouth of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of his broad and long tongue.”
"I wish to hear with joy and desire the rules of practice for Bodhisattvas and those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle; what are their matters?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

"To the northwest of here, having passed beyond twenty-four Ganges-sands of world-systems, and further passing beyond another twenty-four Ganges-sands of world-systems, there is a Buddha-land named Pore-Light (Vimalaprabhā). There, the Buddha is named Dharmadarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles."

That land is pure; all sentient beings therein possess the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and their supernormal powers and transformations surpass those of the worthy ones (*ārya*) and sages.

There are bathing pools there, no different from those described above; all have been born there by virtue of their past vows. Having shaved off their hair and beards and donned the dharma-robes of the *kāṣāya*, they are fully endowed with the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*)—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and the number of sentient beings they deliver is beyond measure.
The bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of that land surpass those in my own land who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

Why is this so? Because these bodhisattvas have attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) after a hundred kalpas of teaching and transforming others, leading them all toward the gateway of the Way, each having achieved accomplishment and established themselves in non-retrogression.

It does not equal the number of sentient beings transformed and delivered by the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of that land in a single day—hundredfold, thousandfold, or hundreds of billions of times greater; it cannot be compared by any analogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse to Śāriputra:
"Pure as refined gold, And like the moon among the stars,
One who is fully endowed with the prohibitions and dignified deportment Shall be born in that Buddha-land."
The Great Sages contemplate the Dharma; having accumulated immeasurable practices over many lifetimes, they possess wisdom that discerns the void.
With minds upright and free from further conceptualization, they preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, with assemblies numbering as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
I have caused all to be fully perfected in the vehicles of the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.

In the past, my resolve was mistaken; I underwent immeasurable ascetic practices, yet because I did not provide them with the necessary causes and conditions, I have become king in this world of five turbidities.
Although I have now attained the Way of the Buddha and travel with sovereign supernormal powers,
if I wish to reach that land, there is no means by which I may do so as they do.
The realms of the Buddhas differ, and their vows are each distinct.
"If one desires to form a connection with him, why would it be too late to make the vow?

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this verse to Śāriputra, ten billion nayutas of devas and people in the assembly all gave rise to a vast and great resolve, vowing to be born in the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Dharmadarśin, among his bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

In that buddha-field, there is no vehicle for bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna, nor is there a vehicle for bodhisattvas of the Pratyekabuddhayāna; there is only the vehicle of the śrāvakas for bodhisattvas. All who are born in that land do so together to enjoy one another’s company, having attained birth there through their past vows.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Now that we have heard the Tathāgata speak of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s Bodhisattva Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattva Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Bodhisattva Śrāvaka-yāna, all sentient beings will fully practice, believe in, delight in, and accept them.”

We now request the Tathāgata to speak of the Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Mahāyāna vehicles; of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle for Pratyekabuddhas; and of the Śrāvaka vehicle for Pratyekabuddhas. We long to hear this so that our minds may be liberated from doubt.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
I shall explain each point to you in detail."
Śāriputra replied, “So it is, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Forty-four *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of] Ganges rivers away from here to the northwest, there is a buddha-field named Thunderous Roar (*Ghoṣābhigarjita*). There, a Buddha named Yathārtha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is fully endowed with the ten titles."

That land is uniquely distinguished, perfected with the seven treasures; its sentient beings are virtuous and gentle, possessing eloquence and wisdom as vast as the ocean. Their speech is never uttered in vain, for they proclaim pure and wholesome matters as their precepts, and every dharma is accomplished without mutual conflict or opposition.

He possesses bathing pools as described above; within those bathing pools are lion thrones made of the seven precious jewels and diamond, high and broad, reaching upward beyond the realm of sentient beings.

All pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna will be born in that land; they will respect and accord with one another without conceit, never deviating from the conditions they originally established nor from their vows, and they will dwell for as long as the sands of the Ganges, possessing mastery of supernormal powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Śāriputra:
"Space is without limit; Pure and white conduct varies from one to another.
The mind is as it was originally, devoid of wisdom; This is the realm through which Pratyekabuddhas pass."
The vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas are attained by virtue of having resolved [for enlightenment] in the past;
their radiant marks naturally adorn them, and they do not calculate the superiority or inferiority of practices.
They are forever free from all suffering and affliction, and they are never deficient in the characteristics of all phenomena.
Thus, through countless ages, he practiced until attaining Buddhahood.
The True Dharma is like space; the four great elements have no cause.
Their aggregation and dispersal occur in an instant; they are without birth, nor do they arise or perish.
Human existence is full of anxieties and concerns, bound and attached by external conditions;
that land is tranquil and settled, free from these manifold afflictions and distresses.
If all classes of living beings would cultivate merit with diligent effort, [they too would attain such liberation].
If you wish to attain the Dharma of immortality, you should aspire to be born in that land.
Even if that Buddha, mindful of you, wishes to come to my realm,
if there is no karmic affinity and no thought arises [in him], he will ultimately never come to this land.
Thus, the Buddha-lands of all Buddhas are each distinct and unique;
due to the vows made in former lives, those whom they deliver differ from one another.
With the eloquence of Dharma, they expound the wondrous meaning; with the eloquence of meaning, they resolve the doubts of the multitude.
One should explain this according to the retribution of sound; these four [means] are all fully present therein.
If one wishes to establish accomplishment and aspires to that Buddha, with vast and great vows, one’s resolve shall not be false or deceitful.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking these verses to Śāriputra, seventy thousand bhikṣus seated there—who had originally sought the Lesser Vehicle to sever outflows and attain realization—all turned their minds away from that aim and vowed to be born in that land as pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and followers of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, there were countless devas and humans who attained the fruit of srotāpanna.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Hearing the Tathāgata speak of the three paths and three vehicles of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and further expounding upon the path of the pratyekabuddha and the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattvas, the entire assembly was filled with joy; their merit became complete and wholesome minds arose within them!
"Now I wish to hear about the pratyekabuddhas and the pratyekabuddha vehicle; what is their meaning?
May it also cause the minds of sentient beings to attain awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"To the northwest of here, at a distance of eighty-four *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of] Ganges rivers, and passing beyond that number, there is a buddha-field named Pure Beryl. There dwells a Buddha named Śarīravyūha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles."
That land is vast and expansive, free from all impurities and evils; the buddha-field is level, smooth, and unobstructed.

Therein are bathing pools, cool and sublime; in the center of each pool is a high seat made of the seven treasures, lofty, broad, and magnificently adorned, reaching to the limits of the realm of sentient beings.

All those who have attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha or belong to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle appear throughout that land to wander and teach, expounding the wondrous Dharma and its sublime practices.
All those who have made the vow to be reborn there shall fulfill their original aspiration without any hindrance along the way.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to Śāriputra:
"With a mind and consciousness directed toward a single goal, Holding fast to the will so it cannot be moved,
Drawn by the power of their original vows, They are born in that Buddha-land."
Accumulating merit like the sands of the Ganges, one seeks to uproot the very source of birth and death;
the fundamental nature is originally non-existent and eternally quiescent—this is the pure bliss of Nirvana.
For those of the Pratyekabuddha and Pratyayabuddha vehicles, they maintain a mind that knows no bounds.
The Vaidūrya realm is wondrous, where the Tathāgata dwells with his physical marks.
His face is like a white lotus, its fragrance perfuming all realms;
he does not undergo the fruits of other paths, having attained the most essential and subtle liberation.
The Buddha-realm is vast and boundless; those delivered therein are beyond reckoning.
It is the essential gathering place of Pratyekabuddhas, where the preaching of the Dharma’s meaning is inexhaustible.
Understanding emptiness such that there is no emptiness to be found, their resolve never regresses.
Having transcended the realm of divine seers, he is thus called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
If one wishes to honor the profound and subtle, the unattached practice of the Tathāgata,
and if all together make equal vows, there will be no difficulty in attaining Buddhahood.
"Sentient beings are of high, middle, and low capacities; their mental applications each differ.
One should simply gather the mind into one-pointedness, and the fruit of the Way will naturally arrive.
At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking these verses to Śāriputra, seventy thousand bhikṣus all made a great vow to be born in that land.

Furthermore, there was an immeasurable multitude of bodhisattva practitioners who wished and desired to behold the bodily marks of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, as well as the pratyekabuddhas of that buddha-field.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings, emitted a light from the mark of excellence upon his crown that illuminated that Buddha-land; like viewing a jewel in the palm of one's hand, it was brilliantly radiant, and they saw entirely that land—pure, flawless, and a realm of great sages and worthies.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his radiance and drew it back into the crown of his head.
The assembly of bodhisattvas was greatly awakened with joy; they immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now we have received the Great Sage’s unfolding of the transformative teachings of the Way. Having been graced by this radiance, we have been able to see that land. We pray that our bodies may cast off these forms and lives, and that we may joyfully desire to be born in the Vaidūrya Buddha-field."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas:
“Sons of noble family!

You have conceived vast and expansive intentions, and your great vows are profound and firm. Each of you shall be born in that land, where you will simultaneously attain buddhahood and fulfill all merits.”
When the bodhisattvas had seen that they were granted their predictions, they rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and returned to their original seats.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Now, having heard the Tathāgata teach the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattva Pratyekabuddhayāna, the Bodhisattva Śrāvakayāna, the Pratyekabuddha Bodhisattvayāna, and the Pratyekabuddha Pratyekabuddhayāna, all sentient beings gathered here have achieved faith and each has attained realization of the Way.

We have not yet heard the Tathāgata speak of the vehicles of the pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas; we only pray that you will explain them and instruct us accordingly, so that all those gathered here may hear and understand them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

"To the northwest of here, at a distance of one hundred and seventy million *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges sands), there is a buddha-field named Udaya. There dwells a Buddha named Prabhāsa-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who currently resides there preaching the Dharma and delivering immeasurable beings."

The world is pure and wondrous, fully endowed with manifold virtues; their aspirations are identical and they do not conflict with one another. With the four immeasurables, they treat all equally with compassion; they circulate through the world to teach and transform others without departing from their fundamental practice, manifesting the sublime Dharma through supernatural powers and transformations.
There he has bathing pools adorned with the seven treasures, their radiant lights illuminating one another such that one never tires of gazing upon them.
Within these bathing pools grow various flowers and fruits, their fragrant scents wafting so luxuriantly as to be beyond measure.
In the center of the pond was a high seat made of the seven treasures, its length, breadth, height, and depth reaching up to the Brahma Heaven.

All the Great Sages gathered in that land to proclaim the Tathāgata’s six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). Wisdom, learning, and giving were never separated from their original vows; the sixteen sublime and profound treasuries of the Tathāgata were each fully realized and manifested before them.
The sentient beings in that land are free from lust, anger, ignorance, and false views.
As for those bathing pools, the first is named "Exhausting Defilements" and the second is named "Receiving Realization.

If there are Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas whose original vows are firm and whose mental aspirations are pure, they will be born in that realm with all faculties purified and the six sense organs complete. They shall all go to the bathing pools to indulge their desires; immediately upon the banks of the pools, all dust and defilements are exhausted, and they attain the path of the Pratyekabuddha, the Bodhisattva, or the Śrāvaka vehicle, achieving the Way of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. Their bodies are adorned with the various marks, such that one can never tire of beholding them; this results from the fulfillment of their past vows and the realization of the fruits of the Path.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Śāriputra:
"The mind is the root of all practices; It guides one across the precipice of consciousness.
With great vows as one's own charioteer, One attains perfect enlightenment without fear."
Forgetting emptiness and not reckoning form, one eliminates the mental conceptions of phenomena;
having cast off the burdens of form within the three realms of existence, the Way is spontaneously realized.
The Buddha fundamentally cultivated the wisdom of emptiness, seeking neither in this nor in that.
Completely extinguishing both preceding and succeeding thoughts, one thus attains the fruit of the Way.
This present life is not a future life; it is a provisional designation that gives rise to its name.
People are deluded by illusory dharmas and sink into the deep abyss.
The excellence of this buddha-field is most sublime, where all the sages gather like clouds;
the Honored One, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, dwells therein to teach and transform.
The Buddha-mind is never unsettled, and his resolve is firm and unshakable.
When practice is perfected and the fruit is attained, one is born in that land.
Its ponds possess the flavor of the eight liberations; those who drink from them are rid of all afflictions.
Their fetters are naturally untied, and they immediately attain the unsurpassed path.
The vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas possess merits that are inexhaustible;
with their resolve firm and undivided, they immediately follow the conduct of the Tathāgata.
With light they reach out to transform others, expounding upon their meritorious deeds.
The mind is pure like a bright pearl, unstained by the dust of desire.
That land is truly extraordinary, and its manifold practices are inconceivable.
For those who wish to aspire to it, there shall be no doubt before me.
I shall support and receive you, My majestic power shall protect your person;
Do not give rise to thoughts of indolence, For regret later will be of no benefit.
Throughout countless kalpas in the past, You have not encountered worthy sages.
"Once one has lost the foundation of the human path, it is exceedingly difficult to seek it again.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking these verses to Śāriputra, seven thousand lay followers (*gṛhapati*) in the assembly abandoned their arrogance and cast off their conceit. No longer clinging to worldly splendor, they reproached themselves within, saying:
"We have been deluded and defiled by secular life for a long time; now we hear the profound and essential True Dharma of the Tathāgata."
