Each rose from their seat, stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, and immediately before the Buddha made this great vow:
"We wish and desire to be born in that land; we only pray that the World-Honored One will extend his divine power to receive us, so that there may be no obstacles among those who share this vow."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the householders and others:
“It is truly rare for you to have resolved to attain the Way; I shall bear witness to your attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment.”

At that time, when the lay devotees heard the Buddha bestow this prediction, they immediately rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and returned to their original seats.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Now we have heard that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has already expounded the practice of the three paths and three vehicles for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and has further expounded the practice of the three paths and three vehicles for Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas.

All those who have gathered and heard this True Dharma have resolved to attain unsurpassed, equal, and perfect enlightenment; they should practice the single characteristic, never losing the ultimate limit, and perform the inconceivable Buddha-work of the Buddha.

We have not yet heard the Tathāgata explain the practices of the three paths and three vehicles for śrāvakas and bodhisattvas; we only pray that the World-Honored One will now, knowing the proper time, expound the essential doctrine to this assembly, so that all doubts may forever be eliminated and no longer remain.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
I shall distinguish each point for you one by one."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“To the northwest of here, passing through as many hundreds of thousands of billions of Ganges-sands of world-systems, there is a buddha-field named Siṃhamukha. There dwells a Buddha named Dharmasamudgata Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who is currently preaching the Dharma.”

The Great Sage’s conduct is all-pervasive; he is fully endowed with all the dharmas of the bodhisattvas. His buddha-field is pure, his majestic deportment and rituals are complete, and his lifespan is exceedingly long. There are no three evil realms there; they delight themselves in the fragrance of ethical virtue, taking the fivefold dharma-body as their precept.
There are bathing pools there, pure and extraordinary, their fragrant scents wafting everywhere without exception.
That land is empty and tranquil, devoid of stones or sand; it is free from filth and impurity, and likewise lacks mountains, rivers, or rocky cliffs.
There is a bathing pool there, deep and cool, where all the holy ones assemble to bathe and enjoy one another's company.
Within the pool dwells a dragon of immeasurable divine virtue with thirty-two heads, who sends down rain at the appropriate times to universally moisten the world.

In the center of the pond was a high seat made of the seven treasures, one hundred million *yojanas* in length and breadth. All those who had attained the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas would go to that fearless seat of the seven treasures to expound the thirty-two extraordinary deeds of a Bodhisattva, the six perfections, the four immeasurables, and the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing; they were able to be born there by virtue of their past vows.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Śāriputra:
“The vehicles of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, Their meritorious achievements are inconceivable;
Their radiance shines everywhere, And they no longer give rise to the notion of names.”
The buddha-field is utterly pure; With the wisdom of the Path, one finds self-delight.
Forever free from all sensual desires, The True Dharma shines eternally.
Day and night, one practices and cultivates the Way; One’s conduct is pure and undefiled.
Not seeing the fundamental nature of phenomena, one perceives the existence of habitual dwelling-places.
The Buddha-treasury is profoundly subtle; its fruit is never in vain.
Pursued by former vows, one is then able to be born in that land.
In that land, all are sages and saints, who proclaim the Dharma of ambrosia;
they eliminate all impurities and evils, so there is no birth, old age, sickness, or death.
They expound the various scriptural canons, delivering immeasurable numbers of people.
"May all proceed to the ocean of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), Tranquil, attaining parinirvāṇa.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking these verses to Śāriputra, there were seven hundred million nayutas of sentient beings in the assembly. Having heard the Tathāgata and Śāriputra discourse upon the practices of the śrāvaka, bodhisattva, and Mahāyāna, these individuals—who had originally sought the state of a śrāvaka to sever their fetters and receive realization—now heard the Great Sage speak of the śrāvaka, Mahāyāna, and bodhisattva practices. Each rose from their seat, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha:
"We vow and desire to be born in the land of Siṃhamukha, where the Tathāgata Dharmasiddha resides, to cultivate pure conduct and aspire to the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!”
Your minds are vast and boundless; that you are able to give rise to this Mahāyāna mind of the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas will surely fulfill your aspirations without fail.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s bestowal of the prophecy, those people were filled with joy and delight; they circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and returned to their original seats.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Now we have heard the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, speak of the three paths and three vehicles of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; we have heard him speak of the three paths and three vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas; and we have further heard him speak of the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva vehicles.”

"We have not yet heard the Tathāgata speak of the vehicles of the śrāvaka, bodhisattva, and pratyekabuddha; we only pray that the World-Honored One will expound them at this time, so that those gathered here may forever be free from doubt."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"If you wish to hear concerning the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now expound them."
Śāriputra said to the Buddha: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

To the northwest of here, beyond a distance equal to the sands of ten billion Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-field named Zhòudu (Jambudvīpa). There, a Buddha resides named Qingjingguan (Vimaladarśana) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.”

The Buddha-lands are pure and they maintain total retention without forgetfulness; the dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas are inconceivable; they transform and deliver sentient beings while single-mindedly cultivating the Way; all dharmas flourish as they attain the holy conduct of a Buddha; and through the transformations of their supernormal powers, they encounter no obstruction whatsoever.
There he has bathing pools that are pure and free from impurity, where various fruits flourish and fragrant scents waft about.
Within the waters of those pools grow various kinds of flowers:
blue lotuses (utpala), kumuda lilies, padma lotuses, and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka).
Furthermore, there are hundreds and thousands of species of extraordinary and wondrous birds that sport together within those ponds.
All those who have attained the Way—whether of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Bodhisattva vehicles—are born in that land.

In the center of the pond is a throne made of the seven precious jewels, equal in length, breadth, and height to one hundred million buddha-fields, extending upward beyond the limit of sentient beings; all those who have resolved their minds to seek the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas are born in that land.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Śāriputra:
"In the pure land of Cāturmahādvīpaka, All the sages have gathered like clouds;
Together they discourse upon the various teachings of the Way, Their transformations being without end."
One contemplates the Tathāgata with purity, brought about by the power of his original vows;
in every thought-moment, there is no other thought, as one cultivates only the unsurpassed path.
Having abandoned the root and eliminated darkness, the Buddha’s radiant wisdom is manifested.
Both internally and externally completely pure, Free from the afflictions of the three poisons.
All classes of sentient beings, Upon hearing the Dharma, immediately attain awakening.
The Bodhisattva’s vehicle of the three paths— Without conditions, one cannot be born there.
Those who follow the three vehicles of the pratyekabuddhas likewise cannot be born there;
only those of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles can be born in that land. You, Śāriputra!
"Behold that pure realm; those to be delivered there are immeasurable, beyond what I am able to reach.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses to Śāriputra, there were again hundreds of thousands of countless sentient beings who thought within their hearts:

"We have been deluded and obscured by ignorance, sinking in the cycle of birth and death, and have not heard the Tathāgata’s great Dharma of fearlessness. Now that we hear it said that that land is pure and fully endowed with roots of goodness, we vow and long to be born in that realm."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings, addressed the devas and humans, saying:
"In a future life, you shall all be born in that pure land; sharing the same day and the same name, you shall all attain the Way of Unsurpassed, Perfect, and Complete Enlightenment."

At that time, when the sentient beings heard the Buddha bestow their predictions of enlightenment, they were filled with such joy and exuberance that they could not contain themselves; they immediately rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and returned to their original seats.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Having heard the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha speak of the three paths and three vehicles of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and further having heard of the three paths and three vehicles of the pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas, and having heard of the śrāvaka-bodhisattva vehicle, and further having heard of the śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha vehicle, the entire assembly is without exception filled with joy.”
"I now request the Tathāgata to explain the vehicle of the śrāvaka-śrāvaka and the bodhisattva vehicle, so that all those in this assembly may attain full understanding.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"If you wish to hear about the śrāvaka-śrāvaka and the bodhisattva vehicles, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!"
"I shall distinguish each one for you.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Eighty-four times the number of sands of the Ganges rivers to the northwest of here, there is a buddha-field named Akṣaya (Inexhaustible). There, the Buddha is named Vyapagataśrotra (Pervasive Hearing) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.”

That land is pure, and its sentient beings are gentle and harmonious; they take the wisdom of the three periods of time as their path and teaching. Practicing the Dharma of Bodhisattvas, they do not lose the *dhāraṇīs*. All sentient beings therein are of one mind, reverently practicing the True Dharma and finding mutual joy in it. Immeasurable *samādhis* manifest before them, and as they practice the contemplations of all Buddhas, they do not lose the fundamental essentials.

There is a bathing pool there, subtle and peerless, a place where the Worthy and Holy Ones sport with great compassion. It constantly turns the Wheel of Dharma through non-regressive practice, causing all bodhisattvas to achieve full realization. All who have resolved their minds and do not regress along the way shall be born in that inexhaustible buddha-field.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Śāriputra:
"In an inexhaustible, pure land, The realm of the Tathāgata is heard throughout;
Attained through his original vows, All manifold conceptions are fully realized."
All the worthy and holy ones, having fully reached those buddha-fields,
are adorned with their own manifold virtues and proclaim incomparable teachings.
They transform and enlighten all people, causing them all to partake in that supreme flavor.
Entering into samādhis such as the "Equal Entry," they are fully endowed with all practices.
Having practiced skillful means for countless kalpas without forsaking their vows,
and possessing the ten powers and fearlessnesses, they are thus born in that Buddha-field.
The World-Honored One, with the universal canopy of compassion, takes pity on all people;
with mindfulness and aspiration never departing, he spontaneously attains perfect enlightenment.
Just like the radiance of the sun, it illuminates all myriad things.
"The compassion practiced by the Bodhisattvas brings universal benefit to all.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking these verses to Śāriputra, there were thirteen billion sentient beings who all resolved to attain the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment], vowing to be born in that land as śrāvakas of the Śrāvaka Vehicle and to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya) above all else.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembled multitude, smiled; from his mouth issued light of five colors, which circled the Buddha three times and returned to enter through the aperture of his face.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"

These five thousand virtuous men have cultivated the bodhisattva path and have already entered the profound Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata; their practice surpasses that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: “Stop! Stop!”

"Why is this? Because these wicked people have, from countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas past, always delighted in slandering and reviling the True Dharma.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha:

They shall now undergo the hardships of diligent suffering, and even after a thousand Buddhas have passed, they will still not attain deliverance."

Among these five thousand virtuous men, the foremost is named Courageous Wisdom (Vīramati); although he practices the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, he will ultimately be unable to attain buddhahood.

Suppose, for example, there were a man who wished to construct a palace of the seven treasures in mid-air, adorned with the five colors—black, yellow, red, white, and blue—and carved with intricate engravings. Could such a son of good family or daughter of good family actually accomplish this?
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One.”
"Why is this? Because space has no form and cannot be fashioned.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"This Bodhisattva Vigorous Wisdom was a lion king during the time of the Buddha Prabhāsa, while I was a brahmin practicing pure conduct.

At that time, the lion king stood motionless in six postures during the early morning; he shook his body and let out a great thunderous roar, causing the running beasts to crouch and the flying birds to fall. Thereafter, he went into the wilderness, mountains, and marshes to patrol his domain and search for game. He encountered an elephant king, killed and ate him, but a thigh bone became stuck in his throat; he died and then returned to life."
At that time, there was a woodpecker before the lion, seeking out soft insects to eat them.
The lion opened his mouth and said to the woodpecker, "Help me pull this bone out; later, when you have found food, I shall repay your kindness."
Upon hearing this, the woodpecker entered his mouth and exerted all its strength to pull out the bone, thereby enabling him to escape.
Later, when the lion king went out to hunt and slaughtered many beasts, the woodpecker remained by his side and repeatedly begged for a small favor, but the lion did not grant it.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"At that time, the lion king replied to the woodpecker with this verse:
'I am the lion king; killing is my ancestral vocation.'"
I ate your flesh and drank your blood, making this my constant meal.
Since you did not measure your own strength, you escaped the hardship of my teeth and emerged from my mouth; how could I ever forget this kindness?
At that time, the wood-sparrow replied to the lion with this verse:
"Though I am but a small bird, I truly should not begrudge my life;
yet the King does not acknowledge my kindness, while I myself bear the weight of my solemn vow."
"If you could be slightly more generous and bestow even a small portion of your kindness upon me,
I would have no regrets until the end of my life and would not dare to voice any criticism.
At that time, the lion king ultimately did not repay his debt of gratitude, but abandoned him and departed.
The woodpecker thought to himself:

"My kindness was most profound, yet I have been treated with such contempt. Now I must follow after him; I shall wait for an opportunity to strike at the lion. Until my vengeance is exacted, I will never leave this world, nor will I ever part from him, wherever we may be."
At that time, the lion king again slaughtered the herd of beasts and ate them at his pleasure; once satiated, he fell asleep without any fear.
Then the woodpecker flew toward the lion and perched upon his forehead, exerting all its strength and power to peck out one of his eyes and destroy it.
The lion sprang up in alarm and looked around, but seeing no other beasts, he beheld only the woodpecker alone upon the tree.
Then the Lion King said to the woodpecker, "Why have you now ruined my eyes?"
Then, the wood-sparrow replied to the lion king in verse:
"Gratefulness for heavy kindness is unknown to you; On the contrary, you have even conceived a harmful intent.
I have now left you one of my eyes; How can this kindness ever be forgotten?"
"Though you are the king among beasts, your conduct is devoid of constancy;
from this point forward, each of you should desist and no longer create conditions for mutual encounter.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Was that lion king anyone else at that time?
Do not entertain such a thought; for it was none other than this Bodhisattva Vīrajñāna who was he then, and the wood-sparrow was none other than you, Mahāmaudgalyāyana."

These noble beings have, from that time until now, constantly engaged in slander and failed to believe in the essentials of the Tathāgata’s three bodies; they shall now undergo the sufferings of the hells.
The Buddha again addressed Maudgalyāyana:

“If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who cultivate the pure *adornment* (*viśuddhālaṃkāra*) and attain the concentration of the three bodies (*trikāya-samādhi*), they sport with supernormal powers (*ṛddhivikrīḍita*) without obstruction, acting as a heavy responsibility for others and bearing their manifold sufferings.”

Just as the realm of space covers everything without exception, so too is it with the Dharma of the three bodies adorned with pure and wondrous ornaments; it fulfills the aspirations of all sentient beings.
For example, just as the great ocean is deep, vast, and pure, and does not admit foulness or any impurities;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who has attained the Dharma of the three bodies adorned with pure and wondrous necklaces—such a one does not accept the dust, defilements, fetters, attachments, or inversions.
For example, the radiance of a mani-jewel shines through with penetrating clarity, such that it cannot be obstructed or eclipsed by the light of the sun, moon, or stars;

likewise, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the pure and wondrous necklace of the Dharma of the three bodies cannot be constrained or suppressed by the incantations or divine medicines of the immortals possessing the five supernatural powers.
Just as one who has realized the four paths and attained self-assured supernormal wisdom has transcended the five destinies and cannot be detained by various heterodox views;

and just as one in the meditative absorption of cessation has burned away all past conditioning, so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva exhaust the root of birth and death, his faith being firm and steadfast, never giving rise to slander.
For example, just as a man who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel finds that whatever he thinks of appears before him at will;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who attains the wish-fulfilling right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Observing those among the classes of sentient beings whose faculties are fully matured, he gradually trains and guides them each to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), just like the dharma of non-retrogression, so that they no longer fall back or become defiled by attachment to birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: although dwelling within birth and death, they harbor no fear, saying, "I shall ever again regress and remain within birth and death."
For example, if a person who is neither male nor female were presented with the five exquisite pleasures, they would not give rise to a mind of attachment or lustful desire;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who circulates through and teaches all beings by entering the five realms of existence. Knowing them yet remaining unattached and free from conceptualization, he delivers sentient beings in an immeasurable way.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Maudgalyāyana:
“The original intention of the Bodhisattva is pure, Like a mountain of diamond;
His resolve cannot be destroyed, And he receives realization as swiftly as a finger-snap.”
Though dwelling in the world to teach and transform, he does not cling to the thoughts of conditions or origins;
having mastered all dharmas, he raises high the great banner of the Dharma.
It is like two men, each holding a different skill in their minds.
They led one another to the hall of performance, each wishing to display their skills.
Mount Sumeru, made of the four precious substances, is vast and exceedingly steep and high;
its measurements are three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand yojanas.
One person stands on the mountain peak, holding a vessel of ambrosia;
another stands at the foot of the mountain, holding a vessel to receive the ambrosia.
The writer does not spill it, and the receiver does not discard it.
Those individuals were all ordinary worldlings, Having not yet attained the path of supernormal wisdom.
How difficult was this for Maudgalyāyana? Is this not extremely hard?
Though it is hard, it is not yet remarkable; The three bodies of the Dharma are exceedingly difficult.
Throughout billions of kalpas, those who wish to hear the Pure Garland and discern the wisdom of the three bodies find this Dharma most difficult to attain.
You should now have no sorrow or anxiety; you have already transcended all suffering and affliction.
Having heard the essentials of the three dharmas, one saves oneself and further saves others.
If there is a son of noble family who practices the Dharma with sincere faith,
he will exhaust all outflows in this present life and roam with mastery through supernormal powers.
"The land where one is born shall be pure, Palaces of the seven treasures shall be formed,
All faculties shall be complete and perfect, And the mind shall be as pure as space. At that time,
while the World-Honored One was speaking this chapter with Maudgalyāyana, there were billions of nayutas of devas and humans who all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
"May the lands where I am born all share a single characteristic, and may there be none who revile the three bodies of the Dharma.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and returned to his original seat.

33. Chapter on the Characteristics of the Dharmas of the Three Times (11). The *Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra-sūtra*, Chapter Thirty-three: The Characteristics of the Dharmas of the Three Times. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mṛdusvara:

"In the past, when I attained Buddhahood, I accumulated merit and performed practices until I personally realized the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. I abandoned my kingdom and renounced my wife, having no greed for honor or position; I proclaimed the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, transforming and liberating beings according to their individual capacities."
Just as a king of physicians treats and rescues various ailments by administering medicine according to their severity,
so too does the Bodhisattva know and protect sentient beings who, though currently manifest in this present life, have planted the seeds of past illnesses;
or those sentient beings whose bodies have already passed away but have planted the seeds of future illnesses— the Bodhisattva likewise knows and protects them.
At that time, the Venerable Kapphiṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a son or daughter of good family, while dwelling in the present body, plants the seeds of past illnesses?”
"What is it that constitutes a body sowing the seeds of future illness while existing in the past?
And what is it that constitutes a body existing in the future while sowing the seeds of present illness?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kapphiṇa, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
It is of great benefit that you have questioned the Tathāgata regarding this matter.”

Why is this? It is because the treasury of Dharma proclaimed by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present constitutes inconceivable dharmas that perform the Buddha-work, adorning the Bodhi tree and proceeding toward the attainment of Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Kapphiṇa:
“With a pure and gentle voice, heard throughout the realms of the ten directions,
endowed with all roots of goodness, he uproots suffering and leaves behind all evils.”
Discerning the activities of the three periods of time, there is no entry and nothing produced;
the Tathāgata observes all this, uniquely virtuous and without equal.
From the first moment he gave rise to the mind of great vows, it was not for the sake of a few people alone.
His mind is as vast as space, saving beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Now, beneath the King of Trees, his various marks naturally adorn him;
having subdued all non-Buddhists, he reverently practices the teachings of the True Dharma.
With the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment upon his head, Clad in the raiment of shame and remorse,
With a serene countenance and a mind of patience, He walks alone without hindrance.
Fearless as a lion, His courageous wisdom is unimpeded.
The form and likeness are like the new moon; gazing upon them, one never tires.
All beings from the worlds of the ten directions come to make offerings to the Honored One;
according to their original vows, they all return to the gate of liberation.
The vow I have originally made is not limited by the duration of kalpas;
out of compassion for all sentient beings, I shall expound the nectar-like Dharma.
To seek a human body is difficult; to hear and receive the True Dharma is difficult.
It is difficult to be born in the Central Land; it is difficult to encounter a True Person.
It is difficult for the wealthy and noble to maintain faith; it is difficult for the stingy and envious to practice giving.
It is difficult for those bound by attachment to receive realization; it is difficult to discern the three periods of time.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Kāśyapa:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who discern the diseases of lust, anger, and delusion throughout the three periods of time, remaining far removed from bondage and attachment so as to be free from further arising and ceasing, their supernormal powers will be autonomous and their transformations limitless."

In this way, such sons and daughters of good family enter the samādhi of the concentration of the three periods of time; they fully know the practices of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and all roots of goodness appear before them.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, advance toward Nirvana by means of the Eightfold Noble Path; this is why the Buddhas appear in the world—to observe sentient beings, exhaustively investigate their fundamental natures, and cause them to know the gateway to the Dharma. Through the Tathāgata’s three types of supernormal knowledge, he observes the phenomena of the three periods of time as immeasurable, limitless, and inconceivable.
There may be sentient beings who should hear the teachings on the past; for them, the Tathāgata speaks of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena in the past and their non-arising.
There may be sentient beings who should hear the teachings on the present; for them, the Tathāgata speaks of the present correct instruction that distances one from bondage and attachment.
"Or there may be sentient beings who should hear the teachings on the future; the Tathāgata then speaks of the future—those dharmas that have not yet arisen and are neither produced nor extinguished.
At that time, the Venerable Kapphiṇa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
How is it that for those sentient beings who should hear the teachings on the past, the Tathāgata explains to them the cessation of all past formations and their non-arising?

How is it that for those sentient beings who should hear the teachings on the present, the Tathāgata explains to them the correct instruction of the present regarding the distancing from bondage and attachment?
"How is it that sentient beings should hear of future dharmas, and yet the Tathāgata speaks to them of future dharmas that have not yet arisen and are without arising or cessation?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Kapphiṇa:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!"
Kapphiṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
I wish most earnestly to hear it."
The Buddha told the Elder Kapphiṇa:

"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who contemplates and fully understands the three periods of time as immeasurable, limitless, and inconceivable—this is not something that can be attained by pratyekabuddhas or arhats."
Why is this? Because that which the Tathāgata practices is not within their realm.

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, dwelling in the present with all practices fully perfected, is to receive a prediction from a past Tathāgata, they will hear the present Tathāgata preach the Dharma of the past: that the past has been extinguished and all practices do not arise. Their mind then attains awakening and they receive the prediction, becoming a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, while dwelling in the present, should hear the Dharma of the past; [for him] the past has ceased and all conditioned activities do not arise.
The Buddha again addressed the Elder Kapphiṇa:

“Furthermore, there is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, while dwelling in the present, should hear the Dharma of the present, receiving a prediction from a present Buddha—such a one as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.”

This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the present body and experiencing the present distinct [realms], yet remaining detached from bondage and attachment, free from the notions of arising and ceasing.

Furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who, while dwelling in the present body, should hear the teachings of the future; the Tathāgata then explains to them the future, unarisen dharmas that are neither produced nor extinguished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind immediately attained realization and received the prediction of enlightenment as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in the present explaining future dharmas—dharmas of the future that have not yet arisen and are subject neither to origination nor cessation.
At that time, the Elder Kapphiṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Do only bodhisattva-mahāsattvas discern the destinies of all practices throughout the three periods of time?”
"Do Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also possess these practices?
The Buddha told Kapphiṇa:

"From the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi) and the stage of vision (darśana-bhūmi), up to the stage of the Samyaksaṃbuddha, all possess the infinite, limitless, and inconceivable multitudes of practices throughout the three periods of time toward which they proceed; thus they receive their respective names."
At that time, the Elder Kapphiṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

How is it that from the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi) and the stage of vision (darśana-bhūmi), up to the stage of the Samyaksaṃbuddha, all possess the attainment of names and titles through the infinite, immeasurable, and inconceivable multitudes of practices directed toward the three periods of time?"
The Buddha addressed the Elder Kapphiṇa:

“If you wish to know extensively how the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha distinguishes the destinies of all practices throughout the three periods of time, I shall now expound their meaning one by one—from the stage of faith, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, and the stage free from lust, anger, and delusion, up to the stage of the Srotāpanna and even the Samyaksaṃbuddha—all of which are distinguished according to their destinies throughout the three periods of time.”

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the stage of faith, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, and the stage free from lust, anger, and delusion, discern the destinies of all practices throughout the three periods of time?
"In this regard, noble son!

If a good man or a good woman, through faith and liberation, attains the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold right path, they may at times achieve them and at other times fail to achieve them."

Such persons as these, whether in the stage of the noble ones or in the stage of ordinary beings, from the point of non-retrogression up to the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood—these are called bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have forever left behind the state of ordinary beings and received the prediction of the Tathāgata. This is what is meant, O son of good family!
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas differ individually according to the stage of faith, the stage of attenuation, and the stage free from lust, anger, and delusion.
At that time, the Elder Kapphiṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, from the stage of faith up to the stage free from lust, anger, and delusion, may be in the stage of the noble ones or in the stage of ordinary persons?
The Buddha addressed the Elder Kapphiṇa:

"If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, having first resolved to seek the unsurpassed path, hears the teachings of the past while dwelling in the present, yet fails to believe in or delight in them and abandons them."
Why is this? Because they lack fundamental faith and joy, they harbor doubt; thus, they regress midway and fail to reach the ultimate goal.
At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyān seizes his opportunity, transforms himself into the form of a Buddha, and goes to where the bodhisattva is, urging him on, saying:
"Good son, do you understand? What I previously spoke was not so;

what I am saying now is the truth. You should have heard the teachings on future dharmas and received the prediction of enlightenment, yet now you hear me speak of past dharmas. Your efforts are thus in vain, and you shall not achieve the fruit of retribution."
"Why do you not quickly abandon your original intention and instead give rise to a great vow? Only then shall you achieve unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva felt hesitation in his heart and immediately regressed, remaining at the stage of an ordinary person.
"This is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who does not attain unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment regarding the dharmas of the three periods of time.
The Buddha again addressed the Elder: "Kapphiṇa!"
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva discern the destinies of all practices throughout the three periods of time, so as to dwell firmly in the noble stages without falling back?
In this regard, son of good family!

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, from the stage of faith up to the stage free from lust, anger, and delusion, dwells in the present and hears of the various practices and destinies of past dharmas, without doubting, without finding them difficult, and without fear, their mind immediately opens and they achieve sudden, great awakening; they then hear the Tathāgata bestow upon them a name, declaring that they shall become an unsurpassed, truly real, and perfectly awakened one.
At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyas manifested the form of a Buddha, came to where the Bodhisattva was, and said to him:
"Good son, do you not know?
"What I previously said was wrong, and what I am saying now is right; if you can repent and follow my teaching, you shall attain unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment."
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with joy, thinking:
"Is it not Māra, the Evil One, who has manifested as a Buddha-image to come and thwart my resolve?
His mind was like a diamond, indestructible and unshakable.

In this way, such sons and daughters of good family leave the stage of ordinary beings and constantly abide in the stage of the noble ones; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose mind does not regress upon hearing the teachings of the past.
The Buddha again addressed the Elder Kāśyapa:

"Regarding what you have asked, from the stage of srotāpanna up to the samyaksaṃbuddha, one distinguishes the destinations of all practices throughout the three periods of time, whether they belong to the stage of ordinary beings or to the stage of the noble ones."
"In this regard, O son of noble family!

If there is a good man or a good woman who hears the teachings of the past with their present body, they should attain faith and understanding based on those past teachings; yet instead, they follow the evil path spoken by Pāpīyān:
'Good man, do you not know?'"

Past conditioned phenomena have already ceased and possess no fundamental basis; the worlds of the ten directions are empty, quiescent, and formless. Why not seek skillful means and resolve to give rise to the great vow?
A practitioner who acts in this manner will attain Buddhahood before long.
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva immediately harbors hesitation, thinking:
"Is what I am currently practicing not indeed like this?

He then abandons his original vow and withdraws from the bodhisattva practice, intending instead to cultivate the teachings of Māra; this is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s retrogression regarding past dharmas.
The Buddha again addressed the Elder Kapphiṇa:
"Regarding what you have asked, concerning the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have already attained the Noble Grounds and departed from the level of ordinary beings—reflect upon this well."
"In this regard, son of good family!
It is as if there were someone who, while existing in the present, hears the teachings of the past and feels no fear in their heart nor any doubt or difficulty.
Then Pāpīyān comes again to corrupt and destroy the bodhisattva, saying:"

"What I have spoken was a provisional expedient, a combination of numerical designations, and not the ultimate reality. You should now abandon your former original intention and instead resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; you shall accomplish the path of a Tathāgata before long."
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"I have already received the prediction of my attainment of the Unsurpassed Way; this one is not a Buddha, but rather the evil Māra Pāpīyān."
"Having thus abandoned them, he departs and does not engage with them.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva leaving the stage of ordinary beings and firmly abiding in the stage of the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to Kapphiṇa:
“The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, discerns that the three periods of time are empty;
forever free from all fetters and attachments, he has attained the stage of the noble ones.
The Tathāgata bestows upon him the prediction of enlightenment and proclaims the name of his buddha-field.”
Not destroyed by Māra, his mind cannot be moved.
Through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, his concentrated mind remains undisturbed;
he naturally attains awakening and thus accords with the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
"The Eightfold Noble Path truly leads to right awakening; It ferries one across all sufferings and calamities.
One should not be attached to wealth or treasures, But always strive against [the defilements] with one's very body and life.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses to Kāśyapa, there were seven hundred million sentient beings in the assembly who, upon hearing this teaching on the Dharma of the equality of the three periods of time, all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, there were further immeasurable sentient beings seated in the assembly whose minds had not yet attained awakening and who each harbored doubts, reflecting within themselves:

"Today the Tathāgata has expounded the teachings and proclaimed the Dharma of the three periods of time; regarding the reception of predictions for attaining Buddhahood, each has its own sequence of priority."

"Will the Buddhas of the ten directions also preach this Dharma of the three periods of time? At that moment, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly, emitted from the mark between his eyebrows a radiance that universally illuminated immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions. Within each ray of light were hundreds of thousands of billions of lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; within each land were hundreds of thousands of billions of lotus flowers; within each lotus flower were hundreds of thousands of billions of mani jewels; within each mani jewel appeared hundreds of thousands of billions of lecture halls made of the seven treasures; within each lecture hall appeared hundreds of thousands of billions of high thrones made of the seven treasures; and upon each throne appeared hundreds of thousands of billions of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Each and every Tathāgata fully expounded the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) and the various practices of Bodhisattvas throughout the three periods of time.

At that time, the entire assembly beheld the extraordinary and marvelous transformations throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Each addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How extraordinary! How marvelous!
Never before have we seen such a thing, nor have we ever heard of it.
"Today the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has emitted this radiance so that we may universally behold the dharmic principles practiced by all Buddhas.

Some see sentient beings receiving their prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) before the Tathāgata; some see sentient beings listening to and receiving the Dharma; and some see sentient beings whose bodies are adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Thus, what was seen by the assembly varied; in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, offerings were presented, with fragrant flowers and silken banners filling the trichiliocosm.

At that time, the World-Honored One observed the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings and, further employing his supernormal powers, moved immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions, inviting all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas to expound the True Dharma of the equality of the three periods of time.

To the east of here, at a distance of eight Ganges-sands of world-systems, there is a buddha-field named Cintā. There dwells a Buddha named Amoghasaṃkalpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. With a single paryañka posture, he pervades the trichiliocosm, and then, amidst the great assembly, he spoke these verses:
"The various practices of the past lead to the realization that the root of arising and ceasing is not to be seen;
Only through liberation and receiving the prediction [of enlightenment] does one correspond to the stage of the noble ones."
The nature of phenomena is detached from all existence, Not creating the dust of the three periods of time;
With valor it transcends all conditioned practices, Like a flower that naturally blooms.
The Tathāgata manifests his instructions, Universally nourishing all sentient beings.
Pure as a bright pearl, the mind is firm as Mount Anavatapta.
Possessing all the merits of the Buddhas, forever free from all sensory pleasures, it restrains the desires of the dust; naturally, there is no defilement.
The Buddha-dharma is truly extraordinary, beyond the reach of the two vehicles;
through expedient wisdom it manifests manifold transformations and is endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body.
I, too, received this without a teacher and did not learn it from conditioned phenomena.
"Bathing in the abyss of ambrosia, one’s body is adorned with liberation.

Eight *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands] of Ganges rivers to the south of here, there is a buddha-field named Adorned. Its Buddha is named Pure Adornment Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. With a single cross-legged posture, he pervades the trichiliocosm and, amidst the great assembly, speaks in verse:
"Today, the Buddhas of the ten directions Universally manifest transformations of spiritual power."
Each explains the root of the three periods of time, exhausting the karmic deeds of the Tathāgata.
The single characteristic is fundamentally formless; one enters deeply into its boundless precipice.
Preaching the Dharma for others to receive, it is like space, free from any conceptualization.
The Dharma drum resounds throughout the great trichiliocosm;
Complete with the merit of the ten wholesome paths, it rescues those of inferior capacity, Causing them to forever leave the sea of birth and death.
For this reason the Buddhas appear; Their transformations are immeasurable.
Through causes and conditions, the fruit of the Way is realized, thereby corresponding to the stages of the worthy and the sage.
Multitudes gather from the lands of the ten directions, each expounding the Dharma of the three periods of time;
they spontaneously attain the True Dharma, and the concentrated mind manifests before them.
From each and every pore, He emits hundreds of thousands of light rays, Proclaiming the teachings of all paths, To extinguish the root of the three poisons.

To the west of here, past as many worlds as there are grains of sand in eight Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-field named Pure and Further Pure. There dwells a Buddha named Vimalaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Seated cross-legged, he fills the entire trichiliocosm and, amidst the great assembly, speaks these verses:
“The natures of sentient beings are diverse; They do not contemplate the wisdom of liberation.
The dharmas of the three periods of time are eternally abiding; Their arising and ceasing are like the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
When the noble ones enter meditative concentration and observe, They discern the twelve links of dependent origination.”
Contemplating the three dharmas in seven aspects, they all return to the nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
One does not aspire to birth in the heavens, nor does one seek fortune through worldly dharmas;
this is called clarifying the three periods of time and constantly mindful of selecting virtuous friends.
Planting merit clarifies wisdom; this is the foremost ultimate truth.
By discerning the notions of existence and non-existence, he is thus called the Honored One among Men.
All phenomena each have their own nature, yet all that is practiced ultimately returns to emptiness.
As one who seeks to fathom space must first distinguish the body,
so too, beholding the countenance of the Tathāgata, all dharmas are naturally complete.
His mouth utters the eightfold tones, delivering immeasurable beings.

"To the north of here, at a distance of eight Ganges-sands of *koṭis* of world-systems, there is a buddha-field named Manifestation by Transformation (*Nirmāṇa*). There dwells a Buddha named Unstained Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, complete with the ten titles. Seated cross-legged, he fills the entire trichiliocosm and, amidst the great assembly, speaks these verses:
"The four great elements have no inherent nature; They arise spontaneously and perish naturally.
I do not create their conditions, And in every thing, nothing exists."
Asanga proclaims liberation, drawing others forth and showing them the nectar of immortality;
he fulfills the original aspirations of all people, causing each to attain the realization of the fruit.
In the past, when I practiced the perfection of giving, I ruled over the realms of the ten directions.
The seven factors of enlightenment are natural treasures, Filling all people.
Remaining to teach and transform sentient beings, They do not dwell on the four formless attainments;
Forever free from the eight unfavorable conditions, They always abide together with the noble sages.
Originally following the threefold penetrating wisdom, having heard this wisdom of the three periods of time,
now free from the dust of the three defilements, he received the prediction of enlightenment from the World-Honored One of the three periods.
Having practiced giving without ever regretting it, he focused his mind on being free from perversion.
"To all those who are on deviant paths, he shows the way of the true path.

Eight *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* sands of world-systems to the northeast of here, there is a buddha-field named Kṣānti-mati. Its Buddha is named Gandhavyaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. With a single paryañka-sitting, he pervades the trichiliocosm and, amidst the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"The nature of phenomena arises spontaneously; It is formless and cannot be seen.
Practicing the noble prohibitions and precepts, Which are beyond number and not subject to calculation;
Abiding in the fundamental yet without abiding, Investigating the source where form does not exist—
Profound and difficult to fathom, This is that which corresponds to the Noble Ground.
Discerning present phenomena, one is untainted by emptiness or the signless;
past births are already exhausted, and one attains liberation from the afflictions of the three times.
The body is a vessel for manifold sufferings, leaking forth all manner of impurities.
Able to relinquish [the world] and enter right wisdom, one gradually reaches the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
With a mind upright and unstained by the heterodox, not abandoning the mind of the Great Vehicle,
and with a mind as pure as refined gold, proceeding toward the Way is likewise not difficult.
"Human life within the five realms of existence Is distinguished through internal contemplation of the body.
From what do the three periods of time arise? It causes people to harbor folly and delusion.

To the southeast of this place, across as many *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (sands of the Ganges) as there are grains of sand in eight rivers, there is a buddha-field named "Universal Assembly of Sages and Worthies" (*Śrāvaka-ārya-samudita*). There dwells a Buddha named Avalokiteśvara-duḥkha-tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. With a single paryañka (cross-legged) posture, he fills the trichiliocosm. Amidst the great assembly, he spoke these verses:
“The Buddhas contemplate all things as empty and signless throughout the three periods of time;
with wisdom they sever the root of craving and thus correspond to the stage of the noble ones.
They resolve their will upon diligent ascetic practice and make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
Possessing all forms of wisdom, he is thus called the Hero among Men.
Faith is the nectar-like Dharma; with no mind of dualistic views, he stands among the multitude like a lion, his teaching shaking the ten directions.
The various defilements and turbidities of birth and death have no root to be found;
having thoroughly understood the afflictions of the three periods of time, one draws near to the discipline of the Tathāgata.
For those who wish to seek the Buddha-way, wisdom is truly the foremost.
He burns away the thicket of doubt, so that naturally there is nothing to be thought of.
The Buddha wanders through immeasurable realms; wherever the light of his wisdom shines, he purifies all phenomena and discerns the activities of the three periods of time.

"To the southwest of here, at a distance of eight *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges] *yojana*s away, there is a buddha-field named Immeasurable Treasury (*Anantagarbha*). There dwells a Buddha named Kṣāntijñāna Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Seated in a single *paryaṅka* posture, he pervades the entire trichiliocosm, and amidst the great assembly, he speaks these verses:
"Mindfulness sustains the root of all dharmas; The conceptualization of conditions cannot be destroyed.
When practice reaches the firmness of spontaneity, One then accords with the ground of the sages."
The Buddhas employ skillful means, transforming sentient beings through their virtuous teachings;
the Bodhisattvas cultivate great vows, wherein the four immeasurables neither increase nor decrease.
They advance upon the path of the unconditioned, pure and untainted.
Spreading everywhere like clouds of wisdom, they extinguish the afflictions of the three periods of time.
When sages appear in the world to transform others, they cause them to cultivate the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
by discerning each [phenomenon] with wisdom, one then accords with the path of the sages.
The intrinsic nature of the three periods of time is empty; Thoughts and perceptions are inconceivable.
Arising and ceasing alternate and flourish, But upon entering meditative concentration, they are eliminated.
By not clinging to the existence of the triple world, One then attains the inexhaustible.
For the sake of others, he manifests majestic deportment, And forever attains a state of peace and security.

To the northwest of here, passing through lands as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-field named Kalyāṇa. There dwells a Buddha named Kalyāṇamṛdu Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. With a single paryañka posture, he fills the trichiliocosm; amidst the great assembly, he speaks these verses:
“The Tathāgata manifests skillful wisdom, Ruling over the realms of the ten directions.”
Discerning that the three periods of time are empty, one then accords with the practice of the noble ones.
The Dharma-realm is immeasurable, like space, without end or limit;
having attained the Buddha’s samādhi and dharma-patience, one does not give rise to a mind of dualistic views.
In the past, I received the prediction of my future enlightenment, Discerning the emptiness of both the internal and external;
Now, having personally attained perfect awakening, I have escaped the suffering of the three periods of time.
The Tathāgata’s broad and long tongue Is naturally adorned with a hundred merits.
Eliminating conceptual thoughts, with single-minded sincerity and no dualistic karma;
the Buddha is the root of all practices, expounding the twelve gates.
By stilling the mind, one completes the traces of the Path and shall no longer wander through the five realms of existence.
"Just as when shooting upward into the sky, The momentum is exhausted and one falls back down;
So too, though the Dharma of the three periods of time is proclaimed, It is immeasurable and cannot be exhausted.

Eight *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sands) of world-systems away from here in the zenith, there is a buddha-field named Auspiciousness (*Śrī*). There, the Buddha named Kṣayajina Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, sat with his legs crossed, pervading the entire trichiliocosm, and spoke these verses amidst the great assembly:
"The worthy sages of the past proclaimed the true and correct scriptures;
being unstained by the phenomena of name and form, they thus accorded with the discipline of the worthy sages.
The Bodhisattva, having originally resolved his mind, now cultivates the teachings of the Tathāgata."
The profound Dharma neither increases nor decreases; no person is seen who attains liberation.
Hearing through all immeasurable ages, they discern the faculties of sentient beings;
with single-minded concentration, they realize the existence and non-existence of phenomena.

Signlessness is not the presence of signs; not recollecting the consciousness of the three periods of time, one contemplates and realizes that nothing exists, and thus attains the title of Honored One among Men.
The source of all dharmas is formed through the convergence of causes and conditions.
Contemplating formless dharmas, empty and still, fundamentally without form;
The dharma of the ten stages of the path, with a mind that does not regress;
Through a single practice, one achieves perfect enlightenment, No longer subject to birth, old age, or death.

Eight *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands] of world-systems below this place, there is a buddha-field named *Gambhīra*. Therein dwells a Buddha named Ratnaskandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Sitting cross-legged, he pervades the trichiliocosm and, amidst the great assembly, speaks these verses:
"Patience, wisdom, and the fruits of cultivating the path, Forever transcending the root of the three times;
Being pure oneself and purifying others— This accords with the Dharma of the noble ones."
He teaches the Unsurpassed Way, moving about without fixed direction;
Wielding skillful means, he exhausts all practices, delivering beings without weariness.
To encounter the worthy and holy is joy; to hear the Dharma and receive it with faith is joy.
The joy of delivering others and severing defilements, the eternal tranquility of Nirvana—
having traversed the three realms, I have distanced myself from karma that leads to evil retribution;
having gained intimacy with virtuous friends, my hearing of the Dharma increases day by day.
Transcending the three realms, one wanders through the void with supernormal powers;
though formless, appearing as if having form—this is what the deluded practice.
Through the Mahāyāna Dharma of the Six Perfections, forgetting oneself, all things are exhausted.
"Having attained the ascent to the ten stages of abiding, he therefore returns out of compassion to transform us.

At that time, the Elder Kāśyapa, having heard of the Dharma of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and the various practices toward which they tend, his mind opened and his understanding was resolved; he suddenly attained great enlightenment, rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and returned to his original position.

There were incalculable numbers of devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, mahoragas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahāragas, and others—both human and non-human—all of whom resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Furthermore, there were countless devas and humans who, upon hearing the Buddha expound the fundamental nature of the dharmas of the three periods of time, all marveled at the Buddha’s profound virtues and immeasurable meaning; they praised that the Dharma-body of the Buddhas is indestructible and cannot be attained even by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.

At that time, the entire assembly all vowed to joyfully discern the internal and external three periods of time within their own bodies, advancing toward the site of enlightenment and attaining non-retrogression.
*The Sutra of the Bodhisattva’s Necklace*, Scroll Eleven.
*The Sutra of the Bodhisattva’s Necklace*, Scroll Twelve, also titled *The Present Retribution*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty. Chapter 34: On Purity (12). Chapter Thirty-Four:
On Purity. At that time, the Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Now that we have heard the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, expound upon the dharmas of the three periods of time, the devas, humans, and the eight classes of spirits all offer worship. They guard and protect the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are advancing toward Buddhahood; for the Buddhas of the future, past, and present expound the wisdom that distinguishes the three periods of time, thereby kindling and inflaming the arising of all dharmas.”

Furthermore, through the power of his supernormal faculties and the Way, he transformed and moved the trichiliocosm; practicing with a resolute mind, he did not abandon his original vow, purifying his buddha-field and cleansing the traces of sentient beings.
At that time, the Elder Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who cultivates the dharma of the single mark of original non-existence, he inwardly contemplates and discerns the marks of the body, such that it is pure both internally and externally, and no defiled attachment arises.”
"How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva inwardly contemplate and discern the characteristics of the body so that it is pure both internally and externally?
"In this regard, son of good family!"
If there are good sons or good daughters who practice the six perfections—the path traversed by all Buddhas—all dharmas will be entirely pure.
In what way are all dharmas entirely pure?

Thereupon, these sons and daughters of good family discern that all things throughout the three periods of time are utterly non-existent; they do not perceive anyone who has achieved the path of the Three Vehicles, from the *srotāpanna* up to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, all of whom cultivate pure conduct across the three periods of time. Internally observing their own bodies and discerning their perceptions and thoughts, they find that at times these are pure and at times they are impure.
How is it that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is sometimes pure and sometimes impure?
In this regard, son of good family!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family discerns the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and does not perceive a self, a person, a being, a life-span, or any phenomena, then from the stage of srotāpanna up to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, they are said to be pure.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
The three dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)—which are unattached, without arising or ceasing, and consist of the analytical contemplation of emptiness—are sometimes pure and sometimes impure."
What are the three dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that are sometimes pure and sometimes impure?
In this regard, son of good family!

Within the future, one discriminates all phenomena; regarding each of the right dharmas practiced, one contemplates them one by one through the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of *savitarka-savicāra* samādhi, which is sometimes pure and sometimes impure.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how is it that for one who is beyond training,

unattached, and free from arising and ceasing, there can be times when the three unconditioned dharmas— discriminated through the contemplation of emptiness— are pure, and times when they are not pure?”
The Buddha told Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"If there are those who have completed their training or those still in training, they discern all future dharmas, forever eliminating and severing them so that defilements do not arise."
Furthermore, to extend this Dharma widely to all sentient beings is called "sometimes pure.
Moreover, son of good family, daughter of good family!
When a practitioner cultivates the intention to sever [afflictions] so that future defilements never arise again, this is called "sometimes impure."
Thus it is, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Among those who have attained the three states of no-more-learning, they accomplish this one dharma. Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

When those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those still in training (*śaikṣa*) discern all present phenomena through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of *savitarka-savicāra*, causing the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be forever extinguished and never to arise again, this is called "purity at times.

When a practitioner at the initial stage of cultivation discerns and contemplates present phenomena through the meditative absorption of *savitarka-savicāra*, causing them to be forever extinguished, this is called "impurity at times."
"In this way, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
there are times when the three unconditioned dharmas are not pure.
The Buddha again addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:

"Sometimes an adept or a learner, regarding past phenomena, discriminates all dharmas that have arisen, contemplating each one without vitarka (applied thought) and without vicāra (sustained thought), forever severing and extinguishing them so that no further afflictions arise; thus they accomplish the three unconditioned dharmas. This is called 'sometimes pure.

If a practitioner, regarding present phenomena, discriminates and contemplates them without vitarka and without vicāra, likewise causing them to be severed and extinguished so that no afflictions arise, this is called 'a son of good family who is sometimes impure. The same applies to the discrimination of the three conditioned dharmas across the three periods of time."
The Buddha again addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"Those who have completed their training and those still in training should further distinguish that the nature of the three vehicles is entirely pure and non-existent."
How is it that the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) and the one in training (śaikṣa), within the three periods of time, differentiate the three inclinations (triniyāma) yet find them to be non-existent?

In this regard, the one beyond training and the one in training differentiate the arising of all phenomena (dharmas) in future dharmas as being sometimes pure and sometimes impure; this, noble son, is called the accomplishment of one dharma among the three conditioned dharmas (saṃskṛtadharma).
The Buddha again addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:

"As for those who practice and study, they further discern in the future that all dharmas and all things that arise are entirely empty, entirely quiescent, and non-existent; they cause them to be forever severed and extinguished so that afflictions do not arise. This, noble son, is called being pure at times and impure at other times."
The Buddha again addressed Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra:

“For those who have completed their training and those still training, regarding the dharmas of the present, they should further distinguish the correct practice of wishlessness (apraṇihita), which is at times pure and at times impure; furthermore, they should bring about its cessation so that afflictions do not arise. This is called being at times pure and at times impure with respect to conditioned dharmas.”
The Buddha again addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:

"As for the practitioner who, regarding present phenomena, contemplates and discriminates the signless samādhi—sometimes it is pure and sometimes it is not pure—and furthermore causes the cessation of afflictions so that they do not arise, this is called being sometimes pure and sometimes not pure with respect to the three unconditioned dharmas."
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is it only these three emptinesses and three gateways that are sometimes pure and sometimes impure?"
“Are there any dharmas that are sometimes pure and sometimes impure?
The Buddha told Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: “It is so, it is so.”
Son of good family!
As you have asked,
all dharmas are at times pure and at times impure.
From the stage of stream-entry up to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, there are times when they are pure and times when they are impure.

From the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, there are times when they are pure and times when they are impure.
At that time, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is it that at times there is purity and at times there is impurity?”
The Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"Do you wish to hear how, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there are times when it is pure and times when it is impure?"
“Is it because you wish to hear that all dharmas of the three periods of time are sometimes pure and sometimes impure?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I wish to hear how, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there are times when it is pure and times when it is impure.
The Buddha told Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"All dharmas are innumerable and not subject to calculation; they neither abide nor do they not abide. This is called attaining purity regarding the dharmas of the three periods of time."
If there are good sons or good daughters who neither perceive abiding nor perceive non-abiding, yet give rise to a defiled mind by conceiving attachments to abiding, this is called impurity.
The Bodhisattva’s great vow is to universally save all classes of sentient beings; though he delivers these beings, he harbors no expectations—this is called purity.
If, however, he should again give rise to thoughts of conceptual attachment, this is called impurity.
"To manifest the light of wisdom and eliminate darkness is called purity;
to give rise to conceptual attachment within that state is called impurity.
To guide sentient beings so they dwell forever in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called purity."
To perceive that there are sentient beings to be delivered and to harbor a defiled mind is called impurity.
To direct one’s single-minded focus solely toward the unconditioned path and to cause sentient beings to attain what one has attained oneself is called purity;
yet, to claim for oneself, "I have delivered sentient beings," is called impurity.
The Way resides within the human heart; to teach and transform according to the capacities of beings, practicing with diligence and vigor without harboring indolence, is called purity.

To exert oneself in cultivation with a mind that does not regress, yet to harbor attachments and conceptualizations while desiring to achieve the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way, is called impurity.
"To discern that all conditioned phenomena are empty, non-existent, and by nature inherently so is called purity;
yet to again discern them while not severing one's hopes and cravings is called impurity."
To know that the activities of countless bodies are all empty, and not to give rise to the thought of accomplishing anything, is called purity;
to praise one's own merits and become attached to bodily phenomena is called impurity.
That the teachings expounded by the mouth have no boundaries, and that one does not even conceive of the way of existence or non-existence—this is called purity.
That one is able to relinquish all things to advance in the cultivation of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), desiring to attain the unsurpassed, truly correct Way—this is called impurity.
"To distribute the characters of the *dhāraṇī* that retain all dharmas in memory without forgetting is called purity;
not seeing that the characters give rise to all dharmas, and lacking faith in the wisdom of emptiness that accomplishes the Way, is called impurity."
That all conceptualizations ultimately return to emptiness is called purity;
that which is originally nameless yet is given a name, and further desiring to achieve the Unsurpassed Way therein, is called impurity.

When sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attachment and without bondage, and when one seeks their objective realms and finds them to be non-existent, this is called purity;
when the consciousness-principle is unconditioned and not something seen by the eye-faculty, yet one still earnestly desires to know its nesting place, this is called impurity.

When one does not perceive the reception or entry into any phenomena, yet seeks to give rise to the various paths, remaining unconfused therein and accomplishing the Way of the Teacher—this is called purity.
Although phenomena arise, if the mind wavers and harbors thoughts of the three vehicles—this is called impurity.
"Diligently practicing the wisdom that accords with the dharma-realm and attaining its realization—this is called purity.
Knowing that all Buddha-dharmas are one and not two, and further understanding them to be without arising or ceasing, empty, quiescent, and formless—this is called purity."
To abide in the ten powers without being distant from the ten stages, advancing in the cultivation of clear wisdom to transform all realms—this is called purity.
To observe all phenomena and be forever free from the three poisons—this is called purity.
“The Mahāyāna True Dharma transcends birth and death; this is called purity.
All dharmas are without attachment, yet consciousness and perception arise spontaneously; this is called impurity.
All dharmas are without instruction, yet they give rise to the six perfections; this is called purity.”
To know the Dharma of the wheel-turner as having a fixed locus is called impurity.
To cultivate all dharmas as being of one single characteristic is called purity.
To speak of the non-arising of all dharmas while giving rise to a dualistic mind of views regarding birth and origination is called impurity.
The Tathāgata, having attained sagehood, turns the Great Wheel of Dharma; emptiness is formless and eternally abides in nirvāṇa—this is called purity.
Not seeing any phenomena and not seeing nirvāṇa, yet harboring these two thoughts with the desire to achieve the unsurpassed, true, and correct path—this is called impurity.
The dharmas of the three periods of time have superior, middling, and inferior qualities; to receive and realize them in their proper sequence without any attachment is called purity.
To give rise to conceptualizations regarding them and perceive a subject who realizes them is called impurity.
"That which is fundamentally without increase or decrease and entirely returns to emptiness is called purity;
if one perceives increase or decrease and discriminates among phenomena, this is called impurity.
That all phenomena are unborn and that one realizes the realization of non-arising is called purity."
If one perceives that all phenomena have an origin, giving rise to the conception of consciousness and recording their names and designations, this is called impurity.
Not seeing phenomena as coarse or soft is called purity;
if one again discriminates and sees them as coarse or soft, this is called impurity.
That all phenomena are unsurpassed and seen as devoid of movement or change is called purity;
if, however, one discriminates and perceives movement or change, this is called impurity.
That all phenomena are eternally quiescent and cannot be maintained or grasped is called purity.
Furthermore, if one discriminates and grasps at various dharmas, thinking, "This is a wholesome dharma; this is not a wholesome dharma," this is called impurity.
All dharmas have neither interior nor exterior; to understand and know that the body and all phenomena ultimately return to emptiness is called purity.

If, moreover, one discriminates between internal and external dharmas, thinking, "This is an internal dharma; this is an external dharma," and possesses these two [dualistic] minds, this is called impurity.
That all dharmas are deaf and do not hear sounds is called purity;
if one further discriminates among dharmas, asserting that there are both the deaf and sounds, thereby giving rise to dualistic views, this is called impurity.
That all dharmas accomplish all factors of the path is called purity;
to perceive a means of escape or to perceive the fruits of the path is called impurity.
That the hundreds of thousands of millions of practices are inexhaustible, all returning to emptiness without conceptualization, is called purification.
To see the exhaustion of outflows, the severing of fetters, and the removal of bonds is called impurity.
That all dharmas are empty and formless, that what arises does so of itself and what ceases does so of itself, and that neither arising nor ceasing is perceived—this is called purity;
if one further discriminates and perceives the occurrence of arising and ceasing, this is called impurity.
All dharmas are likewise not received from a teacher; awakening to them spontaneously and accomplishing the eightfold equal practice is called purity.
If, moreover, one perceives that there is something to be learned from a teacher and distinguishes between high and low, this is called impurity.
When the mind of patience does not arise and one attains a mind of gentle forbearance, severing all fetters so that they are forever stilled and do not arise, this is called purity.
If one can contemplate without reckoning fundamental activities, yet there is arising and ceasing, then there is the dualistic mind that discriminates among phenomena; this is called impurity.
To seek the Way and associate with virtuous friends is called purity;
