if, however, one contemplates with a mind of indolence and harbors thoughts of retreat, this is called impurity.
To receive instruction through the sounds and echoes of the Dharma being turned from beginning to end is called pure;
if, moreover, one perceives the sounds and echoes of the Great Wheel of Dharma being turned while receiving the teaching, this is called impure.
When there are no dharmas of the twelvefold dependent origination, yet one is able to discern them immediately, relinquish them, and not follow them, this is called purity;
to see that which is blazing as being the extinguisher of the fetters is called impurity.

"All dharmas are most marvelous and extraordinary; they cannot be exhausted in their departure nor are they depleted in their arrival. To ferry sentient beings across and enable them to reach the other shore is called purity;
if one further perceives a 'crossing to the other shore,' this is called impurity."
To contemplate that all dharmas of the future are eternally extinguished is called purity;
to perceive that there is arising and ceasing in the future is called impurity.
To discern the eighty-four modes of conduct within the present, thereby adorning the majestic countenance and physical appearance of the Tathāgata, is called purity.
To see that which exists in the present and give rise to a mind of craving and attachment toward its physical appearance is called impurity.
To realize that all phenomena are unarisen and devoid of fabrication, naturally corresponding to the discipline of the *pāramitā* of deliverance, is called purity;
if one perceives the fabrication of all phenomena and gives rise to such a mind regarding the prohibitions and precepts, this is called impurity.
"All dharmas are without form or image; they all return to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and correspond to the unsurpassed path—this is called purity.
If, moreover, one perceives the transformations of forms and colors and gives rise to conceptual thoughts, this is called impurity."
All dharmas are solitary and without companion; that all dharmas are ineffable and that no verbal teaching is perceived is called purity.
To perceive the existence of spoken dharma or verbal teaching is called impurity.
That all phenomena do not arise and are unstained by the three periods of time is called purity;
to see the phenomena of the three periods of time as having arising and ceasing is called impurity.
That all phenomena are without dependence and do not cling to the triple world is called purity.
To see that there are those who rely upon and are attached to the three realms is called impurity.
That all phenomena are bodiless and have only the Dharma as their essence is called purity;
to see a dharma-body that transcends knowledge and vision is called impurity.

"The Buddhas of the future, past, and present—those who have departed are innumerable and those yet to come are inexhaustible—and the teachings they proclaim are each without discrepancy; this is called purity.
If, moreover, one were to speak of the teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods as being subject to increase or decrease, this is called impurity."
That all phenomena are formless and devoid of physical appearance is called purity;
that one further constructs physical appearances from all phenomena is called impurity.
That all phenomena cannot be seen and are as tranquil as empty space is called purity.
Furthermore, if one proclaims that all phenomena are visible, this is called impurity.
That all phenomena are immeasurable and non-contradictory is called purity;
to see phenomena as having measure and number is called impurity.
All dharmas have neither objects nor lands; to teach and transform sentient beings and purify Buddha-lands is called "purity.
If one perceives sentient beings as purifying Buddha-lands and transforming sentient beings, this is called "impurity."
“The equality of all dharmas and their single nature as nirvāṇa—this is called purity;
to see that there are those who receive fruits and accomplish the Path—this is called impurity.
That all dharmas emerge from the essential and do not dwell upon the retribution of dharmas—this is called purity.”
To perceive that there is an escape from existence through the retribution of receiving dharmas is called impurity.
That all dharmas are ultimately devoid of birth and eternally free from form and color is called purity;
to perceive that there is liberation from birth through the reception of form and color is called impurity.
That all phenomena are eternally settled and never undergo change is called purity;
to perceive them as moving, transforming, changing, or unstable is called impurity.
That all phenomena cannot be perceived and that no one can trace their tracks is called purity.
"Whatever has visible traces that can be sought after is called impure.
The Buddha again addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:

"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who maintains and practices both the pure and the impure, he will immediately in this present life attain the samādhi of inexhaustible wisdom and the concentration of right reception; he will then be able to transcend the realms of all Buddhas, traveling from one buddha-field to another, teaching and transforming sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields."

He discerns the destination of each and every phenomenon, universally moistening all beings with the four immeasurable minds; he instructs them gradually, leading each to cross over, and fulfills each according to their original vows. Furthermore, by observing with the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, he thoroughly understands their fundamental roots and purifies their conduct.

"At times, when a bodhisattva enters right concentration (*samādhi*) and attains the wisdom of supernormal powers, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, further bestow their majestic spiritual power upon them. They discern the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which arises spontaneously and ceases spontaneously; its arising is not my arising, and its cessation is not my cessation."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not have such a thought as:
"Because of my birth, this dharma arises; because of me, this dharma ceases.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not have such a thought.

"I have now become a bodhisattva, while so-and-so has not; I have perfected the bodhisattva-dharma, while so-and-so has not; I have attained the ultimate, while so-and-so has not; I have mastered the bodhisattva’s illusory arts, while so-and-so has not; I have accomplished the bodhisattva’s transformation of beings, while so-and-so has not; I have realized the bodhisattva’s resonance, while so-and-so has not; I have attained the bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom, while so-and-so has not; I have entered the bodhisattva’s realm, while so-and-so has not; I have transcended the root of all practices, while so-and-so has not; I cultivate the bodhisattva precepts, while so-and-so does not; I purify the bodhisattva-field, while he does not."
"In this way, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
From the very beginning, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not harbor the thought of discriminating among dharmas as being superior or inferior."

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva attains this meditative absorption of the samādhi of focused intent, they travel by means of their supernormal powers according to their own thoughts, maintaining a mind that neither increases nor decreases with respect to any phenomena.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who attain this state of meditative concentration, they will be capable of traveling about to teach and transform sentient beings and purify Buddha-lands. From one Buddha-land to another Buddha-land, they shall pay homage and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Furthermore, through skillful means and expedient devices, they shall act as spiritual friends for others, subtly expounding the teachings of the Way until they reach the Way of Non-action (*asamskṛta*). They shall also cause sentient beings to establish firm faith, regarding one another as father, mother, elder brother, or younger brother, each without any divergent thoughts. Thus, teaching and instructing one another in turn, they shall fully accomplish the fruits of the Way according to their aspirations.
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva entering this samādhi, whereby he is able to fully perfect all dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"The source of all dharmas Is the gate of their ultimate convergence; Though the gates differ,"
The realms of each are distinct, and the dharmas they practice are likewise so.
I have taught the path of purity; its manifold practices are inexhaustible.
Now I shall briefly explain them to you, so that you may purify those practices that are impure.
The Buddhas are immeasurable, and their teachings are inexhaustible;
now I shall briefly explain the essential points, distinguishing the fruits of the various paths.
The meaning of the Buddhas is vast and great, yet the wisdom of emptiness is not different [from it].
Each having achieved full accomplishment, they all return to the gate of liberation.
With the faculties of their various wisdoms purified, they are praised by all Buddhas;
severing discursive thought and eliminating all perceptions, they preach with the perfection of manifold wisdoms.
The teachings expounded by all Buddhas cause one to know the afflictions of affection and craving;
by forgetting existence and not dwelling in existence, one thus attains the status of the Honored One among men.
The Buddha, having accumulated past practices from the beginning, attained for himself the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Fully endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva, they propagate the activities of the Mahāyāna.
With manifold wisdoms manifest before them, they thoroughly know the origins of sentient beings and discern that there is neither arising nor ceasing.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:

“If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who attains the full perfection of the various pāramitās, discerns the subtle practices of the dharma-realm, increases in wisdom, and expounds and disseminates instruction so as to cause it to pervade everywhere, they shall attain the four fearlessnesses and mastery over the manifold wisdoms.”

Furthermore, having attained the essential departure [from suffering], they deliver those not yet delivered; they bring to mind all dharmas so that they appear before them; their meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are perfected; mindfulness and consciousness serve as their sustenance; the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is their body; and dhāraṇī is their practice. They constantly traverse the buddha-fields, causing all sentient beings to be fully endowed with everything, to accomplish the Buddha-way, to discern various concentrations, and to practice skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

The practices of all Buddhas transcend all measure; according to the thoughts of sentient beings regarding good and evil, they are able to discern them all and transform them accordingly. For countless billions of koṭis of kalpas, they enter meditative concentration with a single mind, never violating the True Dharma nor harboring any other divergent thoughts.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra with these verses:
"In the past, when I sought the Buddha-way, I had not yet received the prediction of a bodhisattva;
Yet for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, My meditative concentration remained unshakable."
Having thoroughly realized all phenomena, One does not give rise to thoughts of defiled attachment;
From this, one attains Buddhahood, Becoming the Honored One among humans.

[The original manuscript lacks seven gāthās from this point onward; they have been recorded here according to the translator’s notes. "All dharmas are inconceivable, and the realm of sentient beings is likewise so."

Furthermore, if a good man or a good woman enters the formless samādhi and surveys the trichiliocosm in its entirety, they shall likewise perceive those sentient beings who are ready for deliverance; they shall likewise perceive those who are infinite and immeasurable and not yet ready for deliverance; and they shall likewise perceive the arising and ceasing throughout the three periods of time.
"In this way, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who attains this meditative concentration practices both the pure and the impure.
**Chapter 35: The Questions of Śakra Devānām Indra** (12) *The Bodhisattva-Necklace Sūtra* At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught that all dharmas are to be made pure, and that the immeasurable Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are as pure as space and entirely non-existent. Now, we further hear it said that one should fully awaken to and know all dharmas.”
"How can one seek to awaken to and know all phenomena when, among all phenomena, there is no form and they are invisible?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra-devānām-indra:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Kauśika! You are indeed able to inquire about this meaning before the Tathāgata. I shall now provide you with a series of analogies one by one; for the wise understand through metaphors.

It is just as a master illusionist conjures all manner of things: kingdoms, cities, palaces, halls, houses, food and drink, beds and couches, the poor and the lowly, the wealthy and the noble, names, surnames, parents, brothers, servants, attendants, and even conjures people to stand as his left and right guards.

Just as when a magician perceives his own magical transformations, and for the duration of many eons provides whatever is required—clothing, food and drink, medicine, beds, and bedding—the recipient truly receives them and the donor truly gives them.
"As you observe it, does it truly exist?
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying, "It does not."
World-Honored One! Why is this?

All dharmas are empty and quiescent; they are illusory transformations and not real. The foolish, being deeply attached to them, fall into perversion. There is no coming and no going, no attachment and no bondage, no exhaustion and no non-exhaustion. These illusory transformations have no form and cannot be relied upon.
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra: "So it is,
so it is, Kauśika!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having attained the Samādhi of Illusion and the spontaneous concentration of mind, they discern the arising of all dharmas; being without conditions and without attachment, they perceive neither success nor failure. They transform and guide all classes of sentient beings, yet they perceive neither one who is saved nor one who is not saved. There is nothing saved and nothing transformed; all is empty and quiescent, further devoid of arising and ceasing.

Why is this? Because the samādhi of the concentration of mind like an illusion is profoundly deep, subtle, and boundless; its illusory realm is inconceivable. Only a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can universally observe it and thereby attain full realization; therein, one perceives neither arising nor ceasing, nor does one perceive that which is yet to arise, nor does one perceive that which has already arisen.
Why is this? The entryway of the bodhisattva is inconceivable; it is not something known by arhats or pratyekabuddhas.

That which the bodhisattva delivers is like empty space; that which empty space delivers has no form and no image. The illusory samādhi is also like this: it has no east, west, south, north, nor the four intermediate directions, nor above or below.
“Kauśika, you should know that I shall now provide you with an analogy.

It is like an ordinary person who originally lacks form or color and is unable to discern the root of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Such a person does not know birth when there is birth, nor do they know non-birth when there is non-birth; furthermore, they do not know what is yet to be born or what has already been born. They are unable to reach the ultimate realization of the phenomena contemplated by the mind; they neither see abiding nor see non-abiding, and they neither see exhaustion nor see non-exhaustion.”
Why is this? Because the mind is fundamentally formless and cannot be grasped or clung to; it is also beyond the capacity of the three vehicles to conceive or imagine.

Kauśika, you should know that it is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: having entered this illusion-like samādhi, all dharmas appear before them, yet they have no limits and no objective sphere; therein, existence is not seen as existent, and non-existence is not seen as nonexistent.
Why is this? The realm of the bodhisattva is inconceivable, and the principles of their practice pervade the trichiliocosm.
"Kauśika, you should know that I shall now provide you with a simile."

It is just as when the Dragon King Sāgara intends to send down rain: if it is for the six heavens, he sends down ambrosia; if it is for those above the Four Heavenly Kings, he can send down the seven treasures. When the Dragon Kings Nanda, Upananda, and Mānasvin send down rain upon the six heavens, it becomes clothing, ornaments, fragrant garlands, and flower wreaths;
if they send down rain upon the fourth heaven, food and drink appear spontaneously, each providing full sufficiency.
"How is it, Kauśika? Is this action performed by this nāga something that truly exists?"
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying: “No,
World-Honored One.”
"Why is this? It is solely because of the merit of those devas that the dragon kings and others present these offerings.
The Buddha then asked Śakra-devānām-indra:
"How is this so, Kauśika?

These palaces of the seven treasures, as well as the garments and ornaments, were originally non-existent, having been bestowed by the nāgas; yet now you yourself claim that it is because of the merit of the devas that the nāgas cause the rain of these treasures to fall."
"Are the various dragons and precious objects existent or non-existent?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
In truth, neither the Dharma nor the teaching exists, nor are there dragons, nor are there precious objects. Why is this?
All phenomena are empty and quiescent; even my own body and the heavens do not exist.
"The rain sent down by the dragon is neither rain nor non-rain; it is neither seen to be exhausted nor seen to be inexhaustible.
It is only deluded and ignorant people who give rise to perceptions and conceptions of it.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

“In this way, Kauśika, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the illusion-like samādhi, he thoroughly contemplates all dharmas and the arising of all dharmas; yet he perceives neither arising nor non-arising.”

He saw that all dharma-gates have both exhaustion and non-exhaustion; he saw that the gates of illusory and transformative dharmas have both exhaustion and non-exhaustion. Furthermore, he saw immeasurable and limitless gates of teaching and transforming; he saw immeasurable and limitless gates of the walking and pacing of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. He saw immeasurable and limitless gates of penetrating the net of various faculties; he saw immeasurable and limitless kalpas of the formation, destruction, and conflagration of Buddha-worlds. His mind was vast and great, transcending the gates of dharma practiced by all Buddhas.
Thus it is, Kauśika!

You should know that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; it is only because sentient beings give rise to their own conscious attachments, fail to enter meditative concentration to observe the human mind, and do not understand the wisdom of emptiness that they fail to attain non-arising.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
“The gateway to the essential departure and entry into the Path, Discerning the activities of the three periods of time,
Transmigrating through the five realms of existence, One destroys being and does not dwell in being.”
The Bodhisattva contemplates according to reality, clarifying the path through discerning wisdom;
the practices originally performed by myself have now finally been realized.
The world is entirely like space, free from the dualistic notions of "self" and "other."
Reverently honoring all Buddhas, you have now attained the crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa);
your countenance is like the udumbara flower, with broad and long eyes that cover the face.
Neither born nor extinguished, your virtue makes you the Honored One among devas and humans.
Kauśika, you should remember the origin: all practices are without deficiency or omission;
with courage and without indolence, one realizes that from beginning to end all is empty.
While sitting, do not give rise to conceptual thoughts; do not perceive anyone standing upon their feet.
Not relying on the foundations of various practices, one is therefore called a śramaṇa.
In reality, there is no nirvāṇa, nor are there the five destinies;
yet the place where Bodhisattvas roam is where they manifest birth through skillful transformation.
For incalculable eons, he has been without desire and without greed;
from the beginning, he has never had a mind of regret, much less any attachment.
Since that time, he has cultivated goodness without departing from its source.
In a single practice, one attains the Way of the Buddha, And gains the turning of the unsurpassed Dharma.
Reposing within the midst of birth and death, One teaches and transforms countless people,
Causing them to know the Dharma of non-arising, Spontaneously responding to the Way and its teachings.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking these verses to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, countless hundreds of thousands of devas and humans attained the mind of non-arising right there on their seats.
Furthermore, there were countless devas and nāgas, all of whom resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
The Buddha again addressed Śakra-devānām-indra:
"If there are good men or good women, as well as the fourfold assembly:

Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who receive, uphold, recite, and chant this inexhaustible dharma of the concentration on the illusion-like will be able to fully possess the immeasurable treasury of the Dharma.
What is the immeasurable treasury of Dharma?
Those who wish to be fully endowed with the eloquence of a Tathāgata should study this inexhaustible treasury of Dharma, which is the concentration of mind on the illusion-like state.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters wish to attain ultimate awakening to the Buddha-wisdom, they should study this inexhaustible samādhi of the mind of illusion-like concentration.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to travel to the worlds of all Buddhas to draw near to them, they should study this inexhaustible samādhi of the concentration of mind on the illusion-like.
The Buddha again addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma as turned by the Buddha, and who wish to be fearless amidst the great assembly, they should study this inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma—the concentration of mind on the illusion-like."
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to obtain the hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇīs of all Buddhas for their own enjoyment, they should study this inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the concentration on the mind of illusion.
The Buddha again addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, and desires to purify buddha-fields and manifest transformations through supernormal powers, they should study this inexhaustible treasury of dharmas, the concentration of mind like an illusion."
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to cause the immeasurable sentient beings of the various Buddha-worlds, with their immeasurable dispositions and conducts, to all attain the same destination, they should study this concentration of mind on illusion and the immeasurable treasury of dharmas.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to cause the immeasurable Buddha-fields of the various worlds to merge into one, with a color like pure gold, they should study this inexhaustible treasury of dharmas, the concentration of mind on the illusion-like.
Why is this? All Buddhas are born from this; all Buddhas of the past attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path through this concentration of mind on the illusion-like nature of reality.

The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions in the present also all attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path from this inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the illusory-like meditative concentration.
"Innumerable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the future shall also practice this inexhaustible Dharma-gate of the samādhi of the illusory-like mind.
The Buddha again addressed Śakra-devānām-indra:
"I shall now provide you with a parable; through analogies, the wise understand for themselves."
It is like a fierce fire, its flames blazing and intense, which, when further supplied with fuel and fanned by a great wind, becomes even more vehement.

It burns away mountains and forests without ceasing until the grasses and trees are exhausted before the power of the fire finally subsides. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having resolved to train in order to deliver sentient beings, he discerns and contemplates the course of the Dharma-realm, extending even to countless lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. He further observes the origins of the faculties of sentient beings within the void, and again reflects upon the intentions and the origins of the minds of sentient beings in countless worlds throughout lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Discerning each one individually, he further deliberates: "By what wisdom shall I fulfill their vows?"
Having analyzed each point regarding the direction of the Dharma, he considered which dharmas should be turned and how they should be taught.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected:
"I originally made a vow to fulfill all virtues and to transform sentient beings everywhere so as to satisfy my aspiration."

Furthermore, he himself fully perfected his deportment and etiquette, turning toward the fundamental practice of the three periods of time. He reflected upon turning the Dharma wheel and entering the inconceivable.

Thus, he deliberated upon those who should be saved and those who should not, whether all worlds exist or do not exist. He again traversed the infinite, immeasurable, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds, circulating among them to establish meritorious karma. Without severing his solemn vow for the essential path of the True Dharma, he practiced great compassion and maintained a heart of vast resolve, exhausting the cycle of birth and death without any deficiency or diminution in his mind.
Why is this? Because they are fully endowed with all forms of wisdom.

Furthermore, they observe the thoughts and intentions within the minds of sentient beings to discern by what path they may be guided, constantly mindful of sentient beings as a mother loves her child.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, maintaining this mind of immeasurable diligence and austerity, further enters into immeasurable and limitless samādhis; observing the world without abandoning his original vow, such is his vast and boundless efficacy.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"When a Bodhisattva first resolves his mind, His great vows are most vast and wide;
Only when he reaches the very limits of space Will his aspirations be fully fulfilled."
When delivering sentient beings, one perceives no one being delivered;
understanding that the three periods of time are fundamentally based on causes and conditions that do not endure,
the mind remains upright and unshakable, its true foundation responding to the Way and its teachings.
Constantly seeking skillful means, one proceeds step by step until liberation is reached.
Without harboring any timidity in the mind, one contemplates the Dharma day and night;
through this single practice, one attains Buddhahood, and does not receive it from a teacher.
Body, mind, and faculties each proceed on their own; through the power of the Way, one knows purity.
Having gone forth into the empty wilderness, one enters meditative concentration with the body unmoving.
Blazing intensely, all dharmas universally illuminate the worlds of the ten directions.
"By cultivating the knowledge of past lives for oneself, one then knows the faculties of sentient beings.

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma to Śakra Devānām Indra, everyone in the entire assembly was not without joy; they all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

36. Chapter on Past Deeds (12). *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Diadem* (Bodhisattvamaṇyālaṃkāra-sūtra), Chapter Thirty-six: Past Deeds. At that time, there was a devaputra named Saṃghaśīrṣamaṇyālaṃkāra. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes, and composed his faculties. Having constantly practiced the pure life (brahmacarya) since the time of previous Buddhas, he had exhausted the three bases [of existence] and fulfilled his vows. With his right knee touching the ground, kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying: “So be it, World-Honored One!”
"The realm where you dwell is extremely distant from here; whatever you wish to ask, if you are granted permission, I dare to receive your inquiry.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maṇikuṇḍala, Leader of the Assembly: "Excellent, excellent!"

"Noble son! As a leader of the multitude, you have brought forth the awakening of the ignorant, erected the great banner of the Dharma, and spread the radiance of wisdom. Now is the very time for whatever doubts or knots you may have; the Tathāgata shall analyze each one for you, responding to your questions so that you may attain understanding and liberation."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maṇikuṇḍala, the leader of the assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is it possible for a Bodhisattva in his final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) not to further cultivate the unsurpassed, right, and true path, yet still attain Buddhahood?”

Is there perhaps any bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the faculties, virtues, and powers, even up to a bodhisattva mahāsattva of the eighth stage, who does not further cultivate and advance toward the unsurpassed, right, and true path?

"Are there any among the devas who, having fulfilled all practices and established themselves in non-retrogression, with their faculties complete, can attain Buddhahood without again taking a human body?
Indeed they can, World-Honored One!"
"You should dispatch them by means of skillful expedients.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Maṇikuṇḍala, the leader of the assembly, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Noble son! You are indeed able to let out a lion’s roar before the Tathāgata.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!"

From the first generation of the aspiration for enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, the various dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas differ; there may be some Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, in the mere twinkling of an eye, seek the Bodhisattva mind and immediately achieve the unsurpassed, right, and true path without passing through days or nights.

There may be bodhisattvas who, from their first resolution, do not abandon their great vows and advance toward the Buddha-way through the sixth stage, yet they subsequently regress and fail to achieve success.

"Or there may be bodhisattvas who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment up to the seventh stage, proceed toward the attainment of Buddhahood without passing through the eighth stage.
At that time, the leader of the assembly, the Bodhisattva Maṇikūṭarāja, asked: "How is this so?"
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to the Bodhicitta for even the duration of a finger-snap, they shall attain the Buddha-way without passing through days or nights.
Why is it that from the first production of the thought of enlightenment up to the sixth stage, there are those who regress and do not achieve success?
"How is it that a bodhisattva, even up to the seventh stage, advances toward Buddhahood without passing through the eighth stage?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Great Ornament (Mahā-Ābharaṇa), the leader of the assembly, saying:

"If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, in the mere twinkling of an eye, seeks the bodhisattva path and attains Buddhahood without passing through days or nights—this son or daughter of good family has all faculties complete and has never before experienced the hardships of birth and death. Perhaps they have come from some assembly to be born here after suddenly cultivating the celestial path; or perhaps they have come from the Buddha-field of Aśoka to be born here; or perhaps, having heard the Tathāgata once preach the path of the emptiness of beginning and end and the absence of arising and ceasing across immeasurable Buddha-fields, they immediately attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."

"Or there may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having fulfilled all practices, attain the Tathāgata’s clear wisdom and Dharma-contemplation; they further cultivate the Tathāgata’s recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, recollection of the devas, recollection of ānāpāna, and recollection of death; they recollect the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; they associate with virtuous friends, do not indulge excessively in lust, anger, and delusion, increase their roots of goodness, and also cause sentient beings to be fully endowed with roots of goodness."
Although he was in the sixth stage, doubt arose in his mind:
"Alas! Could it be that I am not yet a Bodhisattva of the seventh dwelling?"
Or again, they may think to themselves:
"I am certain of this, without doubt.
Then, manifesting as a counterfeit bodhisattva, they speak to ruin this bodhisattva, saying:
"You have now attained the wisdom of emptiness regarding both the beginning and the end.
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, thinking:
"Now that I have heard the testimony and verification from the Bodhisattva Śrīguṇarāja, I shall surely attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
"In this way, before long, they will regress from the sixth stage and fall into the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Maṇikūṭarāja:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having already fulfilled the bodhisattva practices in the sixth stage, further reflects to themselves:"
"I now truly know that I am in the eighth stage and shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Furthermore, before long, he will approach a spiritual friend who, through skillful means, will explain the practices of the eighth stage, saying:
"Good son, do you not know?..."
"You now abide within the eighth stage; do not be conceited and disparage other bodhisattvas.
In this way, son of good family, it will not be long before you shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."

Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he then followed the instructions of the good man and, in a secluded and quiet place, focused his mind on self-reflection.

"In this way, that bodhisattva stands within the eighth stage of practice as one established in non-retrogression; performing the work of a Buddha, they will attain Buddhahood before long after passing through the succession of kalpas.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Maṇikuṇḍala, the Leader of the Assembly:
"If there is a good man or a good woman practicing the bodhisattva path who is further exhorted by another bodhisattva:"
"You shall now accomplish the Buddha's teaching and transform sentient beings before long.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"I do not possess such conduct; how then shall I accomplish the unsurpassed, right, and true path?"
"Could it be that this person has prevented me from attaining final perfection?
Holding his resolve firmly, he was able to advance further and attained the stage of non-retrogression in the seventh bhūmi.
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva being in the sixth stage, wherein there is both regression and non-regression.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maṇikuṇḍala, the leader of the assembly, asked:
"Is it the case that a Bodhisattva in the eighth stage immediately attains Buddhahood without passing through a womb, or is this not so?"
The Buddha said: “There are.

A Bodhisattva dwelling in the eighth stage contemplates all dharmas as being like space and like an illusion—empty, quiescent, and formless. The dharma-principles he practices are likewise like space. Though he desires to deliver sentient beings, he has no perception of ‘sentient beings. He travels to the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions to hear and receive immeasurable dharma-teachings; yet regarding all Buddhas, he fundamentally has no perception of a body. He should also discern that both the internal and external are formless, and he shall inquire of all Buddhas about all dharmas without ever becoming weary.”

Furthermore, one should instruct all sentient beings to abandon what is erroneous and embrace what is correct, entering deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Whether sitting, one should know when to sit; whether lying down, one should know when to lie down. If transforming sentient beings, one must not miss the proper timing, preaching the profound Dharma so that all classes of beings may attain complete liberation.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus endowed with such practice, they immediately attain the Buddha-samādhi, transforming sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields. Having purified the buddha-fields, they enter the essential path of the bodhisattva; having entered this essential path, they are able to give birth to all dhāraṇī dharma-gates; and being fully possessed of these dharma-gates, they can manifest unhindered eloquence.

The Dharma teachings expounded by all Buddhas of the future, past, and present are entirely complete and possess infinite transformations; these dharmas are fully realized without any confusion, capable of purifying the defilements of the minds of all sentient beings, whereby one attains liberation and the unimpeded wisdom of the Dharma. All Buddhas of the ten directions will come to protect these good men and good women, who shall accomplish all dharmas, be endowed with the ten powers, and be entirely free from fear.
"The Bodhisattva thus discriminates the thoughts and consciousness of sentient beings, selecting each one individually and never abandoning them.

He establishes all people so that they may attain the wisdom of original and terminal emptiness, settling them in the Way and its teachings throughout immeasurable and limitless worlds in the ten directions. While there are separations in various aspects, there are also unions throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
Furthermore, in immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—adorned with the garlands of manifold wisdom—appear before him.
Moreover, he clearly discerns the names, titles, and clans of each of the Buddhas in those immeasurable lands;

just as he discerns the names and clans of immeasurable Buddhas in one direction across immeasurable Buddha-worlds, so too does he discern the names and clans of the Buddhas in all realms throughout the ten directions.

“Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva causes the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions to expand or contract; just as he has expanded and contracted the worlds of the ten directions, he further uses the power of wisdom to expand or contract immeasurable and limitless lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
Furthermore, within each and every name, one beholds the faces of immeasurable and infinite Tathāgatas, who, through the power of wisdom, either expand or contract them.

In this way, one distinguishes the names of all Buddhas throughout immeasurable and infinite Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; one thus distinguishes the names within the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas of the ten directions. Yet, all these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, come to protect and sustain this Bodhisattva, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.

"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains this Mahāyāna intention and enters the samādhi of the emptiness of the fundamental and the derivative, they do not lose the rules of Bodhisattva decorum; they are able to universally observe the roots of sentient beings and further know the thoughts and mental activities of all Buddhas."
That bodhisattva should not be called a "bodhisattva," but rather should be called a "Tathāgata.

Why is this? Because they understand all dharmas and transcend all practices; they harbor no doubts regarding any dharma; their conduct is equal to that of a Tathāgata; and they have attained the true Dharma of all Tathāgatas.

They may know one lifetime, or know a hundred thousand lifetimes, or know immeasurable and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddha-dharmas; they receive, uphold, recite, and chant them, accomplishing the path of the Buddha without ever forgetting them. They enter into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) without perceiving a self, awakening to and knowing the dhāraṇīs of all Buddhas with powerful memory, never forgetting them.
"That Bodhisattva perceives all phenomena as the vision of light; with the illumination of wisdom, he dispels the darkness of ignorance, and his wisdom is non-retrogressive.
That Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), teaches and transforms sentient beings without any hindrance."

That bodhisattva has already attained immeasurable dharmas; with the faculty of hearing purified, he hears inexhaustible teachings, responding through spontaneous transformation according to faith yet not following it blindly.

That bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by means of immeasurable and limitless powers, manifests various transformations of the bodies of sentient beings; he may manifest countless forms and then merge them back into one, or again proceed from formlessness to countless forms, causing all classes of sentient beings to believe and understand. Extending his broad and long tongue, he universally covers the trichiliocosm and then retracts it back into one, thus teaching and transforming countless multitudes.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Great Being Maṇikuṇḍala:

"If there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who can fully comprehend the limits of the void throughout the worlds of the ten directions and all these various practices, he shall be called a Bodhisattva who fills the place of a Tathāgata."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Maṇicūḍa with these verses:
"Hearing the Dharma-realm throughout the ten directions, Manifesting the path for sentient beings,
Practicing the deeds of all Buddhas— O Honored Bodhisattva among men!"
Having accomplished the path amidst the multitudes, Thoroughly knowing the conduct of Bodhisattvas, Transcending all modes of practice, The Ten Powers are unimpeded.
All Buddhas constantly protect him; They stand before his face, appearing in person.
Praising his meritorious virtues, he extols the Dharma as being unsurpassed.
*The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Scroll 12;
*The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Scroll 13, also known as *The Present Retribution*.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter 37: Hearing the Dharma (13). Chapter Thirty-Seven: Hearing the Dharma.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, who rose from his seat, composed his dignified demeanor, and approached the Buddha. Kneeling with his right knee on the ground and joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it so, World-Honored One?

It is called 'attaining the unsurpassed, right, and true path through hearing the Dharma' because one hears as being equal to emptiness— empty and with nothing heard— and there are likewise no characteristics of dharmas, whether good or evil."
"The Dharma has no form or characteristics; how is it,
World-Honored One,
that one speaks of receiving, upholding, reciting, and chanting the wisdom of the emptiness of both beginning and end?"
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not reply.
Then, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha once more:
"Regarding those who hear the Dharma, is it by means of verbal instruction that they come to hear the Dharma?"
"Is it by means of wordless teaching that one attains the hearing of the Dharma?
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha a third time, saying:
"Phenomena have arising and ceasing; phenomena lack arising and ceasing. Regarding the wheel of Dharma turned by all Buddhas:
does it turn, or does it not turn?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
"What do you think, noble son?"
All Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma; yet there is both turning and non-turning.
As for what you have now asked, do you inquire about turning, or do you inquire about non-turning?
Then Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That which is now being asked concerns both the existence of turning and the non-existence of turning.”
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!
The True Dharma of all Buddhas neither revolves nor does it not revolve."
Mañjuśrī asked again: “In what way is there neither turning nor non-turning?
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas are like emptiness; therefore, there is no turning, and therefore there is no non-turning.
Mañjuśrī asked again: "Does the Tathāgata turn today?"
Is there no turning back?
Are these bodhisattvas and sentient beings hearing the Dharma,
or are they not hearing the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
"Noble son! All dharmas are pure, and the assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise pure."
"For this reason, there is neither turning nor non-turning.
Mañjuśrī asked again: "In what way is there turning and non-turning?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “Sentient beings have no turning;
it is the wisdom of the emptiness of beginning and end that is called ‘turning.
All the assemblies, my own body, and you yourself—all these are said to have no turning; it is the wisdom of the emptiness of beginning and end that is called ‘turning.’”
Mañjuśrī asked again: "In what way is there turning?
In what way is there no turning?"
The Buddha said:
“Where there is cessation, there is no turning; where there is no cessation, there is turning.
Where there is arising and ceasing, there is no turning; it is where there is neither arising nor ceasing that one speaks of turning.”
Mañjuśrī asked again: "What is meant by 'there is turning' and 'there is no turning'?
The Buddha said:
"To have a limit to one's fetters and attachments is called 'no turning back'; to have no limit to one's fetters and attachments is called 'turning back.
Mañjuśrī asked again, "What is meant by 'turning back' and 'not turning back'?"
The Buddha said:
“When all the world perceives phenomena as burning and blazing, this is called ‘non-turning’; when all the world does not perceive phenomena as burning and blazing, this is called ‘turning.’”
Mañjuśrī asked again: "What is meant by 'there is turning' and 'there is no turning'?
The Buddha said:

"Purifying immeasurable merit to bring blessings and protection to sentient beings is called 'non-reversal'; seeing the purification of immeasurable merit to bring blessings and protection to sentient beings is called 'reversal'.
Mañjuśrī asked again: "What is meant by 'reversal' and 'non-reversal'?"
The Buddha said:
“To purify the root of immeasurable sentient beings and thereby accomplish all-knowledge is called ‘non-reversion’; to perceive the purity of all immeasurable sentient beings is called ‘reversion’.”
Mañjuśrī asked again: "What is meant by 'turning' and 'not turning'?
The Buddha said:
“Furthermore, there is neither turning nor non-turning; therefore, it is called ‘turning and non-turning.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking to Mañjuśrī regarding turning and non-turning, eight thousand bhikṣus and three thousand bhikṣuṇīs attained the wisdom of the emptiness of both origin and end, and their minds became non-retrogressive.

Furthermore, there were countless sentient beings who, upon hearing this unprecedented Dharma, all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; in future ages, they shall all become Buddhas with identical names, possessing diligence and valor no different from my own.

Chapter Thirty-Eight: The Śuddhāvāsa Devas (13). The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-Eight: The Śuddhāvāsa Devas. At that time, while the World-Honored One was expounding this "Chapter on the Turning and Non-Turning of Hearing the Dharma" to Mañjuśrī, there was a Śuddhāvāsa deva-son who had planted various roots of merit under immeasurable Buddhas of the past. Having served and made offerings to those Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, he traveled from one Buddha-field to another, exhausting the entire treasury of the Dharma with unimpeded eloquence. Practicing great compassion and having attained the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dharmatā*), he manifested through skillful means (*upāya*) as being born among the devas, desiring to deliver them. He then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and together with his retinue, stood up with solemn dignity.
Then that deva-son approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We devas have planted roots of merit in past lives and now enjoy birth in heaven, delighting ourselves in the five kinds of celestial pleasures. Our attendants on all sides respond spontaneously, and we sport in bathing pools with inconceivable happiness. By cultivating what merit did we attain birth in the heavens?”

"The palace where I dwell is forty-nine yojanas in extent; its halls made of the seven treasures are more marvelous than anything in the world. Behind it lies a bathing pool surrounded by seven tiers of trees made of the seven treasures. By cultivating what merit have I obtained such blessings?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, saying: “Excellent, excellent, O devaputra!
That you are now able to inquire about this meaning before the Tathāgata—listen well and reflect upon it!

All the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, have also taught this meaning; all the Buddhas of the present and the future shall likewise teach this subtle and wondrous Dharma.
"How is it? Devaputra! I now ask you; you should answer me one by one."
"Can you recall anything that occurred before the deity who presides over the place where you dwell? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The names and titles of the devas of the past are beyond calculation or record. “In what way?”
"Son of Heaven!
Is this body of yours now permanent,
or is it impermanent?"
The devaputra replied,
“As for my present body, it is a phenomenon that is permanent, not impermanent.
The Buddha spoke again to the devaputra:
"If your present body were an eternal phenomenon, where would the devas of the past now be?
He replied, "They have been extinguished."
The Buddha said: "How so? Son of Heaven!"
"All the devas of the past have utterly perished; how then can this body of yours exist now?
The deva replied, "All the Buddhas of the past have entered parinirvāṇa; by what cause has the World-Honored One been born today?"
The Buddha asked the devaputra,
"Are the Buddhas of the past and my present body the same or not?
The devaputra replied:
"No. Why is this? The Buddhas of the past were manifest as the past within the past."
"How can it be said that all past Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa?
The devaputra asked again:
"Are there three periods of time?"
"Are there no three periods of time?
The Buddha replied to the devaputra:
"There are names for the three periods of time, yet the activities of these three periods differ."
The devaputra asked again:
"I have no doubt regarding the Tathāgata’s present statement that there were past Buddhas.
Nor do I have any doubt regarding his statement concerning the Buddhas currently existing throughout the ten directions."
"How is it that the World-Honored One speaks of the existence of Buddhas in the future world?
The World-Honored One replied,
"When you now question me, do you ask about the past, the present, or the three periods of time?"
"Are you asking about the three periods of the present,
or are you asking about the three periods of the future?
The devaputra addressed the Buddha:
"I do not inquire about the three periods of the past, the three periods of the present, or the three periods of the future; today I ask only about the Buddhas of the three periods.
Why is it that in the future they shall be called 'Buddhas'?"
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"There are two causes and conditions for future Buddhas. What are these two?"

There were also Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, who practiced great compassion and were endowed with all the marks; they employed skillful means to enter the five realms of existence, teaching and transforming sentient beings without ever violating the Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, appearing in the secular world, they may manifest as Brahmā or take the form of Śakra; concealing their Buddha-form, these are called bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have not yet attained Buddhahood.

There may be bodhisattvas who, having received the wisdom of the Tathāgata, perform the works of a Buddha, traveling throughout the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system to make offerings to and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Since they have not yet attained Buddhahood and their various marks are not yet complete, whether they manifest as celestial beings or as ghosts and spirits, they do not destroy the dharma-realm. O Son of Heaven!
This is what is meant by having the causal conditions for attaining Buddhahood in the future.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, also had two causes and conditions. What are these two?
Having attained the Lion’s Rush Samādhi, dwelling in a secluded place with a mind free from attachment, he inwardly contemplates the immeasurable merits of ten dharmas.
What are these ten kinds?
This Bodhisattva cultivates the dharmas contemplated by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; this is called the inexhaustible practice.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva discerns all the dharmas of the Tathāgata, this is called the inexhaustible practice."
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
When a bodhisattva transforms sentient beings so that they all proceed toward the unsurpassed, right, and true path, this is called inexhaustible practice."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,

when a bodhisattva discerns the infinite worlds of the Buddhas, purifies Buddha-fields, and transforms sentient beings without impairing his wisdom, accomplishing them according to the Dharma as he contemplates it— this is called inexhaustible practice."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

A bodhisattva practices the prohibitive precepts and cultivates the dharma of liberation just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has done; by means of these precepts, he transforms immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path. This is called the inexhaustible practice."

"Furthermore, O Devaputra, the Bodhisattva contemplates the essential path of transcendence of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present: beneath the King of Trees, he subdues the hosts of Māras, maintaining a mind as steadfast as the earth, incapable of being shaken."

At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyān manifested various transformations to come and terrify the Buddha; appearing sometimes with a human head and an animal body, or an animal head and a human body, or with four eyes, eight eyes, up to hundreds of thousands of eyes; or appearing as monkeys, tigers, and leopards to frighten the Buddha, [the Buddha] held his mind as firm as the earth, remaining unmoved—this is called the practice of the inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

A bodhisattva brings forth the power of retention (*dhāraṇī*) through which he maintains mindfulness for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. Whether it be from one lifetime up to a hundred thousand lifetimes, or from the recollection of one kalpa up to a hundred thousand kalpas, he discerns each and every action performed therein—whether virtuous or non-virtuous—and never forgets them; this is called the practice that is inexhaustible."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

A bodhisattva is able to discern the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three periods of time, such that all virtuous merits manifest before them. In the mere twinkling of an eye, they can cause all classes of wriggling and crawling beings within the trichiliocosm to fully realize the path of unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment, or to attain the paths of arhat, pratyekabuddha, or solitary buddha. This is called inexhaustible practice."
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva further recollects the physical, verbal, and mental conduct of the sentient beings saved by countless Buddhas of the past; he does not destroy any phenomena, but proclaims and spreads wisdom extensively to all—this is called the practice of the inexhaustible."
In this way, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who attains this "Lion’s Boundless Display" samādhi is able to fully realize all dharmas of the three periods of time.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
At times, a bodhisattva discerns the ten dharmas that are signless.
How does he discern these ten signless dharmas?

Thereupon, the son or daughter of good family internally contemplates their own body, discerning that various formations and faculties have reached maturity; there are wholesome actions and unwholesome actions, and at times they are pure, while at other times they are impure.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family externally contemplates the bodies of others, discerning each part—whether their faculties are mature or immature, or whether they are at times pure or at times impure—this, O Devaputra, is called the first practice of signlessness."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
If that practitioner internally reflects and collects the mind so that it is not distracted, practicing as I do without contradicting the sacred scriptures;

and if at that time the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—whose coming and going and walking are in accord with body, speech, and mind; who cherish the treasure of the Dharma and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma; and who, with a mind of non-arising, teach and transform the sentient beings of the three periods of time who have not yet been delivered—therein he shall obtain the spontaneous wheel of Dharma, entering the discipline of the Law limitlessly and immeasurably. This is called the second dharma of signlessness."
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

If a good man or a good woman gives rise to a great vow that pervades the trichiliocosm, their wisdom and contemplation are likewise inexhaustible; their resonance is fluent and unimpeded as they distinguish the voices of all sentient beings. Whether responding to a hundred thousand million voices with a single sound, they expound the Way and its teachings, universally moistening all classes of sentient beings. This is called the Dharma of the Three Signlessnesses."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma to extensively transform sentient beings, causing them all to attain parinirvāṇa while remaining unstained by the three periods of time; and if this wheel has never been turned before by gods, humans, Māras, or celestial Māras, but is turned solely by the Buddha—this is called the fourth dharma of signlessness."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, throughout their entire life, leaves the household life to study the Way, shaves off their hair and beard, and upholds the prohibitive precepts, so that their own person is pure and they cause all others to rejoice in what they themselves rejoice in—this is called the fifth dharma of signlessness."
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

If a good man or a good woman, whose nature and conduct accord with emptiness, comes and goes through the immeasurable and limitless from within emptiness, yet ultimately does not act for their own sake nor for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings, transcending and surpassing emptiness without encountering any obstruction—this is called the sixth dharma of signlessness."

"Furthermore, O Devaputra! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family proceeds unimpeded and alone among all sentient beings; expounds the meaning of the wisdom of universal penetration regarding the knowledge of all phenomena; sits emitting light that reaches everywhere throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions; manifests the meaning of impermanence by entering parinirvāṇa, or remains present, or passes away; or displays the primary and secondary marks, or conceals them—thereby teaching and transforming immeasurable sentient beings and purifying Buddha-lands—this is called the seventh dharma of signlessness."
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
If a good man or a good woman possesses a supernormal wisdom called 'Subduing Māra,' and attains this meditative concentration, they shall subdue the four Māras:

the Māra of craving, the Māra of desire, the Māra of death, and the celestial Māra. To enable a Bodhisattva to rely upon this Dharma and achieve accomplishment, and to become the foremost among those who wish to be Kings of Dharma, one must first practice this meditative concentration of Subduing Māra; this is called the eighth Dharma of signlessness."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family thoroughly studies all dharmas, penetrates deeply into their essential core, and fulfills the roots of goodness, they shall also cause immeasurable sentient beings to enter this essential core. They perceive the power of the Bodhisattva, which increases through the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and have already exhausted the inexhaustible dharma that is without arising or ceasing."
Although one perceives appearances, there are fundamentally no appearances; to sit, lie, and contemplate the various practices of the Bodhisattvas—this is called the ninth dharma of signlessness.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
If a son or daughter of good family is fully endowed with the roots of the ten wholesome paths of action—

what are these ten? They are the three of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind— and they possess mastery over all dharmas without being stained by attachment, delighting in the immeasurable unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and further being able to delight in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), wherein each and every concentration transforms immeasurable sentient beings.
These are called the ten dharmas of signlessness.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!

One who practices the Dharma should practice the non-dharma; taking non-action as action and non-contemplation as contemplation—this is called the most subtle among all royal practices, praised by all Buddhas, performing the work of a Buddha, and being without equal.
At that time, the devaputra again addressed the Buddha,
saying: "How is this so,
World-Honored One?"

The Buddhas of the three periods of time have no "three periods"; as the World-Honored One has taught, the Buddhas of the past return to the present, and the Buddhas of the present proceed to the future.
The dharma-realm is not fixed; how then can the World-Honored One speak of the three periods of time?
This interpretation is incorrect. Why is this so?
The past has already ceased, yet you provisionally bring it back to the present; the present is as yet unarisen, yet you further speak of the future—these various dharmas are mutually contradictory.
How then can you say that the number of past Buddhas is like the sands of the Ganges?
"Will the number of Buddhas to come be like the sands of the Ganges?
Or will the number of Buddhas currently existing be like the sands of the Ganges?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
That which you have now asked is entirely sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, which has enabled you to inquire about this meaning.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
I shall explain each point to you in detail.
The Devaputra said:
“As you have been instructed! So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha asked the devaputra,
"In what way is the past considered 'past'?
The devaputra addressed the Buddha:

"It is called 'past' because it arises and ceases gradually; it is called 'past' because yesterday's form is not today's form; it is called 'past' because yesterday's body is not today's body; it is called 'past' because yesterday's strength is not today's strength."
At that time, the World-Honored One again asked the devaputra: "How is it so,
son of good family?"
"Is the body different from perception?
The devaputra replied to the Buddha, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha asked again:
“Are name-and-form and contact different?”
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “No,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha asked again:
"Is there any difference between the path that leads out [of suffering] and the ultimate way? He replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said to the devaputra:
"Stop, stop! Son of good family!
The Buddha-treasury is vast and expansive; it is not within your sphere."
Knowledge of the past is limited; knowledge of the present is limited; knowledge of the future is limited. Why is this?

Because all dharmas arise from one another and perish from one another; fundamentally, there is no dharma that exists. There is no past, future, or present; nor is there good or evil conduct in this life or in future lives; nor are there noble ones who realize the fruits of realization. This, O son of good family, is what is meant [by the limits of knowledge].
"How can it be said that there are dharmas of the three periods of time?
At that time, the devaputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How do the designations of the three periods of time arise?"
"By what means is it extinguished?
The Buddha told the devaputra:

"Birth is fundamentally without birth, and extinction is fundamentally without extinction; all dharmas are likewise thus—birth is fundamentally without birth, and extinction is fundamentally without extinction."
"Why is this? Because their nature is naturally empty.
At that time, the devaputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the Tathāgata today in existence,
or is he non-existent?”
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"As for the body of the Tathāgata, in the past, future, and present, it neither exists in birth nor in non-birth; therefore, there is no past, future, or present."
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is it only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha who is without birth in the past, future, and present?"
“Are all phenomena entirely without arising?
The Buddha told the devaputra:
“All phenomena are entirely without arising; neither arising nor non-arising is perceived.”
The devaputra addressed the Buddha:
"From the self, persons, life-span, and sentient beings, up to the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), are these subject to arising,
or are they non-arising?"
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"Arising is not seen as arising, nor is non-arising seen; all dharmas are unattainable yet are spontaneously accomplished, and for this reason they are called 'unborn'."

The Buddhas of the three periods of time are without desire and without defilement, nor are they born; because they are not non-born, they do not arise. Samādhi and right reception are likewise so: because there is nothing to be spoken, there is no verbal teaching.
The devaputra addressed the Buddha:
“Are the four reliances and the four paths characterized by arising,
or are they without arising?”
The Buddha told the devaputra:
“The four reliances and the four paths are fundamentally non-arising; how much less could they arise now?
They will not arise in the future either.”
At that time, the devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Nature, the Stage of Thinness, the Stage of Original Non-existence, and the Stage Free from Lust, Anger, and Ignorance subject to arising?”
"Is it non-arising?
The Buddha told the devaputra:

"From having reception and grasping, up to all dharmas—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness; ignorance, craving, contact; up to birth, old age, sickness, and death; and from the stage of srotāpanna up to the unsurpassed path—these neither have arising nor are they non-arising."
At that time, the devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! What is birth?”
"What is non-arising?
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"One who has attained the perfection of mastery over the mind (ṛddhipāramitā) therefore neither perceives arising nor perceives non-arising."
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the perfection of mastery (vaśitā-pāramitā) such that there is neither arising nor non-arising?
The Buddha told the devaputra:

“From this shore to the other shore, one does not see any sentient beings who arise or who perish, nor does one see any place of abode or nest; therefore, one neither sees arising nor sees non-arising.”
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding all dharmas and the body of the Tathāgata, do they exist within the realm of arising,
or do they exist within the realm of non-arising?"
The Buddha told the devaputra:

"It exists both in the state of arising and in the state of non-arising; yet one neither perceives arising nor perceives non-arising. Therefore, the Samyaksaṃbuddha likewise exists neither in the state of arising nor in the state of non-arising."
The Buddha told the devaputra:

"If a son or daughter of good family attains this samādhi of supernormal wisdom and contemplates all dharmas with clear understanding, they find them neither in existence nor in non-existence. The Tathāgata’s sūtra-dharma is likewise: it is neither in existence nor in non-existence."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation; for this reason, one subdues the four māras.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:
"If there are good sons or good daughters who have accomplished wisdom, they will be able to fulfill all dharmas and should further cultivate ten practices."
What are the ten? First, to draw near to virtuous friends and seek them as companions;
second, to practice great compassion that extends widely to all beings.
Third, to fulfill the wishes and thoughts of others;
fourth, to purify all realms and sever all fetters and afflictions;
fifth, to cultivate the pure path as a heavy responsibility for others.
Sixth, to shoulder all manner of suffering without disparaging those who undergo it;
seventh, to transform the ignorant by instructing them in the essential truth;
eighth, to teach and admonish the deluded so that they may believe in the Right Path.
Ninth, to accord with the Dharma and not disparage the acceptance [of it] by others;
tenth, to single-mindedly uphold the Dharma and not associate with or participate in heterodox factions.
These, O son of good family, are called [the ten qualities].
“If a son or daughter of good family cultivates and upholds the True Dharma and attains this state of meditative concentration, they will be able to fully realize all dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One further addressed the devaputra:
“If there are men or women who revere their teacher, they should furthermore practice the ten unimpeded dharmas.”
What are the ten unimpeded dharmas?
First, traveling to the ten directions to pay homage and serve all Buddhas—this is called the first unimpeded dharma of a son of good family.
Second, regarding all wisdom, being neither bound nor liberated, and contemplating the dharma of cessation and extinction—this is the second unimpeded dharma.
Third, the three unhindered knowledges (*trivimokṣa*), wherein the mind is tranquil and extinguished amidst all suffering and pleasure;
fourth, the four unhindered knowledges (*catur-vimokṣa*), wherein one dwells in secluded places contemplating meditative concentration with an undisturbed mind;
fifth, the five unhindered knowledges (*pañca-vimokṣa*), wherein the seven essential paths of the Bodhisattva’s fundamental Dharma are neither increased nor diminished.
Sixth, all forms and appearances are fundamentally non-existent and their place of origin is not seen; this is the sixth unimpededness.
Seventh, reckoning that they are fundamentally formless and subject neither to arising nor ceasing, one understands impermanence; this is the seventh unimpededness.
Eighth, entering meditative concentration with a single mind, one realizes that the Way is fundamentally spontaneous and does not cling to any phenomena.
Ninth, a single intention and a single practice that accord with the Dharma and do not contradict it;
tenth, neither abiding within nor abiding without, arising and ceasing spontaneously—these are the ten non-obstructions.
Thus it is, son of good family!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family contemplates and reflects upon the ten unimpeded [knowledges], they will be able to fully realize all dharmas.
The Buddha told the devaputra:

“If there are sons or daughters of good family who, in the space of a single moment of single-minded mindfulness, are able to fully perfect all dharmas, they should cultivate ten dharmas for the sake of the ultimate meaning eloquence (paramārtha-pratibhāna).”
What are the ten? First, the arising of knowledge, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising and non-extinction;
second, the four immeasurables practiced with equanimity, free from the notion of self.
Third, they joyfully maintain self-restraint and do not lose the fourfold faith;
fourth, their words accord with reality and do not contradict their original vows;
fifth, their aspiration for the Way is firm and all dharmas are accomplished, such that their practiced right view does not deviate from its fundamental nature.
Sixth, one cultivates the contemplation of the six dharmas of respect, observing that they are fundamentally without marks;
seventh, one regards enemies and kin as equal, being free from notions of right and wrong;
eighth, one directs the mind single-mindedly toward faith, realizing the fundamental nature of what is produced.
Ninth, when expounding and teaching all dharmas, one does not harbor the notion of a dharma;
tenth, with the mind of adamantine concentration, one does not destroy suchness.
These, noble son, are called—
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is endowed with these ten dharmas, they will be able to fulfill all dharmas.
The Buddha further addressed the devaputra:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family cultivates the ten dharma-gifts while remaining free from the notion of giving, they will be able to fulfill all dharmas."
What are the ten? First, sitting beneath the King of Trees with a mind that does not waver;
second, always delighting in secluded dwelling and not remaining in tumultuous confusion.
Third, cultivating the threefold concentration that leads toward the gate of Nirvana;
fourth, through meditative stillness and concentrated mind, extinguishing one's own distracted thoughts;
fifth, restraining the mind and practicing the Way so as to be forever free from greedy attachment.
Sixth, they give neither the gift of Dharma nor the gift of material wealth with conceptual attachment;
seventh, their physical marks and signs naturally adorn them, illuminating the world;
eighth, through skillful means, they cause those who lack realization to awaken.
Ninth, to illuminate the True Dharma and manifest the light of wisdom;
tenth, to undergo suffering on behalf of others without seeking recompense.
These, O Devaputra, are called [the ten qualities].
If a son or daughter of good family practices these ten kinds of giving and does not give rise to worldly thoughts, they will be able to fulfill all dharmas. Why is this?
The minds of these good sons and good daughters are like vajra, indestructible; such are the dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas, which are not known even by arhats or pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family cultivates the ten pure dharmas, they will further be able to fully realize all dharmas."
What are the ten dharmas of purity?
First, the path should be pure; turbidity is not the path.
Second, the path should be single-minded; manifold thoughts are not the path.
Third, the Way requires contentment; excessive desire is not the Way.
Fourth, the Way requires reverence; arrogance is not the Way.
Fifth, the Way requires restraint of the mind; negligence is not the Way.

Sixth, the Way should be manifest and radiant; self-concealment is not the Way. Sixth, the Way should be continuous and connected; non-practice is not the Way. [The third version of the text repeats this sixth point.
Seventh, the Way should be diligent and energetic; indolence is not the Way.
Eighth, the Way should be awakening and enlightened; folly and delusion are not the Way.
Ninth, the Way requires transformation through teaching; stinginess is not the Way.
Tenth, the Way is near to virtuous friends; associating with the wicked is not the Way.
These, O Son of Heaven, are called [the ten ways].
Sons and daughters of good family who cultivate these ten dharmas will be able to fulfill all dharmas.

Just as the light of the sun forever dispels the darkness and illuminates the people of the world so that each may obtain sight, so too is it with the Bodhisattva: by practicing these ten dharmas, they are able to fulfill all dharmas.
