"Son of Heaven, you should know that just as genuine gold is luminous and pure both inside and out, such that whatever vessel one wishes to fashion is fully accomplished;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who is internally free from dust and defilement while externally illuminating all things, just as space universally covers everything."
The Bodhisattva is also like this: while practicing these ten dharmas, he has no conceptualization, thinking, "I have accomplished something;
I have taught and transformed sentient beings, severing all fetters and attachments."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
It is like Sumeru, the king of mountains, which is composed of four jewels; yet Sumeru, the king of mountains, does not harbor this thought:
'I am composed of four jewels and stand firmly in the midst of the four oceans.'"
It is the same for a bodhisattva who attains the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): they do not dwell upon these knowledges when speaking as is appropriate.
Why is this? Because from the very beginning there is no conceptualization.
It is just as the great earth universally supports all things, such that trees, flowers, fruits, and all medicinal herbs grow and flourish;
yet the earth has no such thought:
"I am able to bring about the growth and nourishment of these things."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this; he does not form this thought:
"I shall transform sentient beings through the practice of great compassion, traveling from one Buddha-land to another Buddha-land to protect and sustain all those who have not yet been delivered."

“Son of Heaven, you should know that it is like the four great oceans from which various kinds of jewels emerge; when sentient beings go there to gather these jewels, they return with whatever they desire, yet the ocean waters do not think:
‘I have produced these various jewels to give to sentient beings.’”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he rescues those suffering and bestows upon them the seven treasures.
These so-called seven treasures are the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). Furthermore, the Bodhisattva does not form this thought:

"I bestow the treasure of the seven factors of enlightenment; through the perfection of these roots of goodness, I shall adorn the tree of the Buddha and embellish myself with the various marks of excellence."
Why is this? Because from the beginning there has been no conceptualization.
"Son of Heaven, you should know that it is just as the Dharma-realm gives rise to all dharmas, great kindness, great compassion, and the six perfections."
The Dharma-realm also does not form this thought:
"I give birth to all dharmas, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the six perfections.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise; though he gives birth to all dharmas to teach and transform sentient beings, he also does not think or say:
"I have something to deliver.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know that it is just as when a bhikṣu who has entered meditative concentration eliminates all perceptions and his mind does not waver.
That bhikṣu in concentration likewise does not form this thought:"
"I now enter meditative concentration through the mastery of my supernormal powers.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise accomplishes all dharmas according to his thoughts; what he says is truthful and does not deviate from his original vow.
“Son of Heaven, you should know that it is like a vajra, which cannot be destroyed or broken.
Why is this? Because its original nature is inherently so.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: being in accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they do not lose the primordial limit (koṭi).
Just as a bright mani-jewel shines extensively, the moon-bright jewel does not form the thought:
"I am shining, causing sentient beings to see its radiance."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this.
Just as a person who has attained the way of the immortals (ṛṣi) is able to accomplish whatever they wish for,
that person with the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) likewise does not form such a thought:
"I have now accomplished everything I intended.
The Bodhisattva is also like this.
He is like a skilled artisan well-versed in the six arts, who may use a sword or a spear to defeat a great multitude.
That artisan also does not think:
"What I have now created is the most supreme among men; it subdues the great multitude, and there is none who can equal me."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: entering immeasurable samādhis and the concentration of right reception, he moves the trichiliocosm, yet he does not praise himself, saying, "I possess such supernatural power that it moves all worlds without exception."

"It is just as when a Wheel-Turning Sage King, having originally cultivated the ten wholesome paths and the five precepts, fully governs the trichiliocosm; his thousand sons are valiant, he is endowed with the seven treasures, and all the minor kings come to pay him homage."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King also did not form this thought:
"I am now fully endowed with manifold virtues, my body is adorned with the primary and secondary marks, and I rule over the four realms."
Why is this? Because the nature of merit is such that it does not conflict with itself.

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: practicing the Bodhisattva path and respectfully upholding the Buddha’s teachings, they constantly engage in the work of transformation, whereby devas and humans receive his grace, and the number of sentient beings he delivers is beyond measure.
Why is this? For the bodhisattva likewise has no such thought:
"I shall deliver immeasurable sentient beings and cause them to enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder."
“Emptiness is inherently so; there is no sentient being who can cause it not to be so.

It is like a farmer who sows at the proper time without missing the season: the seed before is not the seed after, and the seed after is not the seed before, yet each grows large and mutually integrates with the other.”
Yet that grain seed does not think:
"I am being produced, and that [other thing] is being diminished. Why is this?
Its intrinsic nature is thus of itself; there is no person who can cause it to be otherwise.

So too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: having universally studied all dharmas and practiced the bodhisattva path, they further use the root of the merit of the ten wholesome deeds to purify the faculties of sentient beings, causing them all to advance toward the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva does not form this thought:
"I am now delivering someone from here to there. Why is this?
Its nature is such of itself; there is no person who causes it to be otherwise.
It is like sweet rain descending according to the seasons, causing the hundred grains, grasses, and trees to flourish in accordance with the seasons.
Yet those clouds and rains do not form this thought:
"I have moisture that brings about growth and nourishment. Why is this?

Because they are fundamentally without [discursive] mind, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise: when the single rain of the Dharma-cloud descends, it universally moistens the trichiliocosm, causing all classes of sentient beings to obtain nourishment, while they do not abandon their original vows as they practice the bodhisattva path.
The bodhisattva also does not form this thought:
"I am now able to let fall the rain of Dharma, universally moistening the trichiliocosm and causing all classes of sentient beings to attain complete understanding."
Why is this? Because from the beginning there is no mind or intention; the nature of the heart of the great vow is spontaneous.
Thus, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters this samādhi of concentrated intent, they can cause sentient beings to reach ultimate purity—a purity that is not of another kind.
It can bring sentient beings ultimate peace and security, not merely other forms of peace;
it can enable sentient beings to reach the other shore, not merely other ways of reaching it;
it can enable sentient beings to attain the infinite liberation (pāramitā), not merely other means of crossing over.
It can cause sentient beings to attain ultimate joy, rather than any other form of joy;
it can cause sentient beings to sever the fetters and latent tendencies, rather than any other means of severing them;
it can cause sentient beings to dwell securely in the field of merit that is truly auspicious, rather than any other means of establishing them therein.
He can enable sentient beings to receive the blessings of the faithful’s offerings and deliver all; none other can receive such blessings and deliver all.
He can enable sentient beings to enter the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones (*ārya*); none other can enter the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones.
He can enable sentient beings to establish themselves in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*); none other can establish them in the stage of non-retrogression.
It can enable sentient beings to attain all-knowledge throughout the entirety of the trichiliocosm, whereas others cannot pervade the trichiliocosm;
it can enable sentient beings to act as leaders for others, whereas others cannot act as leaders.

Why is this? Because when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice this meditative concentration, their immeasurable Dharma-practices universally encompass all beings so that they may receive salvation. They open the gateways of the Dharma-nature and great vows, which are inconceivable, limitless, and vast; they do not purify the Bodhisattva path for a single person alone, but extend it to all sentient beings who are difficult to save, establishing therein the infinite task of delivering those who are to be saved.
"At times, for the sake of rescuing a single person, a bodhisattva sacrifices his life to undergo suffering on their behalf.

Or there may be a bodhisattva who, for the sake of one person, does not abandon them from kalpa to kalpa, vowing that he will only enter parinirvāṇa himself after that person has attained liberation."

There are some bodhisattvas who, desiring to purify their own realms and sever all fetters and attachments, cleanse the fundamental nature of sentient beings and establish them in the essential deliverance of the pure, true Dharma.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who diligently practice asceticism without clinging to celestial blessings, constantly circulating through the five paths of existence to teach and transform others.
“Some bodhisattvas attain the four fearlessnesses, teaching and transforming sentient beings without harboring any timidity or weakness.
Some bodhisattvas attain the four analytical eloquences, such that when people come to interrogate them, their principles are penetrating and unimpeded.”
There may be bodhisattvas capable of expounding the Dharma, who do not cling to glory or seek profit through fortune-seeking.
There may be bodhisattvas who have attained the gate of *dhāraṇī*, who discern the contemplation of dharmas and cultivate the practice of impurity.
There may be bodhisattvas who attain the Buddha’s concentrated mind, establishing omniscience while not abandoning discursive thought.
There may be bodhisattvas who attain the Buddha’s essential deliverance, causing all people to leave the household life and study the Way.
There are some bodhisattvas who attain the wisdom of supernatural powers and employ skillful means to enter [the world] in accordance with the forms [of beings].
There are some bodhisattvas who attain the Samādhi of Formless Contemplation, entering the realm of empty space and practicing the inconceivable.
There may be bodhisattvas who attain the samādhi of cessation, manifesting entry into parinirvāṇa yet not abiding in nirvāṇa.
There may be bodhisattvas who attain the sevenfold path of contemplation, externally manifesting dignified deportment while internally remaining truly fulfilled.

There are some bodhisattvas who attain the supernormal power of the divine eye, by which they universally observe the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, receiving teachings not yet heard and finding therein their own delight.

There are some bodhisattvas who attain the supernormal power of the divine ear, by which they universally hear all sounds and distinguish between the good and the evil; they immediately go forth to deliver those beings so as not to let them fall.
There may be bodhisattvas who attain the supernormal power of the mind and, by means of their psychic powers (*ṛddhi*), go to deliver beings.

There may be bodhisattvas who attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), whereby they know their own past lives as well as the origins from which others have come; thus, they subdue beings according to their respective types without falling into extremes.
“Some bodhisattvas attain the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows and are able to sever the fetters and bonds of all sentient beings.

Some bodhisattvas, sitting beneath the king of trees, attain the Buddha’s divine virtues, majestic demeanor, and legal precepts; they achieve perfection in their majestic demeanor, perfection in their spiritual lineage, perfection in their parents, and perfection in their household life.”
There are some sentient beings who, having obtained the Buddha’s radiance, abide in the mind that dwells where the Buddha dwells, with progress like the waxing moon.
There are some sentient beings who abide on the ground of the Buddha’s wisdom, able to sever the defilements with the sword of knowledge.

In this way, through these seventy-five dharmas and the inconceivable practices of the Tathāgata’s profound treasury, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the realization of Buddhahood and never regresses; this is beyond the reach of arhats and pratyekabuddhas.
"In this way, O Devaputra!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains this concentration of manifold practices, he can cause the entire trichiliocosm to become the color of gold and summon all classes of sentient beings, leading them all toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path."
"In this way, O Devaputra, one should transform sentient beings through these dharmas; this alone accords with the discipline of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are twelve dharmas that a bodhisattva cultivates, through which their conduct becomes unimpeded as they advance, pause, move, and come, practicing the bodhisattva path."
What are the twelve? First, subduing the armies of Māra while manifesting the ten powers;
second, sharing in merit without the notion of arising or ceasing.
Third, they are able to fulfill all vows through their supernormal powers;
fourth, relying on the power of non-attachment, they behold the transformations of the Buddhas;
fifth, according to the roots of goodness and merit they have planted themselves, they are able to bestow them upon all beings without regret or parsimony.
Sixth, to cultivate the foremost dharma beyond the measure of the Buddhas;
seventh, to know that birth is suffering and thus remain unstained by the three realms of existence;
eighth, to find personal delight in the inexhaustible root of the Path.
Ninth, knowing the practices of the śrāvakas yet remaining unstained by or attached to them;
tenth, knowing the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas and abandoning them without following them;
eleventh, practicing the nine successive stages through the dharma of the unobstructed path.
Twelfth, one should transform one’s parents and kinsmen so that they achieve fulfillment.
This, O Devaputra, is called the twelfth basis of the unimpeded, pure path; a bodhisattva should mindfully cultivate it to bring its fruit to fruition.

“Son of Heaven, you should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice single-minded concentration and cultivate the ten aspects of the knowledge of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), thereby knowing the past, future, and present, exactly as the Buddha acts, without any difference.”
What are the ten matters regarding the cessation of perception and cognition?

First, one contemplates that the forms and images of matter are fundamentally non-existent, and thus does not give rise to thoughts of form through attachment; the bodhisattva-mahāsattva acts in this way, no different from the practice of the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva cultivates the perfection of the primary and secondary marks; each and every mark is no different from what the Buddha practiced.

The Bodhisattva’s divine wisdom and transformations are boundless; he responds to and transforms sentient beings, proceeding to deliver them according to conditions, just as the Buddha practiced, without any difference.

At that time, the Bodhisattva manifested immeasurable bodies with forms and appearances of the highest excellence; with eight kinds of vocal tones, he exhorted and guided sentient beings, acting no differently than the Buddha himself.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva purifies buddha-fields, observes the thoughts and intentions of sentient beings, maintains dignified conduct and etiquette without violating the prohibitions and precepts, and acts exactly as the Buddha does, without any difference.

At that time, the Bodhisattva again entered the meditative absorption of *samādhi*, whereby he was able to recollect and distinguish the voices and sounds of sentient beings, retaining them with firm memory and never forgetting, just as the Buddha acts without any difference.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva practices the ten wisdoms of illumination, which are infinite, immeasurable, and inexhaustible; he also causes sentient beings to study this fundamental dharma, and according to the needs of the time, he turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, no different from what the Buddha has practiced.

Furthermore, those bodhisattvas attain the four fearlessnesses and roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly; they do not sever the sublime and holy True Dharma of the Tathāgata, and they further use this Dharma to transform sentient beings, causing them all to achieve and attain the Unsurpassed Way, reaching all-knowledge without any hindrance, acting no differently than the conduct of a Buddha.

Furthermore, the teachings emanated from the mouths of those bodhisattvas pervade all things and enter into the practices of the three periods of time; they exhaust all outflows to accomplish untainted practices, and through their supernatural powers and wisdom, they are able to transform all beings just as the Buddha does.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva attains the fearlessnesses and the ten powers of a Buddha; seeing the purity of the Buddha-lands and sentient beings, it is no different from the conduct of a Buddha.
"In this way, O Devaputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these ten matters, he will progress toward the attainment of Buddhahood without difficulty. Why is this? "

All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; they neither come nor go. All dharmas are signless, and even signs themselves are non-existent. All dharmas are soundless, for sound is fundamentally formless, and their intrinsic nature is itself empty.
Why is this? Sound emerges from emptiness and returns to emptiness; sentient beings, being defiled, give rise to perceptions based on consciousness.

Son of Heaven, you should know that when I formerly sought the Way, I analyzed the origins and ends of things for incalculable eons, yet I was still unable to fully exhaust the single dharma of concentrated mind.
What is this one dharma? It is so-called non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*).
When a bodhisattva attains the meditative concentration of non-conceptualization, they perceive that all dharmas are entirely formless.
"In this way, O Son of Heaven!
By means of this single practice, I have now attained Buddhahood and realized the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
At that time, the Son of Heaven from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the conduct of Bodhisattvas as we have now heard it, all dharmas are immeasurable and difficult to fathom to their ultimate limit. Since the various faculties of sentient beings differ in so many ways, how can one wish to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path?”
Furthermore, I have heard the Buddha’s words that they are no different from what the Buddha himself practiced.
Now I ask the Tathāgata: in what way are they no different from what the Buddha himself practiced?
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain each of these in detail.
At that time, the devaputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The practices of bodhisattvas differ according to their respective dharmas; the directions toward which their aspirations tend and the traces of their conduct are not the same."
"How is this so,
World-Honored One?
If the bodhisattva does not differ from what the Buddha has practiced, for what reason is he not called a Buddha?"
For what reason does one who lacks the ten powers fail to subdue the palace of Māra?
For what reason is one not called "Omniscient"?
For what reason is one not called "One who has awakened to the understanding of all phenomena"?
For what reason is he not called one who universally observes and practices the bodhisattva path?
For what reason does he not sit at the site of enlightenment to proclaim dependent origination?
For what reason is he not called the Most Perfectly Awakened One?
Why is this? Because they do not know the true Dharma of the three periods of time or the conduct of the Buddhas;
for what reason do they not remain for the duration of an eon to proclaim wisdom?
For what reason do you not rely upon all phenomena to cultivate right reception and meditative concentration?
For what reason do you not discern the dharma-realm and advance immeasurable wisdom to instruct bodhisattvas as your retinue?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Son of the Pure Abode Heavens,
saying: "Excellent, excellent,
son of noble family!"
Regarding what you have asked, it transcends all measures; I shall now explain it to you.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
O Devaputra!

Now, regarding the question that the practice of a bodhisattva is no different from that of a Buddha: all good sons and good daughters realize that all dharmas are formless and invisible. Yet the bodhisattva’s great vow extends widely to all beings—past, future, and present—who possess form. Through their mutual support and accomplishment, they have not yet attained the pure contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-darśana*) of wisdom; however, were they to attain such wisdom, they would be called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Relying on the bodhisattva’s wisdom, they transform and deliver sentient beings, attaining it themselves and then bestowing it upon others. This is called the Bodhisattva Path, which can sever the three poisons, refrain from the ten non-virtuous actions, and exhaustively reach the realm of the Tathāgata; this is what is called the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).

Having already transcended the stage of ordinary beings and established oneself in the tracks of bodhisattva practice, with a mind that does not waver from the unsurpassed, right, and true path—this is what is called a "bodhisattva.
Furthermore, if a son or daughter of good family discerns the dharma-realm and enters into its shared characteristics, this is what is called "omniscience" (sarvajñā).

Just as all dharmas are fundamentally without marks or characteristics, yet each has a name and designation for the sake of sentient beings—knowing what is to be approached and approaching it, knowing what is to be abandoned and abandoning it—one does not depart from the root of goodness while practicing the bodhisattva path; this is what is called being a "bodhisattva."
"Just as a bodhisattva discerns neither one nor two, naturally giving rise to the various *pāramitās*,
and further awakens to this himself while causing all people to likewise accord with its dharma-characteristics— this is what is called a Buddha."

Just as that bodhisattva does not perceive the arising of two or three dharmas, but skillfully examines them without forgetting, contemplating and thoroughly understanding: from what do dharmas arise?
From what do dharmas cease?
Who is the one that turns the wheel of Dharma?
Who is it that hears the Dharma?
One who is able to understand and know all dharmas is called a bodhisattva.

Just as a bodhisattva, with the eye of wisdom, surveys the trichiliocosm and perceives those with minds of desire and those without minds of desire, those with minds of delusion and those without minds of delusion, and those with minds of anger and those without minds of anger—and further, is able to contemplate and completely sever their roots—it is for this reason called the "eye of wisdom."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva with the Eye of Wisdom travels back and forth, roaming through the realms of all Buddhas; he fully knows the thoughts and mental activities of sentient beings, whether they are ready for deliverance or not. Being thus able to enter into transformation and deliver them according to their respective types, he is called a 'Bodhisattva'."

Just as a bodhisattva universally illuminates all realms with various radiances and demonstrates immeasurable wisdom, recollecting the profound and abstruse teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—this is what is called being a "bodhisattva."

"Just as a bodhisattva is able to illuminate the realm of space with the light of wisdom, so too does the divine wisdom of the Tathāgata manifest before them. He closes the gates of transgression and opens the path to nirvāṇa; furthermore, he is not defiled by or attached to the eighteen fundamental bases, being without clinging and without bondage. This is what is called a 'bodhisattva'."

It is as if a bodhisattva, through the majestic deportment of a Buddha, cultivates discernment; the Tathāgata walks alone without peer, fully knowing the beginning and end of every sentient being across the three periods of past time—including name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, becoming, and birth-and-death—and is thus called "without equal."

"Just as a bodhisattva succeeds the Tathāgata, ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed and performing the Buddha-work—wherein those who arise do not know they arise and those who perish do not know they perish; wherein there is originally nothing, yet it is quiescent and endowed with the four immeasurable minds; and wherein one further discerns that what was originally non-existent now exists, and what was originally existent now no longer exists—understanding all to be empty and giving rise to no manifold thoughts—for this reason, one is called a Buddha."

Just as a bodhisattva, having attained the wisdom of supernormal powers, observes sentient beings and perceives that kalpas are either near or far—neither feeling distress when a kalpa is distant nor feeling joy when a kalpa is near—and likewise regarding the kalpas of formation and destruction, one who restrains the will and maintains the mind without distraction is therefore called a bodhisattva.
The Buddha again addressed the Śuddhāvāsa devaputras:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices the bodhisattva path, they should further contemplate all dharmas from the first generation of the mind until the attainment of Buddhahood, without reckoning a self, a person, a being, or a life-span. When their practice naturally severs all defilements and impurities, this is called cultivating the bodhisattva path."

"Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have set out to seek the Way; they shoulder the burden of ascetic practices for the sake of all sentient beings, yet they do not perceive anyone who has attained the Way. They are also able to deliver incalculable and immeasurable sentient beings—whether there are those who receive certification or those who do not—and while receiving their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) therein, they remain unstained by attachment. This is what is called cultivating the bodhisattva path."
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family discerns the three profound and immeasurable dharmas of emptiness and knows them as they truly are.
What are these three emptinesses?
First, with applied thought and sustained thought;
second, without applied thought but with sustained thought;
third, without applied thought and without sustained thought.
"These are called the three emptinesses, which are the practice of the bodhisattva.
He further addressed the devaputra:
"There are another three emptinesses."
What are the three?
First, the emptiness of exhaustion;
second, the emptiness of non-exhaustion.
"Third, the emptiness of neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion.
These are called the three emptinesses, which constitute the practice of the bodhisattva.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:
"Furthermore, there are three kinds of emptiness:
first, the emptiness of arising; second, the emptiness of non-arising;
[and third, the emptiness of ultimate reality]."
"Third, the emptiness of neither arising nor non-arising.
These are called the three emptinesses, which constitute the practice of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:
"Furthermore, there are three kinds of emptiness. What are the three?
First, the emptiness of abiding;..."
"Second is the emptiness of non-abiding;
third is the emptiness of neither abiding nor non-abiding.
At that time, the Devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present, do all sentient beings possess birth and extinction, attachment and cessation? Do these three kinds of emptiness exist within them?”
The Buddha told the devaputra:
“I shall now speak to you; listen well and reflect upon it!
What is meant by ‘dwelling in emptiness’?”
That which is called "dwelling in emptiness" is precisely this: unconditioned tranquility.
Son of Heaven, you should know: what is meant by "non-dwelling emptiness"?
It is your body and my very self.
"What is the emptiness that is neither abiding nor non-abiding?
It is all conditioned phenomena of the three periods of time.
The Buddha further addressed the devaputra:

"If a son or daughter of good family understands these three emptinesses, they will be able to fully understand all dharmas; the body of the five aggregates of clinging is likewise thus—this is called the path of the bodhisattva."
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:
"All dharmas are neither joined nor dispersed; they are neither seen as pure nor seen as impure. Furthermore, they do not think to themselves:
'If I attain Buddhahood, I shall be born in such a place, with such a kingdom, county, parents, kinsmen, clan name, and personal name.'"
Nor does he further think:
"I am born in such-and-such an eon with a lifespan of such length.
Furthermore, he does not think to himself:
"With a body the color of gold, sitting beneath a flowering tree, he shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

This is called the Bodhisattva having already fulfilled the Way, attaining non-retrogression and practicing the mind of non-arising; since there is originally not even one mark, how much less could there be two?

"At that time, the Bodhisattva discerns that all phenomena ultimately return to emptiness and stillness; he constantly guards himself so that the evil Māra finds no opportunity. He proceeds where there is nowhere to proceed and turns where there is nothing to turn. Having thus entered the immeasurable wisdom of emptiness within the Dharma-realm, he is able to adorn himself with the dharmas of all marks."
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra, saying:

"Just as the eye and forms have no master within or without, and it is through the coming together of these three factors that visual consciousness is produced, so too it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; when the internal and external conditions are fulfilled, the various types of consciousness are produced."
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"I shall now provide you with an analogy, for the wise understand through analogies.

It is like the Naga King Elāpattra, who dwells upon a side of Mount Suvarṇabhadra; his palace is made of the seven treasures, its walls are of the seven treasures, and its trees are of the seven treasures. Its staircases and streets are all fashioned from the seven treasures, adorned with carvings and engravings composed of various jewels."

At that time, the Naga King Elāpattra’s body was as pure white as snow or crystal; a golden parasol followed behind him, his body was fragrant, and his necklaces were all fashioned from the seven treasures.
Furthermore, he fashioned food vessels from the seven treasures and crafted flower garlands from pure purple-gold.

He also made bells, drums, and musical instruments from the seven treasures. His seven parts of the body were level and even, his teeth were even and upright, and his countenance was dignified and majestic; one could never tire of gazing upon him. He was pure, fragrant, and clean, turning left and right without encountering any obstruction. Possessing these manifold virtues, they were beyond measure.

"Furthermore, Śakra Devānām-indra, the most honored among the kings of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, can conceive a thought in the time it takes to snap one's fingers and cause the Naga King Elapattra, who dwells on the side of Mount Suvarṇāvabhāsa, to arrive at the Trāyastriṃśa heaven in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm; his attendants and servants reach him immediately without obstruction."
At that time, Śakra, the Devānām Indra, wishing to have the various devas witness his meritorious virtue, immediately donned a dragon’s body adorned with the seven treasures.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, mounted this divine dragon and traveled east and west to observe his domain. During that period, the Dragon King Elāpattra again employed his supernatural powers to manifest various kinds of offerings, serving and honoring Śakra with reverent obedience.

The dragon transformed its form spontaneously, possessing thirty-two heads; on the upper mouth of each head were seven tusks, and upon each tusk were seven bathing pools. Within each pool were seven hundred lotus flowers, and upon each flower were seven hundred jade maidens. Each jade maiden, in turn, led seven hundred attendants, performing songs, music, and dance for their mutual entertainment.

Furthermore, if Śakra-devānām-indra, the Heavenly King, desires rest, he proceeds to the rear of the seven-jeweled palace to a bathing pool named Fragrant and Pure; there he personally enters the pool and, mounted upon the nāga king Airāvata, sports at his pleasure.

"At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, having entered a magnificent bathing pool and mounted this dragon, adorned his body with a variety of precious jewels; he indulged in the five desires through music and performance, sporting and enjoying himself in ways beyond description."

At that time, the Naga King Elapatra cast off his original form and ceased being a naga body; by his own supernatural power, he transformed himself into the likeness of one of the Thirty-three Gods. He then entered a bathing pool together with those gods and their various jade maidens, enjoying themselves in mutual play just as Sakra, the Lord of Devas, does, without any difference.

Looking around at this transformation, they saw that the bodies of the devas and the bodies of the nāgas were indistinguishable from one another; their forms were identical to those of the devas and their complexions were identical to those of the devas. Dwelling together in a single bathing pool without any difference, the body of Śakra and the body of the nāga were one and not two.
Why is this? It is all brought about by the accumulation of merit from past lives.

Had these two individuals originally sought the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, they would have attained Buddhahood today before long; for practice follows from the mind, and when the mind is pure, the Way is accomplished. Just as those celestial palaces originally have no known point of origin and no destination to which they go, so too all practices are empty and quiescent.
“Son of Heaven, you should know that this body of yours, as well as those celestial palaces and the deities of the sun and moon, all return to extinction and cannot be maintained for long.
Therefore, Son of Heaven!

One should understand the nature of phenomena regarding their success and failure, their destinations, and their arising and ceasing; among these, only nirvana is most peaceful and most sublime, for it cannot be destroyed or ruined by swords, blades, or incantations.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the devaputra:

"The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: having attained the concentration of unimpeded intent with firm and steadfast vows, he adorns himself with the seven jewels of bodhisattva samādhi; he embellishes his body with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment and dwells well within the concentration of unimpeded intent without distraction, emitting radiance from his body that illuminates everything."

Striking the Dharma-drum, its sound resonates throughout the ten directions; erecting the Dharma-banner, it proclaims majestic deportment. With the skeletal joints of his body as strong as a chain, his power surpasses that of devas and humans; he increases all the *pāramitās* and achieves complete mastery in the natural laws of the Dharma.

His muscles are supple and fine, untainted by dust or grime; he turns the wheel of the Dharma of wisdom, the most excellent among Dharma Kings, having entered the profound treasury of the Dharma. He takes all Bodhisattvas as his retinue and uses the bathing pools of the eight liberations to wash away the defilements of the mind.

Without severing the root of my great vow for the sake of all beings, I sat beneath the Bodhi tree and abandoned all worldly karma; I was not stingy with royal splendor, but used this as a gift to bring about the path to Buddhahood.

Then I uttered these words: "Today is the very hour; if I do not attain Buddhahood, I shall not rise from this seat. Only when I have awakened to that which is to be awakened will I rise from this seat—let only the earth and the tree spirits know my heart."

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke these words, eighty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas endowed with supernatural powers from immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions all arrived together, and heaven and earth shook violently.
The Buddhas of the ten directions each, from their respective quarters, extolled his virtue and announced it to the fourfold assembly:
"Today, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, in the Sahā world-system, shall realize the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
"Those among you who are capable of reaching that place should maintain your dignified deportment and go there to pay your respects.

At that time, the bodhisattvas of the ten directions endowed with supernatural powers, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command, all rose together in reverence and circumambulated the Buddha three times. Each one took fragrant flowers and proceeded to the Sahā world, where they presented offerings and surrounded the Bodhi tree. Their praise was immeasurable; their minds of patience were like the earth, their hair did not stand on end, and they fixed their attention before them without looking left or right. Their hearts of compassion grew ever more intense as they felt pity for those in suffering and distress.
"The reason I now desire to attain Buddhahood is out of compassion for all beings.
When these words were spoken, heaven and earth shook in six ways.

At that time, the World-Honored One gazed straight ahead for seven days without moving. The various devas, nāgas, spirits, and the eight classes of beings all came to surround and protect the Bodhisattva, so that he might attain Buddhahood and reach ultimate perfection.
I, too, do not abandon the practices of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven,
when a bodhisattva practices the six noble dharmas through their supernormal powers and advances toward the attainment of Buddhahood, they then accord with the Way and its teachings.
When I previously attained Buddhahood, I practiced great compassion through these six modes of conduct.
What are the six? First, to be benevolent and compassionate toward those who have not yet been delivered; [the remaining five follow].
Second, to practice giving universally so as to encompass all;
third, to extensively expound noble wisdom without advancing or retreating;
fourth, to practice the wisdom of the three emptinesses to purely purify the lands.
Fifth, to embrace a land with a mind free from advancing or retreating;
sixth, to receive the seal of the Buddha and certify sentient beings.
These are called the six matters by which one attains the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:

"Furthermore, there are six matters by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva keeps sentient beings in mind through transformation without harboring indolence or pride, thereby fulfilling the aspirations of all sentient beings."
First, to diligently sever all outflows and fetters;
second, to practice austerities without abandoning the mind of the Way;
third, to maintain self-awareness and restrain body, speech, and mind.
Fourth, to follow a teacher and seek to receive the True Dharma;
fifth, to cultivate virtue for the sake of sentient beings;
sixth, to enter meditative concentration and observe the fundamental source.
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, being endowed with these six matters, shall possess supernatural wisdom.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, by practicing these six dharmas, attain the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way; they extensively transform sentient beings, turn the profound Wheel of Dharma, and enter the gate of *dhāraṇī*."
What is the dhāraṇī? That which is called the dhāraṇī is the dhāraṇī of the purity of delighting in the Dharma.
When a bodhisattva enters this dhāraṇī, they are able to cause sentient beings to enjoy the joy of the Dharma-joy.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:
"Furthermore, there is the Boundless Dhāraṇī; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī enables boundless sentient beings to establish themselves in the eight liberations."
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:
"Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the uninterrupted turning of the Dharma; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they cause all sentient beings to hear the Dharma without interruption."

Furthermore, there is the Bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī for awakening to the path and comprehending the origin of sentient beings; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī enables incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings to know their original point of departure.
Furthermore, there is the unimpeded dhāraṇī of the traces of practice; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they know that the natural dharma is without arising or ceasing.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṛṇī of reciting the Dharma without forgetting; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they obtain all dharma-gates without giving rise to the notion of dharmas.

"In this way, O Devaputra, the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇīs number in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis and are not objects of mental recollection; by means of these dhāraṇīs, the bodhisattva attains mastery over hundreds of thousands of samādhis."
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:
"There are four kinds of noble Tathāgata eloquence; when a bodhisattva attains this noble eloquence, they proceed toward the gate of nirvāṇa without any obstruction."
What is the eloquence of the noble ones?

In this regard, O Devaputra, there may be a bodhisattva who, with the initial thought, enters meditative absorption, and with the subsequent thought, directs the mind toward the practice of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, without destroying the intention of the initial thought that entered absorption. This is called the noble eloquence of a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, O Devaputra, when a Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, his preceding and succeeding thoughts are tranquil and unmoving; he is able to manifest the primary and secondary marks for the sake of the world, surrounded on all sides by Bodhisattvas as his attendants. This is called the noble and sagely eloquence of a Bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

There may be a bodhisattva who manifests as if entering meditative concentration, while his mind roams through immeasurable worlds of the Buddhas, gathering the sublime and wondrous laws and teachings of the worthy ones and sages, such that no sentient beings are aware of it."
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

There are also bodhisattvas who enter the formless right concentration of the samādhi of cessation, and upon arising from that concentration, they perform countless transformations such that no sentient beings perceive them."

He may manifest a single kalpa up to a hundred thousand kalpas; he may manifest one month, or one day, or even seven days; or he may manifest the attainment of Buddhahood and the entry into parinirvāṇa.
"This is what is meant, O Son of Heaven!
The merit of a bodhisattva’s eloquence is immeasurable.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Son of Heaven, saying:
“If there is a bodhisattva who walks alone through the three realms and makes offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, they should first practice this noble and holy eloquence.

If one wishes to surpass the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, wishes to make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, wishes to exhaust the immeasurable dharmas of the three periods of time, wishes to attain liberation such as the liberation of a Buddha, or wishes to cause all sentient beings to attain Buddhahood simultaneously—thus it is, O Devaputra!”

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice this noble and holy eloquence, receiving, upholding, reciting, and explaining it to others; though they may not be able to do much, doing so during the first watch of the night is sufficient;
though they may not be able to do so during the first watch, doing so for a single period is sufficient;
though they may not be able to do so for a single period, doing so for the duration of a finger-snap is sufficient.

Why is this? Because all the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all paths arise from this; it serves as the light of the world, and those who suffer in various afflictions naturally find peace and security.

If there are good men or good women whose bodies are afflicted with sores and leprosy, with pus and blood flowing profusely, upon hearing this noble and holy eloquence, they shall immediately be healed and restored to health.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family—whose spine is bent as if bearing the heavens, whose eyes are blind, whose ears are deaf, and who is mute and unable to speak—should encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who explains to them the eloquence of the four noble ones (ārya), they will immediately receive liberation and be free from all suffering.
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
If I had not attained the four noble analytical eloquences in the past, I would ultimately never have accomplished the four noble analytical eloquences. Why is this?

The merit and blessings of this are difficult to measure; even if one were to praise this Dharma for a single kalpa up to a hundred thousand kalpas, or for countless kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there would still be no adequate analogy.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra: "I shall now briefly state the essential point.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who go to the presence of the Tathāgata and prostrate themselves at his feet, taking this as their starting point, and continue thus throughout immeasurable lands in the ten directions, performing acts of worship and making offerings with unflagging faith; using various flowers, incense, suspended silken banners, and canopies; inquiring of the Buddha about profound meanings to increase their merit; knowing that all dharmas are like illusions and transformations; and further teaching the path of the bodhisattvas to all beings while discerning the Great Path of equality in every detail."
The various practices of the bodhisattvas differ in many ways, and the natures and behaviors of sentient beings are likewise so.

There are various bodhisattva realms, various bodhisattva wisdoms, various bodhisattva dignities, various bodhisattva sublime conducts, various bodhisattva supernormal powers, various bodhisattva means of deliverance, various bodhisattva entries into non-attached realms, and various bodhisattvas who, with minds free from delusion, find joy within themselves.
The various essential dharmas of bodhisattvas, because they differentiate immeasurable teachings;
the various supernormal wisdoms of bodhisattvas, because they observe the ripening faculties of sentient beings;
the various path-wisdoms of bodhisattvas, because they do not abandon the stability of the fundamental and the derivative.
The various profound contemplations of bodhisattvas, because they enter the state of meditative concentration;
the various great vows of bodhisattvas, because they do not contravene their original aspirations;
the various heroic efforts of bodhisattvas, because they bring all dharmas to fulfillment.
The various forms of bodhisattva diligence, because they harbor no indolence;
the various forms of bodhisattva arduous effort, because they do not dwell on whether kalpas are distant or near;
the various forms of bodhisattva great compassion, because their minds are impartial.
The various forms of a bodhisattva’s great compassion arise from pitying all beings;
the various forms of a bodhisattva’s joyful mind arise from never giving rise to anger;
the various forms of a bodhisattva’s protective mind arise from relinquishing all things.
The various bodhisattva contemplations on impurity, because they internally observe all internal phenomena;
the various bodhisattva counting of inhalations and exhalations, because they inwardly collect and restrain the mind;
the various bodhisattva [contemplations on] the twelve links of dependent origination, because they personally extinguish all phenomena.
“Various Bodhisattvas contemplate the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) because they intend to sever all conceptualizations.
‘Thus it is, O Devaputra!

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as inconceivable; purifying all traces and corresponding to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), he accomplishes the root of the single path and returns to the single *nirvāṇa*. Only then does he correspond to the eloquence of the noble ones (*ārya*) and discern the sūtras and precepts spoken by the Tathāgata.’”
"What is meant by 'sūtra'?

That which is called sūtra refers to: the *sūtra* (discourse), *geya* (verses), *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), *nidāna* (origins), *itivṛttaka* (past events), *jātaka* (birth stories), *vaipulya* (extensive teachings), *adbhutadharma* (marvelous phenomena), *avadāna* (causal narratives), *upadeśa* (explanations), and *vedalla* (analytical discourses). These, O Devaputra, are what is called [sūtra]."
“A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who studies this Dharma will be able to fulfill it completely.
The Buddha further addressed the devaputra:

“If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the complete physical marks of a Tathāgata—the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty secondary characteristics, the eight qualities of the *kapila* voice, and the seven-foot halo—[they should study this].”
Those who wish to attain such marks as these should study the eloquence of the noble ones.
Those who wish to attain the Dharma-body of a Tathāgata, fully endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body, should study the eloquence of the noble ones.

"If one wishes to encompass all bodhisattvas who are fully endowed with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), and to achieve omniscience (sarvajñatā) and the fullness of the Buddha-dharma, one should study eloquence (pratibhāna).
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:

"If there are sentient beings who wish not to sever the continuity of all dharmas, nor to rely upon the four great elements (catvāri mahābhūtāni), but to penetrate the profound and subtle dharma of the Tathāgata—if they wish to attain such as this, they should study the noble and holy eloquence."

Those who wish to enter the profound abyss of wisdom and, riding upon the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividyā*), sport within hundreds of thousands of samādhis, should study eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

Those who wish to extinguish their original names and titles to achieve the name and title of a Tathāgata; those who wish to be free from bondage and attachment and take no pleasure in dwelling amidst worldly affairs; and those who wish to attain such states—these should study the eloquence of the noble ones (*ārya*).

"In this way, Devaputra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thoroughly studies all dharmas and thus perfects the path of the Mahāyāna; he fulfills his original vows, accomplishes the purification of Buddha-fields, and purifies sentient beings. He encounters no obstruction within the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, understanding that all dharmas are like illusions and echoes, like plantain trees, like reflections in a mirror, like what is seen in a dream, and like magical transformations—all of which are utterly non-existent."

In this way, O Devaputra, when a bodhisattva understands all dharmas, they are able to pay homage and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; traveling from one buddha-field to another, they listen to and receive the Buddha-dharma, entering the profound and wondrous treasury.
The Buddha again addressed the devaputra:

"If there are good men or good women who wish to obtain the seven treasures and the retinue of a Wheel-Turning Sage King to govern the four continents; or who wish to become a Brahmā Heaven King or Śakra Devendra; those who wish to attain such things should study the precepts of the noble ones."
At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these words, nine hundred and eighty million who had attained arhatship were filled with remorse. They came before the Buddha and said:

"Our transgressions are grave; having abandoned what we originally practiced, we have now fallen into the extremes. We only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion and provide instruction, so that we may cultivate the eloquence of the noble ones."
Thus he requested a second and a third time, and the Buddha silently granted his consent.
Furthermore, upon hearing this Dharma, countless sentient beings were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
The Buddha addressed the devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven:

"After seven hundred buddhas have passed in this Bhadrakalpa, you shall become a buddha, named Jñānakośa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."
The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Scroll 13;
The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Scroll 14, also titled *Pratyutpanna-vipāka*,
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter 39: The Ten Directions and the Dharma Realm (14) Chapter Thirty-Nine:
The Ten Directions and the Dharma Realm At that time, the World-Honored One, being about to enter parinirvāṇa—after ninety days had passed—announced to the fourfold assembly:

"In the past, I attained Buddhahood in the kingdom of Magadha. After my attainment of Buddhahood, while I was at the Hall of Dharma Joy, all the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, gathered like clouds and came to my presence, each exhorting me to preach the Dharma."
"At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Utpalapuspa-garbha who addressed me, saying:

'The people of this world are largely ignorant and do not recognize the true Dharma. I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound the correct meaning, so that all beings may attain liberation.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Padmagarbha who came to where I was and addressed me, saying:

'We are submerged and obscured within birth and death, wandering through the five realms of existence. We only pray that the World-Honored One will open the gate of ambrosia, so that those who have long suffered from hunger and emptiness may receive deliverance.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Priyagarbha who came forward and said to me:

'In this world, many suffer from afflictions and are bound by the twelve links of dependent origination; they do not behold the countenance of the Great Sage. I only pray that you will deliver them.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Candanagarbha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this world where the five turbidities boil like a cauldron, the true Dharma is not recognized. Now that the Sun of Wisdom has descended, we pray only that you will dispel the darkness."
Then another bodhisattva named Vajragarbha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Sentient beings are burning with intense fervor, constantly craving and attached to the five desires; they do not recognize the nature of the Tathāgata. We only pray that you will proclaim the Dharma."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Balagarbha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'All worlds are impermanent; birth and extinction each have their limits. Since Your Honor has now manifested your form, why do you not preach the Dharma at this time?'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Vimalagarbha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'O Honored One, you are now like a lotus flower, unstained by any dust or defilement; being equal in both internal and external aspects, you manifest and spread the Dharma of the Tathāgata.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Viśuddhagarbha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The Celestial Teacher has long been absent from view, and the people of the world have remained in perpetual darkness. Now that the Honored One has manifested his form, we pray only that you will preach the Dharma at this time."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Tathāgatagarbha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past all appeared and preached the Dharma; why, O Honored One, do you now remain silent?"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'It is difficult to be born in this world and encounter a Buddha; it is difficult to hear the Honored One’s sublime Dharma; it is difficult to obtain a human body; and it is difficult to deliver and liberate sentient beings.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Maitreya who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'All sufferings and afflictions arise from affection and love; in this world there are many who act contrary to the Dharma. We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant us awakening.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Siṃha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'If people wish to hear the Dharma, they must sever the three obstructive forms. You, O Honored One, are now the unsurpassed teacher; we pray that you deliver all beings.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Immeasurable Realm who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The power of the Buddha is fearless, and the Dharma-realm is inconceivable; the Buddhas of the past and the future have preached the Dharma in this place.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Gaganagañja who came forward and addressed the Buddha:
'The Original Unborn Samyaksaṃbuddha is undefiled and unstained; he brings all people across to liberation with equanimity. For what reason do you remain in such profound stillness?'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Prajñākāra who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Birth and death are exceedingly painful, like a person submerged in a deep abyss. You, O Honored One, are now a great master mariner; I only pray that you will ferry us across at this very moment."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Guangzao (Light-Creator) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"All practices are now exhausted; you have already departed from the suffering of the triple world. With the four immeasurable minds of compassion and kindness, your original vow is present here today."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmakāra who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The realm of sentient beings is immeasurable; all meet through bonds of affection, yet the Three Jewels have long been severed. We pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma at this time."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Asaṅga who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The light of wisdom has descended, illuminating and dispelling the darkness of the three poisons; for the five sufferings and afflictions of the world’s people, may only the World-Honored One expound the True Dharma."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Abhaya who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"With a resolve as firm as a vajra and vows most steadfast, with a mind as pure as space, I pray that you will rescue all those in distress."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Hugjue (Huguojue) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Wise One has already manifested his form; he shall deliver countless people. I pray that he will rescue and provide relief for all, enabling them to reach the other shore."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Anutpāda who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The True Dharma is inconceivable, and those who have attained thorough mastery of it are exceedingly few. Having accumulated practice over incalculable eons, I pray that its merit not be in vain."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Shenzu (Divya-ṛddhi) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'The Eye of Wisdom has now descended; it shall deliver those of inferior capacity. Through the wisdom of primordial non-arising and equality, it shall cause them to leave behind all suffering and affliction.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Ghoṣadatta who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The root of all practices is wisdom; with intelligence one reaches all people and clearly severs all defilements. World-Honored One, now is precisely the right time."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Ghoṣadatta who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The Buddha is supreme beyond all; his wisdom and conduct span incalculable eons. He is self-born and naturally extinguished—the immeasurable, faultless Honored One.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Constant Compassion (Sadāśoka) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'World-Honored One, you originally accumulated ascetic practices and endured the hardships of birth and death; now that the Sun of the Buddha has risen, let no one remain in the darkness of ignorance.'"
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Māyā-vinirmita who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When one contemplates all phenomena, even illusions and transformations are not real; the Way should be approached through equanimity. I pray that the World-Honored One will now expound upon this."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Anikṣipta who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'The suffering of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time has not yet heard of the Eightfold Noble Path; now that the Most Victorious One has descended, we have long yearned for the Teacher of Heaven.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Courageous (Vīryavanta) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Because throughout countless lifetimes you have accumulated immeasurable practice, and your majestic spiritual power covers all things, I pray that you will eliminate all afflictions."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Awakening Knowledge who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and the exposition of the Dharma is inexhaustible; you abide in the fundamental yet do not abide therein. I pray that you will turn the wheel of the true Dharma."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Sukṛtakārin who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Non-arising is fundamentally non-arising, yet today the Honored One has been born; manifesting your form within the five turbidities, we pray that you deliver all people.”
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Right View (Samyagdṛṣṭi) who came forward and addressed the Buddha:
'O Most Honored One of the three realms, worshipped by devas and humans, you who turn the Dharma wheel that shakes the great trichiliocosm, why do you now remain silent and still?'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmaviśuddhi who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Even if one were to spend countless kalpas extolling the virtues of the Honored One, exhausting every hundredfold meritorious deed, it would not reach even a hair's breadth of their full extent."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Wu-xiang (A-lakṣaṇa) who stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The fundamental non-existence is itself without marks; yet now you, O Honored One, manifest amidst all marks. Having exhausted all practices, you shall attain Buddhahood—why then do you enter meditative concentration?"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Acintya who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"All classes of sentient beings do not perceive the suffering of birth and extinction; they have realized the source and understood all phenomena. O World-Honored One, we pray that You will attend to us at this time."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Daoshou (Leader), who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All dharmas are empty and arise through the convergence of causes and conditions. Since you have not turned the wheel of Dharma for so long, why do you enter into right concentration?"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Wheel-Turning who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'You are impartial and free from hatred or love, for you compassionately regard all beings. Since the Honored One has now deigned to visit us, why do you still sleep? "
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Amitapratibhāna who came forward and addressed the Buddha:
'O Great Sage, Honored One among Men, having exerted yourself through the passage of kalpas, you have now attained perfect enlightenment; I pray that you will take pity on all people.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Jātisamkṣaya who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The root of all conditioned phenomena ultimately returns to impermanence; the eternal body is not an eternal body, yet the World-Honored One now reckons it as an eternal body.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Benmo Kong (Fundamental and Ultimate Emptiness) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Space is boundless, and sentient beings are difficult to awaken. Since no Tathāgata has appeared from the very beginning, please expound [the Dharma] now without hesitation.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Bahukaruṇā who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"One who wishes to benefit oneself must first deliver all people; since the Honored One has emerged from among the masses of beings, to now violate your original vow is improper."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Xiande who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'The dharma of immeasurable supernormal powers and the six perfections neither increase nor decrease; your various marks naturally adorn your body. We pray that the World-Honored One will deign to bend his divine power for our sake.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Ekacitta who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Bodhisattvas from the ten directions have all come to this Sahā world, desiring to hear the True Dharma; may the World-Honored One please awaken us at this time.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Avitatha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One of great compassion and pity, you have contemplated and entered right concentration; immeasurable and beyond measure, the time has come—please preach the Dharma.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Prāmodya who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I know that birth consists of immeasurable practices, and these practices transcend the limits of the triple world. You, Honored One, are now the Honored One of the three periods of time; I pray that you deliver those within the triple world."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Benwu (Original Non-existence) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'World-Honored One, you are now most divine and wondrous; the power of your Way is inconceivable. Having attained Buddhahood for the sake of sentient beings, why do you not turn the Wheel of Dharma? "
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Mahāyāna, who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The three vehicles share the same destination, yet we have not heard the words of the True Dharma. World-Honored One, you should now provide a detailed analysis so that the essentials of Nirvāṇa may be understood."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Kalasaṃkhyāna who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Human birth must end in extinction; having abandoned one life, one proceeds to another. I only pray that the World-Honored One will subdue [this cycle] so that there is neither birth nor further extinction.”
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Śrutaviniścaya who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The pains of birth, old age, sickness, and death—wherein the five aggregates are the source of calamity, and the twelve links of dependent origination are the bonds—O World-Honored One, we pray only that you will deliver us."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Amoghadarśin who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The lands where we dwell are very far from here; we only pray that the World-Honored One will now preach the Dharma so that we may hear it.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Swift Wisdom who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'World-Honored One, you possess the seven factors of enlightenment and are fully endowed with the four immeasurable minds; you shall awaken those who have not yet awakened—may the World-Honored One deliver and liberate them.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Constantly Raised Hand who came forward and addressed the Buddha:
“The Great Man’s marks are complete; you proclaim all dharmas. Having already attained freedom from all attachments, you also cause sentient beings to be free from them.”

"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmamati who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying: 'The past Tathāgatas taught the Dharma in immeasurable measure; now that you have attained Buddhahood, O Honored One, we pray that you will turn the Wheel of Dharma at this time.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Candrasūryaparipūrṇa who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The world is entirely impermanent; all things return to emptiness. One who understands that nothing is produced is the Honored One, supreme among men."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Amitayaśas who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"With a pure body one does not commit evil; with a pure mouth one speaks with sincerity and faith. Such a person transcends all others above and surpasses all devas and humans."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Asamasama who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata is born from Suchness and has descended in spirit to deliver beings from birth and death; yet you only preach the Dharma at this time—why do you harbor hesitation?”
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Dūrībhūta who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'From incalculable kalpas, a Buddha appears only from time to time, like the sun appearing when flowers bloom; why do you not manifest your radiance?'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Weishen (Majestic Power) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The One of Ten Powers is peerless; you have attained emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Your Dharma-body is like Mount Sumeru; I only pray that you will open the gate of ambrosia.”
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Daoli who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The contemplation of emptiness is free from conceptual thought, and practice is likewise tranquil and extinguished; from this one attains Buddhahood, revered by gods and humans."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Anāśrita who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Sentient beings are of many kinds and do not recognize the gate of liberation; they must be led by the Honored One before they can reach the place of fearlessness."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Quiet Contemplation who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The human mind is like flowing water; in every thought-moment it gives rise to evil. World-Honored One, you should sever its root so that it is forever extinguished without even a sprout."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Akṣayamati who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Having crossed the ocean of birth and death and purified the practice of the holy life, you satisfy sentient beings who are deeply famished by preaching the Dharma.”
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Adhṛṣṭaśraddha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'The three realms are entirely ablaze, and sentient beings have no one to rely upon. World-Honored One, you should look upon them with compassion and mercy, and for their sake, preach the truly essential Dharma.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Skillful Manifestation (Upāyapradarśana) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"You have thoroughly exhausted all treasuries and dwell securely in the realm of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); you have fully investigated the practice of primordial non-existence—what are you contemplating now, O Honored One?"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Daben-yuan (Reaching the Fundamental Source) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The four great elements gather in one place entirely due to the activity of past consciousness; ignorance and craving arise together. We pray that the World-Honored One will manifest the Dharma.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Śaila who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The reason the Buddhas appear is to deliver the three thousandfold world, so that sentient beings in ignorance may forever sever the three evil paths."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Daibaku (Attained Awakening) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'That which was not yet attained has now been attained; you have not planted the root of birth and death. World-Honored One, your mind is always in samādhi; we pray that you will arise from this meditative concentration.'"
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Bhadrapāla who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The source of all dharmas is that neither arising nor ceasing occurs; through wisdom one penetrates the suffering of the three realms and completely severs all outflows."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Asamasama who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Dharma of all Buddhas is not different; it takes the transformation of sentient beings as its foundation. This foundation arises from impartiality, and great compassion is present therein."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Mahādeva who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'Sentient beings have limited lifespans from their past lives; though they have been able to behold the form of the Tathāgata, they have not yet heard the Dharma of the True Truth. I only pray that you will expound it at this time.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Xingdao (Practice of the Path) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now, observing the marks of your physical form and seeing that you are fully endowed with all practices, and having attained perfect enlightenment through utmost sincerity, why do you not perform the deeds of a Buddha?"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Vigataraja who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The vows originally made by the World-Honored One span incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya), so that those who are inverted may behold the true path."
At that time, there was another bodhisattva named Akṣaya who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Your countenance is like a blooming flower, and your appearance is peerless. Your merit transcends the eight difficulties; for what reason do you remain so silent?"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Nirāśa who came forward and addressed the Buddha:
"The One of Ten Powers has compassionately appeared in the world to teach and transform gods and humans; from this shore to the other shore, he practices the deeds of the noble sages."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Buddhajñāna who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this limit of space throughout the worlds of the ten directions, all have come desiring to hear the Dharma, to wash away the afflictions and impurities of their minds."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Renben who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The three realms are entirely suffering and affliction, and there is no place from which to escape; only by being received through your divine power can one attain eternal peace."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Devendra who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"There are three hundred and five impurities of the body that constantly defile the minds of people; one should use the light of wisdom to eliminate them so that none remain."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Anunaya who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I have come from the realm of Equanimous Wisdom to visit and pay my respects to the Honored One, desiring to hear the immeasurable Dharma and to cultivate the practice of original non-existence.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Aniccha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I recall that in a past life there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni who exhorted me to preach the Dharma, no different from what Your Honor has done.'"
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Rūḍhadhyāna who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
