“I have heard that after attaining the Way of the Buddha, you turned the wheel of Dharma three times; why do you now remain silent, so that we do not hear the sound of even a single turning?”
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Sāgaralakṣaṇa who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Now that I have attained penetrating wisdom and have heard the true Dharma from all quarters, out of compassion for those sentient beings, I exhort and entreat the Tathāgata.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Siṃhanāda who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The single characteristic is fundamentally without characteristics; all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent. Yet sentient beings do not realize this; O Honored One, you should now distinguish it for them."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Mahāśrī who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The World-Honored One is most majestic, with a multitude of marks beyond compare. I wish to hear the Dharma of the *ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (the Necklace Sūtra) in order to awaken all people.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Raticara who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Just as the udumbara flower appears only once in hundreds of millions of kalpas, so too does a Buddha appear even more rarely than that; why do you now manifest yourself and yet conceal yourself?"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Qudao (Path-Approacher) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Phenomena arise from the self-nature of phenomena; they do not cling to existence within the three realms. I pray that you will rain down the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, universally moistening all people."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Dharma-Expositor who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Sentient beings have no conceptualizations of conditions; they should be [guided] by the causal conditions of the Dharma. With a mind that is empty, pure, and free from defilement, may the Honored One fully analyze this."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Cakṣur-abhijña who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'World-Honored One, you originally made this vow: "I shall deliver those not yet delivered. Now that the appointed day has arrived, I pray that you will preach the wisdom of emptiness and non-existence.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Anuttaralakṣaṇa who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The world is truly pitiable; sentient beings are mostly subject to perversion and are deluded regarding the Right Path. We pray that you will show us the place of wisdom and illumination.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Prāptadhāraṇī who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'I recall that in past lives, I made a great vow together with the World-Honored One: "We shall deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, leading them to the shore of the unconditioned."'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Asamasama who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One, your broad and long tongue now covers the face like a flower; this is entirely due to your preaching of the True Dharma, whereby you have obtained this meritorious retribution."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Mahādāna who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One, you originally bestowed gifts upon others without hoping for their recompense; now you have attained the status of the Honored One among men, and your majesty is truly such as this."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Ultimate Purity who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The great wisdom of the six perfections should pervade the world, causing those who are ignorant and deluded to all proceed toward the practice of fundamental non-arising."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Asaṅgadṛṣṭi who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) are unattached; they respond to all people, resolving each and every doubt, all of which arises from the conditions of past retribution."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Priyadarśana who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, by means of spiritual friends, you accomplished the dharma-gate of the Path; now that you have attained Buddhahood, how could that which is not the Dharma be the fruit?"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Gambhīrajñāna who came forward and addressed the Buddha:
“The undertaking of all practices and the self-adornment with myriad virtues—only the Buddha can expound these fully, from their existence unto the ultimate limit.”
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Puṣpamālāputra who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Virtues accumulated over many kalpas, understanding the dharma of the non-existent limit; that one's merit becomes honored throughout the three realms—this is the retribution for hearing the Dharma."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Rūpalakṣaṇa who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The Tathāgata’s body of one zhang and six chi is made of vajra and is most difficult to destroy; I pray that you will use the formless Dharma to universally reach all nascent beings.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Contemplating the External Body who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Just as the light of the sun shines upon all, universally dispelling every darkness, yet we have not yet beheld the Buddha’s radiance; we pray that you will manifest your majestic marks.”
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Sampannalakṣaṇa who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“One should constantly contemplate impermanent phenomena, fix the mind to enter meditative concentration, leave behind defilements to transcend the three realms, and deliver all people.”
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Pure Mature Faculties (Viśuddhendriya) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The Dharma practiced by all Buddhas has as its sole purpose the deliverance of sentient beings. Since you have already fulfilled your original vow, how wonderful it is that you preach the Dharma at this time!"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Indriyavicitra who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Dharma-realm is inconceivable, and so too are the faculties of sentient beings; I pray that by the power of your spiritual footprints, you will manifest this for all."
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Tonghui (Universal Wisdom) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'Your radiant marks are like the Snowy Mountains, revered and looked up to by the people of the world. Although we have now beheld one treasure, I only pray that you will speak of the second treasure.'"
"Furthermore, another bodhisattva came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'The Way of the Buddha is exceedingly profound and subtle; it expounds and transmits all dharmas. It shall reign as sovereign over the three realms, for all things arise from the root of these dharmas.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Subtle Atom (Sūkṣma) who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The World-Honored Ones of the ten directions have sent us here solely because they wish to hear the True Dharma; we do not delight in the silent seclusion of the worthy sages.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Rūpakāya who came forward and addressed the Buddha:
'The immeasurable Buddhas and their equals, fully endowed with pure precepts, have attained them themselves and bestowed them upon others, thereby fulfilling all aspirations.'"
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Pure Sound who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The ten wisdoms and the ten non-arising states; the knowledge of the extinction of the ten conceptions of phenomena; the perfection of the merits of the ten stages—O One of Ten Powers, please preach the Dharma!”
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Constantly Abiding in Samādhi who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'I am now the most inferior among them, and my manifold wisdom is not yet broad or universal. I only pray that the World-Honored One will today show me the path of supernatural power.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Ananta who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'From the beginning I have made a vow that I must hear the spoken teachings; since you, O Honored One, do not now preach the Dharma, I shall never depart.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Jvālāprabha who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The Buddha-way is exceedingly difficult; the arising of dharmas is inexhaustible. Only one who can purify all defilements should enter the truth of the Way.'"
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Dharma-Eye who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The immeasurable gates of dhāraṇī resound through heaven and earth; you preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, enabling them to attain the Way of the Buddha.'"
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Maitreya who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"All dharmas are exceedingly profound and subtle; like space, they have no beginning or end. Having realized that fundamentally there are no paths, you are therefore called the Honored One among Men."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Ekayāna who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The dust and toil of birth and death, with the eight difficulties as its walls—this suffering cannot be rescued by any other; only the Buddha can deliver one from it.”
"Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Śrīprabha who came forward and addressed the Buddha:
'Alas for old age, sickness, and death! The three realms are a great affliction. Now that the Sun of Wisdom has descended and appeared, why do you remain silent and not preach the Dharma?'"
Then another bodhisattva named Jīvaka came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The lifespan of worldly people is short; they are bound and attached by further cravings and devoured by the six consciousnesses. I only pray that the World-Honored One will extinguish these."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Saṃkhyāna who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All classes of sentient beings are shrouded and obscured by the three poisons; I pray that the World-Honored One will descend in spirit and treat them with the medicine of the Dharma."
Again, there was a bodhisattva named Saṃpuṣpita-pāṇi who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“His voice resounds throughout the ten directions; through the Way, he brings down the rain of ambrosia. As for this inexhaustible and profound treasury of Dharma—who other than a Buddha could proclaim it?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"These hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas have each exhorted one another to give rise to reverence for the Dharma, and each has earnestly entreated the Buddha."
At that time, I emitted light from the mark of my broad tongue, which shone universally throughout the trichiliocosm. Having withdrawn the light, I addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas:

"The reason I have now attained this broad and long tongue is that I have discerned all dharmas to be utterly non-existent; furthermore, by means of the eightfold voice, I cause the infinite Buddha-lands of the ten directions to tremble, so that all may hear and know."
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, spoke in verse:
“The source of all dharmas Arises from the convergence of causes and conditions;
All lands throughout the ten directions Are empty, quiescent, and formless.”
The aspiration for the Way naturally manifests; the multitude of marks of merit is fulfilled.
One discerns internal and external phenomena, which are formless and non-existent.
Having heard that once one has attained Buddhahood, one delivers and liberates all people.
There is a Great Dharma Garland, adorning the purity of the Buddha-lands.
If you wish to hear it and exhaustively realize that both the beginning and the end are empty,
each and every one of you should distinguish these truths, leading yourselves to the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In my past four great vows, I pledged to deliver those not yet delivered;
why must I wait for the requests of others, causing each of you to harbor resentment?
From the very first moment I resolved my mind, I did not limit myself to the people of Qi alone.
"However, because their conditions have not yet reached the Path, they remain silent for now.

At that time, when all the bodhisattvas in the assembly heard the Buddha speak these verses, each leaped for joy beyond measure. They all exclaimed, "Excellent! and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence:

"The Tathāgata is about to expound the teachings of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings and bring them to the realization of the Dharma-realm, so that all those who suffer through the three periods of time may receive liberation."

At that time, more than twenty thousand ordinary persons on the seats who had not yet attained supernatural powers all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; each made vows and gave rise to wholesome thoughts, desiring to hear this Great Dharma Garland.
Chapter 40: The Ten Knowledges (14). The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Chapter Forty: The Ten Knowledges. At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

How is it so? What dharmas did the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first practice, and what merits did he possess, such that he attained unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment and became worthy of the great dharma-garland?
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"Excellent, son of good family!"
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to achieve unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment and correspond with the great dharma-garland; who wish to sever the root-source of birth and death; who wish to cause the True Dharma of the Tathāgata to flourish and manifest; who wish to attain immeasurable concentrations like those of the World-Honored One; and who wish to attain playful mastery within suchness and the nature of phenomena—such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study the gateways of immeasurable wisdom.
"What is the gateway of immeasurable wisdom? Maitreya,
listen well!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses ten kinds of clear wisdom; in a single thought, a single moment, and a single instant, he fully knows the realms of immeasurable sentient beings, discerns and contemplates them without losing the Dharma-realm, and thereby attains unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment.
"What are the ten kinds of clear wisdom?

As for these ten kinds of clear wisdom, in a single moment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to be born in the Tuṣita Heaven, where they collectively cultivate wholesome deeds with no discordant thoughts among them, while ensuring that other sentient beings remain unaware of this."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

In a single moment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to accomplish the path of a bodhisattva and achieve the realization of each dharma, enjoying themselves together with the noble sages, while other sentient beings remain unaware of it."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

In a single moment, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm who have not yet established the power of their faculties and virtues to simultaneously leave the household life and practice the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya). They shave off their hair and beards, don the three dharma robes, hold alms bowls in hand, and practice the twelve dharmas; when the time comes, they go on alms rounds to bring blessings and deliver all beings. At other times, they sit in meditation and perform the contemplation of the body (kāyānupaśyanā), yet there may still be sentient beings who possess no awareness or perception."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

In a single moment, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to accomplish the path of a Bodhisattva, proceed beneath the king of trees, and sit cross-legged upon the auspiciously offered grass. He reflects within himself:

'Today I shall surely attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; of this there is no doubt. First, I shall move all worlds, so that the sages and holy ones who have attained the Way through supernormal powers may come to protect me, while other sentient beings remain unaware. "
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

In a single moment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm to accomplish the bodhisattva path and turn the wheel of Dharma. They cause them to realize the Four Noble Truths—the truth of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and enable those beings to practice and attain liberation, achieving the fruits of the three vehicles according to their inclinations, while ensuring that other sentient beings remain unaware of this."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

In a single moment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to have their faculties fully matured, to be endowed with the fivefold dharma-body, to be complete in the various marks, and to achieve their great vows; they perform buddha-works and subdue the armies of Māra, yet other sentient beings remain unaware of it."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

In a single moment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to accomplish the path of a bodhisattva and fully achieve the realization of a Tathāgata, Samyaksaṃbuddha; they enter the Buddha-mind samādhi and each manifest emanations to teach and transform sentient beings, leading them into the discipline of the noble ones, while ensuring that other sentient beings remain unaware of it."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

In a single moment, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to accomplish the path of a bodhisattva and enter the concentration of sovereign will (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*). He causes all mountains, rivers, stone walls, tiles, stones, grasses, and trees to transform into the seven treasures, providing for the poor and suffering until they are universally satisfied. Only then does he preach the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), while ensuring that other sentient beings remain unaware of it."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

In a single moment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm to accomplish the bodhisattva path and enter the diamond-like samādhi (vajrasamādhi). He can transform them all into a golden hue, identical in appearance to that of a Buddha without any difference, causing them all to achieve the Unsurpassed Way, while ensuring that other sentient beings remain unaware of it."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

In a single moment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm to accomplish the path of a bodhisattva, attaining the faculties, powers, and factors of awakening of a Buddha—past, future, and present—and discerning emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, realizing that all phenomena are entirely non-existent, while causing other sentient beings to remain unaware of this realization."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices these ten kinds of clear wisdom, they will certainly and without doubt attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
At that time, Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having now heard the True Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, I have attained clear and great awakening; I pray that all sentient beings may likewise attain this wisdom.”
Chapter 41: On Timeliness (14). *The Bodhisattva’s Necklace Sūtra*, Chapter Forty-one: On Timeliness. At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamitra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva advance in the practice of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment? By maintaining dignified deportment and conduct appropriate to the occasion, how can they become fully endowed with the great dharma-necklace?”
The Buddha told Dharmamitra:

"If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to fully attain unexcelled, truly real, equal, and perfect enlightenment, and to be fully endowed with the great dharma-garland of the Tathāgata, they should cultivate the ten wisdoms of the great dharma-garland; thus they will be able to be fully endowed with the great dharma-garland."

"Therefore, noble son! If there are good men or good women who wish to hear the timely practice of the Great Dharma-Necklace of the Tathāgata, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!"
What are the ten? These ten are as follows:

when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows for himself that the time has come to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he does not miss the appointed hour and proceeds beneath the king of trees. Holding fast to his heart of great vows, his mind is like space, having severed all conceptualizations. This is called the timely practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Dharmamitra!

If a bodhisattva, having thoroughly known for himself, reflects: 'Now the time has come for me to transform those sentient beings; their clans, surnames, and names do not exceed the boundaries of this realm; I must certainly deliver all sentient beings before I may rest,' this is called the timely practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Dharmamitra! If a bodhisattva, having deep self-knowledge, thinks:

'I shall now attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; furthermore, I shall bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon other bodhisattvas, [determining] their buddha-lands, their retinues, and the regions where they will dwell,' this is called the timely practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Dharmamitra!

If a bodhisattva, having thoroughly known this for himself, thinks: 'I have now attained mastery over all wisdoms; I shall cause sentient beings to be no different from myself,' he immediately enters among them to teach and transform them, universally causing all sentient beings to attain this unimpeded dharma of mastery. This is called the timely practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Dharmamitra!

If a bodhisattva enters the gates of liberation to perform the Buddha-work, transforming all phenomena characterized by form and obstruction so that they all return to the inexhaustible treasury, and causes sentient beings to likewise attain what he has attained himself—this is called the timely practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Dharmamitra!

When a bodhisattva has clearly realized for himself, 'I have now attained the formless dharmas of the four dhyānas of emptiness, as well as the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity,' and further uses these concentrations to transform sentient beings, causing all universally to attain what he himself has obtained—this is called the timely practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Dharmamitra!

If a bodhisattva, having thoroughly understood this for himself, maintains dignified deportment without losing propriety; knows when to walk and knows when to sit; is diligent day and night without transgressing the teachings of the Way; enters the city at the proper time without looking left or right; brings blessings and salvation to sentient beings with immeasurable wisdom; and also causes sentient beings to attain what he has attained himself—this is called the timely conduct of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Dharmamitra!

If a bodhisattva, having clearly known this for himself, examines whether sentient beings are ready to be saved or not according to their fundamental nature, he accepts the faithful offerings given by them while eating only as much as his stomach requires. Returning to a quiet and secluded place, he sits or lies down and reflects:

'The alms I have now received shall sustain my four great elements so that I may practice the Way and attain supreme perfect enlightenment; furthermore, I shall transform and guide all beings with this Dharma, causing all sentient beings everywhere to obtain what I have attained myself.'"
"This is called the timely practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Furthermore, Famiāo! If a bodhisattva, having thoroughly known himself, realizes:

'As I am today, I should accord with the discipline of the noble ones (ārya), guiding and transforming all beings without increase or decrease; I shall gradually advance into the five destinies (gati), observing their minds and delivering them.'"

If he enters the human realm, he proclaims the prohibitive precepts for them, causing those sentient beings to understand the suffering of committing offenses; he shows them the right path and delivers them.

If he enters the heavenly realms and dwells in celestial palaces, he expounds the dharma of impermanence and decay, exhorting them to cultivate the ten virtuous actions and to relinquish their lofty heavenly positions to practice the unsurpassed path.

If one enters among the animals suffering in pain, one preaches for them the ways of conflict, deception, and fraud, so as to cause them to give rise to wholesome thoughts and the principle of reforming themselves.

If one enters among the hungry ghosts in their ugliness, one preaches for them the mind of stinginess, greed, and attachment, so as to cause them to develop wholesome thoughts, abandon their past ways, and cultivate themselves for the future.

If they enter the hells to undergo retribution among those people, they preach for them the dharma of the five heinous crimes that are difficult to save from; furthermore, they cause the sentient beings in hell to open their minds and understand, so that wholesome thoughts may arise, and having completed their bitter suffering of retribution, they may return to the human realm.
This is called the timely practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Dharmamitra! If a bodhisattva, having thoroughly known this for himself, has perfected all practices and attained mastery over all wisdoms, reaching the inconceivable, he should then move all things with his supernormal powers.

Having personally tested their supernormal powers and found them unimpeded, they travel from one Buddha-field to another, serving the Buddhas and paying homage to the World-Honored Ones; they are dedicated to cultivating the pure conduct and receiving what they have not yet attained, and they cause all sentient beings to share in what they themselves have gained.
This is what is called, O Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates these ten wisdoms as timely practices, they shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, thereby becoming fully endowed with the great dharma-garland.

42. Chapter on the Ten Inconceivables (14). *The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Chapter Forty-two: The Ten Inconceivables. At that time, the Bodhisattva Son of the Supreme Path addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enter into the five realms of existence, circulating and coming and going therein, to teach and transform sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and achieve unexcelled, truly real, and most correct awakening?
"Do you practice the inconceivable great Dharma-garland?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmī:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!"
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and practice the inconceivable great dharma-garland, they should cultivate ten dharmas.

What are the ten? If there is a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who enters the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence to transform beings according to their kind; who, by sitting cross-legged once, fills all Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions; and who, further, causes the sound of his voice to shake the trichiliocosm, thereby teaching and transforming all sentient beings therein so that they all resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment—yet without causing those beings to have any conscious awareness [of this]—this is called the right Dharma practiced by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, which accords with the inconceivable.
"Furthermore, Son of Noble Lineage!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters among the beings of the five destinies to teach and transform them, and with a single phrase of meaning suffices all buddha-worlds so that every sentient being with form hears and understands it, yet those beings themselves do not even realize it, and from the Dharma they have heard they all give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment—this is called the inconceivable practice of the True Dharma cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subāhu! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters among the beings of the five destinies to teach and transform them, emitting a single radiance that universally illumines the trichiliocosm, such that all who see this light conceive the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, yet do not perceive his physical form, and causes all of them to enter the gate of liberation—this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the inconceivable practice of the True Dharma."
"Furthermore, Son of Superior Path!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters among the beings of the five realms of existence to teach and transform them, then within a single thought, a single mindfulness, and a single moment, they pervade the trichiliocosm with a single dharma-body, causing all sentient beings everywhere to hear and know it, and leading all beings to be fully endowed with the dharma-realm. Yet those beings do not know from where they have heard it, and they all resolve their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment. This is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the True Dharma in accordance with the inconceivable."
"Furthermore, Son of the Conqueror!

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters among the beings of the five realms of existence to teach and transform them, using his power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*), he transforms all sentient beings throughout the entire trichiliocosm until they all take the form of Buddhas. Then, each of them teaches one another, expounding the twelve ascetic practices (*dvādaśa-dhūtaguṇa*), so that they may together bring immeasurable numbers of beings across to liberation."
Yet those sentient beings do not realize for themselves by whom they are being delivered;
this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation of the True Dharma in accordance with the inconceivable.
"Furthermore, Son of the Victorious Path!

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters among the beings of the five realms of existence to teach and transform them, he uses a single wisdom to discern all formless dharmas without any obstruction, universally enabling those with form to understand this essential method and thereby attain liberation."
If those sentient beings do not themselves realize, "By whom am I being delivered today, as I am now?
this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the True Dharma in accordance with the inconceivable.
"Furthermore, Son of the Victorious Path!

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters among the beings of the five realms of existence to teach and transform them, they are able, within a single thought-moment, to universally perceive all dharmas. They discern the dharma-realm and perform inconceivable deeds, causing all sentient beings to hear this teaching of the Path, so that they simultaneously attain enlightenment without any obstruction."
Yet those sentient beings do not themselves realize from whom they have heard it; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the true Dharma in accordance with the inconceivable.
"Furthermore, Son of the Victorious Path!

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters among the beings of the five realms of existence to teach and transform them, causing those beings to all attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and roam freely through the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions; and hearing the Dharma preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions, they come to understand that all phenomena are like illusions and like transformations.
Yet those sentient beings do not realize or know for themselves that "I am today awakening whom.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s cultivation of the True Dharma, which should be regarded as inconceivable.
"Furthermore, Son of a Conqueror!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the five realms of existence to teach and transform sentient beings, causing all embodied beings throughout the three periods of time to achieve and fully accomplish equal and perfect enlightenment—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the true Dharma in accordance with the inconceivable."
"Furthermore, Son of a Conqueror!

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters among the beings of the five destinies to teach and transform them, enters the profound treasury of Dharma to discern subtle wisdom, transcends the past, future, and present, walks alone through the three realms without equal, and further causes sentient beings to be no different from himself—this is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the True Dharma in accordance with the inconceivable."
"This is what is meant, O son of the Victorious One!

The power of the virtues of the five faculties of a bodhisattva enters into the five realms of existence to teach and transform sentient beings; these dharmas are so preeminent that they cannot be measured, nor can they be known by arhats or pratyekabuddhas."
**Chapter 43: On Non-Self (14)** *The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Chapter Forty-three: On Non-Self* At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Citta-mati who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, through the contemplation of the body, discerns and understands the notion of non-self, how does he accomplish the contemplation of the bodhisattva path?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Citta-mati, saying:
"If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to achieve the contemplation of the bodhisattva path, they should practice ten dharmas."
What are these ten?

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, though not yet abiding in the bodhisattva stage or dwelling in the unconditioned, has perfected the fundamental path and fulfilled his great vows; who observes non-self within himself and transforms sentient beings as if they were no different from himself—this is called the practice of non-self of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Citta-mati!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can transform a formless body into one that appears with form, and again transform a body with form into one that appears without form; and by taking what has a self as being without self, and taking what is without self as having a self, thereby guiding and transforming all sentient beings therein—this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s fulfillment of the dharmas of the mind-knowledge."

"Furthermore, Citta! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, they should cultivate a mind of non-arising and understand that all dharmas are fundamentally not objects of delight. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attainment of the realization of a selfless mind as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Furthermore, Citta-mati!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained the mind of emptiness, understanding that there is no self and neither arising nor ceasing, and further uses this Dharma to teach and transform all beings so they know the mark of non-self; and possessing such wisdom, he does not praise himself, being foremost among all those who dwell in profound dharmas—this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the foremost path of non-self."

"Furthermore, Citta! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or if any son or daughter of good family, discerns the characteristics of all dharmas, yet does not perceive the root of the manifold characteristics of dharmas—and likewise the root of all dharmas is also thus—giving rise to the notion of non-self regarding sentient beings, internal and external dharmas, and omniscience; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the practice of non-self."
"Furthermore, O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family sees the formation and destruction of kalpas, or sees the non-formation and non-destruction of kalpas, they do not rejoice in formation nor grieve over non-formation; in the interval between these two, they do not give rise to the notion of a self. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the dharma of non-self."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Citta-mati:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who relinquish all bodily existence and enter the samādhi of extinction, discerning the root of conditioned activity to know its origin, and emerging through the essential path of non-action to reach the Great Way—this is called the practice of selflessness of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Citta! If there are good sons or good daughters who attain the mind of non-self and discern all twelve links of dependent origination—such that those who arise do not know why they arise, and those who cease do not know why they cease—and who perceive no notion of self in the fundamental nature of all phenomena, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of non-self regarding the fundamental nature of all phenomena."

"Furthermore, Citta! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva discerns the root of all dharmas, seeing neither near nor far, and realizing that they are fundamentally unarisen and unoriginated—this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of non-self."

"Furthermore, Citta! If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, through the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), understands that consciousness is entirely non-existent, and therein attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—neither perceiving its attainment nor its non-attainment—this is called the practice of selflessness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Thus it is, Citta! If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to fully accomplish the practice of non-self, they must reach a state of firm resolve and will ultimately achieve the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."
"Furthermore, Citta! If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to be fully endowed with all dharmas, they should study the dharma of non-self."

What is meant by non-self? That which is called non-self is as follows: even when one has ultimately attained perfection, this too is non-self; when one analyzes the four great elements and contemplates their origin, this too is non-self; even when all Buddhas appear in the world to teach and transform others, this too is non-self. Not seeing any sentient beings who are to be delivered or liberated, and having no sense of the subduing of Māra’s armies beneath the King of Trees—all these are non-existent. This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of non-self.

Not perceiving the fundamental source of the dhāraṇīs of the three periods of time, the wisdom that is free from attachment does not abide within or without; when analytical reflection finds that nothing at all exists, this is called the bodhisattva’s practice of non-self.
The Buddha again addressed Citta-mati:

"Furthermore, if a son or daughter of good family enters the meditative concentration of emptiness and thoroughly penetrates the profound Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata—realizing that it is neither here nor there, and understanding that all things are entirely non-existent."
Furthermore, if a son or daughter of good family, through the power of supernormal faculties, enters into meditative concentration and manifests the contemplation of all signless dharmas—
what is meant by "signless"?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach and transform all beings and deliver them not by means of verbal instruction;
this is called "signlessness" (*animitta*).
What is signlessness? All Buddhas sport spontaneously within the fundamental nature of sentient beings; this is called signlessness.
Sitting beneath a single tree, one attains the unsurpassed, truly correct path; this is called the practice of signlessness. Thus it is, O Citta!
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices and upholds this dharma and realizes the dharma of non-self, they shall attain the unsurpassed, truly correct path.

44. Chapter on the Equal Vehicle (14). *The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra*, Chapter Forty-four: The Equal Vehicle. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Viśuddhacakṣus. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his hands joined in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "How is it so?"
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle and reaches unimpeded wisdom, by cultivating what dharma does he eliminate the traces of the Great Vehicle?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Pure Eye:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
That you have now raised these questions is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
I shall dispel your doubts with a verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One does not attain the path of equality by destroying form;
by observing that form and the path are not different, one is able to mount the Great Vehicle.
Contemplating form and the path, their suchness is likewise the same."
One does not perceive a path subject to decay; this is the practice of the wise.
The nature of the path is fundamentally indestructible; it cannot be exhausted through investigation.
It corresponds most perfectly to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); by mounting this, one reaches the unobstructed.
The mind of the fool is inverted; seeking the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, he is stained by attachment to the three realms and does not escape the portion of rebirth.
All phenomena are without grasping—above, below, and in between.
Seeing no scattering or dispersal— this is called entering the Mahāyāna. If one sees both dharma and non-dharma,
yet remains unmoved within these two states and gives rise to no dualistic views,
then the setting forth [upon the path] is likewise so.
The two are conditioned phenomena, yet they are also called unconditioned phenomena;
by eliminating the two and not perceiving the two, one accords with the unsurpassed path.
Having transcended the stage of ordinary beings, yet not having reached the path of the noble ones—
Though the destination has not yet been attained, one is still a field of merit for the world.
Able to remain detached from the eight worldly concerns, like a lotus flower that does not cling to water,
and having transcended the practices of a hundred kalpas, one then proceeds toward the Mahāyāna.
Everywhere correcting his karma, he manifests supernormal powers in every place;
saving beings without appearing to save them, his actions are secret in body, speech, and mind.
He does not retreat upon the path of birth and death, nor does his mind ever succumb to cowardice.
Holding one's resolve as adamantine, one should most appropriately possess unimpeded wisdom.
In empty space there is neither good nor evil; the dharma-realm is eternally pure.
Since dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, how could there be any defilement?
Not seeing the abandonment of false dharmas, yet cultivating the unsurpassed path, and having no person of inferior capacity—this is the characteristic of the Mahāyāna.
All dharmas are fundamentally without marks; like space, they cannot be grasped.
Seeking the characteristics [of phenomena], one finds they are empty from the very beginning; the wise should realize this.
Those who wish to practice without obstruction take skillful means as foremost;
fulfilling the aspirations of sentient beings, they lead them to the site of enlightenment.
With a virtuous friend for the sake of the True Dharma, Firmly maintaining it without forgetting or abandoning it,
Forever leaving behind the aggregates, bases, and elements, One does not practice with doubt or the hindrances.
Whether a Buddha appears in the world Or enters into parinirvāṇa,
The True Dharma exists eternally, never changing or altering throughout.
All phenomena possess authentic realization; good and evil do not decay or perish.
The nature of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is likewise: it abides perpetually and is immovable.
The practice cultivated is exceedingly profound; There is no attachment even within the realm of Māra.
All phenomena are likewise thus; They are forever free from the faction of false views.
Seeking the unsurpassed path, One does not cling to the dharmas of cultivation.
Neither having perception nor being without perception—this is the unimpeded wisdom.
The Buddha’s wisdom is free from attachment; in all phenomena, nothing is produced.
Seeing neither arising nor ceasing, nor any path—this alone accords with the practice of the Mahāyāna.
Some give away their heads and eyes; with a faithful mind, they have nothing to relinquish.
They do not perceive a recipient, for their deluded thoughts have no point of attachment.
All dharmas are fundamentally unarisen; when investigated, they have no nesting place.
The characteristics of phenomena are likewise thus; their origins cannot be seen.
If a person wishes to investigate emptiness and desires to know its boundaries, though they contemplate and recollect it day and night, their efforts will be in vain.
The deluded and confused cling to a self, Calculating it as permanent, they cannot escape;
They fall into the hardships of the three miserable realms, And fail to attain the ultimate state.
The path of the True Persons and Noble Sages Is unimpeded by the three types of supernormal knowledge.
If even the vast expanse of emptiness has not yet been exhausted, how much less so for those of such a kind?

All people reckon these things as permanent; lacking the light of wisdom to illuminate themselves, they nurture and increase the suffering of birth and death—by what means could they ever reach liberation?
The gift of wealth is without attachment; yet if one seeks the unsurpassed path, the gift and the path cannot coexist—how much less so when seeking ultimate perfection?
By practicing the conduct of the precepts and non-self, one dwells securely in the foremost Dharma.
Furthermore, there is no such sign; through the practice of mindfulness, precepts, wisdom, and the perfections, one attains them naturally without cultivation.
Wisdom eradicates the root of ignorance, and the precepts perfect the pure path—pure like the moon, free from defilement.
The body is like a mass of foam, and like lightning flashing before the eyes;
the faculty of mind is like a mirage, while the precepts constitute the path of purity.
Most supreme and peerless, the Sage among all sages and gods.
Stilling the mind of all evils is the perfection of tranquility.
Whether one violates the precepts or upholds them, whether the mind is concentrated or distracted, there is no difference;
by discerning the various realms of phenomena, the precepts become the path to the outflow-free state.
Having attained the perfection of patience, one is able to endure all suffering;
with universal compassion for all sentient beings, one harbors no thoughts of superiority or inferiority.
Recalling past phenomena, one sees that birth and cessation do not remain for long.
Regarding the dharmas of praise, blame, defamation, and fame, how could one find any advantage therein?
Even if one’s body were dismembered limb by limb, one would ultimately not give rise to an evil thought;
discerning internal and external phenomena, body and mind abide with resolute steadfastness.
When enemies come seeking to harm me, I shall extinguish this fragile and precarious body;
I endure them as the earth bears all, reckoning neither good nor evil.
With the great vow of patience, I remain free of conceptual thought when confronted by others.
Thus, all sentient beings who behold them cannot fail to rejoice.
Desiring to cross the ocean of the Mahāyāna, one must carefully avoid harboring cowardice;
by straightening the body and rectifying the mind, one shall immediately attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
From countless eons past, wandering through the cycle of birth and death,
for the sake of even a single sentient being, you have personally donned the armor of the great vow.
All phenomena are without arising or ceasing, and furthermore, they are devoid of any notion of decay or destruction.
The minds of fools are inverted; they do not understand the wisdom of the past.
The nature of the dharma-realm is eternally abiding, yet those who study it do not reach its ultimate depth.
One should thoroughly understand both the root and the branches: that which is born is ultimately unborn.
Sentient beings do not deeply penetrate the subtle and unimpeded wisdom;
they should seek skillful means to eliminate their inverted minds.
Though the Buddhas appear in the world, there are those who are not met with for deliverance.
Furthermore, he does not abandon diligence, possessing courageous and powerful strength.
He discerns all phenomena as being like illusions, mirages, or light;
seeking their reality yields no fruit, for they are like emptiness, observed as formless.
Sentient beings do not contemplate with clarity, But give rise to thoughts of defiled attachment;
I gradually show them the path to the ultimate truth, Causing them to know the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
If one contemplates this meaning through skillful means (*upāya*), That which is wished for will surely be attained.
Contemplating each and every thing through reflection, unimpeded wisdom is perfected.
Mindfully maintaining both internal and external conduct, one seeks emptiness everywhere;
free from dependence and without attachment, the beginning and end of birth and death are purified.
Advancing in learning, one delights in seclusion; dwelling alone, one has nothing to fear.
Contemplating dhyāna, samādhi, and wisdom, one skillfully proceeds toward the six supernormal powers.
Amidst the multitude, one remains like a wild creature; with a single mind, free from distraction.
Not losing the laws of dignified conduct—this is called the subtle and wondrous concentration.

The dharmas of concentration are manifold; the practice of stilling the mind and the outflow-free (anāsrava) conduct, along with the two superior liberations—this is called the subtle and wondrous concentration.
Universally observing all phenomena, The mind dwells peacefully without wavering;
Counting one after another, This is called the subtle and wondrous concentration.
The aspiration for the Way becomes firm and stable, The defiled mind is extinguished and forever stilled.
To guide and deliver those of pure and gentle character— this is called the subtle and wondrous concentration.
Constantly recollecting the Perfectly Enlightened One and the Tathāgata’s path of the Dharma-body,
while feeling weary of all perceptions of form— this is called the subtle and wondrous concentration.
Furthermore, one cultivates the six recollections, Not deviating from the sequential practice;
Eliminating thought through mindfulness and being free from ideation— This is called the subtle and wondrous concentration.
The four pairs and eight classes of persons Follow from birth the path of the unconditioned.
Countless and beyond numbering—this is called the subtle and wondrous concentration.
The wise cultivate the four dhyānas; they do not rely on the concentration of emptiness through consciousness.
Discerning the internal and external body—this is called the subtle and wondrous concentration.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, from afar beholding these sentient beings,
do not see them through the eyes perceiving forms, yet naturally bring about their realization of the Way.
They likewise behold these people preaching the Dharma in every direction.
Without giving rise to perceptions of ear or sound, consciousness ceases and no longer clings.
Though the perceptions of sentient beings are immeasurable, one knows them all with a single mind;
without giving rise to dualistic views, various thoughts then arise.
Recalling past kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and beyond counting, his former mind was as it is now: courageous and untiring.
He further traveled through immeasurable lands, manifesting the path of supernatural powers.
The mind abides and the body follows of its own accord, causing one to know the dharma of transformation.
He proclaims the path of ambrosia, never losing the practice of progressive advancement;
from one kalpa to a hundred kalpas, his unimpeded wisdom remains inexhaustible.
Having attained the perfection of wisdom, he discerns the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
for the sake of others he preaches the sublime Dharma, yet he does not conceive of a self.
Practicing the path of skillful means, he regards lust, anger, and delusion as equal.
The causes and conditions are free from defilement and attachment, causing one to know the path of purity.
My own original actions were self-created; through liberation, there is nothing to fear.
Through the equal conjunction of conditions, all phenomena are without a fixed location.
Contemplating oneself and contemplating the Buddha, Contemplating emptiness and the nature of phenomena is likewise so;
The path between birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*— Only the wise attain awakening.
Thoroughly understanding the nature of wisdom, They cause seekers to pursue the light of wisdom.
For billions of years the world was shrouded in dust and darkness, until suddenly a great radiance appeared.
This wisdom is called Great Wisdom; the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable.
Guiding the multitudes of sentient beings, it brings them to the accomplishment of this unsurpassed wisdom.
Now, when one calculates all forms of omniscience, there is none that can surpass this;
by cultivating these various wisdoms in their entirety, the fruit of the Mahāyāna path is accomplished.
Though other forms of knowledge exist under various names, they do not possess the true path.
This wisdom is supreme among all wisdoms, rescuing one from every difficulty.
If you wish to seek wisdom, it is like seeking the nature of space;
even a mindless state is swifter than that, so how much more so when discursive thoughts arise?
The realm of space is immeasurable, formless and invisible;
this wisdom is likewise so, infinite and without bound.
Should all people board the vessel of this wisdom, [they shall cross over].
Sporting upon the shores of birth and death, One reaches at last the ocean of Nirvana.
Even if a person were to spend hundreds of thousands of kalpas Seeking to praise these merits,
the great brilliance of this torch of wisdom Would be such that no one could exhaust its treasury.
Inexhaustible and incapable of being exhausted, And free from the eight states of no leisure,
One who can recite with unimpeded wisdom Is the most honored among gods and humans.
Never falling into the evil realms, The six sense faculties are always complete.
Born among gods and humans, They shall be the most noble and eminent among the masses.
All classes of sentient beings Shall all attain the wisdom of the Way;
By upholding this True Dharma, They shall never harbor fear.
Upholding the root of the True Dharma, dwelling securely in the Way of the Unconditioned,
you shall turn the Wheel of the True Dharma and manifest it throughout the world.
For hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, you shall never again fall into the cycle of birth and death.
One will surely attain equal and perfect enlightenment, This arises from unimpeded wisdom.
A hero supreme among men, He subdues the hosts of Māra’s officials;
With vigor and powerful wisdom, He maintains total retention without forgetfulness.
Suppose there were a person who thought, "I shall drink up all the waters of the rivers," and traveled throughout the four quarters; yet he could not exhaust their source.
The wise one, through skillful means, reflects within himself:
Only by drinking the waters of the four seas can one reach everywhere; likewise,
if one upholds, recollects, chants, and recites [this teaching] to accomplish the unsurpassed path and the light of unimpeded wisdom, one will receive the prediction of enlightenment before long.
Although no Buddha has yet appeared in the world, By manifesting the thirty-two marks,
he performs the work of a Buddha And extensively delivers immeasurable beings.
Now I have attained perfect enlightenment, The foremost honored one in the three realms.
"This arises from upholding this treasury of unimpeded great wisdom.
When the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, it was profoundly deep, immeasurable, and inconceivable, beyond the reach of arhats and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, ten thousand devas and humans in the assembly all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Furthermore, thirty-seven thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, there were immeasurable bhikṣus whose minds with outflows attained liberation;
forty-six *koṭīs* of sentient beings, having exhausted all defilements, attained the pure Dharma-eye.

Chapter 45: The Three Realms (14). The Bodhisattva’s Necklace Sūtra, Chapter Forty-Five: The Three Realms. At that time, there was a bodhisattva named King Pure Gift who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I have heard from the Buddha, the essential Dharma is profoundly deep; if there were a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who accepted the designation of a bodhisattva’s prediction, they would thereby accept the sixty-two views and the paths of deviance.
Why is this? The sixty-two views all give rise to the bodhisattva and give rise to the fruit of the bodhisattva path.
As for the fruit of the path, it in turn gives rise to the sixty-two views.

Why is this so? The fruit of the bodhisattva path is not attained from the desire realm, nor from the form realm, nor from the formless realm; it is not attained from the conditioned or the unconditioned, nor from the outflowing or the non-outflowing.

Why is this? Because the name "Bodhisattva" cannot be apprehended and has no location; likewise, the names and designations of the sixty-two views and heterodox paths are also thus—fundamentally and ultimately pure, formless, and invisible.
"How is this so, World-Honored One?

It is as if there were someone who wished to investigate the limits of space, measuring its boundaries and distinguishing its colors—blue, yellow, red, or white—and furthermore, assigned names to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; [declaring] that these arise or cease, are conditioned or unconditioned, are with outflows or without outflows, are eternal or impermanent, and are suffering or happiness."
"How so? World-Honored One!
Does this person possess wisdom regarding the profound Dharma?"
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva King Pure Giver:
"Space is formless and invisible; how can one establish characters for it or give it a name?
To seek space within space—this is not possible."
At that time, the Bodhisattva King Dāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, World-Honored One!

The fruits of the bodhisattva path and unimpeded wisdom, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and the sixty-two views—all these are non-existent and cannot be seen. They are like space, formless and incapable of being maintained; the characteristics of all dharmas cannot be obtained through aspiration or seeking.”
Why is this? Because from the beginning there has been nothing that exists; it transcends the three realms and surpasses the three periods of time.

If it were otherwise, the paths of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would give rise to dualistic views. Where there are dualistic views, there are dualistic perceptions; where there are dualistic perceptions, one falls into heterodox factions. Having fallen into heterodox factions, one enters the five destinies and wanders through birth and death. One then slanders the path of the worthy and holy, claiming it is not the true path, and neither acknowledges nor speaks of the laws and teachings of the worthy and holy.
Deluded and ignorant people say among themselves:
"The Buddha is different, the Way is different, and birth-and-death is also different. Since birth-and-death is different, how could there be Nirvana?
Furthermore, there is no Buddha who cultivates the Bodhisattva path; how much less could there be one who attains unimpeded wisdom?"
"This matter is not so.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Kūṭastha who asked King Viśuddhadatta: "How is this?"
“Noble son! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle and possesses unimpeded eloquence and wisdom, they shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva King Pure Gift.

“If there is a bodhisattva who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, practices the bodhisattva conduct and does not fail to practice it; who neither abandons the true Dharma to practice false deeds, nor perceives that they are practicing the bodhisattva path, nor perceives that they are not practicing the bodhisattva path—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, having transcended the stages of practice, practices that which is without anything to be practiced.”
The Ultimate Bodhisattva again asked King Viśuddhadatta: "How is this so,
son of good family?"
"How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by transcending the stages of practice (*bhūmi*) and cultivating that which is not cultivated, train in the unsurpassed path and attain the title of 'Bodhisattva'?
King Viśuddhadatta replied to the Bodhisattva Paramārtha:

"By not grasping the characteristics (*nimitta*) of any phenomena—whether of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind—and because one has transcended these realms, one surpasses the stages and cultivates that which is not cultivated."
The Ultimate Bodhisattva asked again: "How is this so,
son of good family?"
"By transcending the stages of practice, does one cultivate that which is not cultivated?
Bodhisattva Viśuddhadānarāja replied to Bodhisattva Niṣṭhāgata:
"One does not universally transcend all stages while cultivating the bodhisattva path."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas give rise to the path of the bodhisattva.
Ultimate Bodhisattva said:
"What do you think,
son of good family?
Do all phenomena (dharmas) further possess a sphere of objective range?"
"Why is it said that one transcends all stages and practices nothing that is practiced?

The Bodhisattva King Pure-Gift replied, "The suchness of all phenomena and the nature of the Way are both such; neither a time of coming nor a time of going is perceived. For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to the Way and its teachings while practicing nothing that is practiced."
The Bodhisattva Kṣayamati addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhadānarāja, saying:
"Noble son, how does one set out toward the mind of enlightenment?"
King Viśuddhadāna said,
“It is as the Way is.
The Bodhisattva Paryantagata said:
“What is the suchness of the Way?
King Viśuddhadatta replied:

“As for the suchness of the Way, it does not exist in the past, the future, or the present. Therefore, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive the nature of the Way within the three periods of time as being either pure or as suchness itself, only then does he give rise to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Just as the suchness of the past, the suchness of the future, and the suchness of the present are naturally empty of self-nature, neither coming nor going, and tending nowhere to which they tend—so too can one give rise to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, practicing that which is practiced nowhere.”
The Bodhisattva Qiongjiu asked again:
"How does one resolve upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment so as to practice that which is practiced without anything to practice?
The Bodhisattva Jingshiwang replied:

"Those who have lost their way are able to set out upon the Path; endowed with great compassion, they cause others to be free from fear. Though they dwell within the triple world or the five places of immediate retribution, they do not harbor weariness. With an impartial mind that pervades all, they are able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and practice that which is practiced as nothing."
The Bodhisattva Kujaku (Ultimate) asked again: “How is this so,
son of good family?”
If one were like one without eyes, how could one see?
I now feel doubly suspicious; I only pray that you will explain this to me, so that my hesitation may be removed and my mind may attain awakening.

As you have said, those who have lost their way can set out upon the unsurpassed path; through the addition of great compassion, they are made free from fear, and within the dharma of equality, there is neither increase nor decrease.
"This illness can be cured by no one; only you, son of noble family, may expound it for me, so that my heavy doubts may become somewhat lightened.
The Bodhisattva King Pure Gift said:
"Excellent, excellent!
"Noble son! Those who have prompted you to ask this question are all moved by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
Now, Mañjuśrī is the foremost among the assembly; you should request him to explain this so that the nature of these transformative capacities may be understood."
Then, the Bodhisattva Niṣṭhāgata said to Mañjuśrī:
"I was previously filled with doubt regarding what King Viśuddhadatta said."
"How is it? Son of good family, you are able to understand.
We only pray that you will expound this so that no further difficulties remain."
At that time, Mañjuśrī replied to the Bodhisattva Ultimate Perfection:

"The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion is unimpeded throughout the three realms; if he enters the profound and wondrous, his understanding of those dharmas is thorough and precise. He practices without anything to practice, and he is without attachment, without doubt, without difficulty, and without fear."
If it is thus, one has already attained compassion; one dwells at the fundamental limit and finds rest for the body. Those who have no place of refuge find in this their refuge.

Although one remains within the three realms and the five places of immediate retribution, one does not diminish one's diligent effort; with an impartial mind that pervades all, one is able to give rise to the aspiration for the Way and practice that which is practiced as nothing.
The Bodhisattva Kiu-ching (Kṣāntivādin) asked again:
"How is this so, Mañjuśrī?"
What is its basis?
If, as you say, one practices without practicing, could there be any difference in the arising of all phenomena?
Could there be any difference in the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?
"Is the great compassion of a bodhisattva different from [ordinary] equanimity?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Cease! [Such questioning]."
Stop, son of good family!
That which is called the Way is not a "Way" that exists.

If one does not conceive of a self, a life-span, or the category of sentient beings, this constitutes the attainment of great compassion; with an impartial mind that pervades all, one is able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and practice that which is practiced as nothing.
The Bodhisattva Kiu-ching (Kūṭastha) asked again:

“Mañjuśrī! Since the nature of the Way is suchness, neither upholding the triple world nor abandoning the triple world, how can one give rise to the path of unsurpassed, most true, and perfectly complete enlightenment?”

Mañjuśrī said: "The mind holds nothing and has no objects of perception; it does not depend on the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind; it does not rely upon the five aggregates of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; nor does it give rise to the six defilements within the six sense-fields."

One does not dwell on the presence of virtue nor the absence of virtue; one is not attached to the mundane nor gives rise to the mind of the Path. There is no thought of sin or merit, no wisdom and no folly. One does not perceive anything remaining, nor does one perceive nothing remaining. Furthermore, one does not perceive the aggregate of precepts, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the vision of liberation. One does not perceive the entanglements of birth-and-death or defiled attachment, nor Nirvana or purity. One does not perceive any fundamental existence of arising and ceasing, nor of attachment or severance.

Furthermore, they do not perceive anything as permanent or impermanent, nor as suffering, empty, or non-self; they contemplate all phenomena as utterly tranquil, quiescent, and like space. Those who abide in this way abide in non-abiding. Having attained equal compassion and the equality of non-duality, they practice that which is practiced by none. They attain the arousal of the unsurpassed, truly real, equal, and right enlightenment, and though they dwell within the three realms or even the five places of immediate retribution, they do not shrink from such toil.
When the Bodhisattva Kiu-ching heard this Dharma, he leaped for joy even more intensely than before,
unable to contain himself: "I only pray, Mañjuśrī,
that you may cause me to attain this practice of non-practice, to obtain the foremost unimpeded Nirvana, and further, through this Dharma, to achieve peace and security."
Mañjuśrī replied: “Noble son!

If one dwells on the stage of training and practices that which is not practiced, yet harbors expectations regarding all phenomena, there will then be an objective referent through which one desires to attain peace.”
This is not so. Why is that? If there were no object of focus (*ālambana*), there would be no peace; how then could one attain Nirvāṇa by depending on conditions?

This Dharma is quiescent and comes from nowhere; it does not depend on past thoughts that cease without interruption, nor does it conceive of the present as having a mind that calculates permanence, nor does it concern itself with the future as being either with or without opposition.

Therefore, all dharmas do not abide in habituation, nor is there anything to be habituated; they are not seen as having mindfulness, nor is there anything to be mindful of; they have no stability, nor is there anything to be stabilized; they are neither arrogant nor subject to annihilation. All dharmas are without hearing, without sound, and without resonance; one sees neither the "with remainder" nor the "without remainder. This is called attaining the peace of the dwelling place and obtaining *nirvāṇa*, penetrating all dharmas without the notion of arising or ceasing.
Mañjuśrī further addressed the Bodhisattva Ultimate Perfection, saying:

"If a son of good family contemplates without contemplation and does not give rise to thought, there will be no intention in the interim and no calamities thereafter. Should one give rise to thought such that calamities occur, this would be a state of unrest."

From the beginning until the end, one is neither liberated from affliction nor without affliction; if one makes no such distinctions and perceives neither calamity nor its absence, this is called attaining Nirvana and dwelling forever in peace and security. There is no longer coming and going, neither habituation nor non-habituation, which accords with the ultimate truth.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣṭhāgata said:
"How is it so, Mañjuśrī?"
If there were a person who spoke thus:
"Does emptiness abide? Or does emptiness not abide?"
"Does emptiness have habitual tendencies or not?
Does it have arising or not?
If one says "it does," what is the meaning of that?
Mañjuśrī said: “How so, son of good family?”

If emptiness has a dwelling or no dwelling; if emptiness has reliance or non-reliance, practice or non-practice, arising or non-arising, aspiration or non-aspiration, perception or non-perception—one who contemplates these things, how could they attain Nirvana, which corresponds to non-practice?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣṭhāgata said: "How is this so,
son of good family?"
Emptiness neither abides nor does it not abide; it does not depend on duality, nor does it depend on unity, and furthermore, there is no intermediate state.
Apart from these, how else could one attain Nirvāṇa, the supreme state of non-practice?
Mañjuśrī replied: "If emptiness has a dwelling, it dwells nowhere;

if emptiness has no dwelling, it fundamentally dwells nowhere. There is reliance and non-reliance, practice and non-practice, birth and non-birth, vows and non-vows, marks and non-marks. Fundamentally there are no marks, yet it is not that marks do not exist; marks are themselves non-marks, and non-marks are also non-marks."

All dharmas are likewise thus: one does not see creation, nor does one see non-creation; it is neither that there is no creation nor that there is no non-creation. One does not see marks or marklessness; one does not see difference or non-difference, seeking or non-seeking. One does not think, "I have something to do" or "I have nothing to do. One does not rely on the body, speech, or mind regarding words or conduct, whether good or evil. This is what accords with the foremost state of non-practice.

Why is this? Because they are free from the notion of birth and death; they do not cling to the conditioned nor cling to the unconditioned; their fundamental basis is deep and firm, not conditioned by the three periods of time; and they do not speak of nirvāṇa as being eternally quiescent and unconditioned.
"O son of good family! This is what is meant:

from the first generation of the aspiration for enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to such [thoughts] during that interval, they should abide in the unsurpassed state where there is neither practice nor non-practice."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣṭhāgata asked again:
"How is it so, Mañjuśrī?"

What is meant by a bodhisattva awakening to desire—whether there is seeking or no seeking, whether there is birth-and-death or no birth-and-death—and not dwelling on the three periods of time as having an end or no end, reaching or not reaching, permanence or impermanence; furthermore, awakening to the increase and decrease within the dhyānas and samādhis of all dharmas?
"If one acts in this way, how could there be birth and death? Mañjuśrī replied, "How so?"
"Noble son! Where does birth and death cease? He replied:
"To dwell in non-dwelling. He asked again: "How so?"
"Is it united with the Way?
He replied, "Birth and death are united with the Way; the Way is itself birth and death."
The Bodhisattva Kṣayamkara said: "How is this so,
son of good family?"
“Do the sun and darkness ever come together? Mañjuśrī replied, “Noble son!”
Light and darkness are joined, yet you do not see them and thus claim they are not joined.
Ultimate Bodhisattva asked again: “How so?”
“Son of good family!
Where does this cessation in darkness reside? Mañjuśrī replied:
"That which is invisible is called darkness.
It dwells nowhere. Why is this?
Because it has no place of abiding."
If the sun rises while the moon also shines together with it, how could one say that the moon is of no benefit to the light?
They mutually accommodate one another and cannot be separated.
Son of good family, listen!
When the sun rises, where does darkness go?
Does it return to the east, the west, the south, or the north? Where does it abide in the four intermediate directions, above, or below?
Do not give rise to such a view.

Why is this so? Darkness always exists without any place of refuge or destination; light is likewise joined with darkness. One should contemplate this principle: birth-and-death (saṃsāra) is conjoined with the Way (mārga), and the Way is thus birth-and-death.
Mañjuśrī spoke again to the Bodhisattva Ultimate:
“To take a nearby analogy for comparison, let the wise person realize this for themselves:

Mount Sumeru is golden in color to the east, crystal-colored to the south, lapis lazuli-colored to the west, and white silver-colored to the north. Yet, for those who approach it, does the color of the mountain ever truly differ?”
Do not form such a view.
Why is this? Form is one and there are no many; it is only that the ignorant conceive of it as being different.
Therefore, O Noble One!
The Path merges with birth and death, and birth and death merge with the Path; he who understands this finds that all dharmas are likewise so.
Why is this? Because all things are entirely empty.
How can one give rise to the thought that among all phenomena there is anything that does not accord [with reality]? Such a thing is not so.
Then, the Bodhisattva Kṣayamati again asked Mañjuśrī:
"Does one who is not yet liberated unite with liberation? He replied:
"So it is. He asked again: "In what way?"
"Noble son! Are liberation and non-liberation conjoined? He replied:
"Those not yet liberated are liberated; those already liberated do not think that there is liberation, nor do they think that there is no liberation.

That which is without liberation is without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); that which is without intrinsic nature is without arising; that which is without arising neither sees a time of coming nor sees a time of going—this is called the Path and also Nirvāṇa."
He asked again:
"In what way is it that being without seeking and without liberation constitutes the Great Way? Mañjuśrī replied:
"To not conceive of liberation even while in liberation is itself non-liberation; this is the Path. One who does not give rise to dualistic views is one who accords with Nirvāṇa.
Ultimate Bodhisattva then asked:
"Is that Path different from Nirvāṇa?"
Mañjuśrī said: “No, son of good family!”
"The Way is one and without duality; the Way is Nirvana, and Nirvana is the Way; there are no distinctions between them.
Ultimate Bodhisattva asked again:
"Is there any dharma that transcends Nirvana?"
He replied, "There is none. He asked again:
"Who is it that dwells in nirvana and speaks of nirvana?

Is there any dharma that has come from somewhere, such that one could say, 'This is a worldly dharma,' 'This is a supramundane dharma,' 'This is the dharma of birth and death,' or 'This is the dharma of nirvana'?"
