Mañjuśrī said: "That which has no location is nirvāṇa; it neither goes nor comes, it is without birth and without cessation, and it is without attachment or abandonment."

Those who know the Way are likewise so: the Way is equal and Nirvana is also equal; though one seeks them, they cannot be seen, nor do they have a location. Therefore, the Way is equal and Nirvana is also equal.
The Bodhisattva Kṣāntivīra asked again:
"Is there a skillful means by which one dwells in non-abiding while training in the Way? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Does abiding in non-abiding differ from the Path?
Do you wish to learn the Path through this dharma?
Ultimate Bodhisattva asked again.
"What is the path? What is not the path? Mañjuśrī replied:
"To dwell in non-dwelling is itself the Way; how could one learn the Way by dwelling?
This is not so. From conditioned phenomena to unconditioned phenomena, and from the body of pure precepts, the body of samādhi, and the body of wisdom—can one learn by dwelling?"
This is also not so. Therefore, one should know that the Way is not learned from non-abiding.

Now, those who study the Way do not learn the Way by relying on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor by precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; nor by the various dhyānas, samādhis, physical marks, and secondary characteristics; nor by expedient manifestations and adaptive transformations; nor by giving, morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, wisdom, and liberation. To study the Way through such dharmas is not correct.
Why is this? The Way is neither study nor is there one who studies; it is not seen as arrogance, for it abides in non-abiding. One who acts in this manner is truly in accord with the Way.

One does not form conceptualizations regarding the wisdom that analyzes the three realms, nor does one perceive any phenomenon as constituting the Unsurpassed Way; for one who practices this contemplation, there is a place of abiding, wherein the nature of the Way is empty and Nirvana is likewise empty.
"Therefore, O Noble One!
Do not give rise to doubt regarding the path to Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kūṭastha again asked Mañjuśrī:
“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family desires to seek the unsurpassed, truly real, equal, and perfect enlightenment, what dharma should they practice to attain the Way?
Mañjuśrī replied: “Noble son!”

If a son or daughter of good family, from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, does not lose the mind of the Way during that interval, then even while dwelling in the five places of immediate retribution, they shall have no further fear. Neither the five aggregates, the six sense-decays, nor birth, old age, sickness, and death; nor the worldly afflictions, Māra, or the celestial Māras—none of these can prevail against them.

If men or women desire to seek the Way, they do not perceive any phenomenon as being permanent or impermanent, conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows, liberated or unliberated; nor do they perceive any phenomenon as "mine" or "not mine," as self, person, or life-span, or as the destination of good or evil. All are empty and all are quiescent; the nature of all phenomena, including both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, is likewise so.

All mundane dharmas and those that transcend the world—the Buddha-dharmas of ordinary beings, the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training, as well as those of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—are universally equal and without distinction. Understanding emptiness and signlessness, abandoning all seeds, non-arising, and non-conditioning, one cultivates such practice toward these dharmas; distinguishing them according to what is appropriate and training in this way is what is called the Way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣṭhāgata praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! That which you have spoken benefits all beings."
I have reflected upon this and do not dare to harbor doubts regarding the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Why is this?
As for these phenomena, there is no "mine" and no self, nor is there a life-span; through the analytical contemplation of phenomena, one perceives them as equal and non-dual.

The Tathāgata, the Truly Enlightened One, is liberated without obstruction; only a Buddha can perceive, disseminate, and expound this. Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*);

the defilements of craving, desire, sound, and form have never arisen again. The World-Honored One has completely cast off the web of greed and attachment; the sufferings of birth and death have been severed without remainder. Abiding through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) yet dwelling nowhere, he assumes a physical form to teach and transform others, laboring for their sake. For the sake of all sentient beings, he expounds the sūtras, leading them toward the unconditioned Great Way of Nirvāṇa. That which was to be exhausted has been exhausted with nothing further to exhaust; that which was to be delivered has been delivered with nothing further to deliver. Thus he performs the Buddha-work, extensively saving immeasurable beings.

Furthermore, by means of noble wisdom, he gradually crosses to the other shore; solitary and virtuous, he has neither companion nor peer. He accords with the discipline of Perfect Enlightenment and practices that which is practiced by none. His mind is free from agitation, focused with single-minded diligence, and he always maintains a sense of shame and remorse as if he were ashamed of his own shortcomings. Internally and externally pure like clear, still water, his noble wisdom and moral virtue are like the ocean, never satiated. With a concentrated mind in samādhi, he wanders through immeasurable realms; the noble sages remain in silent composure for their own enjoyment, having realized the Truths and remaining forever without doubt.

Now, Mañjuśrī! You have been granted such immeasurable and unfathomable virtue as to manifest this inconceivable dharma-gate of dhāraṇī, and you have also enabled those who are lowly and base to attain this profound treasury, bringing great benefit and moving all beings.

At that time, while Mañjuśrī was preaching this Dharma, seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas established in practice dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, and all attained the treasury of the profound Dharma.
Furthermore, immeasurable sentient beings all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.

Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits all offered worship, scattering flowers and burning incense, directing their respectful and subtle intentions toward Mañjuśrī.
The Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra Sūtra, Volume Fourteen.
